I have to give this game a negative review. Do I regret playing it? No. Would I recommend it to you? Yes. Let me explain...
This spoke to my soul on so many levels. I had a best friend who was I felt was altogether more interesting than me, she was always getting herself (and me) into trouble whilst I just wanted to kunckle down and get an education. I think even if you don't have this perspective, you will find a part of yourself in Max and you will see someone you know or used to know in Chloe - the writers were very smart about the way they approached these two characters, they are absolutely intoxicating. The supporting characters are also extremely well written, add to this a completely mind bending story-line, the ability to undo time (let's face it, everyone at some point in their lives wishes they could rewind something and try again) and a skin-tingling soundtrack and you have one of the best story-based games I've ever played.
So why am I giving it the thumbs down?
During your journey in this game you will make some absolutely nail-biting decisons. Your cursor will be hanging for minutes between two crucial decisions which you know will impact the story in some massive way. And impact the story it does. However, if you're looking for a game with a huge range of multiple endings based on those chain of decisions you've made, well - you're going to be disappointed. In the end, none of it matters and it all comes down to one ultimate decision that decides one of two endings for you. Now, I know its all about the journey, blah blah blah (I've heard it all before with Mass Effect 3) and you can look back and say, "well, clearly the message is - don't mess with time or time will mess with you" but no, I'm sorry. This game could have been so much more with multiple endings.

So I'd like to start off this review with a fact: Garys Mod is incredibly fun. The graphics are more than dated, but Prop Hunt and Trouble in Terrorist Town are different some fun game modes to play to pass some time.
With that being said, however, the sheer unfun of microphones and headsets will leave you exhausted.
I picked up Garys Mod in July of 2016, and, upon joining my first server, was met with helpful players. Terrific, I thought. The game still has a supportive player base who are willing to help new comers. After learning the very simple rules and how to play, I ventured onward to a more populated server.
That was the first and last time I would find even remotely supportive players and I wish them luck in getting out of the hell hole they are stuck in.
You'll be very lucky to find anyone over the age of 14-16 who isn't a complete waste over the mic. In a game like this, I prefer to use my headset and talk to others, whether it's during prop hunt or TTT, and it has just been riddled with children, mic spammers, and the such.
Now children are not inherently bad, there's nothing wrong with kids. I have a kid and one day I will put her on the PC to join me in glorious pc gaming. But I'll also be monitoring her, as I was when I was young. These kids are not being monitored by their parent (I assume their father or mother left them at an early age due to some of the things that comes out of these kids mouths) They will spew profanity over the mic and it just sounds wrong. It hits the ear wrong. Hearing a nine year old tell me my mother is a ♥♥♥♥♥ and he ♥♥♥♥ed her with his 12 inch ♥♥♥♥ just sounds wrong. Hearing it from a grown adult, alright, I can deal with it. But this is something I haven't had the pleasure of hearing over a mic often enough apparently.
You also run the risk of joining a server that has a female on it. Now, as I stated, my little girl will be playing games one day. There is nothing wrong with being a female gamer, and if you are one, props to you and all that jazz. BUT, adults, children, and everything in between loses their ♥♥♥♥ing minds when it comes to an online girl. In every game. But Garrys Mod is certainly the absolute worst case I have ever seen.
I just got done playing on a server with twenty people on it. This one female who was British started telling people she would smother them with her breasts. She was an admin on this server. She had the ability to kick, mute, ban and etc.
No admin jobs are not 'jobs', but I would like to think the people in charge of these servers would hold a little bit of respect.
With all that stated, and this rant pretty much over, I'd like to just state that if you have friends that play this with you, this could possibly be a lot of fun as youtubers have shown poorly. But if you go in it, alone, expect what I've laid out before you. This is not a Garry's Mod is garbage review. Garry's Mod is extremely fun. It's the community that makes it unplayable for me.

Life is Strange is quite simply the best modern adventure game out there, hands-down. Its characters feel genuine. The world - a picturesque love letter to America's pacific northwest - is lovingly-crafted in a painterly aesthetic. The story is grounded, yet fantastical, always letting the player know the gravity of real life. The mechanic of time travel allows for a clever re-framing of the modern adventure game trope of big, momentous decisions by allowing you to see the consequences of most actions instead of just one. Most importantly, this game really does ask you to make decisions that can question your worldview and give you genuine moral dilemmas. It's a remarkably lovingly-made experience with a great sense of aesthetic, cinematography, character development, intensity pacing, and novel mechanics, and more than that, it's an IMPORTANT game.
Play this game now. You will not regret it. It is my new favorite game, and it's only $20.

This is, simply put, the best adventure game I have played. It starts off as simply a story about a high school girl who is a typical loner, but then it grows into so much more. The final episode, which came out two days ago as of this writing, was a perfect conclusion to the narrative (don't listen to the haters).
Pros
+Unique (and meta) rewind ability
+Cast of diverse characters
+Plenty of Easter Eggs
+Solid, engrossing story
+Replay value
+Fairly long, compared to other games of the genre
+BEANS
Cons
-Game can sometimes be seen as "juvenile" because it is set in a high school environment, but it is fairly realistic in this regard. Once you get past it the story becomes more mature and complex.
-I personally don't view it as a con, but many people expected every choice to have a big impact on things, when, as with every other game of this nature, the final outcome is much more about the journey than the destination. Enjoy the game while it you can, and don't stress about the ending.
Overall this game is near-perfect to me. It was an 18 hour-long journey that made me question myself more than once. Even now, hours after finishing it, I'm replaying the moral decisions I made throughout the game. Would reccomend to anyone.

After completing the final episode i thought it was time to write a spoiler free review about this game.
Life is Strange is probably now my favourite episodic, story-rich adventure game. It starts off light hearted and develops into a dark compelling story. It will make you feel a range of emotions as you make consequence based choices in-game and you will become attached to a wide range of character types/personalities. It has fantastic artistic imagery and a well implemented soundtrack that complements the atmosphere of the game. The voice acting is phenomenal except there are some lip-syncing issues in game which can be a bit off-putting at times.
I enjoyed everything about this game apart from the ending(s). I appreciate the amout of work and effort that went into this game but i finished it feeling disappointed. Dont get me wrong, the endings were 'good' and i understand were Dontnod were going with them but i felt that they were too predictable and all of a sudden all the choices you have made throughout the game dont really matter or affect the outcome, only your final choice does. There are still a lot of questions i have about the game that are left unanswered and i really feel that they should've been addressed or explored further which could potentially have led to more interesting endings.
Life Is Strange rating: 10/10.
Life is Strange endings rating: 7/10.
I would definitely recommend you play this game.

Okay, so first things first: I give this a negative rating only because I think the devellopers deserve it. This game, in the end, was worse then any Telltale game for making you believe your choise matters, when it really doesn't. This is a very bad thing, because during all first 4 episodes, your choises DO matter. With your actions can befriend people or make them your enemies. You can save people, or kill them. Hell, you can even kill your plant if you don't watter it properly. But in the final episode, all of this is taken away. I will not spoil the endings, but I will say this: there are only TWO. No matter what choises you made in the game, at the end you get one final say, and it is that choice, and that choice alone, that determines how the game ends. And it is not even an ending like in Dishonored, where you get either the bad or the good ending, but they leave out the people that died. No, it is either ending 1, or ending 2. None of your previous choises reflect in this.
I really want to reccomend this game, I do. I loved it. Just loved it. Right from the beginning it gave off such a strong feeling, with the music they picked and all. Some epidsodes had points I liked a little bit less, but overall they were all great, and left me impatiently waiting for the next one, which I would play the moment they were released, no matter what other stuff I had to do (well, 15 minutes after they were released, as I first had to get over the fact that after this, there would be one less episode to play, which was sad). So yeah, I loved it. Right up untill the final episode.
I still love it, and am glad I played it. But if you buy it (which honestly, you really should, despite my negative rating) be prepared to face a major let-down at the end.

Life is Strange is quite simply the best modern adventure game out there, hands-down. Its characters feel genuine. The world - a picturesque love letter to America's pacific northwest - is lovingly-crafted in a painterly aesthetic. The story is grounded, yet fantastical, always letting the player know the gravity of real life. The mechanic of time travel allows for a clever re-framing of the modern adventure game trope of big, momentous decisions by allowing you to see the consequences of most actions instead of just one. Most importantly, this game really does ask you to make decisions that can question your worldview and give you genuine moral dilemmas. It's a remarkably lovingly-made experience with a great sense of aesthetic, cinematography, character development, intensity pacing, and novel mechanics, and more than that, it's an IMPORTANT game.
Play this game now. You will not regret it. It is my new favorite game, and it's only $20.

This is, simply put, the best adventure game I have played. It starts off as simply a story about a high school girl who is a typical loner, but then it grows into so much more. The final episode, which came out two days ago as of this writing, was a perfect conclusion to the narrative (don't listen to the haters).
Pros
+Unique (and meta) rewind ability
+Cast of diverse characters
+Plenty of Easter Eggs
+Solid, engrossing story
+Replay value
+Fairly long, compared to other games of the genre
+BEANS
Cons
-Game can sometimes be seen as "juvenile" because it is set in a high school environment, but it is fairly realistic in this regard. Once you get past it the story becomes more mature and complex.
-I personally don't view it as a con, but many people expected every choice to have a big impact on things, when, as with every other game of this nature, the final outcome is much more about the journey than the destination. Enjoy the game while it you can, and don't stress about the ending.
Overall this game is near-perfect to me. It was an 18 hour-long journey that made me question myself more than once. Even now, hours after finishing it, I'm replaying the moral decisions I made throughout the game. Would reccomend to anyone.

Okay, so first things first: I give this a negative rating only because I think the devellopers deserve it. This game, in the end, was worse then any Telltale game for making you believe your choise matters, when it really doesn't. This is a very bad thing, because during all first 4 episodes, your choises DO matter. With your actions can befriend people or make them your enemies. You can save people, or kill them. Hell, you can even kill your plant if you don't watter it properly. But in the final episode, all of this is taken away. I will not spoil the endings, but I will say this: there are only TWO. No matter what choises you made in the game, at the end you get one final say, and it is that choice, and that choice alone, that determines how the game ends. And it is not even an ending like in Dishonored, where you get either the bad or the good ending, but they leave out the people that died. No, it is either ending 1, or ending 2. None of your previous choises reflect in this.
I really want to reccomend this game, I do. I loved it. Just loved it. Right from the beginning it gave off such a strong feeling, with the music they picked and all. Some epidsodes had points I liked a little bit less, but overall they were all great, and left me impatiently waiting for the next one, which I would play the moment they were released, no matter what other stuff I had to do (well, 15 minutes after they were released, as I first had to get over the fact that after this, there would be one less episode to play, which was sad). So yeah, I loved it. Right up untill the final episode.
I still love it, and am glad I played it. But if you buy it (which honestly, you really should, despite my negative rating) be prepared to face a major let-down at the end.

(REVIEW WITH NO SPOILERS)
So, I chose to wait until all episodes were out to write my review, just to make sure my opinion about the game wouldn't change (cough Dexter cough), and finally, it's done. My opinion didn't change, and boy, am I glad about it. The game is fantastic. It is very well written, and the voice actors are extremely talented, which is something really needed for a game like this. The waiting for every episode to come out was excruciatingly painful, as the devs did a nice, evil job to always end their episodes on THAT scene that you simply need to know what happens next.
STORY
You follow the story of Max Caulfield, a somewhat anti social, 18 year-old photographer to-be, and her life on a pretty well known school and interactions with the other students. After discovering she has powers that allow her to go back in time, and saving a girl from being shot in the bathroom by manipulating actions she knew would happen, Max starts using her powers to make things go the way she wants to, since if something goes wrong, she can just rewind and do it again differently.  Sounds like the game will be a generic teen drama fest, doesn't it? Well, episode 1 is kinda FLOODED with that in fact, so I'd say people who has no patience with that kinda thing would start with the wrong foot, unfortunately.  Don't worry, because things get reaaaally heavy later on. Life is strange gets progressively darker and darker with each episode, and from something fun, Max's powers start screwing up with nature and with herself, and the story gets filled with blood, murder and psychopaths. Yep, from teen drama it goes all the way to you screaming on your chair "OH MY GOD, WHAT IS GOING ON". So even if you didn't like Ep.1 that much, give it a chance for the others.
CHARACTERS
Some of them you hate, some of them you love, some of them are completely worthless. Dontnod put some characters there, with backstories of their own, but in the end they are just fillers that don't add much for the story (I'm looking at you, Samuel). Is that wrong? Well, that's exactly how life is, isn't it? Everyone knows someone who you just say "hi" and talk about the weather now and then, but isn't really that important to you, especially when you're at school. So I really liked the fact that LiS has a lot of characters that won't be game changing per se, but are there if you want to chat or whatever. Good ol' chill moments.
The main characters, however, do reveal a good development as the episodes go on, and you can easily see that on Ep.5 they weren't the same they were on Ep. 1. While Max is a likeable, awkward person, Chloe has a stronger personality because of her past, and thus divides the players whether you like her or not. With their constant interaction, Max starts to become a little bit more of a "screw it, just do it" person, and Chloe, from a punk line of thought of "I don't really care about anything" reveals more and more a common sense about caring about other people and whatnot.  Althought they both do fall on what could be called "generic way of teens to think", they are far from being bland characters.
GAMEPLAY/CHOICES
The gameplay is pretty much the same as Telltale games: mosly composed of dialogues, Life is Strange also offers sections in which you control Max and can interact with people or objects, mostly to solve puzzles and continue the game. What I'd say is better on LiS over Telltale is that it feels like your choices DO matter much more here. Don't get me wrong, I absolutely loved the walking dead series from Telltale, but when the game gave you the choice of saving either one person or another, the game was "spoiling itself", as those two persons would definitely die anyway: you'd just extend the life of one of them. Although in LiS the main theme is time manipulation, and thus, you will be able to undo actions and your own choices, the game works better with giving you the feeling that the story did change because of your option, and so did the way Max thinks (since she always remembers what happened on the last timeline).  I HAVE got to say, WITHOUT SPOILERS, though, that people that got mad over the ending of Mass Effect 3 will most likely have the same feeling with LiS: your choices DO matter during the whole game and they do change how other characters act towards you, but the final choice, the one that defines the ending, will be the same. I don't really care about that and I don't think at all that this butchers the feeling of choice in the game (hell, Mass Effect is one of my all-time favorites), but well, if you do, here's the warning.
VISUAL/VOICE ACTORS
Life is Strange is a beautiful game. It doesn't have top notch graphics, and sometimes the camera even zooms in on low-rendered objects (which made me think "didn't they see that this thing is pixelated? It literally ocuppies 50% of the screen!", but it has really well done sceneries and once, I even stood looking at a water puddle because damn, that was a beautiful water puddle (random, I know). One thing that I've seen that people had issues with was that the lipsync of the characters is not perfect: the devs, however, did talk about it, and said that they didn't have that high of a budget, and between that and dialogue quality, they chose the latter, and thank god they did. Honestly, I did get a little bothered by it at first, but by Ep. 2 I didn't care about it at all anymore.
As already stated, the voice acting is amazing, and you can see the improvement of all the cast as the story goes on. By the final episode, the actors speak with such real emotion that it really gets to you, and makes the story much richer. Well, LiS has its dose of teen awkward dialogues (it is filled with wowsies and for realsies, so be prepared), but I thought that was funnier than cringy, so it's all good for me.
SCORE : 8.5/10
I simply loved this game, for real. I didn't expect to like it this much. I give it an 8.5 because even though I don't really care about any of the flaws (lipsync, teen slangs, game ending being always the same choice) I listed here, I know that a lot of people do, and therefore they are problems that potentially could exist to anyone that plays it.

Video games as an art form. The best example when this happens is Life is Strange. Definitely my game of the year 2015, and alot better than the Telltale series. For my review I've waited for the release for the 5th and therefore last episode.
The story starts calmly, you get to know the characters and you're allowed to browse in the protagonists diary, learn everything about her life and hobby and take some pictures or talk with your classmates. You just try to be part of the whole typical school life we all have (or had once). Until the next episode starts and you feel like your emotions are going from 0 to 100, you have to make tough decisions no one of us wants to make and live with the consequences. Till the end you're wondering things like "Why?" "How could you?" "I thought". Who's looking for difficult puzzles, action and challenges is wrong here, Life is Strange is all about dialogues, decisions and a catching story.
++ atmospheric and incredibly emotional soundtrack, the part at the end of every episode always gives me the creeps
++ interesting (and easy to handle) implementation of a time travel feature, which establishes new options to carry on an conversation. Do you regret what you just said? Did you missed something and you can't go back? Here you can try out everything you want, be the best friend, be the weirdo or the evil bit...
++ breathtaking and intoxicating story, you'll abandon your own theories pretty fast
++ incredibly adorable (and lesser adorable of course) characters, it's easy to pick a favorite and you're not forced into a settled way, romance, whatever
++ beautiful graphics, especially for people who dislikes Telltales comic style
++ really tough and confusing decisions, like "Do I have to water this plant? And the next day too?"
++ very detailed and lively world, you can interact with almost everything and get some additional information or a pointed remark from the main character
The very last decision feels like the hardest bossfight you ever had. There is no right "choice", like which decision is the better one, just with which decision you can learn to live. An impressive experience and the emotionally most touching game I've ever played.
And at last one of my favorite quotes from the game: "FIND MY CAT PIX. PLEASE. MY HEART IS BROKEN."

Das beste Beispiel wenn Computerspiele zur Kunst werden. Defitiniv mein Spiel des Jahres 2015, übertrifft die Telltale Games noch um Längen. Für mein Review hab ich den Release der 5. und somit letzten Episode abgewartet.
Du tauchst entspannt in eine ruhige Story ein, lernst die Charaktere kennen, darfst im Tagebuch der Protagonistin stöbern, ihrem Hobby nachgehen und Fotos schießen und versuchen ein Teil dieses typischen Schullebens zu werden. Bis du in den nächsten Episoden von 0 auf 100 geschmissen wirst, extreme Entscheidungen treffen und mit deren Konsequenzen leben musst. Und damit meine ich du trägst deine Entscheidungen bis zum Ende mit dir rum, sie werden dir immer wieder vor Augen gehalten und du wirst mit den Fragen konfrontiert. "Warum?" "Wie konntest du?" "Ich dachte". Wer schwere Rätsel, Action und Herausforderungen sucht, ist hier falsch. Life is Strange lebt von den Dialogen und der Geschichte.
++ stets stimmige und fantastische Musik und Sounduntermalung
++ interessante Umsetzung eines Zeitreise Features, welches einem neue Möglichkeiten sich zu unterhalten eröffnet und ein tolles Gameplay bietet. Bereust du was du gesagt hast? Hast du etwas übersehen und kannst nicht zurück? Hier schon
++ atemberaubende und mitreißende Story, eigene Theorien werden schnell über Bord geschmissen
++ unglaublich sympathische (und weniger sympathische natürlich) Charaktere, man findet schnell seine Favoriten und wird nicht direkt in eine vorgegebene Richtung geschoben
++ wunderschöne Grafik, gerade für Leute die Telltales Comicstil nicht besonders mögen
++ äußerst harte Entscheidungsmöglichkeiten, teilweise bei nebensächlichen Handlungen, nur um einen zu verunsichern
++ sehr detailierte lebendige Welt, man kann sich so ziemlich alles ansehen und erhält Zusatzinfos oder mal einen spitzen Kommentar der Protagonistin
Die allerletzte Entscheidung wirkt wie der härteste Bossfight vor dem man je stand. Es gibt keine "Wahl", keine Entscheidung die besser oder schlechter als die andere ist. Nur mit welcher man besser leben kann. Eine beeindruckende Erfahrung und das emotional bewegendste Spiel welches ich bisher spielen durfte. Ein großes JA zur Kaufempfehlung.
Zum Schluss eines meiner Lieblingszitate aus dem Spiel: "FIND MY CAT PIX. PLEASE. MY HEART IS BROKEN."

Some of them you hate, some of them you love, some of them are completely worthless. Well, that's exactly how life is, isn't it? Everyone knows someone who you just say "hi" and talk about the weather now and then, but isn't really that important to you, especially when you're at school. So I really liked the fact that LiS has a lot of characters that won't be game changing per se, but are there if you want to chat or whatever. Good ol' chill moments.
The main characters, however, do reveal a good development as the episodes go on, and you can easily see that on Ep.5 they weren't the same they were on Ep. 1. While Max is a likeable, awkward person, Chloe has a stronger personality because of her past, and thus divides the players whether you like her or not. With their constant interaction, Max starts to become a little bit more of a "screw it, just do it" person, and Chloe, from a punk line of thought of "I don't really care about anything" reveals more and more a common sense about caring about other people and whatnot.  Althought they both do fall on what could be called "generic way of teens to think", they are far from being bland characters.
GAMEPLAY/CHOICES
The gameplay is pretty much the same as Telltale games: mosly composed of dialogues, Life is Strange also offers sections in which you control Max and can interact with people or objects, mostly to solve puzzles and continue the game. What I'd say is better on LiS over Telltale is that it feels like your choices DO matter much more here. Don't get me wrong, I absolutely loved the walking dead series from Telltale, but when the game gave you the choice of saving either one person or another, the game was "spoiling itself", as those two persons would definitely die anyway: you'd just extend the life of one of them. Although in LiS the main theme is time manipulation, and thus, you will be able to undo actions and your own choices, the game works better with giving you the feeling that the story did change because of your option, and so did the way Max thinks (since she always remembers what happened on the last timeline).  I HAVE got to say, WITHOUT SPOILERS, though, that people that got mad over the ending of Mass Effect 3 will most likely have the same feeling with LiS: your choices DO matter during the whole game and they do change how other characters act towards you, but the final choice, the one that defines the ending, will be the same. I don't really care about that and I don't think at all that this butchers the feeling of choice in the game (hell, Mass Effect is one of my all-time favorites), but well, if you do, here's the warning.
VISUAL/VOICE ACTORS
Life is Strange is a beautiful game. It doesn't have top notch graphics, and sometimes the camera even zooms in on low-rendered objects (which made me think "didn't they see that this thing is pixelated? It literally ocuppies 50% of the screen!", but it has really well done sceneries and once, I even stood looking at a water puddle because damn, that was a beautiful water puddle (random, I know). One thing that I've seen that people had issues with was that the lipsync of the characters is not perfect: the devs, however, did talk about it, and said that they didn't have that high of a budget, and between that and dialogue quality, they chose the latter, and thank god they did. Honestly, I did get a little bothered by it at first, but by Ep. 2 I didn't care about it at all anymore.
As already stated, the voice acting is amazing, and you can see the improvement of all the cast as the story goes on. By the final episode, the actors speak with such real emotion that it really gets to you, and makes the story much richer. Well, LiS has its dose of teen awkward dialogues (it is filled with wowsies and for realsies, so be prepared), but I thought that was funnier than cringy, so it's all good for me.
SCORE : 8.5/10
I simply loved this game, for real. I didn't expect to like it this much. I give it an 8.5 because even though I don't really care about any of the flaws (lipsync, teen slangs, game ending being always the same choice) I listed here, I know that a lot of people do, and therefore they are problems that potentially could exist to anyone that plays it.

Video games as an art form. The best example when this happens is Life is Strange. Definitely my game of the year 2015, and alot better than the Telltale series. For my review I've waited for the release for the 5th and therefore last episode.
The story starts calmly, you get to know the characters and you're allowed to browse in the protagonists diary, learn everything about her life and hobby and take some pictures or talk with your classmates. You just try to be part of the whole typical school life we all have (or had once). Until the next episode starts and you feel like your emotions are going from 0 to 100, you have to make tough decisions no one of us wants to make and live with the consequences. Till the end you're wondering things like "Why?" "How could you?" "I thought". Who's looking for difficult puzzles, action and challenges is wrong here, Life is Strange is all about dialogues, decisions and a catching story.
++ atmospheric and incredibly emotional soundtrack, the part at the end of every episode always gives me the creeps
++ interesting (and easy to handle) implementation of a time travel feature, which establishes new options to carry on an conversation. Do you regret what you just said? Did you missed something and you can't go back? Here you can try out everything you want, be the best friend, be the weirdo or the evil bit...
++ breathtaking and intoxicating story, you'll abandon your own theories pretty fast
++ incredibly adorable (and lesser adorable of course) characters, it's easy to pick a favorite and you're not forced into a settled way, romance, whatever
++ beautiful graphics, especially for people who dislikes Telltales comic style
++ really tough and confusing decisions, like "Do I have to water this plant? And the next day too?"
++ very detailed and lively world, you can interact with almost everything and get some additional information or a pointed remark from the main character
The very last decision feels like the hardest bossfight you ever had. There is no right "choice", like which decision is the better one, just with which decision you can learn to live. An impressive experience and the emotionally most touching game I've ever played.
And at last one of my favorite quotes from the game: "FIND MY CAT PIX. PLEASE. MY HEART IS BROKEN."

Das beste Beispiel wenn Computerspiele zur Kunst werden. Defitiniv mein Spiel des Jahres 2015, übertrifft die Telltale Games noch um Längen. Für mein Review hab ich den Release der 5. und somit letzten Episode abgewartet.
Du tauchst entspannt in eine ruhige Story ein, lernst die Charaktere kennen, darfst im Tagebuch der Protagonistin stöbern, ihrem Hobby nachgehen und Fotos schießen und versuchen ein Teil dieses typischen Schullebens zu werden. Bis du in den nächsten Episoden von 0 auf 100 geschmissen wirst, extreme Entscheidungen treffen und mit deren Konsequenzen leben musst. Und damit meine ich du trägst deine Entscheidungen bis zum Ende mit dir rum, sie werden dir immer wieder vor Augen gehalten und du wirst mit den Fragen konfrontiert. "Warum?" "Wie konntest du?" "Ich dachte". Wer schwere Rätsel, Action und Herausforderungen sucht, ist hier falsch. Life is Strange lebt von den Dialogen und der Geschichte.
++ stets stimmige und fantastische Musik und Sounduntermalung
++ interessante Umsetzung eines Zeitreise Features, welches einem neue Möglichkeiten sich zu unterhalten eröffnet und ein tolles Gameplay bietet. Bereust du was du gesagt hast? Hast du etwas übersehen und kannst nicht zurück? Hier schon
++ atemberaubende und mitreißende Story, eigene Theorien werden schnell über Bord geschmissen
++ unglaublich sympathische (und weniger sympathische natürlich) Charaktere, man findet schnell seine Favoriten und wird nicht direkt in eine vorgegebene Richtung geschoben
++ wunderschöne Grafik, gerade für Leute die Telltales Comicstil nicht besonders mögen
++ äußerst harte Entscheidungsmöglichkeiten, teilweise bei nebensächlichen Handlungen, nur um einen zu verunsichern
++ sehr detailierte lebendige Welt, man kann sich so ziemlich alles ansehen und erhält Zusatzinfos oder mal einen spitzen Kommentar der Protagonistin
Die allerletzte Entscheidung wirkt wie der härteste Bossfight vor dem man je stand. Es gibt keine "Wahl", keine Entscheidung die besser oder schlechter als die andere ist. Nur mit welcher man besser leben kann. Eine beeindruckende Erfahrung und das emotional bewegendste Spiel welches ich bisher spielen durfte. Ein großes JA zur Kaufempfehlung.
Zum Schluss eines meiner Lieblingszitate aus dem Spiel: "FIND MY CAT PIX. PLEASE. MY HEART IS BROKEN."

The last episode of Life is Strange came out yesterday. I've been really rooting for the creators and hoping they will manage to deliver a satisfying finale for this game.
And they did.
For those unfamiliar with it – it’s an episodic ‘drama adventure’, as they claim. It is basically like a tv series (pretty good one) but with a lot of interactivity. The choices you make either have a huge impact on the story or at least they are very good at pretending they do – either way it works for me.
(Don’t laugh). Life is Strange tells a story about a girl who discovers she is able to rewind time. At first she uses this ability to solve stereotypical High School drama problems, but with every single episode the story gets deeper. And darker. Don’t be fooled by the beginning. It’s not, of course, a Lovecraft level, but not so far from King's.
What else I can say without spoilers – it’s really good. Made me wait (2 months each!) for the next episodes to come (cliff-hangers…) and cause serious deficit of sleep today. All episodes were fine, but the second one destroyed me, I don’t remember when I was that emotionally engaged in a video game. Also, they thought about the story from the start, so there are no loose ends.
I highly recommend.
Also – the soundtrack is pretty good !

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding lemon bars recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1) 2 cups Flour
2) 1/2 cup Sugar
3) 1/4 teaspoon Salt
4) 2 sticks (1 Cup) Salted Butter, Cut Into Small Cubes
5) Filling
6) 1-1/2 cup Sugar
7) 1/4 cup Flour
8) 4 whole Large Eggs
9) Zest And Juice Of 4 Medium-sized Lemons
10) Powdered Sugar, For Sifting
Directions:
1. For the crust: Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F. Grease a 9-by-13-inch pan with butter.
2. Stir together the flour, sugar, and salt. Add the butter to the bowl and use a pastry cutter to cut it all together until the mixture resembles fine crumbs. Press into the prepared pan and bake until golden around the edges, about 20 minutes.
3. For the filling: Stir together the sugar and flour. Crack in the eggs and whisk to combine. Add the lemon zest and juice and mix until combined. Pour over the crust and bake about 20 minutes.

The last episode of Life is Strange came out yesterday. I've been really rooting for the creators and hoping they will manage to deliver a satisfying finale for this game.

For those unfamiliar with it – it’s an episodic ‘drama adventure’, as they claim. It is basically like a tv series (pretty good one) but with a lot of interactivity. The choices you make either have a huge impact on the story or at least they are very good at pretending they do – either way it works for me.
(Don’t laugh). Life is Strange tells a story about a girl who discovers she is able to rewind time. At first she uses this ability to solve stereotypical High School drama problems, but with every single episode the story gets deeper. And darker. Don’t be fooled by the beginning. It’s not, of course, a Lovecraft level, but not so far from King's.
What else I can say without spoilers – it’s really good. Made me wait (2 months each!) for the next episodes to come (cliff-hangers…) and cause serious deficit of sleep today. All episodes were fine, but the second one destroyed me, I don’t remember when I was that emotionally engaged in a video game. Also, they thought about the story from the start, so there are no loose ends.
I highly recommend.
Also – the soundtrack is pretty good !

My Game of the Year so far, and one of the most engaging experiences I've ever played in videogames. I got really attached to the characters and the setting, and you know it's good when you feel sad about having to let go of it because you've finally finished it.
If you like adventure games with focus on the narrative aspect, good. Play it and you'll probably be satisfied by it. Its pace is slower than, say, many games made by Telltale Games (they are very similar to Life is Strange in terms of gameplay), but it fits well with how the story is told and how it's presented. I wouldn't have it any other way.
If you want an idea of how the game is, Life is Strange is inspired by Catcher in the Rye (the main character in LIS has the same last name as the novel's protagonist, after all!), Twin Peaks and Gone Home. The game also uses game design notions from games made by Telltale Games as I've mentioned earlier, and it's also inspired by Ghost Trick (or Remember Me, Dontnod's previous game) for the time powers aspect.
But even then, it's also its own thing. It has a lot of love and thought put into it which make the game unique and memorable, at least to me. And I'd like to mention the fact that the developers actually listen to feedback, and one episode after another they made adjustments to the script and scenes according to what the players thought of the game which is really cool and proves that they're making a good use of the episodic structure.
Even though I won't deny that there are some hiccups here and there as far as how the story goes, ultimately I thought it was greater than the sum of its parts and when I've finished it I was very satisfied by the whole experience. I definitely recommend it.

I had to wait until episode 5 was in the can to give an accurate review. Narrative and gameplay wise, it basically combines all the best parts from my two current favorite game styles: that being the intimate, emotional and tenderly wrought personal story of a Gone Home and the branching third-person, colorfully-characterized flair of a TellTale game.
From the word go, I enjoyed the presentation. Echoes of Donnie Darko, Back to the Future, Detention, My So-called Life, and Buffy the Vampire Slayer, presented like an indie film. Time travel seems to be perfect for a high school setting -- the time in our life when we make the most little mistakes we would like to take back, and the time in our life we all wish we could relive after we get the hang of the world.
The internal narrative felt very real (as well as I can remember how my mind worked as a teen), and Chloe in particular is probably one of the best characters I've ever had the pleasure of getting to know through a narrative. Realistic and frustrating and amazing in the ways only a real person whom one loves usually is. That's important, because ultimately the entire narrative of the game pivots on how you feel about Chloe, whether you care about what she cares about, whether you care what's happened to her -- and what's going to happen to her.
Most of all, games like Life Is Strange and Gone Home, as well as a myriad of the new movement in indie gaming, are injecting the gaming world with something it desperately needs (not forced into something like Metal Gear, but rather as an alternative to such a game):
Empathy.

This game completely changed my perspective on my own life, it made me question the choices I have made up until this current point. It challenged me to go the extra mile and to learn how to never anticipate the future. In its own vision, it explained the extreme weight that certain decisions can hold unto you into your own life and those around you. This game cannot be compared with other episodic games such as ones published by Telltale Games or other companies, this game, this piece of raw art is one in a million. Nothing like it has been made or attempted to be fabricated, it's just something unlike anything out there. Everything was unveiling throughout the progression of the story and it used you to create it. You were the one crafting the beginning, middle and end of it, and you didn't realize it until it has already been undone. When the ending is at its peak, it opens the blinders and shows you the complete maze of choices and outcomes that have been either done outright or rewound through time itself. Many people see this game as a "movie" or something of that sort with its somewhat long cutscenes, but I don't see that in its own image. What Life Is Strange™ tries to do it to make you think that you're in the drivers seat, controlling the outcomes on the peoples lives of Arcadia Bay and playing God. Rather, in actuality, at the point of no return, the end, you see the unraveling of everything you love, you've become to love. Everything that you've grown accustomed to. Being altered by one flap of a butterfly. So rather not watching a movie, but experience a human beings life and watching them evolve, being their guardian and ensuring safety for you and those around you with the use of your power to alter time. A movie fades into the past, when life begs to be pushed forwards and onwards. We accept death as an inevitability, it is how we assume such things, that make us human, and unique.
Life Is Strange™ takes you into a second life, a life completely different from yours and puts you in a false sense of command. It turns on you, wrenches at you, makes you feel things you didn't think were possible in a "game". What this game does, tries to do and morally accomplishes it astounding. I would recommend this game to anyone with a sense of what art stands for and to experience marvels not yet foreseen.
Life Is Strange™ is by far, one of the best games ever created.

A re-review after playing the final episode.
First of all: YES I am recommending this game, whole-heartedly. Amazing characters, gorgeous visuals, brilliant voice-acting, tense situations and interesting challenges... a game structured around teen drama that makes the premise not only non-obnoxious, but profoundly emotional and affecting. Far as I'm concerned it's a can't-miss and one of the best games of any genre I've played in a long time.
Now: there's a certain amount of complaining after "Polarized" that the endings negated any sense of choice. This really isn't true -- since the choices the player makes live on in the development of the main character regardless of the ending -- but if you're playing in the hopes of a brass ring, a happy ending, or an ending that's carefully and exhaustively explained, the final act of LiS will disappoint. On the other hand if you're attracted to this sort of game, there's a good chance that the main character's development, which stays intact no matter the ending, will matter to you regardless. Various opinions about the final act notwithstanding, LiS offers plenty of bang for your adventure gaming buck. GET IT.

I had to wait until episode 5 was in the can to give an accurate review. Narrative and gameplay wise, it basically combines all the best parts from my two current favorite game styles: that being the intimate, emotional and tenderly wrought personal story of a Gone Home and the branching third-person, colorfully-characterized flair of a TellTale game.
From the word go, I enjoyed the presentation. Echoes of Donnie Darko, Back to the Future, Detention, My So-called Life, and Buffy the Vampire Slayer, presented like an indie film. Time travel seems to be perfect for a high school setting -- the time in our life when we make the most little mistakes we would like to take back, and the time in our life we all wish we could relive after we get the hang of the world.
The internal narrative felt very real (as well as I can remember how my mind worked as a teen), and Chloe in particular is probably one of the best characters I've ever had the pleasure of getting to know through a narrative. Realistic and frustrating and amazing in the ways only a real person whom one loves usually is. That's important, because ultimately the entire narrative of the game pivots on how you feel about Chloe, whether you care about what she cares about, whether you care what's happened to her -- and what's going to happen to her.
Most of all, games like Life Is Strange and Gone Home, as well as a myriad of the new movement in indie gaming, are injecting the gaming world with something it desperately needs (not forced into something like Metal Gear, but rather as an alternative to such a game):
Empathy.

This game completely changed my perspective on my own life, it made me question the choices I have made up until this current point. It challenged me to go the extra mile and to learn how to never anticipate the future. In its own vision, it explained the extreme weight that certain decisions can hold unto you into your own life and those around you. This game cannot be compared with other episodic games such as ones published by Telltale Games or other companies, this game, this piece of raw art is one in a million. Nothing like it has been made or attempted to be fabricated, it's just something unlike anything out there. Everything was unveiling throughout the progression of the story and it used you to create it. You were the one crafting the beginning, middle and end of it, and you didn't realize it until it has already been undone. When the ending is at its peak, it opens the blinders and shows you the complete maze of choices and outcomes that have been either done outright or rewound through time itself. Many people see this game as a "movie" or something of that sort with its somewhat long cutscenes, but I don't see that in its own image. What Life Is Strange™ tries to do it to make you think that you're in the drivers seat, controlling the outcomes on the peoples lives of Arcadia Bay and playing God. Rather, in actuality, at the point of no return, the end, you see the unraveling of everything you love, you've become to love. Everything that you've grown accustomed to. Being altered by one flap of a butterfly. So rather not watching a movie, but experience a human beings life and watching them evolve, being their guardian and ensuring safety for you and those around you with the use of your power to alter time. A movie fades into the past, when life begs to be pushed forwards and onwards. We accept death as an inevitability, it is how we assume such things, that make us human, and unique.
Life Is Strange™ takes you into a second life, a life completely different from yours and puts you in a false sense of command. It turns on you, wrenches at you, makes you feel things you didn't think were possible in a "game". What this game does, tries to do and morally accomplishes it astounding. I would recommend this game to anyone with a sense of what art stands for and to experience marvels not yet foreseen.
Life Is Strange™ is by far, one of the best games ever created.

A re-review after playing the final episode.
First of all: YES I am recommending this game, whole-heartedly. Amazing characters, gorgeous visuals, brilliant voice-acting, tense situations and interesting challenges... a game structured around teen drama that makes the premise not only non-obnoxious, but profoundly emotional and affecting. Far as I'm concerned it's a can't-miss and one of the best games of any genre I've played in a long time.
Now: there's a certain amount of complaining after "Polarized" that the endings negated any sense of choice. This really isn't true -- since the choices the player makes live on in the development of the main character regardless of the ending -- but if you're playing in the hopes of a brass ring, a happy ending, or an ending that's carefully and exhaustively explained, the final act of LiS will disappoint. On the other hand if you're attracted to this sort of game, there's a good chance that the main character's development, which stays intact no matter the ending, will matter to you regardless. Various opinions about the final act notwithstanding, LiS offers plenty of bang for your adventure gaming buck. GET IT.

I loved this game.
It's not for everyone, of course.  Fans of Telltale will find themselves right at home here. It's a story-driven game that uses an obvious hook (in this case, time travel) to tell a character drama about a protagonist caught in the middle of something they can't really control and are just trying a sort of balance again.
Protagonist Max Caufield is a photography student at a private academy in a quiet, west coast, seaboard town.  Her life is immediately thrown a curve when she witnesses a tornado, a shooting, and discovers an ability to rewind time.  Her quest to figure out why all three have happened (and if they will happen again since she's averted them) drives her forward through five episodes and countless conflicts.
Dontnod Entertainment has managed to take what Telltale was doing with Walking Dead and Wolf Among Us and push it just a little bit further along, adding in better movement controls and eliminating the awful ticking clock forcing you to make decisions within 5 seconds.  It results in a game that is both more casual and more harrowing than its predecessors.
Without the presence of a clock, and with the ability to rewind time, you truly have the ability to pick the version of events you like the best.  Does a line of dialog get said the wrong way?  Rewind and pick a different one!  You might think with such a power that all choice would become meaningless, but no, for all of the tailoring you can do for each interaction, Max can't rewind a whole day.  So, eventually you have to give up your rewinds and your replays and let time progress forward, hoping you've worked out the best combination.
As far as gameplay is concerned, that's it.  Everything else rests on the story and the presentation, and this game hits both right out of the park.
The graphics are not photorealistic and they're not intended to be.  The game finds a pleasant medium between the the blocky, comic book style of Telltale and the more down-to-earth stylings most major games choose.  It's streamlined, and definitely artistic, and at times looks beautiful.  A justifiable choice for a game about artists.
The story, well, it worked for me.  Everyone's tastes are different, but Max and her quest to reconnect with her best friend she left behind five years earlier while balancing a potentially dangerous adventure/investigation with said friend, managed to be both charming and suspenseful.  And each chapter ends with a cliffhanger that will beg you to start the next one right away.
As a caveat: there are gripes out there right now about the ending.  I think people were hoping too much for their fan theories to play out and are dissapointed that the developers couldn't implement their dream ending.  The truth is this: while the story has its rocky points, and the game is uninterested in explaining things that don't have an impact on Max, taken together the story is fun, follows narratively, and the endings make sense.
Yes, endingS.  There are two.  Set your expectations properly.
I wholly recommend this game for anyone who loves a good story and doubly so for anyone who has loved what Telltale has done.  It was an amazing ride and I am glad that I went along.

What can I say? Nothing can be said to encapsulate Life Is Strange. It is a wild ride. Maxine Caulfield is an 18-year old photography student who suddenly manifests the ability to manipulate time itself, and you must use her powers to uncover the truth of Rachel Amber's mysterious disappearance and avert Max's vision of an apolocalyptic storm laying waste to Arcadia Bay. Along the way, you'll meet many characters, most of whom are deeply-flawed but well-meaning. You might save lives, or end them. Max is an earnest heroine who genuinely wants to do good, but are good intentions enough? Is it worth it to save some one, if in doing so you warp the fabric of reality to the breaking point? You'll just have to find the answer for yourself.

Hmm. I'm not really sure how to do this one. Actually i've been delaying reviewing this game all day because I was hoping I would have a better idea of what my thoughts really are... but I don't. So here we go...
In short, it's basically an episodic adventure game thing not so different from the stuff Telltale has been doing for the past few years... except this isn't by Telltale. The gameplay is pretty similar in the sense that you make dialogue choices and those choices make things different. The new stuff is that there are no silly quicktime events and that you have the ability to literally rewind time and redo events either as part of the main plotline or to actually redo a choice you just made that you don't like the results of. It's more interesting than it sounds, and the "redo" is pretty short-term. Unless, of course, you decide to actually replay entire sections of the game.
The "redo" thing is here because time travel is the central thing going on in this story. Annnnd, as usual with these stories, your meddling with time results in alot of weird stuff happening. Is it all your fault? Probably, but... honestly I am not sure how. Therein lies my biggest problem with this game: little is truly explained. Why can Max rewind time? What's up with the massive tornado? Is this a better time travel story than Steins;Gate? To answer those in order... I don't know, I'm not entirely sure, and HELL NO. I had hoped that Ep 5 would shed some light on things, but it left me confused and unsure what to think. If the devs wanted to head♥♥♥♥ me much like how Max was being head♥♥♥♥ed (not literally) in the later half of Ep 5, then they succeeded. It felt like I had taken a bunch of medicine and resulted in me having a foggy head unable to think deeply about stuff. I pretty much didn't know what was going on anymore.
This is a real shame, because up until Ep 5 this game was easily the best of this sort of game i've played since Walking Dead Season 1. I'm no fan of (western) stories set in high school settings, but this one has time travel and mystery stuff going on. It also has real drama that can really get to you. But unlike TWD Season 1, where Ep 5 was arguably the best of the season, here it is the worst. Unfortunately since endings tend to be really important, having a mediocre one messes up the whole experience. This game is living proof that storytellers really need to put alot of effort at creating solid endings or else the entire story will suffer as a result. People remember how stuff ends. No matter how interesting things were before that, if the ending is weak it won't be forgotten.
...Ok i'm going to stop writing.
Overall thoughts? Ep 1-4 were great, with Ep 4 having a particularly sinister ending that made me REALLY freaked out. But Ep 5 kinda messed things up here. This was an unqualified "yes" before that. Now... it's a "yes" still, but with the large asterisk that the ending is likely to be disappointing. Will there be a sequel and is that why things ended with so much left unexplained? Or was this just a case of good writers suddenly finding themselves at the end and just hastily coming up with something to fill in? Both suck in their own way, though I'd honestly feel better if it was the latter. Sadly, the former is probably the truth.
A superb game that outdoes Telltale at what Telltale does best (or used to)... and then messes up. God damn it. :(
I'm still giving this a "yes", right? ♥♥♥♥ it... I guess I am.

If you're a fan of Telltale's games like The Walking Dead, The Wolf Among Us, Game of Thrones, etc., chances are you'll also enjoy this. The majority of choices are determined by what the player wants. There is also room to change your decison if you don't like the immediate outcome, which I actually really enjoyed, because I could fix my mistake if I ♥♥♥♥ed up a decision/Max reacted differently than how I thought she would.
The story is intense. I found myself totally immersed in the game no matter what was happening. The characters are also fleshed out quite nicely, despite the fact that a few people made me role my eyes about how cliche some of their actions were. But, this is a game with high school aged kids, so it's easy to look past it.
Some things that I found a little annoying, however, is that I found that very few voice actors were cast. Meaning that a lot of background characters sounded extremely similar to the protagonist and her friends. Also, it's easy to see that the voice actors have not had very much experience in acting, as sometimes the lines seemed forced.
And while I do recommend this game, I'm doing so because the experience throughout the story was engaging and full of emotion. The ending however, lacked the creativity that I had seen time and time again throughout the chapters.
The ending was everything I was expecting emotionally-wise, but unfortunately, DONTNOD dropped the ball when it came to coming up with a decent ending.

I just finished the last episode and I'm still EXTREMELY overwhelmed and in pain, so forgive me if this review gets a little messy.
I kept up with Life Is Strange since the very first episode, I tried it out and decided to stick around because it had a really nice vibe that you don't see in most games, it seemed like a nice and casual experience.
Well, I was wrong. Entirely. This game isn't nice and casual at all and it will leave you a wreck and don't let the initial impression trick you into believing that it's 'nice'.
Anyway. You play as Max Caulfield, a hipster and an aspiring photographer who got into a private school in Arcadia Bay, her hometown she moved away from five years ago. A certain chain of events ends up with her discovering that she has powers that allow her to travel in time, and she uses said powers to try to save Arcadia Bay from a certain doom you see at the beginning of the game. Max reunites with her former best friend, Chloe, and those two do their best to solve various mysteries in the town while rebuilding their friendship (and, depending on how you play, maybe something different too)
The plot is absolutely unique and the way Life Is Strange went from the first episode to the last is remarkable - it advances, gives answers that only lead to more questions and then ties it all up in an extremely satisfying way. This game has you deal with some very hard situations and will throw multiple choices at you that make you want to never play it again so you don't have to decide - and those choices actually (mostly) matter.
The two main characters, Max and Chloe, are both very well-written and they have an amazing dynamic between them - I honestly enjoyed the relationship between them more than I did anything else in the game. The side characters deserve some mention too, because each and every one of them is so unique that hey, you even remember who they are while waiting for months until a new episode comes out.
The gameplay is nice and simple and it works, even though there are some needed tweaks here and there. What I did like was the mechanic that lets you reverse time - it's interesting and leads to many of the optional things you can explore while playing, so I believe that Dontnod did a good job with that.
In the end I just can't give this game anything but my biggest 10/10. I'm entirely satisfied and I wish I could experience Life Is Strange for the first time again - it's not the kind of experience that you can replace with anything else and I admit that I'll miss waiting for the next episode.

Basically good game for episodes 1-4. Lots of ups and downs, really keeps you on the edge of your seat, waiting for more. Really great story line. The last episode however was a major letdown. It basically comes down to 2 choices that pretty much nullify every other choice you've made in the entire game, both with incredibly anticlimactic endings.
The 5th episode took it from my number one favorite game, down to something I almost regret ever wasting my time on. I still enoyed the story, and the gameplay, but both end options are just a slap to the face, and leave you feeling hopeless either way you choose. Of course, this is just my opinion. I'm just really disappointed this is the path they chose to take in ending something that could have been so great.
I loved this right up to the last decision, at which point my love turned into pure hate. I feel like the creators could have done better with the very end. At least give some story or SOMETHING after you choose what you do. It's almost as if they thought "We'll this is the end, and we already got their money. Let's just be done with it." and stopped it there.
TL;DR: No matter what your choices, the ending of this game is super anticlimactic and depressing. Won't be recommending to anyone.

Having almost 500 hours in this game at the moment of writing this... yeah, it's okay. WHEN IT WORKS.
The HL2's Source Engine did not age well, as this technology from 2004 can make even the most powerful of modern PCs cry with its basically nonexistent optimalisation... You can run GTAV on Ultra in 4K and in 120 FPS, but Garry's Mod simply does not give a f**k and sometimes forces you to watch a slideshow just because it didn't like a certain map or because you spawned more than 10 of a certain laggy prop. Sure, it looks good for its age, but at what price... And even when it runs smoothly for you don't let your guard down... it's about to crash any second. It's also lovable that with each update they manage to break the game more and more, SOMEHOW.
All in all, though, the game had to do something right, because I love it to bits, and that "thing" would be hitting right home when it comes to roleplaying. And not just roleplaying normal boring life, mind you (but that's also a thing if you're into that), but roleplaying things like saving the world from evil Raptor Nazis by carpet bombing their military base in a volcano with a flying fridge (that has a cupholder, paintwork with flames and a stereo installed) that deploys angry badgers. It's basically a tool for people that can have fun with their own imagination - it gives you tons of tools to do almost literally whatever you want with the physics engine. It may be a bit hard to have a great time on your own, but if you can get at least one friend to play with you online then you're just about golden. There are also hundreds of thousands of different items available on the Steam Workshop so you will virtually never run out of content to play with, which is pretty amazing.
If this game was made on some better engine that had more realistic physics and didn't randomly crash it could as well be my personal Game of The Century.

The game boils down to a binary "choose your ending now" choice (with one of the endings being incredibly unsatisfying due to them running out of budget) without any of your previous actions mattering, just like a Telltale game really. Although, in one of those two endings there's a 5 second scene that gets changed if you made one or two specific choices in previous episodes (hence the tiny fraction). Aside from that, this is basically a Telltale game with a unique story, a different form of story telling and lovely characters. You're in this game for the journey, not the destination.
Buy it knowing that it's basically a Telltale game with a lot more choices thrown in that don't really matter to the ingame world in the long run, only to you. Also, don't forget to check your ingame journal & texts throughout, it really adds to the experience.

Play it, get your friends to play it and then talk about your respective choices for hours.
You won't believe how well LiS is written and how deep your choices could alter the narration and how seamless it reconnects with the underlying story course.
There is nothing more to say (except for exceptionnal music ambience, strong artistic direction and flawless gameplay).

To me Life is Strange defines what a storytelling game should be. The storytelling was perfect in every way shape and form, the art style was great, the characters were touching and realistic, the voiceacting was great and the sound track was top notch. Life Is Strange is one of those few adventure games that try to really make you feel engaged into the story and the characters. And after all 5 episodes, I can tell you that they did it right. The story is based around the endless posibilites that time traveling could give to us. We would never make mistakes and we would always do everything correctly, in the best possible way. Or would we? The game makes us realise that the answer isn't always so simple and our decisions might in the end turn out to be not really decisions, that we are all going to confront our destiny anyway. The game gives a lot to think about and offers a great, engaging story in the same time. Is it worth playing? Absolutely, both gameplaywise and storywise. The game will pull you in from the first few minutes.

I try to be honest after playing all five episodes. It is really difficult to evaluate this game.
Actually I cannot believe I give a negative review because this game is in many aspects one of the greatest I have ever played and yet I feel almost cheated by the developers. Let me explain:
Pros:
- Stunning, beautiful soundtrack
- Nice implementation of "choices" (see Cons) and time travel
- Very great effort to small details
- Deeply touching and emotinal in a beautiful way
Cons:
- The Ending... Are you kidding me? We got through 5 episodes with like hunderts of desicions that sometimes really touched us and we felt like doing something and then..... nothing matters.
There are only two purely linear and fixed endings. The decision which ending we take is the last thing we do in this game. So in fact, nothing that we did so far had any influence. This has nothing to do with a morale or a deep meaning this is just cheating the player.
Conclusions:
I loved playing episodes 1-4 very much and deeply satisfied lingered in the moments of beauty. Episode 5 was a bit more freaky and disturbing but that was cool and added some weird feeling horror to the game. Great so far. Then, after so much joy, the game provides us with nothing more then two fixed ending movies, the decision is made right before them.
I say it again, in my opinion this cannot hide behind a beautiful morale or the deep meaning of the butterfly effect or something else. This is just f*cking with the players. They feign a huge spread tree of decisions and instead of making something cool out of it the developers just droped everything one did in the end and nothing has a real influence at all. And feeling no real influence of the decisions you make throughout the game is literally the worst thing that could have happened. I know it is not easy but that was your damn job. You had this one job, to make the player feel influence of decisions, and you failed in the end completely.

If you are looking for a fast paced fps, or a light hearted sidescroller, look elsewhere, but if a deep, involving, and touching story is what you desire, you've come to the right place.
Backed by great characters, dificult decisions, an excelent time-travel mechanic, and the looming shadow of consequence, "Life is Strange" manages to tell a story like no other. What starts out as an almost cliché "high school drama" quickly evolves to become a captivating narrative that truly shows the developer's attention to detail.
The time travel mechanic adds yet another level of depth to this already detailed game by giving the player the choice to revert his or her actions. One might imagine that this could take away form the feeling of weight that decisions carry, as the palyer is able to see all outcomes and choose the most favorable one, enter the game's amazing writers, that give each choice multiple imediate outcomes, none of which "good" or "bad", as well as other distant outcomes that one could never even imagine.
I waited this long to publish my review since most games of this style tend to screw up in the final act, but through a last episode that mixes dark gritty elements with deep feels, a final choice that puts the player in a position I wouldn't wish upon my worst enemy and multiple satisfying endings, none of which can be called the "good one" or "bad one", the game manages to guarantee a very high note for it to end upon.
Cudos to DontNod for the excelent game!

To me Life is Strange defines what a storytelling game should be. The storytelling was perfect in every way shape and form, the art style was great, the characters were touching and realistic, the voiceacting was great and the sound track was top notch. Rarely do I find a game that I define as a "perfect" game but this one I have to say is a perfect game, it is the perfect representation of what a storytelling game should be, more than often I found myself tearing up or overwhelmed with emotion forcing myself to pause the game to rethink what I had just done, storys like these that get to you and last are what we as a gaming community need more and for that I give Life is Strange a 10/10.

Life Is Strange is one of those few adventure games that try to really make you feel engaged into the story and the characters. And after all 5 episodes, I can tell you that they did it right. The story is based around the endless posibilites that time traveling could give to us. We would never make mistakes and we would always do everything correctly, in the best possible way. Or would we? The game makes us realise that the answer isn't always so simple and our decisions might in the end turn out to be not really decisions, that we are all going to confront our destiny anyway. The game gives a lot to think about and offers a great, engaging story in the same time. Is it worth playing? Absolutely, both gameplaywise and storywise. The game will pull you in from the first few minutes.

Sigh. What to say about a game that decided to throw all of its potential into the trash with the very last episode?
Smart, I guess, since the game had everybody hooked with the first four episodes. But like the great Freddie Mercury sang: “It started off so well”…
First, the good.
Life is Strange is a game that depends on the relationships between characters, and the attachment that grows between player and characters. What made Life is Strange powerful for me was the coming-of-age story that it is – for teenage characters to come to terms with, and confront, difficult concepts like grief, loss and ultimately, acceptance, was great to see and executed with a bittersweet, very human touch. Chloe is a beautiful example of this – she starts out as an angry, defiant hellraiser, even with her estranged best friend, but develops into a mature, appreciative woman in a matter of days through the difficult events that are testing the residents of Arcadia Bay.
There’s a lot to explore in the quaint little coastal town of Arcadia Bay and its high school, Blackwell Academy. Through exploration, you discover more about the backstories and problems of minor characters – even if they have given you reason enough to dislike them in the main narrative. It’s easy to pass up or miss some of these opportunities, but it wouldn’t make the game quite so good if you did. DONTNOD have created a sufficiently immersive world in that regard, because it feels like something’s always simmering in the background in Arcadia Bay. Max’s adventures are not all there is to the world; some of her schoolmates are wrestling with their own demons too.
Of course, the rewinding of time is a neat little mechanic too. What makes Max’s powers poignant to me is how they mainly exist to help her grow and mature as a character. What starts out as a convenient power to have then teaches her the danger involved in defying ‘fate’ and the difficulties involved in trying to shape events that should be beyond anybody’s control. The ability to use your rewind powers in tiny situations – such as when you’ve upset an acquaintance – is a nice human touch, because who hasn’t wished they could take things back? Who hasn’t ever hoped for a chance at a do-over? Even one of the core mechanics to the game is intended to appeal emotionally to the player.
Then, the not-so-great.
At times, the twists are unnecessary and feel as if they exist purely to shock – but that I could handle, because they do still serve a purpose in the story, and in this game, the objective really seems to be the growth and development of all characters involved. Still, the dialogue and the events could’ve used a more subtle, nuanced touch at certain points, but most people would be willing to overlook these flaws because the focus has always been on the people and relationships in the narrative. One criticism has been that the dialogue can be forced and cheesy.
Finally, the dealbreaker.
I regret to say that the closing episode really killed the entire game for me. I’ll always have fondness for the first four episodes, but in Episode 5, the game tried too hard to be things that it was not and decided to shelf the minor details in favour of the main ‘story’ about Max and Chloe. Perhaps a prudent decision, but not particularly satisfying or helpful lore-wise when you remember that many potential plot points, like the overarching influence of the Prescott family, the strange popularity of the missing girl Rachel Amber, and the native American symbolism woven like a thread throughout the fabric of the game, all remained woefully underused. Even things that were directly mentioned in the game went neglected in the final episode.
Bearing in mind the deeper sufferings and motivations of even the side characters, the story’s main villain was a mere caricature by the beginning of Episode 5. The first half an hour or so was a mad rush of exposition and nonsensical ramblings of a madman. Not exactly the best use of your time and resources, DONTNOD. Then, the game takes you through a series of trippy dreamscapes – very out-of-place, considering that although Max’s powers are very magical, she’s always dealt with reality and the myriad possibilities that are constantly in flux through the narrative. The hour or so of navigating unrealistic nightmares suddenly felt very foreign and overused to me – what is with everyone who wants the player to experience some kind of bizarre psychological acid trip within the game? (Far Cry 3 boss battles anyone?) Also, it was a poor choice to spend all that time recapping the ‘crucial’ moments of the game while the episode was in progress. People forgave the atrocity of this episode precisely because of the attachments they had formed to Chloe and Max – there was definitely no need to remind us of the emotional moments again. Then, the classic Mass Effect 3 mistake. Red, Green or Blue (although there were only two choices in this game) that served to negate every single meaningful decision in this game. Perhaps it was fitting that Chloe has to remind Max that we live for the journey and not the destination – perhaps they anticipated the criticism and meant that to be a direct message for the player, because that definitely reverberated through the fourth wall and felt like a patronizing, direct slap to the face.
Sorry, DONTNOD. I’ve been known to revisit games and replay them countless times, but Episode 5 wasn’t a closer, it really was the nail in the coffin.
Rating: “Was it all wasted, all that love?” 5/10, 5 whole points taken off for the disappointing finisher. Play for the first four episodes and just write your own fanfic ending afterward.
