Sigh. What to say about a game that decided to throw all of its potential into the trash with the very last episode?
Smart, I guess, since the game had everybody hooked with the first four episodes. But like the great Freddie Mercury sang: “It started off so well”…
First, the good.
Life is Strange is a game that depends on the relationships between characters, and the attachment that grows between player and characters. What made Life is Strange powerful for me was the coming-of-age story that it is – for teenage characters to come to terms with, and confront, difficult concepts like grief, loss and ultimately, acceptance, was great to see and executed with a bittersweet, very human touch. Chloe is a beautiful example of this – she starts out as an angry, defiant hellraiser, even with her estranged best friend, but develops into a mature, appreciative woman in a matter of days through the difficult events that are testing the residents of Arcadia Bay.
There’s a lot to explore in the quaint little coastal town of Arcadia Bay and its high school, Blackwell Academy. Through exploration, you discover more about the backstories and problems of minor characters – even if they have given you reason enough to dislike them in the main narrative. It’s easy to pass up or miss some of these opportunities, but it wouldn’t make the game quite so good if you did. DONTNOD have created a sufficiently immersive world in that regard, because it feels like something’s always simmering in the background in Arcadia Bay. Max’s adventures are not all there is to the world; some of her schoolmates are wrestling with their own demons too.
Of course, the rewinding of time is a neat little mechanic too. What makes Max’s powers poignant to me is how they mainly exist to help her grow and mature as a character. What starts out as a convenient power to have then teaches her the danger involved in defying ‘fate’ and the difficulties involved in trying to shape events that should be beyond anybody’s control. The ability to use your rewind powers in tiny situations – such as when you’ve upset an acquaintance – is a nice human touch, because who hasn’t wished they could take things back? Who hasn’t ever hoped for a chance at a do-over? Even one of the core mechanics to the game is intended to appeal emotionally to the player.
Then, the not-so-great.
At times, the twists are unnecessary and feel as if they exist purely to shock – but that I could handle, because they do still serve a purpose in the story, and in this game, the objective really seems to be the growth and development of all characters involved. Still, the dialogue and the events could’ve used a more subtle, nuanced touch at certain points, but most people would be willing to overlook these flaws because the focus has always been on the people and relationships in the narrative. One criticism has been that the dialogue can be forced and cheesy.
Finally, the dealbreaker.
I regret to say that the closing episode really killed the entire game for me. I’ll always have fondness for the first four episodes, but in Episode 5, the game tried too hard to be things that it was not and decided to shelf the minor details in favour of the main ‘story’ about Max and Chloe. Perhaps a prudent decision, but not particularly satisfying or helpful lore-wise when you remember that many potential plot points, like the overarching influence of the Prescott family, the strange popularity of the missing girl Rachel Amber, and the native American symbolism woven like a thread throughout the fabric of the game, all remained woefully underused. Even things that were directly mentioned in the game went neglected in the final episode.
Bearing in mind the deeper sufferings and motivations of even the side characters, the story’s main villain was a mere caricature by the beginning of Episode 5. The first half an hour or so was a mad rush of exposition and nonsensical ramblings of a madman. Not exactly the best use of your time and resources, DONTNOD. Then, the game takes you through a series of trippy dreamscapes – very out-of-place, considering that although Max’s powers are very magical, she’s always dealt with reality and the myriad possibilities that are constantly in flux through the narrative. The hour or so of navigating unrealistic nightmares suddenly felt very foreign and overused to me – what is with everyone who wants the player to experience some kind of bizarre psychological acid trip within the game? (Far Cry 3 boss battles anyone?) Also, it was a poor choice to spend all that time recapping the ‘crucial’ moments of the game while the episode was in progress. People forgave the atrocity of this episode precisely because of the attachments they had formed to Chloe and Max – there was definitely no need to remind us of the emotional moments again. Then, the classic Mass Effect 3 mistake. Red, Green or Blue (although there were only two choices in this game) that served to negate every single meaningful decision in this game. Perhaps it was fitting that Chloe has to remind Max that we live for the journey and not the destination – perhaps they anticipated the criticism and meant that to be a direct message for the player, because that definitely reverberated through the fourth wall and felt like a patronizing, direct slap to the face.
Sorry, DONTNOD. I’ve been known to revisit games and replay them countless times, but Episode 5 wasn’t a closer, it really was the nail in the coffin.
Rating: “Was it all wasted, all that love?” 5/10, 5 whole points taken off for the disappointing finisher. Play for the first four episodes and just write your own fanfic ending afterward.

After the interesting yet disappointing Remember Me, Dontnod's decision to make their next game an episodic story-based adventure game seemed like a unique direction for the studio to take. With the genre's rise to popularity due to companies like Telltale crafting beautiful games like The Walking Dead and Wolf Among Us, I wondered how this new studio would fair with this ambitious project. Being a new IP, something that even Telltale hasn't done as of recently, the risk was even higher. If Dontnod couldn't pull this off, the studio would be screwed.
They pulled it off. In the most beautiful way possible.
Life Is Strange easily rivals and in some cases even tops anything done by Telltale or Quantic Dream. This game crafts a beautiful story in an even more beautiful world. The characters are relatable, even if the situation might not be. The voice acting is superb, probably some of the most heartfelt performances in gaming. Ashly Burch as Chloe in particular nails every emotion that her character goes through. The writing and tone is more melancholy than other adventure games for the most part, giving the game a more relaxed tone. This is not saying that the game doesn't have its crazy moments, and the later episodes definitely have their intense moments. Every moment in this game, whether intense or mellow, is handled carefully and is well-thought out. The soundtrack is also spellbinding, with many of the licensed songs finding their way onto my spotify playlists.
There are some drawbacks, as they always are. While the world and asthetic are beautiful, the graphics can sometimes glitch out. Nothing too serious, but it lacks the polish that the rest of the game has. Also the lip-syncing in the first few episodes is pretty bad, however this has been reported to be fixed with a patch, (I could not verify this at the time of writing, hence why its mentioned here.) Next, while there aren't any lines that made me slam my head against any surface, the dialogue in episode 1 is a little too forced. It's not awful, and the writing does pick up later in the episode and onward, but some of the lines are a bit cliche high schoolerish, if that makes sense. Finally, while I really liked the ending, it tends to be a bit polarizing. It won't be seen with ME3 in any "Worst game endings of all time" lists, but the community is pretty slpit as to whether or not it matches the quality the rest of the game shows.
In short, Life Is Strange is definitely worth checking into. The amount of games coming out now that have deep and engaging stories is growing by the day, and i'm glad I could play one that I know will be referenced in the years to come as an example of how it's done right. I've had more fun and engaging times with this game than most films, books, and other video games. Definitely worth the $20.

I'll come back to that, but first, there is a lot to actually like about this game. The visual style is pretty, with good looking 3D models and textures that often look like they are hand painted. The game often looks realistic and for the most part doesn't approach the uncanny valley. The time travel mechanic adds a really interesting angle to both the story and the gameplay, often giving you a choice and showing the short-term consequences before having you decide and make it permanent, but not letting you know until later what that choice could mean for the long-term future of the characters. On that note, the story itself is very well written and the voice acting is very good, for the most part. Without spoiling anything, it is both a beautiful tale about the life of an adolescent girl and an interesting story about time travel.
There are some minor anoyances in the game. The visuals, though beautiful to look at, sometimes look awkward and break the immersion. The game can also be a bit buggy, particularly with the time travel system. I have had the game be stuck a couple of times where I was supposed to be given dialoge options after rewinding time, but they never showed up, forcing me to restart the checkpoint. This also meant I had to listen to the same dialogue again, without an option to skip, which completely took me out of the experience.
Yet these are not the reasons why I don't recomend this game. Before I explain, I'm going to put in a SPOILER WARNING. I'm not going to reveal any major plot points, but I am going to talk about the ending, so you have been warned.
The main reason I feel disappointed is because this game made the same mistake that most choice-based games make. They advertised that the choices you make throughout the story have major consequences and even determine the ending you will get. I'm sorry to say that in most cases, these consequences boil down to some different dialogue at some later point, where they simply point out what you did or said earlier and are either happy, sad or angry. There are exeptions, but not enough and not big enough to claim that your choices matter. What I also find a shame is that the time travel powers are never explained, and instead is just taken for granted. This might be for the best, as those explanations usually don't make any sense, but the way it is left now, it feels like deus ex machina. As for the ending: yes, there are multiple endings, but they don't emerse from the choices you made throughout the game. Before the very last scene, you get a choice, which on its own determines the ending you get. This is the reason I won't recommend this game.
Let me end this review by saying that I really did enjoy playing this game and the only reason I don't recommend it is because of the false advertising. If you want a beautifull story driven adventure game with some interesting and unique time travel mechanics, than you will probably love this game, as I have. However, if you are looking for the revolution in choice and consequence games, I'm afraid you should look elsewhere.

What a fantastic game! If you're a fan of adventure games, then don't miss this one. Dontnod nailed how a modern adventure game should be made and I only hope they get to perfect their work in the future.
It's a low-budget indie game and it has some technical flaws/shortcomings, like subpar lipsyncing or the occasional sound glitch but they never get in the way of the plot or your enjoyment of the game.
However, it excels at what it set to do. A larger than life story about choices, consequences and destiny. You have to make some big choices that might affect the people around you and how events will unfold in the future. All with the help of a mysterious time travel power that is given to the main character. A power that gives you fun and interesting gameplay mechanics that will become necessary to advance the plot and unravel what's really going on in this universe.
I personally hope this game shines a nice guiding light on how future adventure or interactive story games should be made in the future and that Dontnod will become a familiar name to a lot of people in gaming.

I am writing this review minutes after I finally finished Life is Strange. It took me some time to recover.
-FOR LAZY READERS AND TECHNICAL DETAILS, SHORT VERSION BELOW!
Dontnod created a living and breathing world, with complex characters that I have come to call "people" throughout the episodes, heartbreaking situations and wonderful moments that I will cherish in my small gamer heart, as well as disturbing yet interestingly mature concepts that made me, and many others I'm sure, sit and ponder about life, reality, existence and ultimately ethics.
Life, reality, existence and then ethics... that order might seem strange, but it is exactly the one adopted by the developers: Max Caulfield, our heroine, first cuts her place in our hearts by exposing how much her life and ours are alike, so that we can understand how her sudden and thraumatizing encounter with sci-fi might have impacted on her, then as we follow the story, as we follow Maxine delving deeper and deeper into the undiscovered, the "twilight zone" (a needed reference given the load of pop culture and nerdy hints throughout the game), we are faced with questions about the nature of our world which can only lead to unsure and hypotetical answers, in perfect fit with the whole "chaos theory" and "butterfly effect" theme that the game chooses to follow.
But in the end, all that matters is, again, ethics: joy, sorrow, friendship, bullism, love, rejection, the need for a young girl to be accepted as she makes her first steps into the real world, to pursue the dreams in her heart, to have people she cares for around her and shield them from harm.
Life is Strange is a parable on life that I am willing to accept as a field guide for my own.
-SHORT VERSION
Life is strange is a technically flawless game which will addict you from the first episode with stunning visuals (just expect some pixels here and there, it's not a DX11 eye-candy title), interesting characters that will make you remeber them (especially a certain punk) and a wonderfully written story (plot twists!), with a perfect soundtrack to top it off.
The game is based on the mechanic "choice=consequence" and you lead the story, making your own mistakes and getting all proud over the right choices. Every action you take ripples through the rest of the game, either in the main story or in the character's dialogues.
Little word of advice: read everything, chat with everyone and always check a new sms!
WHOLE-HEARTEDLY RECOMMENDED 10/10

tl;dr - Awesome story, amazing and likeable characters, a surreal emotional rollercoaster, if you get attached to the characters. Would happily pay a lot more for the game.
Coming from a gaming background with years of mostly multiplayer FPS and MMORPG games, Life is Strange still managed to be the game with which I identify myself the most. With well-written characters, an interesting story and a lot of though decisions to make along the way, the game really struck home to me, emotionally.
Life is Strange puts you in the shoes of Max Caulfield, a 18 year-old aspiring photographer who returns to her hometown of Arcadia Bay after 5 years, to study photography at Blackwell Academy. The story initially appears to be the typical high-school drama, with pretty much every stereotype character in it, but you soon realize that there's a lot more to it. As the game progresses, you are presented with a series of choices that may or may not alter the course of history.
Personally, I immediately resonated with Max's personality, from the start of Ep. 1. That made me care even more of what was happening to her throughout the story and urged me to really think through each and every decision that would affect her and her friends. And believe me, you will probably take a very long time to make up your mind in some of the decisions, if you really care about the characters.
The relationship between Max and her bff is heart-warming, to say the least. I really enjoyed seeing their friendship re-bloom after Max's 5-year absence period, in such a meaningful way. After both being through all sorts of shenanigans (and some horrific moments)  together, the game shows you the pure core of their friendship and how much they really care about one another, which I found beautiful...probably because it's the type of relationship most of us would actually strive to have in our lives (and probably only comes true in movies).
The story is complimented by amazing hand-painted scenery. It is clear that the devs put in a lot of effort to get the mood of each scene right. From the lighting to the top-notch voice acting, it all comes into place nicely. And don't get me started in the soundtrack! I'm mostly a hard-rock and metal guy, but I couldn't imagine a more perfect set of songs for this type of game. The most emotionally intense scenes along with the soundtrack can't help but to get me teary-eyed.
One of the minor negative aspects that most people mentions is the lip-sync. Recent patches improved upon this issue, and, although it's not as good as the lip-sync in TLoU, for example, it is still pretty accurate.
With this all being said, the season pass really is a bargain at 20€. I would happily pay 3 times as much for it, given all that I've been through with Max, playing the game. If you're still unsure about buying this, I hope this review will convince you to do so :)
You can also watch a playthrough of the game, but I really advise you to experience the game on your own. I watched a playthrough of ep. 1 before buying it and it felt much more emmersive to make decisions on my own.

Life Is Strange is a game about choices, and a deconstruction of games about choices.
In the first episode, the protagonist, Max Caulfield, discovers she can rewind time - by accidentally saving a girl from being shot in a school restroom - and everything spirals from there. We spend five episodes exploring the consequences and limitations of our abilities, and exploring the motivations and histories of the people around us.
Your expectations will inform what you get out of this game, I think: it is an exploration of the butterfly effect, and it allows you to rewind and rewrite almost any interaction or conversation you enter into. Almost. What it doesn't do is let you off the hook for the decisions you settle on. There are no objectively "good" switches that you flip to build your perfect ending. There are only actions and consequences, and some of those consequences are immense.
If to you a game about choices means picking the right options and getting the slideshow you want, Life Is Strange will probably disappoint you. If you're interested in following through on your choices as a means to explore the people and places around you, though, there's never been a better medium.

So now that the final episode has been released and I've had a chance to play through it, I can finally give my thoughts on the game as a whole. The short version for those that want a tally of positive vs negative reviews? I liked it, despite some flaws, it was an enjoyable experience.
Much like the popular Telltale games, in this story you get to make choices that will alter the future events within the game, but after an unexplained instance Max is gifted with the ability to rewind time and finds herself able to reverse these future-altering instances and meld a future that she thinks is ideal. The caveat, however, quickly begins to make itself apparent that there is cause and effect to everything, and things aren't always going to end the way you want them to.
Along with her childhood friend Chloe, you embark on a time-travelling adventure to solve the mystery around a missing student, Rachel Amber, after her sudden and inexplicable disappearance. But during the investigation some things start to come to light, and it appears there's much more going on than it first seemed...
With a very impressive soundtrack and some not so impressive lip-syncing issues, the game managed to keep me quite involved. There was one particular character that is always getting into unfortunate situations and her voice just made me want to let her face the brunt of it every single time, but my good nature got the best of me up until the end. But if you're a fan of these graphic novel with a choice style games, you're sure to enjoy the weird and wonderful ride that Life is Strange manages to deliver.

I am writing this review minutes after I finally finished Life is Strange. It took me some time to recover.
-FOR LAZY READERS AND TECHNICAL DETAILS, SHORT VERSION BELOW!
Dontnod created a living and breathing world, with complex characters that I have come to call "people" throughout the episodes, heartbreaking situations and wonderful moments that I will cherish in my small gamer heart, as well as disturbing yet interestingly mature concepts that made me, and many others I'm sure, sit and ponder about life, reality, existence and ultimately ethics.
Life, reality, existence and then ethics... that order might seem strange, but it is exactly the one adopted by the developers: Max Caulfield, our heroine, first cuts her place in our hearts by exposing how much her life and ours are alike, so that we can understand how her sudden and thraumatizing encounter with sci-fi might have impacted on her, then as we follow the story, as we follow Maxine delving deeper and deeper into the undiscovered, the "twilight zone" (a needed reference given the load of pop culture and nerdy hints throughout the game), we are faced with questions about the nature of our world which can only lead to unsure and hypotetical answers, in perfect fit with the whole "chaos theory" and "butterfly effect" theme that the game chooses to follow.
But in the end, all that matters is, again, ethics: joy, sorrow, friendship, bullism, love, rejection, the need for a young girl to be accepted as she makes her first steps into the real world, to pursue the dreams in her heart, to have people she cares for around her and shield them from harm.
Life is Strange is a parable on life that I am willing to accept as a field guide for my own.
-SHORT VERSION
Life is strange is a technically flawless game which will addict you from the first episode with stunning visuals (just expect some pixels here and there, it's not a DX11 eye-candy title), interesting characters that will make you remeber them (especially a certain punk) and a wonderfully written story (plot twists!), with a perfect soundtrack to top it off.
The game is based on the mechanic "choice=consequence" and you lead the story, making your own mistakes and getting all proud over the right choices. Every action you take ripples through the rest of the game, either in the main story or in the character's dialogues.
Little word of advice: read everything, chat with everyone and always check a new sms!

When I first heard of Life is Strange, I had my doubts, but after finishing Episode 5 just now I can wholeheartedly recommend this series to anyone looking for a great story experience. This series has shown that gameplay in its most simplest form can make any person feel invested with the game's characters, setting and plot.
The game has always managed to keep me invested  in the story. From the main choices, to roaming around some areas and reading flyers scattered around. Choices and their consequences rarely go through tropes and often leave you wondering of their impact later on in the plot. Puzzles are simple and intuitive, not the toughest, but they are fitting for the game's style and narrative context.
Some final and more personal thoughts, this game was a real emotional ride that gave me highs and lows that no other game has given, Some moments really hit me hard and even affected me as a person. For a work of art I really do appreciate it more than anything. Life really is the star of this game, and everything that comes with it.

This game is essentially a virtual toybox: there's no overarching goal, only a bunch of weapons, props, vehicles, NPCs and other knick-knacks to do whatever you want. Want to make a gun-carnival? Go right ahead! Want to drive a tank into a crowd of unarmed (or armed!) people? Knock yourself out! Want to NUKE THE WHOLE MAP!? Sure, wipe the map CLEAN!! Basically, the better question is; What CAN'T you do in Gmod?
This is only possible with mods, but that's EXACTLY the purpose of this game; it's a blank canvas that you can (and should!) mod to hell and back!
Once you had your fun in Sandbox mode, give any of the other game modes a try!
-Prop Hunt is a game similar to hide-and-seek, but instead of hiding behind an object, you ARE the object! The Props' goal is to blend in to the environment until time runs out, and the Hunters' goal is to find the player-props and kill them before time runs out.
-Death Run is an all-vs-1 game where the solo person must activate traps on an obstacle course to stop everyone else from completing it. Each trap only activates once.
-Trouble in Terrorist Town is a game where one person is the Traitor and must secretly kill everyone else without giving themselves away, while everyone else has to guess who amongst them is the Traitor.
-There's more gamemodes than just these. TONS more!
My verdict?

So, now that all episodes are out and I played all of them I feel I can give a fair analysis.
I have mixed feelings about this game, to make it simple I will list the pros and cons first.
-- PROS:
- Great story: time travel stories are always fun, specially when they base the story on real life time travelling theories.
- Great music: appropriate for every scene, specially for the most plot intense parts the music add a lot to the feeling of the game.
- Great gameplay mechanics: One strong point on the game mechanics is that when you travel back in time everything around you change to a previous state, but Max doesn't move of her place (which makes sense because is time travel and not space travel), this gives the developers a lot of opportunities for puzzle solving (which I feel could have been used a lot more).
-- CONS:
- Relatable characters: for the most part, I feel the main character [Max] goes off character a lot in episode 4 and 5 just for the sake of making the game dramatic, and that's just not good storytelling.
- Your decisions do NOT matter: for a game that pushes the idea of the importance of choice, it actually doesn't show it. I mean, you can make ANY decision you want and the development of the plot will not change AT ALL besides some lines and references to previous choices.
All in all the game is ok, i would recommend it if you want a good story with lots of feeling but not if you are looking for a mass effect like malleable plot.

*SPOILERS, YOU HAVE BEEN WARNED.*
Life is Strange is one of many games that promises you the diversity in the outcome of your experience based on the choices you make throughout your game. With the release of the final episode and the DONTNOD team failing to meet these expectations, this game is still worth your money and your time.
Most of this game's meaty bits lie in the character you play as and the ones you meet along the way. Life is Strange introduces reletable and likeable characters who are more than what you initially see in the first one or two episodes. While it conforms to dull stereotypes, it also isn't afraid to introduce touchy material that we rarely see in video game media. From mental-illnesses to same-sex relationships this game offers what most don't dare to introduce in their own games. This experience was an emotional rollercoaster and despite the predictable ending I still found myself crying miserably over the fate of your best friend, or the fates of the others you became close to in Arcadia Bay.
With that said some DLC should definitely be in order. With the journey you went through not enough was touched on the endings (specifically if you decide to save Chloe) after the emotional struggle you went through to get there. Life is Strange struggles with what Mass Effect 3 did in that there are too many loopholes and questions left up in the air after it's all said and done, which is definitely disappointing.
Strangely enough with how easily predictable and lackluster the ending was this did not sway my feelings towards the game in the slightest. Could we have gotten better endings? Most definitely. Was the one we got completely terrible? I don't think so. As stated your choices have little meaning in the story's end-game, but the choices you make in earlier episodes do change the path that the story takes to reach that final point.
All in all I would not rate Life is Strange as a "story-rich" game, but instead as an emotional thriller. Despite that this game is definitely worth the time if you haven't already picked it up.

So,,,it's been a long road since the release of Ep.1, but every road must come to an end.
You know, i always recognize a great piece of art from a simply...good one, by the way i feel when it ends. Sadness, emptiness, the realisation that the story is over, these kinda feelings. For me it's always this way, when i read a book, watch a movie, play a game - when i'm sad and depressed after the end, i know it's a great one. Surely, i can replay the game - which, mind you, i'm totally going to do - but you can only really expirience a piece of art once. Nothing beats the first impression.
And oh man, did this game leave a lasting one. I'll probably think about it for months, remembering every little detail of the story.

Okay, let me just say: Wow. This has got to be one of the most amazing games I've played, period. An emotional rollercoaster from the very start, Life is Strange will have you begging for more after each episode.
The story is amazing. Even though it is a work of fiction, there is an amazing degree of realism. From the characters, to the setting, you really begin to feel as if you're in Arcadia Bay, and by Max's side every step of the way.
The graphics and visuals are pretty great, too. Even with a low budget and all of the settings on low, the game managed to not be a total eyesore. Every sunset we see is breathtaking, and every view we get of the storm forces us to be afraid of what's coming.
The characters are so, so relateable. There's a wide spectrum of people that you can meet, not only in LiS, but also in real life. Dontnod captures the essence of human contact in a spectacular story of strong emotion.
If you have some money left over, or you're just looking for another gripping story to play through, buy Life is Strange. Not only will it help Dontnod create more amazing games, it'll help you find another perspective in life.
Also, don't time travel. You could kill a person.

That's just the tip of the iceberg. If i went into detail this review will be the size of the english dictionary.
General pros:
1. Good commuity with alot of different sub-communitys to get into.
2. Amazing devs and players working on filling the workshop. ( Almost 1 million addons)
3. MASSIVE range of gamemodes and servers!
4. Finding a community that you like to be apart.
General cons:
1. Glitchy the more you use the game E.G spamming props and general stuff that would tip the source engine overboard    ( loopholes exist however)
2. Sub-communitys can be toxic ( E.G Server owners selling admin - Toxic regular players on 1 server)
Conclusion.
Gmod is a community based game. There's a community for everyone. You just have to find it.

I held back on writing a review for Life is Strange initially because I felt that if I were to judge it fairly, I could only do so as a finished product as only then can it be truly judged.  What began as an intriguing tale, set in a sleepy Oregon coastal town tinged with science fiction themes set to a 'hipster haven' back drop, quickly evolved into an even deeper and richer storytelling experience than I could even have imagined.
As a game, it isn't really much of one (though that is not a criticism).  There's not really a great deal to the standard 'game-y tropes' beyond a bit of simple puzzle solving, some stealth here and there, and a few collectables for the achievement completionists.  However, this isn't a game really.  The reason to really throw yourself into the game is for the depth of the experience, and it is exactly that.  An experience.  All I can really say about the game-y elements is that they serve their purpose and do the job reasonably well.  It works.  It's relatively bug free.  There's not much else you can say about it beyond that.
Its real selling point is the decisions you have to make.  As long as you can immerse yourself in the world and the characters, the decisions you are forced to make are hard.  Damn hard.  Unlike the Telltale interactive novel games where you have to make decisions on a time limit, Life is Strange gives you all the time in the world to make them, and even then, you often find yourself still needing even more time to do so.  Many decisions I made in my own playthrough came with a sucker punch of regret.  It's that reason that just made me love the game even more with each episode.  I've played hundreds, maybe even thousands of games in my lifetime, and I have forgotten many.  I can safely say that this won't be one of the forgotten.  The storytelling has left a scar, and with it, some of the licensed songs from the game now have new memories attached to them that will always be a reminder of my experience in Arcadia Bay.  One day I will return, but I want it to only ever be this story and this game.
Thank you, Dontnod Entertainment.  Life is more than just strange.  It's heart-wrenchingly beautiful.
~LokusT

Game Rate: 10/10 (Beyond Excellent)
Life Is Strange (Ep 1- 5)
Summary & Review
Played as Maxine Claufield, who is a photography student who discovered that she is able to manipulate or reverse time regardless the situation.
She is able to reverse the time by using a photograph & also “teleport”.
Each decision made will alter the past, present & future. She had repeated vision that  her town Arcadia Bay will be wiped out by a tornado in the future.
Maxine or Max saved her only best friend Chloe from countless death in all alternate realities.
Unlike any American school drama, Max lecturer, Prof. Jefferson, who is a psychopath takes photos of his victims tied & drugged then killed them afflicted with another high prestige student named Nathan involve in this crime.
Nathan ended up kill by Prof. Jefferson.
And finally the psychopath lecturer had been apprehended by the police.
By using too much of her ability to save Chloe had caused the environment to be altered too hence ended up a catastrophic event for Arcadia Bay.
Max tried to save the one she love but every action have a reaction aka The Chaos Theory.
Max regretted not spending time with Warren, who had a crush on her before travelling back time to prevent the end of Arcadia Bay.
And thinking that’s the ending but nope. Max was stuck in a time dimension what all realities appeared in front of her blaming for everything.
In the end, you were given the choice to save Arcadia Bay by sacrificing Chloe (means you didn’t save her in the early stage) or sacrifice Arcadia Bay but keep Chloe alive.
It’s your choice whether you think it’s right or wrong.
Pros: Awesome soundtracks, alternate endings etc.
Cons:  Lip Synch & audio is not synchronized

Okay, let me just say: Wow. This has got to be one of the most amazing games I've played, period. An emotional rollercoaster from the very start, Life is Strange will have you begging for more after each episode.
The story is amazing. Even though it is a work of fiction, there is an amazing degree of realism. From the characters, to the setting, you really begin to feel as if you're in Arcadia Bay, and by Max's side every step of the way.
The graphics and visuals are pretty great, too. Even with a low budget and all of the settings on low, the game managed to not be a total eyesore. Every sunset we see is breathtaking, and every view we get of the storm forces us to be afraid of what's coming.
The characters are so, so relateable. There's a wide spectrum of people that you can meet, not only in LiS, but also in real life. Dontnod captures the essence of human contact in a spectacular story of strong emotion.
If you have some money left over, or you're just looking for another gripping story to play through, buy Life is Strange. Not only will it help Dontnod create more amazing games, it'll help you find another perspective in life.
Also, don't time travel. You could kill a person.

Gameplay: 11/10 (No words needed)
Graphics: 5.5/10 | Since the game is really old, of course the graphics can't hold with the new games. (But I still think it is really beatiful if you max out all the graphic settings!)

It is still probably better than the CS:GO or COD community, but it is still kind of sad to see cancerous trolls abusing everything and just ruining the fun of other players. Overall: 9,5/10 | Everything in this game is just right, but the community isn't the best anymore, and the community is a big part of the game, unless you wanna play offline only.

Excellent game. As luck would have it I bought it just two days before episode 5 came out, so I could play through episodes 1-4 in one sitting pulling an unplanned all-nighter, and then play through episode 5 when I woke up a second time. The game is jsut that good.
There are a lot of very meaningful choices as far as the evolution of the plot is concerned, but the final choice is the most meaningful of all, without going into details.
While it left a lot of people disappointed, the reason is not that it's actually meaningless like it was in ME3, but that it's emotionally hard to execute, as it's a very big choice. Might be the biggest choice in gaming yet, and it certainly is the biggest among the games I played.
Aside of that there's not much to criticise. There is indeed a huge plothole that I only realised later because I forgot about a critical detail towards the end, and it detracts from your satisfaction when you finished the game if you realise it, but it's still a great experience throughout.
The worst aspect of the game is that it eventually ends and ends too soon. You just don't wanna say good bye.
CAUTION, PHOTOGRAHPY AND HIFI GEEK CRITICISM AHEAD
Also photography is awesome, so yeah, that theme is just totally cool. Even though I think a lot of the collectible shots you can make are pretty damn lame and forgettable, like from some amateur "woo I can shoot pics with my iphone, snap all the things!" instagram. Some really stand out though.
The visuals and audio are fantastic. Extremely well put-together and produced - maybe too well produced, hearing that clear sound coming from Chloe's cheap bedroom stereo was pretty weird, and I'm 100% certain that Max's earbuds are not 200$ IEMs either, but I'm sure my geek complaints are irrelevant to 98% of people. And I guess it's much better like this than suffering the actual sound of compressed MP3s on cheap 5$ earbuds.
Also it's made to look like you're looking through a camera lens, but I think this part, while the idea is cool, was not well executed. There is an extreme drop in sharpness at the outer edges of the screen, suggesting a low-quality or portrait glass (from the top of my head I think there are some CA too, but don't quote me on it), but not once did I see an ACTUAL lens-flare (not the "dirty camera" visual vomit that the reet-arded art direction at Ubisoft consider lens flares, the real thing that more or less streaks across the picture) or any kind of bokeh, which would've been rad as hell. This needs some improvement if they get the opportunity to use the lens optics again.
Anyway,
TL;DR Buy the game, it's ♥♥♥♥ing fantastic.

I don't think that any review I write will ever do this game justice. I did not expect much out of Life is Strange. I began the game thinking it would be little more than high school drama overpacked with cliches, but the concept seemed interesting enough to be worth trying.
I have never been more pleased to be wrong.
The game's story rose to incredible heights that I never expected it to rise to. The more the mystery unraveled, the more hooked I became. I was on the edge of my seat by the end of Episode 2, and it just got better and better from there. The story had several twists I never would've expected, was emotionally gripping and heartwrenching, and it felt like the choices made actually mattered.
The only drawbacks that I felt toward the game were related to the endings, as I felt one obviously had more depth than the other. Additionally, it felt that some subplots to the story were touched on yet not detailed later, so I wish we had been given more information regarding certain characters in the story to add more substance.
All in all, however, Life is Strange is a brilliant game that I unexpectedly enjoyed to an immense degree. I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a mysterious, interesting story complete with a rollercoaster of emotions, fun characters, and impactful choices.

This is coming from the perspective of one who has played each installment of the game as it came out. I had the first episode day one and am now just writing this review after completing episode 5 and taking a few hours to think about it.
This is a story-driven game (yes it is technically a game because it has fail-states). I encourage you to try this game even if you value mechanics over story BECAUSE I believe that this game handles the story-driven elements in such a unique way because of the rewind "powers".
Let's start from the beginning. You're Max Caulfield, a LOL SO QUIRKY (this is not a bash, as it fits the story quite well and I wouldn't have it any other way) main character. You attend a pompous art school by the name of Blackwell Academy. Frequently, by the game, you're told to make choices. Some small choices like watering a plant that you might not even notice if you don't look hard enough, some slightly larger choices in dialogue trees that make certain characters react to you in different ways, and the much larger choices. The larger choices are given to you on an anxiety-inducing red-tinted screen with sounds playing in the background that intensify the severity of this choice. Most choices can be reversed with a time-travel mechanic that lets you tailor your choices to exactly what you would want them to be, as directly after the choice you can see some of the short term effects of the choice. This mechanic is also the basis of many puzzle elements in the game, which involve memory puzzles, timing, and trial and error. This is all the information I will elect to give to you about the game because I believe it's quite beneficial for you to go in un-biased and blind. Tune out of this review right now if you want to go along with the whole "un-biased" thing, as I will be expressing my opinions in the next portion
Now, for my thoughts on the game as a whole: It was an amazing experience. Despite things like clunky lip-syncing and numerous bugs on release (that got largely patched out fairly quickly), this game was absolutely worth the time and money (well, my friend's money) invested in it. In my opinion, this game does player choice very well. You can see a large choice coming, and you dread it, and then the choice screen pops up and you're left to sit and contemplate what might be the best option. There were also some "large" choices that were incredibly easy to make, which I also think was intentional on a certain level. Now what this game does well is letting you essentially demo your choices to a certain point, which is very useful on choices that are more gray or murky. The way this game handles situations makes a lot of moments in the game deeply emotionally affecting. Overall, this game had me chomping at the bit for the next episode, and never disappointed me from a story standpoint.
+ Engaging story
+ Realistic characters
+ Intense situations
+ Hard choices
+ Very pretty game
+ Lots of story to pick up on/look at through character dialogue and examining objects
+ Journal that reflects on main character's more complex thoughts
+ Many bugs were very quickly patched out after launch
+ Collectibles
+ Pricefield
- Bad lip-sync (even after the recent patch, though it's a LOT better)
- Some puzzles are clunky
This is my first review of any game I've played on steam, mostly because this one affected me in such a way that I had to to share. I hope you enjoyed this review.

PROS
+ Nice Artstyle
+ Interesting puzzle ideas
+ Plenty of freedom
+ Nice soundtrack
+ 2nd half sets things up nicely for future episodes
CONS
- Dull first half
- Teens don't talk like this
- Mixed Voice acting
- Tropes galore
Overall - 6/10
Episode 2 - Out of Time
PROS
+ Deals with realistic themes
+ Relationships between friends is handled better
+ Strong ending
+ Choices do have some interesting consequences
+ Soundtrack is still excellent
CONS
- TEDIOUS fetch quests longate the already 2 hour long episode
- Set pieces feel uninspired and recycled
- Writing is hit and miss
-  Teens still don't talk like this
Overall - 7/10
Episode 3 - Chaos Theory
PROS
+ Plot is finally coming together
+ Strong Character building moments
+ Twists time mechanics a little bit
+ Tries new ideas
+ Soundtrack is still on point
+ Voice actors finally starting to get comfortable
CONS
- Not much actually happens to progress the main arc
- Puzzles are a mixed bag
- Stealth sequence is welcomed if poorly made
- Teens once again still don't talk like this
Overall - 8/10
Episode 4 - Dark Room
PROS
+ Plot progession
+ Main arc resolved
+ necessary lengthy episode
+ Strongest character moments in the series
+ Puzzles feel rewarding
+ Side characters are actually developed
+ Soundtrack of course
CONS
- Some bizarre puzzle solutions
- Sorry, but Teens do not talk like this still
Overall - 9.5/10
Episode 5 - Polarized
PROS
+ Strong opening act
+ Soundtrack is great
+ Attempt was made
+ Determinantly emotional ending
CONS
- Once developed side characters are one dimensional and forgotten
- Wastes its 2.5 hour long episode on a 40 minute nightmare sequence
- Poorly made stealth sequence
- Underwhelming ending
- Plotholes galore
- retcons previous choices
- Ruins what made the previous episode brllliant
- Teens ESPECIALLY don't talk like this (EVEN IN A DREAM!)
Overall 3/10
Despite its incredibly dissappointing and messy ending, Life is Strange is a game worth checking out at the very least on sale. Although episode 4 is the best of the series, the disaster of ending can still leave an awful taste in your mouth.
OVERALL - 6.7/10

I'm not going to give an extrordinarily in depth review, because I can't.  This game NEEDS to speak for itself.  When explained as an abstract, it loses the tremendous quality, character and cohesion that make it such a great game,  Though none of the individual elements sound impressive, or like they work together, they do.  They work together brilliantly.
The story is emotional and gripping, and deals intellegently with a lot of very mature issues.  It can feel over-dramatized at times, but never to the point of being tiresome.  It has had a greater emotional impact on me then any other game, along with most books I've ever read.  The fact that you're making the decisions, and the consequences play out in all sorts of subtle and unexpected ways only enhances the impact, though many of your smaller choices have a greater percived effect then actual effect on the overall narrative.
Overall, I highly encourage you to try this game.  It's incredbly well done, and the result is best (and worst) romp through time that you've ever experienced.  And it's worth it all the way.

The game drags you inside, you become one with Protagonist Maxine Caulfield and you go through five episodes of pure emotion. I just finished the game so my mind is still heavily blown and emotions are overflowing (to be honest I think I'll get emotional issues for the end of the week XD)

I wrote a review on this game after episode 2 that went into talking about graphics, gameplay, sounds, etc...  After playing the final episode I decided to delete all of that.  You know what, that stuff doesn't matter.  It's the story... Oh my god the story...  If you don't buy this game and play all the episodes you'll miss one of the most amazing story games of our generation.  This should be nominated for awards.   Everyone at Dontnod Entertainment who worked on this project should be proud of themselves.  I'd give this a 100/10 if I could, but for now I'll just recommend it.
---------------------------------------------------------------
UPDATE - 24 Hours Later
---------------------------------------------------------------
Here I am, still awestruck at the ending of Life is Strange.  The method in which I played this game (1 episode at a time with months between) was by far the best experience I can imagine.  The break between episodes gave you time to reflect on the story and build theories as to what was coming next.
Speaking of theories (without dropping spoliers), it was probably easy for most to decypher exactly what was going on with the big "event" that the character kept flashing back to.  That would lead to you anticipating that last important decision.  Anticipating that decision should have lowered the impact of said decision.  It didn't.  If anything, everything you went through up to then makes it one of those situations you know is going to happen but silently pray it doesn't.  It catches you off guard.  You aren't ready for it and it hits you like a ton of bricks.  It was an amazing experience that I've never had with a game before.
If I had to sum up Life is Strange it would be something like this.  It was like reading a really great book and getting so engrossed in it that you move beyond the letters on the page and begin to relate and feel what the characters are going through.  It becomes a personal experience and hits you with emotions you never expected a game to be able to bring out. PROS
+ Nice Artstyle
+ Interesting puzzle ideas

CONS

- Teens don't talk like this

- Tropes galore

Episode 2 - Out of Time
PROS
+ Deals with realistic themes
+ Relationships between friends is handled better
+ Strong ending
+ Choices do have some interesting consequences
+ Soundtrack is still excellent
CONS
- TEDIOUS fetch quests longate the already 2 hour long episode
- Set pieces feel uninspired and recycled
- Writing is hit and miss
-  Teens still don't talk like this
Overall - 7/10
Episode 3 - Chaos Theory
PROS
+ Plot is finally coming together
+ Strong Character building moments
+ Twists time mechanics a little bit
+ Tries new ideas
+ Soundtrack is still on point
+ Voice actors finally starting to get comfortable
CONS
- Not much actually happens to progress the main arc
- Puzzles are a mixed bag
- Stealth sequence is welcomed if poorly made
- Teens once again still don't talk like this
Overall - 8/10
Episode 4 - Dark Room
PROS
+ Plot progession
+ Main arc resolved
+ necessary lengthy episode
+ Strongest character moments in the series
+ Puzzles feel rewarding
+ Side characters are actually developed
+ Soundtrack of course
CONS
- Some bizarre puzzle solutions
- Sorry, but Teens do not talk like this still
Overall - 9.5/10
Episode 5 - Polarized
PROS
+ Strong opening act
+ Soundtrack is great
+ Attempt was made
+ Determinantly emotional ending
CONS
- Once developed side characters are one dimensional and forgotten
- Wastes its 2.5 hour long episode on a 40 minute nightmare sequence
- Poorly made stealth sequence
- Underwhelming ending
- Plotholes galore
- retcons previous choices
- Ruins what made the previous episode brllliant
- Teens ESPECIALLY don't talk like this (EVEN IN A DREAM!)
Overall 3/10

Garry's Mod is a physics sandbox. A quite brilliant one, in my opinion. Other than most games, in Garry's Mod there is no goal. Well, there might be one - and that's having fun. Sure, this game still has a lot of problems, but for a game which is older than most of it's player nowadays (sadly). You could simply download some addons from the workshop (there are a lot of them..) and have fun offline, or you could join a gamemode and enjoy it.
Gameplay: 11/10 (No words needed)
Graphics: 5.5/10 | Since the game is really old, of course the graphics can't hold with the new games. (But I still think it is really beatiful if you max out all the graphic settings!)
Multiplayer: 8/10 | Don't get me wrong, the multiplayer is really great, there are a lot of gamemodes you must try out, but the community is not what it used to be. It is still probably better than the CS:GO or COD community, but it is still kind of sad to see cancerous trolls abusing everything and just ruining the fun of other players. Even worse, there are way too many trolls.
Replayability: 10/10 | Once you find a great gamemode you enjoy, you won't stop playing this game. You will soon reach 100 hours, then 500 hours, and so on. You get my point. It's more addictive than heroin.
Controls: 8/10 | Controls are very simple, not hard to use (unless you got Parkinsons)
Creativity: 10/10 | In my opinion this game is full of creative minds. Every gamemode is creative on its own way, but you can be also creative on Sandbox or offline.
Fun: 64/10 | Once you find the right gamemode, and the right server - you can't have no fun.
Overall: 9,5/10 | Everything in this game is just right, but the community isn't the best anymore, and the community is a big part of the game, unless you wanna play offline only.
But you should really get the game, you won't regret
spending thousands of hours on this game!

What would I do, if I could do it all over again? What if I could change the past, alter the very fabric of time for my own purposes. What would happen then? There's bound to be repercussions to such a violation of physics. Even a minor change could magnify over time to create the unexpected.
This is the idea behind the storyline of Life is Strange, an episodic adventure in the style of Telltale's games. A refinement over the formula well-worn by telltale in gameplay and design, Life Is Strange offers over the course of 5 episodes of about two hours each a story themed around concepts taken from chaos theory, but moreso from the everyday life of today's youth. And this is where it excels where so many other games fails.
This is an interactive story about friendship, love, life and death, choices and consequences, creativity and identity. It has emotional depth like few stories have. Characters that feel real, with down to earth and realistic dialogues that gives the piece a grounded and real feel. And we're talking about time travel here. You will fall in love with its characters and their lives. You will feel each struggle with intensity and urgency, in great part due to the impeccable voice acting. The story propels you forward to the next heatbreak with a perfect pacing that strings you along and never feels wrong.
It's not to say that Life Is Strange is a perfect game. The story could've been more profound and in a way, less predictable. The ending could've been less telegraphed. The lip sync could've been so much better. But put against it's qualities, these become squabbles.
If you have just one game to play this year, make it Life Is Strange. It will leave you in awe.

What would I do, if I could do it all over again? What if I could change the past, alter the very fabric of time for my own purposes. What would happen then? There's bound to be repercussions to such a violation of physics. Even a minor change could magnify over time to create the unexpected.
This is the idea behind the storyline of Life is Strange, an episodic adventure in the style of Telltale's games. A refinement over the formula well-worn by telltale in gameplay and design, Life Is Strange offers over the course of 5 episodes of about two hours each a story themed around concepts taken from chaos theory, but moreso from the everyday life of today's youth. And this is where it excels where so many other games fails.
This is an interactive story about friendship, love, life and death, choices and consequences, creativity and identity. It has emotional depth like few stories have. Characters that feel real, with down to earth and realistic dialogues that gives the piece a grounded and real feel. And we're talking about time travel here. You will fall in love with its characters and their lives. You will feel each struggle with intensity and urgency, in great part due to the impeccable voice acting. The story propels you forward to the next heatbreak with a perfect pacing that strings you along and never feels wrong.
It's not to say that Life Is Strange is a perfect game. The story could've been more profound and in a way, less predictable. The ending could've been less telegraphed. The lip sync could've been so much better. But put against it's qualities, these become squabbles.
If you have just one game to play this year, make it Life Is Strange. It will leave you in awe.

Review after completion of Episode 4 for the PC: (~SPOILERS~ Obviously)
Life Is Strange is a game that, on the surface, is incredibly pretnetious.  The protagonist, Max is a Hipster Mary-Sue.  She also has a unique power that lets her sometimes rewind time, in order to fix mistakes, or to gain access to areas without being detected (as well as other powers that are introduced in later episodes).  Her best friend Chloe appears to be a stereotype of teenage rebellion.  Together, they try to solve the disappearance of Chloe’s friend, Rachel Amber.
However, below the surface, there is a shocking amount of depth that is introduced in later episodes.  The emotional reaction the series has garnered from me shows me that all the stupid surface drama was intentional, and the subtleties allowed me to have such a response to the game.
Do not get me wrong, I did enjoy the first 2 episodes.  While I found it pretentious, I enjoyed the art style, the setting, and found the characters, for the most part, engaging to interact with.  Max’s rewind ability never felt gimmicky because the developers spent a lot of effort making it seem useful as opposed to just a “cool mechanic”.
However, the game really surprised me with the events that turned Episode 3, and the beginning of Episode 4, into a truly complex work of art.  The character Chloe, despite her appearing as a walking stereotype, begins to show a lot of depth, especially regarding the death of her father.  There are moments sprinkled in the first 2 episodes, but it becomes apparent towards the middle of the episode how much her father’s death has truly affected her.  It is done in a really authentic, believable way.
This is when Max discovers a new ability.  She is able to temporarily transport through a photograph and is able to alter history by preventing the death of Chloe’s father.  Once she is brought back into present time, it becomes apparent how much her decisions have changed her life.  Unfortunately, while Chloe is surrounded by both loving parents, in this timeline, she is permanently paralyzed because of a car accident, the same thing that killed her father in the previous timeline.
This is where the game truly got me.  I didn’t cry, or even tear up, but just the way the developers handle this is perfect.  They never overplay their hand, they simply present the situation as it is, and allows the player to truly understand what their decision has done.  Regardless of your efforts, your friend’s life is destroyed in some way.  Coming from a game that’s entire premise is built around decision making, it gives the player this hopeless feeling that they cannot do anything to truly save “Chloe”, and I think it’s masterfully done.  In the end, you are faced with a hard decision to either end Chloe’s misery, or to not accept your friend’s pleas for help.  It’s gut wrenching.
In the end, you are able to revert back to the timeline in which Chloe is alive and healthy, but the time you spent with Chloe paralyzed has forever changed Chloe to me, in a complex way that makes me feel more connected to her.  Throughout the game Max consistently talks about never leaving Chloe, and by the end of the situation, the player truly feels as if they cannot leave her as well.
After those emotionally devastating events, you are thrust into a full on murder mystery.  The second half of Episode 4 pieces together a lot of missing clues revolving around Rachel’s disappearance.    It is enthralling, and pretty much comes to an “a-ha!” moment where everything comes together and you finally think you know the truth.  Until the ending where everything you thought you knew comes crumbling down at the last moment.
Unfortunately, the game is not immune from some legitimate criticisms.  The animation is, for the most part, pretty good.  However there is a lot of polishing that could be done.  There are issues with clipping and some of the textures are pretty half-heartedly done.  The hair textures are also incredibly static and could really use some work.  Graphically, my biggest issue is the lip movement.  There is literally almost zero syncing between the dialogue and the actual movement of their lips.  It’s distracting to the point where I choose to read the text instead of watching their mouths move because it’s just really off.  On top of graphics, I have been waiting for something to really take Max off the pedastool of perfection.  She is nice, kind, sweet, dorky (but not too dorky), shy (but possesses amazing social skills).  I like her, but I want some genuine flaws that make her feel believable.
These issues fail in comparison to the overwhelming quality of the game though.  Definitely recommended to anyone who loves story driven games.

Short version: A good game, but not the GOTY people are claiming it is. Worth the asking price of 20 dollars, even more worth it on sale.
Long version:
Life is Strange is an episodic story-based game with branching paths based upon your choices. It's one of those Heavy Rain or Until Dawn type games, where there's not much actual gameplay, but is instead essentially a very long, interactive movie.
In it, you play as Max Caufield, a teenager who gets to go to a fancy shmancy art school in her hometown, who suddenly finds herself with the ability to rewind time after seeing her old best friend get shot in the bathroom. She gets these visions of her hometown being wiped out by a giant tornado, so she has to try to figure out a way to make everybody not die. Schooltime drama gradually shifts into a much larger plot as Max tries to reconnect with her old friend who almost got murdered, solving a mystery of a missing person, conspiracies, all that fun stuff.
The gameplay is what you'd expect from this kind of game. Walk to the next plot point, press buttons when you get a turn to speak, and what you just said will change what other people just said. There aren't even quick-time events, reducing the challenge from "minimal" to straight-up "non-existant." There's no penalty to rewinding time, so you don't even have to worry about you making a wrong choice (Aside from one important conversation at the end of Episode 2.) The only challenge comes from the rare puzzle, of which there are about 2 in the first 4 episodes.
The voice acting is, for the most part, great. Every character is very well acted, but special mention goes to Chloe. Her actor's being nominated for some award for her role, and I think she absolutely deserves it. It's a shame that the voice acting is so good, because the dialogue is not nearly worthy of ther preformances.
Now, Dontnod is a French company. But, this game takes place in very recent America, 2013 to be exact, focusing on two teenagers for the most part. The dialogue is often very poorly written, trying to use teenage vernacular and failing miserably. Examples include one "stoner kid" at a party reffering to marijuana as "Dank Kush," or the previously mentioned Chloe dropping "Hella" every other sentence.
The characters are also very one-note for the most part. In an interview, the game's writers claimed that they "intentionally set up classic high-school character cliches so they could subvert them later," but thus far there hasn't been a lot of expanding in the character department. Max is a geek, Chloe is a punk, Victoria is the ♥♥♥♥♥, so on and so forth.
Miscillanious thoughts:
-The game's art style is gorgeous.
-The soundtrack is pretty good, especially the game's main theme. Primarily composed of acoustic guitars.
When all is said and done, I'd probably give Life is Strange a 6.5 - 7 / 10. I feel like I ragged on it a lot in this review, but I have actually enjoyed my time with it, and I'm excited for Episode 5's release, which is 5 days away at the time of writing.

Accompanied with the gorgeous art direction, enhanced by its fitting music, the atmosphere of the setting and story truly make a wonderful and unique experience.
This game is one I think anyone needs to experience at least once, but is also one of the few, if not the only game, I can say I was more engaged and excited while playing a second time. Life Is Strange. Rarely has a game ever had a title that contained so much truth! But life for Max, our protagonist, is even stranger than most. It's not enough that she has to cope with moving back to the hometown she left five years ago, studying, preparing her entry into a photography contest and putting up with seemingly every high school cliché character (don't worry, that's just the first impression of the characters, there's a lot more depth than that) but she also discovers she has the power to rewind time... just after witnessing a girl get shot.
The controls are a simple and very effective modernisation of the traditional point and click adventure games and should appeal both to those familiar with the classics and newcomers to the genre.
Unlike many traditional adventure games there's no insane puzzles that defy logic or have you tearing hair out. On the flipside it'd be fair to say that the puzzles are too easy. However the difficulty isn't in the puzzles, it's in the decisions, since you'll find yourself caring about the characters in the game and the consequences your choices will have for them.
Your rewind power allows you to undo decisions you're not happy with, but you only get to see the short term consequences before it becomes too late to undo.
If you're a fan of story driven games, classic adventure games and/or games with genuine emotional impact, you owe it to yourself to give Life Is Strange a try.

Life is Strange is a great example of modern adventure games, where the experience is more about your version of the story than just solving puzzles in a linear plotline. It does a good job of making you feel like you can influence the story and in writing it's characters three dimensionally.
It can be a hard line to walk to write young adults who feel their age, in some ways even more than children. But the game managed this, in several cases making me think back to when I was Max's age. It added an extra level of not-quite-nostalgia, despite a few cringe inducing attempts at teen slang in the first episode. Her classmates- and even Max herself - can be mean, but they weren't in a cartoonish villain way. And that added to them feeling more like teenagers, and like people. Throughout the game they do a good job of fleshing out Max herself, important since you are clearly playing as her and not some player avatar.
The game does have puzzles using Max's time abilities and a few with minor detective work, which overall I enjoyed. They seemed a good balance of requiring thought, but no sudden difficulty spikes. There was one or two that felt like they shouldn't have needed rewinding, but they were easy to handwave as Max's fault. And I did really enjoy that Max uses her rewind powers for some pretty dumb stuff, and overall is not an overly-competent protagonist the moment she gets her powers.
I would recommend this game even to those not traditionally interested in story focused game, my only real hesitation would be some of the subject matter if someone is sensitive to things like abuse and suicide. Otherwise I think this game would surprise most people with how quickly it worms its way in.

This game starts off and finishes strong! At first, the controls are confusing (You have to hit the word rather than the object you want to interact with, which turned me off and confused me at first.) but are easy to adapt to. The plot is killer, there are a lot of small details that keep you entertained if you're into the characters and their quirks, and there are a lot of ways to keep you busy, adding hours of gameplay.
A few things that I feel are negative in this game is the dialogue, skipping conversations, and graphics on lower-end PCs. After playing through the entire game, I wasn't fully impressed as I have been with other titles affiliated with Square Enix in this aspect. The character interactions feel slower than their real-world counterparts, and I feel that turns me off as a player, seeing that a lot of this game is so dialogue-centric. Also, since the conversations get repetitive if you rewind to fix a choice you made, I would skip pretty often, causing me to break the cutscene by putting it in super slow motion or Max just stands there with characters frozen or stuff floating in the air and have no way to fix it unless I reload from the last checkpoint (And that is SO inconvienent.). Finally, my brand new laptop doesn't run the game very well (Asus w/ an Intel Pentium processor - 2.16 GHz; 4GB RAM; 64 bit running Windows 8.1) for some reason, though I run the game on low settings and 800 x 600 resolution and it still lags a bit.
Long story short / tl;dr: The game is great, but there are a few flaws that get in the way of having a truly great experience, but it is overall a great game.
Also: WARNING; if you are prone to feels, DO NOT play this game. It is a total feels trip.

There are very few games that I'm not sure I can do justice in a review. Life is Strange just happens to be one of them.
I've played all sorts of games of different genres. Action, RPG's, Puzzles, ect. Choice and Consequence games are bit different and still have to capture that emotional connection to characters that the 8-32 bit era of gaming did. Awesome graphics are more commonplace now, so the time is ripe for great storytelling to rise again and I was pretty impressed with Life is Strange so far.
Now the first episode, without revealing much starts off with what seems like typical teen drama. Some of the characters fall into the usual stereotypes both by appearance and personality. So right away I wasn't super impressed. However as the game revealed more of itself I started to suspect this was done on purpose and things were much deeper than what they first appeared.
The game doesn't shy away from profanity, drugs, and violence, and this actually makes the storytelling more believable. It touches some sensitive issues with what the characters deal with and they grow on you. At certain points of the game I'd had to pause and step away for a moment because of how emotionally impacting it can be. This is the very thing most modern games just fall short of these days.
If there was any game made in the spirit of Donnie Darko or The Butterfly Effect, this would be it. Episode 5 is still on the horizon, but I've enjoyed 1-4 so far. I really hope Dontnod creates more titles. Working with them is probably one of the better choices Square Enix has made in recent years. Looking forward to more.

This game starts off and finishes strong! At first, the controls are confusing (You have to hit the word rather than the object you want to interact with, which turned me off and confused me at first.) but are easy to adapt to. The plot is killer, there are a lot of small details that keep you entertained if you're into the characters and their quirks, and there are a lot of ways to keep you busy, adding hours of gameplay.
A few things that I feel are negative in this game is the dialogue, skipping conversations, and graphics on lower-end PCs. After playing through the entire game, I wasn't fully impressed as I have been with other titles affiliated with Square Enix in this aspect. The character interactions feel slower than their real-world counterparts, and I feel that turns me off as a player, seeing that a lot of this game is so dialogue-centric. Also, since the conversations get repetitive if you rewind to fix a choice you made, I would skip pretty often, causing me to break the cutscene by putting it in super slow motion or Max just stands there with characters frozen or stuff floating in the air and have no way to fix it unless I reload from the last checkpoint (And that is SO inconvienent.). Finally, my brand new laptop doesn't run the game very well (Asus w/ an Intel Pentium processor - 2.16 GHz; 4GB RAM; 64 bit running Windows 8.1) for some reason, though I run the game on low settings and 800 x 600 resolution and it still lags a bit.
Long story short / tl;dr: The game is great, but there are a few flaws that get in the way of having a truly great experience, but it is overall a great game.
Also: WARNING; if you are prone to feels, DO NOT play this game. It is a total feels trip.

Overall a very absorbing game through Episode 4 (5 hasn't been released yet.)
The story is the high point of the game, full of unexpected twists and turns. There are only a few parts where it seems the story was "stretched" by the addition of more-or-less meaningless "fluff," but overall I looked forward to see what new development each day's playing session would bring.
Another brilliant design feature is the ability to replay specific episodes without revising already-made decisions just to pick up any collectibles you may have missed during the first playthrough of that episode. Brillliant concept and well implemented in this game.
In my opinion, however, the excellence of the story and "collectible replay" is let down by three flaws:
1. Inexplicably rudimentary, crude-looking graphics- 1980 all over again! I saw several excellent-looking game graphics online (check the top of the page at
for an example) that I at first thought were screenshots. These online graphics showed a much higher level of detail (note Max's nuanced, feathery hair and clear, vibrant eyes in the online example I cited above) than what was obtainable in-game. Despite several tries to set in-game graphics to a higher level of detail, they were already set to the maximum the game allows, but everyone's hair looked thick, blocky, static, monolithic and untextured... as did pretty much every other graphic in the game. The depiction of eyes in this game is particularly washed out, dead and "cloudy" looking, reminding me of my grandmother's eyes, cataracts and all. I suppose DontNod was going for an "artsy" look, but the 3rd-Grade-coloring-book graphics really eliminated any sense of immersion I tried to attain.
2. This game is purportedly set in the state of Oregon, which is in the U.S. However, there are some giveaways that this is a European-developed game. The trains, in particular, which form the backdrop as well as a plot device for much of an entire episode, are clearly modeled on 4-wheel freight cars that resemble the Euro-style "wagons" and not any train that has run on U.S. rails in the past 100 years- almost all U.S. freight cars have 8 wheels, 4 at each end. Then we have the Blackwell Transportation School Bus, with its 2-axle rear end. This simply isn't a design commonly found in the U.S. The only commonly-seen dual-rear-axle buses in the U.S. are the over-the-road designs used by Greyhound and other large cross-country bus operators, but ALL of these dual-rear-axle buses have blunt front ends- "cab over engine" rather than the engine under a long hood out in front of the driver. School buses pretty much NEVER use the dual-rear-axle design because they are not designed to haul enough weight to need 2 axles in back. Yes, these are nit-picky flaws... but such gratuitous incongruities greatly detract from immersion (for anyone in the U.S. at least) and could have been easily avoided simply by going online and Googling "US freight train images" (here's one from 1926:
and "US school bus images" (here's a typical large U.S. school bus:
.
3. I played this game on a PC using an Xbox controller. I found that the movement controls had a "soft-lag." Joystick movement and "look" inputs don't *quite* produce the expected movements, or produce the expected movements after a half-second or so lag... this movement and look-direction infidelity actually made me dizzy a couple of times due to the "cognitive dissonance" between what I expected my control inputs to do and what they actually did. Also, I always invert  my Y axis controls, probably due to my experience as a pilot- it just feels more natural to me to pull back to look up and vice-versa. However, the Y-axis inversion worked fine in the main game, but not in the context views when the player "focuses in" on something to manipulate it. A perfect example of this is in Episode 4, where the mini-views of the evidence board require that you "zoom in and look around" to select among 6-8 objects on the board. Y-axis inversion reverted to not-inverted and was extremely disconcerting.
So, on a scale of 1-10, here are my ratings:
Story: 9
Graphics: 3
Controls: 4
Playability: 6
Replay Value: Unknown until Episode 5 is released
Overall Game Rating: 6/10
