Pros:
Fully voiced (and appropriately voiced imo!)
Fascinating story
Player make choices
Short/long-ish term consequences of choices
Easily accessible list of choices made
Easy to obtain achievements
Cons:
Limited skip feature of previous choices
Section in episode for redoing choices not readily apparent
Episodic game can break immersion of story
Ending(s)
Maxine, or Max as she is called by her friends, is the protagonist in this interactive drama. The gameplay reminds me a bit of Heavy Rain, which is a great thing, there needs to be more games like it around! The big thing of games like these is the immersion of the player into the world and situation that the characters are in. As such the voice acting and music greatly influence the degree which this is done and LifeIsStrange delivers on both counts. I've sat just listening to the title screen music for some while writing this, it's quite nice :) One of the things that I enjoyed most in LifeIsStrange is the main character comments on things as you interact with the world. You can click to look at a poster and she will make a comment that helps develop/reinforce the player's understanding of her as a person. In addition, despite a guy, I didn't feel awkward while playing the game with exception in a few cases (tampon dispenser anyone?).
Although I still throughly enjoyed the game, the last episode (Episode 5) is one that still holds a lot of contention among players. I agree with many others that it didn't quite live up to my expectations of what they promised to deliver (Mass Effect 3 anybody?) but it still was enjoyable overall. As a result of how the game ended however, I do not see myself eager to replay the game anytime soon if at all.
The one thing I would recommend new players to do is to try and play out the choices you made the first time around. It greatly increase the level of immersion into the story playing this way. Although the skip feature is limited to the dialogue choices chosen in the current play session of the current chapter, hopefully they may remedy this at some point.
In conclusion, I still recommend the game but wait for it to go down in price. They shoulud also come up with a new genre for this type of game. I put forward "Interactive Fable", anyone else agree?

Despite several tries to set in-game graphics to a higher level of detail, they were already set to the maximum the game allows, but everyone's hair looked thick, blocky, static, monolithic and untextured... as did pretty much every other graphic in the game. The depiction of eyes in this game is particularly washed out, dead and "cloudy" looking, reminding me of my grandmother's eyes, cataracts and all. I suppose DontNod was going for an "artsy" look, but the 3rd-Grade-coloring-book graphics really eliminated any sense of immersion I tried to attain.
2. This game is purportedly set in the state of Oregon, which is in the U.S. However, there are some giveaways that this is a European-developed game. The trains, in particular, which form the backdrop as well as a plot device for much of an entire episode, are clearly modeled on 4-wheel freight cars that resemble the Euro-style "wagons" and not any train that has run on U.S. rails in the past 100 years- almost all U.S. freight cars have 8 wheels, 4 at each end. Then we have the Blackwell Transportation School Bus, with its 2-axle rear end. This simply isn't a design commonly found in the U.S. The only commonly-seen dual-rear-axle buses in the U.S. are the over-the-road designs used by Greyhound and other large cross-country bus operators, but ALL of these dual-rear-axle buses have blunt front ends- "cab over engine" rather than the engine under a long hood out in front of the driver. School buses pretty much NEVER use the dual-rear-axle design because they are not designed to haul enough weight to need 2 axles in back. Yes, these are nit-picky flaws... but such gratuitous incongruities greatly detract from immersion (for anyone in the U.S. at least) and could have been easily avoided simply by going online and Googling "US freight train images" (here's one from 1926:
and "US school bus images" (here's a typical large U.S. school bus:
.
3. I played this game on a PC using an Xbox controller. I found that the movement controls had a "soft-lag." Joystick movement and "look" inputs don't *quite* produce the expected movements, or produce the expected movements after a half-second or so lag... this movement and look-direction infidelity actually made me dizzy a couple of times due to the "cognitive dissonance" between what I expected my control inputs to do and what they actually did. Also, I always invert  my Y axis controls, probably due to my experience as a pilot- it just feels more natural to me to pull back to look up and vice-versa. However, the Y-axis inversion worked fine in the main game, but not in the context views when the player "focuses in" on something to manipulate it. A perfect example of this is in Episode 4, where the mini-views of the evidence board require that you "zoom in and look around" to select among 6-8 objects on the board. Y-axis inversion reverted to not-inverted and was extremely disconcerting.
So, on a scale of 1-10, here are my ratings:
Story: 9
Graphics: 3
Controls: 4
Playability: 6
Replay Value: Unknown until Episode 5 is released
Overall Game Rating: 6/10

Life is Strange is the best episodic adventure game I have ever played and I have played just about all of them. Dontnod Entertainment, a small developer based in Paris France, has taken the episodic genre to new levels of excellence in story, character development, art style, music and soundtrack, so let me discuss those topics.
Story: Life is Strange is about a girl age 18, Max Caulfield, who wants to study to become a professional photographer. She learns that a school in her hometown, Blackwell Academy, has hired one of her favorite professional photographers Mark Jefferson, and she decides she needs to move back to her hometown to enroll in his classes. That is the normal part about this story and nothing else in the story can be considered "normal" in any way shape or form. Each new episode takes the story in a surprising direction that the player will be astounded by, and never able to predict which way the story will go. This is practically unheard of in game stories because most of them are so predictable and cliche by the time you get to the end of the game you know exactly what will happen. Life is Strange is 100% different in that category.
Character development: The main characters in this game are so well done that you will form emotional bonds to them and if something happens to these characters you will feel it as though it is happening to you. Be prepared because you WILL NEED a box of tissues for your tears close by in LiS, and that is a guarantee. Nearly every single person I have conversed with on the Steam forum for LiS has admitted to shedding tears and lots of them, yes the characters and the story are that good rivaling even great best seller novels I have read, and I have read thousands of novels.
Art style: The art style in Life is Strange is not photorealistic like many games now days attempt to achieve instead it is very stylish in the way the Dontnod team has done it and it is perfect for a game like this. Along with the amazing camera work in LiS I think it deserves awards in all three categories I have mentioned so far. All the art in the game is hand drawn and hand painted and it really does show in the finished product, in fact I have a folder on my PC with about 400 screenshots from LiS that I run on a 5 minute timer for my desktop background. I finished playing LiS back in October of 2015 when the final episode released and I STILL have that folder running as my desktop background the art is amazing!
Music/soundtrack: The music in Life is Strange is modern day artists and one of them Syd Matters, the Dontnod team worked closely with the lead person in that band Jonathan Morali and he adapted some of their songs specifically for LiS. Because they use current artists is adds yet another level of realism to the game because you are hearing songs that young adults age 16 to 25 would be listening to in their every day lives. The music selection also really sets the mood for the game and again it deserves an award for the excellence and quality.
About the only thing I would mention as a "con" to Life is Strange is that the lip sync quality is not very good. However in interviews with the Dontnod team they said they spent the games budget in areas they felt would better serve to make the game a work of quality and the story, characters, art style, and soundtrack are so good that you will hardly notice the poor lip sync, at least that was the case for me playing LiS.
If you are a gamer and you don't have this title in your library you have missed out on the best game of 2015 without a doubt and likely one of the best games of all times, yes it is that good.
Edit: I wrote this review when the game was only at three episodes released and though the 4th episode was as good as the previous three, episode 5 the final was not as good as the rest of the game. Dontnod did not do the endings justice to the story in that there was more then one choice at the end and those choices were not equal in length and quality with one of them being much, much better in length and quality then the other was. Both endings were good however one was shorter and not as good as the other, this made for a lack luster ending for me because I preferred the choice of the shorter ending and I would have liked to have seen it show more then it did.
Please note that though I thought the ending could have been better it in no way makes Life is Strange a failure or a bad game, in fact it remains my favorite game for the last decade and likely my favorite game of all time.

Each new episode takes the story in a surprising direction that the player will be astounded by, and never able to predict which way the story will go. This is practically unheard of in game stories because most of them are so predictable and cliche by the time you get to the end of the game you know exactly what will happen. Life is Strange is 100% different in that category.
Character development: The main characters in this game are so well done that you will form emotional bonds to them and if something happens to these characters you will feel it as though it is happening to you. Be prepared because you WILL NEED a box of tissues for your tears close by in LiS, and that is a guarantee. Nearly every single person I have conversed with on the Steam forum for LiS has admitted to shedding tears and lots of them, yes the characters and the story are that good rivaling even great best seller novels I have read, and I have read thousands of novels.
Art style: The art style in Life is Strange is not photorealistic like many games now days attempt to achieve instead it is very stylish in the way the Dontnod team has done it and it is perfect for a game like this. Along with the amazing camera work in LiS I think it deserves awards in all three categories I have mentioned so far. All the art in the game is hand drawn and hand painted and it really does show in the finished product, in fact I have a folder on my PC with about 400 screenshots from LiS that I run on a 5 minute timer for my desktop background. I finished playing LiS back in October of 2015 when the final episode released and I STILL have that folder running as my desktop background the art is amazing!
Music/soundtrack: The music in Life is Strange is modern day artists and one of them Syd Matters, the Dontnod team worked closely with the lead person in that band Jonathan Morali and he adapted some of their songs specifically for LiS. Because they use current artists is adds yet another level of realism to the game because you are hearing songs that young adults age 16 to 25 would be listening to in their every day lives. The music selection also really sets the mood for the game and again it deserves an award for the excellence and quality.
About the only thing I would mention as a "con" to Life is Strange is that the lip sync quality is not very good. However in interviews with the Dontnod team they said they spent the games budget in areas they felt would better serve to make the game a work of quality and the story, characters, art style, and soundtrack are so good that you will hardly notice the poor lip sync, at least that was the case for me playing LiS.
If you are a gamer and you don't have this title in your library you have missed out on the best game of 2015 without a doubt and likely one of the best games of all times, yes it is that good.
Edit: I wrote this review when the game was only at three episodes released and though the 4th episode was as good as the previous three, episode 5 the final was not as good as the rest of the game. Dontnod did not do the endings justice to the story in that there was more then one choice at the end and those choices were not equal in length and quality with one of them being much, much better in length and quality then the other was. Both endings were good however one was shorter and not as good as the other, this made for a lack luster ending for me because I preferred the choice of the shorter ending and I would have liked to have seen it show more then it did.
Please note that though I thought the ending could have been better it in no way makes Life is Strange a failure or a bad game, in fact it remains my favorite game for the last decade and likely my favorite game of all time.

Hello, I have written a couple of reviews of games before but not like this. It is because I feel that Life Is Strange deserves a review because the game is just so well made.
The game starts with the player getting introduced to "Maxine" Caulfield or how she wants to be called Max. She is the game's protagonist. She just moved back to her old hometown Arcadia Bay in Oregon. She has not been there since she moved away when she was 13 years old, along with her family to Seattle. She entered Blackwell Academy which is a fine art school with the help of a scholarship. It all begins with that she dreams that she is at a lighthouse, and its dark out there suddenly an accident occurs, and something is about to hit her when she wakes up in a classroom. She thinks that it is strange because this dream was so realistic. So goes out to the bathroom trying to understand it all, when she hears a boy entering talking to himself. Max is hidden behind a wall so nobody can see her. She takes a picture of a butterfly that comes flying in, and at that moment a girl with blue hair comes walking in and talks with the boy. The girl insults him and he takes out a gun and shoots her. Max screams and stretchs out her hand trying to stop the bullet, but in some weird way she rewinds time itself. That is the whole idea of Life Is Strange. There is also so much happening in the game that you as a player will see. Therefore you will notice that changing time will have fatal consequences when tampering with the past and future. That was just a little short summary of the start of the game story.
The people in the game:
Max:
Max is the game's protagonist and we get to know a lot about her. You get told with she thinks about the people around her in the school, and also how she feels about how people are treated there. The parents also show how much their love their daughter and how proud they are of her getting into such a prestigious art school. They also form our perception of Max as a human being. Max as a person is smart and friendly. She only want whats best for people if you choose it that way.
Chole Price:
She is Max's best friend when Max was living in Arcadia Bay. They were always together and that is shown with flashbacks, pictures and when these two meet each other you can tell that these two have have been friends for a very long time. The two characters have a connection with each other that cam be experienced because they have known each other for so long. Chole is fearless and cheeky that's not how Max remembers her as. But Chole has not had it easy after Max went away. She felt abandoned by her best friend in one of the most difficult times in her life. But Chole also manages to be an irreplaceable person in the game that you just want to hear more about, and be with when playing as Max.
The game's graphics:
The graphic for the game is perfect for a game with that price and even more top notch. The graphics perfectly match the atmosphere, and the whole environment is laid out so the user can gaze at it. The graphics look beautiful and the way it is made just provide a greater value to the game.
The game's decision and consequences of time rewind:
The game makes use of choices where you as a player have to put yourself into different people, and how you intend to behave towards them. But you can go back in time and make the mistakes you feel you have made changed. But you have to make a decision. This system is why i fell for the game because you can explore different outcomes in the dialogues, and try them all. There is a time when something happens to one of Max's friends at school that makes you have to had explored a place and try to talk the person from doing what she is doing. Here I was needed to take a break as the game crept under my skin. I was struck by all the emotions running through you when such an incident occurs. It just hits you so well that it all most feel realistic with what is going on in the game, and you also feel so much for the characters in the game, you care for them. The script is made so spectacular and magnifiecnet.
The game's grade:
I give the game 10 as a unified whole. If you find it interesting to rewind time and like a game with deep characters, and a good, well-written story that captures you and also have desicions with consequences. Then i can recommend this game for you.

Episode Reviews as I play them.
Episode 1 : So far not so good.  Ill chalk it up to setup syndrome, however, the first episode should really pull you in.  I was getting Gone Home flashbacks with all the pointless item inspection.  I feel that games like this need to really compensate for a lack of interactivity with a very compelling storyline and/or character development.  Walking Dead had both. This does not really have either.  I feel like im stuck in a teen movie at the moment.  The major mechanic (turning back time) could have been interesting, but its telegraphed everytime its needed and really only serves to give you endless mulligans which takes away any chance of making a mistake in time sensitive situations.  I received this code for free, so Im going to stick with it.  Lets hope the rest gets better.
Episode 2 : This episode is an improvement on the first in a couple ways.  1)They found a way to use the time bending mechanic in more interesting ways, requiring you to actualy pay attention to events as they unfold 2) Decisions from episode 1 seemed to finally pay off in this episode, and there were a few new decisions that really had me deliberate the decision i was about to make.  Seeing the negative result of previous decisions added even more weight in how I thought about approaching new ones.   On the negative side, the plot didnt seem to move forward much in this episode.  In fact, you really learn nothing new about the central mystery.  Overall, Im still not able to recommend this game after 2 episodes.

For starters, you get to relive your high school years complete with catty rich ♥♥♥♥♥, cheerleaders, nerds, jocks, and creepy artist dude. Life is Strange (LIS) takes place in a remote Pacific Northwest town, Arcadia Bay. You get to play as Max, an average social outcast, who wants to become a photographer. Shortly after her arrival at her new school as a high school senior, she develops "rewind" powers where she can travel back in time.
LIS plays like a standard investigative point and click adventure, and despite the danger of a time travel cliché, LIS definitely delivers. The story is phenemonal and better than many blockbuster movies. The voice acting is also impressive. The lipsynching looks a bit strange and off, but take it how you will. I think you'd be missing out if you held off on buying this based on a lipsynching issue.
LIS is clever in the usage of rewind/time travel, because the power comes with a finite limit. You can only rewind to the beginning of each zone/area you are currently in. So while you can redo all your actions/choices in a single area, you have to replay from previous zones if you have any regrets. There are also some areas where you cannot rewind and must "live with" your decisions. At the same time, your choices do have impact on the game, more so than in other games. You still follow the same overarching story, but the details of the story differ based on the choices you made previously, as well as how the other characters see Max.
One of the things that was kind of a let down is when you replay scenes (which are nicely divided by zones/areas) for collectible mode or for other reasons, you cannot skip cutscenes. You can only skip when you rewind and play through it for the second time in that playthrough. That means if you miss a photo, you will be sitting through the cutscene all over again. Not a big drawback, but it was kind of annoying when I went back right after I finished the area just to grab the photo.
The puzzles are pretty cool and involve everything from investigating clues to remembering details and of course, using time travel to make life easier for Max and possibly other friends throughout the story. I think the characters are really fleshed out and multifaceted that really add to the experience of the game. LIS would not be the same without them or its amazing story. There are highs and lows, love and loss, and LIS is a must-have for a gamer's collection.

Alright, reviewing Life Is Strange.
First off I would like to say that I usually watch playthroughs of story driven games on youtube (Last of Us, Uncharted, etc.). But as this game have choices that matter, even if the main plot stay the same, that wouldn’t quite cut it. I would even go so far as to call this an RPG as you play the role of Max.
So I decided I would play it myself so I’d get the maximum impact of the choices. There was one small snag though, it was episodic and not even halfway done. As I hate waiting for the next part I held off until it was more complete. Que this friday and the sale when I finally bought it.
Secondly I want to put the scores above the review itself as it could be considered kinda spoilery.
Gameplay: 7/10 This isn't all that important in a storydriven game like this but there are things I found annoying and there was pontential for more.
Graphics: 8.5/10 It looks good and I like the style, but there were small things that annoyed me. I'm also debating whether or not they should have made it more realistic.
Story: 9.5/10 So far it's been amazing and I expect that i'll be a 10 when it's done. I would also like to give a bonus point for the internal dialogue of the main character, all to often the character is a blank slate when it comes to RPGs but the characters have had a life before you took over and Life Is Strange gives character to Max while leaving the choices to the player.
All in all I would give it 9.5/10 With the motivation that the story makes up for mistakes in the other categories.
Anyway review, I’ll try to keep it vague but as I said it’s kinda spoilery.
The game starts out with a playable prologue that establishes the main character and introduces you to the story. I found it to be a extremely effective hook for the story as it didn’t take more than a few minutes for me to get sucked into the story, and this was before the main gameplay mechanic was introduced.
After the prologue transitions into the first episode the main gameplay mechanic is introduced step by step. First you’ll get to know what it is without being able to control it yourself, but moments later you are in control as both you and the main character experiments with this new ability and learning it’s uses. The rest of the episode serves to further establish the world and it’s characters and gives you a few different choices, both major and minor, that will have an effect on the world.
With the tutorials out of the way the second episode can focus more on the story and world building, but not before it teaches you that you need to pay attention to the details. This was also the first time the weight of my choices became apparent as the stakes rose quite sharply.
Episode three further improves your understanding of your abilities (or at least it did for me) and introduces another side of the ability that seems to be limited to story purposes, a bit of a shame since it could have been utilized in the rest of the game as well. The story keeps going with the risks and weight of your decisions increasing.
In episode four the story is still on a high note since the end of episode three and an early choice left me speechless as I struggled to make a decision. Afterwards the fact that you need to pay attention is hammered in once again as information you have collected throughout the other episodes come into play. And as episode five haven’t been released it all ends on a cliffhanger which make me restless as a wait for the conclusion.

Life is Strange, AKA when videogames meet art.
No really, slightly less than a game and slightly more than  a movie, Life is Strange is a total masterpiece.
Lets go through the Pros and Cons:
PROS
+The bond it creates with the main character, Max: it's absolutely astonishing how you find yourself teaming up with the main character as the plot unravels, trying to understand her thoughts and anticipate the next ones. You will love the experience and her for sure.
+Graphics: the graphics have their own unique style. They fit very well with the plot and create an awesome atmosphere that will really get you into this game.
+Soundtrack: once again, the soundtrack suits perfectly the feeling this game gives you. It gets very dark-ish sometimes, exaclty as the game does.
+Setting: the setting is recreated as realisticly as it could get. You feel like you're actually dealing with American teenagers in a classic American school. They act, speak and think like they would in the real world.
+Character design: the design of the character couldn't be better. Even when a character represents a stereotype, it doesn't always act only accordingly to what you expect, and often you will eventually find out new information about them that will make you second guess.
+Gameplay: Life is Strange is definitely not you average point-and-click type of game. There are no complicated puzzles to be solved, which helps you get involved in the game from an emotional poin of view. The gameplay is very minimal, and I find the mechanics very well-thought for the plot.
CONS
-Facial expression and animations: this is the game's weak spot. It really sucks not to have good animations and next-to-no facial expressions, which you would expect from a very psychological kind of game. I personally think that this might be due to the low budget they had in the making of the game. The awesome scripture accounts a bit for that, though.
-Episodic structure: I find this to be a flaw in a game when every choice you make affects the future (and the past too, sometimes). It does not kinda feel suitable to the spirit of the game. Maybe this is low budget's fault again?
All in all, this is a great game. Don't expect some hardcore adrenalynic FPS action like CS:GO of course, nor mind-breaking seemingly unsolvable puzzles like Monkey Island or something that requires strategy and game sense. Life is Strange is not made to present you a challenge, it is made to make you think. It does require empathy and social skills though, i.e. the capability of getting in tune with the people you have to interact with in your everyday life and understand their thoughts: the ability of going back in time and re-think your choice does not helps you that much. Also, on the plus side, you'll pay 20 bucks for around 20 hours of play, which is great considering how much games cost nowadays and how few they offer. I'm really looking forward to a great ending in episode 5.
My personal vote is 9/10. You really must play this game.

Episode 1 Starts off by introducing you to the game, and is designed to make you see the effects of your choices. It starts a little strange, but as you go on through the game, you uncover puzzle pieces bit by bit, presenting a story that could be a reality. Life is Strange confronts issues with time travel, power/money, and evil, and uncovers events in a somewhat shocking and horrifying way at times.
It is designed to cause strong emotions in the player, and does so well; in this day of video games being normal and desensitivity, the only way for games to hit the gamer with emotions, is to force the player to see 'what could have been'. The only other game that I have played that compares is "Wolfenstein: The New Order", which presents what a world where Nazi's won WWII, and the horrors that could have been.
The game consistently follows a specific style of gameplay; you know what you're going to be getting from the first chapter onwards. There are some game mechanics that I think could have been worked on a bit better, such as the abiltity to 'space skip' dialogue (such as in collectible mode). (If you haven't heard dialogue in the game yet, you aren't able to skip it).
I have conflicting feelings about the achievements/photography. It is a bit repetitive and seems pointless, but at the same time the photography is vital to the story, and taking the photographs/completing the achievements may help players that have not done photography understand about the art of photography and how that relates to the story.
Overall, I'd give the game a 9.5/10; Thankfully, there were no bugs or crashes that I experienced, and the issues I have I mentioned above. The games environment is extremely well thought out in each scene, and has made this game a game that I identify as a "classic Square Enix game": Virtually bug-less, fun to play, and extremely well thought out. Over time, I have built a preference for specific developers, and I can easily say Square Enix is one of them.

The game, as a whole, is both dark and quaint, and the first time I saw it it filled me with nostaliga. I 100% recommend this to anyone willing to try out the first episode for the meager 5 bucks, and the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th episodes only build and improve, as DONTNOD is very receptive to criticism. A must play, and my GOTY for 2015.

Edit: Leaving the rest but after finishing all 5 episodes I can change this review to simply
"This is, hands down, the most beautiful game I have ever played."
Like playing a brilliant TV show.
This game absolutely nails the episodic "game as TV series" format. It's a perfect example of how this genre of games should be done. I find myself thinking (ok, borderline obsessing) about the game a lot between play sessions and wanting to dissect the character's actions with friends and coworkers in much the same way as I do with my favorite shows.
The plot is revealed slowly, allowing the player to gain an appreciation for the lore and backstory of the game as new plot points are revealed and complexity is added. Given that the "tutorial mission" introduces time travel and involves a murder attempt, this is no small feat. Invoking classic "light sci fi" mysteries (Twin Peaks, Veronica Mars, Donnie Darko, and Primer are clear, sometimes blatant, influences), this continues within and between episodes and keeps expanding on a tone that draws you ever deeper into the story.
Also like a great show, the character development is absolutely brilliant. While some of the characters are set up as quasi stereotypes (the quirky girl, the rebel, the quiet religious kid, the 'mean girls clique,' the hard♥♥♥♥♥veteran stepdad, etc...) the effect of this is to allow the player just enough ambiguity to make their interactions with these characters provide a sense that one is actually having an influence on the game world. As you interact with these characters and have the protagonist Max begin to develop relationships with them based on your decisions, you begin to truly care about these people and their lives.
Even though there is dialogue which was clearly written by people much older than the main characters, it always feels authentic in its substance if not always its phrasing and I find my eye rolling "no way an 18 year old girl would actually say that" moments more often than not serve to make the character easier to connect with. There are also moments where, as the player, I can see blatant foreshadowing and unspoken truths which the main character is mostly oblivious to. Again though, this usually serves to deepen my connection to the character and has me wanting to jump into the game world and talk to her.
The game's central storytelling device of choice and consequence really serves this beautifully as well. I find myself playing most situations as "what would she do" rather than "what do I want to do" and the feeling becomes one where you are guiding someone you care about along a perilous path rather that taking control of her life. Time travel and the ability to go back and make different decisions, rather than negating the importance of choice, actually adds gravity to those decisions; as in life sometimes there just is no "right answer". There are situations where you know what the immediate reaction to your decision is but going back and changing it opens new uncertainty and doubt that return to haunt you in later parts of the game. The result is that "trying both outcomes" increases the difficulty of the decision rather than eliminating it. While I initially found the "crap, which is the right decision?!!!" thing annoying, it very quickly won me over and has become one of my favorite aspects of the series.
While there are occasionally gameplay annoyances that initially seem to break immersion a bit, these mostly serve to give the player a chance to explore the world and organically discover the lore (i.e. Do I seriously need to walk around a junkyard looking for freaking empty bottles?! Oh, wait, this hut has a massive amount of subtle plot hints and significant character development? Cool!). Since most great TV shows have subplots that do little else but give the viewer a chance to "explore" a bit, this is certainly forgivable.
I have not yet completed all 5 episodes (ep 5 was not yet available at the time of this review) nor would I say every extant episode is perfect, but I have fallen in love with this game and would say it is one of the most surprising and enjoyable titles I've played in recent memory. The emotional and intellectual experience of Life Is Strange has me eager for more and desperately hoping this "show" has a very long run.

There really isn't a good way to describe the allure of Life is Strange. It's a mystery, but that's not why you should play it. It's a slice of life, but the term begs an impossible comparison to other slice of life media.
Life Is Strange is a game about choices, which is nothing new. The plot has caught some people off guard, but people who consume a lot of media won't find much here that hasn't been done before. I suspect that, following episode 5's release, I'm not going to be left with any profound thoughts about the nature of humanity or existance that change my view on anything. That's not what makes this game endearing.
The value here is in a whole that is profoundly superior to the sum of its parts. As a highly critical consumer, it is easy for small errors to tear me out of the experience. LIS has little errors in droves, to the point that listing them all would make me sound spiteful. There are animation quirks, sound issues, lip synching issues, and unintuitive puzzle mechanics. If I was reviewing any specific part of this game, I would give it a much lower score than I do now.
Thankfully, I get to review it as what it is. And what it is, in my mind, is an almost unnervingly personal take on the process of coming into one's own. While I started episode one getting hung up on every little flaw, that quickly began to melt away in the face of how alive the whole experience was. I wasn't being blown away by the gameplay, or the spectacle, but just by the fact that it all felt so real. The characters are filled with the personal desires and inner conflicts that allow one to manifest humanity. Every thing that you're allowed to interact with reflects so personally on Max and those around you that it's impossible not to empathize with the MC.
The art style and pacing feed into the feel brilliantly, with a flow that's surreal enough that your suspension of disbelief is hardly challenged. Even the songs that are chosen for the montage sections are lovingly placed, fitting in both feeling and lyrics.
8/10 is my tentative rating. When I finish episode 5, this has the potential to go up or down a point. Regardless of what happens, I will say that I enjoyed this game. Maybe more than I've enjoyed a game in a long time. And that feeling of simple pleasure is exactly why I think you should play Life Is Strange.

This is one of the most fabulous games I have played in a very long time.
Life Is Strange is a game that contains fantastic roleplay and decision making, the characters and atmoshpere are amazing and the story is beautifully written, so much mystery, plot twists and crazy moments you feel as if you yourself are in the game, boy what a thriller!.
Not to mention the soundtrack is absolutely great, it really fits into the moment of every occasion & truly gives you the chills and feels when you see and hear what is unfolding before you.
When I played this game I felt as if though I was Max Caufield (The Protagonist), as If though I was going through all she was going through, It was a fascinating journey and story. This was a  game where I felt like I was involved in the story Physically, Mentally and Emotionally, making friends, checking up on people, and learning the reverse time power I sustained, I would always find myself exploring, talking to everyone and inspecting everything, It is truely a magnificient journey and shows you how to cope with Life, when "Life is Strange".
Life Is Strange has Happy, Sad, Funny moments, its just an all around beautifully written and designed game, It will surely give you an emotional journey and reflect on one's self in certain occasions. This game touches upon the topic of family, friends, bullying, depression, suicide, happiness, love & what we truly fight for in life.
I love this game, and I truly enjoyed it from the very begging to the end.
In terms of 2015, this is by far the best game for me It certainly takes the cake bringing In every aspect of a beautiful story, though this game is no action shooter It will certainly keep you entertained and throughout will make you want to continue the game wondering what will happen next.
This is a pretty short review because honestly, I refuse to give any spoilers or feedback on the story, you must experience this masterpiece and embrace it yourself to truely understand my point of view on this emotional rollercoaster.
When a game can bring tears to my eyes, I know its all around beautiful.
UPDATE: (Spoilers)
Episode 5.... Grand Finale
The Ending was kind of depressing, and its sad that such a great game had a Bad/Mediocre Ending when it could have been way more. Your choices made throughout the game are thrown out the window to 2 Final Decisions to choose from for your Grand Finale. Everyone assumes that Saving Chloe is the best option here (The other ending is played out more sad/feels like you wasted your time), but back to terms with Save Chloe Ending it leaves a bitter taste on your tongue with the ending cutscene with lots of questions to be answered, and the lack of emotion given to it.
WE HAVE TO GO BACK KATE! WE HAVE TO GO BACK!

Life of Strange is a spunky, awesome game that takes a heartwarming, friendship-inducing and scary spin to the 'every choice has consequences' style of gameplay.
Taking the role of Max, the geeky teenage girl who mysteriously wakes up in class with time-reversing abilities, you venture your way through many situations where you connect with classmates and set your heart on what you think is the right choice for Max to make in certain situations. Outcomes will change story for better or for worse and what other characters feel and think about you.
Max starts to sense danger for her town and while the first episode, taking a pinch of slice of life, eases you into the world of her school and mind, continuing on, it all starts to spiral into something magically... Strange.
I can't recommend this game enough, if you love The Walking Dead or any other of Telltale's choice based story games.  Life is Strange defeniely kicks it up a notch and it's one of the most deep adventures you could have playing as a girl who likes to take pictures of butterflies.
EDIT: Finishing epsiode 5, oh my jeebus, amazing game. Made me drop my jaw plenty. Definetley give Life is Strange a pickup.

Honestly until Episode 5 comes out, I can't give a FULL Review of this game.
But I will say this, If you played the games The Walking Dead & Wolf Among Us - YOU WILL LOVE THIS GAME!
Each episode is jam packed and long!
Get the 1-5 package! Episode 1 is a good feeler episode, but if you ONLY play the first episode & judge the entire game on JUST that episode, I feel sorry for you.
The story is DEEP. There are quite a bit of points where YOUR memory will be VITAL.
As a suggestion: Play it like you ARE Max. She has a good heart. She is a geek with cameras (not a negative). She wishes she was a bad♥♥♥♥♥ but its not in her nature. Even with her enemies/bullies she still manages to see the good. She WANTS to be a Professional Photographer!
As you progress, it'll feel like she's awakening her inner Sherlock Holmes and her inner Wonder Woman.
If you love games that REALLY know how to make a great story, then seriously, PLAY THIS GAME!
I'll hold my rating til Episode 5 comes out, but honestly, even with just 4 episodes this game can EASILY achieve 9.5/10!
Side note: The asking price from this game is PHENOMENALLY AWESOME! This is one of the Gems that would make sense to be at LEAST $30.00. The amount of effort put in to this game is spectacular and frankly, DONTNOD deserves MORE than what they are asking!

I'm not a big Adventure game player, this is the first one since the 90's I tried, and it captured me 100%. I was trying to identify why I liked it so much, but it's how everything just meshes together into the whole.

4. Art style - fits with everything else
My only complaints:
1. I have to wait for the next episode to be released. I enjoyed it so much, waiting for them to finish and release episodes is going to be an ongoing struggle.
2. Sometimes the graphics degrade over time. It's a subtle thing and may have nothing to do with the game, but sometimes the degredation gets so bad it breaks the immersion and I realise how terrible it looks.  Relaunching the game seems to resolve this.
Overall I would recommend this to anyone that has some interest. Not my typical game, yet I'd rate it as one of my favorites so if something catches your attention, give it a try like I did; may be pleasently surprised.

After playing this game, I can easily say that I'm going to play through all 5 episodes (fingers already crossed for a season 2). This game offers a (so far, very rich) storyline that is at times a light-hearted and comedic jab at overly-dramatic teenage angst and high school dynamics, and at others, a more serious depiction of a small Oregon town, filled with jaded characters whose lives are full of longing for escape to an idealized "somewhere else." It gets pretty dark at times and touches on some serious themes of psychological abuse, rough family and social lives, depression, desperation, and morality, among others. It does this all while facing you as the main character with a string of choices that affect the relationships of those around you, as well as their perceptions of you, as sinister or benevolent as you'd care to make her. The sci-fi kicker: TIME TRAVEL! So, as you make said moral choices, you are able to instantly rewind time to assess the most beneficial outcome as your character constantly plays the Devil's advocate and tries to persuade you otherwise, "Hmm...maybe that wasn't the best idea." [I had to play through the first episode twice to acheive an outcome I was alright with.]
Visuals-wise, Life is Strange utilizes Unreal Engine's slick development tools pretty effectively. The scenery, character detail, and lighting effects are all pretty stunning, in my opinion, with the only minute detail that bothered me slightly being the characters' speech animations not being synced to their dialogue. (Didn't reach the uncanny valley effect by any means, but in a game with so much dialogue, more attention to accurate speech animation would have perfected it for me. Unrealistic expectation, I know...)
I would say this game is a rough mix of Braid, Mean Girls, Fable, The Butterfly Effect, and Donnie Darko.

Life is Strange's basic style of game will be immediately familiar to anyone who played a recent Telltale adventure game - puzzle-lite, dialog-rich, and choices that change the game as you progress. But LiS comes with a several huge twists on that formula, and manage to do so in a way that should have broken the fourth wall outright. It's as if someone sat down and said "how do I make a game in a way that would both fracture the fourth wall *and* make reloading almost irrelevant?"
Of course, that's not the key of the game - contemplation is. This is a slow-paced, thoughtful game. Observation rewards you with more character depth and detail about the world around you, with even small, indistinct, but above all *human* interactions making this game far longer and more nuanced than it would otherwise look. Put into the observational, smart, and shy head of a young teenage girl, you'll soon discover that every small action *does* count to some degree. Some big, some small. All of them give you a world with greater depth, much like Gone Home does for those familiar, but with far more interactivity rather than *merely* observation.
Few games give you a deep emotional and moral set of considerations as you go through it. Heck, both Telltale and Bioware taught us that choices don't matter *that* much beyond window dressing and cosmetic appeal... (though Telltale *did* take a huge step in the right direction with Tales from the Borderlands on that count)... Here, tiny insignificant details wake you up, and the "Consequences" notification in-game does not actually cover all possible consequences and choices unlocked in-game.
Rush through, and you'll mostly get high-school drama with some supernatural twists. Dive in deep, and you'll get some of the best storytelling to feature in video games.
So, you know that argument about art and games? This is art. And game. Just sayin'.

"Life is Strange" is a series of episodes that follows the story of a photography student, Max, who discovers an ability to partially reverse time and uses it to interfere with the timeline to improve the outcome of the plot. The game also incorporates themes of nostalgia, the departure of adolescence into adulthood and the loss of innocence throughout time. Life is Strange also uses a choice-based system that, unlike the Telltale Games' choice system, actually matters. Every major choice you make sticks with you throughout the game, and the importance of these decisions never die down throughout the episodes, meaning that if you make hasty and poor decisions, it WILL come back to bite you (bacon omelette or Belgian waffles, bacon + eggs or pancakes.. very serious stuff).
Pros:
-Excellent character development and interactions, from both major and minor characters
-Solid soundtrack
-Amazing plot
-A choice system that is incredibly complex and holds you to your decisions
-Most decisions in the game can be undone thanks to the "rewind" mechanism Max possesses, so even if you make decisions you're not happy with, you can fix it
Cons:
-Some aspects of the gameplay can be tedious. For example *minor spoiler alert*, there is a part of the game where you have to focus on a photo for plot reasons and the controls can be annoying to learn and perform the focus properly.
-Serious attention to detail. This isn't really a problem for the earlier episodes, but later on you have to memorise very small details as they can help you out. You need solid sleuthing skills (which you may or may not enjoy). If you miss your opportunity to notice these details, too bad.
All in all.. 9/10. Definately worth the money and provides a thought provoking experience from episode one.

For anyone that likes Telltale's style of adventure games (i.e. The Walking Dead, The Wolf Among Us) are going to enjoy this. Anyone into films like "The Butterfly Effect" are going to enjoy this. People who enjoy realistic teen dialogue... are not going to enjoy this.
Although it certainly will become a classic, I don't see how so many reviews are glazing over the dialogue. It's both written and acted at times, in an increidbly cringe-inducing way. It baffles me. The voices themselves are fine, but I'd liken it to the Star Wars prequels, stilted dialogue often voiced in a way that makes me think the voice-actors were thinking "really? I don't think she'd say it like that...". It's a shame as it sometimes takes me out of the mood of the scene. I guess it's also a bit like Dawson's Creek where the show as a whole is fine, but the way they talk is not representative of "kids" that age.
Other than that, graphics are solid, the story is gripping and the choices although arbitrary, are hard to pick at times.
I'd happily settle for a 7/10 on this, and just wish the writing didn't feel like it was done by a 47-year old man trying to write teenage girl dialogue.

N.B: This review was written after completing Episode 4 of 5.
Headline summary: If you like story, characters and mystery, buy this game.
Full Review:
This game is definitely worth a look if you value stories with a feeling of mystery and nostalgia. The art style is compelling, if a little lacking in detail (which sometimes makes it hard to tell the age of characters etc.). The controls are a little frustrating, particularly when trying to get the optimal angle for those optional photos.
The choice system presents some genuine dilemmas. There are situations when the stress of not having enough information, coupled with the compelling nature of the characters, gives you a feeling of unrest and immediacy that drives the experience forward. This feeling of unease is cleverly enhanced by the rewind mechanic, which makes you just powerful enough to see the immediate consequences your choices have, whilst not providing you with enough insight to be sure that your final decision was bullet-proof. This is a unique experience in adventure games and to be seriously applauded.
However, other situations have a clear morally optimal option, which - particularly when combined with the rewind mechanic - can make them feel like a choice between the 'right' option and everything else. This is not a serious issue, as most 'optimal' solutions are harder to get, which can make reaching them seem like something of an achievement. Nonetheless, I expect that it will limit replay value for anyone who does not enjoy the feeling of deliberately making the 'wrong' choice just to see what happens.
The rewind mechanic itself is a very nice touch and extremely well implemented. It enables the game designers to create some interesting and counter-intuitive puzzles, which whilst not particularly complex, add gameplay depth to a predominantly narrative driven experience.
Nonetheless, by far and away the best part of this game is its cast of characters, who even the hardest of hearts will grow to care about. Max is a compelling lead who manages to combine strength of character with self-doubt and teenage awkwardness in a thoroughly believable manner. Without going into too much further detail - no spoilers I promise - the other characters do not fail to disappoint either. Some tend to be a little cliche at times but those with the most screen time have depth and realism.
The voice acting is solid, if not mind-blowing, with some lines being delivered a little flat and mechanically. Nonetheless, the writing is all there and really drives the game along. It is worth spending time just walking around and chatting to people to pick up those little extra hints and easter eggs, which are reminicent of those that made old school adventure games so much fun.

+ Journals & character biographies hold massive amounts of information and behind-the-scenes storytelling
+ Voice-acting is absolutely top-shelf, almost across the board
+ Soundtrack is well-selected and is implemented flawlessly; complements the narrative atmosphere
+ Choices really matter, and the consequences of said choices reverberate throughout the rest of the narrative
+ Does well to handle myriad mature themes, and does not do so in a manner that comes off as crass or over-saturated
+ Intensely atmospheric; game can be played in marathon sessions without a distinct feeling of being drained or drawn-out
+ Camera work is very well done, and gives interactions a decidedly cinematic feel; is very effective at moving the story forward, visually
+ All characters, even supporting cast, enjoy applaudable depth and development; it must be said that the player is likely to develop emotional attachment to some of the characters, making the game an effective experience
+ Player is able to replay scenes and actions, so as to explore the effects of one's decisions
+ Environments are very detailed, and boast largely competent lighting effects
- Atrocious lip syncronization
- Visuals and textures are mostly underwhelming, and feel somewhat dated (does not necessarily detract from one's appreciation of the art-style, however)

For anyone that likes Telltale's style of adventure games (i.e. The Walking Dead, The Wolf Among Us) are going to enjoy this. Anyone into films like "The Butterfly Effect" are going to enjoy this. People who enjoy realistic teen dialogue... are not going to enjoy this.
Although it certainly will become a classic, I don't see how so many reviews are glazing over the dialogue. It's both written and acted at times, in an increidbly cringe-inducing way. It baffles me. The voices themselves are fine, but I'd liken it to the Star Wars prequels, stilted dialogue often voiced in a way that makes me think the voice-actors were thinking "really? I don't think she'd say it like that...". It's a shame as it sometimes takes me out of the mood of the scene. I guess it's also a bit like Dawson's Creek where the show as a whole is fine, but the way they talk is not representative of "kids" that age.
Other than that, graphics are solid, the story is gripping and the choices although arbitrary, are hard to pick at times.
I'd happily settle for a 7/10 on this, and just wish the writing didn't feel like it was done by a 47-year old man trying to write teenage girl dialogue.

This game is so good that I'm going to show everyone one of my amazing recipes:
For the slow-roast tomatoes
2 tbsp olive oil
3 ripe plum tomatoes, trimmed and halved
few thyme sprigs
3 garlic cloves, left whole
1 tbsp balsamic vinegar
handful basil leaves
For the lamb
1 x 8-bone rack of lamb, well trimmed (see tip, below)
1 tbsp olive oil
25g butter
4 garlic cloves, smashed but with skin on
few thyme sprigs
For the warm bean salad
200g podded broad beans
200g fine beans, trimmed
85g mangetout
1 tbsp olive oil
2 shallots, finely sliced into rings
small handful toasted flaked almonds
For the dressing
2 tbsp olive oil
1 tbsp balsamic vinegar
Method
Heat oven to 220C/200C fan/gas 7. For the tomatoes heat the oil in an ovenproof frying pan (if you don't have an ovenproof pan, use a standard frying pan then transfer to a roasting tray before putting in the oven) and fry cut-side down. Add the thyme and garlic and cook for 3 mins until coloured. Turn over the tomatoes, drizzle with vinegar, then roast in the oven for 20 mins until soft and caramelised. Leave to rest.
While the tomatoes are roasting, cook the lamb. Season the meat generously and heat the oil and butter in another ovenproof frying pan. Place the lamb, fat-side down, in the pan and scatter round the garlic and thyme. Brown the lamb really well, then turn over.
Baste the lamb with the pan juices, then transfer to the oven for 10 mins for lamb that is pink. If you prefer it more well done, give it 5 mins more. Leave the lamb somewhere warm to rest.
While the lamb is cooking, prepare the bean salad. Bring a large pan of salted water to the boil and cook the broad beans for a few mins. Scoop them out with a slotted spoon straight into a bowl of ice water, then slip them from their skins into a bowl. Boil the fine beans for 2 mins, then add the mangetout and cook both for 1 min longer. Drain, plunge into iced water (this keeps their bright green colour), leave for 1 min to cool down, then drain again.
Heat the oil in a frying pan, quickly cook the shallots for 1 min until starting to soften and colour, then add the fine beans and mangetout. Cook for about 1 min to heat through, then toss in the almonds and finally toss through the broad beans.
Scatter the basil over the tomatoes, saving a few of the very small leaves for garnishing. Make the dressing by simply whisking the oil and vinegar together. Carve the lamb into cutlets on a board with a very sharp knife (see tip, below). You are now ready to plate up.
Place the salad to one side of each plate. Line up three tomato halves down the other side of the plate. Lay three chops on top of the salad, slightly overlapping, with the bones pointing in the same direction. Drizzle the dressing around the plate and scatter the small basil leaves over the tomatoes.

It gives a completely different approach to the situation, and makes it feel even worse when you make a bad decision because you had the power to avoid it much more in this game than in Telltale games.
The graphical style of the game are really charming and beautiful, the music fits in very well and creates a very enjoyable atmosphere. If you like achievements or collectibles, they also have some really nice ones in there too which with Collectible Mode are easy to hunt for. in case you missed one the first time.
Best story based choice game ever!

First let me just quote one of the best lines in the game:
Chloe: "Did you JUST say Hella? I think im a good bad influence on you"
And like Chloe said, I have to say that this is one of the best long short stories I've experienced in video games. I could play it a couple of more hours exploring and touching things but I just had to progress with the story. Maybe it was on of the shorest stories I played in, but DAMN, It's the most emotional and touching games I've ever played, so deep and epic.
I actually played this game with a close friend (a girl) watching me playing and in some parts we really shed some tears and was shocked of what's happening, it was amazing.
This game really isn't that much about gameplay but I can say it's smooth and and fits the stor. Such an intresting plot which can chance according to what I decide to do and really affects the future of the game, i'm very intrested to see how can it be diffrent to choose a path that normally I wouldnt.
It was very beautiful to see how the main character also known as Max. develops during each episode and keeps learning new things about herself and her surroundings.
The dialogue between the characters was an amazing thing which everything you say affected the way they act and what they say next.

This game is so good that I'm going to show everyone one of my amazing recipes:
For the slow-roast tomatoes
2 tbsp olive oil
3 ripe plum tomatoes, trimmed and halved
few thyme sprigs
3 garlic cloves, left whole
1 tbsp balsamic vinegar
handful basil leaves
For the lamb
1 x 8-bone rack of lamb, well trimmed (see tip, below)
1 tbsp olive oil
25g butter
4 garlic cloves, smashed but with skin on
few thyme sprigs
For the warm bean salad
200g podded broad beans
200g fine beans, trimmed
85g mangetout
1 tbsp olive oil
2 shallots, finely sliced into rings
small handful toasted flaked almonds
For the dressing
2 tbsp olive oil
1 tbsp balsamic vinegar
Method
Heat oven to 220C/200C fan/gas 7. For the tomatoes heat the oil in an ovenproof frying pan (if you don't have an ovenproof pan, use a standard frying pan then transfer to a roasting tray before putting in the oven) and fry cut-side down. Add the thyme and garlic and cook for 3 mins until coloured. Turn over the tomatoes, drizzle with vinegar, then roast in the oven for 20 mins until soft and caramelised. Leave to rest.
While the tomatoes are roasting, cook the lamb. Season the meat generously and heat the oil and butter in another ovenproof frying pan. Place the lamb, fat-side down, in the pan and scatter round the garlic and thyme. Brown the lamb really well, then turn over.
Baste the lamb with the pan juices, then transfer to the oven for 10 mins for lamb that is pink. If you prefer it more well done, give it 5 mins more. Leave the lamb somewhere warm to rest.
While the lamb is cooking, prepare the bean salad. Bring a large pan of salted water to the boil and cook the broad beans for a few mins. Scoop them out with a slotted spoon straight into a bowl of ice water, then slip them from their skins into a bowl. Boil the fine beans for 2 mins, then add the mangetout and cook both for 1 min longer. Drain, plunge into iced water (this keeps their bright green colour), leave for 1 min to cool down, then drain again.
Heat the oil in a frying pan, quickly cook the shallots for 1 min until starting to soften and colour, then add the fine beans and mangetout. Cook for about 1 min to heat through, then toss in the almonds and finally toss through the broad beans.
Scatter the basil over the tomatoes, saving a few of the very small leaves for garnishing. Make the dressing by simply whisking the oil and vinegar together. Carve the lamb into cutlets on a board with a very sharp knife (see tip, below). You are now ready to plate up.
Place the salad to one side of each plate. Line up three tomato halves down the other side of the plate. Lay three chops on top of the salad, slightly overlapping, with the bones pointing in the same direction. Drizzle the dressing around the plate and scatter the small basil leaves over the tomatoes.

Life is Strange became one of my favorite games ever. It does what Telltale has been striving for, and does it better. Don’t get me wrong, I loved “The Walking Dead 1&2”, “Wolf Among Us” & “Game of Thrones”, but they fail at something that Life is Strange does right.
I mean, I never thought someone would put so much effort into a point click adventure. To compare it to “The Walking Dead”, for example, which has a very unique art style that is inspired, but still lacking. It has nothing new to give us, no unique shots, angles, color scheme or the use of locations and lighting – all the things that Life is Strange succeeds in. No shot is boring, there is always something to look at, something to admire, whether it’s the beautiful sunset or the glowing moonlight, a crooked angle that gives depth or a shot from above for no other reason than to create an unusual setting for a scene. If you’re a person who appreciates the small things and enjoy the art of cinematography, this one definitely uses all of the tools right. All of these and more make this game eye poppingly stunning.
At first it might seem like another high-school teenage drama stuff, but it conceals much deeper, darker, mature not-so-teenage problems. I cannot fathom the grotesque story as it rolls on, and find myself pausing a scene just to comprehend what just happened.
Yes, you heard me, they actually make a difference. If you were bothered before by a game that promised you a story tailored by your decisions (I’m looking at you, Telltale), this one does it right. I found myself fumbling to understand what is going to happen next and what my decision might do in the future. I consider each decision as if it were real, weighting out the endless possible outcomes of each one. My decisions change the story, and yet I have never felt the need to start a new game with new choices, because I felt confident in them. They built up a story tailored uniquely for me.
Let’s say you’re in your room with an objective, you’ll actually find yourself looking around at everything else before continuing with the “main goal”. Every little detail in each scene has something to enrich the story, and most of the time you’ll find something that will aid you later on in a conversation.
That is all.

The punk, the A-hole, the self-obsessed rich snob, the nice teacher and the bad guy actually come up to characters you’re invested in. You care about them, and try and hurt the ones you hate and will sacrifice anything for the ones you love.

Here I go writing my first review on a game here on steam, I'll be honest in saying that this game came out of no where for me and at first glance it looks like the usual teen drama type of game. Boy was I wrong and thank God i was wrong because this game is now my number one game of all time! I have never played the tell tale games like TWD but i have watched lets plays of them, and I am grateful I didnt do that for this game. This game takes you on an emotinal roller coaster and it sure was hella worth the price of admission.
Lets talk about the visuals in the game. First off the lighting in this game is beyond phenomenal! When the time reaches the "golden hour" of the day... MY GOD! The vibrant color of the orange sunset is just amazing. The modeling and texturing is definetly better then TellTale but with these types of games I think they dont have to be over the top for it to convey the the world.
As an animator I feel that the animations were limited and could have used some more refinement in order to convey a certain emotion or feeling, certain facial expression could have been pushed a little more but I also do understand there are some limitations when working on a team, especially a game studio, that get in the way or just brushed aside because it might not be most optimal choice, but that is just my two cents on that.
The score and the sound design in general is just to good not to mention. Playing with the music is a must because it brings together the whole game, like my proffesor used to say "sound is only 50% of the film", and for this game it sure was.
Here is my closing thoughts:
If you like a good narative, and adventure games then BUY this game! If you dont, then I still say give it a shot! You might be surprised at what this game offers. Dont speed through it either because you might just miss the little things in the game that make it what is.
Its the little things in life that are the most important, and you know what? Life really is Strange like that.

I always loved the tell your own tale stories in books like some of the old Dungeons & Dragons mini books with choose an option and turn to certain pages for the next outcome. This game lives to capture that escense with the perfect art & imagination of dream worlds.
As soon as I finished the 1st Episode and saw its climax... It instantly popped into my head that this game took a huge concept from the two movies Butterfly Effect (1st, not the crappy sequels) and Donny Darko (again not the Sequel). To me this was a BOLD choice and unique for this story. Im sure its been done else where but Life is Strange has certainly captured both into one detailed, alluring, suspensful and emotional story. Yes, I said emotional. I hardly ever physical express an emotion towards video games and/or their sequences that happen. At least nothing major since the first time I and im sure most of us saw Aerith die in Final Fantasy VII, I was 12 at the time. I did cry the first time around seeing that and by the end of Episode 3 of Life is Strange, I started to cry... and im a near emotionaless (at least i thought until now) prick of a dude now too.
For now, im going to hold off on playing Episode 4 until Episode 5 releases. Ive read 4 is fantastic and suspensful so, I will update my review again once Ep. 5 drops.
So far I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys Emotionally Deep Stories, Choice Options to direct the story, Butterfly Effect & Donny Darko.
One last thing, use a Gaming Controller like a Logitec Gamepad or XBox 360/One controller. Keyboard controls were aweful imo and I usually play Mouse and Keyboard. Thats my only complaint.

Pros:
-Immersive story
-Unpredictable events
-Nice visuals despite the somewhat cartoony art style
-Good variety in characters and atmosphere/pacing for each episode
-Motha ♥♥♥♥in time travel
-Lots of small references, easter eggs, or random things here and there throughout the game that add to make it even more enjoyable
-No performance issues on PC, well optimized
-Cheap price tag
Cons:
-Somewhat cheesy dialogue and occasionally the characters' voice and mouths don't sync properly
-Linear gameplay. Not much exploring outside of each given "area" you're currently in. And the story choices mostly only have minor impacts so far.
-Interacting with stuff ingame is a bit awkward with a mouse + keyboard. It generally plays more comfortably with a controller, though.
-Still no imgame option to turn off chromatic aberration or adjust field of view, though at least turning off CA is possible through config files.
Overall definitely worth it if you enjoy any kind of story driven game. In fact, I wouldn't really call this a game as the gameplay is almost exclusively walking around, interacting with people, finding stuff out about them or the story, make choices, etc. But it's got that tv series feel like a telltale game should, so it's a nice change of pace from other games.
This game also has nice replayability, because you can start another playthrough and make completely different choices to see how it changes how the other characters interact with you later on. There's tons of combinations of outcomes here!

When I first saw the trailer for this game, I was intrigued. I had never played an episodic game before, but I was familiar with the principle. I immediately bought it. (I think it's the first, and so far only, game I paid for before it was released.)
I was excited for the release of the first episode, and the wait was definitely worth it. After each episode, the waiting became even worse, as the game had drawn me in so much that I just had to know what was going to happen next. Now, with only one episode left, waiting is almost torture.
What is it that has drawn me in? It's not like the dialogue is the best. It's even cringeworthy at times. The gameplay is nice, and it suits the game itself, but it's not an amazing thing in and of itself. (I don't know how it compares to other episodic games, since this is the only one I've ever played.)
The thing that makes this game so brilliant, the reason I would recommend it to anyone without any further thought, is the story. It starts out fairly innocently, with fun characters, and just a hint of something dark on the horizon. However, the further you get, the darker it becomes. I am not ashamed to admit that I cried multiple times while playing this, and I'm sure the fifth episode will not let me get away without shedding any tears. The choices you have to make are difficult, very much so, at times. You don't know what effect your actions will have, but you have to act anyway. I'm curious to see how my actions will affect the ending of the story, which is drawing nearer and nearer, and I dread the way my mistakes might come back to haunt me.
Also, you can be marvellously gay. You can't say no to that.
Awesome game, but not worth buying unless you want all the 5 chapters.

Life is Strange is my favorite game possibly ever. I don't tend to enjoy adventure games much, because of illogical puzzles, or puzzles in general, but Life Is Strange is more like a visual novel. You can't "get stuck" in this game, because it's like real life. It keeps going whether you figure it out or not. The only difference is that they give you a rewind button so that you can experience both immediate outcomes to your choices. So when you decide to help someone, or not, you get a chance to change your mind.
For those of you who know nothing about it, the story revolves around Maxine "Max" Caulfield. She's returned to her hometown after living in the big city for 5 years, and is going to a prestigious high school for her senior year for their photography program. She's estranged from her childhood BFF Chloe, and is too shy to make many friends, though she has a few. Quite quickly, she comes into the power to control time, or specfically, reverse it in order to change her recent past. This plays out like Groundhog Day at first, but quickly becomes a sci-fi thriller as the search for a local missing girl her age throws everything she knows on its head.
The plot, characterizations, development and everything in between is absolutely outstanding. The game gives you a little bit of information at a time, so you form first impressions of characters you may think are bad, or one dimensional, but then as you interact with them more, or find out more of their background, or ultimately realize they're not all that different from you.
Also quite amazing is the sound design. Music is everywhere, but it only plays when there is a logical source of it, usually a CD player or Max's earbuds. And oh my lord, it is so beautiful and fitting. I often will find a seat in the game, or lie back on Max's bed and wait for it to play out while she contemplates her actions and the mysterious around her. It goes so far as to make the music suddenly drop when she pulls off her earbuds, drowned out by the environment that the music once overwhelmed, until she turns it off and puts her earbuds away. It's a small touch, but something that puts you into her shoes so well at the beginning, that Max becomes the teenage girl extension of yourself, but still 100% Max. It's so strange that this, to me, is more RPG than anything I've ever played.
I cannot recommend this game more for everyone who likes video games or good stories. It hit me right in the feels and lingers in my mind as I think about the repercussions of all of my actions, and the seemingly unalterable fate that befalls Max and Chloe.

Warning: This whole review will sound pretentious but here goes.
I hate to throw around superlatives. They become meaningless if you do so but to me, this game is a real pice of art. A lot of different elements come together to make something that's very special.
I don't want to get bogged down in details but Life is Strange is basically a story based game very much in the vein of Telltale games like The Walking Dead or The Wolf Among Us. What differs Life is Strange from those games in that the setting is far more down to earth and mundane, which actually in my mind, counts as a huge strength. Every single one of us has experienced being a young person and dealing with problems, both big and small, in life. I consider this a strength as the story is so much more relatable and immersive. The player character, Max Caulfield, is likeable and easy to relate with. She finds herself in instantly recognisable situations and feels familiar emotions. On the surface, it would seem the opposite. Yet, in keeping within the realms of reality (apart from the time travelling mechanic of course) the characters and plot lines are so much easier to idenity with. To compare with The Walking Dead, the choices there concern such abstract situations in comparison. The vast majority of people never have to act in life or death situations, to kill people or make choices in harsh moral situations. Life is Strange's story is of such familiarity, that the themes are far more intriguing. We've all had to deal with difficult things in regards to growing up. What we want to do in life, who our friends are, the trials and tribulations of education, wishing we could make different decisions and interacting with people. This is the best strength of the game in my opinion.
The other mechanic that sets it apart from the rest is the time travelling mechanic. It allows for some really amazing plot scenarios and works very well in the concept of your choices mattering. Never mind having to make the initial choice, seeing the consequences and being able to go back in time adds a whole new layer to the system. Again, this initially seems like a bad idea but it works very well in practice. As the story progresses, it has a bigger and bigger impact. No spoilers though, experience it for yourself.
I'd also like to heap particular accolades on the audio/visual department. The graphics and art style do an excellent job of conveying a dream-like, surreal state. The environment looks superb, especially the vivid sunsets and rays of light. The sound is well done, with the voice actors being of high quality. The music is well-chosen and fitting to the atmosphere of the game. The only complaint I have in this department is that the DOF and blur effects are sometimes a bit overdone but that may be my personal preference.
Overall, I can't reccommend this game enough. One of the best story based games I've played, with a huge emotional punch to it. I can't wait for the finale of the story.

All the big game releases lately, The Witcher 3, GTAV,Battlefield, all huge budgets yet a game like Life Is Strange sneaks in and gives people an unforgettable emotional experience and some of the deepest characters I have ever seen in a game. My game of the year by miles.
