I'm surprised this is rated so highly because this game isn't as wonderful as everyone proclaims. There are definitely some good things going though:
- Unique art style that feels appropriate for the setting
- Clear opening that defines the strange power and Max, the main character
- Attractive premise
So the game is clearly good at drawing people in for a good time. Unfortunately, my experience left me feeling unsatisfied. After meeting the characters and playing through the first episode, I don't feel like finding out what happens to the town of Arcadia. Personally, I'm not a fan of high school settings because they're usually overly dramatized and full of plain annoyances. I'm usually one to empathize with characters I care about but the problem is that I couldn't really find any that I cared for. Max comes the closest only because she's the only nice person I've really found. Strangely, the second nicest person was the Dana the cheerleader (which was unexpected due to the obvious high school archetypes). It seems like Arcadia has a problem population that mostly consists of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who speak in a strange semi-"hip" vernacular. Almost every single character I spoke to was mean to me. The game made me feel alienated and there was nothing that really makes up for it.
Usually, the gameplay would substitute for these charaters but unfortunately these characters ARE the game. There are a few "puzzles", if you want to call them that. I found them to be annoying obstacles more than anything. These parts felt like areas where you should actually make important decisions rather than the "Choose 'A' or 'B'" method the developers employed. These were extremely linear as there was one solution to them and the "choice" was more about what you chose to say to people. I feel like they should have left you multiple ways to deal with these "puzzles" so that the story felt more like it was revolving around your actions. These parts came across as pointless and honestly felt more like artifical game lengtheners. I suppose it was to make the game feel more like a "game" but their focus should have been on better writing since that is the central point.
The way the time reverse power is used makes it seem pretty useless. Only when something drastic happens does it really make a difference but one can only undo one decision at a time. The power itself constantly reminds me that I'm playing a choice based game. Part of me wants the game to stop informing me that I'm being monitored and graded. Maybe that's some sort of parallel they're trying to draw between the surveillance issue, though it's unlikely.
I really wanted to like the game but I really don't like anything that's happening in the story. The setting feels a bit like I've been placed in Triggered, USA. The premise is cool but every character seems like they have serious mental issues or are just plain♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ There isn't much gameplay and the story doesn't make up for it very well. This is the first Steam game which has prompted me to write a review. So, here goes.
This is an amazing game. It has an engaging story for most part, it is masterfully executed, it has a distinctive visual style. The latter, incidentally, is what misled me. I dived into the game thinking that it was a cute teen drama about friendship, bullying, playing detectives and a little time rewind magic.
IT WAS NOT. Well, yes, it was, but only on the surface. This game is like a Dr. Seuss illustration that has been painted over an H. R. Giger, and the longer you play, the more this underside starts to show. Suffice it to say, after finishing Episode 4 the game offers to visit its website to find a support group in your area, should the need arise.
But if you're OK with experiencing (immersing yourself in) a very dark story, the game is very much recommended.

This is nothing like the games that I normally play.  I bought the first episode because it looked like everything I want in the television series and movies that I watch.  After watching the first trailer I felt an excitement for this game that, sadly, no one else I knew shared.  When I first started to play the game I instantly knew that my excitement for this game had been completely and unequivocally justified.
Right from the start this game forces you feel for the main character, and in extension those that she cares for.  The situations that the game, and to a degree yourself, puts it don't feel forced or contrived.  They feel natural and they flow naturally.  Your choices don't just feel like they matter, they actually do matter.  The game doesn't give to time to mull these choices over either, you choose them naturally and hope for the best.  You won't feel the need to pause the game and decide which outcome you want before making your choice, because for the most part you play just like you.  At least the first time.
Lastly, the game doesn't rely on anything other than a good story and good characters to sell itself.  You won't find excessive violence, nudity, or swearing in this game.  You will people acting and speaking naturally in situations influenced by you and the main character's supernatural ability. This game. Oh god this game right here. Let me explain to you the love that I have for this game in the best way I can: This game is literally everything I have ever wanted in a game. It has the best story I have ever seen in a game, and I mean that as a lover of all the telltale games, mass effect, any story rich game thats out there I have probably played and loved. As a matter of fact The Walking Dead was my favorite game of all time. WAS. Then this game happened.
The feels that this game makes you feel are unlike any feels you have felt at a game. Everything in this game is so relatable and real. The focus of this game is around friendship and average teenager life, and everyone can relate to that because they have been through it. This game is one you show to your friends because you know they can relate to it and love the game as much as you do. This is the only game that has truly messed me up so bad that I couldn't sleep because I was thinking about what I had just seen (looking at you episode 4). You may not have the same impact I did because you may not be able to relate as much as I did to this game, but there is a good chance you will.
Oh and don't even get me started on the soundtrack. The soundtrack on this game will change your music preferences. Seriously its that good. This game uses a combination of liscensed and original music and does it really, really well. I mean really well.
Now about the voice acting. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥the voice actors are phenomenal. They do such a good job of displaying emotion in very pivotal scenes in the game and you can just feel it. Its so good. Not to mention the art style and the way the characters act and look work very well. Its a very immersive game in that regard. There's nothing thats going to pull you out of the immersion in the game and it does very well in episodic format. You should take this game in chunks, episode by episode, so you don't stop in the middle an episode and pull yourself out of the game. You won't get the same impact that way.
If you are thinking about getting this game, do yourself a huge favor and do. It is so worth it if you want one of the most special, beautiful, heartfelt, and real gaming experience you have ever had. That is if you like story based games and are ok with not having quick time events or heavy amount of interactivity at all times. If you are ok with that, then buy this game as soon as you possibly can. Seriously do it.

Here, before you, stands a snapshot of the quintessential adventure we faced growing up. Through extreme attention to detail and excellent story writing, you will be subjected to decisions; some hard, some easy, and some quiet unpredictable.
Your choices are what will define Max Claufield, the main protagonist.
With a beautiful quilt woven through sci-fi, horror, pop-culture and all things rebellious, the main theme of photography - of being able to focus and then capture a single, photogenic moment in time - is what drives this coming-of-age story.
Max, who discovers a very weightily power, is attempting to find her place, as she returns home, among lives that have changed, for better or worse. She is faced with the very real and daunting scenario of returning 'home' as a grown up, and dealing with, in this case literally, as the magic of childhood dies and is replaced by a complex, harsh and sometimes funny adulthood with serious consequences.
With the town crumbling below her and the air of mystery heavy, you have the power to decide how Max defines herself among her friends, the popular kids, her teachers, the towns people and even the police while balancing a supernatural ability and a whole lot of questions with complicated answers. The possibilities that lay before you are almost endless - will you be naiive, will you be reckless, will you be wise, will you be dangerous, or even all four at once?
In addition to the amazing writing, that never ceases to amaze - the game is highly photogenic. As a real-world photographer, the artists of this game clearly intended to give us a highly scenic world; filtered through the dichotomy of night and day. The music, which is down-to-earth and usually acoustic, not only sets the mood but fits the place, as most of us associate the indie vibe with the Upper Northwest. The game, through it's combination of writing, music, visuals, and themes, may just define our generation of millennials.
To sum this up, which was hard - The game, it gives you goosebumps to have so much chaos and peace in one setting. It defines the otherworldly of being an adolescent; If you asked Max what she should would say,
'Life is Strange'

I previously gave this game a poor review, as there are so many bugs in it.  There are still those bugs, but I slogged my way through it.

Again, the bugs were there.  You have to be careful when rewinding and then skipping forward.  You misstime your steps, and you're caught unable to do anything except restart from the checkpoint.
Even with my complaints about the game, yes, you should pick it up.  Though I believe Max and Chloe's tale is done, I hope there's some sort of sequel.  After all, even though they're not connected, Squeenix does make all of those Final Fantasy sequels.  This deserves one too.

This game is an absolute rollercoaster.  The setting is so well researched and its one of the few games that manages to capture... I dunno, the normality of life.  Granted, there are sci-fi elements to the story (mainly just the power to rewind time), the game just does a good job of transporting you to the world of the fictional Oregon town of Arcadia Bay.
The first episode will do a good job of teaching you the ins and outs of LiS's decision system and your choices are not that far reaching, relatively speaking, as you get used to everything.  After that, the story really starts to pick up and you'll start to really get into the characters and their subplots.  By episode 3, you'll be full on sucked in the world of Arcadia Bay and start to feel the effects of your earlier choices.  And finally, as you enter episode 4 (the current episode as of this review), you will be so involved in the stories of these characters that you'll be dying to play episode 5 and finish up the story (ITS SO HARD WAITING).
The music is also something I'd like to touch on.  Its an excellent indie/folk licensed soundtrack and opened me up to music I wouldn't normally listen to.  Playing back the soundtrack really brings back the memories of the various scenes that were happening when the music was playing.  The developer said at one point that the music was a good 50% of the experience and they were right on.
Finally, the graphics.  The graphical style is simplistic, but also very unique.  While not the super sharp HD graphics of a lot of modern games, this game showcases a truly special artistic style all its own and will delight the senses as you play through the various areas.
All in all, the gameplay, story, music and graphics really come together for a unique experience that I hope everyone get the chance to really enjoy.

Having played some big-budget, ultra-hype titles this year it's simply great to play a game like Life is Strange. It not only has a suspenseful story, which reminded me of the classic Twin Peaks, it has just the right amount of interactive gameplay which similar games from Telltale lack in my opinion. But there's even more to it. The game may contain some stereotype characters and elements of your typical High-School-drama, but it presents them in an authentic way dispite the supernatural story. Life is Strange radiates a wholeheartedness and a down-to-earth mood which I enjoy very much. Max Caulfield's tale is presented in such a believable fashion and with so much attention to the little things which constitute human life, it's enchanting and enables a degree of identification rarely experienced in digital media (ok, The Witcher 3 managed that too). I'm not only looking forward to play future episodes, now I even want to pick up my camera and shot pictures right away. This is the gaming equivalent of contemporary tv-shows. Thank you Dontnod!

If you are unfamiliar with this game and wantto know what kind of game it is. Some will say it is similar to Telltale's series of games such as : The Walking Dead, The Wolf Among Us, Tales From the BorderLands Those are great games indeed and I would put LIS in the same catagory, but it is a completely different monster in the regard of how the game is played.
You control a charatcer named Max who has a vision of something horrible happening to the city Arcadia. This vision had felt so real to her that she felt a lil uneasy after waking up from the vision, this leads her to going to the bathroom and reflect on what she just witnessed in her mind. However, and event happens which causes her to hide in the bathroom and as this event takesa turn for the worst, she discovers that she can treverse time. This is where LIS sets itself apart from the Telltale counterparts, as dicisions on those games are usually timed, meaning there are certain events where you must make a quick decision, where as LIS, you literally have time in your hands. The decisions you make dont have to be final right then and there. You are mostly given the freedom to actually reverse back in time to redo the whole scnerio to choose a different decision if you didn't like how that 1st decision turned out. However,once you leave the area the last decision you made is final. What's also great about this mechanic is that characters can ask you questions that you may not know, they give you the answer after you have answered incorrectly, then you can reverse time to give them the correct answer, impressing them with your knowledge.
The story wrting in this game is pretyty incredible to say the least I wouldn't say Ocar worthy or anything, but for a video game we are ruly seeing an evolution in storywriting. I also will say there is also impressive voice acting as well These elements are vital to these types of games as really that is mostly what they are selling us on.
Overall, I don't have too many issues with the game only cvertain times the framerate will drop, not too many times to the point that it is unplayable, but I can say I've only experienced this in ep 4, could be just some hiccup on my end. But overall I'd ssay give this game a shot especially if you can find a good deal on it.

Some will say it is similar to Telltale's series of games such as : The Walking Dead, The Wolf Among Us, Tales From the BorderLands Those are great games indeed and I would put LIS in the same catagory, but it is a completely different monster in the regard of how the game is played.
You control a charatcer named Max who has a vision of something horrible happening to the city Arcadia. This vision had felt so real to her that she felt a lil uneasy after waking up from the vision, this leads her to going to the bathroom and reflect on what she just witnessed in her mind. However, and event happens which causes her to hide in the bathroom and as this event takesa turn for the worst, she discovers that she can treverse time. This is where LIS sets itself apart from the Telltale counterparts, as dicisions on those games are usually timed, meaning there are certain events where you must make a quick decision, where as LIS, you literally have time in your hands. The decisions you make dont have to be final right then and there. You are mostly given the freedom to actually reverse back in time to redo the whole scnerio to choose a different decision if you didn't like how that 1st decision turned out. However,once you leave the area the last decision you made is final. What's also great about this mechanic is that characters can ask you questions that you may not know, they give you the answer after you have answered incorrectly, then you can reverse time to give them the correct answer, impressing them with your knowledge.
The story wrting in this game is pretyty incredible to say the least I wouldn't say Ocar worthy or anything, but for a video game we are ruly seeing an evolution in storywriting. I also will say there is also impressive voice acting as well These elements are vital to these types of games as really that is mostly what they are selling us on.
Overall, I don't have too many issues with the game only cvertain times the framerate will drop, not too many times to the point that it is unplayable, but I can say I've only experienced this in ep 4, could be just some hiccup on my end. But overall I'd ssay give this game a shot especially if you can find a good deal on it.

However, the biggest thing I have to praise this game on is the CHOICE MAKING, which actually IMPACTS your game experience unlike the TellTale games! Wow. So many things to say. How can I really describe this game and do it justice?
I bought this game during the Steam Summer Sale, soley based on the plethora of amazing reviews. Finally started playing it 2 days ago and finished the latest episode (4) just now. I couldn't "put it down," so to speak.
There is so much beauty yet so much ugliness encapsulated within this game. The true nature of friendship even as years pass. The searing pain of losing a loved one. The effect a kind word can have on a hurting person. The depression that ensues with rejection. All the ups and downs and smiles and fights and feelings of being a teenager...and a person. The simple pleasure of sitting in silence with your best friend. The dark side of a person that's always been a hero to you. The dangers of ignoring psychological problems.
All these and more are topics addressed in this game...which honestly, plays out like a phenomenal story. A story where your choices significantly impact the future as well as the present.
The twists and consequences throughout this game lend to its haunting beauty and thrill.
You can't not play this game and ponder it (and your decisions) deeply. It is impossible. There is so much to see and so much to think about.
Play this game. Thank me later.
And don't forget to always look for the photo op! :)

Definitely one of the best games of 2015. It is packed with a very interesting story and gameplay.
It tackles everyday problems of teenagers (for instance depression, bullying, authorities) and weaves it into the whole story. Thanks to your time-rewinding powers, you can solve these problems. You also have to deal with the elements of crime and mystery.
It has some very difficult choices thus you can't just be the good or the bad guy. Every choice is a double-edged sword and neither works in your favour. Mostly you have to choose between being a good friend and doing the right thing, or doing what would make your friend happy even if it is the wrong choice. Fortunately you can rewind time and make a different choice so you get to see the short term outcome of your choice.
I would recommend it to anyone who likes games where YOU choose how the story ends (more or less) like the games from Telltale (The Walking Dead: Season One, The Walking Dead: Season Two, Game of Thrones, The Wolf Among Us).

This game is wonderful. Done, there. That's all you need to know. But if you wanna know more, I'll tell you.
Max Caulfield comes back to her hometown of Arcadia Bay to attend a pretentious... I mean prestigious art school. One day she has a nightmare. In the nightmare, there's a giant tornado heading towards Arcadia Bay and then Max gets crushed by a light house. Jolting awake from her dream, she finds that she's in her photography class. After class, she goes to the bathroom and, through a series of dangerous events, discovers that she can rewind time. Later that day, she runs into her old best friend, Chloe Price, and they try to piece together the story of Chloe's missing girlfriend Rachel.
The whole plot of the tornado and the origin of Max's powers kind of takes a backseat to the main plot. The main plot being Chloe and Max's search for answers behind Rachel Amber's dissapearance. Of course, the final episode has yet to be released so everything will (hopefully) be resolved.
The characters that Max encounters and even Max herself are so realistic and three dimensional. They feel like real people to me. Each character has a unique personality and they all have their own motivations. Max for example is nerdy as ♥♥♥♥ and makes dad jokes and stupid puns. Her whole thing is trying to help people using her rewind power. Seriously, she feels like a real person.
The graphics are beautiful. I mean, when it closes up on Max, you can actually see each individual freckle on her cute little face. The graphics are actually what attracted me to the game in the first place. It's obvious that the developers but a lot of love and care into it.
The game itself and the mechanics I enjoy too. It takes a little while to get used to rewinding time, but once you've got the controls down, you're good Thankfully, there's a little tutorial type mission thing in the first episode. The rewind can become tedious for some of the puzzles. Mainly the Victoria puzzle in the first episode and the clues puzzle in the fourth episode. Other than that, they're fun. Also, the decisions that the player makes actually affect the story in a noticable way.
Anyways, this game is super awesome. 100% recommended.

Many games of the "role-playing choices" genre are either about morality or consequences of your choices. This game focuses more on the latter, meaning that your choices actually do matter in the way the plot advances. It makes sure you know it with the haunting butterfly warning you about everything you do, tempting you to rewind time and say/do something different, only to leave you unsure as to which is the "best" choice after witnessing all the possible short-term outcomes because there isn't always a good resolution to a situation. But, as much as I love this game, I also feel the need to be honest about the things it doesn't really get right.
This is my favourite game on Steam and I'd definitely recommend getting it if you're still undecided.
EDIT: While the ending may not feel satisfactory to some fans of the genre, I think that it is more true to the message of the game and that it is the journey there that really matters. Even after already completing the game and knowing how everything will turn out, I found myself making some of the same choices in additional playthroughs instead of trying out alternatives because of how deeply the game makes you feel about the characters.

I've always been a fan of open world and the ability to explore for myself, without being led by the hand from point A to point B. Life is Strange does an incredible job to entice me to scour the world around me (well, around Max), not for items and trinkets to sell, but rather for insight into each of the characters' thorough backstories. If you like detail, you'll adore this game Every new area is well lived-in and expansive with options, setting the stage for you to find out as much or as little about every character as you choose to. Aside from the touching storylines and beautiful visuals, this game really shines in its ability to convey characters in a way that is far from linear. Life is Strange really goes out of its way to convince the player to keep clicking on objects in the world, even if they've found the quest-specific things they need to progress the story. Searching Chloe's room for a music CD in the first episode was truly a highlight for me because without having to listen to a drawl of unnessesary exposition, I could find out for myself what kind of person Chloe was, by looking at all the stuff in her room. All I really needed was the CD to progress, but I wanted to hear Max's running inner commentary about everything I could click on, regardless of relevance.
Snooping game extraordinaire, Life is Strange makes searching for that one hidden item that you need to complete a puzzle way more fun when everything you click on is tied to a teenager-y and snarky comment. Explicitly, it tells you just enough, and then leaves hidden jokes, side activities, and character backstories for you to stumble across at the most unexpected moments. I really loved that I could choose how much to see of each character's life, whether I cared enough to look into every drawer or pick up every letter. That said, the vivaciousness of the Life is Strange world and the looming mystery are just too good not to go digging for every little piece of the story Max can get her hands on.

I've always been a fan of open world and the ability to explore for myself, without being led by the hand from point A to point B. Life is Strange does an incredible job to entice me to scour the world around me (well, around Max), not for items and trinkets to sell, but rather for insight into each of the characters' thorough backstories. If you like detail, you'll adore this game Every new area is well lived-in and expansive with options, setting the stage for you to find out as much or as little about every character as you choose to. Aside from the touching storylines and beautiful visuals, this game really shines in its ability to convey characters in a way that is far from linear. Life is Strange really goes out of its way to convince the player to keep clicking on objects in the world, even if they've found the quest-specific things they need to progress the story. Searching Chloe's room for a music CD in the first episode was truly a highlight for me because without having to listen to a drawl of unnessesary exposition, I could find out for myself what kind of person Chloe was, by looking at all the stuff in her room. All I really needed was the CD to progress, but I wanted to hear Max's running inner commentary about everything I could click on, regardless of relevance.
Snooping game extraordinaire, Life is Strange makes searching for that one hidden item that you need to complete a puzzle way more fun when everything you click on is tied to a teenager-y and snarky comment. Explicitly, it tells you just enough, and then leaves hidden jokes, side activities, and character backstories for you to stumble across at the most unexpected moments. I really loved that I could choose how much to see of each character's life, whether I cared enough to look into every drawer or pick up every letter. That said, the vivaciousness of the Life is Strange world and the looming mystery are just too good not to go digging for every little piece of the story Max can get her hands on.

Many games of the "role-playing choices" genre are either about morality or consequences of your choices. This game focuses more on the latter, meaning that your choices actually do matter in the way the plot advances. It makes sure you know it with the haunting butterfly warning you about everything you do, tempting you to rewind time and say/do something different, only to leave you unsure as to which is the "best" choice after witnessing all the possible short-term outcomes because there isn't always a good resolution to a situation. But, as much as I love this game, I also feel the need to be honest about the things it doesn't really get right.
This is my favourite game on Steam and I'd definitely recommend getting it if you're still undecided.
EDIT: While the ending may not feel satisfactory to some fans of the genre, I think that it is more true to the message of the game and that it is the journey there that really matters. Even after already completing the game and knowing how everything will turn out, I found myself making some of the same choices in additional playthroughs instead of trying out alternatives because of how deeply the game makes you feel about the characters.

Life is Strange probably has the richest story content I've seen in my life when playing games. If you are looking for a great story and immersion, this may be the best choice for you.
Synopsis: You control Max Caulfield, a photography student who discovers she has the power to rewind time. Your main mission is to solve the mistery about a missing student called Rachel Amber. With the aid of your power to rewind time, you can change the story and make decisions that may change your destiny and other characters' destiny as well.
CONS:

PROS:

At first it seems like a teen game that might have had Diablo Cody write a copy of the script (Not that that's a bad thing!) but there are a lot of little moments that add up to a really good experience.  Definitely worth $4 an episode, and I've seen that your choices really do matter.
I like the graphical style of Sims-realish on the people, and the music sounds like what a college student might hear a local artist play in a coffee shop.  Max being a photographer is something I can connect with, and I enjoy the pop culture references.  I especially enjoyed when Max looks at a plasma TV and say's "Man, I might have to sneak in here to watch 'Final Fantasy: The Spirits Within'!  I don't care what anyone say's, that's one of the best sci-fi movies ever made."  Obviously the line is there because it's Square-Enix, but Max's personality works with liking that movie with a slight hipster-ish attitude, so it doesn't feel forced and adds a tinge of realism.
Controls and time reversal work well, but whenever I take too long before plays I forget that you have to click and then drag the mouse.  A little unorthodox, but it works.
I'm looking forward to seeing how everything concludes!

An amazing episodic story-heavy game about a girl, Max Caulfield, who gets the sudden power of being able to rewind time.
The first episode spends time getting to know the characters and making you learn the mechanic of rewinding time, but even then, you will have a lot of choices to make. And unlike some other episodic games, your choices will very much matter. Some more than others.
Rewinding time can be used in short bursts, like after making a decision. This way you can check both decisions, and choose which one you want to stick with. The best thing is that sometimes this actually makes it harder to make a choice, as a lot of times both answers seem like the bad ones at first. You won't always know what a decision will do until the next episode or even 3 episodes later.
Interacting with objects and people is done by walking up to it/them and pressing a button on the controller (or dragging the mouse in a direction) The same mechanic is used for dialog trees. Most objects are easy to spot so you don't miss too many. What you might miss though, are some of the optional photos. They're quite a nice little side-quest to do.
This game's story will give you feels. Have tissues ready.
In all seriousness, the story is amazingly well written, and I wish I could hang out with some of the characters. Through playing this game, it already kinda feels like I am.
And the music in this game... Oh my god the music is amazing. The way episodes start and end with the music is freaking awesome.
Anyway this was my attempt at writing a review for my favorite game of 2015. Hope it was helpful to you.

I don't think I can add any more insights than the 15.000+ positive which came before me. There should not be any doubt: buy this game, and prepare to be swept away by the storytelling.
True, there are a few disturbances on the technical level. Facial expressions could be better, lips could be synced to the dialogue, textures and objects could be more detailed, some dialogue does not really hit the nuances of the gameplay (e.g. how pretty much any comment on Victoria is negative, even if you tried to be nice), and there is always someone who finds the story predictable/cheesy.
But all these minor issues are irrelevant when you play... the interactive story - calling it a "game" somehow does not feel appropriate.
This is not really an adventure, although there are a few puzzles. But they are too rare and not overly complex - I was able to solve them. Dialogues are not a hurdle as you can rewind time. There are no quicktime events (AMEN!), and you can play at a very relaxed pace.
So! Get the download going and prepare for several hours of pure entertainment!

It is frankly rather shocking to see such lip movement in any game in 2015, let alone in game that relies so much on story. Situation with overall facial animations is better, however they too could use improvement.
However, leaving that little flaw be, it really is perfect game, if you look for story-driven experience. I've always liked these games a lot. Go play it!

This review is written right after my first playtrough of chapter 4. I try to leave it devote of spoilers so it all will sound a bit generalized. It is my first review on here and it was written way past my bedtime.. please forgive any typos.
VISUALS:
This game is a treat to the eyes.. A wonder-gem like you wouldnt belive.. So the graphics are simple.. details and particles and everything seems rather simple, but it just works. The characters look real enough that you can really submerge in the game and the main characters are just so.. plausible.
SOUND:
Cant say very much about the sound, but what I can say is it fits so well with the game, it helped me get 100% submerged into it.. I played trough each episode in one sitting and forgot time, went to bed late (and will probably pay for it tomorrow at work). The sounds in the game work. They do what they need to do to complete the image and feel of the game. Voice acting works very well too! Couldnt have found better voices for the characters.
ATMOSPHERE:
It feels genuine with genuine people and genuine situations.. Mostly everything you do in this game feels like it has a reason. You are rarely in a hurry, you get to walk around and look at everything, study and just marvel in the universe they created.
The game has a darkness to it.. There is something thats just a little.. wrong.. something that feels a little off. The feeling of danger, but not really. The impending doom, yet still not.. Sadly I cant divulge spesifics without spoiling it all for ya so you kinda just have to experience it for yourself.
GAMEPLAY:
The choices I get to make.. I dont feel like they directly affect the main plot of the game, but oh my god.. they affect me.. This game will make ya feel good.. it will make ya feel bad and if you make bad decitions, it will make you feel horrible.. The game gives rewards and penalties in a way that leaves you with a feeling and it will keep reminding you of what you have done.
CONTROLS:
They just feel good. The game is simple and gives good visuals wherever you have stuff to do, the manouvering of the character feels okey and responsive, meaning you can focus on the gameplay.
THE NEGATIVE:
-There is a point in episode 4 where our main character is supposed to use a more determined voice.. I dont quite feel it as much as I'd have liked. It comes trough sometimes, but I would love more of it.
-Sometimes our sidekick acts... very slightly unnatural. I would assume this is is to push the story in a direction and I can approve. It happens rarely and not overly so, so I guess one can have a tiny few of those without breaking the game.
- That particle cloud in the sky.. Are those insects? Are those birds? I can never quite tell. In episode 4, I never saw it.. I saw some birds though.. Maybe they changed it?
OVERALL:
This game has shocked me the most of any I have played before. We are not talking jump-scares (Fear, Dead Space.. etc). We are talking un expected, spine tingling, punches and jabs right in the feels.. kind of shocks. Everything comes together well in this game and there have so far been no game-breaking lacks, faults or errors, no parts of the game I felt it could do without..
What I aspecially like about this game is.. it is not in a hurry. You get to spend all the time in the world enjoying all the work they have put into the game, you get to talk to a lot of people, check for stuff, look around.. If you miss something you can in most cases just rewind a little.

For a lot of people, there's a strange window of time in adolescence between high school and college where everything transitions so enormously that you depart from the life you'd been living until then, and you can never quite go back to the way things were before. People go away, they change, they become different people than they were, and sometimes the people they turn into are people you don't get along with, anymore. Sometimes, you aren't sure what kind of person YOU are turning into. It's all in flux, and going home can make it more difficult to sort out, because there are pressures from the past on you to be like you used to be, but you just can't be that person anymore.
Life Is Strange deals with that aspect of life a lot, because that's when the game takes place for its protagonist.
It's also about personal responsibility to others, linked in part to those expectations and questions of identity. Is it always wise to do whatever makes someone else happy? Probably not -- and the game isn't shy about that, either, sticking to realism over the feel-good satisfaction of solving every sticky situation with a feel-good solution. Without saying anything spoilery, I have done something nice for someone particular in every episode (sometimes more than once), and I have this sneaking suspicion that it's setting me up for doing more harm to them than good in the long run. What's neat is that I think that statement could apply to my interactions with almost any character in the game. It's very successful at making you feel as though nothing is cut and dry.
The fact that all of this observation about relationships and growing up are framed by a very cool, supernatural time-manipulation mechanic is just icing on the cake, to me. That period of our lives is so charged with significance and potential, and everything happens so fast...I think many people probably wonder how things could've been different for them. As the game lets you discover, though, sometimes it's better to just take life as it comes, and do the best you can...because you can't fix everything, or everyone.
Life Is Strange has a kind of infectious nostalgia about it, reinforced by interesting characters and surprisingly dark situations. The story shows you a lot of human suffering -- but it's also full of sweetness, and it can be very funny.
Definitely recommended.

This game is fantastic!  Great story, and the choices make a difference.  It isn't just option A or B like telltale games.  (I like telltale, but they really need to improve on their choice system).

For a lot of people, there's a strange window of time in adolescence between high school and college where everything transitions so enormously that you depart from the life you'd been living until then, and you can never quite go back to the way things were before. People go away, they change, they become different people than they were, and sometimes the people they turn into are people you don't get along with, anymore. Sometimes, you aren't sure what kind of person YOU are turning into. It's all in flux, and going home can make it more difficult to sort out, because there are pressures from the past on you to be like you used to be, but you just can't be that person anymore.
Life Is Strange deals with that aspect of life a lot, because that's when the game takes place for its protagonist.
It's also about personal responsibility to others, linked in part to those expectations and questions of identity. Is it always wise to do whatever makes someone else happy? Probably not -- and the game isn't shy about that, either, sticking to realism over the feel-good satisfaction of solving every sticky situation with a feel-good solution. Without saying anything spoilery, I have done something nice for someone particular in every episode (sometimes more than once), and I have this sneaking suspicion that it's setting me up for doing more harm to them than good in the long run. What's neat is that I think that statement could apply to my interactions with almost any character in the game. It's very successful at making you feel as though nothing is cut and dry.
The fact that all of this observation about relationships and growing up are framed by a very cool, supernatural time-manipulation mechanic is just icing on the cake, to me. That period of our lives is so charged with significance and potential, and everything happens so fast...I think many people probably wonder how things could've been different for them. As the game lets you discover, though, sometimes it's better to just take life as it comes, and do the best you can...because you can't fix everything, or everyone.
Life Is Strange has a kind of infectious nostalgia about it, reinforced by interesting characters and surprisingly dark situations. The story shows you a lot of human suffering -- but it's also full of sweetness, and it can be very funny.
Definitely recommended.

I haven't reviewed any of my games before, but after playing through episode 1-4 of this one, I had to write a review.
(Sorry about the badly structured review in advance, try not to bleed from your eyes whilst reading this)
It's pretty hard for me to put into words how good this game is so I'll try and explain bit by bit.
Life is strange starts off really slow, but this isn't necessarily a bad thing. The game does an extremely good job at making itself feel "real". I mean, the way it's presented, how you walk  around the school campus, attend your lesson, actually sit at your desk and listen to the teacher speak, all in real time. It feels so real and immersive. You can interact with almost everything in the environment, examine it and hear your character comment on it. Life is Strange also references real life titles of movies, videos games, anime, you name it, which connects you even more to its world. When you have a classmate text you asking whether you've watched Cannibal Holocaust, or when you read your diary and notice that the main character likes anime like Fullmetal Alchemist, you can really relate to the world and the people in it. The amount of detail that the developers put into each and every environment you explore is huge. I mean you can just wander around the school halls and read posters or notices on the boards talking about extracurricular activities you can join or some guy trying to sell a bike, these little things really flesh out the world and make it feel like you are really there, living out the life of a Blackwell Academy student.
As for the story, I won't say much on this topic as I don't want to spoil anything for potential buyers, but the story is good and I mean really good.  Like I said, it starts off slow, you just got accepted into Blackwell Academy, you're going to live your student life in this great school, etc etc, then about 15 minutes into the game, certain things happen and you discover that you're actually able to rewind time. From that point onward, the game becomes really interesting, the story slowly starts moving towards a more gripping and mysterious plot and it's exciting to just see what's going to happen next. It really grips you and doesn't want to let go. You won't want to put it down.
And this brings me onto gameplay. Life is Strange is much slower in terms of pace compared to a lot of games you might've seen this year. You'll spend most of your time walking around interacting with things around you, talking to people and just being nosy/curious. The biggest part of gameplay is the rewind power. For example, let's say you spoke to someone and said something that you regret. You're able to rewind and repeat the conversation and say something else this time for a different result. There are even puzzles which require you to speak to people and use the rewind ability to obtain information or certain items. The way it’s done is really smart and the amount of choices you can make and the different results they will have later on is incredible.
I mean Life is Strange is really fantastic, this review definitely doesn't do it justice, but here's something that I really enjoyed in the game that blew my mind;
There are moments throughout the game where you can find places to sit down and when you do, your character begins thinking of things that have been happening lately and or sometimes reminiscence about the past, just sort of summing everything up and thinking about how she feels about everything. During these moments, the camera changes angles, sort of showcasing the area you're in and you get some sort of slow peaceful music in the background (The music is fantastic in this game by the way).
It's during those moments that I realized Life is Strange isn't just about following the story, it made me see the big picture it's trying to paint. Seeing life as something that is actually quite strange. Realizing that these small or even big everyday choices we make have an effect on the future, on the people or the world around us. It made me see how life changes from being a kid to being an adult. You know, sort of seeing the transition you went through but on someone else and then looking back on yourself and thinking "Damn a lot has changed" It also made me realize that every person has their own story, I know it’s a cliché, but it really made me see that everybody has their own issues and reasons for why they are the way they are and that we should never really judge a person too quickly. There's just so much it has opened my mind to that I can't possibly explain without looking like I'm repeating myself or making no sense.
I'm not sure what else to say here, but I really, really recommend you to buy this if you've even thought about it a little bit. Life is Strange is a nice change of pace and it will definitely not disappoint if you're patient and enjoy taking a game slowly.
TL;DR
BUY IT!

I recommend Life Is Strange, but with reservations. Firstly, it requires some time investment to get through the weaker first two episodes, and second, of course, it's a game about story, not explosions, fast cars, hot chicks, big guns and sunglasses indoors, so don't bother if those games are your (only) preference.
Life Is Strange follows Max Caulfield, a college student whose life changes abruptly when she finds out she has a special power, one doubtless connected to the strange and ominous events occurring around her. Max is a bit of a gray mouse at Blackwell, but she is recognized as being talented and gifted in photography, the course she takes at the highly-prestigious school. Apart from Blackwell, though, Arcadia Bay, her hometown, is anything but prestigious, a rundown place of poverty and misery, held in the iron grip of the Prescott family and their fortune. This setting is the centre for a series of strange events both wonderful and terrible, and Max and her childhood friend Chloe find themselves the only ones who can uncover the truth behind these happenings.
Life Is Strange is story-driven, and the gameplay is limited to interacting with objects and conducting dialogue, but since it's a game that relies on storytelling, this isn't a bother at all. Players looking for a profound experience instead of quick action (or perhaps as a break from it) will be more than satisfied with the barebones gameplay, since it leaves room for the story and characters to manifest optimally.
When Life Is Strange says your choices matter, it actually means it. Unlike a certain second season of a certain story-based game about the ambulatory deceased, this game makes sure that your choices aren't purely cosmetic, and they don't get overridden two minutes later anyway, "just because the game said so". Your choices have a profound effect on the story, and every little one can matter. On the other hand, due to Max' special power, you will have the option of seeing how many of your choices play out (in the immediate future at least) and change them if you feel they didn't have the intended effect. Your choices, eye for detail, memory, and thoroughness of exploring the environment may determine if people live or die, break up or reconcile families, and form alliances and enmities. And all these effects
, they don't just change a few lines of dialogue, they really change the story in a meaningful way.
And the story you'll change is absolutely memorable and engaging. Once you make it through the first two chapters (see below) the story really reaches in, grabs you by the small intestine, and doesn't let go. The game throws curveballs at you (some more predictable than others) and from chapter three onward, events build up so quickly you'll be unable to put the game down. The ending of chapter three and first half of chapter four may be one of the best-written story segments in a video game ever, and after that, the game doesn't let you go for a moment either.
The storyline is engaging and gripping, but you'll have to invest some time in going through the first two episodes, which are very slow and rather lukewarm in content. I found the first two chapters to be a bit of a drag, without much story progress and without much excitement. Chapter one plays a bit like "High School Drama: The Game" and chapter two does little to help that. However, like I said, when you reach chapter three, you'll be glad you stuck it out.
Another thing that did bother me about Life Is Strange so far is that, well, it's not
hipster as I feared, but it does still aim heavily for the online-millennial crowd, and you can tell a bit too often that the game overeagerly caters to the very same crowd its story is centred on. A lot of the characters are flatly archetypical, even though the game does try to nuance them, and Max, the main character, teeters on the edge of the Abyss of Mary Sue, with Chloe pinwheeling right there next to her. This isn't to say the writing is bad, it isn't, at all, but there's a rather unfortunate bias and eagerness to please The Modern Internet Student running underneath it. Expect trendy social commentary, a negative view of authority and "the privileged", and of course the worship of bacon.
There are more little nagging details, like the lack of proper lip sync which makes the game look like a bad Chinese kung fu-film dub, but those can be readily ignored by anyone with a decent suspension of dibelief.
Lastly, the devs were dead-set on making the dialogue "hip" and "neat", so be prepared to tell yourself a few times that, wowsers, this dialogue can be hella cringey at times.
I was highly skeptical, both before playing and while playing the first two chapters, but my friends told me to stick it out, and I'm really glad I did. So buddy, you stick it out too, I promise, you'll be glad too.

Despite going to an elite school for science and seemingly photography, life is so hard for Max as no one understands her, despite having plenty of friends, no one likes her, despite living in a place that appears to be basked in eternal sunset, it's just so hard being happy, despite suddenly finding you can rewind time at any point (actually only when the game will allow) she finds life so hard to understand. Complain much Max? Despite beautiful presentation, Life Is Strange is constantly dragged down by its dire characters, it's hard to feel any compassion for people that are so entailed and act out their one dimensional lives in a dreadful teen drama. It's like contrasting the problems of Beverly Hills 90210 and that of The Walking Dead. After episode one here's hoping that town gets destroyed by a tornado, but actually over water it's called a cyclone.

This is an absolutely gorgeous, unique game. It pulls you into the story from the start, and keeps you intrigued through each scene. I love the fact that there are so many awesome female characters.
The artwork is strange and beautiful, with the incredible attention to atmosphere as something to be lauded. The lighting, the wonderful environmental sounds, and the heady music all meld together to provide one of the most immersive gaming experiences I've ever had. One of my favorite environmental sounds is the way Max dries her pictures after they are taken. Even the shower curtains sound so perfect, and bring me back to my dorm days.
The voice acting is phenomenal, and their ability to put the depth of emotion into each character is astounding. Some of the characters make you feel empathy and connection, while others do a good job of making you dislike their blatant "teenaged leanings."
Finally, the game play makes you feel as though your actions really matter. Each one of your decisions is important throughout the game, and could have lasting impacts. They allow you to build strong relationships with each character---friend or foe---and those relationships play out in a way that is truly grounded in life.

If you're into games with a strong emphasis on story & narrative, you might fall in love with Life is Strange just as I have. As far as the nitty-gritty mechanics go, it could use some tweaking. The story itself though is amazing.

This is an absolutely gorgeous, unique game. It pulls you into the story from the start, and keeps you intrigued through each scene. I love the fact that there are so many awesome female characters.
The artwork is strange and beautiful, with the incredible attention to atmosphere as something to be lauded. The lighting, the wonderful environmental sounds, and the heady music all meld together to provide one of the most immersive gaming experiences I've ever had. One of my favorite environmental sounds is the way Max dries her pictures after they are taken. Even the shower curtains sound so perfect, and bring me back to my dorm days.
The voice acting is phenomenal, and their ability to put the depth of emotion into each character is astounding. Some of the characters make you feel empathy and connection, while others do a good job of making you dislike their blatant "teenaged leanings."
Finally, the game play makes you feel as though your actions really matter. Each one of your decisions is important throughout the game, and could have lasting impacts. They allow you to build strong relationships with each character---friend or foe---and those relationships play out in a way that is truly grounded in life.

If you're into games with a strong emphasis on story & narrative, you might fall in love with Life is Strange just as I have. As far as the nitty-gritty mechanics go, it could use some tweaking. The story itself though is amazing.

Disclosure: This review was written before the release of episode 5, and will contain some (very minor) spoilers for illustration.
I bought "Life Is Strange" on a whim kind of knowing what to expect as its mechanic is very similar to the type of game Telltale Games makes with their "Walking Dead" series and various other franchises. The story in these types of games is invariably linear, with the player's choices affecting the outcome of the outcome of the story to a certain (usually small) extent while creating the illusion that you've influenced the story a lot.
From a technical point of view, there's very little to criticize about the game. The graphics are decent enough, sound and music is okay, gameplay is fairly standard (with one notable exception) for these type of games, and it does try to have a compelling enough storyline to keep you playing.
The notable gameplay exception and most interesting mechanic in the game (and perhaps the very thing that the game stands out for) is that the player often can rewind time after making decisions, undoing their actions and look for the most optimal outcome to his/her taste. I have rather ambiguous feelings about the mechanic, because while on the one hand it allows you to make the (seemingly) most ideal choice, but on the other hand it only reinforces how utterly futile your choices really are in the greater narrative. The mechanic is sometimes used in an interesting way to solve puzzles, with a somewhat recurring theme of opening locked doors or accessing areas you don't have access to.
It's that very core mechanic which is also the game's weakest point. While you are presented with various moral dilemmas through choices in dialog and actions, the consequences of your choices are just one button away from being undone, and while it is fun to explore the options it quickly gets tedious.
At some point in the game you are presented with the dilemma of euthanizing someone at their request, but the choice doesn't really matter. You can go ahead and euthanize that person, rewind, decide not to, rewind, do it again, etc etc. And it is that very scene where as a player it should suddenly dawn on you: the choice itself just doesn't matter to the story. Not even 5 seconds after what is supposed to be a terribly hard choice that should affect you in some way the game leaves you no other option but to hurl yourself into the past to undo the events that lead up that moment, resetting everything for the sake of narrative continuity regardless of the choice you've made.
The narrative can't carry the weight of the moral dilemmas it tries to present, so it quickly runs off into a more comfortable zone leaving whatever weight your choice might've had as an afterthought for a cheap shot at evoking forced drama. Sure, you could argue that there was a moral to that choice, but whatever it was trying to convey is lost the moment it was reset.
As the story continued I found myself not to care about the outcome of my choices anymore. Pull the trigger or not pull the trigger, solve something peacefully or have someone else shoot a person, throw a dogs toy into the street or somewhere safe, ... In the end, despite the choices the story will continue to head towards its end no matter what with no real difference in the greater narrative other than a few extra dialogue options.
On a side note, I personally find none of the characters likeable with hardly any of them really standing out. The characters are too close to stereotypical: rebel punk grrl, introverted art student, queen b**ch and her troupe of merry henchwomen, jockey frat boy, secluded christian girl, overworked and late on all of her bills waitress mother (talk about cliché), etc. For a game that is supposed to be carried by its writing, the characters in general are incredibly flat, which certainly doesn't help in caring about them when the forced drama sets in. The character design reeks of "design by committee" where the writers sat in a meeting room making a list of traits they'd include and just used that list alone to create one character at a time based on a single trait.
Finally, the game is full of not so subtle references to popular culture and blatant namedropping. From Edgar Allen Poe references, to gollum impressions, to Stephen Hawking and namedropping dozens of photographers. We get it, you have access to wikipedia too. It becomes tedious very soon, and slapping a bunch of internet memes on top of that just isn't helping. We get it guys, you went on the tumblr/reddit/twitters and found some "dank memes" or whatever and now the game feels young and cool and hip... Right? I personally was surprised they didn't come up with "When this wheelchair hits 5 miles per hour, you're gonna see some serious s**t" but that would've killed that shallow moment.
I can't really say that it is a bad game, because it does exactly what is advertised, and it is fairly polished from a technical point of view. I just find the narrative wants to delve into themes it can barely scratch the surface of, which sadly leaves the player with an incredibly shallow experience while hoping the game had a "fast forward" button instead of a "rewind" one.

-----Life is Strange Ep 1 Review-----
Story: Well I don't really want to spoil anything but what I will say is the story definatly got me hooked and it's a driving factor for this game!
Gameplay: Well the gameplay is pretty simple but very cool so far. If you have played games like Telltale's The Walking Dead, or The Wolf Among us it's like that. One thing that is different though is you have the power to reverse time. This power brings up a cool mechanic to solving problems. You can go backwards to undo actions or try to be faster than an NPC cycle. Although I haven't really ran into anything that stumped me yet going through this was really fun! One thing that I like is when you say a certain thing or do an action

The game seems perfectly optimized (I did use a Xbox One controller though) The music is pretty chill and fits the scenes perfectly. First of all, I do recommend this game. I do feel however, it's not really for me, since I - being a mid 40's man - have trouble identifying with a 18 year old teen. Let's start there:
Using a premade protagonist in a game is always risky, since you don't know what people can identify with. In shooters, it doesn't matter that much that you play as Duke Nukem or whatever since the character is unimportant, bot for games like this, the character IS important since you are playing a story. Life is Strange revolves around Max, a girl who recently turned 18. I could, if I stretch my imagination long enough accept that I play like that. However, the developers also gave her an interest - photography - and that plummeted my interest for the game and the character Max even more to the point I don't care any longer. Why? Because I, the player has no interest in photography.
There's that. We then learn about the cliché teens at her school (the cheerleader, the jock, the bullied geek... Only clichés. Not ONE who appears genuine) and there is that problem too. I have no interest whatsover in teen college drama.
The voice acting is uninterested and boring, and not ONE actor makes an effort.
For me, it's a very boring game with some very simple puzzles. But I do recommend it if you can put yourself in the shoes of a boring teen girl. But if you can't, don't bother.

I first started this game late one night on Twitch. I was watching LolRenaynay stream this game for fun, and I came in right when Max discovered her powers. I stuck to the stream like glue until the very end and since then I've been hooked. The only regret I have is not purchasing it myself after Episode 1 and waiting until the fourth installment to do so.
The game itself however is like something out of your best dream; you wish you could be IN it instead of just casually observing it, soaking in every detail like a sponge of emotion.
The game is more than a game. The art style is one of a kind, despite being used on such a popular engine (Unreal). It's simplistic yet beautiful. The soundtrack is peaceful, despite the chaos and tense moments of this work of art, every time you open your journal or pause menu you get this peaceful acoustic guitar riff that eases you away from any sadness or anger (which is plentiful in this game once you get into it). The music outside of the theme (Amanda Palmer, Syd Matters, etc.) is very indie and comfortable that I've begun to listen to it while on the job.
But the story? Chapters 1-3 were very rewarding and had a deep TV show series-feel to them with the epilogues blocking out most of the ambient noises excluding dialogue with indie music like I mentioned above.
Chapter 4 was extremely dark and took myself and thousands (is it thousands? I hope so) of other players to a region we weren't expecting and had, no, HAS us dying to see it through.
It's very bittersweet seeing the final installment coming up in a little over a month, but I have faith in Dontnod and Square Enix that they will send this game out with a bang. Thank you for reading and I hope you have/share the amazing, if not better experience than myself.

There are buzzwords and expressions thrown in like "steampunk, hella, for reals, go ape(?)" and a handful of others that are used inappropriately and cause constant eye-rolling. I really wish the writers didn't try so hard to seem "in-touch" with today's youth because it ruins a lot of the immersion.
The game's choice-and-consequence system is its greatest asset. Unlike the recent Telltale games, the decisions in this game are plentiful and actually change the course of the story. The rewind dynamic is neat and doesn't feel half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ The soundtrack is mellow and befitting of the feel of the game.
If you can look past the almost unbelievably stupid spoken lines, I can recommend this game.

This is an episodic game and as fans of the genre are already aware, it makes generous use of cliffhangers and other means of making you crave for the release of the next scrap of story. At the time of writing I just finished the penultimate episode of this game with the release date for the conclusion currently unknown; it is a heartbreak and a half.
The last time I was invested like that in an adventure game of this style I played the first season of Telltales "The Walking Dead" - that one was already fully available and could be binged on without pause. Which it was. And I do think that made it a better game, as much as I like serials in movies and on TV.
Which is why my recommendation is definitely going to be a positive one - with a catch: everybody that appreciates adventure-games that revolve around exploration, dialogs and decision-making will have a lot of fun with "Life is Strange". That is, if the context of highschool- and teenage-drama is not something one would be averse to - keeping an open mind in that respect definitely helps.
As for the catch - wait until all of the episodes are available. The season pass kept me (positively) anxious for the last couple of weeks/months, but I would have had an overall better time with this if I did not have to wait quite that long; while the episodes are decently long with 3-4h each, the gravity of particularly events do lose some of their impact if they're spaced so far apart.
All in all, thumbs up. If you're unsure, check out the first episode

I haven't really been playing many adventure games lately, but I took a chance on Life Is Strange after seeing some positive reviews and so far I'm really enjoying it. Without revealing too much, it's basically a story that revolves around Max Caulfield and her return to her hometown of Arcadia Bay, Oregon to attend prestigious Blackwell Academy for her senior year. General drama abounds as she reconnects with people from her childhood and navigates the morass that is teenage life.
Gameplay-wise, the game was designed with consoles in mind but is perfectly playable with a mouse and keyboard. The puzzles that you face are rather simple, but I didn't notice that so much; for me, the main draw was in the story. The characters are likeable, and the way the story unfolds reminds me a lot of the show Veronica Mars in that a lot of small stories play out within the confines of a larger story arc.
People emphasize the importance of player choice and its lasting effects in games these days, but I'm not really sold on that vision. There's only so much a writer can do with branching storylines without compromising the strength of the underlying narrative. That said, I think that Life Is Strange does it just right in that there are choices that affect small things—mostly things you would look at and think "huh, cute"—and choices that affect how people react to you later on in more important situations. It doesn't sacrifice the cohesiveness of the main narrative, but still gives you a sense of agency.
All in all, I'd say play it.

I finished episode one and am fully hooked.
I'll tell you now, I don't play many episodic games, never thought they were for me. Telltale games started a genre, and Dontnod perfected it. I have had my heart ripped out, jammed back in my chest, to be ripped out again. It's an incredibly relatable story for anyone who has ever been a teenager just adding to the depth. You won't be disapointed buying this game.
Pros:
+ Visuals - The art style is made to be as it is, not just a lack of caring. The photos that look as though they were drawn adds a nice touch. The scenery is beautiful, looking over the lighthouse is an image that I will never forget. Characters have a distinct style, almost a steryotypical vibe (ie skaters, nerds, preps, etc.)
+ Atmosphere - You will lose yourself in this game. The background music is always there, setting the mood. Very good fading on the music as well, no sudden jumps.
+ Story - The bulk of this game. I can't put it into words and don't want to, you need to play this game for yourself. Just imagine a Steven King book writen in a high school setting.
+ Choices - Unlike 'Whose Line is it Anyway?' the choices DO matter, and you WILL see the consequences of those actions. Some are small, some are big. You WILL see them though, no doubt.
+ Rewind mechanic - An interesting mechanic that the game introduces. Have second thoughts on a decision? You can go back (I personally don't, but can see if you click the wrong way). Also, interesting puzzles are solved via this mechanic.
+ Characters - You will grow bonds with characters as odd as that sounds. You will see a girl and instantly think 'hey this girl is awesome!' I won't say why, but these situations happened multiple times. The characters have depth even with little build up time.
+ Emotion - This game will toy with your emotions if you're into that thing.
+ Techincal - Game seems to run very well on an old GTX 650 with an i7 and 8gb of RAM. Can almost guarantee the game will run on lower specs as well.
Cons -
- Visuals  - This is clearly a artistic choice, but look at the screenshots if you are concerned. I find the art style appealing but can see others not liking it. However, this game shouldn't be discounted based on its graphics.
Seriously, if you have a soul you will like this game. It takes the high school experience and shoves in some interesting sci-fi stuff. Not aliens (I don't think...) but time travel. You will love this game if you look around at all the small details rather than rushing through. Enjoy the immersion in the world.

You might be able to do it slightly faster but aside from missing some things I had to get (Hello, bottles) I got through it pretty quickly. If you actually check out all dialogue options, all people you can talk to, and explore some on the side, you can probably get 20 hours easily, on a single playthrough of the first four episodes. There's also decent replayability: Even if you found everything, there's some things you might choose to  do differently, giving a handful of things you can do every episode. This was especially displayed in episode 4, where I missed out on a certain scene altogether. All in all, you'll get a very nice playtime out of this game, well worth it's price.
The story is... Nothing short of amazing. Of course this'll vary on a player by player basis, but the characters are realistic and feel  really fleshed out. There's endearing characters, there's creeps, and there's straight up ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. However despite sticking to their general behavior, friendly characters can be manipulative or creepy, and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s can be found to have a soft side, or even be sympathized with. Again, based on how you play the game and how you respond to things can make you feel differently, but I thoroughly appreciated the depth of these characters.
Now the presentation, which is in my opinion it's strongest point by far. The visuals are nothing short of beautiful. Combined with the soundtrack, which is also nothing short of amazing, (Seriously, check it out sometime) it makes for one of the most impressively presented games I've played since the Okami re-release, or Mirror's Edge. There's really not much to say here, it's the one thing you really have to see or experience to fully appreciate.
Now you get all this, for either 20 euros if you get it all at once, or 22 euros if you try ep1 first and get the rest if you like it.
In short, the game is a beautifully constructed, well thought out game, that can get people hooked on the story-driven point and click gameplay in the blink of an eye. It's a nice and long story, interesting throughout all of it, and unless you're the most obsessive of explorers it will give you a really nice amount of replayability.
It stands out the most in it's presentation, mixing great visuals with a great soundtrack.
All in all it's an amazing game, but that's not enough: They go and sell it for less than half the price most games cost nowadays.
I'm convinced there is not a single game that'll stick with you as much around the same price, and very few that do in general.
Putting all this together, if you're looking for a number rating I can easily give this a 9.4/10. It's simply good, it's enjoyable, and I've encountered not a single glitch or bug as it should be. There's few games of this quality, and while the wait between episodes is a nasty few months, it is extremely worth it, not to mention it will be fully available once the next episode releases.

I have full confidence that the conclusion to this series will be a fantastic one, if not likely heart-wrenching, like much of the series.
tl;dr: Play this game. PLAY IT, DAMMIT ... and bring tissues... and schedule an appointment with the nearest therapist. *thumbs up*

Amazingly good game, and worth a try even for folks who normally play more "core" games. You play Max, and 18 year old girl who has mysteriously gained a superpower--the ability to rewind time. You must decide how to use this power to solve both simple and complex problems as an overarching mystery unfolds.
Pros:
+Very strong sense of immersion thanks to dialogue, environment details, and pacing.
+Fun core mechanic (rewind) that leads to interesting puzzles.
+You have the chance to rewind after mistakes or dialogue to see what other options would have led to, erasing the need to save/reload constantly.
+Great use of music/soundtrack.
+Fully fleshed out characters that seem human.
+Great writing filled with teenage slang.
+Great exploration and collection mechanics via Max's photography skill.
Cons:
-Sometimes there is no right answer and you'll have to live with the tough consequences of your decisions :-(.
-Small areas require you to suspend belief as to why you can't explore more.
One of the best games I have ever played.

This game completely tore my heart apart from Episode 3 onwards. Awesome!
- The voice acting is fantastic, we're talking major cartoon/animation level voice acting.
- This games causes you to make decisions that would be incredibly difficult to make in real life because of the consequences that come with all of them. It's not a simple case of "do this and you'll benefit in this way". Each character has such a complete personality and the differences you make are obvious and often conflicting with another character's interests. In the most recent episode you have the make the most difficult decision in the entire game - no matter which way you go, you'll be in pieces afterwards. Basically, the story and decision tree is awesome.
- The art style is interesting. In some places the style can conflict with itself due to some items having a complex/detailed appearance whereas the rest of the game has a very basic, solid appearance. Overall, the game looks great - but some areas conflict with the house style.
- The music is warming and intense in the right places. The developers really knew how to make you feel like you're supposed to, given a scenario. The music for major decision scenarios don't punch you in the face with intensity, but it also isn't timid. It's just right.
However...
- Sometimes a character's facial expressions can seem rather blank/empty. This is mostly a concern with minor characters, which makes it obvious that the developer didn't spend enough time with minor characters to complete the experience.
- You rely on camera angles to be able to reach and interact with certain items. When items are grouped together closely, this can be a bit tricky to deal with.
Overall, this game is a heartwrenching and technologically solid experience. I'd recommend it to anyone who loves a heavily story-driven game, particularly anyone who loves a coming-of-age drama. The experience is less clunky than similar TellTale games, which turned me off of this kind of point-and-click style experience. Life is Strange pulled me back in. This is one of the best games I've ever played, and I really look forward to future games from Dontnod.
9/10, please play this.
