I've decided to review this game following the release of the fourth episode, and not the final episode. The reason I've decided to do it this way is complicated, but it basically boils down to "I don't think the ending will have any bearing on my decision." On the game's discussion forum, I've noticed some people talking about the potential endings (I will not reveal any spoilers in this review) and how if it happens one way the game will be bad, or if it happens the other, it will be good.
Not only do I disagree with this, I outright reject it as a concept.
Life Is Strange has hooked me like no other game has, to such an extent that, had you showed me this game before release and told me I'd be this hooked on it, I'd have laughed at you. I like shooters, I like racing games, I like fighting games. Mortal Kombat is one of my favorite games, and while I have enjoyed many indie games and games of this type in the past, this one really opened up the floodgates and exposed me to a whole world I've never considered myself a part of.
Everything about this game is incredibly well done. The story is very interesting, and the fact that I go into frequent old-man rage about today's teenagers doesn't actually get in the way of the fact that this is actually a very accurate representation of those teenagers (with ... you know, a time traveling mechanic added in). Early reviews of the first episode talked about the dialogue being bad, and not sounding authentic. Most of the people saying that have no idea what teenagers sound like, apparently, because this dialogue is pretty damn spot on.
I'm also reviewing this now and not later because I think the Episodic format actually helps this game a lot. After every episode I'm incredibly interested in discussing theories and while the wait has been a little on the long side between them, I don't think I'd have enjoyed the game so much if it were all released at once.
The graphics are excellent for the aesthetic they're going for (I only wish the lip syncing was a little better) and the music sets the tone for an atmosphere that is nailed perfectly. There are points in the game where you have an option to sit down and your character will go over some of the things she's currently thinking, and the framing and sound design of those moments make me never want to actually stand up and resume the game, regardless of how good the game actually is.
I really don't want to spend so much time on the story. All I can say is that I find myself caring about the characters and what happens to them deeply. How I interact with them -- and seeing at the end of each episode how everyone else interacted with them -- is incredibly important to me. I think the story it top notch, and the way it's been handled through four episodes has been excellent. We're dealing with time here -- time travel, time rewinding, chaos theory, etc -- there's bound to be SOMETHING that angers SOMEBODY. But I'm just here for the ride, and I've loved every second of the game through four episodes.
Can't wait to see how it ends.

Incrediblly engaging story, difficult choices that make a huge difference in the story.  One of the few games that I've ever wanted to go back in play through again and again just to see all the different possibilities.

In 'Life is Strange' you start off as an 18-year-old girl named Maxine (Max) Caulfield, with the passion for photography. But during class, she ends up having a terrible vision and later discovers she has the ability to rewind time. From there on, it's up to you to decide how our little pirate should use her powers.
'Life is Strange' takes interactive gaming to an entire new level. Each episode has major significance and meaning, that it gives each character such vibrance and depth. Attention to detail is everything, as any artist would know, which you'll quickly learn once you start up this game. The people in the game don't have as much  detail, but the environments which surround them are an acrylic painting brought to life, right onto your monitor, waiting to be explored. This is especially true whenever Max decides to sit down and reflect on all the crazy stuff happening around her, as her world slowly spins. 'Life is Strange' is so much more than anything I've ever experienced. Minus the time traveling, each event is so relatable that the messages and choices within the game truly make you contemplate the life you've paved, since each choice effects more than ourselves.
The multitude of emotions this game creates through its storytelling is unrivaled in anything you'll find in a book or movie or other game. I 100% believe anyone reading this should immediately buy the game, if not just the first episode to experience exactly what I'm describing.

There are points in the game where you have an option to sit down and your character will go over some of the things she's currently thinking, and the framing and sound design of those moments make me never want to actually stand up and resume the game, regardless of how good the game actually is.
I really don't want to spend so much time on the story. All I can say is that I find myself caring about the characters and what happens to them deeply. How I interact with them -- and seeing at the end of each episode how everyone else interacted with them -- is incredibly important to me. I think the story it top notch, and the way it's been handled through four episodes has been excellent. We're dealing with time here -- time travel, time rewinding, chaos theory, etc -- there's bound to be SOMETHING that angers SOMEBODY. But I'm just here for the ride, and I've loved every second of the game through four episodes.
Can't wait to see how it ends.

In 'Life is Strange' you start off as an 18-year-old girl named Maxine (Max) Caulfield, with the passion for photography. But during class, she ends up having a terrible vision and later discovers she has the ability to rewind time. From there on, it's up to you to decide how our little pirate should use her powers.
'Life is Strange' takes interactive gaming to an entire new level. Each episode has major significance and meaning, that it gives each character such vibrance and depth. Attention to detail is everything, as any artist would know, which you'll quickly learn once you start up this game. The people in the game don't have much detail, but the environments which surround them are an acrylic painting brought to life, right onto your monitor, waiting to be explored. This is especially true whenever Max decides to sit down and reflect on all the crazy stuff happening around her, as her world slowly spins. 'Life is Strange' is so much more than anything I've ever experienced. Minus the time traveling, each event is so relatable that the messages and choices within the game truly make you contemplate the life you've paved, since each choice effects more than ourselves.
The multitude of emotions this game creates through its storytelling is unrivaled in anything you'll find in a book or movie or other game. I 100% believe anyone reading this should immediately buy the game, if not just the first episode to experience exactly what I'm describing.

Though this game's dialogue is painful at times. It has it's moments where it shines and shows it's unique story. If you can tolerate the hipster enviroment that has consumed our planet, I would definitely recommend this game to you.

This is a review of each episode of Life Is Strange because each one has its own strengths and weaknesses. At times they feel disjointed and slapped together; however, there are some outstanding moments in story continuity that continue to baffle me because of how well-tied together some of these events were by the end of episode 4. (Will complete review on episode 5 when released)
Gameplay: 7/10
In Life Is Strange, there are several gamplay mechanics that stand out as unique amongst a crowd of otherwise blank faces in the gaming industry. Foremost is the time-rewind ability. This works extremely well in conjunction with the other RPG-esque dialogue mechanic. Principally, this is how it works: Have you ever wanted to take back something hurtful you said to a friend? Well, with this ability, you can! Spill milk all over your homework? Not anymore, it's like it never happened. The only person who definitively knows the alternate outcomes to anything like this is *you*. Max, the main character, is the only one who retains knowledge of both outcomes.
This is where Life Is Strange most obviously shines and fails at the same time.
For example, if a person goes through a lot of small talk in order to get to the root of a discussion, it stands to reason that if you could go back in time you could alter events to expedite that outcome, cut the crap, so to speak. Life Is Strange does this, but not consistently. If you implement a mechanic into a game it must be an effective constant for the player, reliable. It's like playing a platformer where the jump button only works
of the time. This point could be argued, but not without spoilers. This is an extremely plot-driven game; therefore, I will not expand on specific instances where this is the case. I *will* say that this dialogue-mechanic-hole is hardly noticeable in chapter 1.
Furthermore, the rewind ability itself does not feel gimmicky at this stage in the game.
The third thing that makes this game unique is the Polaroid picture collectables system, whereby Max takes pictures of things that she finds interesting. They only add a little bit of actual enjoyment of the game. I found myself wishing that I unlocked cool stuff by taking pictures of these useless things but was disappointed by the lack of incentive to actually taking these pictures. The main thing this mechanic allows for is character development, but even then, I don't feel like Life Is Strange took full advantage of this.
One last point, the gameplay is slow. It's definitely not a game for everybody. The reason for its apparent slowness falls into the category of the game's...
Story: 10/10
Life Is Strange Episode 1 starts off with a bang. It then proceeds to force your hands down as it makes an even louder bang so that you completely know who is in control of your mental faculties. Then....! It whispers for the remaining duration of chapter 1. Being completely honest, the game can very easily scare people off with how slow it seems after the initial phases of the game. She's a normal, hipster-teenage girl, so you can expect her to do *mostly* hipster-teenage girl things. She can't fast travel (technically, which I have a problem with that will be discussed in further detail) she gets into anime-esque slice of life problems, she has love troubles. All of these things play into the game's
VERY well, but do not necessarily bode well for the gameplay.
That out of the way, Episode 1 establishes who this girl Max is, it sets up her own personal issues as well as her friend's personal issues, it sets up the larger problems with the school, AND it sets up the grand problem threatening something that will not be spoiled. The way the story unfolds is heavily centered around how you treat the people around Max and what you tell her to do.
This, however, again, leads me to a semi-negative subpoint:
Main Character: 7/10 (This ties back into game play)
Ordinarily, I probably wouldn't include this section on a gameplay review, but this game is so extremely story-driven, you need to know what you're in for. So without further ado, I will explain the main character that you are stuck with through the whole game, not necessarily in a bad way...
The BIG problem I have with the main character: our girl, our lovable hipster - is that she only sporadically, deeply thinks about the consequences of her actions, which is HUGE for a person who has the ability to
. Now, you might say that it's up to the player to think about how their decisions will effect everything around them and that's why the game chooses not to explain certain rationalizations that Max makes through the game, even going the lengths of explicitly stating this between episodes. Because it is a game. Here are the flaws with that reasoning; If you are a game designer, don't make me choose between two extremes that are unrealistic in a game based loosely in reality. Every time I wanted to think out of the box for a solution to Max's problems, I was pigeonholed back into the same rut of 'Gee, I sure wish I could interact with this' or 'It sure would have been nice if Max could have said that'. It breaks immersion and I realized that I was playing a story that I only had so much control over because it is a video game/interactive movie that has specific points that it wants to convey. This probably broke immersion for me worse than the loading screens.
Graphics: --/10
This game is practically art about art. Art is highly subjective. I will say that I
enjoy the style they decided to use with this game. It might be a different experience for you, but I think if you're not a graphics stickler, you'll enjoy this game in spite of the -sometimes- lackluster textures.
Gameplay (In line with what I established for episode 1) and Story: 8/10 and 10/10 respectively
Episode 2 of Life Is Strange is better in every single way. The game improves on Max's relationships. It improves on visualizing the consequences of your actions, even minor ones. It feels more emotional, more complete. It even hides smaller character interactions and photo ops better than the first episode, so even though you don't unlock anything significant, you feel a sense of accomplishment at the end of the chapter when you get to see how many people failed where you succeeded.
eg. Say

Granted, it's mildly annoying when you find out you missed something earlier in the chapter because it blatantly tells you instead of you finding out on a later playthrough, but at the same time, it provides an aggravating incentive to want to replay through the chapter, as
as that sounds.
The major difference between chapter 2 and chapter 1 is that chapter 2 is ten times more exciting. The plot picks up dramatically and Max actually does stuff with her time-rewind ability that matter on so many different levels. This, of course, adds to the excitement of using the mechanic that, up until now, has remained static and limited in its use.
At this stage in the episodic arc, the game poses ethical questions more pointedly at the player: If you had Max's power, how would you use it? Would you use it for fun? Granted, there is one instance in episode 1 where this is presented, but it's much more sharp witted in episode 2. Episode 2 also explores the trauma of seeing multiple outcomes to the same event!

Life is Strange gets better with each episode. It starts as a somewhat innocent seeming teenage-high school drama but builds layers upon layers as it progresses. A brooding, unsettling feeling is established very early on in the game. Not everything is quite right in the seemingly idyllic and sleepy Arcadia Bay, and not everyone is as they seem. Life is Strange explores the strength of friendship and the darkest depths of the human condition through the lens of an aspiring young photographer with a special gift that allows her to rewind time and try to do what we'd all like to: correct the mistakes of our past.
The game offers a tremendous amount of content to analyze and ponder in a thrilling, riveting mystery-adventure format featuring a touching coming of age story populated with interesting, multi-dimensional characters. These characters are developed naturally, rather than with clichéd exposition found in lesser narratives. Even very minor characters have the potential for interesting development depending on player interaction. These characters are clearly not only a product of their births, but also of their experiences.
Life is Strange conducts itself with minimal moralizing and recognition of the complexities of human nature. Critiques by reactionary misogynists seem to be unfounded as strong, sympathetic male characters emerge over time (somewhat dependent on player choice). All the while it explores the very real dangers and abuses women suffer by the hands of some psychotic, entitled and insecure men.
Decidedly less 'feminist' concerns such as bullying, corruption, man's ignorance and hubris towards nature, and how society marginalizes its ill are also tackled masterfully. Topics within science and mysticism are a recurring theme and are handled in a balanced, mature manner and seemingly without much bias.
Equipped with a fantastic, fitting and seamlessly immersive soundtrack including Indie selections and original compositions from Jonathan Morali, excellent (for the most part) voice acting and a beautiful, handpainted feel to the visuals. Technical mishaps (most notably the lip syncing in earlier episodes - *now fixed in a recent patch*) have been vastly improved upon in later episodes.
While still early, this could very well be one of the greatest games ever made and is definitely one of the strongest showpieces for video games as art. The unique impact of LiS could not be replicated by any other medium and shows how interactivity is critical to the poignancy and transcendent qualities of this artform when it is at its finest.
Highly recommended
*A couple of quick notes on EP 5 that I will rewrite into the review at a later date:
+ Two emotional 'grey' endings. Somewhat 'predictable' (I prefer to say 'foreshadowed' - how else would it end?). Thankfully no cop out 'happy endings' that insult the player's intelligence with a Hitchcockian explanation of the phenomena and choices in the game (juxtapose with the ending of the Hitchcock film 'Psycho' - the psychoanalysis). Could have really used a plant influenced ending though, clearly not watering the plant and letting it die should have turned the storm into a nuclear holocaust. ;)
+ Phenomenal art direction, particularly in the nightmare / penultimate segment.
+ Themes and philosophical content remained consistently poignant (lack of taking sides on religion / science, environmental concerns etc)
- Minor quibbles with some of the antagonist's dialogue and actions near the beginning but developed well. Will probably resolve with further reflection.

I'm gonna update this review now from it's previous version, because I finished the game long ago. Simply put, this game revolves around a mystery involving the disappearance of a girl, Rachel Amber. The protagonist, Max, investigating said mystery with her old childhood friend, Chloe, also happens to gain the ability to manipulate time. With it, and with the rekindling of her friendship with Chloe, Max tries to put the pieces together and make sense of Rachel Amber's disappearance as well as make sense of her ever growing abilities with time manipulation.
Now, lemme just go on to say, this game has moved me and put me in more emotional turmoil than any other game I have ever played. No book or movie has ever made me cry for and care about something with such passion as I felt during this game. For comparrison, Quantic Dream games like Heavy Rain or Beyond: Two Souls, are kinda similiar. They feel more like movies to be honest, with lots of action involved in terms of gameplay (ie. hopping up and down, shaking your controller, hoping you don't die as a result of your actions).
However, Dontnod's Life is Strange feels more like the chill, down to earth version of those experiences.  It sorta feels like watching a movie, but with the quiet intimacy and immersion of reading a really good book. Everything feels like real day-to-day, but then there are elements that are extremely out of sorts and that's what makes this game such a curious mystery.
You become so thoroughly invested in this story that you feel as if you become the protagonist herself. Her pain is your pain, her joy is your joy. You learn to love and hate the people she interacts with. You become devastated and overwhelmed by your actions. You experience this huge array of feelings, only to come temporarily to your gamer senses long enough to reflect and think, "wait, I'm playing a game? I completely forgot." It is an experience like I have never had before.
It's probably best that this game released in episodic increments, allowing for it to cliffhang its audience quite effectively. If I had to make a reccomendation (since the entire game is out already out), if you haven't tried this game yet and are going to do so, try playing through one episode at a time and taking a short break in-between to give yourself time to theorize and think about what the story is doing. The story paces itself wonderfully as is, but I feel like having those periods of rest allow you to fully appreciate the plot and take in all the game has to give.
Many people have voiced how they didn't like the ending to this game. That everything about it was excellent, save for the ending. And their qualms essentially boil down to "I didn't feel like my choices really mattered in the end", and to be honest, that's true to an extent. You make a series of choices throughout this game, and most of them have short-term consequences and some you see further down the road, but when it comes to major decisions, life works essentially the same way. And that's why I love this game. I honestly don't go day-to-day remembering all the mundane choices of my life, I only spend time reflecting back on major life decisions. This game isn't necessarily about the importance of free choice, but more about the journey of navigating through them. I could go on about this game for ages. This game is a masterpiece to me, whether people agree or not.
In conclusion, please give this game a try if you haven't played it. Hell, play this game even if you're not even that fond of games. If you're fond of hearing a good story, this game is for you. I know a few people that shrugged it off from the get-go during episode 1 just because they felt it was too hipster, or too lame in terms of the story moving at first, but it does develop to be so much more than that.

Life is strange is a masterpiece, in just a week it became the best game I have ever played making my feelings go all around the place, it probably has the biggest and most intense roller-coaster among games and you will never regret buying it (specially in such low cost). I have never felt so connected to a game character, the protagonist made me find something beautiful in every aspect of life while the history, music and small details made me feel like if I was dead inside seeking for the meaning of life itself . As a final comment, when people first see life is strange they think that it is some other "girl story" but do not be tricked after playing one or two episodes you will feel like if every episode affected your life making you see clearer than ever that life is indeed strange.

A lot of the characters are kinda annoying and self destructive, just like real life. Getting them (especially Chloe) to not ruin their own lives is a lot like herding cats.
Each episode gets progressively better, starting out at a resounding "meh" and ending up at a "pretty good".
It's not a terrible investment if it's on sale.

The story so far up into Episode 3 is definitely one that adds to my 'favourites' book. The story is well and truly captivating and the harsh reality many of the students within the game face can be seen as sad and heartbreaking, rude and jock-ish, or funny and heartwarming.
Whilst I am waiting for episode 4 to come out, Episodes 1, 2, and 3 have all had their own shares of gut wrenching, nail biting moments. The characters are all seperate, no two of them alike, and whilst a few do follow the cliche of your typical school-like group of cliques, and yet they all work well in tandem with eachother.
The game mechanics are very nice, the plot is interesting and daunting, and I'm personally happy to say that the game runs extremely smoothly on my PC even on higher settings and ever during more detailed scenes where you would expect framerate drops. The plot-based mechanic of controlling time is also very interesting, a think I've never seen done so well in a game.
The story itself runs very linearly with sides of stories and events branching off. Whilst you will end up in similar situations, the decisions aren't deceptive in that they don't effect the game. In fact, a choice you decide to make at the very start of Episode 1 haunts your words and choices by the end of Episode 3, and decisions from Episode 1 and 2 could either make or break some key moments in Episode 3, and I've never felt so ashamed of myself for having "messed up" my decision making, and the decisions aren't easy to make either.
If you're looking for a Young Adults game revolving the mystery of time control, with an interesting plot, great game mechanics, nice and not too overly complex graphics and modelling, I would definitely recommend this game to you, and I personally would say that the awards the developer's have had so far have been well deserved.

Life is strange is a masterpiece, in just a week it became the best game I have ever played making my feelings go all around the place, it probably has the biggest and most intense roller-coaster among games and you will never regret buying it (specially in such low cost). I have never felt so connected to a game character, the protagonist made me find something beautiful in every aspect of life while the history, music and small details made me feel like if I was dead inside seeking for the meaning of life itself . As a final comment, when people first see life is strange they think that it is some other "girl story" but do not be tricked after playing one or two episodes you will feel like if every episode affected your life making you see clearer than ever that life is indeed strange.

A lot of the characters are kinda annoying and self destructive, just like real life. Getting them (especially Chloe) to not ruin their own lives is a lot like herding cats.
Each episode gets progressively better, starting out at a resounding "meh" and ending up at a "pretty good".
It's not a terrible investment if it's on sale.

The story so far up into Episode 3 is definitely one that adds to my 'favourites' book. The story is well and truly captivating and the harsh reality many of the students within the game face can be seen as sad and heartbreaking, rude and jock-ish, or funny and heartwarming.
Whilst I am waiting for episode 4 to come out, Episodes 1, 2, and 3 have all had their own shares of gut wrenching, nail biting moments. The characters are all seperate, no two of them alike, and whilst a few do follow the cliche of your typical school-like group of cliques, and yet they all work well in tandem with eachother.
The game mechanics are very nice, the plot is interesting and daunting, and I'm personally happy to say that the game runs extremely smoothly on my PC even on higher settings and ever during more detailed scenes where you would expect framerate drops. The plot-based mechanic of controlling time is also very interesting, a think I've never seen done so well in a game.
The story itself runs very linearly with sides of stories and events branching off. Whilst you will end up in similar situations, the decisions aren't deceptive in that they don't effect the game. In fact, a choice you decide to make at the very start of Episode 1 haunts your words and choices by the end of Episode 3, and decisions from Episode 1 and 2 could either make or break some key moments in Episode 3, and I've never felt so ashamed of myself for having "messed up" my decision making, and the decisions aren't easy to make either.
If you're looking for a Young Adults game revolving the mystery of time control, with an interesting plot, great game mechanics, nice and not too overly complex graphics and modelling, I would definitely recommend this game to you, and I personally would say that the awards the developer's have had so far have been well deserved.

Life Is Strange is an episodic game that uses a similar system to Telltale games like The Wolf Among Us and Game of Thrones in which your decisions determine how the story unfolds. The game follows Maxine (Max) Caulfield who is an 18 year old girl whom, after a mysterious vision and a disturbing incident, finds that she now has the ability to rewind time at will but only within a certain time frame. She then sets out to solve the mysteries that surround the small Oregan town of Arcadia Bay and the prestigious Blackwell Academy, as well as search for answers about her newfound powers, her mysterious and foreboding vision and the fate of a missing girl.
Now to begin with, I can not stress enough how good this game is. The choices are honestly really difficult and deal with real ethical dilemmas that have major impacts on the people and world around you unlike other similar games in which only a small group or individual is affected. This is by far the best story driven game I have played in a LONG time or possibly ever. Unlike other games you really start to feel an emotional attachment to the characters and because of this the choices at times are heart-wrenching and you have to begin to think about the big picture and how your choices can ultimately affect the world and everyone in it. In conclusion, this is a game that I would reccomend to anyone that likes a heavily story driven game in wich you're decisions truly DO matter and I give it a 10 out of 10.

Imagine a rollercoaster that was so slow, climbing to the top took forever.. When you finally reached the top, you only had seconds to gape in awe and fear before you were plummeted into the unknown.
That's the effect this game had on me, from the thrilling and saddening parts to the calm and happy parts. Now, I'm typing this review after just completing episode four and.. WOW.. It got so dark.. Everything about the game is BEAUTIFUL, the voices are good, the graphics I love.. But the lip syncing kind-of-sort-of stinks.
You know, what I was expecting from the game was a Tilt-A-Whirl, like a dog (Maybe named Pompidou) chasing their tail, over and over. I expected repetitive things for no darn reason. In ways, it WAS like that. But that's because everything loops back together eventually. Brilliant.. Now, if you excuse me, I must replay it.

She then sets out to solve the mysteries that surround the small Oregan town of Arcadia Bay and the prestigious Blackwell Academy, as well as search for answers about her newfound powers, her mysterious and foreboding vision and the fate of a missing girl.
Now to begin with, I can not stress enough how good this game is. The choices are honestly really difficult and deal with real ethical dilemmas that have major impacts on the people and world around you unlike other similar games in which only a small group or individual is affected. This is by far the best story driven game I have played in a LONG time or possibly ever. Unlike other games you really start to feel an emotional attachment to the characters and because of this the choices at times are heart-wrenching and you have to begin to think about the big picture and how your choices can ultimately affect the world and everyone in it. In conclusion, this is a game that I would reccomend to anyone that likes a heavily story driven game in wich you're decisions truly DO matter and I give it a 10 out of 10.

This game makes me wish I had the power to reverse time. Once you figure out that the choices you make in the game actually matter it becomes a game of click goddamned everything and talk to everyone about everything, but doing so feels so rewarding when the payoff comes around.
Life is Strange gives me that feeling like I'm playing an old point-and-click adventure game with a 3D mix. Solving the puzzles isn't hard as you can just reverse time at any point once you are given the ability to do so. The difficulty of this game isn't whether you're solving the puzzles or not. It's whether or not you're doing the right thing. At times it's obvious what the good choice is or what the selfish choice would be when given certain things to say to a character, but it's possible to make a moral choice and having it blow up in your face later on. The obvious moral choice isn't always the best one.
The story may not be something that would intrigue everyone. It's your typical teen-drama with a not-so-typical time travel aspect thrown in. The typical teen-drama cliches are there, but the time travel of the game makes things different enough to stay interesting.

Life is Strange is an episodic adventure game from Dontnod, whose previous game, Remember Me, was also its first.
In the style of most episodic games, Life is Strange relies on a choice-and-consequence narrative in which players take on the role of high school student Max Caulfield - a young woman with the power to rewind time. While the game focuses on Max's school life, it also sheds a light on her relationships and the mysterious disappearance of a local girl.
As Max, players navigate school life through a linear path, interacting with classmates, teachers and friends through choice-driven dialogue. But these decisions aren't set in stone; once a conversation is over, you can choose to "rewind" time. You can relive a scenario as often as you like with no consequence, though your powers only allow you to back up for a set amount of time.
Let's talk about Life is Strange's most obvious hook: the do-over. We get this a lot in video games, but it's mostly used as a life-saving mechanic — rewinding to avoid spikey pits, fireballs or any number of cartoonish things. With Life is Strange, Dontnod created a world in which conversation is your greatest foe. I spent a great deal of time picking a path, rewinding, and tumbling down the other hole. But you know what? That didn't always make it easier. Sometimes, I found myself second and triple guessing my responses.

This game is truly excellent. Pretty, interesting, engaging puzzles, great story, even (in my opinion) decent voice acting. Very dramatic, which isn't for everyone, but I don't think many would be disappointed with a purchase of this.
Can't wait for the new chapters. Game is episodic, at time of writing 3/5 chapters out. The final two have something to live up to for sure.
Very point and click, choices are interesing though, its like a really good old text based adventure game, but brought into the present. Graphics are good, detail is ok, but the game has an excellent feel, feels warm and welcoming in the right places and gloomy when needed. Choices have genuine consequences and it really seems like there are a lot. Replay value is high in my opinion, I think it's likely that most players will miss some things the first time through.
Sound and music is absolutely fantastic, really adds to the mood and turns the game from great to great AND very immersive.
Character introduction is not all that complete, but in my opinion this adds to the story, as there is a definite mystery to it.
Drawbacks are few in my opinion. Controls feel clunky in tight spaces, but this is vaguely annoying only, as by the time it matters you should be used to it. Game isn't generally fast paced so no one should really ever feel the need to RQ due to this.
It's hard to tell exactly what your choices will do to the story when you make them. I don't necessarily see this as an issue, but I wouldn't be surprised if some did.
Camera can be a little aggravating as it can move unexpectedly, but its contextual. so does help the player progress through the story.
Overall, great game. Would highly recommend/10.

Most choice-based games are very locked to the rails- you're essentially just clicking "next" a whole bunch.

An actually fairly well done (technically) take on the TellTale "interactive story" game. Descisions can actually matter to some extent, and performance isn't abysmal like the TellTale engine.
Fairly interesting story, though there is a lot of deus ex-machina and inconsistencies. There are random "points of no return", or times when your power is limited or disabled, which is odd for a game about rewinding time to fix your mistakes. Also, using the time travel mechanic you can break a lot of story sequences (go past some required conversation, rewind while standing in place, and you now technically 'never had' that conversation). Also, your power manifests with different abilities, but you can never really use those extras on command to fix fairly obvious problems. Overall though, things are handled fairly well.
However, I'm not sure how it's possible, but without fail, EVERY SINGLE CHARACTER comes off as pretentious and an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Honestly. pretty much every single character in this game, I hate more than ANY character in ANY other game. This goes for the protagonist as well. So, if you can't enjoy a story where you hate all of the characters, it may be best to stay away.
Would recommend.

Bought this game because my girlfriend and I are into playing these story-type games together, and it is really good so far. (Chapter 3/5) Typically I play through these games once, and don't replay them because I like the choices I made. This is one of the only games I want to go back and replay.
Some advice, pay attention to everything, even the little details. It will bite you in the butt if you don't, you'll miss key parts of the story and bad things will happen because of it. In an example that doesn't include spoilers, at one point I needed to divert a train to a different track. I was rushing, I didn't look around enough. I broke the train tracks. It worked, I diverted the train. But there was another way that didn't damage the tracks (I found out about it later) and I know breaking the tracks is gonna come back to bite me. Your choices carry stronger and bigger effects in this game then in similar games, and you'll notice that at the end of the chapter when it compares your choices to others. There's a heck of a lot of them. (Many are very minor things, the amount of major choices are about the same as other games. But they all matter one way or another.)

Oh god, wow.  A 3D interactive game where you play as Max, a girl returning home after a few years away so she can go to the best photography school. She is quiet, average girl who is gifted with the power of rewind and her humdrum life becomes bizarre and risky. Soon she learns that all choices have consequences, and even with rewind her choices ripple farther than she could see into the future. On top of this she still has to deal with bullies, drugs, best friend drama, and all the other stress of being a teenager. How do you make your choices? Even good intentions can have dire outcomes.
At the time of this review, we are still waiting on the last two chapters, but are supposed to be released soon (actual dates). Gameplay can get frustrating as you move your “crosshair” over to what you want to interact with, and then slide your mouse in the direction of the choice you want. Many times I made a choice that I didn’t mean… luckily you have the power of REWIND! I also had a glitch when I first installed and had to Google how to fix. Others have posted how to fix this (mine needed a language reset).  All that aside it was fun to play.
9/10

Quite simply one of the best games I've played this year. If you're a fan of the Telltale games but you're looking for something a little different (and better, in my opinion) look no further. Finally a game that takes the lives of teenage girls seriously! I have never so quickly developed empathy for characters in a game quite as fast as I did in this one. Without spoiling anything, the end of the second episode really struck home for me, and it was something I needed to see right now in my life.
The rewind feature is masterfully implemented and it makes you wonder, even if you make a different choice, is it the right one? Is there ever really a right choice, even when you know how all the choices will pan out? The supernatural element is also an interesting addition to the game's narrative, though without having played the rest of the game I am not sure how I will think of it by the end.
If you want to get emotional and maybe cry about fictional teenage girls, this is the game for you.

If you've played the Walking Dead games by TellTale... Then you'll know the type of game this is. SquareEnix apparently thought they needed to get in on it, and they did a pretty good job, except only once have I been hit with the "waaaat" factor that hit me a lot in Walking Dead and Wolf Among Us. It's a slow game, and feels like it drags on and on for the first hour or two during each season especially when you cover every inch of every area to make sure you didn't miss anything... until you take a look at the achievements and realize you missed a lot. Dangit, now I have to replay it sometime (as if the different choices weren't enough reason).
Speaking of the choices this game sort of flips Walking Dead style on its head and lets you look at each and every choice over and over and make the one you want. This gets rid of that (once again) waaat factor and permanent feel of your choices in Walking Dead since you have time to consider it, but at least you'll have some idea of what you're getting into before you make your choice. One complaint I may have is that the game doesn't seem happy no matter what choice you make, and that's a little offsetting to the point of my decisions.
Anyway overall it's an addicting game. Just as you start getting tired of it the story gives you a reason to keep playing, and if you want something that's low stress and on the level of an interactive book with graphics then this (and all the others I mentioned) are games you should get into.

I just finished episode 2 and I must say that this is one of the best game I ever played ! It's like playing in a movie.
In Life is Strange, you are Max, a young student who suddenly discovers that she can rewind time. There is a lot of mystery surrounding the story so I won't spoil anything.. But she keeps having this strange vision/dream of a lighthouse where strange things happen...
This game is really similar to Telltale's games. In each cutscene/dialogue, you have some options about what to say or what to do. Some choices aren't really important but some really matters since it changes the story a lot !!! (and I'm only at the second episode). You can also interact with a lot of objects/posters to know more about characters or just about anything. The good thing about all this information is that you actually care about the characters because they all have a story.. You can even open your diary to see your personal diary in each chapter to understand Max's thoughts, notes about everyone and other things like that, it's really a nice addition to the game.
One of the best part of the game is the music. The music is perfect for this game. It's a relaxing mix of guitar/piano with some really great songs. It's an important part of this universe and it really makes you feel that you're really in there. In that world.
The graphics are gorgeous. Sometimes, you'll enjoy to take a look around just to see every single detail that was put in this game. It's really amazing how it really feels real. Each chapter should lasts about 1h30-2h to finish depending of your interactions with everyone or if you want to observe everything that this game has to offer.
In conclusion, if you like story-driven games, you'll love this game. It's one of the best (if not the best) in this genre and it's really an unique experience. I would recommend this game to everyone because I seriously doubt that someone can hate this game.

TL;DR: This game is absolutely stellar for its art style, music, characters and story, but the PS4 version is better performance-wise if your PC isn't very "high-end."
Wow. This game is such a rollercoaster. It takes you for a ride that you want to go on over and over again. When I've played certain games, such as Telltale's The Walking Dead, I was never completely certain that my choices mattered. It seemed like the story always turned out the same way and was just as easy throughout. But now that the time flow mechanic is added, there is a plethora of possibilities for the game to go off of. And the developers do that in stride. The story of Maxine Caulfield, while cliche, is so relatable and deep that it has driven me to tears at times. It is such a surprisingly action-packed game, and at the same time it has such a deep story with genuinely interesting characters. I also enjoyed the multiple references to The Catcher in the Rye (look for them, you'll find 'em!) and Jack Kerouac. The game could easily get a five star rating off of its symbols alone. I also enjoyed the music in the game for improving the vibe of the autumntime which the game takes place during. It gives the story a whole other dimension that is hard to ignore. Though some games' soundtracks end up detracting from the story, Life Is Strange's does nothing but build upon an already epic foundation. It is also easy to relate to many of the characters because of their common traits and sayings that are connectable to modern life. While it does get cliche at points, and the voice acting is slightly below-par in some cases, for the most part Dontnod does a stellar job with an ensemble cast of interesting and relatable characters. But even if all of the above were non-existant, the game shall truly go down in history for its dedication to story and choice.  Something as simple as watering a plant will have effects on subsequent episodes in the story. However, many of these actions and consequences would go very much unnoticed if you do not look for them, and it is simply one of many examples of the developer's dedication and belief in choice and playing the game you want to play. They can affect entire conversations, or simply affect a small piece of the game's environment. And the main choices in the game are true moral dilemmas that matter. Unlike The Walking Dead, and other Telltale digital products, choices in this game feel important. This is in part due to the relatable characters, but is also due to the enthralling story. This is a very hard combination to find, but the developers certainly do it well. However, if you prefer your games to be high on a graphical standpoint, I suggest getting the PS4 version of the game if you own one. The controls are slightly less clunky and there is certainly less stutter, while still achieving higher graphics. Overall, Life is Strange is excellent and is one of my favorite games of all time by a landslide.

TL;DR: This game is absolutely stellar for its art style, music, characters and story, but the PS4 version is better performance-wise if your PC isn't very "high-end."
Wow. This game is such a rollercoaster. It takes you for a ride that you want to go on over and over again. When I've played certain games, such as Telltale's The Walking Dead, I was never completely certain that my choices mattered. It seemed like the story always turned out the same way and was just as easy throughout. But now that the time flow mechanic is added, there is a plethora of possibilities for the game to go off of. And the developers do that in stride. The story of Maxine Caulfield, while cliche, is so relatable and deep that it has driven me to tears at times. It is such a surprisingly action-packed game, and at the same time it has such a deep story with genuinely interesting characters. I also enjoyed the multiple references to The Catcher in the Rye (look for them, you'll find 'em!) and Jack Kerouac. The game could easily get a five star rating off of its symbols alone. I also enjoyed the music in the game for improving the vibe of the autumntime which the game takes place during. It gives the story a whole other dimension that is hard to ignore. Though some games' soundtracks end up detracting from the story, Life Is Strange's does nothing but build upon an already epic foundation. It is also easy to relate to many of the characters because of their common traits and sayings that are connectable to modern life. While it does get cliche at points, and the voice acting is slightly below-par in some cases, for the most part Dontnod does a stellar job with an ensemble cast of interesting and relatable characters. But even if all of the above were non-existant, the game shall truly go down in history for its dedication to story and choice.  Something as simple as watering a plant will have effects on subsequent episodes in the story. However, many of these actions and consequences would go very much unnoticed if you do not look for them, and it is simply one of many examples of the developer's dedication and belief in choice and playing the game you want to play. They can affect entire conversations, or simply affect a small piece of the game's environment. And the main choices in the game are true moral dilemmas that matter. Unlike The Walking Dead, and other Telltale digital products, choices in this game feel important. This is in part due to the relatable characters, but is also due to the enthralling story. This is a very hard combination to find, but the developers certainly do it well. However, if you prefer your games to be high on a graphical standpoint, I suggest getting the PS4 version of the game if you own one. The controls are slightly less clunky and there is certainly less stutter, while still achieving higher graphics. Overall, Life is Strange is excellent and is one of my favorite games of all time by a landslide.

I am so glad that I only payed $2 for the first episode. Despite some stellar cut scenes and story in Remember me this game is a massive step back and let down on so many levels. The graphics have a low res texture painterly feeling that looks worse than Bioshock Infinite or Dishonored. I can get past that tough as it is, but for a game so focussed on story the muffling, mumbly, fumberly treatment of lip syncing is an absolute disgrace. It's just impossible to take the game seriously when every character looks like a talking baboon. Coupled with the audio hitching issues (more prevalent on laptop audio too) and you have a game that fails epically at the one thing this type of game HAD to be good at...presenting believable characters.
The real disgrace is that the developer is more than aware of the lip syncing issues, but claims they can't be fixed due to imitations of the game engine used and that it "isn't a high priority". Folks it's not 1999 anymore, plenty of graphic engines have supported motion capture and high quality facial animation for many years..there is just no excuse. Please DONT support this terrible drip feed experiment.

(Review written upon completing Episode 3)
Life Is Strange has all of the best qualities of a modern interactive fiction game--the heart of a text-based IF (with nods to such commands as "examine" and "undo" that are so well-known to text-based adventurers) but with the added vitality and immersion that comes with modern game design.  The story is involving and well-crafted while retaining its self-awareness--fully admitting to its influences in easter-egg references of various blatantness--and I was surprised how quickly and deeply I became invested in the characters.  The gameplay isn't particularly difficult, but there's enough nuance in the use of the time-rewinding mechanic that it remains interesting throughout.  And ultimately, the game is far less about gameplay than it is about the story and the anticipation of the varying degrees of effect our choices have on the story.
A brilliant game most definitely worth any player's time.  Highly recommended.

I thought my nose was going to start bleeding from all the repetitive rewinding. Better yet, dontnod needs to rewind and do ep5 again.

I'm two episodes in, and admittedly, I'll probably finish it, because I'm a sucker for choice in games, and it seems like the choices in this game are less illusory than those in most of its ilk. The game has promise, and I hope it delivers.
But right now? The game feels like it was written by someone raised in an isolation chamber whose only source material for "youth culture" is secondhand descriptions of Empire Records,MMO fetch quests, Stand By Me, and Telltale Games. Oh, and Twin Peaks, apparently. This game is not subtle about its influences.
Also, what's with the music? It's pervasive, but it positively screams "I am royalty-free and proud!"
I want to like this. Maybe someday I will like it. But right now, it feels like homework. I'm waiting on the emotional resonance.
Edit: OK, so episode 3 is the clincher. It's got everything. Chaos theory. That Mogwai song that sounds like the Cure's In Between Days (perfect), missed chances, emotional resonance. It's a damn shame it took this long, but I'm glad I made it here.

, but what you don't know is that it's actually
old at this point
.

Okay, okay. Time for the pro/con-section.
Pro:
- The graphics are absolutely beautiful. I did not expect such a polished game at ALL when I bought it. Actually, I don't know what I was expecting but man, did it deliver.
- The storyline is amazing so far, it's exciting and the protagonist is actually quite funny.
- The concept is really interesting, unlike anything I have seen in a game so far.
- SO MANY CHOICES LIKE SERIOUSLY SOOOOO MANY. And they actually impact the story a LOT, unlike some of the other choices matter-games.
Yes, TellTale, I'm talking to you. Watch and learn, young padawans. Watch and learn.
- It's pretty straight-forward, I didn't spend TOO much time running around like a confused little monkey child, wondering what the hell I was supposed to be doing.
- The characters are quite interesting and have their own voice; some of them are utterly adorable, others straight up kickass, and a select few kinda made me want to sucker punch them in the yapper.
All in all, I personally love this game.
The only con I can think of...
- THE LAST EPISODES ARE NOT YET RELEASED and I hate waiting for these things. I wish they were released in a bundle, but oh well. Can't have everything.

I'm totally biased as I've raised this game up to my personal GOTD. Which means something as I've played like TONS of games in my lifetime. But for sure, none has ever hit me in the feels so often like this pearl. Rarely did a game make me care about the protagonists. And I'm usually a stone-cold ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Seriously.
I admit that, if all feelings put aside, the game has some flaws in many aspects. But <beep!> that!

Best way to describe it quickly: A Telltale-game without the pressure of timed events that hits you right in the feels. Regularly. Until the end.
And in case you've never played one of the aforementioned:
It's an adventure. You play as a young dudette who discovers that she has a ...nah, see for yourself!
One thing's for sure: I'm totally not the target demographic, so for me it was a bit awkward to play an 18year old girlie geek-hipster, coz i'm
a 40+ year old male geek-nonhipster. But hey, at least I'm as introverted as she is. You gotta
start somewhere :-)
Did it matter? No.
But it helps if you're fine with tons of teenie-clichés and modern day references. Yes, the game drowns in clichés but it still manages to be damn lovely all the time.
Adventures like this totally depend on their characters and the story (as there is no real "action" or anything else), and both pay off.
The characters are all believable and authentic (even with all those clichés) and the story always has this subtle "wtf is this about?"-tone swinging along even while you do seemingly meaningless tasks. The epic soundtrack (that made me even get the OST) does a big part in setting up the atmosphere.
So if you're ready to ignore some regurgitated stereotypes and, if you're not a female teenie in school, are open minded for a more or less dramatic change in the point of view, you're in for an awesome tale!
Recommended?
If you loved the telltales? YES! YES! YES!
If you hates the telltales? NO! NO! NOOOOO!
If you love adventures for the puzzles and not for story? Nah, stay away, this would bore you to hell.
For all else: Maybe give it a go, you may be surprised (like I was...really)!

I liked the elements of choice found in Episode 1 and the story elements as well.  If the production crew can maintain this level of creativity throughout the episodes, it should be a VERY good experience.
That being said, there are a few technical problems I've experienced.  The interaction tags on certain items, especially in the later half of Episode 1, are very finicky, requiring that you stand at just the right angle in order to interact with them.  And you'll notice how I only talk about Episode 1, because I've encountered a HUGE game-breaking bug of that ilk in the beginning of Chapter 2 where interaction tags refuse to show up in Max's room, so you can't grab the item you need to leave the room, so you can't play the game.  Neither reloading the game nor restarting my computer helped, and I've found a few cases online where people were experiencing the same issues.  It might be a computer specs thing, so really fast computers MIGHT be able to get around it.  It's kind of a gamble though.
The narrative elements are truly promising, and it makes me sad that I can't progress due to this sort of technical issue.
edit: Turns out the issues I had were due to having an improper graphics card.  After playing on a new computer, I can safely say it lives up to my expectations and that you should buy if you're interested.  But seriously, check the system requirements to ensure you have the right graphics card.  It's no fun otherwise.

At the moment of this review, I am 3 episodes into "Life Is Strange." For the purpose of this review, it is probably easiest to simply list the pros and cons, in my opinion.
Pros:
+ Great story with unexpected twists and turns, even for an adventure and movie buff.
+ Great take on visuals and concept of awareness via photography.
+ Plays smooth and acts like an interactive movie that requires some actual thought.
+ Proficient voice acting. While the voice acting is not the best that I have ever heard for an adventure game, where voice acting is paramount next to story, it is convincing enough for the game's purpose.
- Puzzles can be a little too easy at times.
- Some phrases written into the dialogue kind of throw you for a loop. (Who in their right mind says hella?)
- I wish that the choices had more impact on the story itself.
Overall, I give it an 8.5/10. I love(d) the P&C era of gaming, and even though episodic adventures help modernize the genre, they also seem to take away some of what made large and open P&C games of yesteryear so loveable and challenging.
Definite purchase for anyone into an adventure with a great story that throws in some unexpected twists and turns here and there.

I'm totally biased as I've raised this game up to my personal GOTD. Which means something as I've played like TONS of games in my lifetime. But for sure, none has ever hit me in the feels so often like this pearl. Rarely did a game make me care about the protagonists. And I'm usually a stone-cold ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Seriously.
I admit that, if all feelings put aside, the game has some flaws in many aspects. But <beep!> that!

Best way to describe it quickly: A Telltale-game without the pressure of timed events that hits you right in the feels. Regularly. Until the end.
And in case you've never played one of the aforementioned:
It's an adventure. You play as a young dudette who discovers that she has a ...nah, see for yourself!
One thing's for sure: I'm totally not the target demographic, so for me it was a bit awkward to play an 18year old girlie geek-hipster, coz i'm
a 40+ year old male geek-nonhipster. But hey, at least I'm as introverted as she is. You gotta
start somewhere :-)
Did it matter? No.
But it helps if you're fine with tons of teenie-clichés and modern day references. Yes, the game drowns in clichés but it still manages to be damn lovely all the time.
Adventures like this totally depend on their characters and the story (as there is no real "action" or anything else), and both pay off.
The characters are all believable and authentic (even with all those clichés) and the story always has this subtle "wtf is this about?"-tone swinging along even while you do seemingly meaningless tasks. The epic soundtrack (that made me even get the OST) does a big part in setting up the atmosphere.
So if you're ready to ignore some regurgitated stereotypes and, if you're not a female teenie in school, are open minded for a more or less dramatic change in the point of view, you're in for an awesome tale!
Recommended?
If you loved the telltales? YES! YES! YES!
If you hates the telltales? NO! NO! NOOOOO!
If you love adventures for the puzzles and not for story? Nah, stay away, this would bore you to hell.
For all else: Maybe give it a go, you may be surprised (like I was...really)!

I liked the elements of choice found in Episode 1 and the story elements as well.  If the production crew can maintain this level of creativity throughout the episodes, it should be a VERY good experience.
That being said, there are a few technical problems I've experienced.  The interaction tags on certain items, especially in the later half of Episode 1, are very finicky, requiring that you stand at just the right angle in order to interact with them.  And you'll notice how I only talk about Episode 1, because I've encountered a HUGE game-breaking bug of that ilk in the beginning of Chapter 2 where interaction tags refuse to show up in Max's room, so you can't grab the item you need to leave the room, so you can't play the game.  Neither reloading the game nor restarting my computer helped, and I've found a few cases online where people were experiencing the same issues.  It might be a computer specs thing, so really fast computers MIGHT be able to get around it.  It's kind of a gamble though.
The narrative elements are truly promising, and it makes me sad that I can't progress due to this sort of technical issue.
edit: Turns out the issues I had were due to having an improper graphics card.  After playing on a new computer, I can safely say it lives up to my expectations and that you should buy if you're interested.  But seriously, check the system requirements to ensure you have the right graphics card.  It's no fun otherwise.

At the moment of this review, I am 3 episodes into "Life Is Strange." For the purpose of this review, it is probably easiest to simply list the pros and cons, in my opinion.
Pros:
+ Great story with unexpected twists and turns, even for an adventure and movie buff.
+ Great take on visuals and concept of awareness via photography.
+ Plays smooth and acts like an interactive movie that requires some actual thought.
+ Proficient voice acting. While the voice acting is not the best that I have ever heard for an adventure game, where voice acting is paramount next to story, it is convincing enough for the game's purpose.
- Puzzles can be a little too easy at times.
- Some phrases written into the dialogue kind of throw you for a loop. (Who in their right mind says hella?)
- I wish that the choices had more impact on the story itself.
Overall, I give it an 8.5/10. I love(d) the P&C era of gaming, and even though episodic adventures help modernize the genre, they also seem to take away some of what made large and open P&C games of yesteryear so loveable and challenging.
Definite purchase for anyone into an adventure with a great story that throws in some unexpected twists and turns here and there.

After the first "dream sequence" you end up in a classroom where little dust particles float through the sun rays. It just felt very immersive.
I can't reccomend this game enough. Even if this type of genre isn't usually your thing I think it will win you over.

I reeeeeeeally love this game.  Unlike a lot of games that say that "choices matter", this game REALLY means it. I over-watered my plant and that ♥♥♥♥♥ died, and it said that THAT would have consequences. I got so scared over what those consequences might be that I literally restarted from chapter two just so that I didn't drown the plant. I was afraid that my Mom, who specifically texted me to let me know not to drown the plant, would come visit me at school and tell me that I had to come back to Seattle because I wasn't even responsible enough to take care of a plant, let alone myself.
The game is not kidding when they say that there are no real "right" answers, though. That's what I love most about it and also hate most about it. It's very similar to real life in that way, which is a blessing and a curse. It makes the game a lot more stressful, but the fact that I get so emotionally involved in a game definitely says something about how well the game is made. I am legit scared of and for all of the characters. I appreciate all the possibilities that you can pursue-- being nice or mean to people, using your powers to help people or not (poor Alyssa), answering your family's and friends' texts or not. They somehow managed to take the mundanity of teenage high school life and make it interesting.
(Also, I really like that they show you at the end of every episode how many other people made the same choice you did. It really made me feel validated to see that so many other people stayed hidden in Chloe's closet too :P)

In essence, this is a modern adaptation of the "choose-your-own-adventure" genre. You guide the protagonist, Max Caulfield, through her decisions and interactions. The wrinkle that Dontnod added is that Max has the ability to reverse time, thereby allowing the player to undo the most recent decisions and to experiment with the different choices and their respective, immediate consequences. As the story plays out, however, this mechanic reveals the fascinating paradox where even one with the power to manipulate time cannot control the future. A pleasing soundtrack and art style complements a story whose atmoshere alternates between mellow and mysterious; there's Max's typical school life but also her investigations into her powers and the connections between her school and the disappearance of a student months prior. This isn't an action-packed game for those who want to push a lot of buttons; it's more like a movie where one gives the occasional input but mostly sits back and watches the thought-provoking story unfold.

This is my first review of anything and that's because I cannot ignore this game. I started to play it yesterday and just finished episode 3, now I can't wait for the remaining episodes. So, let's begin..
This game is the most immersive game I have ever played in my life..It does not seem like a game at all, and as a 22-year-old male I was surprised how I entereded  in Max's shoes and felt all her emotions as my own. Even my girlfriend that hates the fact that I play games sat by my side and was anxious to know what would happen next, It seemed that the game was a movie and I was the director.
At first I thought the game was going to be cool but not outstanding. However, as you advance in the game the characters start to intrigue you along with the story and the incredible soundtrack.
The synopsis is basically that you are Max Caulfield, a teenage girl of 18 years old that just came back from Seattle to study photography at Blackwell Academy in Arcade Bay (Oregon). After a "Bad Dream", Max wakes up in the middle of a lecture and after it is over she goes to the toilet where she witness the murder of a girl and mysteriously, she is able to time travel and save the girl. After this event, she discovers she can rewind time and is caught in the middle of mysterious events such as the case of a missing girl called Rachel.
The game approaches several subjects of adolescenceand (depression, bullying, love), sci-fi (butterfly effect, time travel), suspense and investigation. In this game decisions trully matter and it possesses several emotional scenes that keeps you thinking about it even when you stop playing and sometimes you think what could have you done to change the past and when you can't, you have to live with the guilt.
To summarize, just play the game, it is awesome and the only downsides you may find is that the graphs are not impressive (it doesn't matter actually), you don't have an open world to explore and you can't do all the stuff you want to do because the game doesn't give you all the freedom to do so. The rest is perfect and it is one of the best games I have ever played, if not the best.

In a medium in which stories are non-existent or deal with big themes such as saving the world, we very rarely get a chance to play a more grounded and subdued game. Life Is Strange is one such game. The player takes over the role of Maxine Caulfield, a shy and introverted 18-year-old whose biggest passion in life is photography. And even though the game doesn’t waste a second to present its time rewind hook, the real focus is still very much on Max’s more mundane problems such as dealing with everyday life and relationships in Blackwell Academy.
The storytelling is the biggest focus in Life Is Strange and I will try to avoid talking about specifics as much as possible so that you can discover everything on your own. I will say that the storytelling truly shines when Max is inspecting the world around her because it expertly reveals information about Max herself through her examination of objects and interactions with people. These inspections also deliver tiny self-contained stories about other characters and places. The way these stories and tidbits of information are delivered through posters or text messages just feels so natural and completely organic. Max is instantly likable and relatable both thanks to some great writing and terrific voice acting. The game does fumble a bit in that regard when certain other characters are concerned as some instances are rather cringe-worthy and unconvincing, but for the most part this is a truly well-told story with interesting characters.
At the very beginning of the game, Max discovers that she has the ability to rewind time. Next to exploration and human interactions, this is the main gameplay element of the game. Basically, Max is sometimes presented with choices that will have unknown repercussions in the future and she has the advantage to try out both choices before committing to one. Max will offer her views, but it’s impossible to know the repercussions and there’s no turning back once she does commit to one. The mechanic can also be used in other situations, sometimes optional, such as some light puzzle solving or gaining favor with characters. For example, when Max doesn’t offer the correct answer to her teacher’s question and another student does so, she can rewind time and offer the correct answer herself.
Life Is Strange takes place in a small town in the Pacific Northwest, specifically Oregon. The atmosphere is strong thanks to a lovely art style and a fantastic licensed soundtrack that hits all the right notes. The way that the opening credits and music are directly woven into the actual gameplay is a small and subtle yet such a brilliant touch. It’s this attention to detail that really brings this world and characters to life.
The first episode of Life Is Strange lays down a fantastic foundation. It’s warm, intimate and personal and it’s impossible not to care about Max’s predicaments and feel genuinely invested in her story every single step of the way. I can’t wait to learn more about her and find out how the choices I’ve made play out in future episodes.

Where do I even begin? Life is Strange is a thrilling tale of a girl who finds herself in a very unorthodox situation where she can reverse time to a certain extent and cause butterfly effects.
The story is absolutely captivating. Throughout the entire series, your goal is to uncover the dark secrets of your school, Blackwell Acadamy, as well as to find a missing girl named Rachel Amber. However with a bit of a twist, you also have to figure out how to prevent an enormous tornado/hurricane from hitting Arcadia Bay, your home town. The entire game is an emotional thrill ride as all sorts of crazy things begin to happen, and Max's life is turned from upside down to inside out real quick. Plot twists and a lack of plot holes make this game phenominal.
There is a sort of hipster style to it with a mix of geek/nerd culture. Lots of movie, game, etc. type references. Unlike some games like it, the choices you make really affect what goes on in the story, and they are really well thought out. From preventing the death of a fellow student, all the way to getting necessary info.
Characters are amazingly thought out. Each of them has a personality unique to them. No cardboard, boring characters. The awesome and mischievous punk friend Chloe, to the geeky love struck Warren. There are some generic ones, like the "bro" jocks/meat heads, and of course the super b**** of the school.
The art style and soundtrack of the game are incredibly pleasing. Both really know how to set the tone and atmosphere of the whole game. From really relaxing music to exciting music that will make you tense in the right situation, this game does it very well. The additional aspect of taking little photos throught each episode is also a neat little thing for completionists.
The game can also be, however, pretty dark as it sometimes focuses on some very real dramatic situations. Both soul touching and epic, I say I am perfectly thrilled by the series.
Overall this game is a wonderful experience. Great characters, art style, soundtrack, story, and more. While it can be dark, it can also be cheerful and bright. Not to mention the game is great right out of the box, not a single bug on any of the episodic releases from my experience. Great for keyboard or gamepad, too. My biased score would be a 10/10, and my critic review would have to give it a 9.5, because as perfect as this game is I know that some people would really despise the sort of hipster-esque character of Max, and if you miss something you'd have to go back and replay an entire episode which will reset your choices for that episode.

So I've played through the first 3 episodes so far. This game is definitely more of a story telling outlet in which the player makes the choices and creates the story. Of course, there isn't too many ways you can diverge the story, but the game gives you many ways to make choices and go about things. Overall, the story is phenomenal and the characters are fun.

This game is not as revolutionary as it would like to claim. Most of the choices you make are still very binary (e.g. your two choices are "comfort this person" and "insult this person", with no option to ignore them), and many sections of the game culminate in a ham-handed reiteration of the choices you've made recently.
Still, it's enjoyable. The story is fantastic and makes me care about the characters--then rips them away from me or gives me very powerful reasons to distrust or distance myself from them.
I feel there's a lot that could be improved on, but as of episode 3 a very solid experience.

I'm blown away by the quality of storytelling, the mood of the sounds/voices, and the overall quality of the experience.  It's not the most complex game that you will ever play. In fact, I don't know how much "game" there is in this... but, as an interactive experience, this is a "must buy".
The experience of Life is Strange will draw you in to the characters & their world (the Pacific Northwest, inspite of the Seattle chill in the air) in a way that many other games don't. The characters have names, faces, and a weight to their history. That's what the game is about, and DONTNOD is successful in getting you into the skin of a young woman in the midst of incredible changes.
Is it a perfect experience? No. And people who want a lot of game to play may ultimately be disappointed. There's no aliens to blast, and no villages to plunder. It's a strange, sometimes meditative, often melancholy world where your choices may lead to unintended & occasionally shocking consequences down the road.

If you're new to the game, I highly suggest playing each episode and then taking a few weeks off to simulate the anticipation and elation we felt at each new chapter's release. Allow yourself time to process everything you experience and formulate your own theories before moving on. Powering through all five episodes in one sitting seems to me like swallowing your favorite dessert whole when you could have taken it in slowly and savored every moment.
The ending left much to be desired for me. Despite this, an unsatisfying ending does not compromise the sheer genius of the gameplay experience

This game has the potential to be my favorite of all time. Jist=This game is art. Get it (before it's finished if you can).
It starts with teen drama and time travel, but ends up hitting on heavy, real themes. The game definitely has something to offer on life and the tensions of adolescence. The largest theme is that "choices matter."
The gameplay equips you with the power to rewind time. Essentially, the game lets you rethink and alter your choices for a short time. Rewinding and comparing outcomes becomes incredibly stressful in the best way.
Characters are realistic and compelling. Never before have I grown so emotionally attached to characters in a video game. They exist and I know them. I know what they would say when something happens. I want to spend time with them.
The art style is pleasing, especially when it comes to nature. Although some closeups are pixelly, the overall effect of the graphics is atmosphere, not precision.
The music compliments the game and is embellished by it. Standalone, the soundtrack is excellent. Standalone, the game would also be excellent. But put together, cinematics in Life is Strange are moving and intense, and the music takes on a greater meaning as I listen to it later in the car.
The episodic format suits this game well. I have not previously had experience with the format, but it drawns out the game in a good way. It allows time for suspense, theorizing, and emotion. Pick it up before it is finished.
Sure there are problems. The lip-syncing of the scenes is pretty awful at times. Some dialogue and flavor texts feels a little too cheesy. Some moments require dull repetition or memorization. However, when a game is so powerful in general, its problems do not matter. I do not just overlook the problems. I see them and do not care. It has no negative effect. In fact, the blemishes add character in and odd way,
Altogether, I love this game. It has an impact on me as an individual. Themes, Gameplay, Characters, Art, Music, and Episodic format are all a +. Only -, you will be very sad.
