Not much in terms of gameplay other than clicking on dialogue options or exploring, but the characterization is so rich that its flaws are largely overlooked. Corny dialogue is a weakness, but each character's charm makes this forgivable.
If you're new to the game, I highly suggest playing each episode and then taking a few weeks off to simulate the anticipation and elation we felt at each new chapter's release. Allow yourself time to process everything you experience and formulate your own theories before moving on. Powering through all five episodes in one sitting seems to me like swallowing your favorite dessert whole when you could have taken it in slowly and savored every moment.
The ending left much to be desired for me. Despite this, an unsatisfying ending does not compromise the sheer genius of the gameplay experience

At its most bare, a modern story/dialog driven adventure game, but one with extrodinary characters/writing/ambience.  This is a game you can absolutely fall deeply deeply in love with, and which is going to use that love to inflict some serious emotional power both with and against you.
You are presented with choices, like many games of this type.  Those choices will have potentially long term lasting consequences, like many games of this type.  Often both paths will be fraught with good and bad outcomes, like many games of this type.  What really sets this game apart however is the unique ability to 'rewind' and second-guess yourself, to try each branch, at least in a limited sense, and try and make a 'better' more educated choice based on that extra knowledge.
Who you are, who you choose to become, both get tangled up in the deep temptation/allure of that rewind, and in a 'meta' sense, how much you allow that power to corrupt  you, as a player, plays out as an additional game element.  Its trivially easy to exploit characters once you can find out what they want to hear, rewind, and parrot it back to them, but it also can become deeply unnerving/amoral.
All that angst and pain though is absolutely deeply engaging and its impossible to not end up emotionally invested in whichever path you choose.
One word of warning though before I close.  This is a game that is absolutely willing to dive deep into potentially impactful/triggering situations.  If you have trouble with fiction that can edge potentially very close to hard and painful situations you have been exposed to in real life, this game should not be undertaken lightly.

*Spoilers from episode 1-3.*
When Life is Strange first appeared on Steam, I wasn't sure if I wanted to purchase the game since, even though I had wanted to play a story based choice and consequence for a while, I knew I'd have to wait for each episode. Jen (my wife) convinced me to buy episode one, and I am so glad that she did! I have since purchased the entire series
So, the game starts with Max Caulfield, the main character, experiencing a horrible storm, and after following a spirit doe, she finds a tornado wrecking the city that she's arrived in (and grew up in), which is Oregon.
Then we find out that this was a vision she experienced while in class, as she is a college student. She attempts to use her new power, which is reversing time, on something simple. Now, Max was one of my least favorite characters in any video game. She's very... Hipster, which isn't a lifestyle I'm into (no offense to any hipsters reading this), and some of what she said was cringe-worthy (not for that reason alone). That being said, she has kind of grown on me.
Max's dream is to become a photographer, so she has a camera with her wherever she goes, and many of the achievements (on Steam) are based around the pictures you take. I've missed a LOT, so I am excited for a second play through.
Max goes into the bathroom, so she can calm down after her dream and test her powers further, and hears two students arguing, so she goes behind the stalls to hide. During this time frame, there's a beautiful blue butterfly fluttering around. I'm still unsure what the doe, and what the butterfly represent.
The argument escalates, and the boy pulls out a gun and shoots the girl in the stomach on accident(?). Max, of course, panics and immediately tries to use her power to stop him and does so successfully.
I don't want to spoil much, so hopefully this will give you an idea on what Life is Strange is about. The world of LiS is filled with interesting characters, some good, some bad, some totally creepy (like Samuel...)
There ARE a lot of choices (like, taking care of Lisa, the plant), more so than I thought there'd be when I first started. Chloe is amazing, and I am hoping there will be something there, romantically, between her and Max. I totally ship them.
There is a guy named Warren who has a crush on Max, but I find him so annoying. I cannot stand people who are too nice, and he's... Yeah. I prefer the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with a good heart type, which is kind of how Chloe, the blue-haired, pot smoking rebel, is.
But why is she like that? What was her past? You'll have to play to find out!
Anyway, moving on, there's two main stories in LiS. Max's power and this super storm that's coming, and the missing student named Rachel Amber. Everyone is trying to figure out if she left, or was kidnapped. If she's alive, or dead.
Lots of people suspect Chloe's step-dad, but...
Here are my thoughts:
I think he's an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, but I truly think he is simply trying to protect the students.
I think Frank (you'll meet him eventually) is an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with a good heart, and didn't do anything wrong.
I think, the culprit is, Mr. Jefferson, the teacher. I don't know why, just a feeling!
TL;DR: Life is Strange is unique, beautifully made, and has an interesting story. Plus, Max's rewind power is something we haven't seen in a game like this before, as far as I am aware. I definitely recommend purchasing the entire season! Enjoy~!

When this review goes up, the game is up to Episode 3
Oh boy here we go, this game is amazing, it throws a lot of crazy♥♥♥♥♥♥at you, in some moments comepletely unpredictable stuff. The story aspect of this game (which is the main feature of this game) is really imersive and interesting, gameplay is admittedly slow but because of this the game is very soothing and calming, a great escape from frustration.
You play as Max(ine) Caulfield, A shy 18-year old photography student at Blackwell Academy, located in Arcadia Bay. Arcadia Bay was your hometown but you moved 5 years ago to another home and now your back, meeting faces old and new to you. during your stay at Blackwell you discover you could rewind time somehow with no sort of origin knowledge. You meet up with Chloe Price, a punk rock chick who was your best friend until you moved, and you investigate how you got your powers together and the mysterious death of Rachel Amber by using these powers. Now that is just the tip of the iceberg.
Pros:
-Amazing and twisty story, although this is a game roughly based around time travel it throws a lot of surprising moments, even if some moments were standard cliches to time travel stories, it still gave shock value, Episode 3 in particular.
-Interactive and immersive gameplay execution, I wont say gameplay alone since this type of experience is really a debate around different genre fans but in my eyes it was done beautifully.
-Artistic textures, it really shows the personality this game gives to the player, relaxing and in-control.
-The soundtrack, The Acoustic Guitar soundtrack they picked for this game is the best soundtrack for a game I have ever heard, next to Batman: Arkham's Orchestrial theme. Side note: I'm listening to it right now while I'm typing this.
Cons:
-Well there is only one and it is minor but lip-sync, I fnd that there was little-medium effort put into this but it doesn't ruin the game anyway.
9.5/10, I believe that nothing is perfect but this is as close as we are going to get so far.

This is one of the most beautiful, intimate, emotionally rich games I've played in my life.

Pfff...I'm literally strugging to cope right now (waiting for ne next season installment ).
Can't stop thinking about this series!! Gorgeous visuals, incredible story, and captivating characters. Many parts of each installment had me gasping pretty loud/shouting "No Way" a tonne, and made me realise how insanely nosy I am (rumaging through bins, looking at peoples phones/tablets/PCs/staring at people/touching everything in sight).
I adored games such as Fahrenheit and Heavy Rain, so Life Is Strange is obviously no exception to the rule of my favouritings. The main game mechanic (rewind), is excellent, and regardless of whether you rewind or not, most cases I was left panicking as to whether I had made the right decision or not. I also got so into it that at times in real life, I had a few occasions where I thought I could rewind time myself, haha...for example, I spilled my drink in the kitchen, and for a really fleeting moment my brain flickered with "Oops! Re..wind...wait...". I get way to into these types of games, for sure.
The voice acting is something left to be desired though. I mean, the individual dialogues are ok to some degree, but I'm pretty sure each actor was popped in a room by themselves with the script, with the person they are interacting with in the story dialogue in a different room altogether, mind. If I'm honest, this wasn't offputting to me, and actually made me giggle in some instances.
I hope the series rolls on, and on, and on. Like my feelings with The Last of Us, this game will break my heart when it has to come to and end. I'll never get over it, haha!

Life is Strange is a lot like the music chosen to accompany it's narrative. Not flashy, but simple, and yet very beautiful. The thing I find I love the most is the subtlety, if you take a moment to pause you can truley see what has gone into the game.  The audio is great (when it doesn't bug out, YOU TOTALLY KILLED THE SCENE!) I enjoyed the option to sit on the swing in the backyard, and through the automated camera angle rotations, you could pick out things like children laughing in the background, and the clock ticking in the kitchen.
This game is very akin to the works of Quantic Dream, at least as far as how you "play", I happen to enjoy that style a great deal.  It's focus is the narrative, the pacing, the atmosphere, good camera angles and lighting.
Do yourself a favor and pick this game up, it's so damn cheap.
Life is Strange is not a great 'game', Life is Strange is a great experience.

*Spoilers from episode 1-3.*
When Life is Strange first appeared on Steam, I wasn't sure if I wanted to purchase the game since, even though I had wanted to play a story based choice and consequence for a while, I knew I'd have to wait for each episode. Jen (my wife) convinced me to buy episode one, and I am so glad that she did! I have since purchased the entire series
So, the game starts with Max Caulfield, the main character, experiencing a horrible storm, and after following a spirit doe, she finds a tornado wrecking the city that she's arrived in (and grew up in), which is Oregon.
Then we find out that this was a vision she experienced while in class, as she is a college student. She attempts to use her new power, which is reversing time, on something simple. Now, Max was one of my least favorite characters in any video game. She's very... Hipster, which isn't a lifestyle I'm into (no offense to any hipsters reading this), and some of what she said was cringe-worthy (not for that reason alone). That being said, she has kind of grown on me.
Max's dream is to become a photographer, so she has a camera with her wherever she goes, and many of the achievements (on Steam) are based around the pictures you take. I've missed a LOT, so I am excited for a second play through.
Max goes into the bathroom, so she can calm down after her dream and test her powers further, and hears two students arguing, so she goes behind the stalls to hide. During this time frame, there's a beautiful blue butterfly fluttering around. I'm still unsure what the doe, and what the butterfly represent.
The argument escalates, and the boy pulls out a gun and shoots the girl in the stomach on accident(?). Max, of course, panics and immediately tries to use her power to stop him and does so successfully.
I don't want to spoil much, so hopefully this will give you an idea on what Life is Strange is about. The world of LiS is filled with interesting characters, some good, some bad, some totally creepy (like Samuel...)
There ARE a lot of choices (like, taking care of Lisa, the plant), more so than I thought there'd be when I first started. Chloe is amazing, and I am hoping there will be something there, romantically, between her and Max. I totally ship them.
There is a guy named Warren who has a crush on Max, but I find him so annoying. I cannot stand people who are too nice, and he's... Yeah. I prefer the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with a good heart type, which is kind of how Chloe, the blue-haired, pot smoking rebel, is.
But why is she like that? What was her past? You'll have to play to find out!
Anyway, moving on, there's two main stories in LiS. Max's power and this super storm that's coming, and the missing student named Rachel Amber. Everyone is trying to figure out if she left, or was kidnapped. If she's alive, or dead.
Lots of people suspect Chloe's step-dad, but...
Here are my thoughts:
I think he's an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, but I truly think he is simply trying to protect the students.
I think Frank (you'll meet him eventually) is an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with a good heart, and didn't do anything wrong.
I think, the culprit is, Mr. Jefferson, the teacher. I don't know why, just a feeling!
TL;DR: Life is Strange is unique, beautifully made, and has an interesting story. Plus, Max's rewind power is something we haven't seen in a game like this before, as far as I am aware. I definitely recommend purchasing the entire season! Enjoy~!
P.S. There's also plenty of replay value, including collecting stuff you may have missed before. Oh yeah... Yaaaay achievements!

Amazing game! I can not recommend this enough. If you like games where you can see the evidence of your actions as you play, then this game is for you. Back in the 90s there was a boon on dull, lifeless and ultimately frustrating games, these were termed the ‘Point ‘n’ Click’ genre and they were incredibly popular at the time despite being filled with endless puzzles, bad humour and a plot that nearly always tailed off halfway through leaving you with a mess of inconsistency at the end. Many people still enjoy this genre, I however disliked them back then and dislike them even more now. It was with this in mind that I ventured cautiously into the world of Max, a student who discovers quite by accident that she can alter time and finds that Life is not only strange but also incredibly exciting.
Beyond knowing that time travel was somehow involved in the plot I knew nothing about this game, perhaps that is why I was so trepidatious in the first place and believed I was about to experience my most disliked genre of gaming. Turns out my fears were not only unfounded but also very wrong. This is not a Point ‘n’ Click though it holds true to certain gameplay aspects of those games, neither is it one of those ‘experiences’ that whilst often engaging tend to lack any real aspect of actual gaming. No, Life is Strange is, for want of a better description, a cinematic adventure and, boy, the game takes you on quite a ride of emotional consequence as you walk Max around her limited but detailed 3D world, interact with items and people and watch the everyday lives of those around you and then, when you choose to do so, affect the lives of those characters be it through an initial choice or the power of time.
Effecting time is not a new thing to gaming and the way one changes the timeline in Life is Strange has been done before but unlike any other game I have played in which you can control outcomes in such a way, this one feels like it matters. Sure, some of the outcomes are forced upon you but this is merely to continue the story and even then it is a joy to discover the correct path but where it really exceeds is when you end up with a multiple choice of outcomes, neither one right or wrong, where Max, and your own moral ambiguity, will result in a fractured path towards the end-game. One such choice affected me greatly and I spent a good ten minutes rewinding over and over again only to find that my final choice left me open to even more decisions and I questioned whether I chose for the protagonist, Max, or for myself. I then realised we were one in the same and the game had truly melded my own consciousness with that of the games. To date, no other game has ever done this to me. Truly, choice and consequence matter in Life is Strange.
The way in which you change time is a simple right click on your mouse and by holding down the shift key time can be rewound even faster. I did notice that when I used shift, Max seemed to take quite a hit as if it caused her pain, whether or not this will be a feature later in the game I cannot say but I did find myself preferring to take the slower option just incase! There are also checkpoints, if you will, within the timeline that you rewind so you can change a little or all of the choices you just made. This adds subtlety to those choices and shows that thought went into the mechanic and it makes it feel less of a gimmick and more an actual tool.
Beautiful to behold, the game lures you in with a popular graphic style that resembles a digital watercolour, sharp detail yet soft colours that compliment the real world. The world around you is also busy and filled with character interactions which you can, if you wish, choose to avoid or dive wholeheartedly into to experience the sub-plots and general gossip of life in a high school environment. You have every typical teenage anxiety and worry living and walking around you as you meander the school grounds and dormitories and whilst I, as an older gamer found myself quoting The Breakfast Club’s infamous line “I don’t even speak your language” you cannot fail to listen in awe at the sound design and voice acting at work. This is a world fully realised and it is this which, in part, helps seal that ‘choices matter’ feeling you get as you decide the fate of friends and enemies alike.
The games beauty does not require a monster PC to run and has been optimised wonderfully for all levels of computers. The graphic options ensure all levels of detail are catered for and have a wide range of sliders for everything from shadows to anti-aliasing, resolution and more. Audio is less catered for but given the high quality of the sound available this is less important in this particular game than some others. I did experience a fairly common issue when loading the game the first time but a quick perusal of Google and I found a fix by reinstalling the Visual C++ redistributable provided for me in the games folder. This is something Steam normally does on a games first run but for some reason this was broken for me. A minute later and a quick reboot however and I was good to go. Given the nature of day one patches of late for triple A games this is nothing and should not detract from your enjoyment of the game
Life is Strange is an episodic adventure game with currently three of five parts available now and the fourth part ‘coming soon’. So far the release of the next episode has been at roughly eight week intervals with little to no delay so those of us who fear an unfinished game seemingly have nothing to worry about, though of course with releases of this nature it is always something to think about though I feel there is already enough game here to satisfy any fear of value for money many of us will desperately want to experience this story to the, possibly, bitter end. I finished episode one in approximately two and a half hours and at the end was left with stats on the choices others made and a desperate need to just get on and play the next chapter, which as I was live streaming at the time I could not do. If I was merely playing this game on my own with no spectators I fear I would have stayed up all night and played one through three in a single session, like a good book it is simply hard to put down.
I honestly cannot praise this game enough and Dontnod Entertainment deserve high praise for such a perfect gaming experience. Can they maintain this level through all five episodes? This I cannot answer but I have faith and that is far more than I do for most game of late. If you value choice, choose this game.

Have a quick Pro/Con list
PROS
*Easily one of the greatest stories I have ever expirienced in a game. AND IT'S NOT EVEN OVER YET!

CONS

This game is without a doubt one of my favorite games this year and quite possibly all time. Perhaps you're like me and considering purchasing this game, I was wondering how the hell could a game about going through high school and living through the eyes of a teenage girl would be fun.
But I'll leave all spoilers out (As I'm sure that's uber appreciative), but that notion I had was dispelled within the first five minutes of the game. I won't say why, but you'll just have to try it for yourself.
If you liked any of Telltale's Games, this one is a must-buy. The story actually does take turns for better and for worse depending on what choices are taken, rather than being almost on rails like many other games like this.
And making groundbreaking choices, with the sounds and visual effects that accompany them as they arise is almost uneasing like it would be in real life, and I haven't felt that in a game for a very long time.
All in all, Life is Strange is a super interesting game, and one that truely took me for surprise. If you like point and click adventures and exploring every nook and cranny of a game world to find things, if you like to feel a wide range of emotions from said point and click adventure game, this is for you.
10/10.

Episode 1: This is a nice demo... lets call it that. So far there are 3 episodes out there and this is a nice teenage-emo novel. If you are into it you will like it a lot. But unless you buy all episodes you will end up with only a fraction of a game (hence "demo").
One thing that bugs me is the brave "choices have consequences that matter" statement written all over.
After playing the 1st episode twice with completely opposite choices the big consequences were that the stats at the end told me which choices I have taken... the story-line didn't diverge one bit. Let's see if episode 2 actually takes your previous choices and presents you an alternative story branch... I doubt it.
Until all episodes are actually available I suggest holding off with buying. Because if they cancel it you will end up with a book which has blank pages at the end.
---------------
Update: Episode 2+3:
So I have played through E2 and E3 now as well (all 5 Episodes are out).
Although limited the "choices have consequences that matter" statement holds true but sadly almost always puts you between a rock and a hard place where it would really matter. That's OK though since it shows you that there just isn't always a good choice to take in life.
The story comes around with nice twists and turns while still staying linear enough for you to not get the feeling that you are too dumb to grasp the plot.
So in general I have to say that the story is nice.
However it is sad to say that the main feature and USP, the rewind feature, has become a pain.
You will have sections where there are choices in the dialog that will lead to the same response, other times you will get more background information which doesn't effect the story (which is kind of nice), then there are those rewind moments to progress in the story (super-power), and there are the choices that matter moments. That is all good until here.
But then comes the events which are exempt from the rewind - but you are not told about that fact (except for one occasion where they also gave a good explanation).
So what is so wrong about that? You are being trained to skip and rewind through the dialogs to get all the background info, find out all the possible choices and near effects and get a feel of the situation and characters. You will even have the nice chance to rewind when the 1-3 word choice caused a completely different reaction than what you have expected.
While this is cool it is luring you into making an exploratory choice instead of what your really would have taken, even when you will not be able to rewind like usual.
My story-line is by now so messed up with choices I wouldn't have finalized that because of this I simply didn't give a damn anymore at one point and kept messing it up even more.
My frustration level is rather high right now.
However I will just barely change my rating to "recommend" because the story (and that is what this novel is all about) is still enticing, the promised episodes have been delivered (although I cannot give a judgment of the quality yet), and the rewind feature is still nice in general. If you are able to cope with the unannounced rewind blocks you will enjoy this story (hint: car driving cut-scenes are one of those).
Also note that it would be OK to only get the first 3 Episodes since there is no real cliffhanger at the end of E3.

Life Is Strange really is something else. It's the first game, at least that I have played, that gets the interactive game-but-really-a-movie right. A big part of this is the rewind mechanic. It fits in perfectly with the surreal, kind of magic realism feel it's going for, but it also allows you to explore any and all choices you make without any (immediate) consequences. That's always been a big turn-off in Telltale Games: sometimes the protagonist will word things differently than you expected and you'd wish you could make a different choice. Well here you can, and it actually makes sense from the story's perspective.
The game feels like the interactive love child of Juno and Veronica Mars, with hints of The Butterfly Effect. The visual style really works for this kind of story and the audio is spot-on. Max is really fleshed out as a character and is not just a carta blanca waiting to be filled in by your imagination, which is great.
Play this game, and watch your sympathy for hipsters grow. I expect the full game to last about 15 (well filled) hours for a single, slow-pace playthrough, so take from that what you will.
It's great. The final few episodes are one heck of a rollercoaster. All in all I can tell you that the story isn't particularly innovative, the graphics aren't the greatest, and sometimes the dialogue gets a bit too Dawson's Creek for my taste.
But beyond that the voice acting is amazing and the music is incredibly atmospheric. The characters are very believable and relatable and even though the story may not be innovative, it's done
well. I won't soon forget this little gem.

I absolutely love this game. I appreciate that each choice you make actually matters and will make a difference with the outcome. I highly enjoy the art style and the music. Definitely recommend.

(These are my impressions on the game after finishing Episode 5. I will do my best to keep this review spoiler-free.)
Max Caulfield is not your average college student. She has an exceptional gift - the ability to rewind time. Naturally, thanks to her unusual gift, her life turns from average student life into a semi-epic adventure.
In Life Is Strange, every choice you make affects the outcome of future events. And I mean EVERY choice. From small to big, no matter the scale - everything you do will leave its mark. And the consequences are always equal in size.
As far as gameplay is concerned, it's an interesting blend of multiple-choice dialogue and light puzzles that involve the manipulation of time. There is not a single dull moment in the game, partly thanks to the top-notch voice acting. Even the less thrilling sequences manage to keep up interest by encouraging exploration. And of course being a photography student, Max can snap photos - sadly not wherever and whenever she wants, but there are opportunities for that, alright.
I also have to applaud the game for getting to me emotionally. If you happen(ed) to see a certain tragic event near the end of Episode 2, you'll know what I mean. The ending of Episode 3 and the junkyard scene in Episode 4 are also rather emotional moments. The plot twist at the end of Episode 4, on the other hand, had me genuinely surprised.
However, even Life Is Strange does have its flaws, and in my experience, they namely concern Episode 5. The constant time traveling got slightly tedious, and it wasn't as emotionally captivating as the previous episodes. Despite those flaws, even Episode 5 managed to keep me interested.
Overall, Life Is Strange left me thoroughly impressed. Dontnod Entertainment have clearly put all of their heart and effort into this game, and it shows. Without the slightest shred of doubt, this game gets my seal of approval.

I'll probably edit this once I've completed the full game. But as of now I've played Episodes 1-3. Just a warning. Minor potential spoilers.
I just want to say that this game floored me, like straight up took me on an emotional roller coaster, and made some of the "perfect" choices unclear. This game is a completely wonderful purchase. I've paid more money for games with less creativity and content, and this game really does make you feel like what you do has fortunate/unfortunate consequences in the future. What I will say is that some of the "language" used in this is more suited to the 15-19 age group, due to the slang used in the game and the swearing but the content, just wow.
Episode one, I just want to say that you can actually take a -lot- more time exploring things than what I thought initially as the game will not continue until you move Max to specific points in the game. You miss clues/photo opportunities quite easily if you don't look around and you don't actually -need- to rush as much as what you think you do. The first chapter is the perfect introduction into a game. It teaches you the controls as you play without it seeming like a boring tutorial level.
The artwork in this game is phenomenal. You can tell it's created by Square-Enix as all of the character's face models are beautiful, The only thing I'll say is that Kate's hair looks way too big and it throws me off, but still, aside from that one character, the rest look like believable prep-school students and the adults in the game DO look like adults. The actual game is flawless in how it runs, there were NO bugs that I noticed and the game despite having heavy 3D visuals will run on a less than perfect PC just fine.
The story in this is amazingly complex because when you perform one action you actually change some of the gameplay and story into making things happen that you didn't expect, and all of the potential bad guys definitely have their bad guy moments. The voice acting fits really well, including the MC Max, and you can get more out of the game by just having Max sit around at certain points where she explains her story and what she's thinking. The journal is also wonderfully done, and it also gives you a way of knowing where you are in the story and what you've done during the duration of the story/chapter you're on.
The gameplay. Honestly I have no complaints with this. Much like A Wolf Among us, the story plays out like you're watching a movie, and I didn't get sick of any of the music (Minus the banjo music option in the cafe*) The entire game feels fluid and carries you through the game with a sense of wanting more. You can also SKIP the credits which is fantastic since A lot of games don't allow you to do so, in such an interesting way.
The downsides that I have personally for this game:
1) You can't replay certain acts in the story and skip forward to skip cutscenes you've already seen if you replay the game.
2) I didn't love the ending to Chapter 3 although it did leave me wanting more.
3) I would like to see Max in more outfits or have the ability to choose what Max wears from what she has in her closet.
Overall if you like movie-like games, like A Wolf Amongst us, or other similar games, You'll really like this game. If you're a fan of Final Fantasy or other Square/Enix franchises you'll probably like the art. And What I love about this is that there are all shapes body-wise, and all kinds of character traits, so you don't get bored and genuinely DO want to know more about the secondary characters. It's a definite "GET THIS." From me. I would recommend it to anyone who likes an easygoing story yet difficult speed related challenges as the game is based on those. Really REALLY great game, to the creators that made this.
Thank you for giving us something so great story-wise. It's engaging, and makes you really feel like you're in Maxine's shoes. So good. I can't wait for Episode 4 and 5 to come out. I'm so curious now. Got me hook, line, and sinker.

I must say I have played many games but 'Life is Strange' is special. Now why is it? Well the answer is not simple. I think it is a perfect mixture of the reality we all face every day with just a pinch or two of something else, something mysterious that makes this game so outstanding. Every episode kept me wanting more! :) There are some intense moment, emotionally intense and sometimes these left me wrecked, but in a positive sense. I must admit that sometimes I nearly forgot that it is just a game, but I won't spoil anything here ;). There are also these moment when you can just wind down, listening to the awesome soundtrack. The music in this game is just 'ubercool' ;). As for the characters I love the protagonist, Max, she's just an ordinary girl, very likeable, and you can very easily relate to her. Chloe is just amazing, as some people point out she's impulsive, makes hasty choice but I guess I love it about her, this plus her style, I simply adore it. What I also love about the game is the setting, Pacific Northwest is without a doubt an amazing place and it fits the story perfectly.
If you are still considering whether you should buy this game, give it a shot if you like good stories, lovely music, involving characters and dialogs as well beautiful landscapes.

- Good exploration and level design; maintains variety of outcomes and freedom of procedure despite generally linear progression
- Flushed out characters; the only one dimensional characters are the mostly one-off ambient NPCs
- Well executed comic/graphic novel visual style
- Very appropriate selection and placement of ambient music
- Much appreciated volume controls and well executed VO and SFX quality
- Commendable performance (based on a mid-high end pc)
- Chloe.
- Occasionally cringey (but perhaps adorable) meta-game
- Episodic release
It's difficult to find flaws in a game that delivers so well and so precisely in exactlly what it promises: a choose your own, RP-adventure.
Dontnod entertainment's previous endeavor was the Capcom action-rpg Remember Me. Since then, it seems they have vastly improved their story-telling retained thier picturesque visual style.
In Life is Strange, you play as Max Caulfield, a college student with a passion in photography -- which becomes the metagame in this story oriented adventure RPG as you capture stills and unlock achievements with your polaroid camera. Other than the slightly cringey forceful introduction to this mechanic, the occurence in the remainder of the game is rewarding.
You soon discover your superhuman ability which is persistent and available in the entirety of the game.
The mix of first and third/over-the-shoulder camera combined with the stream of consciousness narration makes for very convincing and immersive RPG. If you're willing to suspend disbelief in this story of a coming-of-age girl in suburban America: this game is brilliant.
If there's anything to complain about, it's perhaps the episodic release which makes for considerable pauses in a story-oriented game. Then again, several games have done this and it's an extremely minor complaint for what seems to be a very feasible and reasonable business model. The releases have been more than respectably timely, and as of Episode 3, content has not shown any signs of deterioration in quality. The only thing you risk... is your disapproval of the yet to come conclusion to arc of the story.

I really, really wanted to like this game due to the beautiful visuals, the interesting concept, the pleasant sound-track and the reasonable cost, but the further you get into it, the more you realize that this game has been designed by a comittee trying to milk a very specific demographic. Stale pop culture references are shoe-horned in at every opportunity, and the main character is a posterchild for the 90's-obsessed hipster girl stereotype. Literally everything about this game feels like it was chosen to make people think it's more original than it is. As someone else pointed out, it's basically Juno meets Donnie Darko with a lot more preaching. And no "Aren't we artsy?" wank-fest would be complete without preaching. The climate change message is delivered so heavy-handedly that it made me want to chop down a forrest and buy myself a Hummer out of spite.
Just about every character is a shameless cliche, and the worst part is the game openly admits it with frequent self-deprecating humor. It's like the developers are apologising to you.
Okay, SquEnix, if you know you're just barfing out cliches, why did you bother?
"Because cliches sell, and that means more money for us!"
Bottom line, it's yet another Square Enix angst-wank that panders to dumb, angst-stricken teenagers and Tumblr ♥♥♥♥♥s. If you fall into that demographic, more power to you. Enjoy Life is Strange(TM). Otherwise, do yourself a favor and avoid the title. At the very least, don't get it at full price - for the limited amount of content you get, it's just not worth it.
I'll give credit where credit is due though - they still managed to suck me in. I will probably buy the other four episodes just to see how it ends. Maybe, just maybe, characters will be fleshed out in such a way that they end up being more complex than they appear to be in the first episode. If SquEnix manages to wow me, this review might change.

I've had the full version for 3 months now and still haven't updated this review.
It's an RPG without the RPG elements, from the company which is famous for rich stories in games. Life Is Strange isn't really a game, it's an interactive movie. Gameplay is limited to movement, rewind, and your investigative skills -- and that old statement of mine may seem weird, but it has held up as only one time in the entire game are you stripped of your ability to rewind and undo the consequence of failure. The entire package takes about 8-15 hours to complete once, depending on whether or not you try to investigate everything and read all the backstory literature on your first playthrough.
Having played through the game, I feel the creators have somewhat overhyped the importance of choice in this game. Seiken Densetsu 3 had more meaningful storyline branching. Life is Strange's story is ultimately linear, no matter if you're a paragon of virtue or a sociopath throughout the playthrough. What mid-game choices ultimately result in is "do X, get Y cutscene. Do V, get W cutscene". The most major potential difference is losing a 20-30 portion of the game, but the story inevitably goes in the same direction.
Since the game is far more story than game, I need to tiptoe around the storyline to avoid spoiling it. The audio is fantastic, adds to the rich atmosphere of the game. Normally I'd be annoyed by the slow movement speed but again, since investigation and atmosphere are major aspects, it works for this game. The voice acting is pretty decent, my major complaint is the lips don't sync properly to the dialogue. (to the point of being distracting) The characters are a bit on the caricature side, with old and new teenage tropes mixed together, but that doesn't really bother me. This dialogue awkwardness seemed to be reduced in the later episodes.
In spite of its not-non linearity, Life is Strange still manages to be both epic and personal, heartwarming and cruel, comedic and heart wrenching. The writing is top notch, plot holes exist but aren't to the point of distracting, and it compelled me enough to do a second "jerkwad" playthrough after my first "friend of all living things" playthrough. I'll probably end up picking up the second season, but probably not until all episodes are released. (this title handles episodic well, but I'm binge-spoiled by Netflix)

I loved the Walking Dead Season 1 and Season 2 games. Just got drawn in and loved that decisions can affect the story in almost every way. Life is Strange is definitely not Walking Dead, but the story is just as good if not better. The best part, you can “Rewind” and change the outcome of something you possibly did not want to say, something I wished to have a great deal in any game based on big decisions.
The soundtrack is spectacular! The game introduces its outstanding soundtrack in various parts of the game. Sometimes I tend to “fully” explore the area while listening to the sound track. The soundtrack goes quite well without interrupting any commentary while observing and hearing the thoughts of Max Caulfield, the main character.
The story is breathtaking! I honestly didn’t expect the story to grab me very quickly. From the very first moment of the game, I was compelled to explore every corner of the area to hear what the character was thinking and what she wanted to say. Talking to the various students, bring a sense of life to the environment of a school showing you that each character has their own personality that slowly begin to understand as the story progresses. I, for one, can’t wait for all episodes to release, so I can just replay the entire story again in one fell swoop and possibly another time to go down various story paths that I may have not seen before.
The gameplay is unique has never been done before! At least on any game I’ve played. As said above, being able to rewind a conversation and start over really gets you thinking about the story path you want to take. Make a mistake, just rewind and do it the way you want. Make a major decision, and didn’t like the outcome, just rewind and try another path. Unlike The Walking Dead games I have played for many hours, I don’t have to “restart” a checkpoint to change a potentially wrong decision I was not happy with. This gameplay mechanic really helps you out in certain situations as well.
The graphic art style is great! You won’t see graphics that make a high end graphics card sweat, but the unique art style really brings life to the game. The vivid colors used and the environment is crafted in great detail.
With every episode the story gets deeper and draws you in. This is by far one of the best singleplayer experiences I’ve ever had the pleasure of playing. I literally can’t wait until the entire season is released. My only hope, is that after all 5 episodes release, there may even be a continuation of the story, as the characters that have developed so much after the current 3 seasons that are out as I type this. I would hate to see this completely end. Definitely a must buy regardless of the price!

Life is Strange is less of a video game and more of an interactive movie. The experience is extremely story-driven, and there's very little "action". This is not a bad thing. Instead of clicking on heads, you have to navigate conversations and solve puzzles. Since the protagonist, Max, has the ability to "rewind" the last few minutes, the game isn't particularly challenging. Tasks you fail at the first time can be repeated over and over until you eventually succeed, and usually it's as simple as repositioning a soda can so it doesn't spill all over a book. The real draw of this game is exploring the world, enjoying the atmosphere, and getting to meaningfully affect how things play out (unlike in most games, where player choice hardly matters).
Pros:
+The storyline is more interactive and engaging than most, with many of your choices having real consequences later on. I haven't found a way to "lose" the game yet, but it unfolds differently depending on how you act, which is very satisfying.
+The graphics aren't incredibly detailed or realistic, but they still look wonderful. All the models are hand-drawn, and the colors create a very autumn-y feel, which is overall very nostalgic. The game also seems fairly well-optimized, with a consistently good framerate most of the time.
+The characters read like actual people, rather than talking cardboard cutouts. The a-hole security guard has a family he cares about, the girl bully will cut you a break if you're nice to her, and the cool teacher isn't always there for people. There's very little stereotyping that I noticed, and it's harder write off most characters as "good" or "bad".
+Overall, I feel much more emotionally invested in this game than almost any other I've played. If you've come here for phat lootz and headshots, keep on looking. Life is Strange is all about the story, and the story is truly wonderful.
Cons:
-The lip-syncing is terrible. I wouldn't call it immersion-breaking, but it certainly is distracting. Sometimes I can't even tell which character is speaking.
-Because of the way Max's "rewind" works, she reappears in the spot she was standing in "before" she rewound (from her perspective) instead of in the spot she was standing in at the time she rewound back to.  This makes solving time-constrained puzzles easier, but from another person's perspective, she seems to teleport. None of the NPC's notice this, except where it's scripted in. This IS what I would call immersion-breaking.
-It looks like the people who wrote the dialogue researched how American teenage girls talk by reading Tumblir. Nobody says "hella" that much, and from what little I understand, they didn't even use it properly.
The amount of "girl drama" in this story might be a turn-off for some players. Personally, I thought it was kind of fascinating, especially when you can mine a conversation by rewinding it again and again, choosing different dialogue options each time. However, it seems relevant to stress that this game is not for everyone.

This game is absolutely amazing, for several reasons.
1: It actually changes the story based on your choices.
2: It features a female protagonist with a personality unlike many protagonists in video games today, breaking the mold in a lot of ways that are simply beautiful.
3: The story and choices are engaging enough that even after playing it just a few days ago, I want to play through again to see what I missed and what happens if I focus on pleasing certain characters over others.
The only issues? Well, three episodes of five out so far. No one reviewing knows how they plan to end the game, and there's always the risk that the ending wont live up to expectations. The 4th episode will be pivotal, they threw a curveball after the 3rd and.... well... I personally haven't a single clue how they're going to take this. The only thing I can say is that I felt that same way at the end of the second and the third exceeded my expectations in every way, I trust DontNod that they have something amazing in store.
There's also a touch of a wonky perspective. In the first episode this isn't an issue because you aren't doing much looking or finding with it, but in the second and third(Junkyard scene and dark hallways scenes) this can get annoying as your own character blocks part of the view to the left. To be honest I wouldn't change this, it adds to the atmosphere to keep your character in view at all times and the puzzles aren't quite difficult enough to change that, I just wish that they would make things a little more visible or obvious so that I never had to resort to walking along every wall, nook, and cranny to get past a part in the story.
These are small complaints though. The game has a wonderfully well rounded cast where even the most disgusting antagonist has some level of humanity to them, once you discover a little more about them. I feel more like I'm playing a murder mystery at the end with how they've built the atmosphere, and I have no idea who to suspect or what will happen. This level of tension and excitement in the story is why you should definitely buy Life is Strange.

Love, love, LOVE the experience this game provides. The story telling is well done.
I'm an almost 30 dude, so at first I was worried about myself putting up with these bratty hipster kids using their try-too-hard youth lingo and the word "hella" everywhere. I like to imagine writers about as old as I am, writing dialog for the youth of today. The only initial saving grace was that the main character was a super chill, down to Earth, aspiring photographer. But after a while the annoyances just went away and I went with it, because the immersion is so good.
As far as 3D modelling, texturing and character designs go, this game has it in spades, especially for such a realistic style (for an adventure game). Animation is good - but for some reason the lip syncing is god awful, neglected. GOD AWFUL! For how good the rest of the production value is, there's no excuse. It kills me!
As far as adventure games go though, there aren't really any puzzles worth sweating about. If you get stuck, just go back in time and exhaust all your options - especially since solutions to puzzles are always so localized to a single area.
Original adventure IPs of this quality aren't released frequently enough. Artistically everything about the game is gorgeous, great design and story on all fronts. Just don't expect it to be a challenge in any way, think of it more as an interactive TV teen drama. There's a small handful of time travel inconsistencies that my inner nerd wants to call them out on, but it's all good. I also gotta give props to the technical artist(s) who did the hazy time traveling effect, always cool, never gets old.

I had read a whole lot of hype about this game, didnt read any content because of the hype. All I knew going in was that it was a similar "visual novel" type of game to what The Walking Dead and Wolf Among Us are in the Tell Tale Games lineup.
Its really hard to write anything about this game without giving spoilers up, so I will do my best.
You play as Max, a teenage girl with the power to rewind short periods of time and either solve puzzles or get out of precarious social situations and turn them for the better. You attend a reputable art school for photography and are Average Jane to the core personality wise... at least until you start making decisions for her. You will very quickly learn that unlike some games, you cannot please everyone and work all of the angles... with with super powers to rewind time, you're decisions will have consequences.
OH yeah... the main draw of this game. MEANINGFUL CONSEQUENCES. If you make a decision you can change your mind with the rewind power... at least until you leave the areas. But think carefully... and the protagonist is sometimes her own worst enemy as she will internally comment and make you feel bad for the choice you made her take. Still though, the scope of decision making isn't black and white. Some have immediate consequences, but there are a couple that don't have consequences until later episodes... and we aren't even done with the game fully yet. The decisions are the main selling point of the game, that they have an actual impact on the story. The only thing I can say is... yes. Yes they do. You have to take my word for it that they do, but they do... I don't wanna spoil anything for anyone reading this. This is an A+ story telling mechanism some are small, some are large, but they all have some impact later in the game. AAA Studios could take a lesson about gameplay elements from this IMO.
Great soundtrack... nuff said. Doesn't require an indepth explination.
The graphics and art style of the Unreal Engine work for this game so damn well, they crafted a convincing environment in a pretty small scale without it feeling like it was cramped. Half the time you don't even notice because you're so enriched with dialog and decision making that you don't even notice you're in a rendered parking lot with no much traffic or foot traffic in the background. A good job in that regard. I also love the way they present it, smal bayside village where everyone knows everyone... you don't feel the need to go explore everything because its all pretty meaningless to the protagonist.
Some of the support cast are ripped straight from prep school tropes, not a bad thing, but kind of meh as well. I do love the characters, each one adds something to the story of the game. Each and every one. From the prissy princess who bought the world, to the girl who's constantly in the wrong place at the wrong time. The world around you evolves with you and it is all delivered with great dialog.
The voice acting for said dialog is... hit or miss for me. Some of the characters are really well done... I feel like the protagonist doesn't have much emotional range in her voice though, its like watching a Kristen Stewart character come to life... can look past it since the engagement of everything supercedes it and the characters are at least interesting.
Episode 3 left me mouth a gape and wanting more... little regret playing it when its "incomplete" but it will make the release day that much more savory in my mind. Cant wait for Episode 4.
EDIT***Spoilers***
So I just finished episode 5 and holy♥♥♥♥♥♥I stand by everything I said in my review at the end of episode 3. This is story telling done right... its not a snooze fest and the characters aren't boring. The cause and effect system they use is exceptionally well done and the ending... holy♥♥♥♥♥♥the ending strips all of that away...
Dont get me wrong... this is a great game. But the tornado at the end of the game is really a decision making cop-out. I mean spoiler alert, everyone dies or one person dies. There is no inbetween from what I can tell. Dontnod really had a great thing and they ruined it with the final choice... this really feels like Mass Effect 3-syndrome. Its the ultimate "None of the decisions you made throughout the entire game mattered in the end" All of those times Alyssa was helped with her accidents, dead. You convinced Victoria to stop being a colossal ♥♥♥♥♥? Dead. Convinced Joyce to forgive David? Dead. David? Dead. All of the talking, all of the decision making was obliterated by the final decision. Saving Kate Marsh... pointless. Sacrificing Arcadia Bay is the ONLY way to make Max Caulfield make sense - giving a rise to that selfish love story of "I will destroy anything in my path to be with you" including sacrificing everyone else at the cost of that feeling. It is the ONLY thing that makes sense.

Okay, first of all being an Oregon native I'd like to start by saying I REALLY want to like this game. I was hoping this franchise would be the next BIG thing from Square Enix to kind of pull them from the fire, since the decline of the Final Fantasy franchise and poorly done reboot of "Thief".
Second, I don't write a lot of reviews so I will cut to the meat of it.
WARNING: I have only played the first episode of the game and I feel that after it's completion I cannot justify buying any other episodes, hence the review is for episode one.
The Good:
-Beautiful artistic style.
-Decent amount of content in episode.
-the ability to explore each option by manipulating time.
-Some actions will give you the warning of "this action will have consequences", I feel this adds a very positive element to the game. It's intense to do something as simple as make a doodle on a white board and for the next ten minutes sit there like "Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ Oh no no no no, what have I done?"
-Not early access! (Looking at you DayZ)
The Bad:
-"Life Is Strange" unfortunately  is part of the growing trend of  "lets milk every cent out of this idea" by being yet another episode based game. Great move for sales, awful move for the gamer. Developers don't seem to understand, If you make a good game the money will follow, there is no reason for this backhanded extortion "episode" garbage.
-LIS hits EVERY SINGLE stereotype imaginable, the shy new girl protagonist, her unruly and complete opposite best friend, the  paranoid veteran that beats his family while barely holding a security job, the snobby girl who wants to bang the super dreamy teacher, the rich unstable boy that "owns" the town, and finally the weird girl that dreams of being a cool kid. I felt that ninety percent of this game was me slugging through ♥♥♥♥♥♥ stereotypes and even worse Oregon based stereotypes with very little freshness or depth to any character or the location whatsoever
-Dialog is lacking, poorly scripted and story line so far has been fairly predictable.
-Graphics are lacking, while I am a firm believer in "graphics doesn't make a game" it does bother me when they are lacking and poorly optimized. I have a rig that runs ARMA 3 fairly well and the Metro series, I shouldn't have to dumb down the graphics on a game that doesn't have simple things like hair animation to prevent lag.
Final word: "Life Is Strange" turns out to be another game that had potential of be something special but seems to have been bogged down by the pursuit of money rather than excellence and written by teenage girls with no imagination, dependent on cliches and ignorance.

Life is Strange is so far one of the most interesting games that I have played. As a result, I started to think about how time itself is so precious and that it's important to make the most out of every moment. The atmosphere of this game is also very calming and real. There's a small handful of time travel inconsistencies that my inner nerd wants to call them out on, but it's all good. I also gotta give props to the technical artist(s) who did the hazy time traveling effect, always cool, never gets old.

I had read a whole lot of hype about this game, didnt read any content because of the hype. All I knew going in was that it was a similar "visual novel" type of game to what The Walking Dead and Wolf Among Us are in the Tell Tale Games lineup.
Its really hard to write anything about this game without giving spoilers up, so I will do my best.
You play as Max, a teenage girl with the power to rewind short periods of time and either solve puzzles or get out of precarious social situations and turn them for the better. You attend a reputable art school for photography and are Average Jane to the core personality wise... at least until you start making decisions for her. You will very quickly learn that unlike some games, you cannot please everyone and work all of the angles... with with super powers to rewind time, you're decisions will have consequences.
OH yeah... the main draw of this game. MEANINGFUL CONSEQUENCES. If you make a decision you can change your mind with the rewind power... at least until you leave the areas. But think carefully... and the protagonist is sometimes her own worst enemy as she will internally comment and make you feel bad for the choice you made her take. Still though, the scope of decision making isn't black and white. Some have immediate consequences, but there are a couple that don't have consequences until later episodes... and we aren't even done with the game fully yet. The decisions are the main selling point of the game, that they have an actual impact on the story. The only thing I can say is... yes. Yes they do. You have to take my word for it that they do, but they do... I don't wanna spoil anything for anyone reading this. This is an A+ story telling mechanism some are small, some are large, but they all have some impact later in the game. AAA Studios could take a lesson about gameplay elements from this IMO.
Great soundtrack... nuff said. Doesn't require an indepth explination.
The graphics and art style of the Unreal Engine work for this game so damn well, they crafted a convincing environment in a pretty small scale without it feeling like it was cramped. Half the time you don't even notice because you're so enriched with dialog and decision making that you don't even notice you're in a rendered parking lot with no much traffic or foot traffic in the background. A good job in that regard. I also love the way they present it, smal bayside village where everyone knows everyone... you don't feel the need to go explore everything because its all pretty meaningless to the protagonist.
Some of the support cast are ripped straight from prep school tropes, not a bad thing, but kind of meh as well. I do love the characters, each one adds something to the story of the game. Each and every one. From the prissy princess who bought the world, to the girl who's constantly in the wrong place at the wrong time. The world around you evolves with you and it is all delivered with great dialog.
The voice acting for said dialog is... hit or miss for me. Some of the characters are really well done... I feel like the protagonist doesn't have much emotional range in her voice though, its like watching a Kristen Stewart character come to life... can look past it since the engagement of everything supercedes it and the characters are at least interesting.
Episode 3 left me mouth a gape and wanting more... little regret playing it when its "incomplete" but it will make the release day that much more savory in my mind. Cant wait for Episode 4.
EDIT***Spoilers***
So I just finished episode 5 and holy♥♥♥♥♥♥I stand by everything I said in my review at the end of episode 3. This is story telling done right... its not a snooze fest and the characters aren't boring. The cause and effect system they use is exceptionally well done and the ending... holy♥♥♥♥♥♥the ending strips all of that away...
Dont get me wrong... this is a great game. But the tornado at the end of the game is really a decision making cop-out. I mean spoiler alert, everyone dies or one person dies. There is no inbetween from what I can tell. Dontnod really had a great thing and they ruined it with the final choice... this really feels like Mass Effect 3-syndrome. Its the ultimate "None of the decisions you made throughout the entire game mattered in the end" All of those times Alyssa was helped with her accidents, dead. You convinced Victoria to stop being a colossal ♥♥♥♥♥? Dead. Convinced Joyce to forgive David? Dead. David? Dead. All of the talking, all of the decision making was obliterated by the final decision. Saving Kate Marsh... pointless. Sacrificing Arcadia Bay is the ONLY way to make Max Caulfield make sense - giving a rise to that selfish love story of "I will destroy anything in my path to be with you" including sacrificing everyone else at the cost of that feeling. It is the ONLY thing that makes sense.
But wait, if you pick the other option, and sacrifice Chloe... then your decisions didn't mean anything... the entire reason for doing what you did was asininely removed at the end. You were saving your best friend/love interest (maybe/ I like to think). You pulled the trigger on Frank for nothing, you went back in time to try to save Chloe's dad for nothing...
Every decision felt real, it felt like it affected the world. Until the end of the game. Then they took that power away from the player, they took the feeling of consequences and cause and effect, the entire basis of the game and♥♥♥♥♥♥on it.
STILL a great game STILL recommend you buying it and playing it, but the ending felt copped out, and they couldn't loop everything together in a way that made sense so they went with the "your choices meant nothing" route. Which is infuriating.

This isn't your average adventure game, although it might be classified as such. There are some rudamentary puzzles that use the rewind mechanic, but you won't find yourself rubbing things on other things to see if they work. No, this is a game that holds itself up entirely through decisions and dialogue. If you find yourself in need of an action rush, there's nothing here for you, but if you're a fan of storytelling plain and simple, this is a gem.
The story is a simple and sweet tale of everyday life with the time reversal twist to give it some spice. The characters all feel very much alive, and even minor characters have meat to them. They're instantly relatable because they connect readily with people we all know from real life. The decisions that have to be made are also well implemented. There's very rarely a "right" decision. It's often a case of choosing the "least worst" outcome.
tl;dr: Each episode has had me wanting more, which speaks volumes about the game.

From watching the trailers and listening to the pre-release hype I was extremely reluctant to play Life is Strange. I will not lie, initially I thought, “Oh f**k here we go again, another idiotic teen drama game.” What I actually got was something much more interesting in the end. Life is Strange so far has an extremely engaging story that really covers a variety of themes. The game play advances by interacting with the environment and other characters while using the main protagonist’s powers to overcome the big problems. The controls are rather simple with you walking around 3rd person with various camera angles occurring as you move around.
Initially I hated the dialogue and the main characters comments on everything, even now after finishing act 3 I still cringe at times. Life is Strange is told from the protagonists perspective and touches on A LOT of very adult topics mixed with mystery, suspense, and some puzzle solving(light). The best part about this game is developing the story how you want by using the protagonist’s time reversal powers to make choices in a way you want.
My only complaints about Life is Strange are very few. First, the models seem very stiff at times, but I think that is worked into the artistic approach of the game. The second complaint is the lips don’t match the words coming out of the mouths which I suppose should be expect of a game published by Square Enix. The last little complaint is the invisible/visible walls that force you to stay confined in locations for the sake of the story. Though I understand this decision, I really want to explore the environment more but cannot because of the invisible/visible walls.
The story in this game is fantastic and I felt sucked in after about the first 30 minutes (it is a little slow in the beginning, and you end up dinking around with her powers). The music fits the story except for the best friend’s choice in music…you will see…”rock out”…phhfff.  The voice acting is superb with every characters voice matching the model and personality.  The controls do not cause any headaches while playing and I never got frustrated at being unable to perform tasks. I very much recommend this game.
Update Episode 4 release: This episode did not actually keep me as entertained as the previous episodes, the game felt rushed, disjointed, and very under polished compared to the previous releases (AND IT WAS SUPER SHORT!). I do not know if this is due to budget restrictions or square cracking the whip on the developer, but the purpose of episode 4 seems to be to wrap up the story  and set the stage for episode 5 without any consideration to the story pace (or story telling) as a whole. The big reveal at the end was not very surprising either, there were enough clues by the end that made you realize what was going to happen (unlike episode 3, which was amazing).  So though I still recommend the game, unless episode 5 is well paced, not rushed, and has a satisfying conclusion while avoiding the cliché ending options I do not know if I'm to keep my recommendation.

I thought Telltale ruined episodic adventure games for me. Season one of The Walking Dead was great, but between Season 2, Borderlands, Game of Thrones, and all the announced series it was getting to be a bit too much. This game, however, reinvigorated episodic adventure games for me. The characters are great (though Warren is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥, and the art style is beautiful. The story is gripping, emotional, and incredibly well written (barring a few instances of awkward dialogue) and all the voice actors are fantastic. Definitely recommended if you enjoy story centric adventure games, even if you're starting to get a bit weary of the TellTale style of games.

While the over-all plot line is quite intriguing, the writing and characters are awful--cringe worthy. Every character is a cliche and the writing is even simpler.
Also, there are a few inconsistensies and a lack of player freedom in a game that emphasizes freedom so much... Movements and environments are fairly restrictive. (e.g. one can't step up a ledge, you have to find and use the two-step stairs). Generally, there are one or two small areas beside the main one for exploration. Sometimes they have interesting and useful information, sometimes not. There are lot of objects one can interact with, but they are typically the same over and over again (e.g. missing person's poster), giving the illusion of full interactivity without actually creating any new content or introducing new information.
The game doesn't represent (good) photography very well either. As a photographer, the game kind of makes photography feel like a joke...
The game has so much potential, but the core gameplay is so dumb that it makes it hard to play. However, despite cringing through every other interaction; I still have an urge to keep playing it. I want to know what happens! This feeling tells me how great the game could be if it was rethought, rewritten, and polished to a proper extent.
The game does do a good job of highlighting how small actions can affect life and the notion that everything is meaningless in the bigger picture.
Note: I've played episodes 1, 2, and part of 3.

Gameplay: 10/10
The controls were very fluid and very simple. I was using a controller but I assume it'd be about the same with a mouse and keyboard. The mechanics of the game are very straight-forward and not complicated at all. It's more like an interactive movie than it is a game. It has a story that your actions affect, but other than walking around and looking at things you don't do much. That's perfectly fine because you won't be bored as long as you're actually paying attention to the story and the characters. There wasn't much you couldn't interact with and they did a phenomenal job of putting you in her shoes. Things she wouldn't normally do, like going into random rooms, you can't do. Some people may be turned off by that idea and to them I would say: "this isn't an RPG go back to skyrim. This story would be wasted on you anyways"
Story: --/10
Seeing as there are only 3 episodes out and I've only gotten through episode 1, I can't give this a fair grade just yet. I can say, however, In the 2~ hours I've played, I have felt more emotion, connection, and immersion than any other game I've played in a very long time. I will come back to edit this once everything is out and I have the courage to get through it T_T
Music: 5/5
Normally, for me, music and sound doesn't play a huge role in video games and it isn't something I normally look for or grade, but the music and songs used in this game are so so important. They picked the perfect songs to capture the characters and circumstances and atmosphere. It definitely helped to keep me immersed in this world.
Graphics: 3/5
Graphics don't affect a game positively or negatively for me. I'll play anything from the simplest 2D sidescroller to the most expansive and realistic RPG. But, I also expected more from a project backed by Square Enix. The characters' hair didn't move with them. It looked like a hat placed on their body in a program. The world wasn't as detailed in parts where there could have been more detail. The mouth movements didn't even try to match the words being spoken. The characters didn't seem to be looking at each other when they were speaking to each other. The colors were very well done and strangely the environment was well drawn and detailed. Basically, picture playing The Sims in first-person. That's what it felt like. They're just a few short years behind the current graphical standard but it's nowhere near game-breaking.
TL;DR:
I seriously felt like a part of these characters' lives and they felt like a part of mine. They will not leave me as I move on to other games. It's just not possible to forget this gem. If you like your games to have a story that will actually affect you, get this game right now. Otherwise, go back to skyrim kids.

I'll start by saying that I love this game.   Now, I should mention that emotional involvement in a game's story and immersion in the game's world are far more important to me than "challenge" and "gameplay".  As such, I'm ill suited to comment on such things - at least as a recommendation to someone who finds those qualities paramount in choosing a game.  If, however, you're like me and find it easy to settle into the role of a game's protagonist, feeling good when your character succeeds and empathizing when they fail, Life is Strange should keep you entertained.
In the first few minutes of gameplay, you will be presented with the main theme of the story and find that the character you control has mysteriously acquired the power to rewind time.  This rewind power is the chief mechanic of the game allowing one to solve puzzles and affect the outcome of various decision points.
While there are plenty of flavor details to be gleaned from items you can examine in the world, the majority of the story is told in a cinematic fashion through your interaction with non-player characters in the game world.  I found the simple controls and cinematic cutscenes to render Life is Strange into a kind of interactive movie.  My kind of game.
Of course, a movie should have good acting and I was not left wanting here.  I found the performances here to be quite believable and nothing broke my immersion.  Of course, the believability of a performance is directly related to the number of people one has known who act a certain way.  In my case, this worked.  Your mileage may vary.
The music suited the mood of each scene.  I found some quite pleasant, some not to my taste, but all of it fit well where it was used.
The story is excellent.  I find myself quite invested in the lives of Max and her friends.  I want to solve the underlying mystery of the story.  One of the early themes presented is that of "Everyday Heroes".  While a time-hopping protagonist is hardly "everyday", heroism is in what you choose to do - not what you *can* do.  I think Max makes a great hero - at least with certain choices.
Which leads me to replay value...  For me, I'll only replay to change a decision if the ultimate result of a choice leads to something terrible.  If being nice to someone were to result in the death of an innocent later, I'd feel obligated to "fix" it.  Other than that, I'd just be happy to have played a part in an enjoyable, well-told story.  To my mind, replay value is one of the least important traits of any game.  If you love to replay games, my opinion about how replayable something is may not be of much help to you.
If I were to complain about anything, it would be the fact that the movement of the characters' mouths is not as good as I've seen elsewhere, nor is it in very good sync with their speech.  Sometimes I feel as though I'm watching a dubbed movie.  Not a bad thing, but less than perfect.  Other than that, the graphical style of the game is quite lovely and immersive.  I find the facial animations to be quite good at evoking emotion when combined with the well-acted dialogue.
Overall, I'd highly recommend this game to anyone who thinks they would enjoy a cinematic, story driven adventure game with very light puzzle elements.  I'm reviewing this after completing the third episode - "Chaos Theory" - and I am excited about what's to come.
