One of the best games on Steam by far, and perhaps one of the best games I have ever played. It's full of tiny intricate details that culminate to create something truly epic and you really get a sense that all of the decisions you make actually affect how the game pans out. It's a masterpiece.

This game is a masterpiece, not just in integrating player choice, but also in taking an interesting concept- the idea of being able to go back and change one's own actions- and running with it into the sunset.  Unlike some other "choice-based" games, the universe doesn't feel like it's running on rails without you; your decisions leave a very real impression upon the world, sometimes coming back to bite you or help you in a key juncture where your time-bending powers can't save you, and after a key decision leave you wondering just what you've changed down the road.
Rather than having cookie-cutter good-or-evil choices, the game goes one step further and sometimes makes you choose whom to side with in a confrontation between two characters who are both in the wrong.  It does an amazing job of leaving you paralyzed by the weight of your decisions, which is interesting considering one of the main mechanics of the game is being able to reverse your own choices.  The fact that the game can take a mechanic which renders the player almost godlike in power and yet leave them feeling frustrated and helpless in the face of the world does an amazing job of putting players in the shoes of Max, a teen on the cusp of adulthood who, in spite of finding agency for the first time, feels scared and frustrated by the sudden responsibility she's found thrown upon her shoulders.
The writing is magnificent, the characters are rich and multidimensional, and the visuals are completely stunning- so much that you want to join Max in photographing the beauty of Arcadia Bay.  You become invested in this world, celebrating every triumph and feeling the guilt of your failures... including some truely devastating consequences of decisions made in good faith.  This game is everything that Telltale Games' Game of Thrones should have been, and I can't wait for the last two segments.

Another big sale event on Steam.  Like so many others, I buy game after game that is highly recommended, with only the highest reviews.   These games are usually entertaining, fun for awhile.  But, I miss that incredible feeling I had when I played the original CIV for the first time (or Baldur's gate, Planescape Torment, Masters of Magic, Masters of Orion or Wasteland back in the day).  For far too long it has seemed that the days of truly amazing, well written, innovative games were gone.   The industry titans that made these, and other truly great games, are long gone.   SSI, Sierra, Bioware and so many others, gone.
Then I tried Life is Strange, and that amazing magical feeling was back.  (If you truly love computer games you know exactly what I mean.)   The first night I played until 3:30 AM, the second night I was up until 5:15 AM until I finished all of the episodes that are available.  Followed by my restarting.  It was truly incredible.  The graphics are simply beautiful.  Your soul would have to be dead not to admire them (the translucent American flag in Chloe's room is so beautiful) or the characters you meet.
Playing this game was like reading the most amazing book (the story they build is that good), an epic movie, outstanding computer game, and the most beautiful graphic novel all rolled into one.  With the occasional moment to pause to appreciate the beautiful images and the interaction between characters as you go.   Oh, and the music is great too.
It is like some higher power revived Sierra to fulfill the longing dreams of game players everywhere.
This game isn't just another "overwhelmingly positive" on Steam.   It is a titan, a legend, to be mentioned with the best games ever created for the PC.  To be like Masters of Magic, played by all those who love it 20 years from now  as they fondly remember those first sleepless nights they first played it.
I will admit that this game is a lot like the movie the Butterfly Effect (although the game is a million times better).  I also found myself thinking of the comic story line where Booster Gold used time travel to try to save Ted Kord, or the huge story arc where Animal Man went to any length possible to recover his family.
So, If you love time travel stories... play this game now.  I hope the developers seriously consider contacting a comic publisher to get this out as a graphic novel.  Max deserves to be a super hero at a comic shop near you.  I also hope they boldly let you explore Max's feelings for Chloe in the final two installments.
If you have missed that magic feeling, play this game now.  End your search!.

There wasn't much you couldn't interact with and they did a phenomenal job of putting you in her shoes. Things she wouldn't normally do, like going into random rooms, you can't do. Story: --/10
Seeing as there are only 3 episodes out and I've only gotten through episode 1, I can't give this a fair grade just yet. I can say, however, In the 2~ hours I've played, I have felt more emotion, connection, and immersion than any other game I've played in a very long time. I will come back to edit this once everything is out and I have the courage to get through it T_T
Music: 5/5
Normally, for me, music and sound doesn't play a huge role in video games and it isn't something I normally look for or grade, but the music and songs used in this game are so so important. They picked the perfect songs to capture the characters and circumstances and atmosphere. It definitely helped to keep me immersed in this world.
Graphics: 3/5
Graphics don't affect a game positively or negatively for me. I'll play anything from the simplest 2D sidescroller to the most expansive and realistic RPG. But, I also expected more from a project backed by Square Enix. The characters' hair didn't move with them. It looked like a hat placed on their body in a program. The world wasn't as detailed in parts where there could have been more detail. The mouth movements didn't even try to match the words being spoken. The characters didn't seem to be looking at each other when they were speaking to each other. The colors were very well done and strangely the environment was well drawn and detailed. Basically, picture playing The Sims in first-person. That's what it felt like. They're just a few short years behind the current graphical standard but it's nowhere near game-breaking.
TL;DR:
I seriously felt like a part of these characters' lives and they felt like a part of mine. They will not leave me as I move on to other games. It's just not possible to forget this gem. If you like your games to have a story that will actually affect you, get this game right now. Otherwise, go back to skyrim kids.

I thought Telltale ruined episodic adventure games for me. Season one of The Walking Dead was great, but between Season 2, Borderlands, Game of Thrones, and all the announced series it was getting to be a bit too much. This game, however, reinvigorated episodic adventure games for me. The characters are great (though Warren is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥, and the art style is beautiful. The story is gripping, emotional, and incredibly well written (barring a few instances of awkward dialogue) and all the voice actors are fantastic. Definitely recommended if you enjoy story centric adventure games, even if you're starting to get a bit weary of the TellTale style of games.

While the over-all plot line is quite intriguing, the writing and characters are awful--cringe worthy. Every character is a cliche and the writing is even simpler.
Also, there are a few inconsistensies and a lack of player freedom in a game that emphasizes freedom so much... Movements and environments are fairly restrictive. (e.g. one can't step up a ledge, you have to find and use the two-step stairs). Generally, there are one or two small areas beside the main one for exploration. Sometimes they have interesting and useful information, sometimes not. There are lot of objects one can interact with, but they are typically the same over and over again (e.g. missing person's poster), giving the illusion of full interactivity without actually creating any new content or introducing new information.
The game doesn't represent (good) photography very well either. As a photographer, the game kind of makes photography feel like a joke...
The game has so much potential, but the core gameplay is so dumb that it makes it hard to play. However, despite cringing through every other interaction; I still have an urge to keep playing it. I want to know what happens! This feeling tells me how great the game could be if it was rethought, rewritten, and polished to a proper extent.
The game does do a good job of highlighting how small actions can affect life and the notion that everything is meaningless in the bigger picture.
Note: I've played episodes 1, 2, and part of 3.
Amazing game.

Gorgeous, immersive, and gives old school adventure gamers the instant gratification of answering the question of "What would've happened if I did this differently?". Better yet, you can investigate things and retain the knowledge without leaving any evidence of having touched anything. Say something stupid? Rewind! And still, because you can't see the long term consequences of your actions, which means replayability!
Not only does this game have a great concept, it also has been executed really well, with a clear interface. The main character is not just a pretty girl - she has opinions, she is a teen, she has her anxieties. The writers of the game follow the classic storytelling rule "show, don't tell" to give us insights about her personality. Just clicking and looking at the world will tell you not only about the environment, but also about how she feels about it. Also, I can't help it, but an 18-year-old artsy female protagonist does remind me of April Ryan - and that, Maxine Caulfield, is a flattering association!
My only issue with the game was the fact how quickly Max got used to the idea of being able to rewind time. I understand that for the sake of gameplay, the writers felt they had to speed it up a little, but I honestly would not have minded.
This game should be the future of movies.

I don't write reviews very often, but for this game I had to make an exception.
I think this is the first "visual novel" I've ever played, and after watching some videos of Telltale's Game of Thrones game, I wasn't sure what to expect as most of the time it seemed like doing one thing would have (roughly) the same consequences as picking the other option would.
That's not the case with this game, at all.
Now I haven't played through it for a second time to see how you would end up when you decide to take a different approach, but I did try a few different options from time to time, as well as look up what would have happened if I picked the other option. And as it turns out, your choices can have a huuuge impact on how everything will play out.
Now if that's not exciting enough, I really liked the characters. How not everyone is just either good or evil, but also often somewhere in between. Choosing to bond with certain people can feel very rewarding, as their attitude towards you may change dramatically if you treat them nicely.
For me the game was (near) perfect. There was a fair bit of drama, which, I must admit, will always keep me interested. But there's also a lot of mysterious things going on, exciting, but nothing too scary. Which is something I'm pretty thankful for.
The music fits the game perfectly, to me it feels peaceful and melancholic, and it really adds up to the overal experience that you get.
I'm kind of sad that I found out about this game before the last episode was released. Now I have to wait for months before I can finish it *sadface*

I couldn't find anything in this game I did not like, not one single thing. I've tried, but I can't think of any moment that I was not thoroughly enjoying this game. It was engaging, funny, relaxing but also always interesting.
I can't give this game anything lower than a 10/10, I would play it again, and rather sooner than later.

I'm in shock. I thought I was doing well. I was rekindling a friendship from years past. I was following my dreams. Maybe falling in love? I had a plan. I was going to help people, and do my best. Things were good. Not great. I was definitely making mistakes. But things were good.
And then I ♥♥♥♥ed up. I ♥♥♥♥ed up bad. There was an acquaintance. Maybe a friend. She had her demons, but she had a good heart. I really believed in her. Even angered some friends to try and help her when she needed someone.
And then, I lost control. She's dead, and I could have saved her. I keep telling myself: “No matter what you would have done, no matter what you changed, she'd still be dead.” But it's a lie. I could have saved her. I should have. I had the chance, and I messed it all up.
And the scary thing? I know it's all a game. I know it's just bits and bytes. But I still feel the guilt. I see that scene in the back of my head. I've done some crazy things digitally, but none have made me question myself.

I am in love with this game.
Granted, a lot of people would probably not call it a "game" per se - it's really more of a really loveable visual novel. I guess you have to be into this kinda of game to appreciate it. People who don't like being told a story and solving puzzles, and are looking for action and combat are probably not going to be happy.
Everyone else though is in for a lovely, relaxing experience.
Yes, i was thrown a little bit by the occasional weird "youth culture" reference and an 18 year old telling me "I'm an adult now" (no, you're not, sweetie. sit down. xD) but IN being so weird and awkward and trying to be "cool", she is portraying exactly what I remember being a teenager is like. It makes me feel a lot younger again and I appreciate that feeling of nostalgia.
For being relatively low-budget, the game is GORGEOUS (if you can live with the slightly off lip-synching). And the music... I could listen to the soundtrack for literally HOURS.
To make a long story short: If I didn't have to finish a paper right now, I wouldn't put this game down again.
So if you like visual novels, gorgeous art, nostalgia, relaxing games rather than action-packed ones, and mystery stories that involve puzzles and getting lost in a world and its own logic, this is certainly a game for you!

I'm in shock. I thought I was doing well. I was rekindling a friendship from years past. I was following my dreams. Maybe falling in love? I had a plan. I was going to help people, and do my best. Things were good. Not great. I was definitely making mistakes. But things were good.
And then I ♥♥♥♥ed up. I ♥♥♥♥ed up bad. There was an acquaintance. Maybe a friend. She had her demons, but she had a good heart. I really believed in her. Even angered some friends to try and help her when she needed someone.
And then, I lost control. She's dead, and I could have saved her. I keep telling myself: “No matter what you would have done, no matter what you changed, she'd still be dead.” But it's a lie. I could have saved her. I should have. I had the chance, and I messed it all up.
And the scary thing? I know it's all a game. I know it's just bits and bytes. But I still feel the guilt. I see that scene in the back of my head. I've done some crazy things digitally, but none have made me question myself.
I've been uncomfortable. I've been disturbed. I've been afraid. But I've never felt this regret. This guilt. I'm afraid to continue. But I have to. One foot in front of the other.

This review is for Life is Strange up to and including Episode 3, which at the time of writing of this review is all episodes we have of this game. Two more are to come.
In either case Life is Strange is an absolutely stellar, riveting story-telling game. It oozes the developers passion and commitment, it would seem this is a true labour of love coming from DontNod Games.
The characters featured in the game might seem like more or less typical US high school stereotypes but throughout the game and with interaction you start to get the idea that there is alot more to each character than meets the eye.
This is where the game truly shines in my opinion - often I've found myself contemplating alot about what decision to take and what the ramification of either decision might be. This is how a story-driven adventure game focusing on decisions and their impact should be done!
In the end I decided to try and kind of "roleplay" as Max (the protagonist girl you control) in my first playthrough which I think made the experience that much sweeter. Sure it's been one or two decades by now that I've been at high school but I am sure most players will recognise some similarities in their own school times.
Lastly, and I feel like I have to really emphasize on this, the original soundtrack and licenced artist music pieces in this game are one of its kind. Truly outstanding stuff! I kept being amazed at the wonderful choice of music utilized by the developers throughout the game episodes at cardinal points in the story - already bought most of the featured artists' work for personal use as well.
If you even have the slightest soft spot for story-driven, deep and emotional adventure games you should really treat yourself to Life is Strange.

It's amazing that other game companies wanted to change the whole concept of Life Is Strange such as putting in more action, making the main character a guy but, Square Enix didn't want to anything. They left DONTNOD with their project and let it set sail, the way they wanted. Which honestly, was the best idea ever because this game is brilliant, in more than one way. The design, characters, consequences of choice and just the story makes this game replayable worthy. This game also, brings a few tears so be prepared if you choose a bad choice and things go the way you don't want.
The setting of the game is of a school student, and what I find most interesting and somewhat relatable is what the characters are going through. This isn't your typical game where characters spout a few swear words here and there but, they say it often. The thing that I like the most about this game is the main character; Max (Maxine) Caulfield--she isn't your typical busty, overly make up wearing, /popular/ (in school) kid, kind of girl. She's just... average.
She's a photography enthusiast (camera nerd more like), and her tendency to not hand in a piece of work where her teacher is expecting very high of her is very relatable, to most of us.
Being able to rewind time is a unsual concept but, this game does it well. It isn't sloppy as it may look, it's actually really smooth--and it's a lifesaver when you feel as if you've chosen a bad choice. It's always so daunting getting things such as "this will have consequences" with the choice you've chosen to take but the thing is in this game, it specifies that the choices you make will effect the past, present and future.
There are some puzzles in this game, and there are some things to look out for (such as preventing someone getting hit, or other), they're not too challenging, but when you forget that you can rewind time and the things around you revert back into its previous position while you're somewhere else or doing something else can get you off guard. It definitely happened to me on more than one occasion; which was fine--it simply took a few trial and errors.
Another thing that I extremely like about this game is the relationships and the small things you can do to help these people in their class (whether it being science
), social groups, even small fights they have with one another. The other students in this game (aside from you) have that stereotypical role in the school; you've got the nerds, jocks, cheerleaders, popular and the unpopular.
The art style, music, voice acting, and portrayl of each individual characters give Life Is Strange a new feeling, it gives it that something more than from what other games have tried to incorporate manipulating time as a power. I think what ties it all, is the fact that the power Max Caulfield has, is something she has yet to fathom, or understand how to use it effectively.
If you're going to play this game,
to the things around you, and things you can look at. There are some crucial and significant items that link with the main story (such like at the end of episode 2...).

I've been a fan of Square Enix since I started playing video games, and I love a good VN, so I figured I'd give this a chance. The only thing preventing me from feeling like I wasted my money on this garbage is that I get really invested in terrible teen dramas really fast.
The game is pretty stunning visually, and I've read some business about how bad the soundtrack is, but I don't hate ♥♥♥♥♥♥ indie music and everything I've heard so far goes well with the aesthetic of the game. What is really really disappointing is the dialogue. It seems unanimously agreed upon in the negative reviews that if you're a 13-17 year old girl you'll probably be really into this, and that's more or less true. It really panders to the "lol I'm so edgy" tumblr girls... so it doesn't make much sense that the game is on steam, because I'm going to go ahead and assume that not too many of those girls are particularly interested in video games that aren't The Legend of Zelda (knowing a bunch of girls like this irl, I can attest to this). Every conversation feels dry (seriously, "go ♥♥♥♥ your selfie," what is that nonsense), like the writers know they're trying to fill specific tropes and don't even try to hide it. Unfortunately, you can kind of tell that they maybe tried a little too hard here; ending a string of in-depth photographic knowledge with "I'm so nerdy lol" just makes me, the player, feel cheap. Also, it's not like I don't curse, but the amount of times Max uses "♥♥♥♥" feels pretty similar to the amount of nudity in Game of Thrones (read: unnecessary and excessive).
Basically, I really felt like I was in the mind of an angsty 16 year old girl. Which in the end is most likely the point of the game, so I guess they did a really good job there? I don't know, I'm not 16 anymore, and I was never particularly angsty, so it mostly just feels like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
But all of that aside, like I said before, I get way too invested in terrible teen dramas, so I'll probably play this trash if for no other reason than to know how it ends.

It's amazing that other game companies wanted to change the whole concept of Life Is Strange such as putting in more action, making the main character a guy but, Square Enix didn't want to anything. They left DONTNOD with their project and let it set sail, the way they wanted. Which honestly, was the best idea ever because this game is brilliant, in more than one way. The design, characters, consequences of choice and just the story makes this game replayable worthy. This game also, brings a few tears so be prepared if you choose a bad choice and things go the way you don't want.
The setting of the game is of a school student, and what I find most interesting and somewhat relatable is what the characters are going through. This isn't your typical game where characters spout a few swear words here and there but, they say it often. The thing that I like the most about this game is the main character; Max (Maxine) Caulfield--she isn't your typical busty, overly make up wearing, /popular/ (in school) kid, kind of girl. She's just... average.
She's a photography enthusiast (camera nerd more like), and her tendency to not hand in a piece of work where her teacher is expecting very high of her is very relatable, to most of us.
Being able to rewind time is a unsual concept but, this game does it well. It isn't sloppy as it may look, it's actually really smooth--and it's a lifesaver when you feel as if you've chosen a bad choice. It's always so daunting getting things such as "this will have consequences" with the choice you've chosen to take but the thing is in this game, it specifies that the choices you make will effect the past, present and future.
There are some puzzles in this game, and there are some things to look out for (such as preventing someone getting hit, or other), they're not too challenging, but when you forget that you can rewind time and the things around you revert back into its previous position while you're somewhere else or doing something else can get you off guard. It definitely happened to me on more than one occasion; which was fine--it simply took a few trial and errors.
Another thing that I extremely like about this game is the relationships and the small things you can do to help these people in their class (whether it being science
), social groups, even small fights they have with one another. The other students in this game (aside from you) have that stereotypical role in the school; you've got the nerds, jocks, cheerleaders, popular and the unpopular.
The art style, music, voice acting, and portrayl of each individual characters give Life Is Strange a new feeling, it gives it that something more than from what other games have tried to incorporate manipulating time as a power. I think what ties it all, is the fact that the power Max Caulfield has, is something she has yet to fathom, or understand how to use it effectively.

I've been a fan of Square Enix since I started playing video games, and I love a good VN, so I figured I'd give this a chance. The only thing preventing me from feeling like I wasted my money on this garbage is that I get really invested in terrible teen dramas really fast.
The game is pretty stunning visually, and I've read some business about how bad the soundtrack is, but I don't hate ♥♥♥♥♥♥ indie music and everything I've heard so far goes well with the aesthetic of the game. What is really really disappointing is the dialogue. It seems unanimously agreed upon in the negative reviews that if you're a 13-17 year old girl you'll probably be really into this, and that's more or less true. It really panders to the "lol I'm so edgy" tumblr girls... so it doesn't make much sense that the game is on steam, because I'm going to go ahead and assume that not too many of those girls are particularly interested in video games that aren't The Legend of Zelda (knowing a bunch of girls like this irl, I can attest to this). Every conversation feels dry (seriously, "go ♥♥♥♥ your selfie," what is that nonsense), like the writers know they're trying to fill specific tropes and don't even try to hide it. Unfortunately, you can kind of tell that they maybe tried a little too hard here; ending a string of in-depth photographic knowledge with "I'm so nerdy lol" just makes me, the player, feel cheap. Also, it's not like I don't curse, but the amount of times Max uses "♥♥♥♥" feels pretty similar to the amount of nudity in Game of Thrones (read: unnecessary and excessive).
Basically, I really felt like I was in the mind of an angsty 16 year old girl. Which in the end is most likely the point of the game, so I guess they did a really good job there? I don't know, I'm not 16 anymore, and I was never particularly angsty, so it mostly just feels like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
But all of that aside, like I said before, I get way too invested in terrible teen dramas, so I'll probably play this trash if for no other reason than to know how it ends.

I've been a gamer since I was 4 years old. My older brother, 13 years older than me, introduced me to gaming through N64 and Gameboy. He gave me the original Ages of Seasons. I'm now in my 20's. I have played over 500 games easily and spent over 5,000 hours playing video games. Those hours equal over half a year and that's a low estimate.
Out of all the games I have played, Life is Strange is the most immersive. I don't know how and I don't know why; it just is. This game brings you in. For a 22 year old man who works more than games, saying a game where you are a teenage girl is the most immersive experience you've ever had seems absurd....but it's true. This game is amazingly immersive. I can't believe how I'm making these decisions and taking so much time just to think about them because I don't realize it while playing...but I actually care about each decision. I feel like I'm right there and affecting what's going on.
I know I'm going to do a second playthrough of the first few eps with different choices and see what's different about the game. Is this game for you? Probably, if you like plot in stories more than action/shooting/etc. What kind of problems exist in the game or is there a reason not to buy it? The storyline may be a bit linear in the grand scheme of the plot. This isn't really a hindrance though as you will still get to see your choices pan out for the duration of the story. I haven't found any other reason to not buy this game. It's simply amazing.
August 6th Update: The game continues to enchant me, especially in terms of the plot advancement. After playing over halfway through the game, the linear aspect of the plot does become apparent. The story progression, art form, and character development continues to draw me in. If I wasn't already in love with this game, I am now. I'm doing my best to wait until the last episode comes out before I do an Episode 4 playthrough. I don't want to wait until October before I can play Episode 5. This game is fantastic and, to give you a sense of the feeling of waiting between episodes, just imagine that your favorite TV show had a season finale cliffhanger or mid-season cliffhanger and you have to wait 2-3 months until you can get some kind of closure. This game is insanely impressive both in art style, writing, and most importantly immersion.

Adventure games are back in a pretty big way.  Nobody could have expected it.  Point-and-click adventure games were always destined to die as Sierra’s classic franchises each died shrieking, horrible deaths.  King’s Quest decided to become an action game; it didn’t work.  Leisure Suit Larry decided to switch gears towards a college bro demographic; it didn’t work.  And that’s it because literally nobody cares about Space Quest.  Years pass.  Roberta Williams includes a♥♥♥♥♥♥scene in Phantasmagoria.  Rob Lowe becomes a jazz musician (which is too perfect).  And Tim Schafer… well, he did alright for himself.
Then Telltale Games comes along and resurrects the adventure game genre.
Telltale Games have pretty much owned the adventure game genre for a few years now.  It’s just perfect, then, that the best adventure game of the year would come from an even newer development studio.
Life Is Strange is an adventure game that comes to us from developer DONTNOD, who previously brought us Remember Me, and publisher Square Enix.  Similar to Remember Me, Life is Strange is ambitious in scope and impressive in design; dissimilar, however, is how Life is Strange is actually as good, if not slightly better, than it’s recent predecessors in the genre.
Teen drama, photography, a murder mystery, and time travel all mix together into the cohesive Life is Strange.  After a terrible nightmare, Max Caulfield wakes up in class to what will be the worst week of her life.  While the tween dialogue can sometimes be insufferable, attention and care are given to the characters to help give them impressive depth and dimensions; even villains seem to have more going on beneath the surface than expected.  Well-rounded characters are written into thoughtful scenarios to help flesh out an interesting story.  Too bad about that dialogue, though… it’s hella tryhard sometimes, bro.

I've had to solve three really dumb puzzles (memorization and object hunting) and the story has just gotten more frustrating. You know how frat dudes self-insert as the cool sexlord in college movies? I think that Life is Strange wants to do that but for people who had punk vests in high school. It's an entertaining game, though. I got really mad when I had to do the newspaper-under-the-door puzzle in the first episode. There is so much to say about this game. It's not a game first off, it's one of those things that are marketed as a video game but end up sneaking up on you and attacking you, possessing your sole and encompassing your entire being. I have not been this enveloped and in love with a game since my first play through of Ocarina of Time 10 years ago. It is that good. I had been searching, til this game, pointlessly looking for some game to pull me back into the world of gaming I knew and loved in my past, with Legend of Zelda, Final Fantasy, Halo, and many others meriting note that kidnapped me and pulled me into all night playthroughs and lost contact with reality. Then I found Life Is Strange. It is different in a way, it's definitively tailored to a more mature audience (though we'll all agree Phantom Ganon was scary AF), and definitely more of an indie feel, yet remains beautiful and all-encompassing of what a true video-game that can call itself a piece of art should be.
But be warned.
This is not a sunshine, flowers, and does game with just good feelies, beautiful existentialism, and cliches. It is painful. It is scary. It is realistic and--I can't say this enough--utterly engrossing and enthralling. You will be frightened and scared at the most unexpected peaceful moments.
Thank you SquareEnix and Dontnod.
This original, beautiful, thought-provoking piece of art is well worth any amount of money you might ask. 9.8/10

So this game doesn't really need another review. Most of what has to be said, has been said already. It's gorgeous. Not as far as graphics go (although I do like the style), but the way the whole world, town, people in it and the story are being embodied into this virtual piece of art.
Originally, I picked this up just because it had good reviews. I really wanted to be part of this "touching story". Now, just having finished the third episode, I can fully claim I'm sitting here with goosebumps all over.
The characters are relatable. Maybe less for some and more for others, but we've all been teens. We've all been some part of the cast at some point. And we all wanted to change stuff going on in our lives. Now there's this game, which lets you. Sometimes by choice, other times by forcing you to do so to advance the plot. But holy hell, after the end of episode 3, I'm just going to be happy with my live as it is. Because the alternative might not always be better and this game, nay, interactive masterpiece, knows how to make you realise that.
Then again, I wouldn't recommend picking this up if you're not into narrative-driven games. There's limited gameplay. It's mostly just living the story, becoming part of it. I'm pretty sure a certain part of the populace would rather just watch a movie, instead of having this interactive story playing out. But for all the others I can't but try and convince you to pick this up.
<slight update, which I forgot to do after finishing the last episode>
After having experienced all the parts of the whole, I still feel like this is something everybody should go through. Sure, the ending isn't all too great. There are a lot of things to be said about it. But overall, the complete experience matters. Especially since now you can just go through the complete story, without having to wait for episodes.
The aforementioned end of episode 3 feels like it's the peak. But then again, maybe that's because of the way I played it. I recommend trying it. If it seems to scratch your itch, just go for it.

This game and the feels are two things that go hand-in-hand at this point. Just jeez, it would be a bit of an understatement to say I haven't been semi-traumatised after episode 2 and 3, but in a good sort of way. The way you'd expect/want from such a story focused game.
This premise at first with the whole rewind mechanic of the game was a bit sketchy to me, feeling that it would take away from the whole decision mechanic this is based off. Yet, despite this feeling I was pleasantly suprised and proved wrong as I realised it only adds to the overall all experience and tension and untimately stuffing you up at the worst of times but I won't say anymore. I feel it's just executed so well which is absolutely brilliant and definitely added to my overall experience.
As for other features of the game, the music and artstyle is great. The music is very chill and relaxing and ties in with the theme and artstyle really well and as for the looks, it's stunning really. While it ain't your hardcore, realistic, battlefield graphics or whatever game you ♥♥♥♥♥♥ over, its still beautiful in its own right and just suits the art style so well.
I am definitely a sucker for these types of games, but I cannot help but develop feelings for these stupid pixels that make up the characters. They are developed really well and bring out all the feels and making me combat myself based off my decisions.
I will say, it isn't completely perfect (I hardly call any game that) but it's still pretty damn good and managed to keep me on the edge of my seat wondering what is going to happen next. It's action packed in its own way and I would definitely recommend buying it. Just remember to stick with it and also, there's no shame in crying if you feel like it. It's okay, we won't judge

I'm pretty sure a certain part of the populace would rather just watch a movie, instead of having this interactive story playing out. But for all the others I can't but try and convince you to pick this up.

That ending to Ep. 3 really hit me hard and I can't stop thinking about it. Really awesome character building and pacing. The controls (time rewind mechanic) take on a sense of narrative from the beginning, which is usually rare in games and just makes this so involving and interesting.
The lip-syncing with the dialogue is bad just like it is in Deus Ex HR (edit: lip-syncing slightly improved via a patch just before episode 5 was released), but for the story to still be so riveting is a testament to the writing quality. I've never met anyone that talks like the characters in this game, but that didn't bother me, and I don't really understand why that would bother anyone unless it reminds them of something traumatic.
I think it would be unfair to compare this to other episodic games, or movies like the Butterfly Effect, because this game does enough to be its own thing. I really appreciate how refreshing this game is, just sitting down and listening to Max's thoughts isn't something you'd normally do in games, but here such moments help ease the emotional distress this game world inflicts on you, which in turn makes the game personal.
Of all the games I have, this is pretty much the only one I wish I could buy for everyone I know.
Edit: I finished Ep. 4 some days ago and I still can't stop thinking about it. Scenes of this game just keep popping in my head. The emotional rollercoaster just keeps getting wilder and dives into dark places.
Edit: Just finished Ep. 5, an overall awesome experience that I will hold close to my heart forever. Just like Max, I will always remember the time I spent with Chloe during that week.
The endings to the game are set, they conclude a story that was made before any episode of the game was released. If you're OK with an essentially linear story, and are ready to have your emotional and mental state be heavily tampered with, then I highly recommend this game. Thank you Dontnod.

This game and the feels are two things that go hand-in-hand at this point. Just jeez, it would be a bit of an understatement to say I haven't been semi-traumatised after episode 2 and 3, but in a good sort of way. The way you'd expect/want from such a story focused game.
This premise at first with the whole rewind mechanic of the game was a bit sketchy to me, feeling that it would take away from the whole decision mechanic this is based off. Yet, despite this feeling I was pleasantly suprised and proved wrong as I realised it only adds to the overall all experience and tension and untimately stuffing you up at the worst of times but I won't say anymore. The music is very chill and relaxing and ties in with the theme and artstyle really well and as for the looks, it's stunning really. While it ain't your hardcore, realistic, battlefield graphics or whatever game you ♥♥♥♥♥♥ over, its still beautiful in its own right and just suits the art style so well.

I will say, it isn't completely perfect (I hardly call any game that) but it's still pretty damn good and managed to keep me on the edge of my seat wondering what is going to happen next. I liked Dontnod's first game Remember Me more than most, but yeah, it really was rather disposable. But I really think Dontnod has found its steeze with Life is Strange.
Without having to keep so many playes spinning at once, it can get the most out of the whole rewind/redo thing this time.
It's much like Tell Tale's works in that the main mechanic seems to be difficult decision making, but it does something a lot of us having been screaming at games with moral choice systems to do, or rather to stop doing: it doesn't label your choices as nice/neutral/nasty. There are no right or wrong answers, every decision has consequences and rewards.
At time of writing, we're only up to Ep.3, so I hope it doesn't go all David Cage on us at the end and lose the intrigue of the fantastic by turning around and beating us over the head with it, but for now I think its a real stand out in the Contemporary genre in videogames.
It's not really that innovative or mind bending, and it has its share of design hiccups, but it's nice. And I'm okay with just nice.

Life Is Strange didn't have flashy graphics or top notch gameplay, but it will be forever etched into my memory. What it did have was an astonishing storyline, and characters that felt so real to me. The soundtrack was THE best game soundtrack I've ever heard. The feel of the game and what it said without saying words is incredible. Strip away the surface of it, and the core of the game is about humanity. It is about accepting the choices we make and being able to move on. It is about sacrifice. It is about the bonds we forge with other people. It is about knowing that people are more than they seem. It is about accepting the death and the end of good things. It is about knowing that terrible, terrible things happen and often to good people. Trying to reverse tragedy or avoid tragedy can create more. If you want one reversed, then you must accept what is to come
There's not a day that goes by that I don't think of this game. It's changed my life in a lot of ways. The characters of Max and Chloe will always be something important to me. Life Is Strange will always be a part of me.

I have never played a game that I have enjoyed more. The game has a rich, believable story and great atmosphere. The cutscenes are a pleasure, not something to be dreaded. The writing is superb. The music is, too--even if at times overbearing.
The closest comparison I can make, as far as similiar games would be the Dreamfall series, though this game handles the point-and-click-adventure-style puzzles much better, keeping them rather minimal. Not to mention, the puzzles are so organic that it's easy to forget the game mechanic entirely and simply be engrossed. I am not sure how much choices really matter in this game overall beyond adding mere "flavor", but I'm also not sure that I care. The story is that good.
This game messes with your head. It treads a careful line between overt showmanship, ever mindful that it is putting on as much a show as the very teen protagonists it portrays, and an understated look at just what it means to make (and live with) one's own choices. The games premise is very smart in how it brings this to life. This game is saying something to you, and the mechanism of a fully immersive experience that is a video game enables this in a way that any other medium just couldn't.
If I had to find fault, it is that the game seems to want you to play it as many adventure games and obsessively explore every nook and cranny. I felt compelled to play it differently, on account of being swept away from the story, but later I felt that I had missed out when the game presented me with my summary of my play.
Even here, though, I am apt to forgive. I'm reminded of the scene in the theatre in the movie Twelve Monkeys where the character Cole is lamenting how everything in the world is fixed (as a movie) and cannot be changed and he is told that perhaps the meaning of life is to stop and smell the flowers.
Ok. Let's explore. I eagerly await the next installment.

If you have played and liked Telltale games, you will like this game even better. With time travel as a main mechanic of the game, you don't have to play through the whole thing over and over to know what your conciquence your choices will have. You can make a choice, rewind time and try a different one if you don't like the results of your choice. This eliminates the problem I had with Telltale games where sometimes dialogue options are presented unclearly, and you end up making choices you didn't want to.
Another improvement on Telltale games is the unfixed camera. Trying to explore areas and see all the details in the world is much easier with control of the camera.
But enough of comparing it to other things, looking at the story. I REALLY love a story that can do time travel well, and I believe this game handles it rather well. As a mechanic and story element, it just works really well. I don't want to spoil much so I can't give many examples, but there are some interesting Groundhog Day-ish scenes where you can talk with people, get to know them, rewind, and start a conversation with someone for the first time for them knowing all this information about them.
But on the topic of talking to people: the lingo. Some of the things these characters say are cringe worthy at best (who the hell says "ubercool" or "nosh some food"?) and that is one side of this game that seems like either whoever wrote these lines is 50 and thinks this is how kids talk now-a-days, or they had an actual 18 year old helping with the writing and that IS how kids talk now-a-days, and I don't know which option is worse. But I don't think it takes away too much from the game.
Overall, so far through the game (Episode 3 is the last one that has been released so far at time of writing) it has shown itself to be a very well made game and is absolutely worth buying. I personally can not wait for the final 2 episodes to see where this story goes from here.

Life is Strange is certainly unique. As a story, it's compelling, and as a game it's refreshing. There are pros and cons to this type of storytelling, and I while I think that so far (only 3 episodes in!) it's worth the play, there are a few bumpy patches along the way. I have looked at three main categories below: Story, Presentation, and Gameplay.
---
STORY: Life is Strange presents a story of navigating life as a youth, while also trying to uncover a bit of mystery. If you enjoy peaceful cutscenes, lots of character interaction, and slow exploration, you'll enjoy this game. It's not a story that can be rushed (which is both a pro and a con - more on that below). The main character, Max, is an easy protagonist to follow (considering you're making most of her decisions anyway), and her chemistry with other characters only gets better. Without spoiling too much, she and other characters slowly start to unravel other plots happening around the school, and if you weren't paying attention, there are real consequences.
Unfortunately, the time travelling does make the story stumble a bit. The voices work sometimes, and others it seems a bit choppy, since it all has to fit with your choices. Since we don't know the results of all our choices yet, I can't really give a full review on the story. But it is compelling, although a bit predictable.
---
PRESENTATION: I'm not going to linger long here - the presentation of the game is probably the strongest aspect. The dorm rooms are realistic, the campus is gorgeous, and most of all the camera shots are well executed. Since the game takes place in the real world, the characters aren't exagerrated in movement, and there's a variety of different people. It makes sense - the game focuses on artists, so the aesthetic choices are strong. Extra details are appreciated, especially with foreshadowing the next installments.
---
GAMEPLAY: A choice based game. Anyone who's playe video games knows that sometimes if you pick the less desirable option, you do it over. In this case, Life is Strange encourages the player to explore all the options in game through the "time reverse" power, instead of having to reset. This leads to some interesting game play, but in my opinion, Life is Strange doesn't explore this far enough.
The GAMEPLAY aspect is the weakest part of the game. Where many would be content to play through an interactive story, Life is Strange insists on (sometimes lengthy!) fetch quests, almost as if to remind the player "This is a game! Don't forget!" and can really pull you out of the story. In exchange for a great story and an awesome presentation, we suffer less effort in the branching choices, and often it feels like there could be other options if the developers could have added them. There are puzzles, but mostly they revolve around digging for information, and then using new dialogue options. More story-based diggging, and less "go get the eggs and bacon" or "go turn on that light" fetch quests would be beneficial. Even 3/5 of the way through the game, this can sometimes feel like tutorial. I can only hope that, with the addition of the two final episodes, we see Max really get to use her powers in new and exciting ways.
---
CONCLUSION (TL:DR version)
In general, Life is Strange is worth the play, and I really hope that more games move in the direction of slow, explorative storytelling. It's definitely an early dip into this type of game, and by no means perfect, but it's compelling. There are a few bumps along the way (a bit with the dialogue, and a lot with the gameplay tring to emulate traditional gameplay, which it shouldn't feel the need to do). Otherwise, the game is beautiful and the short nature of episodes gives lots of room to explore. Check it out.

This eliminates the problem I had with Telltale games where sometimes dialogue options are presented unclearly, and you end up making choices you didn't want to.
Another improvement on Telltale games is the unfixed camera. Trying to explore areas and see all the details in the world is much easier with control of the camera.
But enough of comparing it to other things, looking at the story. I REALLY love a story that can do time travel well, and I believe this game handles it rather well. As a mechanic and story element, it just works really well. I don't want to spoil much so I can't give many examples, but there are some interesting Groundhog Day-ish scenes where you can talk with people, get to know them, rewind, and start a conversation with someone for the first time for them knowing all this information about them.
But on the topic of talking to people: the lingo. Some of the things these characters say are cringe worthy at best (who the hell says "ubercool" or "nosh some food"?) and that is one side of this game that seems like either whoever wrote these lines is 50 and thinks this is how kids talk now-a-days, or they had an actual 18 year old helping with the writing and that IS how kids talk now-a-days, and I don't know which option is worse. But I don't think it takes away too much from the game.
Overall, so far through the game (Episode 3 is the last one that has been released so far at time of writing) it has shown itself to be a very well made game and is absolutely worth buying. I personally can not wait for the final 2 episodes to see where this story goes from here.

This is a game that is not for everyone, love it or hate it. Life is strange reminds me of old-school adventure games and features a slick time travelling mechanic that is paired well with the choice focused gameplay.
It is not a fast paced game and will certainly not appeal to everyone, however if you take the time to explore you will be rewarded with a great story from the first person perspective of a female student called Max [which is actually presented in a third person play style.]
The player is drawn into the world of young Max through her thoughts and conversation along with her diary and text messages - it allows the player to feel connected with Max and the world around her. The time travel and choice aspects will have you hooked as choices will effect the outcome of the story and it is well worth finding subtle choice gems that are less obvious than others.
Overall, I'd say this is a refreshingly creative game that provides a nice change from all the action packed shooter titles that are so popular these days. Looking forward to the next episodes!

You've probably heard a lot about this game already.  If Telltale Games was told to produce a game with influences from Gone Home and Twin Peaks, but the protagonist has supernatural powers related to time travel, then you would have a good idea of the game's premise.
If you want a game with a lot of action, that doesn't require a lot of thought, or that is fast paced, then this is not the game for you.  Not that I am trying to put down those games, but Life is Strange is the exact opposite of that description.  It's appeal, and what distinguishes it from other games, lies in atmosphere, character development, and learning about the supporting cast.  You can only really advance the game by talking and learning more about other characters and the town that you live in, and making choices on how you ultimately decide to interact with them.  As you make these choices, you develop the protagonist's personality and what others think of her.
What really sets the game apart from others is the premise.  There aren't really any puzzles, the physical setting is not outlandish, plot development is slow, and the focus is on the story.  In many ways, playing this game almost feels like you are playing a television show.  It feels more unique than most other games that focus on story, in the same way that Portal and Portal 2 feel more unique than most games that are first person shooters.
If you want to try something different, then this game would be a very good choice.

Life Is Strange is one of the very few games that have managed to hook me and made me want to play through them without taking a lot of breaks (makes the waiting time for episodes 4 and 5 even more painful).
It is a very mature and story intensive game featuring lots of decisions you have to take during the course of its various episodes. And while it has not ended yet and the entirety of the choices' impact remains to be seen, I already have experienced the impact some of the choices made and have the feeling that their impact will only become bigger in the yet to come two episodes.
So far, I really like both the complexity of the story and the characters. While some clearly have more screentime and get more characterization, I have the feeling that all of them are "real" with their individual personalities and problems, not just some side characters with an slapped on archetype to fill holes.
My final verdict may change depending on the last two episodes, but so far this game has entertained and excited me in a way lots of games these days fail to achieve.

The atmosphere and writing are perfect, and remind me strongly of the attitudes and behaviors my late high school/early college community.
The only things wrong with this game are the complete lack of lip sync (I'm pretty sure the game just generates random mouth shapes whenever a character is talking) and the few fetch quests with sometimes difficult to find objects (looking at you, fifth junkyard bottle).
Some would say the graphics aren't the best, but the 3D models and textures have a very consistent art style that is clearly supposed to represent a watercolor painting, and looks gorgeous by mixing in highly realistic lighting and animations. My only complaint with the graphics is that the graphics programmers cheaped out and seem to have used a simple gaussian blur for the DOF rather than actually doing a proper bokeh simulation, which would have looked absolutely gorgeous in this game.
Loving it, and can't wait for episodes 4 and 5 to come out!

I've played the first three episodes now, and I have to say that Life Is Strange is different from any game I've played before. I really enjoy how each episode adds a new twist to the time-rewinding mechanic. It keeps it from feeling stale and repetitive. I also appreciate that the game's dialogue options aren't as over the top as, say, Mass Effect. When given options there's always at least one I agree with and if I don't like the outcome I can rewind and redo it.
The ability to rewind time has been done in a few games, but this one really lets you explore some of the ramifications and wonder about the consequences. The main character Max is written as a little dumber than she should be I think, but I still find myself empathizing with her and really enjoying walking a mile in her shoes. I have played each episode in one sitting and I keep checking for announcements on the release date of the next one.
The game music is FANTASTIC and for once an integral part of the game. Life is Strange wouldn't be the same without it.
The story is the truly amazing thing about Life is Strange though. Max has to tackle some very real issues that face us every day and there have been several powerful scenes that have really impressed and moved me.
Square Enix and DONTNOD have done something great here.

Wow. This game ... is incredible. I'm only an episode in, but I'm already blown away. It seems that Dontnod really learned from their mistakes with Remember Me, and they've stripped out the really cool mechanic of being able to rewind or "remix" time and put it in a context that works a lot better. I'm not going to go on about Remember Me here, and I want to make it clear that overall I'm a fine of the game, but Life is Strange is, to me, on a whole other level. It feels very real, very human, and I like that your big choices are often ones where it's hard to know which outcome is best (on that front, I think Dontnod definitely owes Telltale for some inspiration) and that even though you can literally go back and change your decision (sometimes multiple times), it's still not an easy choice. I'm very excited to see what comes next.

I wasn't instantly hooked by this game to be honest, it took me 6 months after purchasing it to really sit down and truly enjoy it. I had initially only played it for a few minutes and instantly dismissed it as a cookie-cutter Shenmue wannabe, right down to the clunky and sluggish walk of main character Max. I think that's a better comparison for the game than likening it to TellTale story-based titles as those are point-and-click and feel largely different in terms of gameplay. There was only a single instance in the story for me so far where it just felt like a sluggish "fetch quest" and that's even after developer Dontnod offered up a patch to remedy the situation. You will basically be interacting with objects and selecting dialogue 99% of the time so if you are looking for action this isn't the title for you.
The time-rewind aspect is handled really well and is woven seamlessly into both the narrative and gameplay. It adds to the experience as your choices and their eventual consequences can be weighed out without taking you away from the game itself. The story takes several cues from other time travel based media but it's all done very tastefully and never feels like a rip-off. As a fan of the genre I really enjoyed this particular aspect of the title. Don't worry, a Delorean isn't going to come crashing into the gates of Arcadia Bay (where the game takes place), but it was very interesting to see the title pay homage and reference a lot of other popular works within the genre.
Life is Strange is a great narrative-driven experience that I personally think is a must play for lovers of story-based games. As I'm writing this I still have two episodes left to complete as Episode 3 "Chaos Theory" is the latest one available, and all I can say is WOW. The atmosphere, writing, and characterization is just oozing with style and actually feels genuine, which is really surprising as high school seniors are never really depicted realistically in most videogames I've ever played. The music may be a little pretentious for some but that's not really a fault as it blends perfectly with the setting. The constant pop culture references are a little jarring at first but they really do a great job at enhancing the world-building and drawing you further into the Life is Strange universe.
There are some dark and suggestive themes being presented here that may be too much for younger gamers. Teenagers and up should be right at home as it's not that different than what's being presented on TV (or reality for that matter) these days.
I highly recommend this title and cannot wait to see how the rest of the story pans out for the students of Blackwell Academy. I didn't mention the narrative at all in this review because this game is really something you have to experience for yourself. Give it a shot if you are looking for something different here on Steam.

The writing is painful and cringeworthy at times because it's a bunch of old people trying to write "hip and young" dialogue for teens. The models are terrifying at times as they bend their necks in inhuman manners. The lip sync is nonexistent and the voice acting is passable at best. The plot is confusing and there's a lot of easy to miss side things with little to no indication that they exist. The big bad thing is probably easily predicted (As of this review, Episode 3 is released and I've beaten it) but it makes sense in context. The characters are supposed to be in High School and around 18 but they all look like they're mid teens due to the design.
Despite all of this, this game is fantastic. The writing and voice acting grows on you as you go along. The characters become endearing and have more depth than you would expect. There's a lot to this game and you just keep on finding more and more to explore and figure out. It's very rough but this actually adds to the value of the game. It's got a unique charm that is hard to replicate on purpose and is as hard to describe. The time travel plot is convoluted and almost nonsensical but that's actually not a bad thing. Time travel plots are confusing and convoluted no matter the medium. It's a great game with a unique charm and an actually interesting story. Everything grows on you and you can't help but get attached to these goofy characters as you constantly rewind time just enough so one person keeps getting hit in the head with a football. You'll play it with a bemused smile and find yourself laughing at the immature humor throughout the game, whether it's on purpose or accident.
I fully expect you to become Chronos and end up destroying the world because your time powers have broken the universe or something. I can see the game going there and not batting an eye.

Storyline - Better then I thought it would be and very unique; touches on very sensitive topics while creating an interest in what could happen next
Graphics - Aren't the best I've ever seen, but I've seen much worse then those. Decent, totally worth it to the player who doesn't go by graphics alone.

as soon as I can figure out how to do it without spoiling anything.

EDIT
Okay, now that it's all over... Yeah, still basicaly the same.
This is what the modern point-and-click evolved to. Games like Back to the Future and The Walking Dead are amazing, but this?
Everything you do throughout the (story) game has an impact in later episodes and especially in the final episode, which I do not envy the creator's job for. The final episode is the Ultimate Result of everything you've done. It's... incredible. Every important choice you've made plays a part in the final chapter - and surprisingly insignificant choices make a major difference, too.
*Spoiler Territory*
The very first episode went to great pains to show you what you were dealing with: in the very first major event - the thing that catapults you forward into everything else - there's a butterfly. The ideas and imagery of the Butterfly Effect (the actual theory, not the only-okay Ashton Kutcher vehicle) thump pretty hard through the rest of the game. All your major descisions have an impact, and even something as insignificant as basically writing "Wash Me" on a dirty window impact the later story.
If you're looking for action, look elsewhere. But if you want a story that will resonate for days after you play, then you've come to the right place... and no, this isn't a "walking simulator". It's a young woman's life, with you at the controls. It's... amazing.

Warning: This review is 100% my oppinion, nothing more. Also it contains spoilers, so read at your own risk.
Lets get straight to business. Game has incredible visual appeal, its masterfully crafted from the design point of view, bringing forth an interesting mechanic we dont see used nowadays, just because of how complicated it is to use.

Okay, now that it's all over... Yeah, still basicaly the same.
This is what the modern point-and-click evolved to. Games like Back to the Future and The Walking Dead are amazing, but this?
Everything you do throughout the (story) game has an impact in later episodes and especially in the final episode, which I do not envy the creator's job for. The final episode is the Ultimate Result of everything you've done. It's... incredible. Every important choice you've made plays a part in the final chapter - and surprisingly insignificant choices make a major difference, too.
*Spoiler Territory*
The very first episode went to great pains to show you what you were dealing with: in the very first major event - the thing that catapults you forward into everything else - there's a butterfly. The ideas and imagery of the Butterfly Effect (the actual theory, not the only-okay Ashton Kutcher vehicle) thump pretty hard through the rest of the game. All your major descisions have an impact, and even something as insignificant as basically writing "Wash Me" on a dirty window impact the later story.
If you're looking for action, look elsewhere. But if you want a story that will resonate for days after you play, then you've come to the right place... and no, this isn't a "walking simulator". It's a young woman's life, with you at the controls. It's... amazing.

This will be my first proper review for a game, but I feel like I need to try to explain how amazing this game is for people who are thinking about getting it. I've played hundreds of games in my time, and I can say for sure that this is definitely among my Top 5.
Life Is Strange is about a girl who discovers she has the power to rewind time. That's pretty awesome in itself, but the most awesome parts of this game is the direction and progression of the story, the soundtracks, the art and design of everything, and strangely enough, the down-to-earth relatable real life scenarios.
It sounds crazy to compare real life to a game that focuses on altering time, but you can really get lost in every little detail in this game. Nearly every little object is interactable in the way of your character sharing her thoughts of it with you. You have your own diary, and you attend school and class and live this almost-normal life. Some scenes will have you sit down and take in the scenery while your character has thoughts about her life and the story thus far. The soundtracks mix in with this to create a very calm atmosphere, but there's definitely still a lot of drama and gigantic twists to be had.
You might have played other games that have had "player-made decisions with consequences" before, but trust me when I say that you've played none like this. The decisions you make might seem meaningless at the time, but they can have huge consequences in this game; life or death consequences in some cases, or hugely game changing consequences (as I predict Episode 4 will have).
All in all, I can't recommend this game highly enough. This is one of the best experiences I've ever had, it really throws you into this life and all the fun and crazy emotions that comes with it. For just $20 for the entire series, you're basically buying the best possible use of ~15 hours to do in your day. 11/10 for sure.

Incredible voice acting, characterization, and a gripping story: this is what gaming should aspire to be. BioWare games have interesting characters; this game has characters you love, you hate, and you empathize with. It allows player agency while maintaining a strong narrative, leaving you second-guessing your major choices...not coincidentally, a lot like life.
The story drives you through themes which are rarely touched upon in games, ranging from depression to exhilaration, loyalty to betrayal. You don't simply press 'F' to pay your respects here; you nurture relationships through your dialogue choices and the actions you take; you work for your friendships or let apathy guide your way...it's your choice.
Technical Ratings: The character models and textures are not as great as they could be, especially for the Unreal Engine, but the environmental graphics and overall art direction are quite strong. Audio is also excellent, with a ridiculously appropriate soundtrack.

Episode 1 - You play as Maxine Caulfield, a photography student, studying at Blackwell Academy, who realizes that she can turn back time and has a vision of a hurricane/sharknado/whatever heading into her town thinking that it'll happen days from now. It's a teen, time-travel version of Take Shelter.
This episode is just a set-up for something bigger and for the most part, it has potential. I purchased this game without prior knowledge so I had no expectations. It just looks interesting to me and I love story-driven games. I didn't think it was going to be a teenage drama but with time-travel elements and I could do without the teen drama. Max Caulfield is introduced as a typical but likeable teenager who's up against challenging dilemmas and she can alter the results at her will.
That's the cool gimmick about this game, the choices you make can affect the story but you can turn back time and choose another option before moving on. I definitely want more interactive games with this mechanic as I don't have to play the game all over again to see another outcome. I was shocked at the principle's lack of concern in regards to an armed student since, apparently, he's a guy that you can open up to and so I reversed time to choose an option where you hide the truth from him as that (to me) would result in a better outcome.
On a technical level, the textures are low-res so it can be difficult to see things clearly. I'm not too picky when it comes to graphics but it could've been better. Overall, it's passable. I feel like the graphics complement the game's art direction as well. The lip-sync in this game is terrible. This game wants to be more like a movie but it feels like a dubbed Japanese anime.
Max is a strong character who aims to make things better such as impressing her teacher, resolving awkward teen dramas (cheating boyfriend scandal) and stopping bullies. The outcomes aren't always apparent but an episodic game aims to make it apparent later on and I'm interested in all of it. Every conversation is about a missing student named Rachel Amber, with missing posters all over the game. I'm interested to find out her role in the game and why everyone is so interested in her and why a security guard is interested in another student.
Max is the most grounded and believable character but unfortunately, everyone else are pretty much stereotypes. You have a stoner best friend, a spoiled queen b, a rich jock from a powerful family and a dead-beat step-dad. It doesn't help that the dialogues are cheesy and the deliveries felt phoned-in. I wanted to cringe at certain lines and the way they were delivered, such as the bathroom scene, the parking lot scene, the sexting scandal and the interaction with Victoria. It's a shame because this is an interesting story with believable scenarios and a heart to spare.
It took me about 3 hours to complete the first episode but I took my time with the game as I wanted to explore, interact with secondary characters and take optional photos. Overall, I enjoyed this episode and I can't wait to find out what happens next (although I'd rather wait until all 5 episodes come out before purchasing the rest) despite some writing and acting problems. It doesn't completely ruin everything but it makes it harder to buy into the story that tries so hard to make you care about and relate to its characters. Hopefully, the next episode gets to the interesting parts and tone down the teen crap.
7/10 - GOOD GAME
Episode 2 - So I bought the Season Pass despite my earlier intention of purchasing the rest of the episodes when they're released because I was so interested in this game. This episode has the same writing problems and continues the teen crap that you get from Episode 1. It's arguably a marginal improvement over Episode 1 as supporting characters that didn't work before (especially Kate Marsh and Chloe) now have more depth.
Kate faces constant bullying at school because of a viral video where she was supposedly engaging in sexual activities while being intoxicated. The caring Max that we knew from Episode 1 tries to be more supportive and I sympathized with Kate that I took the best possible options that I thought would result in a better outcome for Kate. But at the same time, Max has other things to worry about as well so I can understand why some players would choose to prioritize other characters (mainly Chloe) and choices instead.
Max's old friend Chloe, who becomes a rebellious troublemaker, brings us closer to the disappearance of Rachel Amber, as she and Rachel has a past. They spent time at a junk yard and we almost see the jealous side of Max that I didn't know existed. Chloe felt abandoned and Rachel was there for her when Max wasn't. This makes the character interactions in this episode more effective than the previous episode.
The junkyard section also embodies a tedious puzzle solving sequence where you collect 5 bottles to test the limits of Max's time-travel ability. Shortly after, we find that Max's ability can have a negative consequence. By the end of the game, I'm still not quite sure what that is but I'm guessing we'll find out later. I think Max can rewind time a certain number of times during the cutscenes though you can abuse her ability during gameplay sections as many times as you want but, of course, you can only go so far with her rewind ability.
In the end, the support characters are more important and even though I feel like they don't interact like real people, I buy them as a character when I didn't before. Like the previous episode, this one keeps me engaged by the end, even if I have to tolerate with the awkward dialogues and bad writing, but I'm willing to endure it again to enjoy its best and find out what happens next.

Original Review -
The only way I can truly describe how this game makes me feel, is to express it as a force. When you're walking in the early morning, feeling the crisp air, hot sun against your face, hearing the cars pass by, the birds chirping. Or when you're in a comfy diner, listening to the rumbling of voices, the chatter of silverware against the plates, the sound of a fresh cup of coffee being poured. While playing this game, you'll be absorbed into this world. Even though it's not that large, it feels immense. The team at Dontnod have gone above and beyond is creating an epic game that hurls you into a meticulously crafted story that truly makes you feel every aspect of the main character's journey. It also deals with heavy subjects like bullying, suicide, drug addiction, etc. It's an unfiltered view of what most of our high school days we're like, but you know, minus the sci-fi twist. I would highly recommend this game to everyone. Sit back, turn off the lights, crank the volume, and take your time going through this adventure. Also, the soundtrack is amazing. The music layered on top the visuals and narration only further this amazing experience. I can't wait for the final two episodes, but I'm not sure if I can take any more of these feels.

Life is Strange succeeds where many other modern "adventure" games fail. A narrative driven experience that simultaneously dabbles in science fiction, teen drama, conspiracy and mystery without ever feeling muddled or bloated. It's sure of itself and wears it's 90s pulpy influences very much on it's sleeve. It's quirky and dramatic and somehow never seems to take itself too seriously. Don't get me wrong, it's plenty serious. But it makes moralistic points without being preachy, it tackles difficult issues without passing judgement or causing offense and it treads a brilliant line between the fantastic and the mundane.
I've never played a game that's kept me guessing this long, that's had me so interested and invested in each and every character that passes by (yes, even the horrible ones) nor have I ever played a game where the choices have left me so unsure of myself. I still don't know if -any- of my decisions are the "right" ones, and that's fantastic.
It looks great and has a style all it's own with brilliantly designed characters and environments, it sounds amazing with a soundtrack that somehow manages to stir nostalgia for songs and places and people I've never experienced before.
Some people have issues with the dialogue, saying that it's clearly written by middle aged dudes who have no idea what teen girls talk like. Well, I disagree. My biggest issue with the game was the overly expositional nature of some of Max's internal dialogue, but that eases by Episode 2.
If you love great, crazy, emotional, keep-you-guessing stories and have a 90s fetish, do yourself a favor and check this out.
