AIGHT LET'S GO.
The main selling point of this game is that it's a choose-your-own-adventure game in which your CHOICES ACTUALLY MATTER. You've seen the hype.
Welp, they might have succeeded in  keeping up that illusion for the first two episodes, but guess what, guys! By the end of episode 3, that's all dashed across the cliff alongside a couple a dead whales.
dontnod wowed a lot of people with the potential death of a main character at the end of Ep. 2. I've got to admit, I was totally impressed by the ambition that must have gone into a game that presents two fully branched, 100% voiced stories. It even allowed me to forgive them for the flat characters, bland setting and poorly researched dialogue. But guess what? The only differences between the branches have to do with various textures in the background. Anything that requires one image to be swapped with another? SOMETIMES different. There are a few dialogue headers that are clearly route specific, but most of the dialogue is totally vague about Kate's condition. Except when it isn't and really really should be! Within the first ten minutes, it becomes unclear whether the primary "bad guy" Nathan has been expelled or suspended. If you succeed in saving Kate, the dialogue refers to his expulsion while notes consistently discuss his suspension. Poor form.
And if you can really forgive all that laziness, the grand finale of Ep. 3 lets you wipe out all of your choices up until that point! Like salt in the wounds, dontnod!
Honestly, I'm still in a haze of "Oh my gosh, what did I just waste my time and money on." Sure, it brings up themes that are important to youth right now, but you can get the same experience by browsing tumblr for a couple of hours. You know what else costs 20 bucks? Dragon Age Origins. Gone Home. A couple of hamsters. Go out there and buy yourself a friend before you throw dosh at this tripe!
PS. The art everybody's gushing over? Everything looks like the very bottom layer of a thumbnail. This is the laziest game I've ever payed money for.
PPS. The music is generic hipster garbage. Y'all should be offended by how blatantly this game has tried to water down youth culture to get into your wallets.
PPPS. Yeah, I'm salty at this game. If you haven't forked over $20, save yourself the headache and pass. If you already have, by some star-crossed twist of fate, you should probably be salty, too.

tl;dr: A slow burner with an awkward beginning. Push on and you'll find a deeply human story, with clever mechanics.
Boy, did this game grow on me. I'll admit, episode 1's initial hit of awkward teen drama combined with minimalistic time travel mechanics did not draw me in. However, the slow burning mystery, beautiful environmental storytelling, and incredibly human character arcs left me breathless by the end of episode 3.
I have learnt this is a game about people, first and foremost. The mystery is simply a driver, and the paranormal a backdrop. It is about friendship, regret, grief, loss, love, change; the death of innocence, the complexity human's hide beneath superficial veneers.
As the plot deepens, so too do the mechanics. Simplicity gives way to complexity, and Max's rewind ability gains more uses than just undo. Though the possibility of rewinding conversations to follow alternative paths is neat, and at times necessary, I found myself using it less and less as I progressed. Max was no longer the awkward, unsure girl she'd started as. Her curiosity had transformed into resolve, and no second guessing would slow her down.
If you're looking for visceral action, you'd best begin with Telltale's Walking Dead, however, if you're looking for a slower, nostalgia-tinged adventure, Dontnod's Life is Strange is a fine choice.

Having sat down to play Episode One, I knew I was going to be hooked and impatiently waiting for this to come to it's full potential. I returned today to find that Episodes two and three had been launched and now that I have played through them all, I finally feel like I have enough to write about it.
Life is Strange gripped me in it's beautifully loving and cruel talons from the get-go. With Max returning to her old stomping grounds it called to me visiting an old town I lived in once. Where everyone knew everyone, the diner employees knew your favorite dishes, and you could get lost just imagining the world for hours. Then... things got crazy.
Graphically, sure it will never match-up to AAA titles, but it's got something that even realistic graphics and physics engines of our modern gaming seem to have lost. It's got heart. It's got the balls to swing against all odds, because it knows it's pretty enough to get there and it knows the real beauty of the game isn't the hand-drawn art that shows how truly hard these artists worked. No, it's not a graphical masterpiece of our time for it's futuristic realism... it's a graphical masterpiece for it's simplicity. I was absolutely blown away by how quickly I fell for this style.
When it comes to audio, I usually crank the music volume down (or off) because it always detracts from my experience with the game. It pulls me out of the moment because suddenly, the boss-fight features the London Phil-Harmonic. Not so with this piece. The music is so interwoven with the story that it feels enhancing, not distracting. Very few games have ever achieved this for me, This War of Mine being among that list (a game I absolutely loved). The voice acting feels real to me, as though these characters are putting weight behind their words, as though their words have meaning. Vocally and musically, even just the ambient sounds really put me in the moment for a lot of the game. Even now, as I write this, the menu music is playing as background noise, it's truly a treat for the ears.
The controls are fairly easy to understand, it's a basic WASD and point/click/drag kind of game. But Life is Strange knows this, it knows it doesn't need fancy lean mechanics or crouch/jump for telling the story. What it gives you is so much more than a list of spells and a big heavy sword. It gives you a mechanic we've all seen, used, and loved. It gives you this and it makes you love it more. The world is at Max's fingertips, your fingertips, with the right use of the rewind mechanic. All from the perspective of a scared, uncertain young adult - something we all were once. Something we'd be in this scenario. I never felt like my immersion was broken by faulty control, it was very well done.
Now as far as the story goes (and this may get long), I do like that (as Telltale does) it lists your choices against other players. I'd like to think we're all on our first play-through here and seeing how the world reacts to this is touching. Knowing I'm not the only person that rewinds time as much as he can to tell that one weird girl about getting out of the way is kinda cool (shame on you guys for letting Lisa die). But it also reveals where maybe we slipped up, took a course of action that later on we can see may have affected our timeline (though, it was awesome to see we all love to hate Nathan). The story doesn't drop you into the middle of a minefield armed to the teeth or dressed to the nines. It drops you into the shoes of a young, socially awkward, confused girl... and then throws more confusion and chaos on top. I did, quite literally, risk going into work late so I could finish chapter two because I was so enthralled. Life is Strange tugs on all the right strings, it knows you want a story and it has a hell of a story to help tell... so long as you help tell it. As I saw another review that stood out to me...
"You can tell a good story in a bad way, and you can tell a bad story in a good way." (Thank you, Dominus) Life is Strange tells the story, for better or worse, in the best way possible. Because it's not just the game's story... it's yours. As a 24 year old male, the times a game has caused tears to well up in my eyes can be counted on one hand. Twice now, Life is Strange has caused that. My ending with Kate and the end of chapter three were written in such beautiful cruelty that I was simply left... as though I had truly been standing there.
When I had picked up Life is Strange, I hadn't bothered to see who made it and it never really clicked until tonight who was behind this masterpiece. I avidly stand firm against Square Enix, their stories, their products. I thought this was an indie developed title, which is why I chuckled so much when I read Dominus' review. It challenged me to think, what if AAA developers cared about making a /good/ game, not just another repeat of everything we've seen. Square Enix definitely brought themselves back onto my radar with this title. Life is Strange is a masterpiece that should be in every gamer's collection, standing proudly alongside games like This War of Mine. I am to put it simply, extremely impressed.
On a side note - Who said DON'T kiss Chloe? Really? Cause the rest of us felt the implied sexual tension. For those of you who said DO kiss Chloe, how quickly did you scroll to that... The menu was barely visible as a choice I scrolled so quickly.

Edit: I've added some comments after episode 4's release.
Edit: I've changed this since episode 5's release.
Pre-Episode 4: This game has truly gotten my attention. I thought the Wolf Among Us was amazing, but Life is Strange blows it out of the water. No pun intended. The ability to change actions done within a small amount of time gives me a whole new feel for Choose Your Own Adventure games like this. I despised when I'd feel like I'd make an awful decision while playing the Wolf Among Us and have to restart the chapter to change it. But now, I don't need to worry. Until the sequence ends. But I feel like I don't need to restart if I f*ck up a decision because I had the chance to change it, but didn't use it, so it's truly my fault in the end, so I should suffer the consequences.
The characters truly catch my eye as well. I can name one person in my life who can match each and every character if only by a little bit. I won't go into detail, but I'll tell you one: I'm definitely Chloe. Minus the drugs and being able to drive (fear of driving).
Also, people always complain about the lip-sync, but I feel like it's a genuine, lovable quirk. Just like how Telltale has their cartoon-y look (excluding Game of Thrones), Dontnod has their (unintentional) nonsynced mouthing. Unintentional because of budgeting.
People also complain about the writing. However, I truly feel like the writing is good. I know when there's truly horrible writing, trust me, and this writing is average. However, I grew slightly disappointed; while I learned the lip-sync problem was unintentional, I learned Dontnod pushed most of their budget in WRITING and voice acting. I would expect if they did such a thing, that writing wouldn't be a complaint among people. Highly budgeted, AVERAGE writing? I mean... I personally have no complaints as the writing makes the game enjoyable for me, but I do see why there is complaints after learning this fact.
All in all, I personally adore the game and would recommend it to everyone I know. Hell, I'm even tempted to see how my mom would go through the game and she hasn't gamed in over a decade.
Post-episode 4: The lip syncing has gotten a lot better. I found LIPSYNC files in episode 4's data which leads me to believe they worked on that during this episode. I have reason to believe after episode 5, DONTNOD will go back and fix the lip synch for the first three episodes. I shall report back if this occurs or I have new comments after episode 5.
Also, major trigger warning through episode 4. I got really upset throughout episode 4 and cried for about a half hour. Be wary as you tread through the game.
Post-episode 5: DONTNOD has gone back and done LIPSYNC files for past episodes and it does look a bit better.
However, episode 5 in itself. It's honestly... Not satisfying. The ending was predicted for the start of the game by loads of people. It was great though, but there are unanswered things that I wanted to get answers to.
-SPOILER WARNING-
Nathan's father is referenced in episode four to be coming to Arcadia Bay. That never happened. In episode three, you can find feminine stuff in Samuel's closet thing, but it's never exactly explained. Sure, maybe it's the squirrel thing, but why feminine things though?
-SPOILERS DONE-
The ending is just completely... Flat. Maybe if they had a episode or two more, then we could get more answers and maybe they could have gotten a better ending wrapped together. The end was so cliche... It's just... Not great because I knew it was going to happen...
Don't get me wrong. Life is Strange is a great game, but it took so much out of me emotionally... That having this ending is disappointing. I still recommend it to those who want to play it. Just don't put yourself too into the game cause it will feel so wasted.
Overall: 8/10

This game will have changed my life. Every now and then I stumble upon a work of fiction that I completely lose myself in. It's usually a book series-- Eragon, Twilight, Black Cat. I forget what's real and what's fiction, and just kind of drop out of reality, swimming in fantasy and emotion. It's been a while since the last time that's happened, probably a few years, but this game really hit me hard. I've never seen or played a game that's wrenched my heart right out of my chest and played my emotions like a piano the way this game has. I watched Jacksepticeye play through the first two episodes, and after the first one I felt like my entire personality, my whole mind went through a complete reset. I went to class that day and forgot all about who I was before; it was like it was the first time I had set foot in the room. It's just that immersive of a story that you can forget reality and live in this fantasy world, and when you step away from the computer it's a struggle to accept that you're not an 18 year old girl named Max who can rewind time, on a mission with a punk♥♥♥♥♥best friend to figure out what the hell is going on in a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥filled apocalypse. It's painful, even.
Long story short, the best story of any game I've ever played by far. If this was a book, it would go down as one of the greatest of our time.

So i was skimming through youtube a while back when suddenly my feed was filled with this little game called Life Is Strange. I watched the first episode as a let's play by one finnish youtuber and i was instantly hooked to the story and characters. I just HAD to buy this and experience the game first hand...
The gameplay is sort of point and click-esque, but not quite. It's similar to Beyond: Two Souls, but not even close. It's so hard to describe because it's so unique. You are solving puzzles, playing with a certain gimmick the game provides (and story is based/revolves around on). The twists the story throws in your face are so well written, it leaves you praying for the next episode to come out quickly.
The episodic nature of the game is something i'm not a big fan of, but the length of the episodes are just right (about two to three hours depending your style of play). The replay value is also high because you want to see how different decisions affect later in the game. And trust me, they REALLY DO affect, unlike in certain titles from Telltale (*Grhm* Game of Thrones *grhm*)
The visuals of the game are amazing. And even for my low-end pc, i still get the full experience because the art style of the game is not that dependent on graphical quality and processing power, like GTA 5 for instance.
I have found a major bug in the game though. When i enter the journal and look at the emails or text messages for two long, my computer crashes to the point of no return, and need to be hard reseted. This is happening only in SMS/email screen, and i don't know if it's a bug in the game itself, or just my computer dying of old age.
Still, i do recommend this game to everyone who likes episodic "choice-games", and for even those who don't because it is so unique and different it would be unfair to compare it to any other game out there.
Give the first episode a try. Or if you are hesitant drop five bucks for it, watch the first episode on youtube, and then make your decision :)

With innovative story and excellent soundtracks, Life Is Strange truly offers a breath of fresh air to a generation filled with action-packed FPS and RPG games. Life Is Strange certainly does not offer the most cutting edge graphic, but its visual style is very comforting; apart from the visual design the soothing soundtracks alone deserve commendations.
Although many players are alienated by the prominent American youth culture and stereotypes throughout the entire game, every single characters in game has unique personalities which arguably brings varieties and hence making the story interesting nonetheless. The character developments are frequent which keeps the story going; as I have just finished ep3, I am excited to see what ep4 and 5 have to offer.
Gameplay wise, Life Is Strange offers exactly what a telltale game should be. The rewind ability truly provides gamers many options and approaches as well as a new level of freedom as they progress throughout the game. In most cases, players could always rewind and go with a different approach each time, which makes the gameplay a lot more flexible than any other telltale games such as The Walking Dead. The possibilities are endless, and it's up to players to decide how the story would go.
As I have just finished ep3, I have made both "good" and "bad" decisions throughout my game time. A lot of the decisions might be completely irrelevant, but then again, I suppose you could say the same when a butterfly flaps its wings. I am looking forward to the ultimate finale.

Having sat down to play Episode One, I knew I was going to be hooked and impatiently waiting for this to come to it's full potential. I returned today to find that Episodes two and three had been launched and now that I have played through them all, I finally feel like I have enough to write about it.
Life is Strange gripped me in it's beautifully loving and cruel talons from the get-go. With Max returning to her old stomping grounds it called to me visiting an old town I lived in once. Where everyone knew everyone, the diner employees knew your favorite dishes, and you could get lost just imagining the world for hours. Then... things got crazy.
Graphically, sure it will never match-up to AAA titles, but it's got something that even realistic graphics and physics engines of our modern gaming seem to have lost. It's got heart. It's got the balls to swing against all odds, because it knows it's pretty enough to get there and it knows the real beauty of the game isn't the hand-drawn art that shows how truly hard these artists worked. No, it's not a graphical masterpiece of our time for it's futuristic realism... it's a graphical masterpiece for it's simplicity. I was absolutely blown away by how quickly I fell for this style.
When it comes to audio, I usually crank the music volume down (or off) because it always detracts from my experience with the game. It pulls me out of the moment because suddenly, the boss-fight features the London Phil-Harmonic. Not so with this piece. The music is so interwoven with the story that it feels enhancing, not distracting. Very few games have ever achieved this for me, This War of Mine being among that list (a game I absolutely loved). The voice acting feels real to me, as though these characters are putting weight behind their words, as though their words have meaning. Vocally and musically, even just the ambient sounds really put me in the moment for a lot of the game. Even now, as I write this, the menu music is playing as background noise, it's truly a treat for the ears.
The controls are fairly easy to understand, it's a basic WASD and point/click/drag kind of game. But Life is Strange knows this, it knows it doesn't need fancy lean mechanics or crouch/jump for telling the story. What it gives you is so much more than a list of spells and a big heavy sword. It gives you a mechanic we've all seen, used, and loved. It gives you this and it makes you love it more. The world is at Max's fingertips, your fingertips, with the right use of the rewind mechanic. All from the perspective of a scared, uncertain young adult - something we all were once. Something we'd be in this scenario. I never felt like my immersion was broken by faulty control, it was very well done.
Now as far as the story goes (and this may get long), I do like that (as Telltale does) it lists your choices against other players. I'd like to think we're all on our first play-through here and seeing how the world reacts to this is touching. Knowing I'm not the only person that rewinds time as much as he can to tell that one weird girl about getting out of the way is kinda cool (shame on you guys for letting Lisa die). But it also reveals where maybe we slipped up, took a course of action that later on we can see may have affected our timeline (though, it was awesome to see we all love to hate Nathan). The story doesn't drop you into the middle of a minefield armed to the teeth or dressed to the nines. It drops you into the shoes of a young, socially awkward, confused girl... and then throws more confusion and chaos on top. I did, quite literally, risk going into work late so I could finish chapter two because I was so enthralled. Life is Strange tugs on all the right strings, it knows you want a story and it has a hell of a story to help tell... so long as you help tell it. As I saw another review that stood out to me...
"You can tell a good story in a bad way, and you can tell a bad story in a good way." (Thank you, Dominus) Life is Strange tells the story, for better or worse, in the best way possible. Because it's not just the game's story... it's yours. As a 24 year old male, the times a game has caused tears to well up in my eyes can be counted on one hand. Twice now, Life is Strange has caused that. My ending with Kate and the end of chapter three were written in such beautiful cruelty that I was simply left... as though I had truly been standing there.
When I had picked up Life is Strange, I hadn't bothered to see who made it and it never really clicked until tonight who was behind this masterpiece. I avidly stand firm against Square Enix, their stories, their products. I thought this was an indie developed title, which is why I chuckled so much when I read Dominus' review. It challenged me to think, what if AAA developers cared about making a /good/ game, not just another repeat of everything we've seen. Square Enix definitely brought themselves back onto my radar with this title. Life is Strange is a masterpiece that should be in every gamer's collection, standing proudly alongside games like This War of Mine. I am to put it simply, extremely impressed.
On a side note - Who said DON'T kiss Chloe? Really? Cause the rest of us felt the implied sexual tension. For those of you who said DO kiss Chloe, how quickly did you scroll to that... The menu was barely visible as a choice I scrolled so quickly.

Edit: I've added some comments after episode 4's release.
Edit: I've changed this since episode 5's release.
Pre-Episode 4: This game has truly gotten my attention. I thought the Wolf Among Us was amazing, but Life is Strange blows it out of the water. No pun intended. The ability to change actions done within a small amount of time gives me a whole new feel for Choose Your Own Adventure games like this. I despised when I'd feel like I'd make an awful decision while playing the Wolf Among Us and have to restart the chapter to change it. But now, I don't need to worry. Until the sequence ends. But I feel like I don't need to restart if I f*ck up a decision because I had the chance to change it, but didn't use it, so it's truly my fault in the end, so I should suffer the consequences.
The characters truly catch my eye as well. I can name one person in my life who can match each and every character if only by a little bit. I won't go into detail, but I'll tell you one: I'm definitely Chloe. Minus the drugs and being able to drive (fear of driving).
Also, people always complain about the lip-sync, but I feel like it's a genuine, lovable quirk. Just like how Telltale has their cartoon-y look (excluding Game of Thrones), Dontnod has their (unintentional) nonsynced mouthing. Unintentional because of budgeting.
People also complain about the writing. However, I truly feel like the writing is good. I know when there's truly horrible writing, trust me, and this writing is average. However, I grew slightly disappointed; while I learned the lip-sync problem was unintentional, I learned Dontnod pushed most of their budget in WRITING and voice acting. I would expect if they did such a thing, that writing wouldn't be a complaint among people. Highly budgeted, AVERAGE writing? I mean... I personally have no complaints as the writing makes the game enjoyable for me, but I do see why there is complaints after learning this fact.
All in all, I personally adore the game and would recommend it to everyone I know. Hell, I'm even tempted to see how my mom would go through the game and she hasn't gamed in over a decade.
Post-episode 4: The lip syncing has gotten a lot better. I found LIPSYNC files in episode 4's data which leads me to believe they worked on that during this episode. I have reason to believe after episode 5, DONTNOD will go back and fix the lip synch for the first three episodes. I shall report back if this occurs or I have new comments after episode 5.
Also, major trigger warning through episode 4. I got really upset throughout episode 4 and cried for about a half hour. Be wary as you tread through the game.
Post-episode 5: DONTNOD has gone back and done LIPSYNC files for past episodes and it does look a bit better.
However, episode 5 in itself. It's honestly... Not satisfying. The ending was predicted for the start of the game by loads of people. It was great though, but there are unanswered things that I wanted to get answers to.
-SPOILER WARNING-
Nathan's father is referenced in episode four to be coming to Arcadia Bay. That never happened. In episode three, you can find feminine stuff in Samuel's closet thing, but it's never exactly explained. Sure, maybe it's the squirrel thing, but why feminine things though?
-SPOILERS DONE-
The ending is just completely... Flat. Maybe if they had a episode or two more, then we could get more answers and maybe they could have gotten a better ending wrapped together. The end was so cliche... It's just... Not great because I knew it was going to happen...
Don't get me wrong. Life is Strange is a great game, but it took so much out of me emotionally... That having this ending is disappointing. I still recommend it to those who want to play it. Just don't put yourself too into the game cause it will feel so wasted.
Overall: 8/10

First and foremost: All of the episodes of this game, so far, have been awesome.
Secondly: This is not a shooter. If you're the kind of person who can't stand dialogue in your games, this isn't for you.
That isn't to say that this game doesn't have adrenaline rush moments, though! I just finished playing Episode 3, and while every episode has ended with a cliffhanger, Episode 3 has been the best yet.
In this game, you play the high school girl Maxine Caulfield, who discovers she has the power to rewind time. Throughout the episodes, she has to use this ability to take decisions that will ultimately affect the way the game plays. And here's the kicker: It ACTUALLY works. Remember the ending of Mass Effect 3? If you felt betrayed by that game's lack of outcomes despite your choices, you will love this game.
There's hundreds of hours of cutscenes and dialogue in this game, and you'll only have the abililty to experience it all for yourself if you make different choices the next time you play.
Another cool thing about this game is the art direction. The graphics mix cartoony with realism, resulting in a kind of hipster-chiq look. The music emphasizes this, as does the writing. Playing through this game feels like playing through an american indie film.
Of course, there are also drawbacks. Sometimes, the gameplay can crawl to a halt if it isn't immediately obvious what you're supposed to be doing. And sometimes the game will require you to look at certain objects or make certain dialogue choices which will require you to rewind time. All of this sounds repetitive, and it is. It can also make the game feel somewhat limited, because it isn't free-roaming and half the time you're either talking or looking at or grabbing objects.
But the actors, writing and animation make you as the player care about the characters and the story. And in a story where the player gets to make choices that really determine how it plays out, I for one can't ask for much more.
If you like dialogue and great storytelling, you WILL love this game.

This is a rare gem and a good improvement over Telltale's approach to episodic gaming.
It takes the existent pseudo-point&click formula, and does something which I had to grin about at first, but since have come to love: it allows you to freely "reload" (you do something in-game, actually) and try out different options when talking or doing.
In a way, save-scumming is the main game mechanic, here.
But the game knows that, and beautifully works with it and presents an absolutely awesome (so far, 2,5 episodes in) story with likable characters with understandable issues. That is, the characters are overdone, but in a good way, they present issues which we can agree with and be moved by, without getting lost in a "full" character, yet at the same time they avoid the Final Fantasy issue of 1-attribute-characters.
In total, warmly recommended.
Pros:
+ Very good narrative (so far, 2,5 episodes in)
+ Well-done presentation, nice work of drawn shapes to highlight objects.
+ Amazing inclusion of save-scumming as a game mechanic.
+ Relatable issues on well-written characters.
+ End of episode 2 leaves you panting.
Cons:
- Short episodes (they're good *and* worth the money, but still short).
- Overdone dialogue "theme" at times, lessens after the first episode.
- Naturally "too easy", but this depends on perspective. Going back and trying different approaches *is* the game's main mechanic, ofc you can re-try until you like the outcome.

At first i felt like i was playing "how to be a hipster without a fedora". But as i continued playing, a fairly good story started to unravel. It pulled me in, I was wrong of my previous opinion the game.

I would recommend this game to anyone, especially people who enjoy story/choice based games like TellTale Games produce (The Walking dead, Games of thrones etc)  I don't do many review but when i stepped away from this game i felt the need to post one.

The rewind mechanic is more like an "exploration" mechanic than a mechanism for tension and drama. It creates a lot of opportunities for characterization that aren't possible in older forms of media (I mean, I guess choose-your-own-adventure, but...). "Did she respond that way because of what I said? Is she in a bad mood? Does she just not like me? Does she just not like anybody?" All of these questions can be clarified for the viewer with the rewind mechanic, at the level of their curiosity. Not to mention the characterization you can create for the player character..

I love games with a unique story and choices. Life is Strange hits all of those marks right on the head. The characters are very well written and the hand drawn art style was a very good choice for the graphics. And when they say that choices matter in this game, they mean it. Even the little things that you think won't matter actually comes up later in the story. And the soundtrack for the game is very good very chill and really sets the mood. I feel like I'm in a TV show and am engrossed in the story. And it goes into time travel and paradoxes so they have some pretty cool puzzles with you talking to someone, learning some information, rewinding back in time, and using that info on someone to progress. This game does have it's flaws though, the characters mouths don't always sync up with their words and that may not seem like a big deal, but for me personally it takes me out of the moment. I have seen some glitches where a character in the background would T pose, but other than that the animations and cut scenes are very fluid. Over all if you love games like Telltales The Walking Dead you will love this game.

It's like a Back to the Future/time travel adventure modern point and click adventure game, except not made by Telltale.

A beautifully executed game where the choices matter in your overall story. I've only played episode 1 so far, but either way each decision had a certain impact on later events as the episode progressed, and really drills that sense of dread when it says that your actions have consequences.

All I have to say is every choice you make in Life is Strange brings about a sense of urgency and actually matters throughout the story.  I was in deep thought before finalizing all of my decisions and it still made me feel uneasy about some of the things I've done despite how good my intentions were as the main character, Max. The fact that you can rewind time in case you changed your mind about a choice is a very useful and convenient feature if you believe the alternative choice is best.  This level of control does not take away anything from the this intense ride, instead puts you in the driver's seat of the story, so to speak.  What you see unfolding isn't predictable either because of this mechanic, that's part of why it's so awesome.
I'm a 23 year old man and I can relate tremendously to Max.  I have zero interest in photography yet I think if this character were real I would be best friends with her.  I have realized how similar I am to her when I was in high school and even to this day.  She's a very likable protagonist.
I only finished episode 1 and this has already become my favorite choice-based episodic game. It's actually turning out to be one of my favorite games of all time even. It's good to note that Life is strange is leaps and bounds better than anything Telltale has dished out recently, a company positively notorious for its interactive episodic titles.
UPDATE: I finished episode 4 and the game continues to get better and better.  My verdict on LiS hasn't changed.
If you are unsure whether to give this game a shot, please take my word and get it.  There is not a single negative thing I can say.  The choice in soundtrack is literally perfect.  The animation and graphics are beautiful.
Simply put, Life is Strange is a masterpiece and easily worth your money and time.

I believe this will be my first review of any game but this is one game that is worth reviewing.
Life is Strange was a game I first saw as a popular streamer was playing but after watching for five minutes I had to turn the stream off because I did not want anymore spoilers. Immediately after I bought the entire collection and the next day played it through. As the first story telling type of game I have ever played Life is Strange was definitely worth starting as I was hooked before the first scene even finished. It immediately had me hooked into wanting to know what I had just seen and why I'm seeing this. As I moved through the game it didn't feel like I was watching just a movie or playing a game. I had just enough interaction to not feel like I was watching a movie but also not like I was playing a game. I felt truly immersed in this game and in the story I was controlling. Everytime I made a choice I thought long and hard about how It may affect the rest of my play and whether I should have or not. Not only did my choices affect the game they always kept reminding me about those choices later as I played and It was incredible. I never felt a wasted moment in the game and I can't wait to play more. I'm not really sure there is anything I can say I disliked about this game because if there was no chapter ending scenes I may have stayed in full immersion until someone or an alarm or something reawakened me to the real world or I finished entirely. Truly a game I will remember and I highly recommend to everyone who feels they may truly be able to enjoy this genre of game and even to some who are uneasy should at least try the first episode out because you may just like it.

So I got 14 minutes into this game before getting stuck.  Actually, it was more like 5...and then a bunch of restarts to see if "that" worked.  Anyone who's played the game is probably trying to figure out what I got stuck on.  The second task...look at a smegging photo on your desk.  Maybe you wonder how the hell you get stuck there...me too.
So as it turns out the circle with the arrow pointing at the photo isn't a indicator of what you should do...despite being labeled look.  Your actually supposed to drag the mouse onto the label.  How...intuitive.  Maybe I just suck at interpreting their directions...but seriously that took way too long to figure out.
Oh, and for a game where you can rewind time...its suspiciously "random" as a game mechanic.  Seriously, when it matters, like saving a persons life, your rewind window is like three seconds...when it means absolutely nothing like a conversation, rewind as far as you like.  Yeah, I'm barely into the game and that already has♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off.  So yeah, still not impressed.
Story and characters and all the strong points everyone raves about?  Yeah, I wouldn't know.  The mechanics of this game have thus far prevented me from finding anything out.  I'll try to play more and see if this game manages to hookme before I give up, but at this point I'm glad I only got ep1.
Penetrated by feels, 10/10. The game takes some building up but it is worth every second.

This is one of my favorite games I think I have ever played.  It's not complicated, it's a lot of just watching and clicking on things, but it's incredible!  It's like a movie you get to take part in...speaking of, it would make an amazing movie or series of.  Unlike the Telltale episodic games most of your decisions in this one can be changed on the fly instead of reloading and replaying because you screwed up or didn't click fast enough.  This allows you to see things from the other way, briefly, before making a final decision...this might seem like a cop-out in a way, but sometimes you are actually supposed to do that and other times you'll see the results far down the road and they can be big.
The main characters Max and Chloe are hella awesome, both character wise and in the voice acting.  The rest of the cast does an outstanding job as well.  The story flows surprising well while also being a jumbled up time traveling mess of wtf is going on, keeping you guessing the entire way through...who is doing what, who is involved where, what happened here, why are weird things happening and what connects them all, where is this photo Max is going to turn in for her project!  Episode 3 especially...holy♥♥♥♥♥♥..not the ending you would expect...plays out like the ending of an epic movie, then blam, major cliffhanger...shock, just wow.  And then they do it to you again at the end of Episode 4, another punch to the face!
Episode 5 is a wonderful rehash of all that is happened with humor and heartbreak and more wtf is happening...which by episode 5 is the only drawback to the game, it's never fully explained...some think that's good, me, I would have like a little something.  The final endings are the biggest disappointment to the game ala Mass Effect 3, lackluster and not enough depth if you go one way, too cliche and defeats the purpose of a lot if you go another, though there is a  lot of emotion and it is done well.
Overall, though, this game is a Game of the Year without question, a Best Games of All Time contender for certain.  I love 'Life is Strange' and I wish there would be a sequel with the same main characters that you grow to love throughout, but sadly the developers have said if they make a second season, it will be different characters.  Max & Chloe forever! <3  ːLIS_butterflyː

I like story rich games.  Especially when what you choose has an effect on the story. This is why I like visual novels in which you are given choices that matter a lot. And this game, has all of that, but also an actual, and I must say, a really enjoyable 3D environment in which you can move around. You can tell they put a lot of work into the environments, the graphics look kind of water painted which gives it an unique look, and it looks really nice, and the scenes are really lively when there are more people around which makes it feel like you're in a real world. Indoors environments are really nice as well, really creative. I love the things written on the wall in Chloe's room. I found myself spending some time on reading them all.
So anyway, on top of that, this game offers exploration, a lot, there is a lot you can look at/interact with.
This is kind of spoilery, but as soon as I started the game and the fact that the main character can reverse time came clear, I had to think of the Butterfly effect. I enjoyed that move a lot so I already knew this game had gotten even better. The story, although kind of cliche at times, is interesting and keeps going at a nice pace. And the choices given sometimes made me wonder if I really did the best thing. It's not like you can reach a bad ending/lose the game prematurely due to choices though as far as I know. Regardless of that; I still had this "uh oh" sense at times when I did something, which proves how well the game makes you experience that what you do will have certain possible consequences, either good or bad.
I had only bought episode 1 first to see if I'd like it enough but I am hooked and am definitely getting the other episodes as well!

Wanna hear something crazy? Supercalifragilistic expialidocious. Wanna hear something crazy and consistent? Life is Strange sometimes when one day you find yourselves eating waffles with David Cameron, the other you're playing the didgeridoo in a mariachi band; Sometimes you'll find you're granted a power to bend the fabrics of the space time continuum while communicating entirely through pop culture references in a strange alien language that closely resembles speech patterns of human communication but doesn't quite grasp the subtleties. Life is Strange when episodic adventure games sets out to do something and then manages to more or less accomplish it.
Life is Strange the game, however, by Dontnod Entertainment are none of the things above and yet it is all of it -- It's an episodic adventure game developed by the creators of Remember Me, which can best be summarized as promising potential that was let down by repetitive combat and weak execution of its gameplay concepts involving memory alteration.
Well, Dontnod, took these shortcomings on board.. and threw them into a fire.
Gone are all of it, instead we get an excellent adventure game with some occasionnaly clever puzzles integrated into the game's dialogue tree, which also brings us to the game's premise of choice; Choices that feel weighty as they are presented to be.
Although the inclusion of reversing time is nothing if not completely ♥♥♥♥ing sweet, but like your average comic book it fails to get in the ring with Professor School Life who always acts like a♥♥♥♥♥whenever they are both in the same room. Relatively speaking, things aren't easy for main character Max Caulfield,18 years of age who attends Blackwell Academy, in the suburbian city of Arcadia Bay at a pivotal moment of embracing the abominable selfie-culture during class, which also serves to pave way for such award winning lines as  "selfie-expression" or "Go ♥♥♥♥ yourselfie" -- Max discovers a strange occurrence of deja vu, like time had just reversed, which incidentally it did at her behest; Things only get more intense from there. In typical French arthouse fashion, or at least by the rule of David Cage, it doesn't take less than 5 minutes before someone is stabbed to death, where Max's powers become handy for the game to demonstrate the magnitude behind them and the responsibility. The player is obliged to take advantage of this power to both score points in class to advance the plot and save people in need. All things considered, while Max is basically channeling the infinite power of Chronos here, there is of course a catch and a burden.. but most importantly, a limit to what she can do. Her story centers itself around making hefty decisions, as mentioned a few phrases ago, which will change not just her life, but those who flock around her if not reality itself. Choices that are more or less soaked in morality, indistinguishable from any concepts of "good" and "evil", they are but choices and it's up to the player to do what is right. A nice change from the usual feeling you get from a game, that would more or less resent you for not aligning in accordance with its moral compass.
The dialogue is dodgy at first but when Max and Chloe are in the same room, then everything is gold -- Chloe is  rambunctious and a wild card, but her close feelings for protagonist Max makes it easy to warm up to her along with the excellent voice acting from Ashly Burch (whom I believe generally steals the show in regards to the overall acting in the game so far). If we forget the cringe-worthy dialogue cluttered in slang, we'll find some genuinely good writing beneath the crap, when the pop culture references play out appropriately like Max and Chloe's ping-pong exchange of Al Pacino's famous Scarface one-liners, then it comes exhilarating and fun. But one musn't forget the emotional content, for if anything, Life is Strange has managed up the scales by a margin with the release of episode 2 & 3, dealing with sensitive topics such as suicide which fiddles into a pivotal character moment for Max and one of her NPC in-game friends in episode 2 SPOILER ALERT, SORRY!
Life is Strange has only 3 episodes so far but it carries with a fair and tight release schedule to make sure that things don't go quiet for too long between the waiting time, in case so we forget the game or anything remotely memorable about it.
Because the truth is that the game has become memorable for me. Its considerate usage of time travel and choice for its storytelling is executed so well through its lighthearted banter between teenagers and emotionally heavy drama that it could potentially end up being  one of my favorite games of the year. If Dontnod continues to up the scales at the pace they've been keeping then that could definitely become true.
The game might not be finished and neither is my review so consider this a recommendation based on what has been seen and/or played so far. It's really good!

I rarely write reviews.
In fact, this is my first one.
But in my quest to get some stuff done on steam, in the name of 'achievements!!' or whatever, I was ultimately drawn to describing how my experience with Life Is Strange was- above any of the other games in my library.
This is an absolutely beautiful game. While it has is ups and downs, the art style is simply gorgeous, and the story and in-game mechanics are so skillfully designed and put into play that it makes up for anything possibly negative.
If anything contributes to any 'cons' this game has, it would at most be some occasional glitches/bugs (time traveling sometimes stops rewinding just to leave the world in slow-motion, until someone's line is finished), or the fact the difficulty is nothing really balanced- seeming to be placed either at the extremely easy setting, or very confusing setting, on one or two occasions. Don't worry, they're easily fixable with the help of Max's tendency to speak her mind.
Either way, those two issues do nothing to damage the complex emotions this game creates. Sucking you in, characters are surprisingly intricate, making any story line with different people interesting and life-like. Characters can also sometimes be difficult to read- exactly like real people. The soundtrack also helps; the lovely indie tunes to this game leaving you entranced and stuck within the indie movie-esque fictional world, until your chapter comes to a close.
I can promise you: at the end of every episode you'll be craving the next.
So don't be so quick to rush through chapters and get missions done; make sure to look at everything, talk to everyone, and most of all don't be afraid to rewind and choose every possible option.
If this game has taught me anything, it's to take your time.
PS. Keep an eye out for those extra parts/photos/clues in the different chapter settings! If you don't start looking at everything from the very start, you'll learn later how much you truly miss.

(I'm writing this after having just completed Episode 3.)
I'm more of one to watch walkthroughs of video games than actually playing them myself, but when I saw the first promos for this, I just KNEW that I had to actually play it myself. And I'm so glad I did. This game has everything I really love about video games, especially the complex storytelling. All of the characters and situations ring true to life, even if sometimes they do seem a bit outlandish or awkward. I love how even the small decisions (like having Max water her plant) end up having interesting impacts down the line. And there's such an heavy sense of nostalgia in the game that really makes it more fun and engaging; we've all been in some of these situations, we've all said and done things the characters have done -- the aforementioned outlandish and awkward bits actually make the game more realistic.
I'm not a huge gamer, I just like the story telling aspect of games and how some games really embrace the cinematic aspect of this form of media (some of my other favorite games are Heavy Rain, Beyond: Two Souls, and The Last of Us). And this game really does a fine job of that. This is turning out to be one of my all time favorite games. Serious props to DONTNOD for this game; for once I actually WANT to be playing, instead of being content to just watch someone else play.

BEFORE I START, I WANT TO SAY THAT EVEN THOUGH I RECOMMEND THIS GAME, DO NOT BUY IT UNTIL ALL 5 EPISODES HAVE BEEN RELEASED. IF YOU WANT THE EXACT REASONS, READ ON, BUT THERE ARE SOME MINOR SPOILERS AHEAD.
OK, just finished Episode 3, and feel ready to review, episode by episode.
This game is a wonderful game involving time-travel in a school setting and involving a deep mystery. It also has one of the best choice systems I've ever seen in a game, much better than any Telltale game (I really like Telltale, but in the end, most of the choices just lead to the same inevitable end). Well, I say it includes it, but that is actually a major gripe I have after playing Episode 3 (detailed below with minor spoilers). I have high hopes for this game, once the last two episodes are releases, however I have some gripes. The main character Max can reverse time in order to change her (your) decisions throughout the game.
1. The game is bugged. In the "reverse time" function, once you have reversed time in order, you have the option to skip dialogue. This function works, however leaves the game bugged afterwards. In Episode 1, the game became unplayable due to me using the skip function and the game going weird, which was fixed by reverting to an earlier save. In Episode 3, while in Chloe's room, I discovered it was the skip function that made it bug out. Sitting through the same 30 lines of dialogue every time you want to change a decision is annoying, and really not cool as that's what I'd expect from a game not involving time travel that includes a choice system. The time-reversing could be a hell of a lot more smooth, and really, it's an oversight on the developer's side of things.
2. Episode 3. My god. That is just a bad episode. Not because the choices are bad, or the story is bad (well, for the most part). However, the final scene is awful. As in, smash my head on the keyboard awful. The game prides itself on its "choose your own path" way of doing things, and then forcefully merges everyone's game to the same point, disregarding all previous choices. While they may spread it back out into the big tangled web that it was previously next episode, at the minute, I sit here♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off and quite close to hitting "No recommend". That's why I'm saying wait until at least Episode 4 has been released. Please.
It's a great game, but the end of Episode 3 has left me questioning the writers, as it felt very forced. Wait until further episodes are released before deciding whether or not to purchase the game.
EDIT: The following is after completing the game:
After finishing the game, I feel heavily disappointed. Previously I talked about the 3rd Episode being a bad episode, and while episode 4 was ok, Episode 5 reached the epitomey of bad writing. Of the 2 hour episode, you only really have 30 minutes of content, filled out by a mass of bad minigames that are, for the most part, illogical and impossible to solve on the first try. Once you wade through 1 and 1/2 hours of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t timey wimey stuff (I say stuff because you finish it with no sense of what you just accomplished, the accomplishment really being sticking with it until the game decides it's time to let you finish), you are left with 2 choices, which lead to two different endings, both quite open, which in some sense is nice, but in another sense is awful because, after seeing the episode, and wading through the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t time-♥♥♥♥ing-up minigames that make the "Focus on the picture" look as appetising as chocolate ice-cream in the summer, having an open ending feels like climbing to the top of a mountain only to be greeted with a man saying "Sorry, you're not allowed to see the view".
Overall, the game is good, it makes you think, deliberate morality of certain choices, and covers some hard-hitting issues, but the gameplay and inconsistent quality of writing (and complete abscence of it for most of Episode 5) really drags this down from a 9/10 to a 6/10. It's a nice game, but I wouldn't buy it in the hopes that it's a GOTY contender, because there are quite a few flaws.

It began with a video; I watched a YouTuber play through the first episode of a game that looked almost too average until, like the wings of a butterfly newly emerged from its chrysalis, the story slowly unfurled into something far more complex, fantasitcally baffling and emotionally invested. Immediately I connected with the main character, Max, as I saw everything about her express her difference from most others in her world; an analogue soul immersed in a digitally driven environment, soft-spoken, introverted and unsure of every step taken like a newborn fawn. The sudden and jarring discovery of her strange ability would propel Max down a rabbit hole she never expected to fall into, revealing that there was much more to Blackwell Academy and Arcadia Bay than she could have ever imagined. Life is Strange is very appropriately titled because, like reality, it's set in a way that is so ordinary that even everyday ocurrances seem profound, which they are, thus giving even the smallest detail more importance and helping the game take on a very organic flow. I found that, while playing, the pace at which things moved and the urgency in certain situations took my heartrate on the rollercoaster ride right along with it. Nothing felt too drastic or slow, though popular concensus would disagree with the events of episode two during the junkyard scene, which most considered slow and frustrating when it came to finding the objects needed to move forward. However, I find that this forced me to become more aware and detail oriented, looking with a photographer's eye so that I wouldn't miss anything (and many times I almost had.) This concept tests the patience of the player, most of whom are used to things going much faster and being more obvious, and possibly even teaches the player to be more self-aware and conscious that even the small things can mean the difference between life and death.
I also enjoy that the ideas and concepts of the game are very closely tied to the Chaos Theory and, possibly, the Butterfly Effect when it comes to Max's power. Though this has been explored in many films and other games in the past through other methods, I like the idea that Max can only rewind a certain amount before it starts taking a genuine toll on her. As we see in episode two, Chloe pushes Max and her ability to a degree where physical rammafications become visible and, by the climax of the episode itself, has a consiquence that forces us to take great care and know that, this time, the choices we make cannot be changed.
Though only 3 episodes in, Life is Strange is rapidly becoming something more than just another episodic game of choice. Though I have yet to play the third episode myself, I have no doubt that it will life up to, and even surpass, my expectations and I can only look forward to what lies ahead, come what may..

I'm always down for a great episodic story game, and Life Is Strange is no exception.

Things I especially love about this game is the unique time rewind mechanic. It adds a whole new layer to the world that the played can interact with. Did you say something you know you'd regret later? Easy, you can just rewind time and undo a decision. The story fantastic, characters are well developed, the environment actually makes me want to explore and find out more. I'm finding myself actually taking the time to read all the journal entries / text messages (which is something I almost never do).
Overall, if you're a sucker for a good story, buy this game: you won't regret it.

At the time of writing this review, 3 of the 5 episodes are out for Life is Strange. I'll admit that during the first episode I thought the gameplay was a bits low and I wasn't completely sold on the story or the rewind mechanic. However, by the end of the first I had grown to respect the game and had an open mind.
It was during the second episode that I really grew to like this game. Some of the moral choices you make have a severe effect on what happens, and yet you might have completely skipped over a few of the things you needed to know to make a fully informed decision.  The way the game/story is set up makes you feel rewarded for exploring and taking every opportunity to find out as much as you can.
Then the third episode came out, and I was just completely blown away by it. Character development, the choices you make, and then the ending of the episode was just amazing. Really looking forward to the last 2 episodes of this game and replaying through many times once they are all out.  I would highly recommend this game if you are interested in episodic, story based games. Even if you aren't a super big fan of them, you can probably get a lot of enjoyment out of this game.

At the time of writing this review, 3 of the 5 episodes are out for Life is Strange. I'll admit that during the first episode I thought the gameplay was a bits low and I wasn't completely sold on the story or the rewind mechanic. However, by the end of the first I had grown to respect the game and had an open mind.
It was during the second episode that I really grew to like this game. Some of the moral choices you make have a severe effect on what happens, and yet you might have completely skipped over a few of the things you needed to know to make a fully informed decision.  The way the game/story is set up makes you feel rewarded for exploring and taking every opportunity to find out as much as you can.
Then the third episode came out, and I was just completely blown away by it. Character development, the choices you make, and then the ending of the episode was just amazing. Really looking forward to the last 2 episodes of this game and replaying through many times once they are all out.  I would highly recommend this game if you are interested in episodic, story based games. Even if you aren't a super big fan of them, you can probably get a lot of enjoyment out of this game.

This game...is unique. That's all I can say. I have completed a review for each episode. All episode reviews are brief and have no spoilers. I'd like to address the reviews saying bad things because of lip-sync issues. Although this is not a lie, it does not affect any story if you're listening to their voices not watching their lips. This can also be expected as the developer is French, so they do not natively speak English.
Episode 1: Chrysalis
A great episode that introduces you to the mechanics and characters, giving you choices that do not really change the story in many ways. This eases you smoothly into the game I'm sure you will love and will be a favourite of your library.
Overall a 8 out of 10 as of Episode 1: Chrysalis
Episode 2: Out if Time
It starts to throw you into the rough water, forcing you to make harder choices, and the characters always make you feel guilty after you choose dramatic decisions. The ending is truly a challenge, and will require you to pick up tiny details of plot to decide which ending you receive.
Overall a 9 out of 10 as of Episode 2: Out Of Time
Episode 3: Chaos Theory
My god... this game steps up the difficulty, stuffing harder choices into your already full arms, with a shocking plot detail at the end that will give you chills to the bone. It is a truly sad ending, and I can't wait to see what happens next. Gameplay still amazing.
Overall a 10 out of 10 as of Episode 3: Chaos Theory
Episode 4: Dark Room
More of a cinematic episode, this episode has a huge plot twist at the end. A definite high point in the series. It gets you wondering how there could be another episode, then bam. A strike to the brain. Not as moving as some events in Episode 3, but still sad.
Overall a 10 out of 10 as of Episode 4: Dark Room
Episode 5: Polarized
One of the most shocking and moving finales to a series, TV or games, as long as you choose the right ending. One ending is, in my opinion, disappointing. However, there are plenty of tear jerking moments between all different characters, with some Bioshock-Infinite-style segment. Events in this game are more dark than previous episodes. More emotions are added to the mix, like love, anger and confusion. A must buy!
Overall a 10 out of 10 as of Episode 5: Polarized

+ Visually appealing: The graphics are quite good and the style suits the nature of this game

Just played through the First Chapter of Life is Strange and here are some first impressions.
First, I’m getting a really strong Gone Home vibe- both the time period this is set in (early 2000s late 90s) and the narration style remind me heavily of Gone Home. The game relies heavily on you making your own exploration of the world in order to tell the story of Max (our lovely main character) and their relationship with those around them. Who are you friends with? Who are your antagonists? Who do you just plain don’t know? It’s all dependent on you to build relationships with those around you. Whether these relationships end up having an affect in later chapters remains to be seen- tho the “this will have consequences” icon that pops up when you talk to people lends to the idea that later relationships will play heavily in later chapters
Second: The mechanics. The reverse time mechanic is very clever imo. Who hasn’t played an RPG, made a choice, and then immediately (or in a second play through) gone back and made a different choice? The reverse time mechanic pretty much take a fact of RPG playing life and turns it into a game mechanic while simultaneously giving it limits: once you leave an area, for example, you can no longer go back and change your decisions. And Max will make comments on ever major decision: whichever you choose Max will wonder what might have gone differently, encouraging the player to go back and see for themselves.
Critiques: thus far some characters have not reacted in a realistic manner to Max’s meddling. While it is expected in an RPG for you to rummage through peoples things without consequences, Life Is Strange seems to be going for a more realistic approach to RPGs (despite the time control powers, of course) and yet at one point you can rummage through a girls bag right behind her without her noticing or poke around a certain long lost friend’s private belongings with no comment from them.
But this is a minor critique- overall this game seems to have a very solid foundation and I definitely do recommend at least buying chapter one-which can be bought separately from the rest of the game on Steam for 5 US dollars. If you do buy the first chapter separately you can later buy chapters 2-5 without having to repurchase chapter 1.
Some Triggers: There is mention of sexual assault in the form of date♥♥♥♥♥♥and some gun violence, implications of stalking, as well as minor drug use. So far, none of these things have been explicit however the tone of the first chapter implies that these things may become major themes throughout the game.

I would recommend this game just because it has a very high production value as far as voice acting, music, graphics, and overall cinematography go.  My recommendation is more of a, "The game isn't terrible, and spending $10 to try it out would not be a waste of money," type of recommendation.
That said, with all the high production values, the game itself does not draw me in.  Maybe it is the purposefully slow pacing, or the kindergarten level gameplay, but the game is definitely not what I expected when I saw the trailer.  I have not seen how this game "revolutionizes" choice-based adventures.  All it does is give you some big flashing warning whenever you are going to do something not good.  Or it just makes you re-do something over again until you get it right.
The only thing it changes is that instead of "dying" in a game, you just "rewind" until you complete a puzzle.  I have only played 3 hours and haven't finished episode 1 yet, but  the game is so slow and dialogue heavy, I find it difficult to play more than a few minutes at a time.
There don't seem to be any negative consequences in the game unless you purposefully choose to do something negative.  I actually don't see any consequences at all.  I guess the only way to tell what might have been different is to play the game over again.   There seems to be an option that you unlock later in the game that lets you see all the alternate possibilities, but then that seems kind of lame and cheap.
Maybe that is just how games like this are supposed to be, except I don't see how this revolutionizes anything.
It's really just a really slow paced game where you are prompted to make a decision every once in a while and you see a story play out that is probably pretty linear with probably a little dialogue change and maybe some scenes happening sometimes and not happening other times.  Maybe that is some huge groundbreaking achievement but it seems like a pretty simplistic concept.
I guess I was just expecting something a lot different, like the way Chrono Trigger or Shenmue played out to me, and those games are decades old.  Or really any game.  You make decisions and the game changes.  Except in this game you only make decisions once in a while in an extremely linear progression.
I just remembered where I've seen this revolutionary game mechanic before.  They used to call it a save point.

Life is Strange is a very interesting game. As the other episodic games out there, such as the Telltale games, its storyline and different path choices makes it a really fun experience, but what it makes it so unique and amusing is the possibility reversing time, as the main character possesses the power of rewinding time, makes this game even more engaging and pleasant. The different puzzles and possibilities that the game creates within the mechanic of time traveling creates an endless enjoyable time (no pun intended). The story is promising and rich as it compels a great emotional feeling over the main character, Max Caulfield, which makes you feel very thrilled towards future actions and what your decisions may take part. With only two episodes released so far it's hard to say more about the game, but I can definitely say that as it stands, it's bound to be an outstanding game.
Update 30/07: This game still doesn't ceases to amaze me. Episodes 3 and 4 are so far my favorite episodes and it just keeps getting better and better.
Update 20/10: A worthy ending for such an outstanding game. Everything comes to a great conclusion that makes you wish that there was more but sadly it has to come to an end. The whole journey spent over the other 4 episodes wraps up here in a satisfying, emotional and heart-breaking final episode. Some may not consider the ending worthy, but it's like they say: "It's about the journey not the destination". Some people will keep playing games thinking that that particular game he played over the extent of hours, days or months, resumes all in the last part, the ending. I just don't agree. What about all the rest of the time you spent? Are they no longer meaningful to you because the end had a different outcome to what you wished for? I just don't agree. You should enjoy the game by its experience not its results.
Nonetheless, if you are looking to buy this game now that all episodes were released, I highly recommend it. It's probably one my favorite games of 2015. It has an incredible emotional, thrilling and immersive story. And thus, by the end of it, you'll finally see, that indeed: life is strange...

"Life is Strange," has us see through the eyes of a female student photographer named Max. Max is given time rewind abilities and we the players are fated to choose her destiny. Her story unfolds in a nostalgic high school setting where dramatic life changing events occur. All of these events are stepping stones that lead to the perpetuated event where we must save the town.
Additionally, "Life is Strange('s)" atmosphere brings this game to life. As you first leave the classroom you are swathed into photographic scenery where you will not believe is a game. "Life is Strange," appeals to both teens and adults playing the game. (Please Know: This game is for mature audiences who are okay with swearing and capable of withstanding disturbing events.) As you play through the game there are so many bits of information given to you. Such as objects to look at, people to interact with, and song selections. Currently, the game is up to Episode 2 and it is well worth the full price of all the episodes.

- Graphics are beautiful
- The music is fantastic
- Story is full of gripping intrigue
- The attention to detail is seriously impressive
You won't regret spending €5 on the first episode, and I can guarantee you that you'll want to buy the rest.

This game is fantastic. The story, atmosphere, art style and animations are fantastic, and combine to make a sort of high-school time-travel drama thingy. The characters are diverse and well-written, and they are realized with superbly well-done mo-cap animations that give so much flavor to the characters that, even by the end of episode 1 or 2, you could probably recognize the major characters simply by body language alone.
The story can best be described as an unusual mix of time-travel crime mystery in a high-school coming-of-age drama setting... and it's ♥♥♥♥ing great! It's also full of vagueness and subtlety that leaves plenty of room for your own imagination and interpretation. If you like over-analyzing, you'll love this game as the attention to detail is incredible. There are no coincidences in this game.
Now, for the few gripes I have with the game. The major characters are all well written and voice acted, but occasionally the dialogue of some of the minor characters will seem a bit off, and this also goes for the voice acting. It was not nearly bad enough to really sour my experience with the game though. There's also a long scene in episode that seems kinda like pointless garbage... perhaps it will make sense later, but it didn't really seem to contribute with anything. The last scene in episode more than makes up for this though. The end of episode 2 is ♥♥♥♥ing intense. No, seriously, if you're not a heartless monster you should get ready for them feels.
Meaningful choices, a very promising story, any Telltale fan can admire the level of detail this game has.

This game is fantastic. The story, atmosphere, art style and animations are fantastic, and combine to make a sort of high-school time-travel drama thingy. The characters are diverse and well-written, and they are realized with superbly well-done mo-cap animations that give so much flavor to the characters that, even by the end of episode 1 or 2, you could probably recognize the major characters simply by body language alone.
The story can best be described as an unusual mix of time-travel crime mystery in a high-school coming-of-age drama setting... and it's ♥♥♥♥ing great! It's also full of vagueness and subtlety that leaves plenty of room for your own imagination and interpretation. If you like over-analyzing, you'll love this game as the attention to detail is incredible. There are no coincidences in this game.
Now, for the few gripes I have with the game. The major characters are all well written and voice acted, but occasionally the dialogue of some of the minor characters will seem a bit off, and this also goes for the voice acting. It was not nearly bad enough to really sour my experience with the game though. There's also a long scene in episode that seems kinda like pointless garbage... perhaps it will make sense later, but it didn't really seem to contribute with anything. The last scene in episode more than makes up for this though. The end of episode 2 is ♥♥♥♥ing intense. No, seriously, if you're not a heartless monster you should get ready for them feels.
Meaningful choices, a very promising story, any Telltale fan can admire the level of detail this game has.

Life is Strange is a choice-driven, episodic story of a young woman named Max, who finds she has the ability to reverse time, enough to undo a mistake or even save a friends life. As an aspiring Photographer, who is enrolled in the elitist Blackwell Academy, Max see's the world through a photographers lens. Detailed Review
09/10 as of now. At the time of the review only episode 1 + 2 are out.
And what to say here.... LOOOOVE THAT GAME! If I would rate it subjectively I would give this game straight crit 13/10!!
But hell yeah, lets go down a little more objective.
First the positives: Very alive chars, all of them appears very emotional and individual. All of them are great, also the ones you dont like are great and well made. So you can easily build up an emotional binding to the most main chars easily.
The athmosphere is AMAZING! The whole world seems just to be allright. You really feel like beeing in a "living" environment. And its beatifully designed.
You can really enjoy the whole game, also in very quiet moments. Just sit around and let your char think. Play guitar in your room and enjoy some rest.
Soundtrack - AWESOME again! I usually listen to hardrock,metal and some faster dubstep.
But in this game, the slow comforting music is all perfect, allways well placed and feels allright!
Also great feature is: no background music (not that I recognized it) if no music plays!
Turn on MP3 player - Music!
The graphics are something special. I love them! Instead of using highly detailed in deepth textures and fail making them look really perfect, they took another approach. Graphics are more minimalistc, but look very great!
Now lets head to the best part so far: Story!
What we got here so far is epic. Very got story in general, storytelling is great. I had not a single: "WTF that was purely displaced" moment. It gives us a lot detail of the place, the persons etc. There is also a lot of "optional" information about almost everything. I don´t want to talk too much about detail here.
Just want to say: very good story and an in deepth detailed world
Gameplay - The idea of the gameplay is cool. Try and fail gets an entirely new approach here. You can rewind time. Thats cool. Gave wrong answer? Rewind. Wanna get some information, but it will♥♥♥♥♥♥off someone - get Info and Rewind. And many more examples. They made a lot out of the gameplay mechanics they have. And they use them in many good ways.
Thats the positiv part. Now the negatives.
Graphics: You gotta like that graphic style. I do, I love it. Cause it beautifully shows the world in this game. But its a question of how you look onto this point. Cause modern engines can do better in point of detailed textures.
Language: only french and english. Im perfectly fine with english. So no worries about that. But to some people this might be a major drawback, or even make it impossible for them to enjoy this game.
Gameplay: Like I wrote above they use their gameplay mechanics very well. Yeah thats true. But in fact there isnt much to do in that game. You can select stuff and rewind time. Done! Thats it.
Its hard to me to describe anything in this game as complex except the story. The game itself is very simple to play. No puzzles yet or something like that. All in game tasks appear very clear and feel almost "hghlighted". You barely have to think about anything. Cause if you fail - rewind and you allready got shown how to do it right.
All in All not too bad cause game clearly focuses story. But the game feels a little too easy to play. And I dont feel really free to do things my way. Only one solution, that gets pointed directly INTO MY FACE.
Making me feel more like havin an interactive movie than a game.
But honestly, its a very very very cool movie.
Final statement: Few minor issues that could be better.
But the game perfectly does what it wants to do. Tell an emotional and immersive story.
Thats wants me get MORE! And I´m so excited for chapter 3!
