One thing to bare in mind though, these episodes are fairly short. It's definitely not a bad thing but something to be well aware of before jumping on board. We're talking 2-3 hours if you take your time and really explore. Less if you're just rushing through.
It's yet to be seen just how strong of a ripple the choices made so far will have on the rest of the game. I've not replayed episodes 1 or 2 since I want to continue a consistent timeline (ironic, eh?) so I'm not entirely sure just how much the choices I've made already have affected the game. However there were a couple of moments that I knew for a fact were directly linked to a choice I made earlier. Subtle things like changes in dialog are one thing, sure. But it seems pretty clear that the game wants to make sure that the choices that say they have consequences, really do mean what they say.
But if none of that interests you, it's worth dropping $5 as a cheap price of entry on purely the amazing sense of nostalgia alone. Nothing major even needed to happen to provoke a strong emotional reaction. Just a beautifully set up atmosphere with all the right ingrediants to give you goosebumps.

Life is Strange will be a polarizing experience. The dialog is lame, dopey at best. The characters are all mostly insufferable♥♥♥♥♥hats, and the puzzles and general gameplay design is lack-luster at best.
However I'm still giving this my recommendation. Because despite all it's flaws and annoyances, Life is Strange strikes a cord that very few games do. it's a beautiful looking game with seemingly a lot of heart, even though at whenever the writing tries to be heart-felt it comes out as unintentionally hilarious.
It's an interesting game with a great art-style and a fun concept, of which there should be many many more.
And hell $20 isn't that bad for a couple hours of campy, time-traveling, whiny, angsting teens doing dumb♥♥♥♥♥♥
Overall enjoyable, not for everyone.

Anyone remember that "Riley Rewind" web series by Ray William Johnson? No? Well, Life Is Strange is kind of like that. Except it's good.
Max and Chloe are re-establishing their lost childhood bond, while messing with Max's newly discovered time-control ability. Sensibly indie Max is a likeable lead, and fire-cracker Chloe brings excitment and danger to the narrative.
Other student characters are generally not people you'd want to be around. They're apathetic at best, or just total♥♥♥♥♥hats. I don't even mean that as a negative - it's pretty freakin' accurate of high school.
Some may disagree, but I find the writing well-structured and authentic for the most part. I also had a teenage girl say "hella" to me roughly 7 times while making my coffee last week, so perhaps my reference point for juvenile dialogue is slightly skewed.
I found the conversation-tree choices I made were, without fail, exactly what I wanted to say. They don't make absolute, hard-line statements; the choices have nuance and reasoning.
By now, many of us have heard about the climax of episode 2, it's been discussed at length in the games media. I knew what was coming, but it surprisingly didn't remove the intensity of the scene. It was a desperate situation, and I was powerless to stop it, literally. I did not succeed, and it felt terrible. Player stats suggest 64% managed to make the right choices and save the day. I suspect this is due to players resetting the checkpoint multiple times to achieve the "correct" outcome. While I understand the temptation, I won't do it. Sometimes we need to live with the result of our choices. Sometimes you can't go back.

So, here goes.
PROS
- A memorable cast of believable, likeable (mostly) characters that you can empathize with.  I care more about what happens to these characters then most of the the characters in TV and movies out right now.
- Believable voice acting.  Helps a lot towards the above point.  Listening to Max voicing her inner dialogue and the soundtrack for this game is like slipping into a warm/fuzzy blanket for me.  Relaxes me better than a cup of warm tea.  o.0
- Enjoyable soundtrack. (some other people nitpicks some of the character's musical choices, but I happen to think those choices gives said character(s) a little bit more of layers and nuances.
- Choices that reverberate through the episodes.  Unlike many other story choice/consequence games, you don't always see the result of your choices quickly or even in the same episode of the game.  Having the game reference your earlier choices later on in occasionally dramatic fashion makes one feel more responsible for those choices.
Also, this is a game that encourages thorough exploration the game world.  Many of the character's back stories are painted thorough these indirect observations of their surroundings, and these explorations can actually open up dialogue choices that those that are just racing through the game would not have access to.
- I appreciate the ability to continue the game on a new save slot from any point.  Makes it a lot easier to go and explore the various story branches without forcing you to play from the beginning
- You learn random factoids!  (My sister who works at an art college mentioned daguerreotypes and I knew what she was talking about)
CONS
- Mostly personal view/nitpicks, but some of these character's reaction to events seem a bit overly dramatic.  These are 18-ish year olds in a combo highschool/college dorm environment, but their reactions sometime seem more appropriate for a highschool freshman.  Again, this is a very personal/minor nitpick just because I feel like I should put something in cons list.
- As is the case with most branching choices games, some of the canned responses don't really jive with the flow of the game/dialogue and feels shoehorned in. (especially the case in the delivery of the lines.  There has been a few points where the character that I'm talking to seem to be pretty chummy with me, but one dialogue segment made them sound like they're upset with me; which breaks immersion)
Especially since this is a digital distribution game and not limited by space on physical media, maybe just record an extra line (I know, I know. if this was done for every instance it would soon balloon to an extra couple hundred of lines.  But I feel that for games where dialogue is the meat and potatos of the game, maybe you should go all out on that front.)
MIXED
- I'm already sad that I'm 40% of the way through the series.  It's like when I'm reading a good book and closing in on the last 50 pages; I know that the end is coming and then I won't have any more to read after I'm done.  Sadness.
CONCLUSION
Personally, my most enjoyed game of 2015 thus far.   If you enjoy story based games I would urge you to get it.  Support DONTNOD so they continue to make more content for us!  :D

If you dont want to read the full review - here the short version.

If you prefer puzzle based and/or action driven adventure games.... naaaah think twice here.
If you look for an FPS, RTS or RPG .... WTF ur doin here?
Detailed Review
09/10 as of now. At the time of the review only episode 1 + 2 are out.
And what to say here.... LOOOOVE THAT GAME! If I would rate it subjectively I would give this game straight crit 13/10!!
But hell yeah, lets go down a little more objective.
First the positives: Very alive chars, all of them appears very emotional and individual. All of them are great, also the ones you dont like are great and well made. So you can easily build up an emotional binding to the most main chars easily.
The athmosphere is AMAZING! The whole world seems just to be allright. You really feel like beeing in a "living" environment. And its beatifully designed.
You can really enjoy the whole game, also in very quiet moments. Just sit around and let your char think. Play guitar in your room and enjoy some rest.
Soundtrack - AWESOME again! I usually listen to hardrock,metal and some faster dubstep.
But in this game, the slow comforting music is all perfect, allways well placed and feels allright!
Also great feature is: no background music (not that I recognized it) if no music plays!
Turn on MP3 player - Music!
The graphics are something special. I love them! Instead of using highly detailed in deepth textures and fail making them look really perfect, they took another approach. Graphics are more minimalistc, but look very great!
Now lets head to the best part so far: Story!
What we got here so far is epic. Very got story in general, storytelling is great. I had not a single: "WTF that was purely displaced" moment. It gives us a lot detail of the place, the persons etc. There is also a lot of "optional" information about almost everything. I don´t want to talk too much about detail here.
Just want to say: very good story and an in deepth detailed world
Gameplay - The idea of the gameplay is cool. Try and fail gets an entirely new approach here. You can rewind time. Thats cool. Gave wrong answer? Rewind. Wanna get some information, but it will♥♥♥♥♥♥off someone - get Info and Rewind. And many more examples. They made a lot out of the gameplay mechanics they have. And they use them in many good ways.
Thats the positiv part. Now the negatives.
Graphics: You gotta like that graphic style. I do, I love it. Cause it beautifully shows the world in this game. But its a question of how you look onto this point. Cause modern engines can do better in point of detailed textures.
Language: only french and english. Im perfectly fine with english. So no worries about that. But to some people this might be a major drawback, or even make it impossible for them to enjoy this game.
Gameplay: Like I wrote above they use their gameplay mechanics very well. Yeah thats true. But in fact there isnt much to do in that game. You can select stuff and rewind time. Done! Thats it.
Its hard to me to describe anything in this game as complex except the story. The game itself is very simple to play. No puzzles yet or something like that. All in game tasks appear very clear and feel almost "hghlighted". You barely have to think about anything. Cause if you fail - rewind and you allready got shown how to do it right.
All in All not too bad cause game clearly focuses story. But the game feels a little too easy to play. And I dont feel really free to do things my way. Only one solution, that gets pointed directly INTO MY FACE.
Making me feel more like havin an interactive movie than a game.
But honestly, its a very very very cool movie.
Final statement: Few minor issues that could be better.
But the game perfectly does what it wants to do. Tell an emotional and immersive story.
Thats wants me get MORE! And I´m so excited for chapter 3!

Life is strange is one of this new and trendy point n' click games with little to no challenge. It is, however, a wonderful cinematographic experience.
I tend to think these games can only be good when you identify yourself as the main character.
The main character is a socially awkward student living her dreams but overthinking her daily life : i live that. I also share a lot of interests with her (music, pop culture...). So yeah, I identify myself, and when I play Life Is Strange, I can feel the emotions of the characters.
The main interest of the world is how well composed it is, almost like a good photography, and since it's moving (but not so fast), like a good (french) movie. Graphics aren't specials in any way, but the atmosphere here is fabulous.
This game is far from flawless : some characters are too much of a stereotype, usually not the most important, but some situations are, which is bad. Generally speaking, the game is not written that well, which is worse, especially for a game based on dialogues choices. Moreover I found myself irritated several times when the obvious good choice did not appear.
As for the content, there is plenty to read or to listen to, but that won't take so many hours. However, I think there is a lot to see, a lot of birds playing on a tree, a lot of people waiting for the bus, a lot of people watching the sunset to observe.
Life Is Strange is an invitation to observe the world with the eye of a photographer, to catch moments and revive them using Max powers. It's also an invitation to feel humans as a sensitive teenager. It is a great experience I'm sorry not to recommand to anyone but to sensitive people because of some bad writtings.

This game has an amazing cast of characters who you will get to know intimately through the use of the very interesting rewind mechanic. The challenges that each character faces is very believeable from daily bullying, unreciprocated love, outgrowing your home, and yes, even Max's struggle to please and fit in with her classmates for which she is fortunate enough to have superhuman powers to help her.
While the ability to rewind might not be real, the desire to do so certainly is as we sometimes fumble through social interactions or do things that we wish we could take back. This game does a great job in showing the consequence of controlling such power, as a high school student is no better equipped to deal with her gift than any of us would be. The episodes thus far have been compelling, and I look forward to each release. I highly recommend this game, particularly if you value a well told human story.

Since the very first moment, this game made me question if I myself am aware of reality or not. The atmosphere seems so believable and unreal at the same time, the music is so sweet and down-to-earth, the emotions expressed are so honest and relatable. I feel immersion like never before and the story keeps me thrilled for sure.
One thing I would advise the developers for, though, is that they should work on talking expressions: lips don't match words and I believe this is reasonable to ask for in our era. Apart from that, I absolutely love the torn notebook UI theme.
I like how the graphics are sharp on the faces but more abstract on the environment - it makes me feel that the game focuses on feelings and characters rather than objects, on the personal angle of the photographer rather than actual reality (if there actually exists such a thing). And for me, so does life. That is why this game is a masterpiece to my heart.

Ah this game... It's very beautiful. It's very relaxed, mainly because of the genius soundtrack, while at the same time it can hit you hard emotionally. At the time of writing, I've finished Episode 1 and 2 and am waiting for the 3rd episode. The end of episode 2 is simply genius, no matter what happens.
So, you play as a teenage girl with the power to reverse time. This allows you to test multiple choices in the moment and potentially make a better decision as to what is going to happen in the future. There's only so far that you can reverse time, so in the end there is a lot of room for speculation and doubt, which keeps the game very interesting. You do feel like your choices affect the outcome. It can be the difference between life and death. It goes a lot deeper than just teenage drama, and you can get a lot of time out of this game. If you easily get depressed however, I don't know if this is the best game for you. It has its fun moments, but also its dark moments. Just saying :)

Absolutely LOVING this game.  This is a game for the Adventure/Story/Character die-hard.
-Protagonist is amazing, so reflective in her mind, yet so subtle.
-Consequences feel real... I know you hear this in a lot of games, but I see the genuine impact of my actions -- and that they are grounded in my earlier decisions, without necessarily understanding them in their fullest at the time.
-Characters are VERY evolved in their behaviors, albeit somewhat unpredictable.
-There is no genuinely right or wrong choices as you make them, but you feel the weight they carry.  This gives the game a very realistic feel.  You kind of have to spend time reflecting on the whole world of what's going on, through the eyes of the characters in front of you.  I'm amazed that a game can do this.
And, although the art isn't quite as evolved as Quantic Dream's games -- I think this has earned its rightful place beside it, if not above it - just because the story has such a deep narrative, and adjusts so wildly to what you do.
(Can't wait until the end! - I want to see the world through their eyes again!)

A game that is inspired by the mechanics of Telltales flagship series, The Walking Dead, but finds it's own path with interesting characters and an intriguing story. Mixed with an interesting time rewinding mechanic the game feels new and exciting in comparison to other story driven point and click games. Unlike Telltales games Life Is Strange does not rely on button mashing to include action into it's game-play to spice up the often dialogue driven world, it uses its time rewind mechanic to provide a new and interesting take on the genre of story driven point and click adventure games.
Beautiful as well as thought provoking, the stylistic choices in Life Is Strange give it a unique feel to other games of today, Adding to it's beauty is its wonderful soundtrack, that makes the world of Life Is Strange a more wistful experience.
Currently Life Is Strange Episodes 1 and 2 are released and I am eagerly awaiting Episode 3, having bought the season pass for $16 dollars after finishing the first episode on a whim when I happened to have a spare $5 dollars in my Steam wallet. All I can say is that my purchase was well worth the price to enjoy this story, as it is more than just a game.

This game is interesting, engaging, comedic, and, most of all, fun. I honestly can't remember the last time I experienced a game with so much personality and such an engaging storyline. You can really feel all the effort and time that was put into this come together to create, in my opinion, one of the finest pieces of interactive artwork modern gaming has produced.
The characters are memorable, and well fleshed out, each with their own hobbies and personalities. The introduction of most of the side characters happens within the main character's (Max's) head, and often the player is simply told about these characters outright, which can make the game's introduction feel a bit overwhelming as the player attempts to learn all they can in a short amount of time. However, if you don't attempt to learn everyone's name in the first few minutes, and simply move along through, most of the characters are reintroduced more naturally later on.
The inclusion of the butterfly icon to notify the player of when she's making a decision that will impact the future feels a bit too mechanical, and takes away slightly from the immersion the game otherwise delivers so well.
The artwork and visual style is simply gorgeous. The beautiful, hand painted textures and thoughtfully crafted models make for game worth the trip just for scenery, let alone combining the story and gameplay.
Speaking of, I already mentioned, but the story has me hooked. I love the charaters, the personalities, the plot; as the game is only just approaching the release of Episode 3, I'm constantly thinking about what's next. I'm looking forward to the release of episode 3, but dreading the release of episode 5 only because it will mark the end of a game I've enjoyed (or expect to enjoy) more than nearly any game released this year.
I'd recommend this game to any player who doesn't need a gun or offensive item in their hands all the time, and can appreciate a game that doesn't explicity put you in immediate danger.

#This review is based on playing ep. 1 & 2
This game is a very nice and touching adventure about college girls. It tells an interesting story about returning to your old hometown and friends, that you somehow forget while moving forward at a certain point of your life. It combines it with a mysterious ability of the main hero called Max to rewind time. She can change what she said and did, but still every choice is hard and meaningful. You can't even pretend that you see where decisions will lead you, and they certainly will.
Playing Life is Strange is a complicated experience, that gives you an opportunity to see a world from an uncommon perspective, think differently and try as hard as you can to fit in a given circumstances. And it's always not enough of this game to completely fulfill your desire to know the world of it better. It's moving fast, arranging stuff as it likes, and you should react as best as you can.
It also makes you nostalgic sometimes. And it often tells you "look how cool and incredibly hard to be a badass teenager".
Anyway, you should be very careful, because if you are looking for something more serious or just can't believe in a little cartoonish characters, then you will probably be dissapointed. But if can truly emrace the setting, you will love this.

I also feel the decisions can have real consequences without spoiling anything major, a serious event can happen by either taking action or not which was felt in the 2nd episode and im very happy that i did what i did in my playthrough to stop such an event however until ep3 is released i can not say if it suffers from Walking deads prevent the envitable so take that comment with a pinch of salt. oh and also actually interact with the characters it makes the game feel more meaningful with various subplots and also not paying attention to some characters can really come back to haunt you.

I was looking forward to playing this game. I really was. However, I will be the first to admit that the writing was a very big turn off for me here. People are thrilled just to see more games with female protagonists lately, but after playing this game I can confidently say I would always rather have a male protagonist than a female one written by a team of male writers.
This game was developed by a team from Paris, France. I am all about international developers, don't get me wrong, but it felt like this game's script was a product of watching too much MTV and disney movies. Every sentence painfully included words like "hella", "rawk", or "krazy". It felt like it was trying to be an experience along the lines of Gone Home mixed with the format of a telltale game but it was much less genuine.
I noticed some other leaving positive reviews and recommending this product because of the plant watering sequence. Why? The time rewind mechanic seemed cool at first but then it was only used to undo obvious outcomes. It felt a little too necessary and less of a toy for players because it was in a linear system. There was also little done to motivate the player to relate to the main character. I found myself shaking my head at all of her decisions and lacking motivation to speak to anyone.
I can't bring myself to recommend this game to others as I would more likely recommend Gone Home or The Walking Dead game more readily. For five dollars, sure it is worth checking out, but this story game certainly did not leave a positive lasting impression.

Life is Strange is a bright spot among darker fare like the Telltales games. Honestly, out of 10 adventure games more than half are usually horror, gore or feature a disturbing theme. For me, reading the news is horrific enough, so I look for something else when it comes to my free time.
In terms of consequence driven games free of horror, gore, undead, Game of Thrones nasty business, whether is sex or action, I have found only two: Dreamfall and Life is Strange. Really, after finishing the last Unwritten Tales, I had a hard time finding an entertaining adventure game.
I will list the pros and cons, as I see them:
Pros
- graphics and voiceover. I read there were some minor issues with the lipsync, but that takes nothing from the engaging world of the game
-  many characters with detailed personalities that will have meaningful interactions with you. You'll like some, you'll hate some (only because they're mean). It's a win win.
- I really liked the educational bits about the history of photography. I miss games that are also un educational experiences, like the Gabriel Knight trilogy.
- although the game doesn't have puzzles per se, I consider the sum of actions that help (or not) save a friend one of the best and most rewarding puzzle-like experiences in a while. More of that please in the next chapters!
- a potential love story. Maybe more?
- you can actually consider gifting this game to a 18+ audience. Maybe even 16+, depending on how adult will be the content for the rest of the chapters. In my opinion, in our time, every teenager already knows about the issues the game tackles like bullying, teen pregnancy, ruffies and bullying-driven suicide.  I like the way they are approached, in a very tasteful and sensitive manner that might have a positive effect on a young audience.
Cons
- three save slots. maybe it's a way to insure replayability, but I don't like they made that decision for me.
- two months is a long time to wait between episodes. One month would have been better. The story is very engaging and it's hard to stop and reengage every time. So, my advice, maybe play the first chapter and then wait until the end to play the full game.
- I kind of disliked the bottle hunting puzzle. Although it fell nice into the storyline, from a game point a view it was more of a filler meant to explore a junkyard. A very detailed and beutifully rendered junkyard, but still. A MacGyver-style puzzle would have been more rewarding or anything character-driven.
- also,  there should be a way to highlight the location of the hotspots as sometimes it's kind of boring to walk around trying to move the camera so you can spot them. Fortunatelly, the enviroment is fun to walk through.
This game is pretty ♥♥♥♥ing awesome... and has a nice style to it. ^^
A great, great game and a brilliant new take on the adventure game genre.
In every way, this story delivers something that is honest and engaging. I can't wait for each new episode.

Developed by DONTNOD and published by SquareEnix, Life is Strange is played in an episodic format that will end with a total of five in all, starting with Episode One: Chrysalis. You are Max Caulfield, future photographer extraordinaire, transfer student in her senior year at Blackwell Academy, a prestigious high school for talented young adults that gives off more of a small college-town vibe. Life is Strange plays out very much like a choose-your-own-adventure novel with simple navigation and interaction with the world around you... almost point-and-click, if you will. At any given time, you are moving from place-to-place just observing or getting a read on the people and objects around you. Max walks through the halls or across her beautifully hand-painted campus to a soundtrack that is reminiscent of films like Juno or Nick and Norah’s Infinite Playlist. I say hand-painted because that is the style of visuals that the game’s creators have taken with this adventure, and it is gorgeous. It is well complimented with a light filter that gives the atmosphere around you the appearance of age that it would otherwise lack. The soundtrack to the game is top-notch so far and one of my favorite parts to experience as I play.
After the terrifying dream of an introduction, Max is brought back to good ‘ol reality and all of the mundane sluggishness that comes with it by waking up in her photography class. For anybody who has played any of Telltale’s recent titles, Square Enix’s take on the genre is all about the scenery and observations of the world around you. The player, as Max, is introduced one interactive moment at a time to a world that is very unspectacular at first glance. She is not a social butterfly, but is more of an introspective and in-her-own-head kind-of girl. The voice actors do a wonderful job at expressing their given character’s personalities, even if the the main character will ironically point out the caricatures that so many of the students and staff take on. You make the choices that determine just how much or little Max chooses to involve herself during every interaction, but the consequences of those choices are never as clear as they would seem at first. It’s a lot like real life and how you first discover this would be spoiler-ish to divulge here. If the game could manage to synchronize its animations of the people who are speaking just a little better, there would be next to nothing to criticize about the overall appearance of the game.
Life is Strange will eventually push you through to learning that Max has the ability to rewind time in small increments, and this is what the game strives to build itself around. This is where I was going with the talk of being in the shower earlier, looking back at conversations that you would do differently. You can go through an interaction with somebody or something, experience the consequences of your choices, and then immediately choose to rewind and try again for a different result. The game has a way of introducing predicaments where you will need to experience one result in order to learn the knowledge required to induce a different outcome. Some of these moments are as simple as knocking something off of a shelf when reaching for it, only to rewind and knowing to prepare the spot that it lands for a safer conclusion. Other moments involve simply arriving at a location and noticing that something is can be interfered with after it occurs naturally for the first time. Whenever a rewind occurs, Max keeps the knowledge of the previous event with her - as well as any items that she picks up, and will sometimes remark on how well something went for her by manipulated coincidence. In this way, it pays to experiment and sometimes be a little snoopy when the situation calls for it. You can retain what you know without consequence… for the most part.
If all of this power and ability makes Life is Strange’s consequences sound too easy to regret, you would be falling for the exact same trap that I did when I first began playing. You see, as capable as Max is at rewinding time on a whim, she cannot do it indefinitely. You are making choices, yes, but many that will have far-reaching and unforeseen consequences that you will never know to see coming. The beauty of the storytelling in Life is Strange is that it does a fantastic job at showing you just how powerful you should feel at first glance while still managing to bring down a truck of regret or hindsight that you’ll be desperate to undo later on… but can’t. This is due in part to how few opportunities you are given in the narrative to simply not make a choice - you’re going to have to choose to to befriend, who to♥♥♥♥♥♥off, who to help. Telltale’s games will often give you the choice of staying silent or being as apathetic as you want to be, whether or not it truly changes the outcome of an event. Life is Strange plays a much more forceful hand in the options that it gives you, and it can come off as unnatural at times. You may not like being wrapped up in the affairs of others as much as the game wants you to be, but life is strange, after all.
With all that the game does right for setting up the atmosphere, it nags me even as I write this that some of the characters within the game itself just do not feel real, or are frustratingly unbelievable. Chalk the problem up to bad writing or blame the limitations that are in place for the choose-your-own-adventure genre, but some of the interactions and reactions that grown adults within the game had me feeling completely back-handed. The worst example of this comes in the form of the high school’s principal, a figure of authority and one that students should be pressed to confide in should anything concern him or her. Where the characters within this world are meant to have believable relationships towards Max and everybody around them, many of the adults in Life is Strange do nothing but make their life harder for the most asinine and vague of reasons. The head of security for the school’s campus is unacceptably cocky and rude to everybody that he interacts with, leaving me wondering how he manages to even maintain his employment. The principle alone has such a downright inappropriate attitude towards the students that approach him with serious life-altering and dangerous concerns that I can not suspend my disbelief enough to buy the act, which could explain the other adults under his employ. There is already enough conflict going on within the game to warrant real concern, so it boggles my mind why the adults have to be written into such antagonistic roles. It feels so unnecessary.
As a point-and-click adventure game with simple puzzles, a gorgeous atmosphere, and a heavy dose of self-doubt after every decision that you make, Life is Strange, Ep.1: Chrysalis is a slow but careful look into the world that you will be manipulating over the next four episodes. The developers at DONTNOD are consciously and carefully manipulating the future of the series based on how the players’ choices play out, meaning that your choices really do have much more of an effect than you realize. While many of the characters have yet to fully blossom with this introduction into the story, it will be fun to see what plays out as Max learns more and more about her mysterious power and the fate of the people around her. I feel that I need more time as the player to learn to truly care about many of the people that I have had interactions with so far. All in all, for $5.00 for the first episode, I might recommend that some people hold off to see how the next episode is received. Should the next episode improve on what the first has established by pushing the narrative and mechanics forward, I will be ecstatic to see where this adventure is going.

I believe that this is the first ever review I have done on Steam and I can't say how pleased I am that my first review is for such a fine a game as this.
Well, where do I begin? I bought this game, purely to study the game's story for it's rich content and as a way to refine my own storytelling abilities. Never had I ever expected a game's story to influence and rock me to the core as much as this one. I write this as a person who had begun episode two, "Out of Time", with the idea that I would be playing just another stage of Max Caulfield's life in this amazing story from Dontnod and Square Enix. As the final scenes played out, I could only sit there and marvel at how heavily my action, or lack thereof, could effect someone's life. I can only say that I wish everyone could play this game. It's unique storytelling aspect may not be up everyone's alley, but I can safely say that this was my best full price purchase on Steam as it is worth every cent.
If you want a story about self discovery and what it means to be a part of a living and breathing world, you needn't look further. This game has it all in spades. The soundtrack is amazingly complimentary and doesn't feel as though it is there for the sake of being there. Everything has a purpose in this game. The gameplay mechanics, though simple, are enough to tell the story in a way that isn't encumbersome. Everything works just as it was meant to and I just cannot recommend it enough.
I have spent enough time contemplating whether or not you need to buy this game. To save you time, the simple answer is, yes. Yes, you do. If you haven't purchased this game yet, make sure you do. I only give credit where it is due and the teams at Dontnod and Square Enix have just proven that the art of high quality storytelling is not dead. for this, I thank them and trust that the next three episodes will be just as powerful and thought provoking as the first two.
Now for the scores:
Story: 95/100
Visuals: 90/100
Gameplay: 90/100
Soundtrack: 95/100
Overall Rating: 93/100

My only criticism is Max's camera - considering the protagonist is a photographer I was expecting a different integration of this mechanic more like akin to Frank's in Dead Rising.
All in all I haven't been this excited about a game in a very long time, and while at first I was dubious of the episodic format I have come to appreciate it now considering I tend to binge-play this game for hours at a time. I hope the future episodes continue to be as awesome!

Stories in videogames?
They generally suck.
But it's nice to see someone working against that trend! I don't think I've ever been as invested in videogame characters as I was with this game. Besides a few bad eggs, they are wonderfully well-rounded and relatable.
...okay, those are over-used words when describing characters. Let me try again:
After finishing the first couple episodes of this game, I actually felt like I knew these people. They aren't perfect, by any stretch, don't mistake my glowing praise for empty hyperbole, but they reminded me so much of what a lot of people were like in my high school days that I could easily believe that this whole cast actually exists, somewhere out there in that beautiful, quiet town.
The relationship dynamics between Chloe/Max and Warren/Max were absolutely brilliant (in that it felt natural), and the visuals of the game, while not much in terms of fidelity, were absolutely stunning in the area of artistic design. It turns out, I don't need perfectly lip-sync or the most polygons money can buy to get invested in a story. Just some talented voice actors and some sharp writing. Well, okay, apart from some cringe-worthy memes and old slang tossed in, but those don't really detract in any noticable way from the strengths of the script.
And the music? Whimsical, calming, and it sets the mood for this game perfectly. I especially love the episode outro montages.
Again, I'm only two episodes in, waiting on the others to come out, but so far?
This was not a "good story for a videogame".
This was a good story.
Please play this game. It is well worth your time and your money.

This is actually my first reveiew, I'm no expert but here goes. I actually really enjoyed this game for the most part... the beginning was pretty bleh though, honestly this game is VERY slow to start and most of the introductions are fairly annoying and slightly opinionated comments about the people the main character interacts with. Add in some cheesy modern slang and pop culture lingo, and the dialogue from a high school senior perspective and to me it just detracts from the experience honestly.
But I suppose thats what this game is all about, High School Drama, stuff most of us playing have already been through, but in some cases taken to a more extreme level.... oh and it has short range time travel!
Now, I'm the kind of person that abhors time-travel as a mechanic in videogames... it often opens up loopholes and things that probably could have been exploited but havent been for plot reasons. I'm not going to write that book today though.
My review sound pretty negative but honestly you have to keep playing to get past all of the annoyances and the boring stuff.
One thing I'm on the fence about is the fact that you can go back in time after, say, examining something that you might have missed earlier prior to a conversation with someone who knows a lot about the topic, getting your answer wrong and being almost rudely dismissed by each person before you  rewind and then try your best to sound like an expert. It screams poser, and it really makes me question the main characters sense of honesty and whether shes trying to make it in school or is just trying to fit in. Not to mention their sudden acceptance of you is rather runrealistic... or at least I feel like it is. On the other hand, it's nice to be able to get hints at all the potential outcomes before you make a decision.
Of course your decisions can impact your social and academic lives thus far, but I get the distinct feeling that every decision that has consequences will require a sacrifice of some sort. Every time I see that little butterfly there is a sense of dread that washes over me, and I have to do my best to ignore it and continue playing the game.
The music is okay but it doesnt really tug at the heartstrings. Some of it I find to be kind of boring actually.
Anywho, it took a while but I did start getting into the story, pretty much right around the time
After that fairly intense moment, the game in its entirety starts to get interesting. More actions have consequences and the game and story start to flow a lot better.
So far nothing seems redundant which is a great thing for me... its been a common pitfall with a lot of games these days.
The art style doesnt seem to fit square enix's usual standard so that had me confused a little bit. I have high hopes for the future installments to this game, though. It looks like itso nly going to get more interesting from here, especially with everything that happens at the end of the first episode.
Honestly so far the biggest thign holding this game together is the story (post introductions), and the ability to make somewhat informed decisions via short range time travel.
Some annoyances I've found  were mostly the music, which is boring for the most part, character dialogue being a bit corny, and character interaction being slightly quirky at times based on decisions made. The game is slow to start and the first day is probably boring because its the usual crap most of us have been through except at select points.
I'd recommend it to some but not many. So its getting a thumbs up from me, but if I were to give the game a number score it might be a 7/10 which is juuust passing by my standards. I really want to score it higher thna that, and my reveiw mightve reflected that but... that pretty much the best its gonna get with what I was given.
It got an extras point because of the price tag... its not all that expensive, andmight be a decfdent play for 5 bucks depending on your standards.

This is a fantastic game, but it is not for everyone.
If you're looking for a game that immerses through gameplay then this isn't really for you unless point and click is your style. The real strength of the game lies in its story ,  characters, and music. The way the story is presented raises many questions that you need to be answered and most of the characters seem to have their own little quirks, while the music seems to fit every scene perfectly.
If you easily care for characters in a game then this is perfect for you and you are able to interact with a large cast of characters.
Its hard to explain without spoiling anything, but if you liked games like The Walking Dead, Heavy Rain, and Farenheit, then try this game, but be prepared to feel many feelings.
If you're more into well told stories and movie-like game then this is for you.

The game has, so far, been giving of a really cozy feel with the very likeable and realistic characters. It's nice to to be able to really interact with so many of the characters in-game.
You play as Max Caulfield, your regular teenager, until she finds out that she can rewind time. She recently moved back to her hometown 'Arcadia Bay' to study at Blackwell Academy. Right after she discovers her power to rewind time she is also reunited with her childhood friend Chloe Price. Max keeps having these visions of a huge storm coming to and destroying Arcadia Bay.
Visuals, environment:
I really love the environment of Life is strange. The school campus, the lighthouse, Chloe's house.
It really just looks... casual, in a really good way. What makes this a super cozy game to me is the way the creators use the sun to just make every scene so beautiful with the visible sun rays (Not sure if this is what it's called...).
The graphics doesnt have to be requiring a GTX 980 to be good. Life is strange proves that. The game is ridiculously good looking without having those "super sick" graphics.  I don't really know how to describe how much I love the visuals.
Visual and environment rating: 10/10 The beautiful scenes are what makes it for me.
Voice acting:
The game has a lot of good voice actors, but sometimes the dialogue between the characters can sound pretty awkward.
At some times I just don't buy it. At least the voice acting in episode 2 gets a lot better. Overall, I still think it's good.
The mouths not syncing with the voices adds to my rating here.
Voice acting rating: 7,5/10
Soundtrack and BGM:
The soundtrack in Life is strange is perfect as it is very "calming" and adds to the cozy feel of playing as a regular teenager. The music itself always seem to fit in with the environment you find yourself in.  I've been listening to the soundtrack non-stop since I played through the first episode.
Soundtrack rating: 9.5/10, as I really love it.
Story:
It has really just been a lot of introduction to the story so far and we haven't really gotten that much into it. But there is a storm coming and a lot to unravel.
Story rating (thus far): 8/10, I'll get back to this rating when I've finished the game.
In Life is Strange, your choices matter. It's a really cozy game and I like how easy it is to bond with the characters. I actually started caring a lot about them.
Overall score: 9/10, again, I'll come back to give it a final rating when I'm done with all the episodes. But even so far, I highly recommend this game.

Life is Strange asks you to suspend your disbelief with the supernatural; it's not the point. Instead, the game is about holding on to memories and letting go. Time travel, aside from being tied to photography and memories, is a way to convey additional information to the player. It offsets the dissonance between the player and Max by enabling the player to make more informed choices, familiarizing the player with Max's experience.
It's often easy to see multiple choices leading up to the same outcome. That's not a fault of the story, instead the story ends up stronger for it. With every piece of dialogue, players color the story with nuances of their own.
The heartfelt story and the characters rise above their stereotypes, twisting expectations of what the story is about. Through excellent script and cinematography they come to express timeless themes of friendship and growing up. Max's heart-warming commentary won me over; reminiscing her first time drinking or simply sparing a thought for books that have been untouched for years is anything but meaningless.

Life is Strange is a five part episodic game that revolutionises story based choice and consequence games by allowing you to rewind time and affect the past, present and future!
I really enjoyed this game. I am confident I will remember the game years from now, . I enjoyed  the Telltale-influences gameplay, and beautifully created world, a amazing story! It has more depth than The Walking Dead or The Wolf Among Us.
The time rewind feature adds an interesting twist to adventure gameplay. It doesn't feel like "cheating" because although you might know the immediate consequences of your decision, you can't rewind past maybe 30 seconds and you can't see how these things will affect the future. Decisions you make do have definite consequences and even little details along the way will have a butterfly effect in ways you won't realize until it hits you like a ton of bricks an episode or two down the road.
The music chosen definitely augments the emotional depth of the game. They did a wonderful job incorporating ambient noises into the scenes, so that you really get the full immersion.
Just get this game. Experience it for yourself!

Life is Strange asks you to suspend your disbelief with the supernatural; it's not the point. Instead, the game is about holding on to memories and letting go. Time travel, aside from being tied to photography and memories, is a way to convey additional information to the player. It offsets the dissonance between the player and Max by enabling the player to make more informed choices, familiarizing the player with Max's experience.
It's often easy to see multiple choices leading up to the same outcome. That's not a fault of the story, instead the story ends up stronger for it. With every piece of dialogue, players color the story with nuances of their own.
The heartfelt story and the characters rise above their stereotypes, twisting expectations of what the story is about. Through excellent script and cinematography they come to express timeless themes of friendship and growing up. Max's heart-warming commentary won me over; reminiscing her first time drinking or simply sparing a thought for books that have been untouched for years is anything but meaningless.

First of all, decisions in this game really do matter. It's not like The Walking Dead, where it doesn't matter what decision you make, because in the next episode the outcome of the decision is basically going to be the same and all that changes are a few dialogue lines and that's about it. No, in here, the decisions you make are remembered by the game properly. You can also check out the different immediate consequences of different decisions by using the game's special "timey wimey rewindy" mechanic.
Now, I could give a lot of reasons why I like this game, but I don't really feel like it right now. Maybe later. I do, however, want to give some constructive criticism for the devs. First of all, the lip-sync is horrible. I've seen better lip-sync in Bethesda games, and I'm not kidding. The animations, at times, are a bit wonky. The voice acting is usually pretty good, but in some places, it really falls short. Usually the moments where it does fall short are because of boring writing. The actors aren't really given much to work with and that is exactly why some lines are delivered blandly. Most of the time, yes, the writing is good, but, like I said, there just are a few moments where it felt rushed and like the writers forgot to flesh out some dialogue. There is also a strange, annoying chromatic aberration filter throughout the game. It's probably there to kinda give the game maybe a vintage camera look, but let's be honest, you don't want your game to look like an Instagram photo. If you don't know what chromatic aberration is, look it up on Google. It makes the game look blurry and the edges of the screen a bit difficult to see properly. I think the game would look much better with it turned off.
Now, other than this, it is a good game, and it is enjoyable. I would definetly give the experience I had with the first two episodes so far a 9/10. It has interesting characters and I don't know why, but I just like high school drama (as in, finished watching all the 4 seasons of The OC and loved it, and I never even thought it'd be my thing). Don't let the pretentious sounding hipster name and the generic "episodic story based choice and consequence game" style drive you away. It puts an interesting spin on it and does it better than some other story games I've seen.
Gameplay: 8/10. The game has a special, interesting time rewinding mechanic. Other than that, it's a standard adventure game. There is a lot of detail put into the world and you can interact with a lot of things.
Plot: 9/10. Life is Strange has a lot of suspsense and I cannot wait to see how it all plays out in the end. It also has a lot of stereotypes... OR DOES IT!?
Graphics: 8/10. For an Unreal 3 game, Life is Strange has pretty good graphics. On the highest settings, you get nice textures, really good looking shadows, god rays, very nice looking depth of field in cutscenes and cool effects when you use the rewind feature. The art style in the game is also really nice. The game just has that autumn atmosphere. Also, every single texture in the game was hand painted. This clearly took a lot of effort. At the same time, the game world doesn't feel fake or made up. It feels alive and real. The game is also littered with tiny details. Good job.
Audio: 8/10. There are some hipstery songs which I didn't really enjoy that much, but I don't know, maybe it's to estabilish Max as a hipstery nerd? The original soundtrack is good and it gives you those school/autumn vibes. It really fits the atmosphere. I would easily give the audio a 9/10 if the dialogue was improved to allow the clearly talented actors to give better performances. The actors' voices are pretty nicely matched with the characters.
Overall, 9/10. Enjoyable with good characters and plenty of consequences. Don't forget to water the plant. Seriously.
EDIT: There's also quite a few morally black and white choices. As in, there are choices that are obviously good and choices that are obviously bad. I think the devs will make some more consequences for their choices in the next episodes, however, so we'll just have to wait and see.

At first, this game seems like a rip-off of the Telltale Games genre that is popular due to the Walking Dead games, the Wolf Among Us, and The Game of Thrones game.  However, once I got into the small-town, quirky art school environment, I found this game very interesting.  The main character is NOT a gruff, angry, scruffy dude with an attitude that needs to protect someone or something.  The main character is an 18 year-old woman who is a photography student and she is returning to her home town after years in a bigger city.  She is not highly sexualized like Lara Croft not is she just a token female character like Faith from Mirror's Edge.  She feels like a real, if very awkward character who has depth to her.  The primary gameplay mechanic is rewinding time, which makes many of the binary choices in the game more interesting because you can make a choice, see the end result, rewind and try the other option.  This kind of game mechanic would feel too "gamey" in something like the Walking Dead or Game of Thrones, but it works here because the characters and the world is just strange in general.  In a lot of ways, this game reminds me of Twin Peaks, though that might just be the omnipresent references and shout-outs to that series.
Overall, pretty solid game.

Its hard to explain Life Is Strange, its a third person time travelling adventure that lets you make choices that effect events in the game. You are a photography student called Max who has returned to the town of Arcadia Bay, Oregon to attend Blackwell Academy. We meet Max three weeks into her first term, she receives a vision during class which is the beginning of events that lead her to some how find she has the ability to travel back in time. The events following will place Max in situations that will require her to use this new found power to change her own and others future.
The game is designed in episodes with four scheduled for future realise, we currently only have the first but the second is due this month. In a similar way to the Walking Dead or Wolf Among Us games,Its a bite sized chunk of an altogether bigger title. But don’t let that put you off, there’s plenty of game here for your money and though it may not be as polished as Square Enix’s triple A titles it is well put togetherand not to far removed from them. And though its a short game being only a day in Max’s life, there’s a fair amount of meat to this title and even some reply value too.
The choices you make in the game really do shape the game too, for instance at one point in the game you have the opportunity to intervene in a confrontation or take a photo of said event. If you intervene
then you will gain favor with one of the party’s involved, if you take a photo you will lose favour but gain a bargaining tool for later in the game. There are many of these choices, all have some kind of effect on the
game and though some events are set to happen, the duologue and way they happen can be altered.
There are some wonderful moments in the game too, one moment that stands out to me is right at the beginning. After the first scene of the game you leave class and find yourself in a crowded corridor
full of stereotypical students, Max puts in her head phones and walks down the corridor. Instead of still hearing the sound of the bustling corridor all sound is muted except Max’s chilled out music. Its a really beautiful
moment, the chilled out tune plays as the chaos around you continues. Some may miss the beauty of this moment, but the contrast when you must repeat this without the music really highlights the difference.
Its not all perfect though, Life Is Strange has one glaring issue that’s apparent from the first five minutes of playing. The writing is not up to par with the rest of the game, some plot moments seem
so badly written in fact that they seem to only be there to create a situation for you to find a solution to. They don’t feel natural and out of place in the world and the students themselves are so stereotypical its almost
like watching American Pie or a Brat-pack film. It doesn’t spoil the game, but does make you wish they had put a little more thought into it. This is the one area the game really shows its not a triple A title and that’s
a shame as this one thing holds the a wonderful game back.
The games controls on the other hand feel great, at least playing with a controller which I did. The face buttons are in a constant state of flux doing different things in different situations but A is
your action button whatever that action that maybe, Y is your look button, X and B are other actions when available. But there are always the on screen prompts to help you out. The rewind time and run are taken care of with
the bumpers, Is an elegant system and works fluidly with out any need to really learn anything before hand.
The HUD or lack of a HUD only shows you what you need when you need it and when it does show its done in a pleasant hand sketched style. its not the first time I’ve seen this kind of drawn style, but
never the less it fits well with the game and works perfectly well.

At first, this game seems like a rip-off of the Telltale Games genre that is popular due to the Walking Dead games, the Wolf Among Us, and The Game of Thrones game.  However, once I got into the small-town, quirky art school environment, I found this game very interesting.  The main character is NOT a gruff, angry, scruffy dude with an attitude that needs to protect someone or something.  The main character is an 18 year-old woman who is a photography student and she is returning to her home town after years in a bigger city.  She is not highly sexualized like Lara Croft not is she just a token female character like Faith from Mirror's Edge.  She feels like a real, if very awkward character who has depth to her.  The primary gameplay mechanic is rewinding time, which makes many of the binary choices in the game more interesting because you can make a choice, see the end result, rewind and try the other option.  This kind of game mechanic would feel too "gamey" in something like the Walking Dead or Game of Thrones, but it works here because the characters and the world is just strange in general.  In a lot of ways, this game reminds me of Twin Peaks, though that might just be the omnipresent references and shout-outs to that series.
Overall, pretty solid game.

First of all, decisions in this game really do matter. It's not like The Walking Dead, where it doesn't matter what decision you make, because in the next episode the outcome of the decision is basically going to be the same and all that changes are a few dialogue lines and that's about it. No, in here, the decisions you make are remembered by the game properly. You can also check out the different immediate consequences of different decisions by using the game's special "timey wimey rewindy" mechanic.
Now, I could give a lot of reasons why I like this game, but I don't really feel like it right now. Maybe later. I do, however, want to give some constructive criticism for the devs. First of all, the lip-sync is horrible. I've seen better lip-sync in Bethesda games, and I'm not kidding. The animations, at times, are a bit wonky. The voice acting is usually pretty good, but in some places, it really falls short. Usually the moments where it does fall short are because of boring writing. The actors aren't really given much to work with and that is exactly why some lines are delivered blandly. Most of the time, yes, the writing is good, but, like I said, there just are a few moments where it felt rushed and like the writers forgot to flesh out some dialogue. There is also a strange, annoying chromatic aberration filter throughout the game. It's probably there to kinda give the game maybe a vintage camera look, but let's be honest, you don't want your game to look like an Instagram photo. If you don't know what chromatic aberration is, look it up on Google. It makes the game look blurry and the edges of the screen a bit difficult to see properly. I think the game would look much better with it turned off.
Now, other than this, it is a good game, and it is enjoyable. I would definetly give the experience I had with the first two episodes so far a 9/10. It has interesting characters and I don't know why, but I just like high school drama (as in, finished watching all the 4 seasons of The OC and loved it, and I never even thought it'd be my thing). Don't let the pretentious sounding hipster name and the generic "episodic story based choice and consequence game" style drive you away. It puts an interesting spin on it and does it better than some other story games I've seen.
Gameplay: 8/10. The game has a special, interesting time rewinding mechanic. Other than that, it's a standard adventure game. There is a lot of detail put into the world and you can interact with a lot of things.
Plot: 9/10. Life is Strange has a lot of suspsense and I cannot wait to see how it all plays out in the end. It also has a lot of stereotypes... OR DOES IT!?
Graphics: 8/10. For an Unreal 3 game, Life is Strange has pretty good graphics. On the highest settings, you get nice textures, really good looking shadows, god rays, very nice looking depth of field in cutscenes and cool effects when you use the rewind feature. The art style in the game is also really nice. The game just has that autumn atmosphere. Also, every single texture in the game was hand painted. This clearly took a lot of effort. At the same time, the game world doesn't feel fake or made up. It feels alive and real. The game is also littered with tiny details. Good job.
Audio: 8/10. There are some hipstery songs which I didn't really enjoy that much, but I don't know, maybe it's to estabilish Max as a hipstery nerd? The original soundtrack is good and it gives you those school/autumn vibes. It really fits the atmosphere. I would easily give the audio a 9/10 if the dialogue was improved to allow the clearly talented actors to give better performances. The actors' voices are pretty nicely matched with the characters.
Overall, 9/10. Enjoyable with good characters and plenty of consequences. Don't forget to water the plant. Seriously.
EDIT: There's also quite a few morally black and white choices. As in, there are choices that are obviously good and choices that are obviously bad. I think the devs will make some more consequences for their choices in the next episodes, however, so we'll just have to wait and see.

I can't think of any possible way to explain how I feel about this.
This is a truly beautiful masterpiece--brilliant visuals, audio, story, and dialogue all combined to form something greater than one singular piece.
I've only played Episode I, but from my experience, the rest will be just as phenominal. Now, on to the review.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The story begins as Max, an 18 year-old girl, has a nightmare while in class, and discovers that she can rewind time. She can use this ability to learn things, travel backwards, and then use her knowledge of the future to avoid outcomes. Everything in this game is about choices and their possible repercussions. While they aren't directly revealed, major choices are followed by Max hinting at what could come later, and you can rewind and choose the other option if you so like. That's the beauty of this. Every choice WILL affect the plot. The characters and dialogue are pretty unique and dynamic, with very little cliché here and there, and the graphical design is just spectacular. You can interact with most things in the environment, and some of them even give you insight into what you should do next, or even information that you wouldn't learn while going throught the storyline progression normally. The dialogue is well-voiced, the SFX are brilliant, and the music fits the mood perfectly, further bringing out the emotions currently present.
Bonus points for beautiful camera pans and the ability to take 'optional' pictures.
Get this game. If you like deep storylines, GET. THIS. GAME. Amazing visuals? Get it. Choose Your Own Adventure? Move your mouse on over to the green Add To Cart button. All those feels? Buy it--now.
BOTTOM LINE--This game rocks.  11 / 10

Life Is Strange is a point and click adventure game that follows you through a week in Acadia Bay where you attend school, meet new people, meet old people, make friends, or make enemies. This game looks very good, using a hand-drawn style to illustrate a very well done perspective. And Acadia Bay is one of the nicest video game environments that I have ever had the pleasure of experiencing. The woods and water in this game look fantastic, and it makes me wonder what exactly this game would turn into if there was an open world element. I'm not saying that there should be, or that it would even work, but it would sure be one hell of a great time. It also has a strange system which the plot centers around which involves the fact that you can go back in time to change choices that you made and try new ones. This works very well in letting you truly explore every single thing available to you in Acadia Bay, as well as letting you have something to strive for after you've finished the game: 100% completion. This game also has one of the best soundtracks in video game history, perfectly describing the challenges that the characters face. It is also extremely well written, with vivid, beautiful dialogue that perfectly paints this game's setting. It is, however, a short game. I cant see it taking most people more than three hours, but there are still tons of achievements to keep you busy. I have completed the game, and have only unlocked three of those achievements out of about fifty, so you won't get bored. I have only played the first part, and I got it on sale, but I am truly impressed. I would say that part one is probably a perfect game for what it is, and one of the best that I have played all year. I cannot wait to play the next chapter.
10/10

Let's just start with this: If you want to play a game that blends Twin Peaks, The Butterfly Effect, and My So Called Life. Then stop reading this review and just buy this game.
Life is Strange is not finished at the time I'm writing this review, but I wouldn't recommend waiting for the full game. Sure, it could all go straight to hell, but right now you're going to want to experience the mystery at a slow boil like you would a good season of TV. The first chapter sets up Max, a girl who has figuratively "rewound time" to end up back at her small hometown to attend the prestigious Blackwell Academy. After a strange dream of doom she finds that she can *literally* rewind time and that's when, well, life starts to get strange.
This game has an excellent story so far, full of characters that have some real depth to them and honestly leave me wondering who I can trust. Max herself is a fantastic and likeable protagonist who combines a sort of nerdy naivette with a charming knowledge of nerd culture which manages to make me laugh without becoming a barrage of memes. The dialogue is mostly good, but there are some moments where it pushes belief (like a character who uses the word "hella" waaay too much for 2013. That shouldn't stop you from enjoying the game, though. In fact, it's kind of part of its weird small town charm.
Don't worry about this game being just another novel in game form, either. I have made some choices that had a real impact, including a moment at the end of the second game that had me cursing myself for my own bad decisions. I heartily recommend this game to anyone who loves sci-fi that has a firm foundation in the human element.

This is the only game I ever preordered. And when it finally showed up in my steam library... I knew my money had been well spent.
This game made me cry. For all the right reasons.
Presented in a format very similar to Telltale Games' The Walking Dead and The Wolf Among Us episodic series, wherein you focus mainly on dialogue, some point-and-click puzzles, and the consequences of your actions in a very powerful way, Life is Strange perhaps has more emotional power than any game I've ever played. I've never become so invested in characters alongside the main character like I did in this game, and whereas in Telltale's two similar games you pick a choice and you're stuck with it (unless it kills you), Life is Strange presents to you the choice to rewind time. That's right, you can go back in time and change your dialogue choices, or actions you've taken, AND retain memory of the previous timeline. This is the superpower of your main character, Max, a student at renowned Blackwell Academy for a photography course and its teacher, Mr. Jefferson, who is Max's idol.
The story precedent set by similar games like TWD and TWAU is high. And Life is Strange meets it without effort. Every character in and outside of the school feels and acts like a real human being, as though you have been dropped straight back into your senior year of high school, only there's no underclassmen to deal with. The world you explore is rich with the reality of it all, and nothing is black and white... save a few things, depending on your perspective. The love and work that was put into this game just oozes out of every pamphlet, every door, every leaf on the trees that appears in the game.
The mechanics are spot-on once you get the hang of them. Unlike TWD, there's no time limit on dialogue choices, but each choice still has its impact and can affect how other people in the game view you and what goes on. Max is a young girl who's recently moved back to her childhood town of Acadia, having left 5 years ago to study in Seattle. Coming back to study photography, Max realises she can alter the immediate past and becomes aware of an impending catastrophe. Max is by no means predestined to be a heroine, but a somewhat introverted, insecure girl with a strong sense of right balanced by general cowardice.
We get the feeling that photography, traditionally her hobby and outlet, is increasingly becoming a source of pressure as her studies toward and aspirations of becoming a photographer hinges on her ability to produce photographies on demand. At the same time, it seems plausible that some of the choices she's about to make may jeopardize her scholarship and thus future chances of becoming a photographer.
There's a real legitimacy to every choice - compounded by the fact that you have the option of exploring every outcome before comitting to your choice. Interestingly, you may find yourself agonizing the more for it - frequently, Max will voice her doubts as to your choice, reflecting that she, at least, is not wholly committed to one choice over the other. As if that wasn't enough, many of the characters you'll interact with place conflicting demands on Max, there's seemingly no way to satisfy everyone's demands, helping might entail forsaking another, driven home by Max receiving SMS messages throughout it all, reminding her of her obligations or subtle hints of her failure to be there for them when needed.
It may seem that I mistake a game review for a character review - but the game *is* Max - the real feat of this game is its ability through narrative, music and aesthetics to cram you into the mindset of seventeen-year-old girl; inheriting her worries, second-guessing, melancholy and general unease in the context of being granted an ability which is both a blessing and a curse, depending on one's perspective.
If you appreciated the Telltale series of games (Game of Thrones, The Walking Dead, The Wolf Among Us) from which this game draws much of its inspiration - or the story-telling and aesthetics of games such as Dreamfall and the Dreamfall Chapters, then you'll appreciate this game immensely.
Though ultimately, comparisons do it little justice, the game definitely has its own story to tell, the question is if you'll afford them the chance to do so - in summary, this is one choice I don't feel the need to unwind and do over :)

This game illustrates some things I rarely see in games nowadays: interesting play on game mechanics, solid storytelling, interesting empathetic characters and a very real vibe to the world. While "your actions influence the story later" and the major game mechanic (I'm avoiding saying what it is because it's spoilery) both have been done before, together it feels like something new.  The main game mechanic is handled in an interesting way and it's core to the story and main character.

This is the only game I ever preordered. And when it finally showed up in my steam library... I knew my money had been well spent.
This game made me cry. For all the right reasons.
Presented in a format very similar to Telltale Games' The Walking Dead and The Wolf Among Us episodic series, wherein you focus mainly on dialogue, some point-and-click puzzles, and the consequences of your actions in a very powerful way, Life is Strange perhaps has more emotional power than any game I've ever played. I've never become so invested in characters alongside the main character like I did in this game, and whereas in Telltale's two similar games you pick a choice and you're stuck with it (unless it kills you), Life is Strange presents to you the choice to rewind time. That's right, you can go back in time and change your dialogue choices, or actions you've taken, AND retain memory of the previous timeline. This is the superpower of your main character, Max, a student at renowned Blackwell Academy for a photography course and its teacher, Mr. Jefferson, who is Max's idol.
The story precedent set by similar games like TWD and TWAU is high. And Life is Strange meets it without effort. Every character in and outside of the school feels and acts like a real human being, as though you have been dropped straight back into your senior year of high school, only there's no underclassmen to deal with. The world you explore is rich with the reality of it all, and nothing is black and white... save a few things, depending on your perspective. The love and work that was put into this game just oozes out of every pamphlet, every door, every leaf on the trees that appears in the game.
The mechanics are spot-on once you get the hang of them. Unlike TWD, there's no time limit on dialogue choices, but each choice still has its impact and can affect how other people in the game view you and what goes on. Sure, it's still mostly scripted, but are you going to be a ♥♥♥♥♥ to the ♥♥♥♥♥, or will you show her a speck of kindness, and perhaps show her forgiveness for just a moment regardless whether you receive it in kind? And if you don't like the result, well, rewind and see how the other choice plays out, and go from there. (Not as easy as one would think.)
The visuals are decent, following a similar cartoonic path that borders a bit more on realistic, but still holds a very different life quality in how it looks. The visual details are simple, but the colors and contrast are quite pleasing and excellently portray the mood of the outside world. There are some issues with lip-syncing at the time of this review, but if you are engaged by story and voice, you will quickly forget about the issue.
Speaking of voice acting - another thing Dontnod did excellently in making this game. The characters aren't just 3D models with lip sync lines - the lines ARE from the characters, and the voice and music go together beautifully.
This game does have some flaws. Like the lip-syncing. Or the emotional impact being so huge that you are thrown out of the game world into memories of your own, where something went wrong. Nah, just jesting. But the game does have just that much power - it can make you genuinely happy for the characters, doubt their actions, and make you burst into tears, as I did. (The emotional overwhelm isn't really there in the first episode other than character attachment, but the second episode Out of Time throws some seriously heavy hitters at you.)
Would I recommend this game? ♥♥♥♥ yes. Show Telltale that not only did they do it right, but they led the way for some even more praiseworthy competitors, in the best way possible. Dontnod, I cannot help but nod to you.

Life is Strange, one of the best games I have every played. This game is defiantly in my top 5 games of all time(with games like Mass Effect 2 and Dragon Age Origins). Life is Strange has some of the best story telling I have seen in a game.
Game play: The game progresses at a very relaxed pace, the time control mechanic fits in well with the story and isn’t as game breaking as you might think-it actually makes choices a lot harder. The world feels alive with out being overly populated like other games.
Story: The story progresses well keeping the player submersed in the world, characters all fit in well and while some might point out that they do not act how people in the real world would, you need to accept this as a fictional world to truly appreciate it. Charters develop well, and all of them have some back story if you are willing to look for it.
Graphics: The graphics in the game are amazing they might not be the most realistic but the art style suits the game well. The art style is refreshing compared to what we see in most games, and the developers did an excellent job with the lighting in the game. The colours in this game are very vivid with out being over the top. Also you wont need a beast of a graphics card to run this game on maximum graphics.
Audio: The sound track in the game really add a lot to the ambiance of a seen, and set the mood for the game, you wont mind reading every little bit of information scattered around the world with this sound track in the back ground.
Pros:
-Amazing story
-Beautiful Graphics and scenery
-Choices fell like they are important
-One of the best sound tracks in a game
-Characters
Cons:
-none
Game Rating 10/10
