Ever wanted to timetravel? Well here is your chance.
The story is about a introverted 18 year old girl called Maxine Caulfield or short Max. Recently she started at a new school and is struggling to fit in. She has a strange power that let's her reverse time for a couple of seconds. This ability allows Max to learn information and redo conversations to get a better result for herself and to change her decisions.
I enjoy these types of games. You make important choices that will influence your faith and that of the living beings around you. Amazing storyline that sucks you in from the first moment. Geniusly athmospheric, amazing soundtrack and beautiful art.
After playing episode 1 I was very impressed by the storyline and immediately purchased episodes 2-5 straight after. This game does, what I miss with Telltale games (in my opinion) and that is, allowing you to redo/undo your choices/conversations/mistakes and see a different outcome. This does not mean that this game is not worth a replay. The choices you make, will have consciences for future episodes. I am looking forward what the future might bring.

I find the game awfully expensive - an other  17 Euros to get the rest of the story.  On top of it being such a cliff hanger. The game is really neat though. And I like the design and story line, but I didn't see much of my decisions affecting the outcome in an obvious way. Like with the drone girl - it didn't matter what answer I picked, I was still not cool in her eyes. Oh well, maybe I'm just a bit quirky that I have to buy the next episode now to see what is gonna expect me there.

Love this game so far. I just wish they'd fix the lip sync issue.
Also, this is my first episodic game and can say the 1-1.5 month wait between episodes is excruciating.

I am truely blown away with this game. I love this story and the timewarping twists that completely throw the story in another direction. When i played the first 30 mins of episode 1, I though this may be a little corny. Soon I realised that this game developed some solid characters and genuinly surprising twists that have had me on edge.
I love adevnture games, and these 3rd person, choice based story games are fanatic. I hopw the writers of this game continue with this kind of quality with other titles in the future. It is no wonder they have won awards for this.
This game is one you can sit back, enjoy like a movie, but with a deep interaction as you control the direction of the story. The choices in this game have a genuine impact on things later on and this too makes the story personal in some ways.
This game gets darker as the episodes go on, so be prepared to go through a rollercoaster of highs and lows of suspence and surprises.
This is easy to play, well narrated, well drawn gfx wise and nice audio production which syncs well with the story.
Play this game, you will not regret it, it is a masterpiece!

Life is Strange is a very heart warming and well thought out story-based video game in which you play as Max Caufield, a 18 year old girl who currently is being schooled at Blackwell Academy, in this decision based game, you will make moral choices which reflect how you play the game, and will give consequences based on said choice, the game is really good at making each choice balanced making each choice a hard one, and ensures that there is no "Good" or "Bad" choice to make.
In my experience, gameplay was smooth and crisp, kind of like my favourite potatoe chip (or what us brits call them, Crisps). Although i've noticed some bugs in the game, they were fixed as soon as i found them, which comes to my next topic that i will cover later, anyway, gameplay, like i said, is very smooth and is obviously shown that they put very hard work into making the game.
The interactiveness (Not sure if thats a word) of Life is Strange is just immense, for example, when you start the game, you head into the corridor, EVERYTHING, including posters and people, are available to be examined, it's just so fun looking at all the details, which got me hooked instantly.
The only complaint i have, which is noticable throughout the whole game (including episode 2) is the lip syncing, but if you get past that, which is easier than you think, Life is Strange becomes a fantastic game....
I give Life is Strange a solid 10/10, it's narrative and visuals make it look like it cam straight out of a indie film, which in my opinion, is a good thing, i recommend this to all gamers, even if you only ploay multiplayer games such as Counter-Strike, this game makes every gamer feel welcome. If you like Telltales "The Walking Dead2 game and "The Wolf Among Us" or even "Gone Home", then this game is almost a dream come true for you!

Life is Strange, one of the best games I have every played. This game is defiantly in my top 5 games of all time(with games like Mass Effect 2 and Dragon Age Origins). Life is Strange has some of the best story telling I have seen in a game.
Game play: The game progresses at a very relaxed pace, the time control mechanic fits in well with the story and isn’t as game breaking as you might think-it actually makes choices a lot harder. The world feels alive with out being overly populated like other games.
Story: The story progresses well keeping the player submersed in the world, characters all fit in well and while some might point out that they do not act how people in the real world would, you need to accept this as a fictional world to truly appreciate it. Charters develop well, and all of them have some back story if you are willing to look for it.
Graphics: The graphics in the game are amazing they might not be the most realistic but the art style suits the game well. The art style is refreshing compared to what we see in most games, and the developers did an excellent job with the lighting in the game. The colours in this game are very vivid with out being over the top. Also you wont need a beast of a graphics card to run this game on maximum graphics.
Audio: The sound track in the game really add a lot to the ambiance of a seen, and set the mood for the game, you wont mind reading every little bit of information scattered around the world with this sound track in the back ground.
Pros:
-Amazing story
-Beautiful Graphics and scenery
-Choices fell like they are important
-One of the best sound tracks in a game
-Characters
Cons:
-none
Game Rating 10/10

A gripping tale about a simple high-school girl who gets an almost ideal power for any indecisive teenager, to rewind and try a different approach, see the immediate reaction but not the long term effect, but at what cost?
There's so many pieces working in tandem here, and by the end of the 5 hour session in which me and two of my students played this, something wonderful happened to them. For two 16 year olds, the most important thing is their phones (an equally important narrative tool in the game) but after the first major decision, immersion gripped them, hard. Phones were of no interest to them, they moved through the world, no longer skipping talking to optional characters, but looking at everything and everyone because they were not playing a game, they were experiencing it. Watching them rewind, repeating, discussing, and even stopping for minutes to really think through choices was one of the greatest joys I've ever experienced!
If you have to compare this to any of the Telltale series (which one might inevitably do), then I'd first tell you to not do that, but secondly I'd say that it's perhaps a bit more black and white with the choices, each decision has a more distinct "good and bad" repercussion compared to Telltale. You get very clear feedback that "this was bad" or "this person will not like that" but I'm alright with that. Why? The game is set in high-school and it caters to that audience, the language is simpler as a result of this, and despite decisions having a clear cause and effect when they happen, I think they diffuse what it actually means at a future point in the story.
And this, my friends, is why I can't wait to play the next episode!
One of the best story based games I've played in a really long time, would recommend to anyone who also likes story driven games.

This review is based on the impression of the first two episodes...so thus it technically isn't of the complete deal.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Ok, so...to cut to the chase, this game is bloody brilliant. I was perhaps fourteen when I realised I played games for the enjoyment of narrative involvement and currently I'm far from disappointed. I'm two episodes in and at times...it can leave you on the edge of the seat, or wondering about how the story might proceed. The story twists and turns as you notice small details that influence the plot heavily or very little making you paranoid about your actions and the exploration you engage in.
Life Is Strange absolutely nails the characters within its story with characters deep and interesting with human quirks and touches of mystery that are interwoven with the story perfectly. The choices are rarely black and white and hold no real 'correct' answer - many of them coming back to bite you in the♥♥♥♥♥a few episodes later making you sometimes consider restarting the game to see how else it could have turned out.
The visuals are absolutely fantastic, with some really beautiful scenes you feel as if you're seeing the world through a photographer's eye. I must also sing praise for the voice acting. The range of emotion conveyed through the varying tones of each actor really helps entice the audience in the story and the choices they have to make. This in combination with the animator's work on facial expressions makes you give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about what each character is saying and helps flesh their personalities out. Hell, I even found that Max's inner-voice interesting (certainly more interesting than mine).  Still, thus far I've seen no QTE-based combat as seen in the recent Telltale works and whilst I can imagine it working for games such as 'The Wolf Among Us', I'm quite content not seeing it feature in Life Is Strange.
Regardless, I look forward to future episodes, the game is a damn fine one - though I feel somewhat guilty calling it a game as it feels more like an interactive story. I'd recommend picking up this game if the stuff I've mentioned to you sounds good and hell...I hope I haven't built you up to disappointment.
Enjoyable, and the time travel mechanic could open up some very interesting puzzles.

I'm not usually one to write a review, however, this game seems to warrant it.
I've been gaming since I was an 8 year old kid, almost 35 years worth of games under my belt at this point.  In every gamer's timeline, there are moments in games that stick with them forever.  The first time you chased down and ate a ghost in Pac-Man.  Hitting a trigger on a floor in Quake and watching as two blocks float up, slowly make their way through the air and into two square holes in the wall, and a door suddenly opening and a creature jumping out at you faster than you can blink (many pants were changed that night, my friends).  Heading to the edge of a platform and turning to head down the ladder when you spot Alma standing there (at this point in my gaming career, I learned wearing pants was really a waste of resources and time).
And then there are games that move you.  Entire games, not just moments.  Games that really suck you in and make you feel for the characters within them, make you actually care about them.  For me, there have been only a few games to reach that status.  Both "The Longest Journey" and "Dreamfall" stand out as storylines and characters that had me hooked and on the edge of my seat throughout the entire game.  After finishing "Dreamfall", I actually had to sit in the dark and contemplate and reflect on what I had experienced.  Other recent ones included "Bioshock", "The Walking Dead", "The Last of Us", and "Skyrim".  These were games that really made me feel real emotions on what was happening all throughout the gameplay.  And I've never replayed any of these games (except Skyrim, lots of alternate options to explore without having to experience the same thing over again), because I didn't feel a need.  Finishing them felt complete.
And then there is "Life Is Strange".  In some games (KOTOR comes to mind immediately), decisions reap consequences.  But many times, those consequences don't really drive your gameplay as much as they should.  Those decisions are a means to an end: getting past a boss in an easier way, getting a much needed item easier by choosing a darker decision over a more "righteous" one, etc.  In the moment, the decision isn't really that hard, because the consequence isn't fully realized until much later in the game and the emotion of that decision isn't immediate.  I've played plenty of games where I wondered briefly what would have happened had a chosen option B rather than option A.  But not in "Life Is Strange".  Soon after the intro of Episode 1, I found myself not only deeply immersed in the storyline and anticipating the next moments, but I found myself fully exploring each decision I had to make and making sure I was OK with the choice I made before proceeding.  The game mechanics are novel and seem fresh, the art direction, music, and voice acting are superb, and the concept is intriguing and compelling.  But the choices you have to make in this game can be gut-wrenching at times.  Some are easy.  Many, though, will have real consequences both immediately after and much later in the game, consequences that may not be fully realized what they are but will definitely be palpable once the choice is made.  The game is still linear and you will still start at Point A at the beginning and arrive at Point B at the end.  But the experience making the journey between those points will vary greatly depending on the choices you make and will affect your journey beyond Point B in ways you can't imagine.  That alone brings me closer to the protagonist and the other characters in ways many games lack.  I not only care about the story and the characters, but I care about the person Max will become based on my choices.
So, I've played a lot of games.  Many were terrible.  Many were good.  Quite a few were great.  A handful were memorable and moving on a personal level.  And then there is "Life Is Strange", which could rank as the best virtual experience I've had in 35 years of gaming.  I hope Episode 2 carries this momentum forward and it continues through to the end of the series.  If so, it will definitely be placed at the top of my list of all-time favorites.

Where do I begin?
Life Is Strange is one of the most heartfelt, unique games I have ever played. I just finished Episode 2 and felt it necessary to write a review. No game has ever had me reacting aloud to what happened in it, until this. It's like a TV show, but this kind of episodic series doesn't feel gimmicky or like a cash grab. It builds up anticipation like no game I've played has done before. If you're considering buying it, buy the whole set. Buy all of the episodes. You won't regret it. It was able to run well (at its lowest graphics settings) on my crummy little laptop, but I was so involved in the story that it didn't make a difference. I eagerly await Episode 3 and I will scream this game's praises until my voice is hoarse. Buy it immediately.

I've only played the first episode of this game (There's only 2 episodes out as of now).  I would have to say this game so far is pretty solid.  If you've played any of the Telltale games you will feel extremely comfortable playing this game.
With me only playing 1 of the 2 episodes available it’s too early for me to judge and explain what the story is about, or where the story is going.  So far the only thing I know is that you're playing a character named Max, and she has the power to reverse time.  And with this power where she has no idea how she obtains it, there are events that happen throughout her day that allow her to start to understand her power.  With this power when an event occurs she's able to make a decision and see how each decision plays out, and even gather information from the future to help her change decisions in the past.
I like that they add an element of reversing time in this game.  This element allows you to look at anything you might have missed, do something without any consequences, and even allows you to view both of the consequences of choosing from two decisions.  While I like this feature a lot, I personally dislike how the character is constantly second guesses herself. While I get the purpose of why the company did this I believe that the second guessing should be left with the player.  I say this because sometimes I want to think about the possible consequences of what's going to happen in the future on my own.  For example when the main character says something as little as "I hope this doesn't conflict with my scholarship" makes me second guess my decision more than I usually would. In a way it doesn't make me feel like I'm making the character how I want her to be. I think the indicator that your decision has a consequence is more than enough.
Just like a Telltale games they show you your decisions compared to everyone else who's played.  It was nice to see that they added a filter to see if you would like to see exclusively how your friends stacked up to your decisions.  They break down your decisions in two parts.  The first of which are your major decisions, and the second being "minor" decisions (You don't know how big of an impact these decisions make on the future of the game just yet).  Minor decisions can be anything as simple as watering a plant to drawing on a dusty car.  Any minor decision you may have missed appears on the list and tells you what you did/didn't do.
The art and graphics the company decided to use compliments this game extremely well.  The lighting especially looks gorgeous.  I'm not saying this game blows something like Battlefield 4's graphics out the water.  But I'm stating for the graphics specifically for this game's theme it looks extremely well just like how Minecraft's graphics look appropriate for that kind of game. The only downfall that REALLY takes away from really good moments of the game is the synchronization of the mouth and voice of the characters; In fact it doesn't even look like they're trying at all.  For example the character can be speaking a sentence that has 10 words and will only move they're mouth 3 times throughout the whole time they're speaking.  This personally kills me because there are some heart felt moments in this game but the voice synchronization take away from me getting emotionally attached to the characters sometimes.
Another pet peeve that absolutely kills me is the typographical error of the usage of the $ in this game.  While it's small it appears multiple times instead of using the dollar sign properly ($20) they display as this: 20$.
The music is also worth mentioning for this game.  Just like the graphics the music compliments this game perfectly.  The music hits the perfect mood and gives you the appropriate emotion for what's happening in the game.  Some of the songs are actually worth Shazaming.
Overall, I would recommend this game to anyone who hasn't tried games where you make a decision and your decision has a consequence for what you've decide.  If you've played this kind of genre in the past I would recommend that you give this game a shot.  Personally I've been on the fence seeing how I don't know what the story is entirely about.  But it's just too early to judge the richness of the story seeing how there’s only 2 out of 5 episodes out right now.  You're just going to have to try it out to see if you like the direction that the company takes you with their story. The first episode is only $5 and if you decide that you like it you can purchase the other 4 episodes for $17 (you lose $2 for not buying the complete season).

The only (minor) mistake I would note is that the dialogue is occasionally dumbed down to appeal to a certain audience, and that the gameplay is slightly choppy, depending on your processor.
This game is essentially about ethics and semantics. Someone who can change time to fix their mistakes, and make everyone like them and make themselves perfect, isn't default the "good guy." Every mistake brings a question, every question make it gut-wrenching to leave the game, anxious to get back into the questionable world of Arcadia.
Overall, 9.5/10. One of the best games of 2015, and I look forward to see if it can become something huge.

This is my first time playing an episodic game while the full story is still yet to be finished and released. At times, I wonder why I took the plunge and didn't just wait for the whole darn thing to be finished and out there, but overall -- so far -- the wait has been worth it. There's so much to explore and discover in Arcadia Bay, and while some of the dialogue has been "entertainingly awful" at certain points ("amazeballs" and "hardcore"? really?), the story and characters' potential leave me eager for future episodes.
In the most general sense, I'm reminded of my own high school days with this game. Though the drama is upped for story purposes (+ that whole time travel thing), they've captured the general essence of high school culture. I can kinda relate to Max (as well as parts of some other characters, like Chloe and Kate), and sometimes internally cringe at how she can sort of remind me of my own inner dialogue as that shy / introverted teenager several years ago. Other times I just wanna smile from the sheer nostalgia she and her experiences with the other characters give me.
Overall, the graphics are aesthetically pleasing (dat art direction mhmm lovin' it), the soundtrack is AMAZING and has already turned me onto some new artists (<3 Message to Bears), and the story as well as the intriguing characters continue to hold promise. Max's ability to rewind time also gives the game a great, albeit torturous dynamic -- should you, should you not?
The tension was amped WAY UP with Episode 2 choices (I was left wanting to just lie down on my bed, stare at the ceiling, and rethink my life choices after one in particular), and I'm excited to see how this game plays out with future episode releases! It's not a "perfect" game by any means -- it has its flaws, but I'd definitely rec it if you're into these kinds of games.

How would the ability to time travel impact your decisions?
Would you use it to fix up and tidy your personal interactions such that people always have the best opinion of you?
Would you use it to hurt those that anger you and then rewind time so that you don't face the consequences?
Would you use it to minimize your guilt and minimize consequences in your life?
Would you prioritize certain outcomes based on how it turns out for those who matter more to you?
Life is Strange is not a perfect game. While it subverts certain adventure game tropes, it falls into the pitfalls of other genres. (E.g. Collection quests, badly designed stealth messages.)
However, it is an important game and it's filled with perfect moments. While I cannot help but wish it strived for more, I would heartily recommend this to everyone.

(Please note this review is only for Episode 1, I will have reviews for the other episodes when I play them. Thank you!)
Max Caulfield is an ordinary girl with an extraordinary power. She wakes up one morning in October, expecting everything to be the same as usual. But one surreal daydream sets her down a path that will lead to something that no-one in the sleepy town of Arcadia Bay was expecting...
Life is Strange is an episodic, mystery, point-and-click game set in the town of Arcadia Bay in Oregon, USA. The story is centered around Max Caulfield, an 18-year-old girl who grew up in the town but for the past five years has been living in Seattle. She returns to Arcadia Bay after recieving a scholarship to go to Blackwell Academy to study photography, although she had to leave her parents behind due to finanical difficulties. Now she lives on campus in Blackwell and has quite the photo collection on her bedroom wall!
What did I think of Life is Strange Episode 1? I wasn't too sure when I started, but I was quickly enticed by the story. Telltale have really made a monopoly on these sort of games lately and it's nice to see Square Enix (Of all people!) to bring out this sort of game that people can relate to a lot more on a personal level than.. Game of Thrones or Borderlands, you get what I mean?
The art department on Episode One did an amazing job, everything from sunsets to lighting was perfect and it was truely reflective of a summers day, although they are few and far between in Ireland!
I enjoyed the wide range of characters in the game, from the super-elite right down to the quiet "geeks" of Blackwell. While some do represent hardcore stereotypes, some are very grounded and.. real, is the right word to use, I guess? Although I wished that there had been more choice to intervene in certain scenes.
That brings me onto my last point, which is the amount of choice in the game, and the impact of the choices you make later on in the game. So far, my choices have amounted to either a momentary mood change in the character I interacted with, or a little variation in a text message I recieve (comparative to other playthroughs that I've seen).
Although I would highly recommend this game to anyone that it new to the point-and-click genre and to anyone looking for a (mainly) feel-good game.
So, what is my final rating for Life is Strange Episode 1? I'm going to give it a solid 9.5/10 as I felt that choice lacked and there could have been more of it.

This game is different than all other adventure game ever made.
It is not based on puzzle-cinematic-puzzle-cinematic walkthrough. Gameplay is much more dynamic. All other characters are not stay at a corner to wait you to solve next puzzle. You don't spend all your time while searching a piece, even if you do, you discover lots of amazing details about the game. Also environment is not stagnant, it's alive! Even watching the sunset is a special experience. Relationship between characters are observable. Purpose of dialogs is not just there to tell you the story. They also really tell you about the characters' interior worlds. When Max talks with Chloe in her room, or at the Two Whales, you fell really a warm talk of two old friends.
The one more thing make this game special is personage of Max. She's not just a tool of player to play game. For example, In Walking Dead, we have really connected with Clementine. But how about Lee? He was just like a dummy. His feeling was too staright. We all guess what will he do. We learned about his past, his feelings about Clementine but not really his inside world. Game left us his personality to us but did not give a real chance to shape it. He was just a weak tool to protect Clementine.
However Max is different. She is not only there to let us discover other things about game. She is also there to let us discover her own world. She is a living person!
And finally musics, they're great. You should find the sountracks on spotify and listen them after you finished current episodes. Also there're lots of details and theories really interesting on YouTube. Have a look at them.

Life is Strange is an engaging interactive story in the Telltale mold with interesting characters, a compelling plotline, and a nifty time rewinding mechanic. The choices you make in the story have more than just a token impact, and for most of the more prominent ones there isn't a right or wrong decision. That means that though the choices aren't the difference between life and death, some are very difficult to make. I found that that gave me an insentive to rewind and see what happens if you go the other way.
The rewind ability is also used for various puzzles. None of them are particularly taxing, but are generally challenging enough to avoid being boring. You can also learn information in a conversation and then rewind and use that information to change what happens. Speaking of talking, that is what a lot of your time will be spent doing, either with other people or to yourself, making observations about the world around you.
The main fault of the game I would put on the dialogue. For the majority of the game it is good if not excellent, but it sounds sometimes like the writers wrote out normal dialogue, then hired a middle-aged consultant and said "Make this teenagery." Suffice it to say, it didn't work very well, and in a game set in a school, it can be obnoxious at times. For example, one of Max's friends says "hella" more times than I can count.
TL;DR. it is a great game worth your time if you enjoyed Walking Dead or The Wolf Among Us with an atmosphere a bit like Gone Home that will keep you intrigued even if some of the characters talk like a 30 something man imitating a teenager.

This game had me conflicted... but only a little.  The feeble gameplay is overwhelmingly shadowed by amazing storytelling, characterization, voice acting, and social commentary.
I am a heavily gameplay-focused player in general and I can't help but point out that gameplay-wise this game is borderline painful.  You control Max with a fixed over-the-shoulder camera that is mostly ok but not what I expect in a PC game.  The game's non-dialogue puzzles range from mildly interesting to busywork, and the time-rewind mechanic they are all based on is very poorly implemented, with the rewinding often being painfully slow even in fast mode, and often continuing even after you release the triggers or just pausing indefinitely and waiting for you to hit the skip button.  The way it rations out your options only after rewinding in a situation is only a little annoying, and seems totally fair for the dialogue-based situations, but can feel downright insulting in certain physical puzzles where the game forces you to screw up and rewind once or twice before even allowing you to do the correct thing.  And the interactivity of the game comes in the form of a very limited set of choices hand-picked by the devs.
The above is what would normally be ever-present in my mind during a game with this format, except that the game's story is so compelling and the characters are so well-portrayed that I managed to get immersed and totally forget about it.  Me, a player who's usual definition of immersion is a first person view and simulationist physics!  This is an amazing achievement for Dontnod.  The choices in the game, while limited and hand-picked, are legitimately interesting, and more importantly, are acted upon in natural ways that give the game a realistish feel, where the equivalent decisions in most AAA games would be either hollow filler material or data points for some uber-shallow good/evil axis.
This game was so amazingly immersive and enjoyable to me in its present form that it's scary to think about what sorts of games Dontnod would make if they put any effort into gameplay.

So I wasn’t too sure what to expect when I first decided to get chapter 1.  I mean, sure it looked good, but as we all know, games like this can go one of two ways, they can be engaging, engrossing and captivating experiences, or they can…well, not be.
And I’m glad to say that Life Is Strange is definitely the former.  I played Chapter 1 a few weeks back and found it great. Just finished playing through Chapter 2 just there. Many small details stand out in the game, how you can affect so many small things, and people remember.  They really do mean it with that whole ‘player-choice driven’ thing, I was seriously impressed by that aspect.
The choice and consequence is amazingly done, coupled with Max’s power to rewind time and for you, as a player to try out other choices with Max retaining all knowledge of what she experienced before in other conversation ‘branches’, plus that notification if something you’ve done/said will bring about a major consequence is something that’s rather helpful.  But even out-with those major choices, there are small things you can do that other characters in game remember.
The game manages to draw you into Max’s life and whilst at first it seems like a whole bunch of teen drama, after a while you find yourself actually giving a damn about the lives of all of the characters, about what’s going on, and as ever, I’m always impressed by a game that can pull of such levels of immersion.
The graphics are pretty, but of course that in itself doesn’t mean much.  What does is the art, and the choices it makes regarding which direction it chooses to go in.  And I have to say, I’m rather pleased with that.  The mood of the visuals, as well as the audio matches the mood of the storyline, syncing up quite well in order to deliver an enjoyable experience.

But don’t just take my word for it.  I seriously recommend giving this game a go for yourself, if you like story-driven games (Telltale Games-esque, in a manner of speaking), then you’ll enjoy Life is Strange .

This evening I decided that my bank account wouldn't scream to loud if I brought the first chapter of this reasonably hyped up game. These are my opinions and hence they are only my opinions on the game and you may have other opinions and that is fine. I chose not to watch any lets plays or read much about the game before diving in so I was really in the dark  accept for the fact it was about cause and effect. Cause and effect is a quite frequently used game mechanic so I was a little skeptical of how they would use this mechanic to create a exciting and gripping game; but oh boy they did.
The graphics of this game are beautifully realistic but the journal effect used to compliment the graphics really catches your eye and makes it something that makes the game feel like a dream. And did I say they are beautiful?
At the start of the game you are plunged into an introductory fast paced scene, and it is the scene that sets up the whole story. The atmosphere in the section is absolutely beautiful, I really like how the character shields herself from the storm and although it is at first frustrating you cannot run which seems to be what your natural reaction would be in a storm of that size. The fact you cannot run ruined the immersion into the storm situation a little for me but I was willing to continue as it was such a sudden scenario and I wanted to know more. After playing through the lighthouse storm scenario you wake up to find yourself in a photography class without really having much revealed about the main character, minus the fact she looks a little like Ellie from The Last Of Us with short hair. This classroom situation gives us plenty to find out about our character and her situation, as well as introducing us to the every games 'how to play' section which was made really interesting by the factor of keeping your brain going with all the information that was made to seem important flashing in front of your eyes.
Now I am going to continue with a non spoiler review for the rest as I want everyone to have an equal change to experience this game first hand without the influence of foreknowledge. The game introduces the mechanic that makes the cause and effect idea truly unique; reversing time. The reversing time aspect makes you think over every little situation carefully before choosing your action. It also allows you to see how different events could occur according to your action which is a nice touch. Most cause and reaction based games don't allow you to do this limiting the choice aspect as it doesn't get you to think how multiple other characters may react to a single choice. For example your relationship with one character may benefit from one choice but your relationship with another could be completely destroyed and effect that characters reactions to you further into the story.
The main character, Max, is a character I can really relate to due to my love of photography and I was totally jealous of her beautiful camera. Although to start with she seems quite a blank character through her inner dialog you really find her voice and she even makes you laugh with her little off hand comments at things. Overall the way I played her she is caring but a little snarky, which is a little like me as it is supposed to be. The idea of her as a character is to be a outreach of your own personality but stronger in aspects that you would normally be reserved about due to it being a game and the recoil of your actions are not real so you do not have to suffer her consequences. Although that is the case I really like her as a base for your own personality to adapt to.
As a whole I really enjoyed playing chapter one and I cannot wait to get my card out again to but the second chapter.

I cried
Truly. Life is Strange is a unique roleplaying choose-your-own-adventure story set in Acadia Falls, Oregon. You see life through the eyes of the akward Max Caufield,  student at the highly prestigious Blackwell Academy. And this life isn't pretty.
Never before have I seen a game tackle such heady issues as teen pregnancy, bullying, sexual assault, drug use, suicide, and domestic violence, much less bite them off in one sitting. Yet Life is Strange grasps all the heartbreaking complexity of life and embraces it. Yes, they overgrasp at times, trying too hard for authenticity, but in this game where Max can reverse time, it works. It is so easy to buy into the world of Arcadia Bay with its corruption, the juxtaposition of wealth and poverty, expansion and decay, that the things thrown at you one after another will leave you in the same emotional state as Max ... battered at every turn.
Everything you look at has a potential consequence, though the number of game-changing consequences are somewhat fewer. Its easy to overlook things in this game, both critical and atmospheric, making it challenging. You don't really get to see the consequences of your actions immediately either, making it difficult to "game" the story.
I strongly recommend this game. It pushes boundaries in a way no game I've experienced ever has. This isn't a "time-waster." It might be an eye-opening experience, though.

This will be a long review and this will feature SPOILERS from both episodes, so be warned.
When I first saw Life is Strange's reveal trailer, I wasn't impressed. I thought of it at first as a Telltale ripoff, just Square Enix trying to cash in on episodic games. When all the reviews came out, I decided "what the heck, it's only $5". I played it through and my opinion of it was turned completely upside down. This game is awesome on so many levels.
In this game, you play as Max Caulfield, an ordinary photography geek who is somehow given time travel powers. First off, the concept of the game is awesome, especially with a female lead. The soundtrack is amazing and it fits perfectly with the indie style of the game. The graphics aren't the best, but to me that's not really the focus. The focus is on the characters throughout the game and how they make you feel that you care about them and what happens to them, especially Kate Marsh, a student who is focused on in the first two episodes. The choices you make in the first and second episode will affect how she views you and this will have a significant impact on the game, or at least this episode. This game is extremely heavy and you may get emotional and feel differently about certain things after finishing it. Just a warning.
There are cons to the game, but I can easily get over them. Some may not, so this game may not be for you. First off, the lip syncing is pretty much non-existent. There are some points it matches up, but most of the time, it doesn't. This bothered me at first, but now I don't notice it. Second is the dialouge. A lot of people have trouble with the dialouge, saying that A) It doesn't fit what actual teenagers would say, or B) The dialouge doesn't fit the character. There are some points in the game where you cringe, more in the first than the second for me, personally, when you hear some characters talk. However, that really doesn't affect me much because I want to see this adventure, Max's and mine, continue. It's not perfect, but for me, this is probably the best game released in 2015 that I've gotten this year. If you liked Telltale's games, there's a good chance you'll love this; if you're skeptical, just buy the first episode for five bucks; you more than likely won't regret it.

I'm not saying this lightly but Life Is Strange is probably the best game I have played so far.
I've seen games with better graphics or with stories that are more epic or with more complex user interaction but the overall fell of this game is what gives it its value.
Before starting Life Is Strange I would not have believed that I would be drawn in by an American teenage story.
This game however is more than just a story. From the music, to the lighting to the small details you notice all around Arcadia Bay, everything is carefully arranged to create a distinct feel you won't notice in many titles.
The complexity of the story is also overwhelming. Where other games sometimes give you a feeling of unfulfillment, of blindly following a path laid down by the developers or of missing options in completing certain quests, this games feels complete. The evolution of the story seems in tune with the symbology of the tornado, where you are accidentally caught in this seemingly random flow of events. In spite of the huge measure of control time travel bestows on the player many times you find yourself helpless, yet every decision, every posible user interaction is crafted in such a way that you feel nothing is missing from the gameplay.
The characters also seem more alive than in most titles and interactions between them and the user natural. Even the thought of Max, often displayed throughout the game add a more natural feeling and a sense of completeness.
There are a lot of games which focus on providing endless quantity of playable content and in this aspect Life Is Strange also exceeds most titles out there by providing not a lot of content but a well-balanced amount of high quality content.
From graphics to story to the finishing touches everything seems to blend in harmoniously. All in all this game is a masterpiece and I eagerly await the release of the next three episodes.

This evening I decided that my bank account wouldn't scream to loud if I brought the first chapter of this reasonably hyped up game. These are my opinions and hence they are only my opinions on the game and you may have other opinions and that is fine. I chose not to watch any lets plays or read much about the game before diving in so I was really in the dark  accept for the fact it was about cause and effect. Cause and effect is a quite frequently used game mechanic so I was a little skeptical of how they would use this mechanic to create a exciting and gripping game; but oh boy they did.
The graphics of this game are beautifully realistic but the journal effect used to compliment the graphics really catches your eye and makes it something that makes the game feel like a dream. And did I say they are beautiful?
At the start of the game you are plunged into an introductory fast paced scene, and it is the scene that sets up the whole story. The atmosphere in the section is absolutely beautiful, I really like how the character shields herself from the storm and although it is at first frustrating you cannot run which seems to be what your natural reaction would be in a storm of that size. The fact you cannot run ruined the immersion into the storm situation a little for me but I was willing to continue as it was such a sudden scenario and I wanted to know more. After playing through the lighthouse storm scenario you wake up to find yourself in a photography class without really having much revealed about the main character, minus the fact she looks a little like Ellie from The Last Of Us with short hair. This classroom situation gives us plenty to find out about our character and her situation, as well as introducing us to the every games 'how to play' section which was made really interesting by the factor of keeping your brain going with all the information that was made to seem important flashing in front of your eyes.
Now I am going to continue with a non spoiler review for the rest as I want everyone to have an equal change to experience this game first hand without the influence of foreknowledge. The game introduces the mechanic that makes the cause and effect idea truly unique; reversing time. The reversing time aspect makes you think over every little situation carefully before choosing your action. It also allows you to see how different events could occur according to your action which is a nice touch. Most cause and reaction based games don't allow you to do this limiting the choice aspect as it doesn't get you to think how multiple other characters may react to a single choice. For example your relationship with one character may benefit from one choice but your relationship with another could be completely destroyed and effect that characters reactions to you further into the story.
The main character, Max, is a character I can really relate to due to my love of photography and I was totally jealous of her beautiful camera. Although to start with she seems quite a blank character through her inner dialog you really find her voice and she even makes you laugh with her little off hand comments at things. Overall the way I played her she is caring but a little snarky, which is a little like me as it is supposed to be. The idea of her as a character is to be a outreach of your own personality but stronger in aspects that you would normally be reserved about due to it being a game and the recoil of your actions are not real so you do not have to suffer her consequences. Although that is the case I really like her as a base for your own personality to adapt to.
As a whole I really enjoyed playing chapter one and I cannot wait to get my card out again to but the second chapter.

This will be a long review and this will feature SPOILERS from both episodes, so be warned.
When I first saw Life is Strange's reveal trailer, I wasn't impressed. I thought of it at first as a Telltale ripoff, just Square Enix trying to cash in on episodic games. When all the reviews came out, I decided "what the heck, it's only $5". I played it through and my opinion of it was turned completely upside down. This game is awesome on so many levels.
In this game, you play as Max Caulfield, an ordinary photography geek who is somehow given time travel powers. First off, the concept of the game is awesome, especially with a female lead. The soundtrack is amazing and it fits perfectly with the indie style of the game. The graphics aren't the best, but to me that's not really the focus. The focus is on the characters throughout the game and how they make you feel that you care about them and what happens to them, especially Kate Marsh, a student who is focused on in the first two episodes. The choices you make in the first and second episode will affect how she views you and this will have a significant impact on the game, or at least this episode. This game is extremely heavy and you may get emotional and feel differently about certain things after finishing it. Just a warning.
There are cons to the game, but I can easily get over them. Some may not, so this game may not be for you. First off, the lip syncing is pretty much non-existent. There are some points it matches up, but most of the time, it doesn't. This bothered me at first, but now I don't notice it. Second is the dialouge. A lot of people have trouble with the dialouge, saying that A) It doesn't fit what actual teenagers would say, or B) The dialouge doesn't fit the character. There are some points in the game where you cringe, more in the first than the second for me, personally, when you hear some characters talk. However, that really doesn't affect me much because I want to see this adventure, Max's and mine, continue. It's not perfect, but for me, this is probably the best game released in 2015 that I've gotten this year. If you liked Telltale's games, there's a good chance you'll love this; if you're skeptical, just buy the first episode for five bucks; you more than likely won't regret it.

A heartwarming game about teenagers in a relatively sleepy, apparently fictional American city/town trying to find their place in the world but facing increasing numbers of obstacles, handling classic themes such as growing up, taking responsibility, showing moral courage, dealing with loneliness, mending broken relationships, valuing solitude or friendship and so on. It has some supernatural/mystery elements that hit in very early (the protagonist has daydreams and can rewind time) and which remain yet to be understood as far as the first episode goes.
I'm not the best to judge because I'm not from America but it seems to have all one would expect: A highschool, bullys, jockeys, nerds, punks, religious types, cheerleaders, divas. Extro- and introverts mashing up all having their own dramas of sorts to endure in today's time (there are many (pop)cultural references - "selfies", social media, Facebook, anime, video games, movies, ...)
Yet despite this possibly stereotypical first look there is always a sincere warmth shining through. It's a thoughtfully designed game showing a great passion and love of detail, being wiser than it perhaps knows and maybe deserving more attention than it gets. Many characters are very likeable despite them filling rather archetypical roles and even the divas and bullys may have more to them than meets the eye. The soundtrack is fantastic (I hope it will be added to Steam later as DLC) and was put into the game in some very interesting, smooth ways. The motion capturing/animation work is great, just like the voice acting. You can talk to a lot of people and examine so many corners and crannies the protagonist, an 18-years old aspiring albeit introverted and indecisive photographer called Maxine Caulfield, will always comment with her voice (talking to people or having mind monologues) making you quickly empathize with her. You will feel her struggles eventually, and of the people she meets - helping them or not, being nice or not, often depending on your choices.
This game can easily stand up to more prominent character-/story-driven titles like those made by Telltale, I dare say it outshines them even. Life is Strange takes some obvious inspirations from them giving you multiple dialogue lines and sometimes critical two-way-decisions to choose from, which will "be remembered" or "have consequences" and, upon finishing an episode, are compared to the choices made by your friends and the whole playerbase.
However it rarely pushes you from one scene to another: You are given relatively great freedom in exploring and examining each area before you move on to your often journal-logged "objective" (which is beautifully designed too, it's rather extensive and really looks like it could be a journal from a young art-ish woman, shown to you in little angles featuring character descriptions and all sorts of sketches, drawings and writings on it as well as photos you can take occassionally adding to the great level of detail of this game). And there is a lot to look at that makes you wonder, giggle, feel sad or simply curious. In other such games there is far less to examine (I'm looking at you, Telltale) and in them I'm often a bit scared by what I do in which pace, fearing - by selecting specific dialogue lines or lollygagging too much even in seemingly more relaxed scenes - to trigger a chain of events I wasn't ready for just yet missing out on things I would have wanted to check on first. That was rarely the case in Life is Strange. Of course there is no "Ready to continue? Yes/No" popup, but you won't exactly trip into things either and more often than not can rewind time. Yet it still has its funny, sad or dramatic moments and a tight red path to follow and to keep the story flowing fluently if you wish so. There is no serious puzzling, just you having to rewind time to get around situations and the very basics of interacting with one item in the world or another, which very much makes you feel like a part of the world and definitely renders it a game (there can be some nitpickers out there). That's the way I prefer so I don't get artifically blocked out from the story flow. I decide if I want to take it more slowly and examine things and talk to people, and I happily do so in this game, having spent like 6-7 hours on the first episode with no idle/afk phases where a Telltale episode would only last me for two or three at best.
The only thing that may put one off a little is that the time rewind feature is sometimes forced on you. There is no hard "Game Over" - if Maxine/the story dearly wants you to rewind, you must do so. This sometimes happens in scenes where you or other key characters would otherwise die or where you would miss out opportunities to clear out and walk otherwise blocked off paths. Sometimes you must rewind because the "correct" answer to a request of another character can only be found out by answering falsely first (a little awkward variation of "trial and error"). That isn't too dramatic, and you can skip dialogue sections anytime, but perhaps it wouldn't hurt to find more subtle and nimble ways to deal with some situations. I hope there will be a tad more feeling of consequence to your rewinding too. It's a feature that allows you to test out many dialogue options and actions without having to replay whole epsiodes or chapters, which I like in itself; a neat trick I would love to see in similar games too, admittedly without necessarily knowing how to pull that off with a less deeply built-in story-related feature. Even with this rewinding feature you won't always find the very best option (as if Life would be that easy), but you often have all the time in the world to find the one you'll feel most comfortable with. I don't think it should, or could, go on like that all the way. Such stories, such characters with such abilities, often seem to demand unpredictable negative sideffects to make sure the protagonist won't get too confident with her "superpowers" and will never forget her responsibilites and that she is gifted in a way. She mustn't do it uncontrolled whenever she wishes to I guess. Maxine has that freedom for now. I wonder how it will work out in the next episodes.
So, I was literally blown away by the game/its first episode despite my initial doubts and reluctance towards teenage drama. But there is just so much warmth and love in this thoughtful, richly detailed game that I cannot dislike it.

I'm not saying this lightly but Life Is Strange is probably the best game I have played so far.
I've seen games with better graphics or with stories that are more epic or with more complex user interaction but the overall fell of this game is what gives it its value.
Before starting Life Is Strange I would not have believed that I would be drawn in by an American teenage story.
This game however is more than just a story. From the music, to the lighting to the small details you notice all around Arcadia Bay, everything is carefully arranged to create a distinct feel you won't notice in many titles.
The complexity of the story is also overwhelming. Where other games sometimes give you a feeling of unfulfillment, of blindly following a path laid down by the developers or of missing options in completing certain quests, this games feels complete. The evolution of the story seems in tune with the symbology of the tornado, where you are accidentally caught in this seemingly random flow of events. In spite of the huge measure of control time travel bestows on the player many times you find yourself helpless, yet every decision, every posible user interaction is crafted in such a way that you feel nothing is missing from the gameplay.
The characters also seem more alive than in most titles and interactions between them and the user natural. Even the thought of Max, often displayed throughout the game add a more natural feeling and a sense of completeness.
There are a lot of games which focus on providing endless quantity of playable content and in this aspect Life Is Strange also exceeds most titles out there by providing not a lot of content but a well-balanced amount of high quality content.
From graphics to story to the finishing touches everything seems to blend in harmoniously. All in all this game is a masterpiece and I eagerly await the release of the next three episodes.

Rarely do I buy games on impulse. I had never heard of this game before, but upon watching the trailer and reading the description, I instantly bought it without consulting reviews or forum impressions.
My instinct wasn't wrong and I was very pleasantly surprised by this fresh, unique and quirky experience. This is like Juno, Ghost Town and Donnie Darko meets the gameplay of The Walking Dead, with a unique time rewinding gameplay twist at the core of it (allowing you to see different outcomes instantly, and deciding which is best going forward). I also get a slight Twin Peaks vibe (and I love Twin Peaks!).
It is unashamedly hipster, and whilst I was tempted to think the writing was just trying too hard to be hipster-ish, to the point of being cheesy, perhaps I'm just out of touch and this really is the way some teenage highschool students speak now. Afterall they're part of the social media generation which is a phenomonen that didn't start until I finished Uni.
Most importantly the story is interesting, I'm intrigued to see what's really going on here, where these characters will end up, and what the ultimate consequences of my choices will be.
On the technical side, I'm happy to say this runs and looks better than The Walking Dead ever did.
I highly recommend this game to anyone looking for a fun and unique experience, at the low price, it's worth checking out.

The time rewind mechanic is awesome. If you feel like crap after the last choice you made, rewind and go the opposite. The puzzles are also built around the time rewind mechanic as well and are very, very clever.
The graphics are suprisingly great as well. I'm a big fan of Telltales games and the stunning visuals in this game were a refreshing change of pace. I can have my amazing story, hard choices, puzzles that I love from Telltales games and beautiful visuals too.
The music is grand. It fits so well within the game. It's not some teenage, emo, crap; however, it does give you a sense of that angst. The music never felt out of place and was very well done.
The only thing negative I can say about this game is the lip-syncing. It's complete crap; however, the amazing voice acting makes up for it. I never really paid much attention to the lips but the quality of the voices themselves.
Overall, if you're on the fence about getting this game. Do it. It's 4 dollars an episode. One of the most engaging stories I've played in a while that didn't come from telltale games.

TL; DR:
For people who are patient enough to seek into deep emotional characters, real choices, and heavy story other than adrenaline rush games like Call of Duty, Battlefield, Counter Strike, look no further!  If you enjoy Telltale games, this game is much better with real choices!
Long Review Version:
I like interactive storybooks such as Dreamfall, the Longest Journey.
Life is Strange has quickly become my new favorite.  So far I'm enjoying Episode 1 and 2.  Although the game kind of starts slow, it manages to introduce the power and limitations of the main protagonist, Maxine, as well as build up emotions for characters around me.  The choices you make depend on how observant and care you are toward your friends, classmates, and environment.  A lot of weight is toward love.  The more love toward the people around you, the better the decisions outcome will be.  Detail care is the key in this game.
Most of the choices you have made in Episode 1 will be reflected in Episode 2.  If you found Episode 1 is too slow, try Episode 2, you will be touched!  The end of Episode 2's message is very powerful even though Maxine's ability is not so powerful!

Pros:
+ Lots of real choices with actual consequences that are reflected later in Episode 2.
+ Pretty diverse dialogue selection tree.  Almost allow the game plays differently everytime.
+ Leaving me feeling quite empty and impatient for the next episodes!
+ Great voice work
+ Soothing music
+ Interesting storyline and characters
+ Sketch style graphics
+ Keyboard & Mouse as well as Controller friendly.  I would prefer a controller so I can sit back to enjoy.
+ Collectible mode where you can go back to each chapter to collect items without interfering the choices.
+ Multiple slots to save the progress for replaying the chapters.  You can experiment as many decision tress as possible.
+ Great use of Bible quotes.  Able to bring a very strong message from the scenarios.
Cons:
- Animations need more work.  (Budget issue most likely)
- It starts kind of slow but advanture games are mostly about patients instead of adrenaline rush.
- Main character is not hot for me :P  Chole and Rachel are hot!
- Sometimes the conversations are conflicting and may not be too logical.

Buy it instantly without hesitation if you liked any of the following:
- Telltale's The Walking Dead
- Telltale's The Wolf Among Us
- Consortium
- Spec Ops: The Line
- Outer Wilds
You may also be interested if you liked the story/dialogue/plot elements of the following:
- Mass Effect
- Deus Ex: Human Revolution
- Wing Commander III
- The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask
Dontnod Entertainment have taken on the Telltale formula, and improved it.
- No QTEs
- Less frustration (Just rewind if you mess up)
- More unexpected hidden choices that can be missed entirely
- Tenser choices that stack across episodes changing what becomes preferable
- More interesting clutter info that can give extra dialogue choices and reveal plot points early.
Episode 1 is good. Episode 2 is godly. (bit like Walking Dead S1). Roll on Episode 3!

Loving this game so far, it fills the hole that games like Dear Esther leave when you finish them. If you like games like Dear Esther this is a must buy.

Following is based actual events the past eight relative hours or so:
Logged on Steam with the exact thought "Damn, it's so boring playing games these days, ever since I got through Bioshock Infinite, nothing really pulls my mind apart in a truly joyful way anymore, wish there would be an equal game around."
Coincidentally, this game appears on the store front in that exact moment. I don't really know why, but I feel this strange urge to click on it, though neither title nor concept art is really intriguing to me.
Doing some casual observance of one of the trailers, and get more intrested. Continue with some minor reading in the reviews. Getting more interested by every word. It seems very promising. I decide to give it a shot and proceed with buying the game, and download it right away.
I'm starting to play the game, and the first impression isn't that catching, I don't really like the feel of the controls nor the camera angle. The first scenario isn't that much of what I had expected either. But I've learned not to be small minded, so I continue on. Every minute I play I become more and more hooked. Eventually even getting over the bad controls and camera angle.
The story continues onward being intriguing in a very new way, but yet not really new, since the story itself isn't much more than average. But the actual time one really spends on making the choices, as one learns very quick that they really do matter, is what makes it so deep. It is the concept of contemplating every possible timeline that could stem from what appears being such a silly choice of not watering ones plant or not.
It is Quantum physics all over again, like back in the Bioshock Infinite, when one was trying to get the pieces of the puzzle in order at the end, but now while one is actually playing the game. Every possibility could eventually mean the end of the world, which you remind yourself of with that bottle of water in your hand.
I snap back to, ehm, reality, for short moments, but the game really get ones attention without really craving it, pulling one in, like a black hole, or stupid vortex.
I proceed with playing through the two available parts, and I feel kind of empty inside now when I'm not really able to continue, yet. But I also feel equally satisfied, like I actually found something that fulfilled my requesting thought when I first got on Steam. And the fact that there are yet three episodes to go really gives something to look forward to.
This far:
9,5/10
Only the controls (in the sense that a refrigerator moves more gracefully) and camera angle being the cons to me.
I also, somewhere, deep down inside, like to think, that I played through this game, went back, and made myself buy and download it, when I already knew how good it was. It would explain that hunch, that feeling.
According to the actual Quantum physics, that would be fully possible, but then again, Quantum physics is weird♥♥♥♥♥♥

I must say, even this early in the year, I can see this game being in my top ten and perhaps even GOTY.
Life Is Strange, a game I did not expect, nor was I thinking I was going to buy. Leave aside the fact that I'm drooling for more after finishing the second episode. I was looking for a game that my girlfriend and I would be able to play together and make choices that we would both care about. To be honest this buy was mostly for her, but now I think I love this game more than she does! Here is the thing, DONTNOD has done an absolutly outstanding job making this game exceed my expectations. Even after episode one, that bar was set high and episode 2 rose the bar again.
Pros:
-The game is gorgeous and has a very unique yet familiar art-style that makes everything look hand painted and very charming.
-Keeps you guessing!
-You are rewarded for exploration, You can find hidden clues that can help fuel your inner conspiracy theorist. These little nuggets you find are gold for bragging to your friends who also play.
-Oh god the music ties the game together.
-Its relaxed experience with bursts of excitment that keep you on edge.
-The games collectible system is unique and works well, if you miss any you can go back and replay individual areas without replaying the entire area.
Kinda Cons:
-Length: not much to tide you over for the next episode, although the perfect length for an episode a sitting.
-Once the game was unclear we just abused the game mechanics untill it all turned milhouse.
Lengths:
Episode 1: 3-ish hours (including backtracking for collectibles)
Episode 2: 2.5ish hours (without backtracking)

I am not a person who replays games.
Especially not story driven ones, because I have a habit of trying to get the *best* decisions on the first go.
However with Life Is Strange, I don't really feel compelled to do that. It kills it. You want to explore so bad, you want to click on every available button and talk to everybody and talk again and explore the consequences of your choices.
Watering a plant has consequences. AND I DESPERATELY NEED TO KNOW WHY.
This good is so good at hooking you. Even though it's a little on the extreme side of teenage life, it's still pretty funny and somewhat relatable, and gives a very unique environment. I love how the little things drastically change the game and how the big choices are affected by all the little things you did. And the detail is INSANE. Notes on the walls, posters, papers, objects. The things you can even walk straight by without noticing are crazy. Unless you decided to look up spoilers, no two play throughs will be alike (unless you follow the same path of choices).
The gameplay is pretty fun too for what the game is. No QTE events, but episode 2 offers some fun new 'ways' to use her ability for fun. And the rewind option? Very unique.
And the characters are all pretty hooking. Not all of them are entirely full of depth, but the way they are interwoven into the story is awesome. That, and the way EVERYTHING in the game has some purpose or other for the most part. The plant defo will. But looking at posters? Important. Talking to people? Important. Grafitti? Important.
Wonderful game that has me totally hooked. Can't wait for more!

TL; DR:
For people who are patient enough to seek into deep emotional characters, real choices, and heavy story other than adrenaline rush games like Call of Duty, Battlefield, Counter Strike, look no further!  If you enjoy Telltale games, this game is much better with real choices!
Long Review Version:
I like interactive storybooks such as Dreamfall, the Longest Journey.
Life is Strange has quickly become my new favorite.  So far I'm enjoying Episode 1 and 2.  Although the game kind of starts slow, it manages to introduce the power and limitations of the main protagonist, Maxine, as well as build up emotions for characters around me.  The choices you make depend on how observant and care you are toward your friends, classmates, and environment.  A lot of weight is toward love.  The more love toward the people around you, the better the decisions outcome will be.  Detail care is the key in this game.
Most of the choices you have made in Episode 1 will be reflected in Episode 2.  If you found Episode 1 is too slow, try Episode 2, you will be touched!  The end of Episode 2's message is very powerful even though Maxine's ability is not so powerful!

Pros:
+ Lots of real choices with actual consequences that are reflected later in Episode 2.
+ Pretty diverse dialogue selection tree.  Almost allow the game plays differently everytime.
+ Leaving me feeling quite empty and impatient for the next episodes!
+ Great voice work
+ Soothing music
+ Interesting storyline and characters
+ Sketch style graphics
+ Keyboard & Mouse as well as Controller friendly.  I would prefer a controller so I can sit back to enjoy.
+ Collectible mode where you can go back to each chapter to collect items without interfering the choices.
+ Multiple slots to save the progress for replaying the chapters.  You can experiment as many decision tress as possible.
+ Great use of Bible quotes.  Able to bring a very strong message from the scenarios.
Cons:
- Animations need more work.  (Budget issue most likely)
- It starts kind of slow but advanture games are mostly about patients instead of adrenaline rush.
- Main character is not hot for me :P  Chole and Rachel are hot!
- Sometimes the conversations are conflicting and may not be too logical.

Buy it instantly without hesitation if you liked any of the following:
- Telltale's The Walking Dead
- Telltale's The Wolf Among Us
- Consortium
- Spec Ops: The Line
- Outer Wilds
You may also be interested if you liked the story/dialogue/plot elements of the following:
- Mass Effect
- Deus Ex: Human Revolution
- Wing Commander III
- The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask
Dontnod Entertainment have taken on the Telltale formula, and improved it.
- No QTEs
- Less frustration (Just rewind if you mess up)
- More unexpected hidden choices that can be missed entirely
- Tenser choices that stack across episodes changing what becomes preferable
- More interesting clutter info that can give extra dialogue choices and reveal plot points early.
Episode 1 is good. Episode 2 is godly. (bit like Walking Dead S1). Roll on Episode 3!

A very intriguing and interesting game that follows the traditional telltale games style. Which, for those of you who do not know, is a series of directional dialogue choices, with some limited third person walking around to point and click at objects. There is some very light puzzle solving, usually interacting with an object, getting a bad result, then interacting with a  different object and trying again. The mechanics are not very creative, however, there is one. The rewind mechanic is very useful and inventive, as I'm sure we've all had moments we wanted something similar, or have committed the infamous "save scumming" before. The pot thus far is very intriguing, but only the first two episodes are out.

Overall, this is so far a really good game. The art style is unique, looks beautiful and fits the game's theme really well. The choices you make actually feel like they make an impact and they really do; it's not just choose option B to get slightly different dialogue - the game, its plot and its characters are changed and deeply affected by your choices. The high school/college (?) setting is done well, the characters feel real and believable and you come to really care for or really despise certain ones you interact with well. The plot after two episodes is still interesting and compelling, and I'm excited to see where it's going.
On the downside, the lip-syncing is terrible. It really bothers me during cutscenes, and Dontnod have basically said nothing can be down about it. There are a few minor bugs here and there, and writing-wise Max's internal monologues (especially the ones where she sits down somewhere) are bloody terrible and come off as completely unnatural. Most of the writing is good though, and these downsides are relatively minor. I would definitely recommend this game.

Let me preface all of this by saying that I play a lot of games, and that I love adventure games. It’s probably my favorite genre, overall.
Why is that important? Because I have to scramble my brain to find any other examples of games that has captivated me so consistently and felt as evocative and powerful as Life is Strange. I can’t even pinpoint why, not exactly anyway. There’s plenty of weak points here, after all. The graphics are nothing to gawp at. The lip-synching is just awful. The story is interesting, but nothing stellar. Not to mention the puzzles, which are not challenging or even very creative. But I find myself ignoring all of that while playing, because the game just sucks me in. It’s one of those rare games that continue to affect me
after I’ve completed an episode. It’s not just me thinking about how I could have affected the choice-driven story differently either. It’s more a sense of wonder. It makes me nostalgic. This game makes me think about my own life. It makes me think about memories I treasure, moments I remember from my youth. I find myself drifting back and forth in my muddled thoughts, thinking how my teenage years were and how they formed me. Life is Strange makes me feel. Not just while playing, but long afterwards. Life truly, is strange. It really makes that statement ring.
Life is Strange then, is one of those games with
. It shows its qualities primarily through its characters; flawed and occationally inconsistent, but so relatable, quirky and interesting. Every person has layers upon layers to them, and they all feel important, even when they do nothing at all but sit there. They feel real. And they keep surprising both me and Max, the sweet protagonist.
The other definitive quality of this game is in its atmosphere. Arcadia Bay, like the characters there, feels like a real place. You just want to explore this world! The visuals and the sounds and music comes together to create a gloriously  calm and warm symphony of lush forests, homey houses and run-down diners. It’s a place that seems to have been lost in time, a small American town that we all could feel some belonging to, no matter what nationality you adhere to. The most inspiring moments in this game comes from just walking and soaking it all in. Or sitting, while Max shares her thoughts with you. It feels precious. It really does.
Oh, and did I mention it’s got a sweet time-control mechanic?
Now that’s just icing in the cake, though.
