Today is Oktober 28th of 2015. Episode 5 of Season 1 of Life is Strange has been out for 8 days now. I am writing this after playing Episode 5 at the day of release and replaying all 5 Episodes again making some different decisions (most importantly looking at the other of the two ending sequences) as well as reading a lot of the discussions about the endings.
But let's start with a non-spoiler explanation for people that do not know Life is Strange and probably heard about the ending controversy, why they should go ahead pay the money and play this game despite all the controversy about the ending.
In short: This game is for sure one of the best adventures featuring choice and consequence story telling out right now. For me it is the best I have played so far. And despite the fact that in two weeks we get Fallout 4 for me Life is Strange is game of the year.
At it's core the game is a mystery-crime-drama story taking obvious inspiration from tv series like Twin Peaks and movies like Donnie Darko and the Butterfly Effect.
The games graphics clearly speak a language of low budget/indie production. But nevertheless the art team did a great job in making it still a great and enjoyable experience by giving everything a handpainted pastell color look that fits the overall theme of the game very well.
The Soundtrack is superb and in combination with the voice acting and the story, which is in large parts outstandingly well written, might as well have been from a high budget TV series.
The Story and the way it is presented is the strong part of this game. It no doubt captivates you and doesn't let you go. Life is Strange is actually the first game that had me keep playing because I wanted to know how the story would go on. Games that make you care about the story in that way are very rare. Especially if you're an adult that doesn't fall for the stereotypical hero saves all the world plot anymore.
And there is two parts to that:
First of all the crime part of the story taken on it's own is done perfectly. If there are hints at all to what really goes on before the end of episode 4 they are so subtle that you actually only notice them after the first playthrough when you already know what's going on. And up until the end of epsiode 4 there are so many different suspects. Uncovering things really is a jaw dropper.
Secondly the drama part of the story is done equally well. It's an emotional rollercoaster. Games rarely get me to tear up. Actually I remember only one time before Life is Strange and that is when Mordin Solus sacrifices himself in Mass Effect 3. When it comes to believable characters that the player can identify himself with and hold dear Life is Strange deserves just as much praise as the Mass Effect series got.
So you might ask what all the current fuzz and outcry is about: It mainly is caused by the mystery part of the story falling apart in the ending the devs chose. And one of the endings offers no real closure on what happens to the side cast of the game while the other shows exactly what every of the characters go through in the end which makes it a very satisfying end to the story's drama part.
Closing this non-spoiler part of the review I want to talk about the gameplay:
There really isn't much new here. We have the typcial WASD + Mouse controls for modern 3D Adventures. We have a time rewind feature much like Prince of Persia the Sands of Time with puzzles very cleverly designed around it. Puzzles even involve the dialogs. Dialogs are multiple choice with consequences to the choices spanning several episodes in some cases.
As far as choice and consequence go in my view it all fits the story very well. You have some impact on minor parts of the story and some of the characters but you are far from full control over every aspect to the story which would be quite unrealistic anyways.

You don't really have to hate people that are not so much your friend, you can ignore them mostly. Also you have diplomatic answer options that allow you not to crawl at their feet, but still not make an enemy for life. The ones you like, you really care for after a short while.
Also nice is to have situations that could happen in real life. Not some dragon you have to conquer.
Storywise it is one of the three best games on Steam for me. I also like to play the maincharacter. Not some supernatural hero. Also the choices I get have almost always one I would also take. Not like some games where you get 3 choices and want a 4th since all 3 are dimwitted.
Also her friend, weird as she is, is someone I would also befriend. Someone you just have to like, not some stupid person you are forced to tag along.
However I must say I am not so much in shooters, even if I play left4dead once in a while. So if you only enjoy games with lots of dead and killed, this might be not our thing. But I would say if you enjoyed RPG's like Dragon Age Origins or Walking Dead you might like it. The negative critics I understand that some macho guys got their feelings hurted, playing a girl for a change. Hey i enjoyed Witcher 2 also, though I was forced to play a guy .... so .... . And why not, that is what roleplay is after all, play the role of someone else.  Anyway, congratulations to the creator that they did NOT agree to replace the hero by a boy as the investor proposed. There are already felt 5 billion macho guy games out there, let us also play a person with feelings using other tricks than a 12 gauge gun for a change. Also nice is not to have to spend the time with pesky fighting engines and 500'000 enemies you must kill. I anyway cheat my way through most RPG's, bored by the many monsters that attack.  I was really tired of, go to cave A, kill all bandits, fetch item B, bring it to NPC C, get so and so much experience ... . In RPG's I enjoy the story and would wish there were less fights. "Life Is Strange" does not give experience and tedious collector filler quests. It is pure story, and your decisions matter !!! I would even say, this game does not give experience, it does not need to give experience, since it *IS* an great experience.
Only part I do not like is this sequel fever. The waiting for the next part is not so much fun. But well i understand it, it helps the Indie to finance the game. So I guess having pesky sequels is preferrable to not have the game at all, since the creator went bankrupsy. But I assume it is allowed to dream on to get such a cool game in one go for a change, hehe.
I would give it 9/10. Must play, even for guys that can jump over their macho ego once in a while.

The first thing I took from this game is that even when you think a choice is right, it may turn out to have dire consequences.
In this fantastic game, you play as Max who has just moved back to her hometown and has reunited with her old friend, Chloe. She goes to a prestigious academy and discovers she has the power to rewind time by a few minutes, ultimately leading her to believe she can change everything.
This mechanic of the game is used well - it means you can see all the choices available before actually making your choice, often unlocking new paths from what characters have said to you. Every single choice you make as Max matters and affects the present and future of the game, or how characters feel about you or react. But then there's times where the game does not let you rewind. Is that a bad thing? No, it's not. It means that you made the choice you thought was right, and now you have to live with the consequences in the game and future episodes. There's no going back to change it - you must move on.
On top of that, both the soundtrack and visuals of the game are absolutely stunning. My only gripe is the facial animations and lip syncing, but they don't impact the way the drama is delivered at all.
10/10

Life is Strange. You follow Max, a blooming photographer who discovers she has the power to reverse time.
This game is not just a game. It's like your own pre-set movie, where you are the director, the writer, the cameraman, and the star. Every choice you make is pivotal, including watering your own potted plant.
The rewind function is the thing that makes the game stand out. You could do a lot with it, including being the Blackwell Ninja. But the important thing is, it lets you explore your choices and at least have an idea of its consequence in the future.
For example, you water your plant. "This action will have consequences." So you chicken out, rewind, and not water the plant anymore.
It has a big difference from Telltale's games, and that is it doesn't really focus on survival, but more on choices and consequences.
Once again, Life is Strange is like your story. You could be a sweet, nice person who's always there for her friends, or you could be the meanest b*tch in the story and bully Victoria using your newfound powers.
Because of the amazing hand-drawn graphics and soothing old-timey soundtrack, I give this game 9/10.
Get ready, Telltale. Life Is Strange is coming.

I will start by saying I'm one of the artists that worked on this game. Since we had a downfall with "Remember me" I was not sure what to think about "Life is strange". Ofc I knew that this will be a completely different game, but I had this strange feeling that this game will fail as RM did...
I really enjoyed working on it...the art direction was great...but that's about all I knew about this game. I had no idea how complex the story will be or how it will feel as a whole.
I must say I’m more of a rpg kind of games guy….I had played a lot of adventures but actually I haven’t really been blown away by an adventure game since the good old days when I’ve played “Grim Fandango” or “Syberia”.
So I've played episode 1. It was a blast. It was the first game in a really long time when I really got emotionally attached with the characters. The story was complex and intriguing....the characters different but with a lot of things to relate with. The art style combined with the great soundtrack and those moments when u can just stay and meditate on your journey (like sitting on the fountain) was absolutely perfect. For me it was a pleasant surprise that this game actually managed to get that realistic feel of a teenager getting through life with all the choices that might seem right at some point and completely wrong after 10 minutes. This movie like feel combined with all those details to explore and the inner thoughts of Max was for me absolutely incredible.  After finishing ep 1 I really thought that this is a masterpiece…a game that actually keeps u there in front of the monitor even if it’s not about getting points, scoring goals and killing monsters. And it was a long time ago when I last played a game that made me feel that way. And for that I am really proud of the job that the guys from Dontnod did.
Then episode 2 was released. I’ve had high expectations and I must say I was not disappointed. Actually the game became more awesome. The story got a lot more complex. The decisions I’ve took in ep 1 had a real impact in the second one. In the first episode the decisions were not that problematic to be honest….they felt a bit dull as long as u wanted to pose in a righteous person….but in this one I had struggles with every damn decision….even answering a god damn phone call….I just cannot express how much I want to see how this will evolve in the next episodes.
Ofc there are some problems with the game…like the lip sync issue…but tbh after 10 minutes into the story u have to be crazy to even care about that. I see a lot of people comparing this with Telltale games. Actually I think that this game is from a completely different league. The graphics and overall style is nowhere near that low budget look from telltale. And ofc it’s like this. We’ve worked almost 3 years on this game….Telltale is making one of those episodes every god damn few months. Imho the only thing that gets together Telltales and Dontnods games is the episodic part and maybe the fact that it’s an adventure. Other than that the games are completely different.
Anyway…I have only one more thing to say. Go and buy this game. U won’t regret it.

Only played the first episode. Very promsing but not without faults. At it's heart the game lies somewhere between point and click adventure and interactive movie.  I say that because, though it plays like the former it has very few puzzels and you are generally just progressing a story.
The player can make choices in the style of Telltale's The Walking Dead game.  This has two new spins as far as I can see - a time travel mecanic allows you to rewind and undo decisions and occasionally that game will inform you not just of when you have made a decision but also when something has happned as a result of one.  The time travel is a nice touch but so far is very simplisticly used and linear.  Bar a puzzle or two It may aswell be replaced with an "I've changed my mind" button.  Hopefully it will be used more in future episodes.  The decision notifications are just annoying.  I don't see how anyone can see "this has happened because of a decision you made" and not get annoyed because they want to know which decision it was.  Personally I have never liked these kind of decisions in games and much preffered games like Heavy Rain where the play often doesn't know they have even made a decision until something happens to make them think "I wonder if I change that by reloading and doing something different".  That would make for excellent use of the time travel trick but sadly there's nothing like that here.
Ultimately its the presentation and story that pull this game though as it certainly has be wanting to see how it proceeds.  That said there are problems with these too, as both of them feel they are trying too hard at times.  Whoever heard of a student who looked at the new TV in the class room and sincerely remarked "I can't wait to watch some documentaries on this bad boy".  Cringe.  Simmilarly the art style whilst mostly accomplished layers the indie vibe on with a spade. Animations made to look like they were doodled in the back of a text book were over-done in 2009 (see
) but Life is Strange using them for everything thing, making it feel less like Indie and more like a very polished homage to Indie. On a related note the game feels almost patronising as all it's teenage characters are exactly the right level of retro to be into the same stuff as it's late 20s early 30s target audience.  Thanks, but I can handle the fact that kids today use digital cameras and don't own CDs.

Life is Strange. You follow Max, a blooming photographer who discovers she has the power to reverse time.
This game is not just a game. It's like your own pre-set movie, where you are the director, the writer, the cameraman, and the star. Every choice you make is pivotal, including watering your own potted plant.
The rewind function is the thing that makes the game stand out. You could do a lot with it, including being the Blackwell Ninja. But the important thing is, it lets you explore your choices and at least have an idea of its consequence in the future.
For example, you water your plant. "This action will have consequences." So you chicken out, rewind, and not water the plant anymore.
It has a big difference from Telltale's games, and that is it doesn't really focus on survival, but more on choices and consequences.
Once again, Life is Strange is like your story. You could be a sweet, nice person who's always there for her friends, or you could be the meanest b*tch in the story and bully Victoria using your newfound powers.
Because of the amazing hand-drawn graphics and soothing old-timey soundtrack, I give this game 9/10.
Get ready, Telltale. Life Is Strange is coming.

I will start by saying I'm one of the artists that worked on this game. Since we had a downfall with "Remember me" I was not sure what to think about "Life is strange". Ofc I knew that this will be a completely different game, but I had this strange feeling that this game will fail as RM did...
I really enjoyed working on it...the art direction was great...but that's about all I knew about this game. I had no idea how complex the story will be or how it will feel as a whole.
I must say I’m more of a rpg kind of games guy….I had played a lot of adventures but actually I haven’t really been blown away by an adventure game since the good old days when I’ve played “Grim Fandango” or “Syberia”.
So I've played episode 1. It was a blast. It was the first game in a really long time when I really got emotionally attached with the characters. The story was complex and intriguing....the characters different but with a lot of things to relate with. The art style combined with the great soundtrack and those moments when u can just stay and meditate on your journey (like sitting on the fountain) was absolutely perfect. For me it was a pleasant surprise that this game actually managed to get that realistic feel of a teenager getting through life with all the choices that might seem right at some point and completely wrong after 10 minutes. This movie like feel combined with all those details to explore and the inner thoughts of Max was for me absolutely incredible.  After finishing ep 1 I really thought that this is a masterpiece…a game that actually keeps u there in front of the monitor even if it’s not about getting points, scoring goals and killing monsters. And it was a long time ago when I last played a game that made me feel that way. And for that I am really proud of the job that the guys from Dontnod did.
Then episode 2 was released. I’ve had high expectations and I must say I was not disappointed. Actually the game became more awesome. The story got a lot more complex. The decisions I’ve took in ep 1 had a real impact in the second one. In the first episode the decisions were not that problematic to be honest….they felt a bit dull as long as u wanted to pose in a righteous person….but in this one I had struggles with every damn decision….even answering a god damn phone call….I just cannot express how much I want to see how this will evolve in the next episodes.
Ofc there are some problems with the game…like the lip sync issue…but tbh after 10 minutes into the story u have to be crazy to even care about that. I see a lot of people comparing this with Telltale games. Actually I think that this game is from a completely different league. The graphics and overall style is nowhere near that low budget look from telltale. And ofc it’s like this. We’ve worked almost 3 years on this game….Telltale is making one of those episodes every god damn few months. Imho the only thing that gets together Telltales and Dontnods games is the episodic part and maybe the fact that it’s an adventure. Other than that the games are completely different.
Anyway…I have only one more thing to say. Go and buy this game. U won’t regret it.

Only played the first episode. Very promsing but not without faults. At it's heart the game lies somewhere between point and click adventure and interactive movie.  I say that because, though it plays like the former it has very few puzzels and you are generally just progressing a story.
The player can make choices in the style of Telltale's The Walking Dead game.  This has two new spins as far as I can see - a time travel mecanic allows you to rewind and undo decisions and occasionally that game will inform you not just of when you have made a decision but also when something has happned as a result of one.  The time travel is a nice touch but so far is very simplisticly used and linear.  Bar a puzzle or two It may aswell be replaced with an "I've changed my mind" button.  Hopefully it will be used more in future episodes.  The decision notifications are just annoying.  I don't see how anyone can see "this has happened because of a decision you made" and not get annoyed because they want to know which decision it was.  Personally I have never liked these kind of decisions in games and much preffered games like Heavy Rain where the play often doesn't know they have even made a decision until something happens to make them think "I wonder if I change that by reloading and doing something different".  That would make for excellent use of the time travel trick but sadly there's nothing like that here.
Ultimately its the presentation and story that pull this game though as it certainly has be wanting to see how it proceeds.  That said there are problems with these too, as both of them feel they are trying too hard at times.  Whoever heard of a student who looked at the new TV in the class room and sincerely remarked "I can't wait to watch some documentaries on this bad boy".  Cringe.  Simmilarly the art style whilst mostly accomplished layers the indie vibe on with a spade. Animations made to look like they were doodled in the back of a text book were over-done in 2009 (see
) but Life is Strange using them for everything thing, making it feel less like Indie and more like a very polished homage to Indie. On a related note the game feels almost patronising as all it's teenage characters are exactly the right level of retro to be into the same stuff as it's late 20s early 30s target audience.  Thanks, but I can handle the fact that kids today use digital cameras and don't own CDs.

So after playing two episodes, I think I'm ready to review this game.
Long story short: if you play games for the story, this is pretty much a must-have.
Others have said this is a mix between Walking Dead, Heavy Rain, and Alan Wake, and that's a pretty fair description.  The story and consequence-based gameplay of the first two combines with the scenic atmosphere of the last to create an experience that is both simple and cinematic at the same time.  However, it avoids the stressful, dystopian nature of Walking Dead, the over-the-top situations of Heavy Rain, and the repetitive gameplay of Alan Wake while keeping the good stuff.
You really get invested in this world and in the characters, which is the sign that they are believable and true.  Despite having control over time, the game makes sure to show you that you don't have as much control over your world as you think, and sometimes no matter which choice you make, there will be consequences.  It also encourages to notice the little things in life; not only rewarding you with snippets of dialogue, but important clues on how to prevent tragedy later on.
While the pace is slow at times, and the graphics, while pretty, aren't very advanced, overall the game manages to tell a story better than most mediums.  And unlike most video games, the situations you deal with here are real and very possible in our world (well, except for maybe the time travel thing, but no complaints about that.)
Overall, I highly recommend the game, and look forward to future episodes.  After all, I need to see what consequences my actions will have, since Max can only rewind so far...

So after playing two episodes, I think I'm ready to review this game.
Long story short: if you play games for the story, this is pretty much a must-have.
Others have said this is a mix between Walking Dead, Heavy Rain, and Alan Wake, and that's a pretty fair description.  The story and consequence-based gameplay of the first two combines with the scenic atmosphere of the last to create an experience that is both simple and cinematic at the same time.  However, it avoids the stressful, dystopian nature of Walking Dead, the over-the-top situations of Heavy Rain, and the repetitive gameplay of Alan Wake while keeping the good stuff.
You really get invested in this world and in the characters, which is the sign that they are believable and true.  Despite having control over time, the game makes sure to show you that you don't have as much control over your world as you think, and sometimes no matter which choice you make, there will be consequences.  It also encourages to notice the little things in life; not only rewarding you with snippets of dialogue, but important clues on how to prevent tragedy later on.
While the pace is slow at times, and the graphics, while pretty, aren't very advanced, overall the game manages to tell a story better than most mediums.  And unlike most video games, the situations you deal with here are real and very possible in our world (well, except for maybe the time travel thing, but no complaints about that.)
Overall, I highly recommend the game, and look forward to future episodes.  After all, I need to see what consequences my actions will have, since Max can only rewind so far...

This is my first ever review and I must say, I'm proud to write it about this game. Never before have I experienced such a blend of media, storytelling and gaming in one. Like a reference within the game, Life is Strange has a definite Donnie Darko vibe. (And Donnie Darko had a reference to Stephen King's IT. What a strange string of twist and turns.)
Enter Max Caulfield, a photographer and student at Blackwell Academy.  Oh yeah, and she has the power to turn back time. This adds another dimension in the cause and effect of decision making and I promise you, this won't always feel safe as the end of episode 2 proved. You must also live with your choices eventually, which have an affect across future episodes.

Cons
This is not free-roaming. Though you still get to move your character to explore each scene.
Some characters are one dimensional like Nathan, the rich bully who seems to own the town.

How can this game pull the same stunt with being a total walking simulator yet be so damn fun?
Well, time travel is always fun, and boy did they do it right. So without giving too much away, you are Maxine Caulfield, (because Catcher in the Rye, get it?) a high school student who is suddenly dropped into the 4th dimension, giving her Cassandra-like powers and weaknesses. So you navigate the choices you make as you and those around you slowly veer towards the incoming disaster - a week away.
The Pros: There are TONS OF CHOICES you can make, so many that I missed a lot of them on my first playthrough. Definitely worth your time to explore. Brief Summary:
Life Is Strange is a fairly new episodic story game with clear and heavy influence from but not made by the telltale games company. This is the first episodic story game put out by Square Enix a reputable producer of story rich games and RPGs. Although more accustomed to the Japanese scene and style, Square delivers an absolutely beautiful westernized game developed by DONTNOD Entertainment which takes place in Arcadia Bay, Oregon at what I believe is a fictional school named Blackwell Academy(correct me if I'm wrong didn't do my research there!). It follows the story of Maxine Caulfield an 18 year old photography student who comes back to Arcadia Bay for the first time in 5 years to study at Blackwell to study under a prestiged photographer, Mark Jefferson.
What you can expect(some great aspects of the game):
-A gripping story with a deep history of each character you come across straight out of the gate.
-Vivid colors and wonderful character design giving each character a genuine human-like feel and appearance.
-A reflectable setting, everybody has been through high school or will go through high school, everybody has dealt with their high school drama, you'll experience scenarios that you see going on every day in your career as a student.
-Inviting game mechanics, the ability to rewind time makes the story forgiving and allows you to choose the way you really want things to go down. You can always replay later if you're curious to see other outcomes but you won't be penalized and forced into consequences you were originally unsure of.
What I would like to see for future episodes:
-Longer episodes, episode 1 was a little short finished it in a little bit under two hours. Call me picky but I have high expectations from non-indie developers. It will never be make or break for the time it takes for me to complete a game, but I'm all about something that keeps me going, I'm satisfied with the content provided in episode one but if another half an hours worth of play was included in future episodes it would simply be a bonus.
-A real conclusion to episode 1, I would like to get closure for what we've seen so far before they dump 15 new characters and a new scenario on top of that. I'm genuinely impressed by what I've experienced so far and the ending of this episode brought out plenty of different emotions from me, I don't want that ruined by a common flaw in many developers which is rushed content.
-More about Max and her family, we've seen so much of the people around her just in one episode but I would love to see more about her personal life and maybe why she's developed the power she now has, where her nightmare came from which provided this power and most of all why her in the first place. A power that great should have a reason!
All in all I'm just ecstatic over this remarkable game. There are no real cons for me and my playthrough so far has been overwhelmingly great. I look forward to the new episodes coming out and can only hope they keep on delivering the bliss episode 1 did.

I can only recommend this based on what is available which is episode 1 and 2.  Usually I'd suggest to wait to review an episodic game before it is released, but I was extremely impressed by this.  As it goes through the rest of the episodes, I will edit this.
You are Max, a girl with a passion for photography who has returned to her home town Arcadia to go to a private school that only accepts seniors.  There are posters everywhere of a missing girl named Rachel Amber.  Very early on in the game, you discover something strange about yourself: you can reverse time.  This has a pretty important role as you can imagine.  Not long after you discover this power, you use it to save the life of your old best friend Chloe who you havn't seen or spoken to for 5 years, until now.  As you two get reacquainted you discover that Chloe was close to Rachel, and now you both want to find out what happened to her.  As things go on, it becomes clear that whatever happened is extremely complex.  Lots of people are involved, lots of things going on, and everything seems to be connected.  They are weaving this story together in an amazing way.  You'll have to deal with some pretty heavy stuff.
<3 Max and Chloe
As you go, you will make all kinds of decisions that will have an impact on the story, and what people think of you, as you progress.  And if right after you make a decision you decide to change your mind?  Reverse time and change it.  It gives you some control over the course of events like that.  However typically the choices you make are difficult ones.  There is almost never a clearly obvious right thing to choose, and I think that's good.  However some decisions can be quite odd too.  All of them really make you want to know what happens next though.
I did encounter a few bugs.  A couple of times during conversation with other characters, people would stop moving their mouths while talking, or freeze completely, and once or twice I had to restart the game.  Overall though, nothing terrible.
The characters are interesting, the story hooks you in and makes you want more and is woven together expertly, the art style is pretty (like a painting), and the music is great.  I think we're in for a really great (and very emotional, possibly even disturbing if it isn't already on some levels) storyline.  I definitely feel tension rising in the storyline.  Things are escalating and building and it's getting pretty crazy.
Life is strange, indeed.

I've played a LOT of games. I used to play games for the "story" before I realized that even the likes of Bioshock, Mass Effect and Half Life just don't hold up to decent books and movies. I had a phsyical reaction (MASS EFFECT 3 SPOILERS) to Samara trying to kill herself and that really impressed me, but I've never been given goosebumps by a games story alone. Life is Strange did that. The attachment you have to these characters is more real than Booker and Elizabeth or Shepard and (insert love interest) or Freeman and Vance. As much as I love the characters in those games, the ones in Life is Strange are real in a way those other characters are not. The lack of actual gameplay and the inclusion of important and ambiguous decisions greatly enhances the connection you feel to these characters and the story is just brilliantly written. If it was just this the game gets an easy 10/10
But it isn't just that and there are problems. For one the lip syncing is archaic and in a game that heavily relies on character development that's nearly disasterous. You need to be able to see the characters emotion and the bad syncing nearly destorys that. Fortunately the great acting, story and graphics very much make up for that. But there's room to make the emotional connection even greater in the next few episodes.
The 2nd major problem is the cinematography. It's MOSTLY good. But occasionally scenes are cut in a very "gamey" and jarring way and not in a fluid movie like way thusly reminding you that you're playing a game. It's not a huge issue but it can easily be better.
Final score for me would be 9.5/10 and simply the 2nd best "experience" there is in the gaming world (P.T. takes the top spot). DEFINITELY a big thumbs up :P
[EDIT for Episode 2]
This is so much more than a video game or a story or a video game with a story. Despite fundamental similarities to other "games" in the genera, particularly Telltale Games, it is safe to say I've never experienced anything like this. Could not recommend more despite continued abysmal lipsyncing that really distracts. Despite this glaring and massive flaw LiS is still on pace to be an absolute masterpiece.

I can only recommend this based on what is available which is episode 1 and 2.  Usually I'd suggest to wait to review an episodic game before it is released, but I was extremely impressed by this.  As it goes through the rest of the episodes, I will edit this.
You are Max, a girl with a passion for photography who has returned to her home town Arcadia to go to a private school that only accepts seniors.  There are posters everywhere of a missing girl named Rachel Amber.  Very early on in the game, you discover something strange about yourself: you can reverse time.  This has a pretty important role as you can imagine.  Not long after you discover this power, you use it to save the life of your old best friend Chloe who you havn't seen or spoken to for 5 years, until now.  As you two get reacquainted you discover that Chloe was close to Rachel, and now you both want to find out what happened to her.  As things go on, it becomes clear that whatever happened is extremely complex.  Lots of people are involved, lots of things going on, and everything seems to be connected.  They are weaving this story together in an amazing way.  You'll have to deal with some pretty heavy stuff.
<3 Max and Chloe
As you go, you will make all kinds of decisions that will have an impact on the story, and what people think of you, as you progress.  And if right after you make a decision you decide to change your mind?  Reverse time and change it.  It gives you some control over the course of events like that.  However typically the choices you make are difficult ones.  There is almost never a clearly obvious right thing to choose, and I think that's good.  However some decisions can be quite odd too.  All of them really make you want to know what happens next though.
I did encounter a few bugs.  A couple of times during conversation with other characters, people would stop moving their mouths while talking, or freeze completely, and once or twice I had to restart the game.  Overall though, nothing terrible.
The characters are interesting, the story hooks you in and makes you want more and is woven together expertly, the art style is pretty (like a painting), and the music is great.  I think we're in for a really great (and very emotional, possibly even disturbing if it isn't already on some levels) storyline.  I definitely feel tension rising in the storyline.  Things are escalating and building and it's getting pretty crazy.
Life is strange, indeed.

Conclusion:
Give it a whirl. It's worth the time.  ;)

On the good side, the idea of a chose your own adventure with the ability to rewind time is very fun, allowing for the exploration of different routes in "real time" and allowing what is every utilitarian's dream, observing the consequences of every possible decision. The few time rewind puzzles in the game are simple so far, but I'm sure they'll be more complicated as the series progresses. The events that are teased in the first episode seem to make for a compelling story arc, but being the first episode, those events weren't explored yet. The teaser for episode 2 was way more interesting than almost anything that happened in the first episode, but it's difficult to tell if it will live up to the hype.
My main problems with the game are in the atmosphere created and how the characters have developed so far. This game has to be one of the most pretentiously hipster things I've ever seen. Every song is some indie guitar strumming ballad. Every piece of art, every character design, nearly every shot in every cutscene bleeds "LOOK AT ME I'M COMPLEX AND RELATABLE." Perhaps this is just my subjective reaction to the director's vision, but I think the game lacks any semblence of subtlety when it comes to its world. If you enjoy that subculture, this game is probably heaven, but if you're not a fan of bands you've never heard of and dank modern slang then this game has a lot of cringeworthy moments. Even the non hipster characters are shallow and cliche. Every adult in this game is blockheaded and unhelpful (EXCEPT FOR THE DREAMBOAT HIPSTER PHOTOGRAPHY TEACHER OMG SO DREAMY). You would swear that this game was written by a 16 year old girl who is moving from that awkward transition from emo 15 year old to hipster 17 year old (which also, by no small coincidence, perfectly describes our protagonist).
Overall, the game did provide about the same amount of entertainment as a 4 episode arc of an average anime, so I can at least give it credit for not being a complete waste of money. Whether or not it is actually worth continuing is something I will still have to consider. I probably will keep playing as the story and gameplay have intrigued me enough to want to know what happens to these mediocre characters.

Life is Strange is one of those rare experiences that was once thought possible only in the pages of unlauded literature or on the celluloid flicker of some low-key movie that you happened upon solely by chance or recommendation. The game taken at face value seems to offer little new, and it is easy to dismiss Life is Strange as simply another indie.
Don't make that mistake.
Life Is Strange is a deeply personal experience. It is the story of a few people, a few choices and the consequences born from those. Also reversing time.
Right from the start Life Is Strange puts you into a world in motion. Events are already underfoot, disasters on the horizon that cannot be stopped and that may only be, with the very best of luck, endured cast long shadows.  Posters of a missing girl adorn walls, vicious teenagers eagerly await the slightest provocation to lash out at you, and the obligatory psychotic school bully is packing heat and is out for blood. It is sex and psychopaths and pregnancies all wrapped into the sort of story John Green might write after a marathon of Back to the Future and a lost bet.
Life Is Strange is a non-combat experience and progress is made by solving puzzles and having conversations. The unique mechanic at play here is your ability to turn back time. More than once did I play through a series of events only to rewind time to find a better way to do things. Struggling with a dilemma does not get easier when you can see both events spiral out to different circumstances. Do you accept this version, or will you reverse time again to make it better? Is doing the right thing now worth the consequences it will have tomorrow? Can you truly save anyone at all? Is there even a right thing anymore?
In short, Life Is Strange is a remarkable experience. It is one of the few games I have enjoyed wholeheartedly. It is by far the greatest non-combat game I have ever played and is well worth sinking about an hour of your time into. The writing is superb and the progression of gameplay feels comfortable and well paced. The only drawback to an otherwise pristine experience is the frankly abysmal lip-syncing, and as far as smudges go that is hardly game breaking.
Experience it right now.

I have a soft spot for narrative-driven games.
Games like these are usually auto-buys for me. The moment I discovered Life is Strange, I was interested. However, after reading many (not entirely inaccurate) reviews that described the game as "Hipster Girl Simulator 2015" and "Feminazi Soapbox Visual Novel: 3D", I ended up putting my wallet away and pushing the game back onto my wishlist for another day.
Well, that day came, and I was finally in the right mood to give the game a chance. Long story short, I'll probably be buying the season pass.
You play as a young girl named Max who has just started attending a private photography school. Early in the game, she gains the ability to rewind time (à la Prince of Persia).
This mechanic is
interesting in narrative situations than in the action scenes of PoP. In a fight, rewinding time acts as little more than an extra life or a continue. In a narrative situation, the possibilities are more complex. You can ask people questions and snoop through their stuff, then rewind time and retain the knowledge gained without having actually performed those actions in your current timeline. This allows you to know things without others knowing that you know, which can give you the upper hand in conversation and future decision-making.
Additionally, rewinding time doesn't affect your own body, so you can move to a new spot before you start rewinding and essentially 'teleport' yourself, or be in multiple places at once (sort of).
Max is a sweet girl and a believable character. A lot of people have described her as an emo hipster. Both of those labels could certainly apply to her, but so could many others. There can be a lot more to her than that but, since you are in control, your own choices are what really shape who she is.
The only character that is really grating to me is
. Her character is basically Hot Topic in human form. She's supposed to be "edgy", but to me she's really just whiny and annoying. She smokes pot, wears "anarchy" shirts and listens to "hardcore punk" music that is really just yawn-worthy garbage. She has her reasons for being the way she is, but I still can't stand her. I hope either she develops quickly into something better, or the player is given the opportunity to shun her.
Time travel mechanic is way cool,
just a gimmick. Max is definitely a hipster, but self-aware and well rounded => it's okay. Chloe is an annoying personification of Hot Topic. Looking forward to episode 2.

Pros:
+Unique mechanic of rewinding time
Because everyone save-scums and tries all the options in choose-your-adventure games. Rewinding gives you and your character valuable information, and a chance to change your decisions. However, the consequences of your choices are pretty unpredictable, and the fact that you can't rewind *that* far back is a good way to reinforce the message of 'your choice matters'.
+Beautiful visuals, although strangely it's taxing on my laptop even though the graphics look somewhat simple. Players with good rigs shouldn't have any problems, and the visual style is pretty unique.
+You're not always in the right
You may try to do good, but others may not take it too kindly. A negative action may save you in the future. This kind of ambiguity makes the story and your choices more interesting.
Cons:
- Somewhat clunky interface
- Awkward dialogue at times. Who says 'uber cool' in daily conversation?

I really enjoyed how this game played.  The music is the biggest highlight of the first episode, I think.  While there wasn't anything too intensely exciting about this episode, I wasn't really expecting it on what is essentially a pilot.  There's a lot of foreshadowing and mystery, and I'm really looking forward to watching every character grow, especially Max and Chloe (and Chloe's father, strangely enough).
There are a lot of seemingly obvious choices I've had to make that made me think twice and thrice, just because I know it will affect the future episodes.  It really shed some light on and allowed me to empathize with "dumb" choices I've watched people make in my real life experience.
The only complaint I have is the lip-syncing.  It's terrible and just seems lazy.  Since I'm playing a story, I'm (pretty much solely) relying on dialog AND visuals.  Because they fail to mesh, my immersion was broken at times.  I don't know what the excuse is for this but I would be happy to hear/read it.
With that aside, I definitely recommend this game.

Life is Strange is a fantastic game that definitely isn’t for everybody. If you’re strictly into first-person shooters or games overflowing with action and noise, LiS isn’t for you. If you’re into deep, interesting, immersive, and emotionally-charged gaming experiences, however, Life is Strange is perfect.
If you’ve played Telltale’s The Walking Dead or The Wolf Among Us, you’ve already got a pretty good idea of what Life is Strange’s gameplay is like. The controls are simple and intuitive; for the most part, you’re only using them to walk around and point-and-click at specific people, places, and/or objects to investigate or interact with them. LiS also features beautiful graphics and a gorgeous soundtrack consisting mainly of alternative music reminiscent of Alt-J.
But of course, Life is Strange’s best and strongest feature is its story. From Episode 1, it’s almost impossible not to be drawn into the life of Max Caulfield, an 18-year-old photography student who inexplicably finds herself gifted with the ability to turn back time. Max’s rewind ability is the driving point of the game, allowing the player to explore the immediate outcomes of almost every action and choice they make. Full of doubts about how you handled a situation? Make a bad first impression? Don’t get the desired outcome? Rewinding a few seconds or minutes solves all those problems and more, and the player is given ample opportunity to use, test, and exploit Max’s powers.
Of course, that’s not all Life is Strange is about. By the end of episode 1, players have plenty of pressing questions to answer and mysteries to solve. Where did Max’s time-turning powers come from? What happened to Rachel Amber, a fellow student who’s been missing for six months? What’s with the eerie, frightening nightmares Max keeps having about a terrible storm destroying the town? The following four episodes work to add to and answer those questions while simultaneously introducing new ones to deepen the plot and keep player’s interests high. The characters are (for the most part) realistic and complex; I found myself caring about and empathizing with Max’s friends and enemies alike. That emotional connection was especially deep with Max and her best friend Chloe, the game’s two main characters. Even if the story doesn’t interest you a whole lot, I’m willing to bet your attachment to Max and the citizens of Arcadia Bay will be enough to keep you playing.
TL;DR: Life is Strange is a deep, interesting, immersive, and emotionally-charged game with great music, beautiful graphics, and complex characters. At least buy and play through the first episode; it's only 2-3 hours long, and if the game isn't for you, you'll know by the time you've finished episode 1.

Life is Strange Episode 1 is a beautiful game with a super engaging story that keeps me interested the entire time. The choices make you sweat because they both seem like good ideas, and Max's responses to them make you want to go back and change it no matter what you pick. That has never happened in a game before, or at least none that I've played, and it's a fascinating idea to have the main character question her every move to make you want to try out everything. Very mild spoilers in my review.
It feels good to be in a high school setting that shows the real struggles of teenagers, as well as the bonds the movies never really care to show. The characters do follow some tropes, but they also have extra elements that make them different than their cookie-cutter counterparts. I know some people may not see this at first, you just have to dig a little deeper, which is what makes the game fun. I highly appreciate the rewind option because I'm a habitual save file reloader when I mess up. The mechanic of time travel is given to you early on in the game with no explanation, so I look forward to the big reveal, as well as the "giant tie in that brings every plot in the game together." I honestly have no true idea how it'll be resolved and that's INCREDIBLE if done correctly. Bear in mind, it's only episode one.
I only hope the developer doesn't send us down common trope lane, such as "the teacher did it" or whatever. So far though the game has been very good with both keeping me very relaxed between walking around scenes and very on edge when the situation is intense. I truly worry about my choices, even though I know I can just replay it.
My one "complaint" might be the lingo the teenagers use, but then again I said weird stuff in high school too! I suppose the only real "ugh really?" moment would be, when put in dire situations, Chloe still uses the term "hella."
All in all, great beginning to a hopefully great series! I hope my review helps!

Good aspects:
+Story: It's a movie worth plot and story. A complex combination of supernatural features with the life of a common 18-year-old teenager. A perfect balance of crazy and not-so-crazy.
+Voice acting: Amazingly immersed voice actors, with the voices matching each character perfectly. Improves the enjoyability of the story immensively. Additionally, Max's voice is incredibly cute.
+Graphics: Who says you need photorealistic graphics to make a good game? Brushstroke-esque graphic style is still just as good and quite a breath of fresh air.
+Characters complexity: Every character is more complex than they first appear, each one having a mysterious but still rich background and a personality that makes it impossible to reduce them to archetypal school youngsters.
+Dialogue and text writing: You really feel the emotions in the writing, texts and dialogues are written in a way that matches the character's personality. Security guard is strict and talks with correct grammar, teenage students write and speak with modern common terms and vices (e.g. using the word "literally" and "totally" in almost every sentence, using modern terms like "selfie", "twerking" and with your fair share of swear words).
+Soundtrack: The ambient soundtracks fit incredibly well with the situation, in fact it almost makes the situation. And the indie-band songs are fantastic.
+Story driven: A surprisingly large amount of things are marked as having consequences. The smallest thing you do may cause ripples that you would never expect.
Bad aspects:
-Lip sync: This is probably one of the things that annoyed me the most, to the point where I avoided looking at characters' mouths as much as I could. I really didn't want to use such adjectives but... the lip syncing in this game is horrible, the lips don't follow the words at all (e.g. they would say something with the letter "o" but their mouths would be wide as in saying "a", they may be saying "you" but if you had to guess you'd probably guess they said "what"),
And the worst part is that even after they finish their sentences their lips keeps moving for a couple seconds. It doesn't sound like much but it's really noticeable.
If I didn't know better I'd say this was made for another language altogether and just dubbed over.
-Player locks: For a game that advertises as "revolutionizing choice and consequence games, and using time rewind to let you redo and explore your other choices", this game sure has its fair share of player locks. In a very large amount of conversations, you're two choices are basically the exact same thing with different wording, which doesn't allow you to mold Max's personality in the slightest bit. I know she has a background and isn't supposed to be made from scratch, but I was expecting a little bit more "paragon & renegade" as in Mass Effect, just a little.
And the time rewind isn't lock-free either. You can only rewind a short amount of time, about 1 or 2 previous actions. Right at the beginning of the game it says that "if you leave this area you won't be able to rewind to this time", well I was expecting to rewind more than just a couple minutes.
Also, the game doesn't allow a lot of exploration, as you progress in the quest line you visit some places and you can only explore them in that moment, once you leave it you can't go back.
And as a personal suggestion, it'd be really nice if we had a button to go into camera mode or something, so we can take pictures of anything we want and review them later in Max's mural. Embrace our inner photographer right?
-Hand-holding: This isn't a really big issue, but I just think the game would be more enjoyable and immersive if there weren't the two messages "This action will have consequences" and "You learned something you might use". Let the player figure it out by themselves, take a little more action in the game and use their heads to figure out if something might be influential later or if the info they got can be used for something. Besides, if a player doesn't know when an action might or might not have consequences, they'll just treat every action consequential, which is good. You get more immersed and take more care in what you say.
All in all, 9/10 would chew my arm off in anxiety again as I wait for episode 2, such intense cliffhangers will keep me awake all night!

Life is Strange Review
Story-rich game genre has become a trend in recent years, and this game, Life is Strange, could be considered as one of the mainstream. I myself feel surprised, however, that Square Enix has an eye on this genre and takes a big risk to open the new market internationally, and I hope Square Enix would pay off. This review here is not about the ‘yeah-or-neh’, but more on what I have perceived after playing the 1st chapter of this series. More review considering later chapters will be provided in the future.
The story involves Maxine, a teenager girl in photographic department of Blackwell Academy, who discovered that she has the power to rewind time. Initially, she used her power just for some trivial matters, such as manipulating her friends or using it for her advantage. However, as she began to get used to her power, she understand that she then needed it to deal with a big premonition she foresees, or not … (after this, no further spoiler given.)
It sounds cliché’, doesn’t it? A geek girl, with teenager’s problems, and adolescent frustration, given a superpower like a superhero. It is like reading a YA fiction plus a commercial fantasy fiction (if applying my field of literacy into this game), and I almost give a ‘meh’ to this kind of plot. Nevertheless, I decided to buy the first chapter as the trial for the gameplay, and, surprisingly, I found this game more fascinating in many points, from the characters, game mechanic, to OST presented in this game.
The first thing is about characters. Though somehow they look stereotypical, they still give the atmosphere of school life very well; school with many kinds of students: nerds, geeks, b-tches, bullies, and so on, living together in the same environment. This way, in order to get us into the story, apart from letting us interact with characters through Max’s point of view, we can understand them even more, even slightly, through Max’s diary, which seems to be overlooked by average gamers. For example, we may know that Victoria, a total b-tch, is treating other friends quite poorly, we can grasp her information linking to Nathan, a total gangster, through Max’s diary as well. As a quiet girl, diary is a medium for her to express what she feels, and this game takes the advantage of this element sustainably, of Max's characteristic as being a geek, with no sense of too extreme introvert or extrovert behaviour.
The second feature to discuss is the selling point of this game, time-rewinding mechanic. Many people may complain on this game being too simple, to some extent I don’t say disagree, but I beg to differ; time-traveling mechanic is the special case for this simplicity. It is like we can reflect what we did and make an instant comparison to the other alternative after we reverse the time. This is an interesting method to demonstrate the plot progression in an interesting way. In other games where consequences affect the whole plot, this mechanic gives us what I might call ‘trial and error’; we may be able to see the upcoming results of the each choice, but that is not the whole story: we can never totally expect the outcome only based on what we see through ‘short-term’ time traveling power of Max’s. This illustrates the concept, if I would need to say, of irony –or specifically ambiguity, which constructs the new attractive feature to this game, taking it closer to game with artistic elements.
Yet, in terms of gaming experience, explore-and-click progress might not please many people who long for exciting, action experience. Rather, this might satisfies those who prefer more story-focus attempt. Story-rich genre never needs too complex mechanic, if I need to make a voice of comment, but it needs to let players keep focus on the story itself without making it too boring to follow. Looking to this game, personally, this attempt is not in vein; I still feel I can follow the story through separated situations despite no amusing or fantastic events happening. Like I said, it’s more like watching a series where we can participate and define the choice and consequences for our own sake. However, puzzles during exploration is nothing special and they need more implemented tactics in order to drive this game to be ‘not totally boring –with something to do on the way’.
Lastly, coming to the most impressive one, I can say, this game contains good OSTs which creates appropriate mood and feeling of being teenagers. I’m not a total pro in music but I can sense that everything offered in OSTs are in harmony –lyrics, tuning, rhythm. They are so moving that I can think back to my personal experience during adolescent years after listening to the songs. Nothing more to say for the music. (If more touching OSTs are added in later chapters, that would be very perfect!)
Conclusion
I may not be able to say that everyone should try playing this game since individuals may have different gaming taste, but I would like to suggest those who enjoy story-rich games to come and try this game for themselves as Life is Strange makes a new slice-of-life to this genre through a very simple way –like Max’s seemingly ordinary life turning into a long and compelling story here.
Score 8.5/10

The story and characters are presented in very broad strokes, so it is up to the user to acually play the game. If the user is presented with a stereotypical character and accepts them as such, then the character is indeed two dimensional (the same holds for the story.) If the user is willing to apply some imagination as well as some effort to look beyond, they will be rewarded with quite a few moments hinting at much more.
Hearing questionable dialog in a game usually shows that the developers are trying too hard to present the character a certain way. What if a silly phrase is not an attempt of the developers to show a character to BE tough, but rather, is a character that is trying to put on a front of being tough or mature?
'Life is Strange' is not a well tread path amoung games and is still a conceptually new style for game design. The use of such well done body language to convey ideas in a subtle manner worked quite well for me, although the lip-syncing is off.
- dialog gives an ambiance that is quirky lending to a non-scripted feel,
- painted textures adds a graphic novel like effect to the visuals,
- setting ambiguity gives a hazy timeframe that can be described as nowish,
All of the above except the lip-sync, seem to be design choices which fit together very well for an exceptional gaming experience.
I would highly recommend this title to anyone who is willing to play with it.

It's strange how this will be the first review I ever write for a game. I always thought it would be written for a game like Fallout, Elderscrolls or some huge open world survival horror. And yet it's this little piece of art that has me aching to write something, if only for a minute.
When I had finished this, a few minutes ago, I couldn't believe that they only charge a pittence for it. I thought to myself that if people can charge you 70 euro for games that are poorly executed and badly made from start to finish, then this game should have a much higher pricetag. It wasn't before looking up and seeing that I just finished the first episode in a mere three hours that I understood their reasoning. I feel, however, obliged to tell you all that the three hours spent in this game were worth more to me than the hundreads of hours I've spent in most other games combined. Not because the story was awsome, or the graphics made me gape in awe, but rather that every single aspect of the game in combination managed to grip me and pull me in so that time became temporarily meaningless. Imagine if games held this standard. Imagine if your favorite action, your favorite adventure game or even your favorite driver had this kind of execution.
You can tell a good story in a bad way, and you can tell a bad story in a good way. The story in this game might not be the most interesting story you've ever heard, but it's good, and in the execution of it you are drawn in, captured by it, moved by it.
Most adventure games will entertain, they'll give you some ups and downs along the way, but ultimately they will feel like games.
I've never felt so fulfilled after "playing a game" as I did today. Original, beautiful and masterfully executed. I can't wait for the next episode.

Life is Strange,frankly,is by far one of the most invigorating game experiences ive had the pleasure of playing.Ever.
Equal parts angst filled teenage high school drama combines with a Walking/Talking simulator that likes to throw in gameplay mechanics from Prince of Persia:The Sands of Time.
In Life is Strange you play as Maxine Caulfield an 18 year old photography student on Scholarship at Blackwell Academy,a private school for high school seniors.
This game features a charming painterly asthetic faintly reminiscent of Team Fortress 2.
The gameplay will definitely remind you of Gone Home as there is heavy interaction with the enviroment as that's a major chunk of gameplay,Coupled with talking to the many unique NPC's.Which is a marvel all on it's as every NPC is an actual character not just a expressionless bystander like in several other games.i need to bring up the enviroment as I haven't seen anything quite reminiscent of it since Rockstar's Bully.The attention to detail is phenomenal.There is a bevy of popculture refrences in this game often times talking about real life artists.as well as more topical things like Akira and The Twilight Zone.Ive sad alot of nice stuff about this game but one of the minor errors is the lip sync.It's off slightly but it didnt ruin my experience with this game so it shouldnt for you.
Overall this game is only $5.00 per episode with 5 episodes over all which is an amazing price.
SO I GIVE LIFE IS STRANGE A 9.5* out of 10.

I want to start by saying that I really enjoyed this first episode of what shapes as an excellent gaming saga.  By far my most played game is dota 2, which proabably tells you something of my proclivities, and to be honest I'm not entirely sure why I picked up this title, but I'm glad I did.
Although a lot of fun, it was not without its flaws which I'll cover first because I want to close with the good stuff.
Some of the negative reviews have pointed out how linear the storyline is.  This is not something that overly concerned me because content thats heavily story driven has a tendency to follow along a linear path in order to maintain cohesiveness.  However, I did feel that there was a lack of opportunity to make a real difference through my actions.  Perhaps this is a symptom of first episode syndrome, given the impact of our choices here wont play out until later in the story.  Either way, there was definitely a lack of opportunity for player driven creativity in episode one.  We were very much funnelled down a narrow path.
Another criticism is the cast of heavily stereotyped characters.  The creative loner coming out of her shell.  The depressed pot head struggling with family problems.  The rich kid bully who gets away with whatever they want.  The ♥♥♥♥♥y queen bee.  The general uselessness of the adults.  Again, perhaps they're setting the characters up deliberately as stereotypes in the opening episode so they can introduce sublety and nuance later on.  Too early to judge.
Third and final criticism is the mostly excellent graphics, which looked extremely plasticy and weird during the storm sequences.
Onto the good stuff then.  First and foremost is the fantastic atmosphere generated, complimented by the pacing of the story.  The slow reveal works really well here because the world of Arcadia Bay is a rich and detailed one that you're happy to take your time exploring.  The graphics, and in particular the lighting (barring the storm sequences), makes each environment feel extremely authentic.  The sense of immersion was almost unparalleled.
The story itself was intreguing, with just enough mystery and teaser to leave me unhappy that we have to wait so long for the next episode, but subtle enough that you dont feel like they're using cheap emotional trickery to get people to reup.  The moral choices were nicely ambiguous, with no overt black and white.  For the most part the dialogue was solid, and well acted by the voice talent.
Inspite of their stereotypical nature, I liked all of the core characters we encountered and look forward to spending more time with them.  I'm particularly interested in seeing how Max's character develops and hope that I can play a part in determining the direction of that in future episodes through my choices in game.
Overall, this game is a must play for anyone who has an interest in the episodic/story driven gaming genre, and I would recommend it to all you dota players who're burned out after your latest loss and looking for a change of pace to recharge your batteries (which is everyone, lets be honest).

The story and characters are presented in very broad strokes, so it is up to the user to acually play the game. If the user is presented with a stereotypical character and accepts them as such, then the character is indeed two dimensional (the same holds for the story.) If the user is willing to apply some imagination as well as some effort to look beyond, they will be rewarded with quite a few moments hinting at much more.
Hearing questionable dialog in a game usually shows that the developers are trying too hard to present the character a certain way. What if a silly phrase is not an attempt of the developers to show a character to BE tough, but rather, is a character that is trying to put on a front of being tough or mature?
'Life is Strange' is not a well tread path amoung games and is still a conceptually new style for game design. The use of such well done body language to convey ideas in a subtle manner worked quite well for me, although the lip-syncing is off.
- dialog gives an ambiance that is quirky lending to a non-scripted feel,
- painted textures adds a graphic novel like effect to the visuals,
- setting ambiguity gives a hazy timeframe that can be described as nowish,
All of the above except the lip-sync, seem to be design choices which fit together very well for an exceptional gaming experience.
I would highly recommend this title to anyone who is willing to play with it.

Well I'm very disappointed... Life is Strange is a character-driven game in which the story supposedly changes according to the player's actions. In addition to this existing interesting concept, it brings a new feature into choose your own adventure, with the player character Max being able to reverse time to change choices in-story while still retaining knowledge, items etc. Mix that with a setting allowing for easily relatable young characters and it's a recipe for success. Unfortunately, the output somehow ended up as "meh."
The key problem with this game? Everybody in it is a ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Even the player character Max. Part of her backstory involves her abandoning her best friend for 5 years without making any contact, during a time in which said best friend, Chloe was going through a very hard time. Max constantly makes excuses for why she was avoiding Chloe, regardless of the player's dialogue options. I can't relate at all to this character, this isn't just a passing mention, it's an aspect of her backstory that is major and is brought up constantly.
But then do I feel for Chloe? Nope. Maybe five years ago I would've. She lost all likability to me when she tried to make Max take the blame for something she did herself, then gets angry at Max for not playing along. Oh and this was after Max saved her life. And in this game all about how your choices matter, Max constantly regrets the decision and says she should've chosen differently.
There's Warren, I think his name is, a good friend of Max's. However in all his attempts to be edgy, he lost any respect from me by trying to make Max watch Cannibal Holocaust. Real animals were filmed being killed for that film. Unfortunately I made a dialogue choice that was positive due to very confusing context making me think it was negative, and this one time I wasn't allowed to reverse. Every other character barely appears or is intended to be seen as an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
There is also way too much "puzzle solving" instead of getting on with the story or optional communication. Why do I have to spend 5 minutes dicking around with a washing machine that some tools are on top of, instead of just climbing up on to the desk right next to it and reaching up? What exactly was added to the story or characters by spending 5 minutes dicking around with a washing machine?
I wanted to like this, I really did. Story-driven, multiple choices, a female protagonist, interesting concept... but a lack of real choice, annoying puzzles and above all,  the game could've still been good if not for this factor, insufferable goddamn characters. Yeah, characters should be flawed but the creators went so overboard that none of these people are remotely likable. And I can't even like who I'm playing as! It's a risky move giving the player character of such a game a flaw and the flaw didn't pay off in this case, perhaps because of how specifically explained the flaw was. I hate to use a game that was ruined by its sequel as an example, but The Walking Dead handled the concept of a player character with an unchangeable flaw well. Vague details here and there, but the overall idea of what he did is still prominent.
Unfortunately, nothing about this game managed to truly pull me in. I don't see any reason to purchase the other episodes. I'm not looking forward to anything that'll happen, as I don't care about any of these people in the slightest.

Life is Strange is different from your average everyday game; it is set within a typical American high school setting with added time travel, and manages to pull this off remarkably well. While some may find some of the characters cliché, this is no different from how students are represented within everyday media. This does result in a number of what could be considered “cringe worthy moments”, but if anything this adds to the believability of the setting as, if you school days were anything like mine, your know this is the norm of this environment.
The game is influenced by titles such as the walking dead, gone home and heavy rain, and players of those games will certainly be able to see their influence here. The main innovation that this game brings is in the form of its time travel mechanic. Through this players can rewind time to change their choices or actions, basing your decisions on how charters react. However there is limit to how far you can travel back; once you leave an area your decisions are fixed meaning you are only able to see the short turn consequences of your actions. This can make choices tricky, and this difficulty is increased by there not necessarily been a correct choice to take. The rewinding time mechanic also adds some intriguing puzzles into the game which give a good impression of the advantages of been able to see into the future. While they are all fairly straight forward in this first chapter, I am hoping that the concept will be extended and built upon in the future chapters.
One thing I must mention is that this game has an excellent soundtrack and the way that it is included within the game is excellent. Rather then been played at random, the creators managed to make it so that most of the soundtrack is played through the actions of your character and this adds to the experience immensely.  The opening scene gives a wonderful example of this, and it is something I hope to see in more games.
Sadly the game does have a number of flaws; prime among them is that the lip-synching is awful to the point of almost been non-existent in places. Whenever this will be improved in future chapters I do not know, but I hope so as it takes something away from the otherwise beautifully crafted atmosphere. Another is that I did not find the controls that user friendly at times; with the mouse movements on clicked objects feeling sluggish I would definitely recommend increasing the sensitivity. However if you can look past these flaws there is a gem of a game here which I feel it will certainly provide ideas to take away and think about once the final chapter is done.

If you've played any of the Telltale Games adventure/story games, then you'll be very familiar with many of the mechanics here. With that said, Life Is Strange does a great job improving on those mechanics, while also introducing some nice intuitive new ones to drive the time-manipulation gameplay, and further offer freedom of decision making for the player. Where I think this game excels, even beyond Telltale's games, is in giving the player a very dense gameworld to explore. Each environment, no matter how small or large, is packed with interactive or inspectable elements that either add to the story, present minor or major choices, or simply flesh out the world and make it feel that much more alive.
Some hokey dialogue and exaggerated colloquialisms aside, the many characters, both main and minor, are all interesting and believable, keeing the game feeling grounded in reality, while still packing on a healthy dose of science fiction.
Definitely recommend to anyone who likes one or more of Telltale's adventure game series, and even to those who didn't. The game uses a lot of the same mechanics, but the difference in tone and presentation of the characters and story may mean you'll like this even if you didn't get into one of the Telltale games.

Life Is Strange is and interesting and beautiful game that stands out amoung many other titles thta you will find. You play as Max, a young woman who discovers that she can control time and must figure out what the visions she is having mean.
Positives-
The game has very beautiful visuals and a soundtrack that fits the games atmosphere. It really is refreshing to see a game that has this sort of aesthetic to it, it feels like something that you could experience in a movie or in everyday life.
What I found interesting about this game is that with Max's ability to control time you can undo certain choices that you made and say new information that you have discovered from the previous conversation. However your choices, as the game reminds you, do have consequences so you must decide which choice you would like to go through with.
My favorite thing about this game, however is the two main characters: Max and Chloe. They are such interesting characters and their chemistry really helps set up the tone in the game. I love the relationship these two have and I hope that the game can further develop it in future episodes. Also I'm very happy to see that the two main protagonists are woman, in the gaming industry you rarely see the main character actually being a woman and it makes me excited to see developers branch out from the gaming norms.
Negatives-
On the downside, the game tries to use teenage lingo and it comes off as incredibly cringe worthy. Please do not have the main character of your game say, "Man are you cereal?" or have the punk character say, "bidness" instead of business. It just comes across as awkward and takes me out of the game when 18 year-olds are talking like 12 year-olds.
Another problem I have is when the game really wants you to get close to someone to talk to them, you have to stand at a very specific areas to talk to them and while you do get used to it's really annoying having to rub up against them in order to talk to them.
Overall-

If you've played any of the Telltale Games adventure/story games, then you'll be very familiar with many of the mechanics here. With that said, Life Is Strange does a great job improving on those mechanics, while also introducing some nice intuitive new ones to drive the time-manipulation gameplay, and further offer freedom of decision making for the player. Where I think this game excels, even beyond Telltale's games, is in giving the player a very dense gameworld to explore. Each environment, no matter how small or large, is packed with interactive or inspectable elements that either add to the story, present minor or major choices, or simply flesh out the world and make it feel that much more alive.
Some hokey dialogue and exaggerated colloquialisms aside, the many characters, both main and minor, are all interesting and believable, keeing the game feeling grounded in reality, while still packing on a healthy dose of science fiction.
Definitely recommend to anyone who likes one or more of Telltale's adventure game series, and even to those who didn't. The game uses a lot of the same mechanics, but the difference in tone and presentation of the characters and story may mean you'll like this even if you didn't get into one of the Telltale games.
