Life Is Strange is and interesting and beautiful game that stands out amoung many other titles thta you will find. You play as Max, a young woman who discovers that she can control time and must figure out what the visions she is having mean.
Positives-
The game has very beautiful visuals and a soundtrack that fits the games atmosphere. It really is refreshing to see a game that has this sort of aesthetic to it, it feels like something that you could experience in a movie or in everyday life.
What I found interesting about this game is that with Max's ability to control time you can undo certain choices that you made and say new information that you have discovered from the previous conversation. However your choices, as the game reminds you, do have consequences so you must decide which choice you would like to go through with.
My favorite thing about this game, however is the two main characters: Max and Chloe. They are such interesting characters and their chemistry really helps set up the tone in the game. I love the relationship these two have and I hope that the game can further develop it in future episodes. Also I'm very happy to see that the two main protagonists are woman, in the gaming industry you rarely see the main character actually being a woman and it makes me excited to see developers branch out from the gaming norms.
Negatives-
On the downside, the game tries to use teenage lingo and it comes off as incredibly cringe worthy. Please do not have the main character of your game say, "Man are you cereal?" or have the punk character say, "bidness" instead of business. It just comes across as awkward and takes me out of the game when 18 year-olds are talking like 12 year-olds.
Another problem I have is when the game really wants you to get close to someone to talk to them, you have to stand at a very specific areas to talk to them and while you do get used to it's really annoying having to rub up against them in order to talk to them.
Overall-
I fully recommended this game, it has a few faults but they are mostly minor and do not take away from the positive factors in the game. I look forward to seeing the rest of what this game has to offer in later episodes.

Published by Square Enix and made by a studio that has showed - with this release- that they have a vision that they wish to pursue despite adversity. I'll gladly support them.

The writers and gamemakers of the studio were told with their first game 'Remember Me' that publishers didn't want to adopt it because it had a female action protaganist and time-warping mechanics. The game did above average.

This time with Life is Strange, they are showing determination with a female character and time-warp mechanics. They realized some issues with gameplay, story, progression, and experience with Remember Me, and the reviews are showing that they are addressing this.

It isn't a AAA by any means, the entire game series is only a fraction of a full releases when it isn't on sale, and it is on sale very often right now even though the first episode has only been out for a few weeks.

Aggressive support from Square Enix with a statement that they are pursuing a very agressive online distribution strategy (along with physical console copies) has shown a lot of fruits.

Finished the first episode in about 3 hours. Not bad. Not perfect, but not bad at all. The biggest thing I can say about it is how realistic it feels in characters, discussions, demeanor, and conversational language. They are some of the most 3D sub characters I have ever seen written. They do have main personalities, but also carry out a subtle archetype to their personalities that very few games can delve into. An example being that despite there being cliques and different groups, that they can still talk to 'the others' and be half-friends with them. They all reacted in realistic manners that I could feel from the tension that were created in situations X Y and Z. Even better, there is a scene where they talk about, and show, a flash drive with pirated movies/content.

Overall, the professional reviews and user reviews are both spot on. The 5/5 user reviews are mainly in support of how refreshing Life is Strange is to the genre while the approx 75+% rating on professional sites does show that it still needs a bit fleshing out.

This review is a NON spoiler. I would hate to ruin the story for you, so I shall avoid that at all costs so you can thoroughly enjoy this game!
Life Is Strange is an incredibly charming, narrative driven point and click game that captures teenage angst at it's greatest. Playing the role of Max Caulfield, an anxiety ridden student that persues her dream in Photography... albeit not so confidently. She quickly finds herself in a very unfriendly situation and realizes she posesses more abilities than she knows about...
One of my favourite things about Life Is Strange is the crazy amount of effort that went into the multiple choices. Going back and choosing each one because of how unsure the character makes you feel with the dialogue after you've committed something supposedly bad. There are so many small steps you can alter with each choice, it's amazing!
Secondly, the voice acting in Life Is Strange suprised me. It's really, really good! You may think "eh, Max sounds quite monotone" but for me, that captures her personality and how she perceives her school life/anxiety. I think they did a great job with casting and the script.
The game has a very beautiful art style. I love the lighting of the game, it's so gorgeous. I love the simplicity of the games art as well. It's not trying to be super detailed, it's trying to be artistic and emotional IMO and it shows. Having only played 1 out of the 5 parts of this game thus far, I feel I need to first note that I've seen a few promising starts in video games go down the tubes by the time you get to the end. In that regard, "Life Is Strange" is quite capable of  letting us down. It has mysterious and fantastic elements which, while excellent for drawing the crowds in at the beginning, will really demand some great writing later on in order for us to feel satisfied with the way they've been used by the end. Some games give us intriguing beginnings such as this, yet eventually begin to feel too convoluted to enjoy, or that their fantasy elements feel so "tacked on" by the end that they become all but meaningless.
That being said, what I've seen of "Life Is Strange" thus far gives me no cause to doubt that these developers are giving us a memorable, staisfying and perhaps even life changing experience, piece by piece.
Part 1 delivers us a wonderfully character-driven story filled with intrigue, drama, thrills and so much depth. It's immersive as hell - you can't help but feel like you really are Max every second your playing this game, living her dramas, reliving her old memories and agonizing over her impossible "no right answer" dillemmas. The rest of the cast of characters are so unique, believable and well fleshed out. This would have to be the most impressive aspect of the game, thus far.
Gameplay-wise, "Life Is Strange" is more an "interactive movie" then a traditional computer game. Most of the game revolves around handling social interactions in just the right way to produce the outcome your most happy to live with (bad choices will come back to haunt you, apparently), but that being said, there are plenty of practical puzzles to keep old-school gamers who were reared on "Myst", ect happy. Without dropping any spoilers, the way the game handles time is an enjoyable little innovation, though perhaps gluttons for a challenge might think it makes the puzzles too easy.
Stylistically, this game reminded me of "Alan Wake". Though it's nowhere near as gothic (yet!), certain elements like the geography, vague supernatural elements that only afflict the protagonist, use of music and especially the turbulent fantasy segments involving creepy lighthouses just made this game feel like it was a child - or some other relative - of "Alan Wake"'s.
One thing I really have to complement about this game is the visual style. Even though the graphics aren't photo-realistic, there is real and constant beauty in the look of this game - especially in it's use of light. But more then simply being pretty, the visual style of "Life Is Strange" is also brilliant, as the outer beauty of "Arcadia Bay" is in stark contrast to much of the ugliness and unhappiness that hides behind it. You can't help but notice how these two elements of the game clash and you just know that this isn't happening by accident. Small wonder that we also find ourselves with a "plain" protagonist who is actually quite beautiful where it counts, and a "beautiful" villainess who is ugly and cold on the inside. You can't judge any books by their covers in "Life Is Strange". The fact that photography is such an important aspect of our protagonist's character also betrays the fact that "Life Is Strange"'s visual style has been very carefully managed to suit the story, by clever, diligent developers.
All in all, from what I've seen thus far, I couldn't NOT reccomend this game to anyone who loves an engrossing story-based adventure. Potential for pitfalls aside, everything I just experienced in my play-through left me thoroughly impressed.
I can't wait to see what happens next!

But more then simply being pretty, the visual style of "Life Is Strange" is also brilliant, as the outer beauty of "Arcadia Bay" is in stark contrast to much of the ugliness and unhappiness that hides behind it. You can't help but notice how these two elements of the game clash and you just know that this isn't happening by accident. Small wonder that we also find ourselves with a "plain" protagonist who is actually quite beautiful where it counts, and a "beautiful" villainess who is ugly and cold on the inside. You can't judge any books by their covers in "Life Is Strange". The fact that photography is such an important aspect of our protagonist's character also betrays the fact that "Life Is Strange"'s visual style has been very carefully managed to suit the story, by clever, diligent developers.
All in all, from what I've seen thus far, I couldn't NOT reccomend this game to anyone who loves an engrossing story-based adventure. Potential for pitfalls aside, everything I just experienced in my play-through left me thoroughly impressed.
I can't wait to see what happens next!

I bought episode 1 of this game nearly as soon as it came out, and I really enjoyed it.
Without spoiling too much, this game does an excellent job at storytelling, and making the game feel immersive while also having pretty and innovative gameplay. The rewind mechanic gets increasingly creative and complex, and it just works so well.
It's hard to criticize this game because most of the problems I have with it aren't necessarily game-breaking, but are more of nitpicky things. The writers of the game tried really hard to reach the teen audience, but what the player ends up getting is dialogue full of slang and un-used teen vernacular. In short, Life is Strange tries very hard to immulate "tumblr culture", and that is were it falls short.
Another thing worth mentioning is the lack of more intense violence. Don't get me wrong, there are some moments with guns, near death experiences, etc, but there is nothing graphic in the game. If you are looking for an experience similar to Heavy Rain, this game is nowhere near as urgent, stressful, or graphic.
Despite these minor flaws, the story is enjoyable, the graphics look beautiful on the unreal engine, and the story is full of memorable moments.
9/10, Buy it while it's on sale!

This is the first episodic game from Square that I know of, and definitley a type of game TellTale games is known for making but I'm glad to see someone else start this kind, I'd like to see them become more mainstream.
In Life is Strange you play as Max, a freshman in her new college which happens to be in the same hometown she moved away from as a preteen.  For some reason Max has discovered she has the ability to reverse time and can see visions of the future as well and you decide when is a good time to use that ability.
Basically, it's a storyline that adapts to your decisions but you can reverse time and remake your decisions if you want to. There are also a few 'puzzles' that require you to reverse time to solve. I mean really, imagine a TellTale-like game with Final Fantasy type graphics in which you could redo your choice and decide which outcome you wanna go with. It's actually pretty cool.  The only real issue I have with this game is the lip syncing to the voice actors. I hate to say it, but it sucked. They rarely lined up at all and it was really obvious.
This first episode is definitley worth five bucks if you are into this kind of game. It's a different kind of episodic game compared to TellTale and I liked that.
Overall, I give episode one 6 out of 10 stars.

So far, this game is like the perfect blend between Heavy Rain, Braid, The Last of Us (no zombies though), and even some Mass Effect. Very detailed and rich environment. There was not one set piece that wasn't thoroughly thought through (whoa, 3 'th' words). Every character is beautifully deep and complex and this game completely puts you right back into the 'everyone's trying to be cool and fit in but are secretly depressed' feeling of highschool.
The developpers have set up a complex gameplay mechanic but introduce it to you in the same way that Max, the protagonist, is discovering it. Her thoughts are your thoughts and you're experiencing everything the same way she does. I will emphasize that gameplay is very similar to Braid, though applied to situations like those in Heavy Rain. The character development seems to be approaching The Last of Us - but its presented in a style similar to Mass Effect in that conversation choices with characters will lead to different reactions and information. I also feel a bit of Mass Effect and Last of Us in the third person sequences, exploring the world, openning cupboards, listenning in on conversations, etc.
I'm really looking forward to each and every other episode. Good Stuff.

This is a great storytelling game. It's too early to tell exactly how substantial your choices are, but it hardly matters because the story is more rich than anything else I've experienced. If you like Telltale at all, you'll love Life is Strange. And, even if you don't care for Telltale, you should still check this out because it is a unique experience. SquareEnix really took some risks, but it paid off. The atmosphere and attention to detail makes the story seem plausible.
The characters are deep, interesting, and believable young adults. I fell in love with the cast right away because they all seem so delightfully human in their flaws. Each character has something to like, something to resent, something to pity. There's a ton to see and explore. Granted, most of the interactables are set pieces that trigger a thought from Max, but even those are a joy to watch because Max is an inherantly quirky and likeable girl.
Do yourself a favor and get this game. Then get it for someone you love.

Every character is beautifully deep and complex and this game completely puts you right back into the 'everyone's trying to be cool and fit in but are secretly depressed' feeling of highschool.
The developpers have set up a complex gameplay mechanic but introduce it to you in the same way that Max, the protagonist, is discovering it. Her thoughts are your thoughts and you're experiencing everything the same way she does. I will emphasize that gameplay is very similar to Braid, though applied to situations like those in Heavy Rain. The character development seems to be approaching The Last of Us - but its presented in a style similar to Mass Effect in that conversation choices with characters will lead to different reactions and information. I also feel a bit of Mass Effect and Last of Us in the third person sequences, exploring the world, openning cupboards, listenning in on conversations, etc.
I'm really looking forward to each and every other episode. Good Stuff.

This is a great storytelling game. It's too early to tell exactly how substantial your choices are, but it hardly matters because the story is more rich than anything else I've experienced. SquareEnix really took some risks, but it paid off. The atmosphere and attention to detail makes the story seem plausible.
The characters are deep, interesting, and believable young adults. I fell in love with the cast right away because they all seem so delightfully human in their flaws. Each character has something to like, something to resent, something to pity. There's a ton to see and explore. Granted, most of the interactables are set pieces that trigger a thought from Max, but even those are a joy to watch because Max is an inherantly quirky and likeable girl.
Do yourself a favor and get this game. Then get it for someone you love.

Life is Strange is extremely good interactive movie-game hybrid. It has emotionally good and bad moments, just like life. If you're considering to buy it, I recommend this game. It's entertaining and relaxing in comparison to playing AAA titles with enraged people screaming at each other all the time.
Episode 1:
The game is an entertaining high school drama viewed by 18 year old girl who's beginning to enter adult world and find her place. She discovers an extremely unique skill to impact time and roll back presumably wrong actions/decisions.
The story itself is set in school and everyday life situations that become unusual at certain points (i.e. Max's nightmare visions).
Characters could be more developed but it's somewhat sufficient to the story of the world. Graphic is quite comic, nicely optimised and runs at steady 60fps on 1080p max with 16xQCSAA (FXAA off - this crap blurs textures and image quality)
Episode 2:
Episode 2 picks up where Episode 1 leaves us. You wake up in your room at the dorm (hate the song here, especially the tiny singing voice, omg). You are dropped right into the storm. Bullying, harrasment, psychological sadism and everything else you can think of. Of course the game has lots of light moments to balance it out. The episode is better than 1st. Characters have been developed better and they are more meaningful. More decision making and most of all a situation you need to deal with without moving back the time! Great episode with compelling story.
Episode 3:
The episode picks up where the last one end. Max is well known now but that doesnt stop her from getting into and out of trouble with her best friend. This episode is so far the best one released, because you get to do things that are just unimaginable. Out of previous episodes this one has the best atmosphere and the twist at the end is highly unexpected! At least it made me jaw drop. Eitherway now it becomes clear what Max has to do in order to bring things back to normal in Episode 4. I recommend all episodes so far :D They're worth every penny.
Episodes 4-5 - to be reviewed

This is an excellent start to what I expect will be a very enjoyable series. Life is Strange: Episode 1 is a very upbeat, colourful, and fun game with a great protagonist.
Max is a relatable and likable girl who suddenly gets the power to reverse time for short periods; a power we all wish we had. This is useful for undoing mistakes, experimenting with different dialouge choices and actions, or solving simple puzzles. This mechanic has lots of potential. I hope they use it in more significant ways in future episodes.
The art style and music are both wonderful. Everything is colourful and vibrant, like a drawing. The music is one of the things I liked the most, very peaceful with a few contextual tracks. This game is ideal for those of you who are tired of dark and gritty video games and want to play something pleasant that will make them genuinely happy.
There are some problems with the dialouge though. The script has the characters saying some hilarious things that you would never hear from the mouth of a real American teenager. They use a lot of slang and 'cool' terms that just sound strange. Admittadly this gives the game a certain charm, although I suspect the writers actually think teenagers speak like this. The lip sync is also pretty bad and can sometimes break immersion.
These two problems are worth dealing with when the overall game was so enjoyable. I can't help but smile when I think of Life is Strange. Buy this game if you want to smile too :D

I'll write a full review once I've played through the whole game (all episodes).
But I'll let you know my thoughts towards this game for now:
So far Life is Strange is very atmospheric. The music/sounds are great and very fitting. The graphics aren't top notch but they have a unique and warm style to them that I really enjoy. The story so far is great and got me hooked instantly, so far it keeps me guessing and I is quite unpredictable. Although I'm not from America and I don't know what high school is like there from first hand experience, I still feel like they have captured the "high school life" feeling really well.
One thing that stands out to me are the characters. I have absolutely fallen in love with the protagonist and I'm genuinely interested in all the side characters as well.
The gameplay itself is simple and straight forward. I played the game on a keyboard but I heard it works with a controller as well.
I also love the options they have added. That you can choose certain areas from each episode and then start your game from there or play it in "Collectible Mode" which I think is a genius idea for all the achivement hunters among us that don't enjoy playing through a whole game again or mess up our original chosen path doing so.
If the following episodes continue on this path I think this game could easily be one of my favourite games of this year.

Review of episode 1.
I ended up really enjoying this game. It's a bit of teen age drama story, but the story is told in such a great way that this was hardly an issue. The different choices were well presented, and I had a hard time choosing from time to time. All though I really liked the choices, I felt like at the moment their impact is not the biggest, but I expect them to matter a lot more in the long run.
The teen age story blends in elements of the paranormal in a really fluent way. The game eases it in so it feels like Max(protagonist) is just as confused as you are. What might be a downside for some is that in order to fully know whats going on, you should read in Max's notes, presented as her notebook. You can read about different characters, you can go trough the game without reading it, and still get a feel for the characters though. However the backstory explains some details that the mainstory skips a bit over.
I expect more replayability if the choices in the first episode impacts the next ones. But episode 1 isn't that expensive, so it didn't matter a whole lot to me. For the price this was a very nice experience.

I am a huge fan of telltale's walking dead series. But the highly scripted QTEs get somewhat annoying at a certain point. I was hesitant to purchase this game because I did not want it to be the same type of story telling game as the walking dead.
I was pleasantly surprised to discover the most important mechanic in the game is something that all of us already employ with quick saves and quick loads (once you start playing for like 15 mins, you will know what I mean). It's as if the developers built an even better method for us obsessive compulsive gamers to truly perfect our choices and get the outcome that we really want.
If you have a few hours to spare for a day or two, definitely give this a go. It's pretty cheap and not high intensity, a very good experience when you just want to relax.
One negative thing I do want to mention is the interaction scheme. While it is refreshing and fun, it is a bit finicky with a mouse, but overall, it does not in any significant way take away from the experience.

Life is Strange is an amazing addition to the library, which reminds me heavily of The Walking Dead, The Wolf Among Us, Indigo Prophecy/Fahrenheit, Beyond: Two Souls and Heavy Rain. While choice and consequence play a significant role in the game, your character has the ability to reverse time and try again. This ability may seem overpowered but it isn't, considering the fact that you only have a short amount of time to reverse and many of your actions' consequences won't reveal themselves until later, when it's too late to go back and change the action.
An awesome, atmospheric title which focuses on current social topics such as teenage bullying, gender specific bullying, possible kidnapping and teen substance abuse. The game gives you a similar feeling to that of movies like Juno, which fits very well for the setting. It also maintains an awesome sci-fi/fantasy feel and if you're into photography or art, you'll get a nice history lesson on those subjects as well. There are so many different choices you can make, with each one changing the story a bit. In fact, there's one significant secret which you will only discover by acting in very specific ways. It'll be hard to have two Let's Plays play out the same.

Episode 4 (edit)
No-one can really explain the ending to episode 4, but holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ I thought episode 3 hit me hard but within the first decision in ep4, ep3 was blown out of the water. Life Is Strange tells the tale of a young photography student Max. She has just started in her new school. Things are already complicated for her but her life takes a strange twist when she gets the power to travel back in time.
Max can only rewind for a few minutes and this is also a gameplay mechanic to be used in puzzles and choices in dialogue. It's really interesting mechanic and it makes the game standout from other modern adventure games. Even though it bothers me a bit that Max always comments when time could or should be rewinded. It would be more fun to figure out these things myself. Also sometimes the story forces you in time more than just few minutes.
There's plenty of things to look at and interact with, for example posters and notes. Or you can just chill for awhile and play some guitar or sit at the fountain on the schoolyard. There are many characters you can have dialogue with, however those conversations aren't unfortunately very long. But many of the characters were really interesting with their own backstories and mysteries. When you make choices in the game, it will notify in the upright corner "this action will have consequences". Unfortunately these choices very rarely affect the game in the long run. In the end you have two choices to pick the ending from. But that being said, every choice you make is part of your personal story. You made the choice and it happened. Just because they don't affect the ending cinematic they shouldn't be disregarded. As they say, it's about the journey not the destionation.

Life is weird...
You'll probably wonder what all of the fuss is about when you first hear about this game. I can tell you with explicit confidence, this game is a journey. You are Max Caufield and you are in a zone of comfort. One day during class you realize something is missing and you want it. You enter an unfamiliar world as a time manipulator. You adapt to this new power. In a few days you get what you wanted, but you pay a heavy price for it. You return to the world you once knew long ago, changed.
This game could be a dissertation for a PHD cadidate.
If you want a feel trip, try something from Telltale. This is a game for someone who wants to know what it feels like to be ALIVE. Friendship and betrayal, love and hate, murder and rebirth, suicide and salvation: you can experience a story crafted in a world unlike any other. This game is about you.
You are the gamer and you like to play games. One day you'll want something more. You buy Life is Strange and adapt to the story driven gameplay. You'll learn to love it by the end of Episode 2 and wonder why you waited so long to buy it, but then at the end of Episode 3 you're so engulfed with the game you'll wonder how you lived without it. At the end of episode 5 you'll close out Life is Strange and return to Steam, wondering why and how games could ever surpass what Life is Strange has done for you.

If you take Life is Strange for what it is, an episodic game with a fairly compelling story so far, beautiful graphics and easy controls, you're gonna have a great time. Don't go into this expecting Telltale Games quality or storytelling.
Goods:
- stunning graphics
- simple but engaging gameplay elements
- decent voice acting
bads:
- lipsyncing is pretty much terrible
- stereotypical characters (I'd give them a couple more episodes to redeem themselves, but for now you've got the lonely hipster, the rich jocks, the b*tchy bully, the cheerleader and so on)
- cringey dialogue (I never want to hear the word 'hella' ever again)
Overall, I was entertained enough by the gameplay and available dialogue options to keep me engaged for the full episode despite a few hitches and a fairly slow start. Hopefully it picks up the pace a bit on the following episodes.

I went and took a chance, spent $20 on the 5 episodes. 100% worth it. This game is one of the most if not the most immersible game I've ever played. The game is so well thought out having the option to go back in time, having the player make the decisions. Taking the time to travel at your own pace just ties everything into the story so much more, I think I took at least an hour touching everything I could find. The more you touch the more you find out and all this is only within the first chapter! The best game I've played this year, cannot wait for the next episode. Great recommendation if you want an immersible single player game to burn hours on a few playthroughs.
Definitely. Recommended.
Episode 2 (edit)
What the hell just happened. This game just leaves me begging for more, I'm asking so many questions and that makes me want to play it even more! Only mishap for me was when the episode 1 patch came out, left disappointed not being able to play the next chapter. ;( I absolutely cannot wait for episode 3! And honestly, the wait for episode 2 was worth it, keep it up devs!
Episode 3 (edit)
Well, I don't have any idea on where this game is taking me. Episode 3 had so many big changes from what's happened in the previous episodes, really impacting. Surprises all over in Ep 3, I feel it was a bit shorter than episode 1 and 2 but the impact on what's going on is so much more. This game is changing rapidly into something bigger, can't wait to find out what happens in episode 4 just from what I've done in episode 3. The feeling of wanting to dive into the next episode is so anticipating, just wanting to see how the game changes! Soooo Goood! Cannot wait until ep. 4
What will happen next? :)
Episode 4 (edit)
No-one can really explain the ending to episode 4, but holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ I thought episode 3 hit me hard but within the first decision in ep4, ep3 was blown out of the water. Out of all the episodes this one had given me butterflies in my stomach even before the first BIG decision was made. This chapter in the story is by far the deepest one yet, and in both good and bad ways. I don't know how to explain what will happen next because the ending came so out of nowhere. I do have one theory though...
I hope everything returns as it was in the final installment, Episode 5.
Episode 5 (edit)
Ouch. You're pretty much thrown into episode 5 really quickly and you end up questioning yourself on how you go about what to do. It's definately strange, I'll give it that, but as the episode progresses and with it's more puzzle based finale, wow. This episode is probably the most in-depth in my opinion, due the the shear slap in the face you get when first playing it. The decisions you have to make though... ouch. I ended up second guessing myself and thinking constantly about what would happen after every decision. It makes you think, alot and I don't mean the 5 minute brainstorm. In all Life is Strange was something I had known nothing about at the start of the year and now It's my Game of the Year. I can't say much more other than to play the game yourself, don't go to youtube or your favourite streamer to watch it. Just do it! (Shia pun not intended) Honestly though, Life is Strange is truly a game to go down in the books. Highly Recomended! Well done Dontnot and Square-Enix!
Thanks,

At first, I wanted to keep my review like this. Two words, one line. But it's impossible.
Do you know these kind of games that lay their arm around you, pull you into a tight grip and then never let you go again? It drags you everywhere, it won't let your mind rest after playing, it wants you to know and see everything.
You might think at the start that this is just another average minor puzzle, major exploration, choice-influenced story heavy game, but believe me, this is what lifts the genre into a whole new light.
Life is Strange is THE choice-influenced story heavy game, standing out of the crowd with its brilliant writing, tricky and twisted story and characters that aren't simply good or bad.
There is never an absolute feeling of having done everything right. You will find yourself at the point of wanting to replay everything for at least a single important decision more often than you might expect. And believe me - it's worth it.
The differences of your choices carrying over into further episodes is visible, the way the other characters interacts with you and end up is based on more than just two or three things you say.
How you act defines who you are and how things will turn out in the long run.
Don't believe the impression that this was a game mainly for girls. It's not true. I have more male friends than female friends who play this and they would all agree within seconds and without hesitation.
Give this game a try, you won't regret it.

Life is Strange is a unique game. It's the most innovative game I've played since Mirrors Edge. Don't get me wrong, the two are completely different games. The only thing they have in common is Unreal Engine. Let me explain. Life is Strange is immersing, has a engaging story line, and beautiful art style. The music is very subtle, yet...memorable. I won't go into telling about what the game is about. That's what game descriptions and trailers are for.
I have completed Episode 1 and looking forward to playing the rest of them. I'm a old school gamer (myst, shadow warrior and the original unreal and original call of duty...classics) and so  I'll always enjoy shooters, rpg, strategy, etc...but sometimes, it's nice to have a breath of fresh air.
I'm not saying this is the best game you will ever play...but I highly recommend it.
The story, how you control made this  game one of really perfect games. although no real gameplay in it, but this story is fantastic.

Great story with some amazing visuals. Most of the decisions you'll have to make are pretty balanced. There are no obvious right or wrong choices. As you progress through the story, you'll begin to wonder if you made the right choices.

I really enjoy this game. It has a unique mechanic that satisfies the urge to replay important decisions without having to start the episode over, the main character has a personality that is identifiable and well written, and the plot, though starting off slow, promises to evolve in an Alan Wake sort of way. I'm digging it.
What I don't dig is the dialogue. To anyone over 20, the game's dialogue will be difficult to deal with, I imagine. With the high school setting comes the... unique way millenials talk and write.
I remember looking over the protagonist's journal, biting my lip every time my generation y tendencies to speak and write like a normal human being were interferring with developing the character as a millenial.
You could chalk it up to being poorly written, but it does bring across this odd dissonance that high school brings. Once you adjust, you'll find something you'll like here. For five dollars, it isn't bad in the slightest.
Though, millenials need to learn how to ♥♥♥♥ing write.

One of the best story/character driven games I've ever played. If you like the spirit of games like Heavy Rain, The Walking Dead (and Telltale in general), Gone Home, Beyond: Two Souls, Dreamfall, etc. then this is the game for you. In my opinion, it has done an even better job of doing what all the above games aspire to. The characters, music, atmosphere, visual style, and gameplay all just meld so beautifully to create the most cohesive story game I have ever played.
My only criticism would be that the writing can occasionally seem like it's trying too hard to replicate teenager lingo, and it can come across as false. These moments are rare, though, and I was able to easily overlook them. Here's hoping the rest of the episodes stack up!

Your options a clearly displayed on the screen to be read at your liesure and decided upon. Your choice is NOT rushed or display in unreadablely small text flying around the screen.
The story and characters are everybit as engaging as HR and TWD but LiS has a soundtrack that draws you into the enviroment even more.
Come for the story. Stay for the soundtrack and because the gameplay isn't annoying.

Having played some of the recent Telltale games and really enjoying them, I thought I'd give this game a try. I'm very happy to say Life is Strange has met my expectations - honestly, far exceeded them - with the execution and flexibility that the game has demonstrated.
The game is set in a high school setting, a special school for photography. Initially I was a bit annoyed when the main character Max starts nerding out about cameras in jargon I didn't understand, but it really grew on me once I started to get to know Max more! Just one of the things in the characters and dialogue that makes it so immersive. It depicts the high school setting very well, in a way that's kind of nostalgic and didn't turn me off like I'd expected it to. There's lots of teen drama, but I think the game makes it easy to empathize with, and you realize that these characters aren't just "stupid teens", in fact they're really resourceful and intelligent.
The gameplay, once you get past the initial figuring-things-out stage, is very smooth. Time rewinding is executed very well and the game adapts instantly to your choices. Finish a dialogue and don't really like it? Rewind, and instantly the people you interact with change according to what you have done in the new reality you've created. There are many small choices that impact what characters bring into conversation with you - leave evidence while snooping and have someone accuse you of it, and don't like that? Rewind, remember not to leave evidence, and watch the accusing character immediately change their body language and what they remember. I don't want to bring up comparisons that much, as I feel this game stands so well on its own, but well, compared with Telltale's games which really have the same story no matter what you do (mostly the difference is person A v.s. person B is dead), this game does feel like storytelling with instant player influence and control.
Overall, I think this game has great immersion and execution, and if you like games like this and would want to play one of the best I've experienced, try this game out! I look forward to future episodes and seeing how things branch out. One last thing - I love the "collectible mode" in the end which allows you to get achievements without affecting your previous choices or going through the hassle of replaying everything - the devs really are super considerate!

I only write Steam reviews about a few games that I either really like or really dislike. This game is the former. I've played a lot of adventure games, from Telltale's games to the old Gabriel Knight games to Syberia to Sanitarium. I'm honestly more a fan of older adventure games for the most part. Life is Strange might be my new favourite adventure game of all time, though, if the next episodes are as good as the first one. I don't expect games to get everything right, but Life Is Strange somehow does. The character models and art direction or perfect, the cinematography is perfect, the soundtrack is beyond perfect, and the story - the most important part - is so far incredibly compelling. One of the problems that adventure games run into is puzzles. Typical adventure game puzzles involve combining two or more items then using them on something. Life Is Strange completely circumvents that: there aren't really many "puzzles," instead there are just decisions you make. None of them seem to be wrong decisions, and
. This isn't a game that's going to make you combine a taser with a butterfly net and a rake to proceed. The actions you make are decisions, and they feel like they matter.
The characters are awesome and relatable and I can't wait to see where the story goes. I really can't imagine anyone playing this game and not really enjoying it. Even if you don't like adventure games, you should give this a shot - it really doesn't follow the gameplay style of most adventure games.

Life is Strange is in that genre of interactive storytelling games which at time straddle the borders of "game".  Generally, I'm not a fan of the genre, but despite this, the game won me over.  First and foremost, the story is a bit of a downer to start with, but it is so in a way I'm sure most people can relate to.  Second, this is not a fast-paced game; things happen roughly at the pace of daily life, but it is offset by having a lot of things to explore and learn about.  The curious sort will find a ton of things to learn about in the world around the protagonists and you'll almost certainly miss something on your first playthrough.
There's a good deal of freedom and flexibility about how you do things, and the "rewind" mechanic will almost certainly leave you second-guessing your choices.  It's fun sometimes to do things just a little differently for a second or third time and see how it plays out.  Overall, I give the game a Strong Recommendation.

Life is Strange is somewhat of a guilty pleasure of mine, considering the premise didn't really interest me. I Just happen to like adventure type games, and this cheap so i went with it. I certainly got my moneys worth with this game.
The Pros:
Presentation: This game is very well done, it feels like a professional type television show you participate in through the main character
Story: While I find the main plot to be good but not spectacular, some of the side stories i found very interesting, and  a big motivator for me wanting to play further episodes.
Graphics: Its well done, the people are fleshed out pretty well, aside from some voice syncing issues i had on PC.
Gameplay: Like most episodic type games you make choices in the world around you, some of which I had a hard time decided which ones to make. Luckily the rewinding of time gives you a chance to see an immediate outcome of different choices.
The Cons:
Teenagers: I Found myself rolling my eyes alot through this game, some parts just felt like cliche teenage nonsense that you'd see in a movie or show and i felt embarressed for myself playing this at times.
Soundtrack: Pretensious Soundtrack, it wasn't bad but i didn't care for it. This game could have used more variety. I'm pretty sure every college student doesn't listen to depressing acoustic low fi music.
Voice acting: This is a minor complaint cause over all i thought it was good, but some of which i found kind of week and super cliche.
In conclusion, if you know what your getting into here, you will certainly have a good time. I'm very much looking forward to further episodes, even if im embarressed to admit that to people in real life

A return to form for Square-Enix, even if it wasn't their dev studio (to begin with). In fact, I may come to think of Life is Strange as better than anything their Final Fantasy team ever produced. Life Is Strange is the best game I've played in a long time. After finishing Episode 1, it's been haunting my thoughts constantly.
It's told from the perspective of an angsty high school senior trying to break out of her shell at her new boarding school. The opening scene was extremely reminiscent of Donnie Darko; that's what made me get the game right away when I saw the trailer on YouTube. In fact, the game is very aware of pop culture and chock full of references to anything and everything.
Gameplay-wise, Life Is Strange feels good. The WASD controls are simple and the mouse-controlled camera functions smoothly. I haven't experienced any framerate issues or game-breaking bugs yet. The best part about the game is that your actions matter; they have concrete consequences that can shift the story onto numerous different paths depending on which actions you take. While recent choices can be "rewinded" immediately for a re-do, this window of opportunity only lasts for a limited time and your decisions stick once you move out of the area.
If you enjoyed TellTale's Walking Dead and Wolf Among Us or Quantic's Heavy Rain or Beyond: Two Souls, you'll love Life Is Strange. In my opinion, this is the most fleshed out game of the genre so far. LIS's controls bring a much higher level of interactivity and engage the player far more than those other titles. Sure, the cutscenes are extremely well done, but you're actually in control, playing the game, instead of just watching a movie. The level design and attention to detail are superb and your actions feel tangibly consequential. Like, you can just tell that a decision is going to bite you in the♥♥♥♥♥in some way down the line when you choose it. But you don't know how. Maybe you should rewind and choose a different path? Or maybe not. I love it. The physical and social settings of the game are beautiful and relatable. Even though the protagonist is an 18-year-old girl, I think everyone can recall the drama and angst of high school life.
It's not often I write reviews for anything, but in this case I just had to. What a strange and beautiful game indeed.
Oh yeah, I almost forgot. The soundtrack is awesome and perfectly complements the beautiful visual scenery.

This game is similar to the "Dreamfall Chapters" game, where you make decisions that affect how the rest of the story turns out. In this game the main character, Max, is stricken with a sudden ability to turn back time. You get to choose the outcome to many situations, and it is not always an easy choice. They give you a lot of power and chances to explore. The more you explore the areas, the more decisions you make and the more you change the story. I found myself reversing several times for each major decision. Ususally I would pick an option and see the result, then reverse to see the other result, and go back to my original choice. However, you never know how the choices you made are going to affect the rest of the story just based on the immediate reaction. After you finish the first episode you get to see how your choices matched up to others. I would highly recommend this game. It is certainly not a fast paced action game, but more like a movie that you control. It still pulls your interest, and keeps you guessing.
The only negative I have to add is that they are releasing the game in 5 episodes at different times. I mean, come on. This isn't a TV show where we have to wait a couple of months to finish the season. This is not the only game doing this, and I think it is a little ridiculous. I don't want to have to wait a year just to finish a game, especially when it only takes a couple hours to go through one episode.

Life Is Strange is the best game I've played in a long time. After finishing Episode 1, it's been haunting my thoughts constantly.
It's told from the perspective of an angsty high school senior trying to break out of her shell at her new boarding school. The opening scene was extremely reminiscent of Donnie Darko; that's what made me get the game right away when I saw the trailer on YouTube. In fact, the game is very aware of pop culture and chock full of references to anything and everything.
Gameplay-wise, Life Is Strange feels good. The WASD controls are simple and the mouse-controlled camera functions smoothly. I haven't experienced any framerate issues or game-breaking bugs yet. The best part about the game is that your actions matter; they have concrete consequences that can shift the story onto numerous different paths depending on which actions you take. While recent choices can be "rewinded" immediately for a re-do, this window of opportunity only lasts for a limited time and your decisions stick once you move out of the area.
If you enjoyed TellTale's Walking Dead and Wolf Among Us or Quantic's Heavy Rain or Beyond: Two Souls, you'll love Life Is Strange. In my opinion, this is the most fleshed out game of the genre so far. LIS's controls bring a much higher level of interactivity and engage the player far more than those other titles. Sure, the cutscenes are extremely well done, but you're actually in control, playing the game, instead of just watching a movie. The level design and attention to detail are superb and your actions feel tangibly consequential. Like, you can just tell that a decision is going to bite you in the♥♥♥♥♥in some way down the line when you choose it. But you don't know how. Maybe you should rewind and choose a different path? Or maybe not. I love it. The physical and social settings of the game are beautiful and relatable. Even though the protagonist is an 18-year-old girl, I think everyone can recall the drama and angst of high school life.
It's not often I write reviews for anything, but in this case I just had to. What a strange and beautiful game indeed.
Oh yeah, I almost forgot. The soundtrack is awesome and perfectly complements the beautiful visual scenery.

This game is similar to the "Dreamfall Chapters" game, where you make decisions that affect how the rest of the story turns out. In this game the main character, Max, is stricken with a sudden ability to turn back time. You get to choose the outcome to many situations, and it is not always an easy choice. They give you a lot of power and chances to explore. The more you explore the areas, the more decisions you make and the more you change the story. I found myself reversing several times for each major decision. Ususally I would pick an option and see the result, then reverse to see the other result, and go back to my original choice. However, you never know how the choices you made are going to affect the rest of the story just based on the immediate reaction. After you finish the first episode you get to see how your choices matched up to others. I would highly recommend this game. It is certainly not a fast paced action game, but more like a movie that you control. It still pulls your interest, and keeps you guessing.
The only negative I have to add is that they are releasing the game in 5 episodes at different times. I mean, come on. This isn't a TV show where we have to wait a couple of months to finish the season. This is not the only game doing this, and I think it is a little ridiculous. I don't want to have to wait a year just to finish a game, especially when it only takes a couple hours to go through one episode.

This review is of Episode 1, so it's not a full review.  Keep that in mind.
I saw this game on steam and thought, "Looks like a new Telltale style game, but in a real world setting!".  Bought the season pass on a whim since I had just finished A Wolf Among Us and a month prior to that  The Walking Dead Season 2.  I rather enjoyed myself on those games.  So much, that I even bought the Borderlands game Telltale made and I didn't look at the reviews of it yet.  But Life is Strange looked like current and real world to me.
Well, it's good, but it's not Telltale.  Do not think it is or will be.  That is a style all unto itself and those folks at Telltale do it with their own style that this does not replicate.  In fact, the only thing that is similar is the part about your choices affect how the games turns out.  Really, that's about it.
In Life is Strange, we get a 3D Unreal Engine and it's a very vibrant and well designed environment.  It's also more interactive.  There are tons of little things to click on - and I'd go so far as to say that's a giant part of the game itself.  Checking out all the different comments and clickable things.  Use a camera, look a facebook pages, enjoy photos, make comments on posters, and in general be a sneaky little mouse going through everyone's belongings.  It's sort of like a creepy thief sim.
Then there is the rewind aspect.  That's neat. Not world shattering, but neat.  I can edit my game choice - for better or for worse.  In the end, though, I still went back to a new save and did a speed run to try other choices ( and achievements ).  I didn't dislike the rewind bit at all, but I did find it a little annoying when I had to do it several times in a row for what would have otherwise been a "click this button quick" event that telltale does so often.  Granted, it was faster than dying and starting over.
Voice acting is good, yet not exceptional.  I've heard better,  I've heard worse.  Dialogue is well written and the actors do a decent job with it.  If it was even marginally bad, the game would be intolerable.   So, kudos to the actors.
There are two things here that to me could be off-putting to some gamers.  One is that the main character is a girl and the game revolves around her life as such.  Doesn't bother me.  It's 2015, I would think we've outgrown the need for all video games to have a male lead character.  But some folks will disagree, perhaps even vehemently.  It's not a feminine game by any means in my opinion and I think the devs made it a point not to specifically set it as such.  But there will be some who just can't get into it because of that. Along with others like me who don't really care.
The second that is that it is completely involved in an American high school setting.  For some it will be a familiar setting, for other nationalities a new experience/surprising similarity to their own background, for some a "I cannot relate" reaction, and for folks like me a general "oh, god a high setting. sigh".  Not a huge fan of high school themes - I was hoping it was a college scene instead.  Oh well for me.  Did I dislike the game because of it?  Honestly, yeah a little.  I played on because I wanted to discover the world and the what happens to the main character, but I could have done without the high school bit.
So, it's a story game. With some super light puzzling.  It's got some real life aspects along with a sort of fantasy bit where she suddenly has a magic power.  It's engrossing, not a telltale, and perhaps not just a "spin" on telltale adventure games.  Is it Gone Home fleshed out?  Well, as much as I hated to say it, sorta yeah.  I as trying hard not to make that comparison, but yep. You could say that. But still, this game is unique enough to call it it's own.  Enjoyed the depth of the world it created , the thoughts behind it, and the daring it took to stick with it as it is ( Square Enix deserves a shout out for not forcing it to be a male lead ).

This review is of Episode 1, so it's not a full review.  Keep that in mind.
I saw this game on steam and thought, "Looks like a new Telltale style game, but in a real world setting!".  Bought the season pass on a whim since I had just finished A Wolf Among Us and a month prior to that  The Walking Dead Season 2.  I rather enjoyed myself on those games.  So much, that I even bought the Borderlands game Telltale made and I didn't look at the reviews of it yet.  But Life is Strange looked like current and real world to me.
Well, it's good, but it's not Telltale.  Do not think it is or will be.  That is a style all unto itself and those folks at Telltale do it with their own style that this does not replicate.  In fact, the only thing that is similar is the part about your choices affect how the games turns out.  Really, that's about it.
In Life is Strange, we get a 3D Unreal Engine and it's a very vibrant and well designed environment.  It's also more interactive.  There are tons of little things to click on - and I'd go so far as to say that's a giant part of the game itself.  Checking out all the different comments and clickable things.  Use a camera, look a facebook pages, enjoy photos, make comments on posters, and in general be a sneaky little mouse going through everyone's belongings.  It's sort of like a creepy thief sim.
Then there is the rewind aspect.  That's neat. Not world shattering, but neat.  I can edit my game choice - for better or for worse.  In the end, though, I still went back to a new save and did a speed run to try other choices ( and achievements ).  I didn't dislike the rewind bit at all, but I did find it a little annoying when I had to do it several times in a row for what would have otherwise been a "click this button quick" event that telltale does so often.  Granted, it was faster than dying and starting over.
Voice acting is good, yet not exceptional.  I've heard better,  I've heard worse.  Dialogue is well written and the actors do a decent job with it.  If it was even marginally bad, the game would be intolerable.   So, kudos to the actors.
There are two things here that to me could be off-putting to some gamers.  One is that the main character is a girl and the game revolves around her life as such.  Doesn't bother me.  It's 2015, I would think we've outgrown the need for all video games to have a male lead character.  But some folks will disagree, perhaps even vehemently.  It's not a feminine game by any means in my opinion and I think the devs made it a point not to specifically set it as such.  But there will be some who just can't get into it because of that. Along with others like me who don't really care.
The second that is that it is completely involved in an American high school setting.  For some it will be a familiar setting, for other nationalities a new experience/surprising similarity to their own background, for some a "I cannot relate" reaction, and for folks like me a general "oh, god a high setting. sigh".  Not a huge fan of high school themes - I was hoping it was a college scene instead.  Oh well for me.  Did I dislike the game because of it?  Honestly, yeah a little.  I played on because I wanted to discover the world and the what happens to the main character, but I could have done without the high school bit.
So, it's a story game. With some super light puzzling.  It's got some real life aspects along with a sort of fantasy bit where she suddenly has a magic power.  It's engrossing, not a telltale, and perhaps not just a "spin" on telltale adventure games.  Is it Gone Home fleshed out?  Well, as much as I hated to say it, sorta yeah.  I as trying hard not to make that comparison, but yep. You could say that. But still, this game is unique enough to call it it's own.  Enjoyed the depth of the world it created , the thoughts behind it, and the daring it took to stick with it as it is ( Square Enix deserves a shout out for not forcing it to be a male lead ).

It’s quite clear where the majority of their focus was however and unfortunately some aspects of the game suffer because of it. I’m often of the mind that graphics don’t matter if the story is strong however Life is Strange’s art style and simplistic lip syncing detracts heavily from its well crafted story. This is somewhat made up for by the novel time rewind mechanic and strong story but it’s hard to escape it when you’re constantly reminded of the rather below par visuals. I am interested to see where this story goes however as it has the potential to set up Dotnod as one of the few developers able to execute well in the episodic game space.

A Great Game, especially if you love stories and character exploration, but a little too much hand holding.
If you take the time to immerse yourself in Max's life at Blackwell, you'll have a great time. The characters seem authentic, the story is interesting for what it is, and it's all around a good time.
The main issue I have however is the hand holding. I'm going to give the developers the benefit of the doubt and assume this was meant to be a tutorial episode so to speak, since it constantly told me when and how to use my powers. I was really disappointed that the game constantly after every major decision had Max wondering if she should try the other path, or saying 'hmm maybe I should rewind'.
The game did have some moments where they didn't give suggestions or hints about using your abilities, and in my mind that's where the mechanic shown. In those moments you were actually Max, and whether you remembered to use your newly found power or not, was entirely up to you, for better or for worse.
Assuming the developers stop giving excessive hints on their puzzles / when to use the games core mechanic, I think this series could become something very, very special. Only one episode is out at the time of writing this, but based on the 3.6 hours i've enjoyed and experienced so far, I'd definitely recommend this game.

There is a lot to like about Life is Strange. Episode 1 offers a great control scheme (which includes the interesting time control mechanic) and a layered story that offeres a ton if character development. Those are things this genre absolutely must have and so far, so good. I'm really enjoying the story and definitely want to see this out to its conclusion.
However, there are a few things that are not fantastic. One in particular is the fact the the characters lips do not actually move along with their speech. This is incredibly distracting and just feels like a shortcut taken. For a game that is almost entirely story driven with almost no action, letting your characters mouths move randomly with no connection to what they are saying is a huge flaw. The other thing that bugs me is that the game holds your hand with the time rewind mechanic and always gives you main character dialogue to remind you it's an option to use. This also pulls away from the immersion some because we aren't truly given control of what to do, but only in very specific situations.
Lastly, the most important thing I am looking for is yet to be seen and that is how our choices will create different paths. If this is going to be a step up and improvement on TellTale games then there needs to be different endings. So far I've found that many options will result in the same dialogue that drives the story forward, but we won't know how deeploy our choices affected the outcome until much later in the series. If this is done correctly and allows for multiple endings then this is a gem despite its flaws. If all paths lead to the same conclusion - well, it's merely just okay.

Life is Strange, a choice and consequence adventure game by developer DONTNOD Entertainment, opens up with what seems to be familiar territory: a high school setting, ominous dream involving a storm and a lighthouse, and a teenage protagonist arbitrarily discovering a mysterious, potent, power.
And really, judging purely from its premises, it isn’t anything new. A time reversal mechanic, bad premonitions, precarious friendships, heroic deeds – you’ve seen these things before. But what sets this game apart is its uncanny ability to deliver with its plot and its characters, engulfing you in a coat of verisimilitude, with the use of an intriguing plot, solemn atmosphere, authentic characters, and sharp writing.
Our protagonist Max Caulfield isn’t nearly as cynical as her apparent connection to Catcher in the Rye‘s protagonist may imply, but there’s still a palpable sense of alienation present from the very beginning; the atmosphere is serene, yet somber, developed through effective uses of Max’s monologues, music, and general attitude. Of course, this doesn’t mean that Max is just a friendless recluse, or we’d have no game; character interactions and relationships play a major role here, and they are handled commendably. Through environmental tidbits and brief conversations, Max’s reputation and past links are subtly developed; her relationship and reunion with Chloe, her intimate friend before the merciless effects of time and distance, was especially breathtaking. Although a lot is expressed between the two of them through dialogue, details in the surroundings and retrospective narrations subtly, yet effectively, add to their intertwining stories. It only helps that the character archetypes are realistic shades of grey, and the dialogue is strong – believably crude with some effective uses of profanity. The quality of the drama and emotional resonance achieved by these amalgamated elements is absolutely beautiful. A calming, almost melancholic soundtrack, and stellar voice work only helps matters.
It’s important to note, however, that because the game places such a great amount of attention in this area, the speed of the plot is relatively slow. Yet, it’s alluring; certain plot events do well to galvanize the pacing, keeping the underlying mystery consistent and – not surprisingly, this episode ends on a game-changing cliffhanger.
For better or worse, the time reversal element of the game seems to take a bit of a backseat to the game’s story and character development; so far, the plot has been much more focused on the human side of affairs, rather than the quasi sci-fi/fantasy aspects. However, Max’s mysterious ability is still cleverly woven into the gameplay, making for some interesting alternate scenarios and puzzles. Unfortunately, the puzzles were straightforward and seemed little more than small bridges between points, and as you might guess, being able to undo any recent actions detracts from the tension otherwise present if choices were permanent. However, details waiting to be scrutinized and tested are ubiquitous, and even seemingly trivial actions, such as watering a plant, may cause the plot to bifurcate, making for some fascinating scenarios.
The visuals are where things get a little slippery. While there are some detailed, authentic level designs and impressive uses of lighting, the game’s visual presentation is bogged down by some stiff animations, blurry textures, and some rough models. Character facial animations, and lip movements in particular, are jerky and often out of sync, which can be fairly detrimental to the show’s otherwise excellent sense of immersion.
So far, Life is Strange‘s captivating plot and layered characters have me enamored; I have little doubt that I’ll be continuing my adventures in the later episodes, and I’ll definitely be returning to see how else my choices will branch out. What was initially a piqued curiosity quickly grew into one of my most remarkable gaming experiences in recent memory, and for its price, I don’t see why it couldn’t be one of yours, either.

There is one thing I'd have to critizise though, that being the pretty stiff facial animations.

tl;dr: This is a great narrative experience for fans of recent Telltale Games Adventure people who love stories that resolve around Teenage/Young Adult Drama.

Note: Instead of revising the review every time a new episode comes out, I'll just keep adding my opinions on each episode into this. This covers episodes 1 to 4.
tl;dr - Excellent first episode with some awkward but endearing writing. Episode two has dry, unnecessarily long excursion from main plot but bounces back to a grandstand finish. Episode three has good atmosphere but also lots of filler and boring revelations before ending with a big event that loses a lot of impact due to the lack of buildup. Episode four is nothing short of a masterpiece. The stage is set. Now end it, DONTNOD. End it well and enter the pantheons of the adventure classics.
Episode 1:
Life is Strange is an intriguing, occasionally awkward blend of high-school drama and outlandish mystery - all tailored to fit the 'modern adventure' template as defined by Telltale's definitive Walking Dead series. While it does not break any new ground, the game is spectacularly successful when it comes to hooking the player in with the multitude of tantalizing subplots, an extremely relatable protagonist, and generally gorgeous art direction that compensates for the relatively simple visuals. The writing could use some polish as certain parts felt rather forced in their attempt to mimic teenage talk circa 2013, but this is otherwise a hugely promising beginning for what could be among 2015's best games.
Episode 2:
This is the proverbial difficult second album and hopefully just a minor blip for the series. While the art direction and music remain just as striking as in the first episode (if not more - especially during the spectacular ending montage), this 3.5-hour chapter goes off to a drab start with an overlong introduction, a drawn-out "prove my powers" scene that sounds neat on paper but rather lifeless in play, and two entirely unnecessary deviations from the core plot set in a junkyard. The blue-haired Chloe, introduced as a huge breath of fresh air and a walking box of mysteries in the first chapter, is simply grating here. However, Episode 2 makes a barnstorming comeback as it returns to school grounds for its grand finale, which delivers an even bigger punch than last time despite some contrived and/or packaged responses to certain major dialogue choices.
Episode 3:
We're halfway through the "season" and it looks like things are going downhill. The third episode begins promisingly enough with a (literally) dark section that is dripping with atmosphere and, once again, more excellent lighting work. However, the escapades in this hour-long bit end up feeling like filler, building up to a half-hearted attempt at a relationship subplot that is not worth the amount of awkward dialogue the player has to plow through. Out of the three investigative segments, two gave us no revelation we did not know beforehand, and one dropped a hint that doesn't seem to fit with the character it's talking about or the tone of the entire series. After all this, the game tries to repeat the second episode's trick with another big finish and is reasonably successful, although the impact is nowhere near that of the previous chapter since this particular big finish has almost nothing to do with anything that came before it in the episode.
Episode 4:
Beauty. Sadness. Discovery. Horror. It's all there. Aside from a short 15-minute downtime early on, this episode is as complete an experience as it gets for an adventure game and up there with the very best the genre has to offer. Flits seamlessly from thrilling to touching and everything in between from start to finish, and so packed with incredible, pivotal moments that it's almost impossible to describe more than vaguely without dropping huge spoilers. Masterfully executed, and more than good enough to lift the series as a whole above all the narrative and pacing problems it stumbled through in episode 3.

This is only a review for episode 1 and it's a good start. If you enjoy Telltale's adventure games, you'll probably feel at home with Dontnod's foray into the genre. One of the most striking things I came to realize was how much better these modern adventure games can feel when they're built with solid technical design. I felt so much more absorbed into the story without all of the stuttering, texture dropouts, and crashes that seem to be so consistent in Telltale games. This game looks and runs like a dream, with beautiful, confident, and unique visual design.
In spite of some cringeworthy dialogue here and there (they lean a little heavy on teenage lingo that's occasionally dated and a little out of place) I found myself connecting and getting invested in the characters and their drives very nicely. The time rewinding mechanic was a fun way to play around with the short term impacts of your actions that I hope will be expanded upon in later episodes. When I finished this episode, I had found myself so enamored with the experience, I played it through one more time to get the achievements and see the consequences of actions I didn't take the first time around.
I'm finding myself slowly becoming a Dontnod groupie after thoroughly enjoying Remember Me and now the first episode of Life is Strange. Their games aren't perfect, but the unique female driven angles they take and solid technical execution are really something I value. I whole heartedly recommend this.

Warning: Review might contain spoilers!
Life Is Strange:  A story-centric, point-and-click, adventure game with an interesting art direction in which the player leads a young protagonist called Max as she deals with her new found abilities, and the problems of those around her.

In Life Is Strange you are able to make decisions that—supposedly— affect the outcome of the story. Regardless of your actions, however, the story unfolds somewhat similarly to a film: Linearly.
The gameplay and mechanics are reminiscent of Telltale Games’ The Walking Dead, and— to a lesser extent— Alan Wake.
The 'indie' soundtrack is interesting. Definitely adds to the overall aesthetic of the game, while re-enforcing its film-like qualities, making it feel less like a game and more like a movie at times; which seems to be the conscious intent of its creators.
Overall, episode 1 of Life Is Strange offers an enjoyable experience that is unfortunately cut very short, leaving the player to wonder if the investment was worth it.

This game is absolutely amazing; the story line is captivating and the use of time travel doesn't add confusion, but instead contribues to the plot line further. Past the game's story line and controls, the graphics and physics in the game are stunning, I often found myself forgetting that I was playing a game and not watching a film during cutscenes. I would highly reccomend this game, even if only one episode is currently available. I eagerly await the next! 10/10

A Great Game, especially if you love stories and character exploration, but a little too much hand holding.
If you take the time to immerse yourself in Max's life at Blackwell, you'll have a great time. The characters seem authentic, the story is interesting for what it is, and it's all around a good time.
The main issue I have however is the hand holding. I'm going to give the developers the benefit of the doubt and assume this was meant to be a tutorial episode so to speak, since it constantly told me when and how to use my powers. I was really disappointed that the game constantly after every major decision had Max wondering if she should try the other path, or saying 'hmm maybe I should rewind'.
The game did have some moments where they didn't give suggestions or hints about using your abilities, and in my mind that's where the mechanic shown. In those moments you were actually Max, and whether you remembered to use your newly found power or not, was entirely up to you, for better or for worse.
Assuming the developers stop giving excessive hints on their puzzles / when to use the games core mechanic, I think this series could become something very, very special. Only one episode is out at the time of writing this, but based on the 3.6 hours i've enjoyed and experienced so far, I'd definitely recommend this game.

There is a lot to like about Life is Strange. Episode 1 offers a great control scheme (which includes the interesting time control mechanic) and a layered story that offeres a ton if character development. Those are things this genre absolutely must have and so far, so good. I'm really enjoying the story and definitely want to see this out to its conclusion.
However, there are a few things that are not fantastic. One in particular is the fact the the characters lips do not actually move along with their speech. This is incredibly distracting and just feels like a shortcut taken. For a game that is almost entirely story driven with almost no action, letting your characters mouths move randomly with no connection to what they are saying is a huge flaw. The other thing that bugs me is that the game holds your hand with the time rewind mechanic and always gives you main character dialogue to remind you it's an option to use. This also pulls away from the immersion some because we aren't truly given control of what to do, but only in very specific situations.
Lastly, the most important thing I am looking for is yet to be seen and that is how our choices will create different paths. If this is going to be a step up and improvement on TellTale games then there needs to be different endings. So far I've found that many options will result in the same dialogue that drives the story forward, but we won't know how deeploy our choices affected the outcome until much later in the series. If this is done correctly and allows for multiple endings then this is a gem despite its flaws. If all paths lead to the same conclusion - well, it's merely just okay.
