The writing could use some polish as certain parts felt rather forced in their attempt to mimic teenage talk circa 2013, but this is otherwise a hugely promising beginning for what could be among 2015's best games.
Episode 2:
This is the proverbial difficult second album and hopefully just a minor blip for the series. While the art direction and music remain just as striking as in the first episode (if not more - especially during the spectacular ending montage), this 3.5-hour chapter goes off to a drab start with an overlong introduction, a drawn-out "prove my powers" scene that sounds neat on paper but rather lifeless in play, and two entirely unnecessary deviations from the core plot set in a junkyard. The blue-haired Chloe, introduced as a huge breath of fresh air and a walking box of mysteries in the first chapter, is simply grating here. However, Episode 2 makes a barnstorming comeback as it returns to school grounds for its grand finale, which delivers an even bigger punch than last time despite some contrived and/or packaged responses to certain major dialogue choices.
Episode 3:
We're halfway through the "season" and it looks like things are going downhill. The third episode begins promisingly enough with a (literally) dark section that is dripping with atmosphere and, once again, more excellent lighting work. However, the escapades in this hour-long bit end up feeling like filler, building up to a half-hearted attempt at a relationship subplot that is not worth the amount of awkward dialogue the player has to plow through. Out of the three investigative segments, two gave us no revelation we did not know beforehand, and one dropped a hint that doesn't seem to fit with the character it's talking about or the tone of the entire series. After all this, the game tries to repeat the second episode's trick with another big finish and is reasonably successful, although the impact is nowhere near that of the previous chapter since this particular big finish has almost nothing to do with anything that came before it in the episode.
Episode 4:
Beauty. Sadness. Discovery. Horror. It's all there. Aside from a short 15-minute downtime early on, this episode is as complete an experience as it gets for an adventure game and up there with the very best the genre has to offer. Flits seamlessly from thrilling to touching and everything in between from start to finish, and so packed with incredible, pivotal moments that it's almost impossible to describe more than vaguely without dropping huge spoilers. Masterfully executed, and more than good enough to lift the series as a whole above all the narrative and pacing problems it stumbled through in episode 3.

This is only a review for episode 1 and it's a good start. If you enjoy Telltale's adventure games, you'll probably feel at home with Dontnod's foray into the genre. The time rewinding mechanic was a fun way to play around with the short term impacts of your actions that I hope will be expanded upon in later episodes. When I finished this episode, I had found myself so enamored with the experience, I played it through one more time to get the achievements and see the consequences of actions I didn't take the first time around.
I'm finding myself slowly becoming a Dontnod groupie after thoroughly enjoying Remember Me and now the first episode of Life is Strange. Their games aren't perfect, but the unique female driven angles they take and solid technical execution are really something I value. I whole heartedly recommend this.

Life Is Strange:  A story-centric, point-and-click, adventure game with an interesting art direction in which the player leads a young protagonist called Max as she deals with her new found abilities, and the problems of those around her.

In Life Is Strange you are able to make decisions that—supposedly— affect the outcome of the story. Regardless of your actions, however, the story unfolds somewhat similarly to a film: Linearly.

I reviewed this game a long time ago when it just had the first episode out, and I'm here to revisit some of those thoughts.
For the record, There will be massive endgame spoilers, because it's hard to talk about this game without addressing some of the backlash.
Life is Strange released in an interesting fashion, bringing some competition to the point-and-click adventure genre that was currently (and frankly, still is) dominated by Telltale Games. It sells itself episode by episode, five dollars a pop. You can choose to get the whole package or just one at a time as your funds permit. After an hour into it, I had bought the entire thing because I was absolutely enchanted by the storytelling and most of all, the music.
The interesting thing is, I could barely tell what the actual game was. LiS was a sort of gateway drug for me, I ended up buying a few Telltale games AFTER playing this one. The screenshots were all scattered around the various cutscenes and the tags were vague like "Story Rich" and "Choices Matter" (oh yes, we'll get to that, spoilers to come). I didn't really know what the big deal was until I actually understood that this whole trend was the resurgence of the point and click genre.
Life is Strange is a game I wished I had started my gaming life with. This nagged at me for a while after I saw the "Made with the Unreal engine" logo pop up. My gaming life started in earnest with the very first Unreal so it already gave me a sense of nostalgia as I played it, but my first gaming experiences were that of violence and basic primal needs to survive. However, LiS is calm and serene with a soundtrack that damn near perfectly sets the tone in every scene. I'm not even a real follower of independent bands, but I've loved every track.
The interesting thing about the music is that it is very often, contextual. You generally only hear it when there's speakers, or when Max puts on her headphones. If not, there's usually a void of sound where you just let the atmosphere take you in. I remember one sequence of walking down dormitory hallways. There was no music, but could hear muffled showers behind closed doors, leaking pipes, and morning birds chirping outside.
We follow Max Caulfield, a photography student returning to her home town of Arcadia Bay after a five year absence. She catches up with Chloe Price, whom Max saves from being shot and discovers that she can rewind time, which ties into the core game's mechanic. Being able to rewind through conversations but keep learned information, and you can use that to your advantage. Chloe is an old friend who has had a rough few years with a deceased father and an overbearing stepfather. She lashes out at Max every now and then, so her damage is clear.
Navigating social structures is part of the game, which I did not expect to enjoy. You can basically pick and choose how you treat various characters throughout the entire game. Will you be empathetic to the local rich alpha ♥♥♥♥♥, or turn the tables on her at every opportunity? Will you try to rekindle your friendship with Chloe, or try to keep her at arms length because of how she has led her life in recent years? All of these things manipulate events and conversations and there's invisible "point" values attributed to these characters depending on how you act towards them, and that can affect how cooperative they are in later episodes.
The game does a good job of wanting me to see what happens next and I imagine that same style will translate well into future installments, including the up and coming "Before the Storm", where we will follow Chloe and the time that predates Max's arrival.
Now, there are a couple of flaws and one of them will include the spoilers I previously mentioned.
The obvious one; the lip syncing is some of the worst in the industry. The game's graphical style is compared to paintings, to which the game does very well. It looks great, but somebody somewhere dropped the ball when the characters actually open their mouths. It takes a full episode or two to adjust and get used to, but the game's other qualities help me overlook it. Many other reviewers did not agree, and it haunted them through their entire playthrough.
Other reviewers talk about very bad attempts at teenager speech and lingo. I however... didn't notice, to be honest. I raised a brow at the use of "Hella" and when Max said "Are you for cereal?" I cringed, only to be recovered when Chloe herself called Max out on silly slang. Everything else I barely noticed, including the "Cool Kidz Club" comment from one character, which I legit heard in my own teenage years. Granted, that does make this outdated but the fact is that to me, it existed.
Now, to the backlash the game received. Last spoiler warning.
Branching storyline games with character choices constantly get this wrong, no game has yet to perfect this. In order for choices to actually matter, the game has to give us like nine or more different endings. Mass Effect 3 made this mistake and paid for it. Life is Strange made the same mistake, and was next on the chopping block.
You see, throughout the game it becomes "clear" (in a muddy sense) that Max's constant manipulation of time is what was causing a massive hurricane to come and destroy the town. She gets several visions of this throughout the game and she slowly unravels the mystery. At the end of the game, she discovers that saving Chloe in the beginning actually causes it. Other forms of media have covered the "Butterfly Effect", and this is basically their version of it. At the end, Max can either rewind all the way back to when Chloe got shot, and let events unfold as they were 'meant' to be... Or allow Arcadia Bay to be destroyed, forsake the power, and leave town with Chloe (Possibly as lovers if you made some specific choices). Cue "Bay or Bae" memes.
If you're following this line of logic, you might already be angry. Despite all the choices, the endgame effectively boils down to two choices, and neither one gets manipulated in any way throughout the game.
...Honestly? It didn't hurt the game for me. I mentioned earlier about how your choices affect certain social structures and that's really what drew me in. Choices did in fact have consequences, they did affect how people treated you and my first game was mostly a "nice" run, wanting to be as nice to everyone as I possibly could. I mostly succeeded, save for a few stubborn jackasses but hey, those exist. Can't please everyone.
Ultimately I chose to let the Bay be destroyed. The game implies that everyone dies but I don't think that's realistic. In what is essentially a "Headcanon", I like to imagine many people were in shelters, underground, surviving. The government might come and help rebuild while survivors live in a sort of encampment just out of town while repairs go underway.
So frankly, I cannot remain annoyed at the endings for very long. In a world short of LGBT stories I wanted so hard to avoid the dreaded "Bury your Gays" trope and just imagine Max and Chloe living happily ever after, but perhaps with a bit of survivors guilt in the mix. Which would make a great sequel by the way, with more choices and social navigation!
Alas, other than Before the Storm, future games of this series will not involve Max or Chloe (allegedly). Developers have already said that they have entirely new characters planned.
I for one, will be following this series to the bitter end. All aboard the feels train!

Navigating social structures is part of the game, which I did not expect to enjoy. You can basically pick and choose how you treat various characters throughout the entire game. Will you be empathetic to the local rich alpha ♥♥♥♥♥, or turn the tables on her at every opportunity? Will you try to rekindle your friendship with Chloe, or try to keep her at arms length because of how she has led her life in recent years? All of these things manipulate events and conversations and there's invisible "point" values attributed to these characters depending on how you act towards them, and that can affect how cooperative they are in later episodes.
The game does a good job of wanting me to see what happens next and I imagine that same style will translate well into future installments, including the up and coming "Before the Storm", where we will follow Chloe and the time that predates Max's arrival.
Now, there are a couple of flaws and one of them will include the spoilers I previously mentioned.
The obvious one; the lip syncing is some of the worst in the industry. The game's graphical style is compared to paintings, to which the game does very well. It looks great, but somebody somewhere dropped the ball when the characters actually open their mouths. It takes a full episode or two to adjust and get used to, but the game's other qualities help me overlook it. Many other reviewers did not agree, and it haunted them through their entire playthrough.
Other reviewers talk about very bad attempts at teenager speech and lingo. I however... didn't notice, to be honest. I raised a brow at the use of "Hella" and when Max said "Are you for cereal?" I cringed, only to be recovered when Chloe herself called Max out on silly slang. Everything else I barely noticed, including the "Cool Kidz Club" comment from one character, which I legit heard in my own teenage years. Granted, that does make this outdated but the fact is that to me, it existed.
Now, to the backlash the game received. Last spoiler warning.
Branching storyline games with character choices constantly get this wrong, no game has yet to perfect this. In order for choices to actually matter, the game has to give us like nine or more different endings. Mass Effect 3 made this mistake and paid for it. Life is Strange made the same mistake, and was next on the chopping block.
You see, throughout the game it becomes "clear" (in a muddy sense) that Max's constant manipulation of time is what was causing a massive hurricane to come and destroy the town. She gets several visions of this throughout the game and she slowly unravels the mystery. At the end of the game, she discovers that saving Chloe in the beginning actually causes it. Other forms of media have covered the "Butterfly Effect", and this is basically their version of it. At the end, Max can either rewind all the way back to when Chloe got shot, and let events unfold as they were 'meant' to be... Or allow Arcadia Bay to be destroyed, forsake the power, and leave town with Chloe (Possibly as lovers if you made some specific choices). Cue "Bay or Bae" memes.
If you're following this line of logic, you might already be angry. Despite all the choices, the endgame effectively boils down to two choices, and neither one gets manipulated in any way throughout the game.
...Honestly? It didn't hurt the game for me. I mentioned earlier about how your choices affect certain social structures and that's really what drew me in. Choices did in fact have consequences, they did affect how people treated you and my first game was mostly a "nice" run, wanting to be as nice to everyone as I possibly could. I mostly succeeded, save for a few stubborn jackasses but hey, those exist. Can't please everyone.
Ultimately I chose to let the Bay be destroyed. The game implies that everyone dies but I don't think that's realistic. In what is essentially a "Headcanon", I like to imagine many people were in shelters, underground, surviving. The government might come and help rebuild while survivors live in a sort of encampment just out of town while repairs go underway.
So frankly, I cannot remain annoyed at the endings for very long. In a world short of LGBT stories I wanted so hard to avoid the dreaded "Bury your Gays" trope and just imagine Max and Chloe living happily ever after, but perhaps with a bit of survivors guilt in the mix. Which would make a great sequel by the way, with more choices and social navigation!
Alas, other than Before the Storm, future games of this series will not involve Max or Chloe (allegedly). Developers have already said that they have entirely new characters planned.
I for one, will be following this series to the bitter end. All aboard the feels train!

An absolute "Yes", judging from Episode 1.
This is a mostly narrative-driven game with some puzzle elements that involve time manipulation.
There's a lot to look at and do in the first episode, worth 5 bucks imho. I'd still compare this best to the Telltale Adventure series of recent times. The story is pretty depressing, the characters are quite cool, though you always get those stereotypes...guess that's why they're stereotypes. You have your cheerleaders, your jocks, your elitist rich guys, the nerds, the punk chick, the control freak and yourself, the shy nerdy 18 yo. I personally found the voice acting to be good, the writing is good as well, so far. The story is interesting. It reminds me of "Butterfly Effect" (movie), which it probably is supposed to.
If you like chill games with a dense atmosphere and believable characters, check it out. There was not a single action scene in it, so bear that in mind.
The only real "negative" thing I can think of is this: You are able to indefinitely reverse time. You can thus also reverse dialogue choices. If you don't like an outcome immediately, you can change it. Of course, you don't know what will happen further down the road, but I still thought this takes away a bit of meaningfulness for the choices, which are mostly just A or B. It's also easy to miss some of the things in your first playthrough. Things that you're made aware of after you see your choices in the aftermath.
Edit: Episodes 2 and 3 were really nice as well. The game can get a bit slow, because you CAN explore lots of different things. Annoyingly at one point I reversed time too much and didn't notice it which had an impact on something...luckily you can just select a scene and redo (or undo) your mistakes or even start a completely new playthrough from that moment in the story or just explore for missed pics and stuff...really great!
Episode 4 was the culmination of tension, everything comes together. Best episode imho....and now to the spoiler....
sadly, this is being unravelled by episode 5, which is not bad, but it can't keep up with ep 4 until the very end in terms of emotions. Basically all your previous choices are made obsolete...repeatedly. It's just a mess of time travel and alternate realities and lots of useless dialogue that doesn't get you anywhere. In the end you have 2 choices, only 1 of which will really fell like the correct choice, the other one having MUCH less emotional impact. Where as before the game also told you about the different choices to make, episode 5 only has that for the final choice, since there are no other choices...I don't know why they did that, maybe they ran out of ideas with the story, but it feels too different from the rest of the game, it feels like tying up loose ends, but that didn't have to be the case. We could have stayed in our current time line most of the time and maybe the ♥♥♥♥ing huge tornado could have had a bigger impact on the Jefferson story line without altering everything back to square 1. Maybe the nosebleeds could also be something noteworthy and not just random stuff we don't care about in the end. I really think they threw the story away in the end. Yet, despite all this, it's not a bad episode, it just can't compete with the other ones in my opinion...that is until the very end and until you make the "right" choice. Then it hits you hard and when you think it's over, it just hits you again. I seriously thought that sacrificing myself would have been a better ending...not being able to save everyone we lost in the past episodes, but at least saving the city and the rest of its inhabitants. Too bad. Oh, well, it's still a great game overall. 15 hours for this price is great.
Episode 1 was a solid entertainment experience. I can't wait to play through the remaining story.

Every angle and point of view put you in the eyes and body of the characters, their relativity to real life personalities makes you feel insecurities in your seat at what you are watching; making you feel as if you are inappropriately watching someone pour out their feelings, and living their fears, while  being vulnerable for you as well. The story and setting of this small town brings forth a desire to explore and to learn what is means to live another life, in this case  Arcadia bay, and to witness more perspectives and personalities of real people. It is this unfamiliarity that draws eyes and heart to want to sit and listen to this young girl's story. And even from the male point of view as a player; each insecurity, and each judgement to go back and do something better is alive in your conscience. It is a fun imaginative storm of harmony for the brain.
P.S.   I highly desire to see this game be given the chance, after the full story is completed, to become a free roam  game. It tickles me with excitment onthe idea of actually living this characters life and recreations in a full encompassing  adventure of the game's world. Everyone who tired out Dontnods last effort Remember Me should agree the strenght of that game was it's time rewinding mechanic which was woefully underutilized there.  Life is Strange is their attempt to take this mechanic and build an entire story around it.  The time rewind function works extremely well and has some pretty interesting uses for choices both big and small.  While some may complain that it's too obvious where to use the mechanic I would counter that there are enough consequences for both doing and not doing certain things that it doesn't matter so much when you rewind time to alter events as much as why you're doing it.  The choices in this game are not easy, and some immediate benefits may haunt you later and vice versa.  The story has an interesting almost Twin Peaks style revolving around the small Oregon Town and a missing girl while also nailing the everyday life of high school kids and the problems they have with authority figures and each other.  Some may not enjoy the slow pace and mundanity of the opening chapter but for fans of story driven, choice based gameplay Life is Strange should definitely be on your must play list.

This is an interesting "game" to say the least. I use the quotation marks because to me it is more like a choose your own adventure movie than a game. Certainly there is much to interact with and a very interesting mechanic for limited time reversal, however there are no real challenges to overcome or problems to solve (or even any way to win or lose). If you are interested in taking an immersive journey through the mind of an awkward, sensitive, social misfit as she tries to cope with not only having dodgy friends and highschool drama, but also a universe where physics is broken, this is the "game" for you. If you'd rather be shooting things, solving puzzles, and generally being challenged you should look elsewhere.
All of that being said if this IS a thing you like, you will positively love Life is Strange. The environment, the music, the characters... this is a work of art. The darkness which lurks on the outskirts of what appears to be a normal school for aspiring artists creates just enough tension to captivate without seeming too hoakey to destroy the immersion. The reversal ability is a very interesting twist and it allows you to know things you couldn't have known and do things you couldn't have done. The options and scope of the powers, although outlandish in themselves, seem 'realistic'. Don't hesitate to buy it.
P.S.- 3.2 hours was my total game time and while the game does have tremendous replayability (just to see all the outcomes which might have been) I choose to play it once in its entirety rather than change the story several times per chapter then go back and do it all again. I can't wait for the next installment.

Developed by French studio, Dontnod Entertainment and published by Square Enix, Life is Strange is an episodic, story focused, adventure game. The protagonist, Max Caulfield, an introverted senior photography student, and has returned to her home town of Arcadia Bay after five years away in Seattle.
The story kicks off with Max experiencing a series of visions during a photography lecture, which seem to be of future events. After class, Max is witness to the shooting of a young girl in the school toilets. Shocked by the event, Max leaps forward from her hiding place and causes time to rewind, back to the start of the photography lecture. From here Max embarks on a journey of time travel discovery, altering the time line in order to improve her situation and help the people around her.
The opening sequence and the way the main game mechanic is revealed is quite well done, but sadly, is not fun to play through, due to hit and miss voice acting, and the over use of teenage clichés and colloquialisms. I knew I was in for a tough slog early on, after flicking through Max's diary where I found the text, and I quote, " Jefferson is supercool and superchill," and of course the classic line about Mr Jefferson, "I think he is a genius. OMG I WANT TO MARRY HIM. Just joking."
The clichés don't stop there either, the dialogue, the teen bullying, the girlfriend/boyfriend sexting dramas and of the over use of the adjective hella, repeated slapped me in the face, and never allowed me to feel submerged in the story. I found this extremely disappointing, as some of the morale decisions in this game are really difficult which is great. I am not sure who the target audience is for this title, but I am pretty sure it's not me.
Life is Strange's time reversal mechanic is interesting in concept, and adds a great level of second guessing to your conversational decision. Sadly though, this great concept doesn't transfer well to the puzzles. While the puzzles are interesting when you solve them, I often found them to be too structured, with only one solution. Also it seems like they force the use of the time mechanic into some very mundane situations. Can't get an item from under some draws, better reverse time, getting a ruler or something to slide the item out is just hella old school.

Life is Strange kicks off to a good start by giving us a well developed game experience, a solid plot (albeit some cliche characters) and what we love the most about interactive stories; the ability to make choices and live with their consequences.
The big plot mechanic to bring some light into the experience, is the ability to rewind time and chance your most recent decisions and actions, which brings up an internal debate with yourself over whether or not you made the right decision, and if you should or not rewind it and chose something else instead.
Despite minor technical issues, like bad lip-syncing (which is disappointing, seeing how good the voice-acting is), camera locking or centering at times you feel it shouldn't, the game really shines by offering side-quests you didn't even knew were there, like rewinding time to make sure one of your classmates doesn't receives a football to the head or finding out about your friend's pregnancy, which not only will make you feel like you're not experiencing the game the way it was meant to be, but will reveal a lot about yourself. Did you went off your way to explore the world and help every living thing that crossed your way, or you kept to yourself and ignored everything and everyone else?
By the end of the first episode (if the linearity of the plot and themes doesn't drives you off) you'll be joining the bandwagon of excited players waiting to play the second episode, to find out about the whole mystery behind your time rewinding powers and be left wondering how your decisions have affected everything and everyone around you.

Ok so, where to start with this game.  I can't really describe how much of an impact this game had on me up through Episode 2.  It really was profound on a lot of levels, and my specific thoughts on Episode 2 are at the bottom of this review.  Yeah this review is a little choppy, but I want to keep the evolution of my thoughts in the review.   From a "it's a fun game with good bits, but needs work, to Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥that was Intense! to Well, it's finally over, how did it handle the landing?"
Short version:  It's good, a very good game, one of a short list of games that's actually made me get emotional about the events and characters.   It's a little choppy at parts as the resolution pans out, but I don't really hold that against it given it's a time travel story, and those are always messy at the end.
Long version:
This game has taken hold of a very special place in my heart now.  It's the kind of game that makes me glad I'm a gamer, and able to experience this kind of interactive storytelling.   It's not perfect, but the parts it falls short on are minor in my opinion, while the parts it gets right, it gets them SO right.
The story continues to build on the events of the previous episodes, each new installment upping the stakes and intensity of events.  While the storm builds outside, a storm is building inside Max as well.  A maelstrom of choices and consequences, and the cascading ramifications of those choices.  She's made to face what she's done, and how it's impacted the things around her, and left with the task of trying to make it all make sense.   She has to go to some dark places, literally and metaphorically to come out on the other side, but whether she comes out intact and sane, is another question all together.
Eh, I'm rambling again.  It's a very good game.  It fumbles a bit at the end, but you kind of have to accept this with time travel stories.  They are messy by nature, and it's damn hard (near impossible in my opinion), to make them hold together from start to finish.  But I think they kept the heart and soul of the game intact, and gave us a very touching story, filled with a lot of care and love.  To say the response to this game was immense is an understatement.  I don't think the people at DONTNOD had any idea it would become this big, but the amount of support and appreciation they've shown the fans is something I like to see from developers.   This really is a grassroots game when it comes to popularity.  The fans REALLY championed this game, and spread the word like only nerd fanatics can.  It's a very inspiring situation, and I look forward to more work by this team.
It's a wonderful game, and a wonderful experience to have as a gamer.  It reminded me what it was like to be a young kid again, to have crazy dreams, and lofty ideals about what you would do with your life, and seeing those dreams come face to face with reality, and how you deal with it.   All mixed in with a fun time travel story, that really had more emotional weight to it than you might think.
Buy this game.

Good game, with some issues.
I really like this game.  It's got a lot of heart behind it.  It's not a perfect game, but the things it gets wrong are fairly minor to me, where as the things it gets right, it does really well.
The mood and atmosphere of the game is very engaging.  It's very rooted in current teen/20's culture, but there are elements of their behavior and speech that do transcend across generational gaps.  Many times I felt reminded of my own highschool/college years, with certain moments and characters, which was a nice bit of nostalgia.   I've played better games for sure, but I've also played a lot worse.   I'm glad I decided to buy it, and I plan on picking up the others as they come out.
Pros:
Interesting story
Believable representation of aspects of American teen life.
Good soundtrack, very mood setting
Visually very pretty, the lighting especially was a delight
Interesting game mechanic in the time rewind.
Significant dramatic tension when presented with choices.
Cons:
Voice acting at times can be sketchy.  Not terrible, except for the skaters, but not outstanding either.
Some of the character archetype cliches were grating on the nerves.  The elitst photo snob guy in the campus yard was especially annoying.  As well as the "gung ho military guy" one too.
Some of the elements aren't believable, and by that I mean that I just don't buy a guy living in an RV **on a highschool campus parking lot**   Or that a dormroom would be designed with deadlock doors, where a person inside them is trapped without a key.  That's a fire hazard and just simply wouldn't happen.
Graphics could be very low rez sometimes, even on the higher settings.  This was mostly with the ambient artwork on the  walls and stuff, so it wasn't a big deal, but I honestly couldn't tell the different between my low quality graphic settings and the highest.
Bottom line:
If you like story driven, dramatic narratives, with a touch of supernatural stuff going on, and can fondly remember your time as a teenager, then you'll probably like this game.  They've got room for improvement certainly, but the work definitely seems to have had a lot of love poured into it, and I can appreciate that enough to overlook the places where they didn't do a stellar job.
**Episode 2 Review**
Ok so, man...the game devs really took the gloves off here.   They sort of trick you with a false impression that the "Choices matter" in Episode 1 seem to be fairly minor things, but they build into a significant situation very quickly.    First off, the choices you make, from the very start in Ep 2 have way more impact, and it's a LOT harder to decide which is the better option.  Ep1 had a lot that were pretty binary in which would be the better choice, but Ep 2, man is it hard to decide the right decision.  So right off the bat, the game ups the stakes significantly.   We learn more about the lives behind the people in Blackwell Academy, and just how messed up some of them are.
I'm not going to spoil anything, but when you get to the finale of this....man, it's an emotional stomach punch.  I'm a 38 year old man, and I was crying at the events of the climax.  And let me tell you, the choices you made in Eps 1 & 2  DO have consequences...and you learn some of them here.   The dialogue at the climax was so intense, I even get upset watching Let's Players' play it.  And they all have the same reaction.  When the climax of the game shows up, all fun and games stop for them.  They get REALLY serious, and really invested in the events.   Anyone who's played it will know exactly why, and I find it to be a FABULOUS testament to the writing of that scene, that it hooks everyone I've seen play it, where they are genuinely invested and care.
The overall writing can still be a little cheezy, as they sometimes forget to make the kids actually be kids, and instead have them behave like characatures of kids.   But other times the kids are spot on accurate.  I still have feelings of nostalgia when I see some of the teen interactions, and some of the characters are eerily similar to people I knew in highschool.
Bottom Line for Ep. 2:
The game continues to impress me, and pull on my emotions strongly.  And from the reactions of everyone I've watched play this, I'm not alone in this feeling.  It's rare that a game makes me invest this much feeling and concern into it, and for that I am grateful.   It's still a little cheezy, and once or twice there are some lines of dialogue that seem out of order, but these are very minor issues on what is an excellent game.
If you haven't picked this game up yet.  You should.  It's worth it.   I've gifted it to everyone of my friends who had it on their wishlist.

Life is Strange is a adventure games with choices that has a consequences, there is no right or wrong, just choices. Yep, the choosing mechanic is very similiar with Telltale Walking Dead series, but don't get it wrong, its similiarity is like Halo has a gun that can reload, just like Call of Duty. Soo, Life is Strange is not a Walking Dead clone.
It tells the story of Max, a geeky girl that have the abilities to rewind time, how did she get that abilities ?? its still a mystery. There's some mystery here and there like why is he like that, or why did she knows that, and why did she get that strange vision at the beginning of the game ?? Of course like all super hero story, when the main character get that super hero power, they tend to use it on everything even the little things. The episode 1 stop with the main plot unfolding, very cliffhanger, but its an episodic game and i expect no less.
The characters in this game is really good, all of them is really lifelike, their behaviour and everything about them is very lifelike, and we even got some anti mainstream main character, that is not really confident with herself, very geeky, not perfect, and like to talk to herself a lot. She even kinda talk to herself about her being nosey when a player go to places they are not suppose to go, like when she go to her friend parents bedroom for no reason whatsoever, except because the player want to go everywhere.
The gameplay mechanic is like i said before, bear the similiarity with Telltale Walking Dead series, like you pick a conversation choices and the game will tell you that there will be a consequences with that choices... But instead of that button smashing dumb quick button event, we got a really cool puzzle that could be solve using the rewind time mechanic, like you don't really like what you said to someone ? Just rewind the time ! Or you really need to hide and crap !! you messed up your hiding spot, just rewind the time and avoid that ! that kind of stuff. Its really soothing because you can take all day to solve the puzzle because if you mess up, just rewind the time and you good to go.
The visual and audio in this game is design to be soothing and beautiful. The soundtrack is absolutely beautiful, i could listen to all of that all day long just to calm myself. the visual is well. Not AAA good, there's some low poly texture here and there, but its usable. Its very pretty in some area and again the visual is design to give the player that soothing atmosfer and combine that with the audio make this game really calming.
In the end, this is a really good game and definitely worth your time and money. I don't know what to say, i'm amazed that the developer really know how to give the player a good atmosfer and they didn't afraid to make the main character not the usual confident heroine type. Its really nice just to see her diary and listen to her rambling about stuff. Buy it now or wait for all the episodes to come out. If you like a good story telling, definitely don't miss this one.

This is now one of my favorite games. With the exception of cut scenes, you do get to walk around and choose what to interact with, who to talk to, where to go, etc. the majority of the game. My only complaint (besides the off lipsyncing that's easy to ignore) is that I have to wait for episode two.

Life is Strange is a adventure games with choices that has a consequences, there is no right or wrong, just choices. Yep, the choosing mechanic is very similiar with Telltale Walking Dead series, but don't get it wrong, its similiarity is like Halo has a gun that can reload, just like Call of Duty. Soo, Life is Strange is not a Walking Dead clone.
It tells the story of Max, a geeky girl that have the abilities to rewind time, how did she get that abilities ?? its still a mystery. There's some mystery here and there like why is he like that, or why did she knows that, and why did she get that strange vision at the beginning of the game ?? Of course like all super hero story, when the main character get that super hero power, they tend to use it on everything even the little things. The episode 1 stop with the main plot unfolding, very cliffhanger, but its an episodic game and i expect no less.
The characters in this game is really good, all of them is really lifelike, their behaviour and everything about them is very lifelike, and we even got some anti mainstream main character, that is not really confident with herself, very geeky, not perfect, and like to talk to herself a lot. She even kinda talk to herself about her being nosey when a player go to places they are not suppose to go, like when she go to her friend parents bedroom for no reason whatsoever, except because the player want to go everywhere.
The gameplay mechanic is like i said before, bear the similiarity with Telltale Walking Dead series, like you pick a conversation choices and the game will tell you that there will be a consequences with that choices... But instead of that button smashing dumb quick button event, we got a really cool puzzle that could be solve using the rewind time mechanic, like you don't really like what you said to someone ? Just rewind the time ! Or you really need to hide and crap !! you messed up your hiding spot, just rewind the time and avoid that ! that kind of stuff. Its really soothing because you can take all day to solve the puzzle because if you mess up, just rewind the time and you good to go.
The visual and audio in this game is design to be soothing and beautiful. The soundtrack is absolutely beautiful, i could listen to all of that all day long just to calm myself. the visual is well. Not AAA good, there's some low poly texture here and there, but its usable. Its very pretty in some area and again the visual is design to give the player that soothing atmosfer and combine that with the audio make this game really calming.
In the end, this is a really good game and definitely worth your time and money. I don't know what to say, i'm amazed that the developer really know how to give the player a good atmosfer and they didn't afraid to make the main character not the usual confident heroine type. Its really nice just to see her diary and listen to her rambling about stuff. Buy it now or wait for all the episodes to come out. If you like a good story telling, definitely don't miss this one.

First and foremost let me just get this out of the way; this review is just for episode 1 as it is the only one available for purchase right now. M'kay?! M'kay!
Life is Strange has to be one of the best episodic games to date. Ever since Telltale's 'Back to the Future' games, I've been hooked. And don't get me wrong, I absolutely adore Telltale, but they've been dominating the episodic space for quite a while now and it's nice to see some fresh blood in the water. When I saw the trailer for Life Is Strange I knew immediately that I was going to be purchasing this game. And boy am I ever glad I did.
I plugged in my headphones, grabbed my controller, and I played the entire episode without noticing 2 hours have passed. From the second you get in to the game, to the second the credits roll, I don't think I took my eyes off the screen for longer than a blink. The music is incredible and suits the game perfectly, the characters all show so much real emotion, and the world the developers have created is... amazing. And beautiful. Actually you know what, if I had to sum up this game with 1 word it would be "beautiful".
I feel so attached to these characters already. Max is a bit of an odd ball and never really feels like she fits in with anyone. She's making a couple friends but, struggling. Normally when I find little journals sitting around game worlds I tend to ignore them. But Max's journal is actually one of my favorite parts about this game. Throughout the game as you make choices Max will write about them in her journal. And the weirdest thing is it ACTUALLY feels like a journal. It doesn't feel like some developers wrote it, or just a simple rundown of everything you've done in the game. It feels like a real person wrote every single word. Not saying developers aren't real people, but you know what I mean! You can feel the happiness, the stress, and the sadness that went in to every story. I believe this is the first time in a game where I actually wanted to read every single poster, sign, and text you come across. It's kind of hard not to when the characters are so fantastic.
I'm not sure why, but looking at Max and Chloe I almost felt a bit of myself in these characters. And I have a feeling that is exactly what the developers were trying to accomplish. You sneaky devs, you.
There is so much I would like to say about this game but I definitely don't want to be giving anything away. This is a game you need to play first hand. This is a game you need to experience alone. This is a game you need to buy immediately. Seriously, stop reading this and buy the damn game.

This game was put together like a love child of Gone Home and Telltale point and click games (TWD, The Wolf Among Us etc) and it pulls this off brilliantly! You're put into the shoes of 18 year old Max, a shy (and VERY CUTE) girl who has come back to her home town to study photography after moving to Seattle for several years. After witnessing a vision of a tornado destroying her home town, she finds out she has the ability to reverse time. As Max sets out on her quest to prevent Arcadia Bay's imminent doom, she must also solve the mysterious disappearance of a Blackwell student.
I love this game especially for its similarities to Gone Home - Max keeps a journal and writes down pretty much everything, I love that feeling of intimacy with the character through the journal and her internal narration. I make this comparison to Gone Home because there is also a lot of teen angst featured through Max's punk rock best friend Chloe much like the girlfriend of Gone Home's protagonist's sister. The journal feature is pretty neatly sorted out in four sections: Max's journal entries, character bios, optional photos taken (these are linked to achievements) and text messages from Max's friends and parents. Much like Gone Home, there are a lot of objects to examine and read, these really help with immersion with the game's universe and Blackwell Academy's past leading up to the present.
The game's style is pretty nice too, it doesn't look very realistic as Square Enix's other games but neither does it look awfully like a cartoon. Text on posters are hand written which is very cool and given with an option to formalize the text for you if you are unable to decipher the handwriting. A lot of the game's textures are very fluid thanks to a style resembling painting which I guess gives off a very artsy vibe. Only con to this game I can mention so far is that the lips moving and audio doesn't sync very well, despite it stated in the credits that this game uses motion capture. Not too much of a bother, just minor nitpicking on my part. The game also features a very nice, soft music soundtrack which makes good BGM as you play.
Every episode plays for as long as 3 hours each if you go over every single interactable object or person, despite this the game can hold your attention pretty long! There are quite a number of characters that Max can speak and interact with, most of which tie in to the events of the story. They are all quite well written and possess their individual ideas, characteristics etc. Max's ability to reverse time can change the outcomes and fates of several events and characters throughout the game, although most of the outcomes are linear, there are a variety of ongoing plots that carry out differently based on Max's actions. It appears there are no right or wrong actions as you can either allow the events to happen as they were or reverse and change their outcomes, save for a few irreversible decision.
Contrasting with TWD and other Telltale games, it appears Square Enix has decided to allow purchasing the first episode of this game separately which I think is a great method for distribution. It allows players to buy one episode and check out the game first before making the move to spend larger amounts of money to obtain the full game. Purchasing the first episode costs a mere ~$5 to purchase - a reasonable price to pay for 2-3 hours of time spent within the game per episode.
TLDR: Cool story rich game, cute characters and interaction, very immersive game world, nice art style, episodes can be purchased as they are released, potential for vastly varying consequential actions within the storyline, get the game!!!

This game was just amazing. The summary of the Steam reviews sums it up really well: "overwhelmingly positive".

You could really well compare it to Telltale's style, even though I think it is even better: more polished, on a better engine, and with a deeper story. It's hard to review it like this.
Don't play this game if you expect something adventure-like, and adrenaline-based, even if you'll get some; the pace of Life is Strange is quite relaxing, and you'll end up believing you're Max, a high-school photography student. Who can control time.
The fact that it's episodic really bodes well. Some people won't like it; but I do like playing episodes as they come out, it keeps it fresh. Of course, I can't say the next episodes will be good at the time I'm writing this, but I can't see how they could be bad.

Telltale Games finally has some serious competition in the modern take on the adventure game genre!
With an interesting art style, very pleasant music, an interesting time travel concept and a fantastic atmosphere... this game's got me hooked. Not to mention that *narrative hook* you've probably seen in the trailer by now.
The game also makes great use of body language. Awkward teenager body language. And I love how you can just sit down and chill in various places throughout the first episode, and all those little details scattered throughout the environments.
Highly recommended.

The music is great, the game play is basic, but has a new mechanic compared to other interactive games, such as Tell Tales games. It introduces a rewind system where you can go back in a limited time frame to remake a decision or undo what has happen in the story. However, you will have to live with the consequences. After all the main drive of this story is making tough decisions. Other than the mechanics of the game, the game runs really smoothly. More so than other games because it's running on the Unreal engine.
Other aspects I enjoy greatly about the game is the music. The company behind the game has gone great lengths in gathering a unique sound track with many indie muscians.  What is off setting about the game is the lip sync. There are some scenes where the mouth flaps of the characters do not match at all with what the characters are saying. To me that is a bit annoying as it takes the player out of the world.
---edit 3/25/15/--- I found out that the reason why the flaps are not sync is because the developers developed this game to be in the language in French. However, they had to make the decision on to spend money on a solid gameplay/voice actors or spend money to fix the flaps. They obviously chose the first. And I full heartily agree that they made the right call for this.---edit----
Other than that, I give this game a 9/10. The minor flaws does not detered me from the main aspects of the game(gameplay,story, music, and art). It is a must play for people who enjoy games similar to the tales series.
------edit 3/25/2015------------------ 2nd Chapter
Just played episode two of Life is Strange and it is just as amazing as the first. There are more nail biting decisions where you, the player, have to make. They added a feature where the individual can go back on a certain chapter to replay that scene. In addition, they added a play mode where you can just collect missing pictures in the game. However, in this game mode the player can not influences his or her choices in the origonal gameplay.
I love the new features that they added and it helps as the player will make mistakes and perhaps want to redo a certain part of the story or complete more achievements by going back.
The music is just as great as the first episode. What is even better is that the game company added more songs to their already large sound track.
Finally, I believe this game still deserves the 9/10 score I have given it. The music, the gameplay, and the story is still amazing. If somehow the first episode still haven't convinced you to buy the rest of the episodes, then you are missing out!
Seriously enjoying this game so far, the music is awesome! Can't wait for the next episodes! I want to know what's happening!

A great game to chill out and play. LiS has an intriguing story so far that plays like a YA book. I definitely recommend exploring your surroundings to get a feel for the other students and their stories. The dialogue is fresh and funny. Also, the art style is looks gorgeous with the lighting definitely taking the cake. Combine with that the atmospheric and well chosen soundtrack. Lastly, the time travel mechanic is a great addition to this type of interactive story. You made a choice with consequences you didn't like? Reverse! Or if you're just curious, reverse! I liked episode one so much I went ahead and bought the whole season.

This game was just amazing. The summary of the Steam reviews sums it up really well: "overwhelmingly positive".
The story is deep and great. The graphics are really good-looking. The gameplay is really enjoyable, and relaxing. You could really well compare it to Telltale's style, even though I think it is even better: more polished, on a better engine, and with a deeper story. It's hard to review it like this.
Don't play this game if you expect something adventure-like, and adrenaline-based, even if you'll get some; the pace of Life is Strange is quite relaxing, and you'll end up believing you're Max, a high-school photography student. Who can control time.
The fact that it's episodic really bodes well. Some people won't like it; but I do like playing episodes as they come out, it keeps it fresh. Of course, I can't say the next episodes will be good at the time I'm writing this, but I can't see how they could be bad.
If this review makes you interested in the game, or even excites you, just p l a y  i t  a l r e a d y. You really won't regret it.

Gonna be honest. The game glitches quite a lot - parts of the background glitches out in black patches constantly, the speech is out of sync for the most part and especially at the beginning of the game with the cutscene in Jefferson's classroom, the speech repeats itself and is considerably jittery.
However, this is a relatively new game so I am going to take the mindset that these glitches will be fixed in due time in future updates. On the whole though, the story is rich and immerseful - it's such a simple environment and concept yet still so endearing, the music is impeccable and is one of my favourite features of this game. The voiceovers were pretty impressive, especially for Chloe. Also I'm really liking this unique art style - this game is bringing something new to the table and I like that. I will be looking forward to the second episode, I just hope you will work on improving some of the technical problems though.

You know, after tediously playing shooting and MOBA games I decided to make a change by trying out an indie game.
After seeing that this was a female protagonist game, I thought to myself ... well, seems like another cliche girl game, but in the end I gave this game the justice it well and truly deserved.
Life is Strange is simply a master-piece. The game is essentially like reading an addictive book, and at the same time watching a movie, only YOU are capable of controlling the events that happen which ultimately affect the storyline.
From realistic graphics, exceptionally fitting music to match the tone of each scene, and a fitting genuine, contuining story which is easily relatable to many real-life ordeals and situations makes this game (mind you, this was more than just a game) an exceptional 10/10.
Honestly, 5$ out of the steam wallet is a small ask for a 'game' of such calibre. So... the next time you have spare cash in your steam wallet, or if you're looking for a change from the many mainstream games in this day in age, try out Life is Strange! It is a continuing story split into 5 episodes so we can all anticipate for the upcoming episodes in the months to come.
P.S
The game is developed by Dontnod Entertainment AND published by Square Enix, so there are no surprises there...
Both companies never cease to amaze in game development and production.

This game is a five-part episodic, and oddly realistic portrayal of small-town college life in the U.S., as seen through the eyes of a likeable young lady named Maxine. One can easily find info on the internet about the storyline, so i won't go into detail there.
Some things i liked:
As a photographer, i appreciated the aspiring photographer storyline in regards to Maxine, and the fact that you can seek out opportunities to take photographs. There's a sci-fi time-rewinding aspect to the gameplay, which harks back to Remember Me, Dontnod's other great game. It's a creative addition to the game, with multiple actions possible for even the simplest of things. Think "Groundhog Day" mixed with "Back To The Future", awesome!
Overall, i absolutely loved this gem. From every catty comment, to the amazing music, wonderful setting, and beautiful visuals. I really hope it gets the recognition it deserves.

Life is Strange is a narrative driven point and click adventure game. You play as a young girl named Max, in school for photography. It does a good job at portraying modern youth but it does have a twist that you'll find out early into the game. With out saying too much that twist will play a fairly large role in the small instances of puzzle solving that's featured in episode one. You'll also be making choices through out the game and each choice will have an impact on the overall outcome.
I'll be honest, I didn't really expect to like the game to much based solely on the theme of the game. I ended up getting it because of it's low price and great looking visuals. I really do like the art design in this game. I features an almost acrylic hand painted texture style that really carries the game's aesthetic.
I'm glad I ended up getting it and playing it through. Life is Strange is well written, the characters, though typical in archetype, has a lot of depth. Both the main and supporting cast all show flaws, and strengths. Traits that may seem obvious, then get's contradicted by a story revel. It is the level of intricacies in each character that I enjoyed the most.
Overall, Life is Strange is a surprising little gem. The theme might not be for every one, but what it does it does pretty well.
Pros:
- Great art style
- Unexpected turns
- Fair payment model
- Good characters
Cons:
- The "Special ability" of this game is under used
- Mechanically, it does nothing ground breaking

Life is Strange has the shape of the game I want to play - but whether or not it ends up being the magnificent sculpture that I hope it is, is dependant upon the next four episodes yet to be released. Still, it's a strong start for Dontnod Entertainment's sophomore effort and I am cautiously, optimistically charmed by this rendering of a small Oregon seaside town. It's pretty much all plot setup for the first episode of the game: meeting all the characters, taking a walkabout the setting and getting absorbed into a world.
That said, some of the writing is a little bit awkward. A lot of a bit awkward, really. Most of it is intentional (I think) since it's a story primarily about teenagers transitioning into adulthood and all the wonderful awkwardness that period of life entails. The story keeps a whole lot of balls in the air: high school drama and the unspoken social hierarchies, rich high school kids with too much money and not enough sense, loners and "the alternate crowd" who are not nearly as rebellious as they think they are, and all of them with private lives they keep hidden to project these "proper" images of themselves. Some (a lot) of it is perhaps a little bit straightforward (the rich ♥♥♥♥♥ turns out to be a lonely girl, the jerkass jock is a bundle of psychological issues) but it's nice to see a game that lets you explore these tiny minutiae of everyday life at a slower, more thoughtful pace.
And then there's the other kind of awkwardness - one which comes from something being originally written in another language and then translated into English correctly on a TECHNICAL level, but perhaps not so much on... the spiritual level? Some of the slang is a bit on the hella off. And if you just winced at my wonky use of the word "hella" in that previous sentence, then you're going to be in for a MARVELLOUS time. That word gets used in ways that were probably never used before until this very game. And I'm willing to forget the one unironic use of the phrase "awesome sauce" if you are. Brrrr. I feel like the script could have used a couple more passes to smooth out some of the rougher spots but it's great for the most part and functional when it's not so great (if, yanno, awkward).
The voice acting deserves a lot of praise, as well. Hannah Telle carries the majority of the game as Max, the main character, and her performance conveys a perfect blend of introverted, gangly klutziness and self-aware hipster youth. Meanwhile, Ashly Burch's rebellious teen Chloe is a real revelation - I really only know her work as Tiny Tina from Borderlands 2 and Hey Ash Whatcha Playin', so to hear her playing this more down-to-earth lower key character is all kinds of amazing. But she still couldn't make that "awesome sauce" line work. Sorry.
I also love the time travelling mechanic used in this game. Basically, at any point you can hold down a button, go back a couple of seconds and redo any major (or minor) decisions you may have made in that time. It's the perfect metaphor for OCD people like me who save and reload games in order to get the "perfect result" from a conversation with a character (tis part of the neverending quest of Dragon Age: Inquisition to get 100% approval with every character). The best part is that Max retains the knowledge of whatever major snafu you rewound back from, which adds a wonderful bit of leaning on the fourth wall: acknowledging the branching nature of the game's narrative design in the game's story itself. This is something I've only really seen in games like 999 and Virtue's Last Reward and wish the concept were explored more in games. It's the kind of narrative device that can only be told in an interactive medium like games, I feel.
Visually, the game's environments have a kind of quiet beauty that leans more towards an impressionistic rendering of high school life. A lot of the environmental details are vague outlines or splashes of colour, with the more important details fleshed and fully drawn in. It's a nicely artistic touch that gently steers the eyes (and players) towards more significant landmarks like other characters and interactable items. That said, some of the character models look a little bit out of place in this mellow setting and the lip synch for dialogue in this game is possibly the worst I've seen in recent memory. Considering how much careful attention to detail was placed in putting together, say, a rebellious teen's bedroom filled with nostalgic memories of the past - the lip synch issue is kind of a strange misstep.
And the music is so hipster. It is soooooooo hipster. I love it. But it is so, so, SO hipster. Acoustic guitars, soft male vocals crooning about soft summers and waterfalls. God, I want to punch myself in the face. But I love it. It's just... the PERFECT match for this game and the mood it's going for and oh no my fist is in my face how did that happen
TL;DR I liked Life is Strange episode 1. Hoping for more good stuff in future episodes.

Have you ever said something and wished you could take it back? Had a conversation or argument and then thought of a better thing to say afterword? We've all been there, had those moments where we wish we could just go back and have a do-over. Max, a photography student returning to her home town for classes, has surely been there. Teen drama, wrong answers in class, a missed opportunity for that perfect shot.
Well this is where Max gets one over on us all. Without knowing why, she suddenly gains the ability to skip back in time, even through important conversations and previous choices. This is the core gameplay mechanic of Life Is Strange. In a game where your choices can have far reaching consequences, being able to change your mind gives players the chance to see an event take place in several ways, as well as to go back and retry a conversation with new information and choices available.
I want to mention that I absolutely love games that are purely story driven, all the more when the player's choices have real effects on how the story turns out. The sense of immersion a player gets from feeling like they are really in charge of their own choices is wonderful, and I think the devs at DONTNOD Entertainment have done a wonderful job on this. Players who enjoyed Telltale's Walking Dead games will most likely enjoy this as well.

Life is Strange has the shape of the game I want to play - but whether or not it ends up being the magnificent sculpture that I hope it is, is dependant upon the next four episodes yet to be released. Still, it's a strong start for Dontnod Entertainment's sophomore effort and I am cautiously, optimistically charmed by this rendering of a small Oregon seaside town. It's pretty much all plot setup for the first episode of the game: meeting all the characters, taking a walkabout the setting and getting absorbed into a world.
That said, some of the writing is a little bit awkward. A lot of a bit awkward, really. Most of it is intentional (I think) since it's a story primarily about teenagers transitioning into adulthood and all the wonderful awkwardness that period of life entails. The story keeps a whole lot of balls in the air: high school drama and the unspoken social hierarchies, rich high school kids with too much money and not enough sense, loners and "the alternate crowd" who are not nearly as rebellious as they think they are, and all of them with private lives they keep hidden to project these "proper" images of themselves. Some (a lot) of it is perhaps a little bit straightforward (the rich ♥♥♥♥♥ turns out to be a lonely girl, the jerkass jock is a bundle of psychological issues) but it's nice to see a game that lets you explore these tiny minutiae of everyday life at a slower, more thoughtful pace.
And then there's the other kind of awkwardness - one which comes from something being originally written in another language and then translated into English correctly on a TECHNICAL level, but perhaps not so much on... the spiritual level? Some of the slang is a bit on the hella off. And if you just winced at my wonky use of the word "hella" in that previous sentence, then you're going to be in for a MARVELLOUS time. That word gets used in ways that were probably never used before until this very game. And I'm willing to forget the one unironic use of the phrase "awesome sauce" if you are. Brrrr. I feel like the script could have used a couple more passes to smooth out some of the rougher spots but it's great for the most part and functional when it's not so great (if, yanno, awkward).
The voice acting deserves a lot of praise, as well. Hannah Telle carries the majority of the game as Max, the main character, and her performance conveys a perfect blend of introverted, gangly klutziness and self-aware hipster youth. Meanwhile, Ashly Burch's rebellious teen Chloe is a real revelation - I really only know her work as Tiny Tina from Borderlands 2 and Hey Ash Whatcha Playin', so to hear her playing this more down-to-earth lower key character is all kinds of amazing. But she still couldn't make that "awesome sauce" line work. Sorry.
I also love the time travelling mechanic used in this game. Basically, at any point you can hold down a button, go back a couple of seconds and redo any major (or minor) decisions you may have made in that time. It's the perfect metaphor for OCD people like me who save and reload games in order to get the "perfect result" from a conversation with a character (tis part of the neverending quest of Dragon Age: Inquisition to get 100% approval with every character). The best part is that Max retains the knowledge of whatever major snafu you rewound back from, which adds a wonderful bit of leaning on the fourth wall: acknowledging the branching nature of the game's narrative design in the game's story itself. This is something I've only really seen in games like 999 and Virtue's Last Reward and wish the concept were explored more in games. It's the kind of narrative device that can only be told in an interactive medium like games, I feel.
Visually, the game's environments have a kind of quiet beauty that leans more towards an impressionistic rendering of high school life. A lot of the environmental details are vague outlines or splashes of colour, with the more important details fleshed and fully drawn in. It's a nicely artistic touch that gently steers the eyes (and players) towards more significant landmarks like other characters and interactable items. That said, some of the character models look a little bit out of place in this mellow setting and the lip synch for dialogue in this game is possibly the worst I've seen in recent memory. Considering how much careful attention to detail was placed in putting together, say, a rebellious teen's bedroom filled with nostalgic memories of the past - the lip synch issue is kind of a strange misstep.
And the music is so hipster. It is soooooooo hipster. I love it. But it is so, so, SO hipster. Acoustic guitars, soft male vocals crooning about soft summers and waterfalls. God, I want to punch myself in the face. But I love it. It's just... the PERFECT match for this game and the mood it's going for and oh no my fist is in my face how did that happen
TL;DR I liked Life is Strange episode 1. Hoping for more good stuff in future episodes.

Life is Strange is a narrative driven point and click adventure game. You play as a young girl named Max, in school for photography. It does a good job at portraying modern youth but it does have a twist that you'll find out early into the game. With out saying too much that twist will play a fairly large role in the small instances of puzzle solving that's featured in episode one. You'll also be making choices through out the game and each choice will have an impact on the overall outcome.
I'll be honest, I didn't really expect to like the game to much based solely on the theme of the game. I ended up getting it because of it's low price and great looking visuals. I really do like the art design in this game. I features an almost acrylic hand painted texture style that really carries the game's aesthetic.
I'm glad I ended up getting it and playing it through. Life is Strange is well written, the characters, though typical in archetype, has a lot of depth. Both the main and supporting cast all show flaws, and strengths. Traits that may seem obvious, then get's contradicted by a story revel. It is the level of intricacies in each character that I enjoyed the most.
Overall, Life is Strange is a surprising little gem. The theme might not be for every one, but what it does it does pretty well.

I bought this game based on the reviews it got and because I thought it would be cool to play as a female photography student. Unfortunately, the game is underwhelming so far and I regret buying it.
Cons:
- Persisting bugs, e.g. with sound duplication, taking away from the enjoyment.
- Only Episode 1 out now, and very, very short. Misleading info on page regarding the other Episodes.
- Graphics and Animation feel outdated (atrocious lip sync for example)
- A lot of boring interaction that does not further the plot. Looped boring music.
- Unrealistic, where it should have been realistic to further immersion:
YOU DO NOT SHAKE A POLAROID! It drives me crazy each time I see her doing this. Unlike what that song says, if you shake a Polaroid while it is developing you do not aid the development but instead run risk of breaking the emulsion layer, ruining the photo. I also have experienced this first-hand, it really detracts from the game. As does the fact that you DON'T SIMPLY TEAR A POLAROID. You cannot tear a Polaroid with bare hands, as the plastic foil is too strong. You only get a few millimeters deep where there is only paper. If you tear from the broad end you tear through the chemicals reservoir spilling the caustic developer paste that can burn/irritate your skin. I also know this from first-hand experience and it shows that the subject has not been researched. Several other issues in the story are also poorly researched. Example: If you get a flu shot and then get a flu-like illness, IT IS NOT THE FLU. It is a viral infection that
and is totally unrelated to the flu shot. The protagonist's view of flu vaccination is highly problematic, as it is being disseminated to a lay audience that could be influenced by this and miss out on necessary vaccinations. Other views/stanced are also problematic, like the friend-zoned "white knight" Warren. What is this crap? This whole hipster take on life by the protagonist ("Chloe would never use animal products") ("If I had taken that picture it would be the deer sitting on your♥♥♥♥♥quot;) is over the top.
Pros: None. Boring. Go play another game. Unless you are a full hipster.
