Where to begin in Life is Strange. *avoiding as many spoilers as possible*
Let's start here. You play as Max Caufield. She just recently had her 18th birthday and attends a popular school for Art and Artistic career fields, in our case, a photographer, taught none other then by Mr. Jefferson. The location is in Arcadia Bay a city in Oregon and a very beautiful city at that. Max has been through tough times and is recently coming back to our school, which is Blackwell Academy. Blackwell Academy may b e an academy of the arts but is still very much a High School, so because of that reason, you will notice a ton of typical behavior from a high  school student. We are Seniors this year and it appears our objective is to enter a photo for the "Everyday Heroes" contest. This contest will be a one photo, approved on the correct paper for entry. Max here hasn't found her "it" photo for the contest at least not yet. You play as Max going through her life, experiencing what every student in high school and even college has or will face at some point in time. The typical, I want to listen to my music and drone out the world, attitude. That will do for our backstory.
Speaking of music though (in our last point) the score is outstanding and you will find yourself wanting to: A) buy the soundtrack and B) explore the game to listen to all of the music. The music has a modern yet very nostalgic feel to it and impacts the game immensly. You will see that the music just fits for every point the game has.
When you put together an outstanding protagonist character, a good role of supporting cast, interesting gameplay and game mechanics, you get a very solid and highly satisfying gaming experience.
You will want to play this with a very high quality headset or speaker as you will spend a lot of time in this game reading the character profiles, checking your objectives, seeing your achievements (so to speak by through the optional pictures to take) and handy Journal mechanic in the game. Throughout the game you will want to check this frequently (or should you prefer it can alert you of just the important things) for updates such as text messages and journal entries and other smaller menu tasks.
Other things to say about this game. Achievements are a breeze in this game because of the oh so handy Collectible Mode. Now without going to far into the game (as to not spoil) this mode essentially allows you to go back and go through the options to get the rest of the achievements without having to alter your game in any way. You can literally go back into a chapter where you may have missed something, get it and continue your game where you left off at the most recent checkpoint.
This game is outstanding and at the price of 4.99 per episode or 19.99 makes for a solid game and very much worth the purchase.
Overall Pros****
-Character Development (reading through the profiles you really learn these characters you will interact with)
-Music (the score is breathtaking and modern in every way but doesn't let the pop culture get to it, very nostalgic)
-Controls (the controls are failry straightforward with minor detailing done well and done right)
-Highlighted items. (this is separate because this feature allows the player to know what they can and cannot interactive quickly and easily without causing any hiccup in game play whatsoever)
- Texture (the shadowing, the lighting, the miniscule details in this game at HD quality are great, nothing fancy just done right)
-Pacing (the pacing of this game is just right, you can do it completely at your own pace.)
-Art design (this games art design is so well done, each character has a design that will fit exactly how you pictured them if they were written on paper)
-Voice Acting (the voice acting in this game is just superb, the quality and crispness of the voices add that to the art design and your characters are memorable, within minutes of reading the logs of each character I had them memorized by name and it made it feel more personal to me.)
Cons*****
-Audio bugs *may not happen to everyone*  During the last segment of the game I had the audio clip out and the framerate drop and that had the final scenes of the game lose audio but with a simple reset it fixed it just fine for the audio not the framerate but that could be any number of things so I am not faulting the game for that.
-Voice Synching: The voice syncing in this game is just terrible, you will have some characters talk but their mouths will never move and many many times the sound coming out of the character will not match the movement or articulation of the jaw, tongue, uvula, etc (This needs to be fixed but it doesn't ruin the game by any means)
Subjectional Cons
-Length, for some people 5 dollars for an hour and half gameplay is too short and feels like a rip off, but that is just for some. My playthrough was just over 4 hours and I enjoyed each and every single minute of the game
-Character. some will find the characters lacking on screen or their personalities not coming through and for some it might not be enough development to get a bonding for these characters which is understandable
-Art style for some the art style alone could turn some players off from enjoying the game but for me I loved it and enjoyed it.
-Swearing. There is a fair amount of swearing in this game as well as sexual innuendos as the game is made around the high school life so there are things that could have been avoided. For my taste there were a bit of swearing. I don't mind a little but I tend to not swear and reading all the logs and character details when there are a lot of swearing then it will put some people off
-Grammer some of the things in the game are flat out grammatically incorrect and spelling errors and slang are used a lot there will be points in the game where reading the text is a challenge because of the font, way its written and how it is written.
Overall Score*****
On a scale, ranging from one-to-ten this game scores a very high 8.4. The game play is simple and straightforward with an easy to learn mechanic that can become challenging or intuitive as the player progresses but not to the point where you don't want to use this mechanic so a good balance. Overall outstanding concept and very satisfactory execution that paces well and doesn't punish the user too harsly for certain actions. The main supporting cast of characters do a great job of setting the protagonist a number of different options each having their own set of consequences that overall can change the game from small little things. Things that don't seem important can change the entire game at a later point without you even knowing it but, the main character fits the role of high school student so well and the music just brings it on home. The voice synching could be done better, more polished, but its not unbearable or game breaking and so with that being said will conclude this review.

tldr: If you like choice-based adventures, a degree of mind-screwiness and an overall rather ponderous, numbly threatening mood, this game is definitely for you.
After the first Episode, I must say that this is different from other Choice-based Adventures (like Wolf Among Us or Walking Dead) in several ways, but with that comes a whole different atmosphere and style, which is what makes it a grand experience. Just try not to pay too much attention to the Juno-esque "teen-speak" dialogue that crops up occasionally.
For one episode, assume a playtime similar to the Telltale games (2 hours). However, the rewind-mechanic (the main character's ability to rewind time and get a redo on a decision she made within the same scene) changes how you make decisions. You now see the short-term benefit or repercussions, but the long-term fallout or fruits of your doing is just as nebulous as ever. Since you do get punished or rewarded right this instant though, you will find yourself taxed a lot harder than in similar games to make the right decision.
Life is Strange is fascinating in that it doesn't really disclose where its story is meant to be going. Sure, there's a fairly huge damocleic sword that appears at the conclusion of the first episode, but where Wolf had already played most of its hand, Life is Strange keeps the player guessing.

I Recommend it. A must have.

In terms of core mechanics, Life is Strange brings nothing new. Overall, the game is very similar in structure to Telltale's adventure games, opting for the modern approach to the adventure genre seen in games like the Walking Dead. Beyond the typical explore, point and click interactions of the Walking Dead, the only novel addition is the "Rewind" ability, which ties into the plot but also has the side effect of allowing you to experience a couple of different actions before comitting to their consequences. This "Rewind" feature comes directly from Dontnod's previous title, Remember Me, which similarly had sequences that allowed you to try out multiple actions before committing to one that worked.
Stylistically, the game is reminiscent of Remember Me, although it was made with a different design team and has an aesthetic more befitting of the tone and setting. On the whole, I think most players will be able to appreciate the visual aspects of the game, which I consider to be a step above those seen in the Walking Dead. One thing to note is that this comes at the cost of performance. I've found that on my machine, I have the same problems for this that I had for Remember Me - occasional hits in FPS coupled with a slowdown in the audio. I've also had to lower graphics settings a bit, but otherwise the game plays well enough on my basic Intel HD graphics.
So far only episode 1 has been released, so it is hard to say much about the plot. In contrast to the Drama/Action feel of the Walking Dead, Life is Strange seems to have a lighter, Drama/Slice of Life feel. The school setting of episode 1 is a bit easy to relate to, especially for younger players who are still in school or who have been in school recently. It will be interesting to see where things go in the later episodes - whether the plot adopts more or less realism. The closest comparison that I can make from what I have seen so far is that the themes of episode 1 are similar to those of a recent anime called Nagi no Asu Kara, which dealt with settling into a new school, encountering hostile students and adults, and trying to grow up against a backdrop of seamingly unlikely environmental changes.
On the whole, I can recommend this game for three groups of people - fans of the Telltale adventure games, fans of Remember Me, and fans of the Slice of Life genre. Unfortunately the same features of the game thay may allow it to appeal to those groups may make it a turnoff for others.

After playing episode 1 of this, I can definitely say this game was made with a lot of love from its developers. The world of Arcadia Bay is very well realized, the characters are believable and the mechanic of Max's powers is intertwined with the game in a way that feels natural once you get the hang of it.
It's like someone noticed the practice of "save-scumming", ie, reloading a save in a game whenever you get an adverse outcome from doing something, and said, "hey, let's make that the character's *actual power*". On a meta level, it's pretty amusing, and it provides for a well balanced power - while Max can fix obvious mistakes, the limit on how far back she can go to change time means she can't always foresee the larger complications of her choices.
The main character herself is adorkable and thoroughly believable as a protagonist. She does second-guess every single major decision no matter what she chooses, but when you have the power to retry something as many times as you want trying to get it "right", wouldn't you?
Cons:
* It took me an embarassingly long time to figure out the 'click and drag' action mechanic. Maybe I just needed more coffee?
* The game goes way too far with having a literal popup saying "THIS ACTION WILL HAVE CONSEQUENCES!!!" at major decision points. If I carelessly leave evidence while searching someone's secret files, or rat out the school's richest kid to the authorities, I shouldn't need the game to tell me that this may come back to haunt me. It's a good thing to have a game where your choices impact the story in meaningful ways, but "show me, don't tell me" applies. An option to turn this off would greatly improve the game.
* The lip synch of the character models can be a little jarring if you pay too much attention to it. Which isn't helped by me pointing it out. But there it is.

Life is Strange isn't a game - it's an experience. It envelopes you in a mix of teenage nostalgia with many moments that even feel like vague memories of your own. When Max is gifted supernatural time-traveling abilities, you feel like you are right there with her. Looking at the world through her lens can really open up your own eyes to how the seemingly insignificant choices you make in real life can have sweeping effects. It is engulfing - a beautiful first episode that plays as good as it looks. The intuitive interface doesn't distract from the immersion of the world - this really shows how character centered the developers were. You can truly tell this game was made with a lot of heart and dedication.

This is absolutely one of the best games I've seen in years.
Similar to the Telltale series games, in that they're episodic and you make choices.
But different in every other respect.  The choices you make can be undone as you rewind time, causing an unpredictable butterfly effect.  And you really can't predict what changes you've made are going to do - it was a lot more obvious in The Walking Dead / Wolf Among Us to see where your decision would lead to.
This is a lot more like real life - you knocked something over, this is going to have consequences... but what - possibly, is it going to do?  You have no idea.  You just have to hope it's nothing bad.
The storywriting is incredible, the carefully selected and amazing soundtrack setting the mood perfectly.  Something strange happens to Max (the protagonist) in the otherwise calm and quiet town of Arcadia - home of Blackwell Academy; a prestigious academy where she studies photography.
And something really bad about to happen.  Or is it?  Can you stop it?
You will just lose yourself in this.  Immersive and revolutionary.
I cannot recommend this enough.

tldr: If you like choice-based adventures, a degree of mind-screwiness and an overall rather ponderous, numbly threatening mood, this game is definitely for you.
After the first Episode, I must say that this is different from other Choice-based Adventures (like Wolf Among Us or Walking Dead) in several ways, but with that comes a whole different atmosphere and style, which is what makes it a grand experience. Just try not to pay too much attention to the Juno-esque "teen-speak" dialogue that crops up occasionally.
For one episode, assume a playtime similar to the Telltale games (2 hours). However, the rewind-mechanic (the main character's ability to rewind time and get a redo on a decision she made within the same scene) changes how you make decisions. You now see the short-term benefit or repercussions, but the long-term fallout or fruits of your doing is just as nebulous as ever. Since you do get punished or rewarded right this instant though, you will find yourself taxed a lot harder than in similar games to make the right decision.
Life is Strange is fascinating in that it doesn't really disclose where its story is meant to be going. Sure, there's a fairly huge damocleic sword that appears at the conclusion of the first episode, but where Wolf had already played most of its hand, Life is Strange keeps the player guessing.

I Recommend it. A must have.

After playing episode 1 of this, I can definitely say this game was made with a lot of love from its developers. The world of Arcadia Bay is very well realized, the characters are believable and the mechanic of Max's powers is intertwined with the game in a way that feels natural once you get the hang of it.
It's like someone noticed the practice of "save-scumming", ie, reloading a save in a game whenever you get an adverse outcome from doing something, and said, "hey, let's make that the character's *actual power*". On a meta level, it's pretty amusing, and it provides for a well balanced power - while Max can fix obvious mistakes, the limit on how far back she can go to change time means she can't always foresee the larger complications of her choices.
The main character herself is adorkable and thoroughly believable as a protagonist. She does second-guess every single major decision no matter what she chooses, but when you have the power to retry something as many times as you want trying to get it "right", wouldn't you?
Cons:
* It took me an embarassingly long time to figure out the 'click and drag' action mechanic. Maybe I just needed more coffee?
* The game goes way too far with having a literal popup saying "THIS ACTION WILL HAVE CONSEQUENCES!!!" at major decision points. If I carelessly leave evidence while searching someone's secret files, or rat out the school's richest kid to the authorities, I shouldn't need the game to tell me that this may come back to haunt me. It's a good thing to have a game where your choices impact the story in meaningful ways, but "show me, don't tell me" applies. An option to turn this off would greatly improve the game.
* The lip synch of the character models can be a little jarring if you pay too much attention to it. Which isn't helped by me pointing it out. But there it is.

In my years of gaming, rarely do I see a game of this magnitude released by the gaming industry. This game takes us away from the fast-pace shooters or the open-world survival games we've all been so engulf by these late years, and gives the gamer something they can actually relate to: Real life. This game takes us into a world that we've all been through, just from different angles, and tries to show us every angle. I find this game hitting close to home, because I lived a life similar to Max (Minus the time turning aspect of course!).
The game is beautifully created, and I dare say "perfected" to be a masterpiece of storytelling. The art is amazing, the soundtrack is fantastic, and the story is mind-blowing. I highly recommend everyone to buy at least the first epsiode of the game, even if your into these types of games, because after the first twenty minutes of gameplay: you will be.

THIS REVIEW MAY CHANGE AS EPISODES ARE RELEASED
I don't know what's up with people overreacting to games with a different approach to storytelling. It seems that everything that doesn't involve explosions and guns is an instant masterpiece for most reviewers. While this game tries to be different from most games by being more story-driven and less interactive (even though we can walk by ourselves and "explore"), it is basically focused on decision making and seeing how that affects the story. Now don't get me wrong, that is a good thing, but the story in this game is too childish for it to attract my eye.
The problem with this game is that they made the characters too young, specially the main one who is 18 buy behaves like a 14-year-old. There's so much teen angst in her personality that it makes me want to rewind time back to when she was a toddler and change the way their parents raised her. Most of her dialogues are simply idiotic, and it seems that she keeps wanting to rewind time just to get the right answers for meaningless conversations. Is there anything more pathetic than that?
So far, the story is bland and poorly executed. I don't want to spoil anyone, but honestly, who gives a ♥♥♥♥ about what's going to happen?
Concerning the main game, there are some issues:
- Lip-sync: as many have mentioned, this has to be one of the worst lip-sync'ed games I've ever seen. They didn't even bother
- FOV (field of view): TOO DAMN CLOSE. I have to almost to 360 turns to see♥♥♥♥♥♥around me
- Graphics: it's clear they approached this "let's make it look like a canvas painting" style to save resources and textures. Some people will like it, some will hate it
- Soundtrack: I read many people saying how awesome the soundtrack in this game was. It simply isn't. Every song sounds like (a couple of chords strum on an acoustic guitar and some soft pop lyrics). There's even a part where a character gets warned to "turn that punk♥♥♥♥♥♥down" when the music sounded more like Lady Gaga than like Sex Pistols.
As a piece of advice, and to sum it up, I’d recommend you to wait for all the episodes to be released and then see if reviews are still positive. I ordered them all after I jumped the hype wagon and I will be playing it and updating this review to reflect my final opinion on this, even though I don’t have high hopes for this.

I loved everything about this. It has a polished and refined presentation which uses the character's love of art to create an interesting and cohesive UI, along with the instagram-esque filters over the top to boost that artistic feeling whilst also adding whimsy and nostalgia for being young. It has characters with depth who all do questionable things and who you actually care about and Max is an endearing and likeably awkward lead. It would take someone younger than me to gauge whether some of the writing is cringey because  teenagers say cringey things, or whether it is just the clumsy writing of somebody trying to write younger than themselves, but having been a teenager, heard teenagers, and with the game being set in 2013, I'm inclined to give it the benefit of the doubt, and it works regardless. I love that it isn't afraid to take its time and that there are parts where you can just sit and contemplate, or read your journal, or take photographs and you are rewarded for exploring. This is most obvious in the rewind mechanic which is not only key for solving a lot of the puzzles, but also allows you to test out the short term consequences of your decisions. By removing the time constraints on decisions it puts greater emphasis on character rather than plot, but without losing any of the impact because the long term effects of your actions may not be felt for a considerable amount of time (the game isn't subtle about its chaos theory references). It has a great soundtrack that adds to the indie-film vibe and it's integrated really well into the characters' lives, further fleshing them out. Finally there's the slightly weird story itself that combines a teenage coming of age tale with a missing person mystery, resulting in a blend of Gone Home, Alan Wake, Twin Peaks and various other bits and bobs to form something compelling and unique. Overall, I went from expecting a flawed, derivative, but interesting experience to being completely drawn into one of the most earnest, genuine and absorbing games which left me with a warm, fuzzy feeling and an eagerness to see where it goes from here.

Great game so far (episode one), looks beautiful, very interesting story. I like that they offer a lot of optional details such as the journal and photographs, as well as a lot of actions that are skippable if you go straight to each destination. Those details really help to make you feel connected to the story.
My main issue with this game is the dialogue which would seem on point if the protagonist was around 15, but she's 18 and an introvert at that, so it feels to me that her thoughts and writings should be a tad wiser, as well as the dialogue of her classmates.
My only other critique is the lack of connections between events. For example, at Chloe's house, I had looked at about 5 different items that revealed the identity of Chloe's stepdad before I found the one item where Max actually reacts (though not a lot) to finding out his identity. Similar issue when Max gets into Chloe's car and doesn't react to realizing she was the one in the bathroom, I feel like a simple voiceover could have cleared that up.
I still highly recommend Life is Strange and don't regret having bought each episode.

This game takes us into a world that we've all been through, just from different angles, and tries to show us every angle. I don't know what's up with people overreacting to games with a different approach to storytelling. It seems that everything that doesn't involve explosions and guns is an instant masterpiece for most reviewers. While this game tries to be different from most games by being more story-driven and less interactive (even though we can walk by ourselves and "explore"), it is basically focused on decision making and seeing how that affects the story. Now don't get me wrong, that is a good thing, but the story in this game is too childish for it to attract my eye.
The problem with this game is that they made the characters too young, specially the main one who is 18 buy behaves like a 14-year-old. There's so much teen angst in her personality that it makes me want to rewind time back to when she was a toddler and change the way their parents raised her. Most of her dialogues are simply idiotic, and it seems that she keeps wanting to rewind time just to get the right answers for meaningless conversations. Is there anything more pathetic than that?
So far, the story is bland and poorly executed. I don't want to spoil anyone, but honestly, who gives a ♥♥♥♥ about what's going to happen?
Concerning the main game, there are some issues:
- Lip-sync: as many have mentioned, this has to be one of the worst lip-sync'ed games I've ever seen. They didn't even bother
- FOV (field of view): TOO DAMN CLOSE. I have to almost to 360 turns to see♥♥♥♥♥♥around me
- Graphics: it's clear they approached this "let's make it look like a canvas painting" style to save resources and textures. Some people will like it, some will hate it
- Soundtrack: I read many people saying how awesome the soundtrack in this game was. It simply isn't. Every song sounds like (a couple of chords strum on an acoustic guitar and some soft pop lyrics). There's even a part where a character gets warned to "turn that punk♥♥♥♥♥♥down" when the music sounded more like Lady Gaga than like Sex Pistols.
As a piece of advice, and to sum it up, I’d recommend you to wait for all the episodes to be released and then see if reviews are still positive. I ordered them all after I jumped the hype wagon and I will be playing it and updating this review to reflect my final opinion on this, even though I don’t have high hopes for this.

I loved everything about this. It has a polished and refined presentation which uses the character's love of art to create an interesting and cohesive UI, along with the instagram-esque filters over the top to boost that artistic feeling whilst also adding whimsy and nostalgia for being young. It has characters with depth who all do questionable things and who you actually care about and Max is an endearing and likeably awkward lead. It would take someone younger than me to gauge whether some of the writing is cringey because  teenagers say cringey things, or whether it is just the clumsy writing of somebody trying to write younger than themselves, but having been a teenager, heard teenagers, and with the game being set in 2013, I'm inclined to give it the benefit of the doubt, and it works regardless. I love that it isn't afraid to take its time and that there are parts where you can just sit and contemplate, or read your journal, or take photographs and you are rewarded for exploring. This is most obvious in the rewind mechanic which is not only key for solving a lot of the puzzles, but also allows you to test out the short term consequences of your decisions. By removing the time constraints on decisions it puts greater emphasis on character rather than plot, but without losing any of the impact because the long term effects of your actions may not be felt for a considerable amount of time (the game isn't subtle about its chaos theory references). It has a great soundtrack that adds to the indie-film vibe and it's integrated really well into the characters' lives, further fleshing them out. Finally there's the slightly weird story itself that combines a teenage coming of age tale with a missing person mystery, resulting in a blend of Gone Home, Alan Wake, Twin Peaks and various other bits and bobs to form something compelling and unique. Overall, I went from expecting a flawed, derivative, but interesting experience to being completely drawn into one of the most earnest, genuine and absorbing games which left me with a warm, fuzzy feeling and an eagerness to see where it goes from here.

This review will be updated as new episodes come out. I'll try my best to avoid spoilers as this is an highly story-driven game!
As of Episode 3 I'll also start giving each episode a rating, as for the game so far.
Ep. 1: I very much like the way the plot slowly thickens, giving you the opportunity to explore everything and everyone at your pace. The choices you have seem to make some impact but I believe, and want them to be, longer lasting than just the first episode.
For now, I'll just say what everyone has been saying: if you liked Telltale's The Walking Dead, this follows the same book but has nice different touches in gameplay and in the characters.
I can't recommend you buy the entire season (although I did), but if you like story and character-driven games, and you liked TWD, I can't recommend this first episode enough! Nice effort by DONTNOD!
I give this one a 9/10 but that can be expected while you're still getting to know the world and its characters.
Ep. 2: This is where you can tell if the episodic format really will work or not, and I'm delighted to say it most certainly will. I like the wider and wider gap in between choices you made before, kind of like the "butterfly effect" most time travel theories base themselves upon. Important decisions made before and during Episode 2 CAN have major consequences in this episode; I really like the variety of outcomes the story seems to be able to take. Also, character development! The money spent on the Season Pass seems more and more like a good value!
I'll give this one a 9/10 too.
Ep. 3: This is when the story starts to grip you, when it all starts to get more serious and your choices start to have real consequences.  Past decisions start to matter to the story and to some of the more important characters as well, including the protagonist! I also like the ever growing character development in this episode, including Max's which is shaped by your own actions. But the best, story-wise (or worst if you started caring for the characters as I did) comes at the end, when you will start questioning YOUR choices and what you could do to have a different outcome in the end. And there's some subtle but very well made irony in this one.
Even if the two next episodes aren't as good (and they have no reason to be, as the quality has only been going up), this episode alone is worth getting the Season Pass.
10/10 definitely. The story starts to grip you and you find yourself at the end of it wanting more.

I just played through the first episode of Life is Strange. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥I really love this game. For those of you that don't know what it is, its a story based episodic game about a girl who discovers she has the power to rewind short periods of time. This time rewind mechanic is used to solve puzzles, but it can also be used to try all of the dialogue options before committing to them. This is really neat because even though you know all the options, it's never clear which is the right one and once a certain period of time has pasted, you can no longer go back and change your choice. Despite the occasional irritating bits of puzzle game logic
, theres something that really draws me to this game. While it doesn't have a whole lot of game play aside from the puzzles (it's kind of like a third person Telltale game), it has a really interesting/ unique premise and the story is well written and compelling enough to make me keep playing to find out what happens next. The voice acting is very good, and the actors do a good job of making their characters feel believable. While some of the art assets are a bit eh (its running in Unreal 3), the game still has a really nice aesthetic which is helped out by a fantastic soundtrack that really adds alot to the atmosphere of the game.
So yeah, thats my terrible review of Life is Strange. You can pick up episode 1 for about $5 on steam right now, I would highly recommend trying it.

Okay, so, I am a big fan of telltale's interactive story "games", and went into this with many past story game experiences under my belt. I was expecting something good, based on steam's reviews and my past experience with such games, and boy was I in for a surprise.
I was expecting something good, but what I got was something phenomenal. Sure, the mouth flaps didn't sync perfectly with the voice acting, but damn it I don't care! Right away I was interested in our main heroine and her journey into becoming a photographer, I expected a slice of life take on entering adulthood and going your own way, but I was immediately surprised by a twist I wasn't expecting, having gone into the game relatively cold of knowledge about it's story. The characters are all believable, and through "natural" voice acting from some lesser known actors, the characters get a new layer of realism and allow you to identify with, and relate to them a little more easily.
The only game I can equate this to from any past experience I've had is probably "Gone Home", it's a very personal quest that Max is on, trying to find herself, and then she gets mixed up in a totally bizarro situation, but the whole thing is sort of grounded in this believable, real world.
I sat down, dimmed the lights, put on my headphones, and lost myself in the awesomeness of this game's atmosphere and character. I beat the first "episode" in about a 3 hour session of play, and that's looking at everything, talking to everyone (sometimes a few times for different results) and generally getting the most out of the chapter, and at roughly 3 hours per episode, this series is looking to be a solid 15 hour epic! And for $5.50 for the first chapter, I'd say it's worth every cent.
I know these thoughts I'm having are sort of all over the place, it's because I'm having a hard time properly expressing just how much I enjoyed the first Episode of this series, and i am eagerly awaiting the next... and next and next installments.
I went into this game expecting a good time, and I came out being a little sad that I had already finished the first part and have to wait so long for the next. This wasn't just a game, it was an experience, I thought about my moments with the first episode for about 2 days after I finished, and am still mulling over the events, the atmosphere, the character, and of course the wonderful soundtrack of in game songs and themes.
So, in conclusion, I rambled a lot, but everything about my time with Life is Strange is great, I enjoyed every second of it, and I hope that everyone else does too. Get this game, if not then at LEAST get the first episode to wet your feet, and see if you like it enough to take the (super affordable) 20 dollar plunge.
YES YES YES, get it.
EDIT: I have since of course finished the entirety of the game, and my thoughts have not wavered. The game gets incredibly more interesting and even quite dark, the feels overwhelm and you find yourself feeling sad alongside these characters you've come to see almost as friends of your own.
Life is Strange is the best game I've ever played, not because it's the most technically impressive, or has the best story, or has the best world... But because when I was playing; it was able to immerse me into this real world, it made me feel like I was apart of the story and interacting with these characters. I love this game, it's my favorite, and I got a tattoo, lest I never forget the impact this game has had on me.

Before posting anything, I would have to say that this game is made with the Unreal Engine, and like many Unreal Engine games, the sound output gets corrupted about 45+ minutes of play into the game along with other UE games like Mass Effect 1 (but not 2), Bioshock Infinite, and a couple other games.
So if you had problems with sound crackling in those games, this game will do it too sadly and there does not appear to be any fix for this whatsoever.
That said, the game itself is story-heavy and uses a consequence system that reminds me of Beyond: Two Souls with seperate paths branching off of each hard choice you make in the game, and the ability to rewind time is a cool idea. From what I've seen thusfar, the story was decently written, and the characters are believable. Pretty much life as a barely-18 girl in college or upper high school with all the things that would normally bring (and of course, the time rewind powers the protagonist has oddly).
If you like story-heavy interactive experiences, this game should be good for you. Also reminds me somewhat of Gone Home, 'cept this game has other characters to interact with and actual choices to make.

I just played through the first episode of Life is Strange. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥I really love this game. For those of you that don't know what it is, its a story based episodic game about a girl who discovers she has the power to rewind short periods of time. This time rewind mechanic is used to solve puzzles, but it can also be used to try all of the dialogue options before committing to them. This is really neat because even though you know all the options, it's never clear which is the right one and once a certain period of time has pasted, you can no longer go back and change your choice. Despite the occasional irritating bits of puzzle game logic
, theres something that really draws me to this game. While it doesn't have a whole lot of game play aside from the puzzles (it's kind of like a third person Telltale game), it has a really interesting/ unique premise and the story is well written and compelling enough to make me keep playing to find out what happens next. The voice acting is very good, and the actors do a good job of making their characters feel believable. While some of the art assets are a bit eh (its running in Unreal 3), the game still has a really nice aesthetic which is helped out by a fantastic soundtrack that really adds alot to the atmosphere of the game.
So yeah, thats my terrible review of Life is Strange. You can pick up episode 1 for about $5 on steam right now, I would highly recommend trying it.

[edit] All 5 episodes completed, with 100% achievements.
I bought this game given it was made by the developers of Remember Me, and liked their trailer. I had no idea of the vitriol about the game before playing it.
You are Max Caulfield, a student with a photography scholarship at a college, a little shy and insecure of her talent, you have to survive school (and a giant tornado, but I'll get onto that later). There's also the case of a missing student which remains unsolved.
Standard WSAD for movement, shift to jog, the only thing that you need to get used to is how to interact with the surroundings, holding the left mouse button down and then moving the mouse to choose the option (usually Look, Open, Photo, etc.). Objects you can interact with are pointed out with white text and arrow, and hovering your mouse over them results in the items being 'sketched' over. Occasionally you can't see the interaction since your character is in front of it (namely in closed quarters), so you have to guess where to aim, though these are few and far between.
Gameplay is not that of a standard game. Comparisons have been made with 'Gone Home', and it does feel like that, you can look at posters and they pop up on the screen showing everything on it. There is even an option click read so all the text is simply written out to read without all the images getting in the way. This is more of an exploration point and click.
If you were to just rush through and get to the end of the first episode, I wager it would take no longer than an hour, if you knew what you had to do.
However, this isn't what the developers had in mind, in my opinion. The world was made to be looked at, and I think I pretty much interacted with everything I could. Overall it took me 5 hours to see everything and test the time reversal power.
This isn't exactly a spoiler, since you see this in the very first scene of the game, but I have blocked it just in case.
This is a great introduction to the time rewind, since we know this event was happening now. A new aspect appears too. When Max doesn't know the answer to a question, and the rival student gives the correct answer, you can choose to rewind time and give the exact same answer!
Note that time rewind can be done by yourself whenever you want; there is no need to even do it once if you don't want to. The first time you really need to use it for the story to progress is to save the girl's life in the bathroom.
Using time rewind to give different answers is a subtle way, but another way you learn to use it is to cause events to happen by changing future events, such as gaining entry to a building and so on. You can even peek into private belongings and learn what there was in there, and then rewind time so the other person doesn't even know you have done so. The only restriction of the time control is that once you leave an area (i.e., school, dormitory etc.) you cannot rewind time to go back into the previous area, so important choices from there remain the same.
Onto the story itself, so far, it is mainly to do with learning about the different characters you can interact with, and also about your own self. It is a typical sleepy town and school, are has a very nostalgic feel to everything, and reminded me about school and university. There are several places you can just sit down and wonder about your life and new powers, leaning against a tree thinking about your choice to come back to the town, playing your guitar with a mellow tune, all lead me to like the character more since she is struggling to find her way in life, and if her choices are right in the end.
The game includes social media, memes (3.14 backwards equals PIE) and other throwbacks in the writing and artwork, references to Lord of the Rings, Twin Peaks, X-Files and other series are easy to find. A Facebook clone is seen in some screens, selfies, even Instagram style filters on certain scenes appear. The music is nothing pretentious and gives this feeling of relaxation overall, good voice acting, though lip syncing seemed to be off in most scenes, nothing game breaking though. Overall, it is quite a post-modernist game which pokes fun at this social media connected world, and quotes and integrates them in daily life. Even one great line appears in the game, which made me chuckle:
"Okay. I see you're a geek now with a great imagination, but this isn't an anime or a video game."
Which it obviously is, thus making me love the game more, since it realises that such things cannot be in reality, yet in that reality, it is true.
Good continuation, and brings more depth to the powers showing them off further, ending in a breath-taking finale.
One plotline is resolved, and we get a brand new power, which is admittedly used only once. Then, there is a horrid scene where you are completely unable to rewind time, which helps you realise how blase you can be without the ability. After this ending, you get an important new power, which changes the whole timelines, leaving you with an evil cliffhanger.
The huge change you made at the end of Episode 3 ends quickly, with a terrible decision to make. As you delve into the mystery of the missing student, you eventually get to find out exactly who was the perpetrator of it all ina nail-biting cliffhanger.
The finale. Using the time rewind power you got at the end of Episode 3, several times, you manage to escape, and then you have to come to terms with what your meddling with time has done.
The ending is a simple decision, and none of your previous choices will affect either one. I know this will upset most people who play the game, but think just how hard it is to actually code in several endings depending on your choices.
Overall, the game starts off like a university social life simulator 2015, later becoming more detective-like and uncovering the mystery. Max comments on big decisions, wondering if the other choice was better, and some choices which may seem obvious will have repercussions in future. Once in a while the game industry shows us that there is still space for gentle and poetic narratives, that gaming isnt all about blood, explosions and violence: it is, of course, a field that requires fantasy - real life is often dull, so, playing any sort of video game is, in a way, a retreat from this world to a more vivid and interesting one.
Still, this game tells the tale of a youngster, dealing with growing up, ostracism, loneliness, facing dreams about what life could be and the terrible fear of the ever dream-crushing reality. We've been there. Some of us are still dealing with it.  Some will never leave this painfull stage of life. That bit of fantasy is what defines the strangeness in "Life is Strange". without it, the title would be, perhaps, just real every-day dull life.

This game has to be my favorite episodic game so far... it's beautiful. The developers know how to bring out your emotions, I was full of hope then torn apart, I felt like a superhero then the next second I felt useless, I loved and I lost, I gained knowledge then felt played. This game made me feel it all happiness, sadness, love, depression, hopeless, hope, struggle, fear etc the list goes on... it's art and everyone should experience it at least once in their lives!
The game has a lot of good things about it and right off the bat is the options it's better than I expected it to be it has fullscreen, borderless and windowed mode. It has decent options plenty to play with but they only go up to high there's no ultra or anything like that. Keyboard and mouse work great and everything is rebindable, a controller also works straight out of the box with no problem. The graphics in this game are very pretty sometimes ugly here and there but for the most part it's gorgeous to look at. The gameplay is pretty much your typical episodic game type stuff except with a twist here you can rewind time giving you so much more possibilities to work with it's great fun! Plus the game has small time puzzles if your a fan of that. THE SOUNDTRACK IS BEAUTIFUL some of the best I've heard in a game to date, you can easily listen to it outside of the game... it's honestly worth a listen too. The story at first is your typical cliche teen flick but then rapidly changes... so don't be fooled by it's looks at first the game opens up a lot later on. The game is a good length I was expecting 12-15 hours and including 100% it's like 17 hours. The game does one thing right with collectibles they don't force you to go looking for them they want you to explore, talk and hell if you don't like that on the first run? You can simply always restart episodes in collectible mode which is super super super good plus one for that!
While I would love to say the game is perfect it's not I mean for one the puzzles there either too easy or too annoying it's not that fun to go through. Sometimes the story just drags on... I guess you get say they left in space to take breathers but honestly I didn't enjoy those parts. The game like I said before does have ugly looking textures, while I usually never complain about dumb crap like that... in this game though it is pretty noticeable like the hands GOD THE HANDS! While I'm sure some people like it there are things to the game that are so easily missable until you see them in the results screen making you scratch your head as in how the hell could you have possibly missed something like that. One minor problem I had was the game is screenshot madness which I love until an item you pick up gets stuck on your screen... bad design choice on that one should have made it a toggle off and on feature.
I think the game is wonderful and I would honestly recommend it to anyone like I said before it's something everyone should experience at least once in their lives... I cannot wait to see what's in store for us in season 2!

Now let me say, this is definitely not an official review because the complete series has yet to be released. That being said, i can already say I am going to really enjoy this game. If you have played any telltale series, this game follows a similar format. That being said, I believe this game is to telltale games as the first Deadspace was to the Resident Evil series. It took mechanics that worked in similar games and improved on them making it better than the original. Life is Strange is an episodic, story heavy, character driven game. However, unlike a telltale game which is cutscene heavy, and seems to focus on quicktime events , Life is Strange is more interactive. You have more control of your character and can roam the world freely. This doesnt just happen in specific areas like in A Wolf Among Us in toads apartment. You can explore dorm rooms, a high school campus, homes, parks, the list goes on. All of which are filled with characters that have some sort of personailty and individuality to them. There are stereotypical highschool characters such as the jocks and skaters which is a shame because they kind of feel forced. The main characters or the ones you interact with the most definitely have some depth. Cloe for example, is Max's old best friend who turned from a shy, fun girl to a depressed punk  individual. Learning her story and how she changed is very engaging.
The biggest and most prominant change is the ability to reverse time. This is a main plot point  so its not just some mechanic thrown willy nilly into the game. It allows you to change a decision you made once you see the outcome, or it helps in opening new dialogue options and story branches because you learned certain information that you can rewind and apply. It is also used for solving puzzles, yes this game actually has puzzles. Are they challenging? Not in my opinion but the way the game uses time reversal to allow the player to do certain actions works really well. Players see how the puzzle plays out step by step, if it works or if it does not, than they can rewind and apply what one has learned. It very rewarding bcause it does not hold the players hand, but also does not leave the player with no pieces to solve the puzzle. This allows the player to feel very rewarded when they have that AHAH! moment.
The sound track is phenominal, and really emphasizes the last and lonley feeling that the main protaganist Max experiances. I couldnt help but turning on music whenever i could because it was so enjoyable. The voice acting is good, not amazing, but definitely better than most games *cough* Destiny *Cough*
This game is not perfect. Though i do like its art style, and its emphasise on artistic view it has some mechanical problems. At times characters are not very fluid and the mouths dont always match the dialogue being said. Also when using certain objects such as the computer in Max's room, it would be nice to be able to click the folders and see certain things. Its a minor gripe and does not really take away from the experiance. I cant wait for the next episodes, I can see were the storyline is going to go but not how my choices are going to pan out which is something I always felt was predictable in the Telltale games.
All in all i give the first episode 9/10. Yes it has some mechanical issues and there are a couple things you really felt like you should be able to do but it is made up by the great story line, interactive world, unique characters, and the rewind function. Like i said its the first episode so it could change once all the episodes are released but I like where it is currently going.
Edit* With episode 2 released I am pleased to say that the game continues what it did well in the first game with adding an emotional crisis that plagues many teens of recent generations. The same techinical issues still exist in the game but overall the story telling trumps the issues and I have to say I never really cared for the outcome or life of a character before. Especially One that was underused in the first episode. Cant wait to see were the next episode takes the story.

I have only just finished Life is Strange and I already want to go back and play it again to see how much different actions have an impact on the story, and to find things that I've missed. There was one decision I agonised over for ages, and knew I'd made the wrong one, but stuck with it anyway. That had a bigger emotional impact on me than I was expecting, which shows just how well-written the game is.
You might think that being able to rewind time makes the decision-making process obvious and easy, and that this is a straight-forward game because of that. You would be wrong. Of course you're given the freedom to play the character of Max how you choose, but if you want to go down the path that you think is the best for her, it really isn't always easy to decide what that is when you know each decision will impact on other people too.
As far as actual gameplay goes, I had issues with stuttering a few times, which could be my PC's fault (my processor isn't the best), and the subtitles weren't always easy to read. Otherwise it was absolutely fine.
Also, I would absolutely love a soundtrack. I really hope the music over the rest of the series continues to be as good.
If you want a game that will get in your head, and is well-written, beautiful and leaves you wanting more, buy Life is Strange now!

Life is strange indeed, so is this game.
Anyone that likes to play point and click adventures should definitely read this review and will probably decide to invest some money into this game, published by Square Enix.
I bought it at
with a 20% additional discount so paid 15 € for all 5 seasons.
Given the first season is not very long, still I think 5 € (reduced Steam price atm) is a fair deal.
As I am not a native speaker this game was a good lesson to polish my english language knowledge, though the language used in the game is very urban, so urbandictionary often enough helped me to understand phrases and situations much better than any Oxford dictionary would have done.
That said the language used perfectly fits the setting and their teenage slang, of course.
You play as Max, a girl that's on a college for photography / art, and just turned 18.
Very soon you will find out that you're not only an ongoing talented photographer but also have another gift:
BEING ABLE TO REWIND TIME
This adventure, unlike many many other I've played in the last 25 years, really cares about your actions and they will influence the story.
At the end of the game (Season 1) you'll get an overview that shows which path YOU actually choosed and which of the other possibilities the OTHER PLAYERS have chosen.
Based on this rating, it seems that the majority of players of "Life is Strange" do have a very righteous tendency I may say - just like me. I had just one exception from the mass. Interesting to know.
Overall rated the game is a great. It has a refreshing and interesting touch, plus is really worth the time and money as some professional reviewers have judged.
I can agree with them and I really liked the sketchy but technically modern graphics (CSQAA / FXAA) based on Unreal 4 engine and I really loved the ambient soundtrack. The characters are stereotypes but well so close to real-life, somehow.
To be honest I hoped for far more decisions and it gets a bit obvious over time that the decisions sometimes can be "undone" by rewinding and sometimes not. Also in dialogues you have options but they don't really influence the game that much as the about 8-9 key situations the first season offers.
- only 9 hours playing time for the Season 1 (other said they did it in just 3 hours)
- controls on PC with a mouse are not that intuitive as it is designed for controllers / Xbox
- some people report more or less severe issues but the staff has a fast pace responding at the Steam community. I can only file one bug as Fraps does not work with the game (taking screenshots will crash the game for me)
- Graphics are okayish but bear in mind the game intentionally has a sketchy style.
- most actions are not that carefully animated (playing guitar etc.) so in terms of motion capturing I've seen better things.
- the really decisive decisions are not that numerous, and there should be more variants in the next seasons.
But well all the criticsm is moaning on a high level.

Episode 1:
Life is Strange is a point and click story game with the same structure of other story games such as The Walking Dead, Dreamfall, and Heavy Rain. The story this time however is different from the usual point and click game; you're not trying to protect a little girl during a zombie apocalypse, or saving two alternate dimensions from collapsing into each other, you're just going through typical drama at a high school, albeit with time travel powers.
The story of Life is Strange is very relatable to me, the character of Max being almost an exact parallel to my current life as a junior in high school (Or at least the way I chose to play as Max). Like The Walking Dead, you are able to make decisions that will both majorly change the story, or perhaps change something minor such as a student's sketch being posted on your Facebook page. With one choice for instance, do you make fun of the typical popular, but ♥♥♥♥♥y girl when her dress gets ruined in public, or do you try and comfort her and become her friend? Unfortunately, aside from one of these choices, the other's consequences do not go into effect by the end of the episode, which hopefully means that they will resonate in the upcoming episodes. The rewind features actually adds an interesting factor to these choices, as you able to see the outcomes of all the possible decisions, and then choose the one that you see is the best one, which may or may not be easier because of this.
Apart from the great story, Life is Strange has a bunch of characters with varying personalities, from the highly religious Kate, and the nerdy tech guy Warren. This episodes main character development though shines between Max and her best friend Chloe. Listening to these two characters talk to each other for the first time in five years is a fantastic experience, with Ashly Burch doing a great portrayal of the troubled 19 year old.
Gameplay, like the story, is a mix of elements from both a typical Telltale Game and a David Cage game (Beyond Two Souls, Indigo Prophecy), with the character limited to interacting with a select few items inside different locations. The rewind feature adds to this somewhat boring concept, allowing several new ways to approach situations involving puzzles.
However, this game does have a few, but very minute cons. For me at least, the game stuttered at some points, with dialogue repeating itself in an echo fashion, but this could just be because of my computer's processing power being a bit low. Also, lip synching could use major improvement, as sometimes really emotional scenes are underwhelming by the lack of mouth movements by the characters.
Overall, Life is Strange Episode 1 has the potential to become something as similar to a video game representation of the Great American Novel, and paves a bright future for the next four upcoming episodes.

So far so good, I enjoyed the first chapter at least. Obviously not a certain purchase considering it's to be delivered in an episodic format...
First off I guess, I particularly liked the setting of the story so far, though it's arguably quite linear (in all fairness this only being the first chapter). Perhaps it hits some cliches, like the "dominant family in a small town" or "feelings of being trapped in a small town" in some instances, but it's not necessarily a bad thing. (arguably I would say the second cliche is completely natural as I went through it myself.... for a very long time)
The main characters Maxine and Chloe are likable and relateable enough, and there seems to be foreshadowing for a butterfly effect with numerous small things done in the story, which to me is really interesting. Characters also don't seem to be morally black and white, and through rewinding time you can see various different faces of the characters, which is also interesting. Perhaps most of all though, I like the fact that Chloe, your former best friend, is also clearly imperfect as well... whether it be by certain sexist (yes, IMO sexist) opinions caused by her circumstance, to her past actions which lead to her (prevented) death (don't think this is much of a spoiler considering it's in the game's description). Life is strange...Well, it's not like we didn't already know that, is it? But for Max, it just got quite a bit stranger than most ever experience.
Welcome to Life is Strange, episode One. And just that is a good thing, because there isn't really more than a couple hours of gameplay to be had here. That having been said, it is a couple hours that will pull you in and move you along. The graphics are very pleasing, with a soft and beautiful tone that feels perfect for the game. The main (female, and there should absolutly be more female protagonists) protagonist is well envisioned, with a clear personality, but with leeway enough hat you can chose either the gentle/kind/caring/positive answer options, or the harsh/nasty/uncaring/negative answer options, and it still feels congruent with the story. And the story, well, it left me wanting more. A lot more. I like the people in the game (Max is awesome!), I want to learn more about them, I want to know what will happen next, and I actually care about making the choices that helps them out.
So why do I hesitate to recommend this game?
The publisher says that the game "sets out to revolutionise story based choice and consequence games.", and it may very well be that it will do so in the comming episodes (the idea of making choices now in an episodic game, choices that will influence what happens in episode 2-5 IS a very good one), but right now, the world of Blackwell Academy and Max's old home town feels like it is on rails. There are too few options when you interact with the story, you are moved from area to area, and you cannot go back. And this is a shame, because every location is so beautifully created that you'll WANT to go back and play some guitar in Max's room, or sit on the swing. So this is where the game fails. You can rewind, but only to your last choice made, you can listen to the dialogue, but excepting different choices, it doesn't differ from time to time. You feel more like you're watching an interactive movie than playing a game that gives you real choices and opportunities to explore.
Even so, even with those shortcommings, this game is a bit of a gem. But like every pretty gem, it needs a nice setting. So developers, please give us more choices in the upcoming episodes. Give us a bit more freedom to explore and go back and forth between areas of the game. Perhaps include some form of a photo system where we can go around and take pictures of other things than the different "hidden shots" you've put in the game. Give us more, because we love what you have given us so far.
Pro:
Awesome art style that really fits the game.
Female protagonist that is really well envisioned.
Cast of characters that you'll want to get to know more about.
Options that feel like they will matter in the next episodes (don't let us down here!).
An interesting story that makes you want that next episode, now dammit!
Con:
The game is "on rails" with very little to do except follow the story as intended.
The options provided in conversations are usually limited to two opposing choices / reactions.
Limited reason to replay the game (may change as more episodes come along).
Very short, with less happening than it feels like. This is basically an appetizer to the comming epsiodes (we hope).
Summary:
An interactive story that really shines in character envisioning, art, sound and storytelling, but hides its shortcommings with an experience that runs on a set track and offers little opportunity to truly explore the (beautifully created) world, Life is Strange is nevertheless a promising start of what could become an experience you wouldn't want to miss, IF more choices and freedom to explore is added in comming episodes!
Score: 6/10 -Recommended
Addendum for episode 2:
So, episode two of LiS (Life is Strange) is out. The game remains much the same with the same shortcomings as before, but luckily, it also has the same strengths! -The episode starts off a bit slow with things happening that seems almost like filler stuff (mind you, it is filler stuff that the game needs to cultivate it's special "feel"), but like any good story, the tension rises as things progress, and the episode ends on an emotional high note that is not unexpected, but still manages to lift the story further and create an intense desire to see what will happen next.
As promised, the game picks up the threads from your choices made in episode one, and binds them into a whole in a nice way. A certain development in the episode also caused me to fear for the main protagonist in a more immediate way than previously, which also manages to add another dimension of "how will this go?" to the game.
As it is, the gameworld remains enchanting but a bit limited in freedom, so the score stands as before at 6/10, but I will remind those who enjoy a good game with a strong emotional tone and interesting character that this IS a gem, and probably better value for the asking price than most games I would rate as a 6 out of 10.
Addendum for episode 3, 4 and 5:
So, the rest of LiS has launched, and I have to say, it got better and better for the most part. There are some emotional gut-punches, some unexpected plot twists and a couple cliffhangers. And two drawbacks, one small, one big. The small one should come as no surprise as it is the same as with every other game that sucks you in: it was over far too soon, and the ending could have been more complete.
The big drawback is, without giving anything of the plot away, a large segment just before the end which felt as it had been tacked on, just to give the players a little more to do in an episode that is, largely, "on rails". Said segment simply didn't fit into the overall theme I felt.
Even with this in mind, I would say that this game deserves an updated score. If I could overlook the flaws the game has (look above for the details), I could easily score it as an 8 or even a 9 for the soundtrack, the "feel" of the game and the unique art style. However, with the aforementioned flaws, I can only justify a 7/10 score, which is a shame since this game is an unique gem well worth picking up.

Episode 1:
Life is Strange is a point and click story game with the same structure of other story games such as The Walking Dead, Dreamfall, and Heavy Rain. The story this time however is different from the usual point and click game; you're not trying to protect a little girl during a zombie apocalypse, or saving two alternate dimensions from collapsing into each other, you're just going through typical drama at a high school, albeit with time travel powers.
The story of Life is Strange is very relatable to me, the character of Max being almost an exact parallel to my current life as a junior in high school (Or at least the way I chose to play as Max). Like The Walking Dead, you are able to make decisions that will both majorly change the story, or perhaps change something minor such as a student's sketch being posted on your Facebook page. With one choice for instance, do you make fun of the typical popular, but ♥♥♥♥♥y girl when her dress gets ruined in public, or do you try and comfort her and become her friend? Unfortunately, aside from one of these choices, the other's consequences do not go into effect by the end of the episode, which hopefully means that they will resonate in the upcoming episodes. The rewind features actually adds an interesting factor to these choices, as you able to see the outcomes of all the possible decisions, and then choose the one that you see is the best one, which may or may not be easier because of this.
Apart from the great story, Life is Strange has a bunch of characters with varying personalities, from the highly religious Kate, and the nerdy tech guy Warren. This episodes main character development though shines between Max and her best friend Chloe. Listening to these two characters talk to each other for the first time in five years is a fantastic experience, with Ashly Burch doing a great portrayal of the troubled 19 year old.
Gameplay, like the story, is a mix of elements from both a typical Telltale Game and a David Cage game (Beyond Two Souls, Indigo Prophecy), with the character limited to interacting with a select few items inside different locations. The rewind feature adds to this somewhat boring concept, allowing several new ways to approach situations involving puzzles.
However, this game does have a few, but very minute cons. For me at least, the game stuttered at some points, with dialogue repeating itself in an echo fashion, but this could just be because of my computer's processing power being a bit low. Also, lip synching could use major improvement, as sometimes really emotional scenes are underwhelming by the lack of mouth movements by the characters.
Overall, Life is Strange Episode 1 has the potential to become something as similar to a video game representation of the Great American Novel, and paves a bright future for the next four upcoming episodes.

This is really really good. Ignoring the sub-par ps2-era graphics, the game itself is a simple point and click adventure with a reverse-time mechanic. Use this mechanic to reverse time so you can change history in this small tale. The character narrative is great, the music OST is truly wonderful and the story is well written, add to that mechanic that does not feel repetitive.
For me the best part of the game was the narrative and the music, the way the story plays out and how you can influence even some of the smaller decisions is fantastic. It makes the game feel non-linear, in a linear environemtn - that is there are set zones where you can do things, you can't go everywhere and change everything and interact with everything, only with things that affect the story. But what's there is really fun to discover.
At first I didn't like the main character, Max, but after getting to "know her" through her story, she becomes immediately likable, if a little naive. It's great that the relationship between the girls and the friends is treated with such care and delicacy. It rarely ever feels cliched, especially with the fact that you can change the outcome.
The music is really really good too, the lyrics to the songs and such are also interesting. I've never been so engorssed by video game lyrics/music, that it makes we wonder if they had professional artists commissioned to do the work, or whether this was all in house. Regardless of which, the OST is just brilliant.
Narrative wise, the game never gets old, and they also added stats at the end of the chapter to compare your results, as well as reveal the alternatives you could have chosen, and world stats on the choices that were made. It feels refreshing that a point and click adventure be made seriously, with the focus on a serious-ish sci-fantasy story. I love the characters, I love the setting, and I loved the music and this particular chapter.
I can highly recommend this chapter to anyone as it only costs under a fiver and you get a good 1 hour-ish of time for each £ you spent. If this carries on the final collection should be around 15 hours.
I'm not surprised at how this game has turned out narrtive wise, it's from the same developers of Remember Me which although combat-wise was clumsy, narrative wise was very strong, and this too shows that DontNod are a vaery capable team that have put a lot of love into Life is Strange Episode 1, if they can replicate this with the remaining Episodes then we are certainly in for a valuable treat to treasure.

Easy Skillet Tacos
Ingredients
1 pound ground beef
1 small onion, chopped
1 teaspoon olive oil
1 tablespoon chili powder
1 1/2 teaspoons ground cumin
1 teaspoon salt
1 (15-ounce) can pinto beans, rinsed and drained
1 (8-ounce) can tomato sauce
3/4 cup water
1/2 cup salsa
1 1/2 cups (6 ounces) shredded Cheddar cheese
1 tablespoon chopped fresh cilantro
Taco shells or flour tortillas, warmed
Toppings: shredded lettuce, diced tomatoes, salsa, sour cream
Preparation
Cook ground beef in a large skillet over medium-high heat, stirring until beef crumbles and is no longer pink. Drain well. Remove beef; wipe skillet with a paper towel.
Sauté onion in hot oil in same skillet over medium-high heat. Add chili powder, cumin, salt, and beef. Cook 5 to 7 minutes, stirring occasionally. Stir in beans, tomato sauce, 3/4 cup water, and salsa. Mash pinto beans in skillet with fork, leaving some beans whole. Bring to a boil; reduce heat, and simmer, uncovered, 8 to 10 minutes or until liquid is reduced.
Top evenly with cheese and cilantro. Cover, turn off heat, and let stand 5 minutes or until cheese melts. Serve with taco shells or tortillas and desired toppings.

I was really, really excited for this game. I thought it looked fun and people were praising it as Heavy Rain mixed with jesus christ magic. I foolishly purchased all episodes instead of sampling the first one like I ought to have, I just had so much faith in the community but I feel bamboozled.
This game is just plain mediocre. It looks okay and the premise is neat but the writing is so bad I can't even believe how many people are praising this. First of all, it's full of characters that don't act like anybody that exists. No teenager behaves in the way that these kids do. They are extraordinarily cruel and the adults are either total one way or the other on the realism spectrum. They are either full on Mr. Belvedere 'we believe in you' perfection or complete Hitlers.
Secondly, I love how right off the bat we're expected to care about this Max character who supposedly 'loves' photography and loves her photography teacher but she can't even be arsed to learn or remember what a daguerreotype is. Her teacher brags in front of the whole class how she has a gift but she doesn't even ♥♥♥♥ing bother to learn basic♥♥♥♥♥♥about photography. But am I supposed to be impressed when she name drops Avedon or whatever who-gives-a-care esoteric reference to whatever? I just don't like her at all. She sucks and is pretentious. Really this whole first episode was me being unsure of whether or not I was supposed to care about these peoples problems.
Thirdly, the controls of this game had be completely baffled for the first fifteen minutes. Maybe it is my fault but I honestly couldn't understand how to select things and the little tutorial at the beginning explained it really ♥♥♥♥♥ily. Also, the game promised me that if I rewound time after picking up an item, that I would keep said item. I guess not when it serves the ♥♥♥♥ing plot though because I decided to take a picture of the
♥♥♥♥ that mechanic then, just♥♥♥♥♥♥it right out of the window along with Max's personality.
I am a gamer. I am also a female. I know there is huge pressure to develop a game that features female leads that inspire and are badass or whatever, but truthfully, I would rather play as Bigby Wolf or Solid Snake than this, frankly, soggy Max Caulfield. She is lame, meek, and just bleh. I'm not saying a character has to be all phwow pizazzzz to appeal to me but they have to at least have depth and something that makes them appealing instead of the opposite. This attempt at grrl power leads was pandering and sad, with the standard issue indie music and 'oooh does she have blue hair? EMPOWERMENT.' oh and that dumb blue haired one kept sayin' 'Hella' ah god why? That's another thing. Characters are completely forgettable and wooden at times. I only remember Max's name and literally nothing else. I wanna say there was a Zoe in there? Maybe a Becca? Even if I knew all of their names I couldn't put them to any one of the generic rando white girl faces I was forced to dialogue with.
This really was a very bitter dissapointment to me because I love games like this one. I LOVE THEM. I took a chance on this game and it was a gamble I lost. It was boring and a far cry from it's lofty acclaim. I think the only reason people are cheering this game on is because they think they have to. I'll let you guys in on something though. When you suck the peen0r of a game as mediocre as this one just because it has a wealth of female roles in it you are setting the standard very low for what a female lead driven game should look like.
In short, I have never wanted a refund so bad in my LIFE. All I am going to feel when the next episode is out is guilt that I could have purchased something better for my money. This game is just so hyped and I fell for it. I hope anyone who reads this maybe dares to take a closer look at this game. If you want to play an incredible story driven visual novel type game with choices and consequences, play Wolf Among Us or any Telltale game for that matter. If you want a game with a cool female lead with asskicking tendencies and a smidge more complexity, play the new Tomb Raider. If you want to be assaulted by pretentious references, tryhard indie EVERYTHING, mechanics that function only whenever they want to, a boring protagonist who's only notable feature is her ♥♥♥♥♥♥, then please play Life is Strange.
Also ♥♥♥♥ you square enix that reference to Spirits Within wasn't cute or funny, it made me sad for you. Really sad.

Life is Strange hits all the points it's aiming for perfectly, creating authentic characters, an engaging and mysterious story line, and mechanics that allow for unpunished exploration of the story, without feeling out of place, something many games don't seem to be able to achieve.
On top of this, the atmosphere is perfect. Oozing with nostalgia, yet feeling modern. You get the real sense of a new generation growing up in a world built upon the sensibilities of the previous generation. You feel the presence of the 90's all around, but there is no doubting that you are exploring in the 10's. The art direction plays in to this so very well, with light leaks seeping in along side beautiful painted portraits on posters. A balance has been struck that makes the ambiance of the game just feel real without hiding it's artistic qualities in the search for perfection.
Mixing Telltale's The Walking Dead, Gone Home and Dontnod's previous game Remember Me, Life Is Strange combines the stronger elements of all three to create a perfect blend that stands above them all. Of course this is only after the first episode, and the next four episodes could ruin all the praise the first has garnered, but I see that as being unlikely. For the price of the first for episode, I would 100% suggest buying this, and then buying the season pass afterwards if you felt it was worth it.
