LIFE IS STRANGE
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Life is strange is a point and click adventure game / movie set in a place call Arcadia Bay. This game is very similar to “The Walking Dead” and “The Wolf Among Us” with a little twist to it.
You play Max (ine), an eighteen year old teenage girl with a passion for photography. During class Max experiences some sort of trance and sees something which is similar to a tornado ripping of Arcadia Bay lighthouse, and then she is suddenly back in the classroom totally confused. Finally the class ends. After wandering around the Campus our main character witnesses a crime and, believe it or not, she is teleported back to relive her previous 10 minutes in class. A classic case of Groundhog Day! Then, she realises that she can rewind time. Fabulous idea, especially that all your actions have consequences (just like The Walking Dead but you are not rushed into it). And you can decide which one sounds the more appropriate to lead you into the story.
Episode one sets the stage and story beautifully. You will meet interesting people including Chloe, Max’s childhood friend.
The visuals are superb with plenty of opportunities to take great screenshots. Max will certainly envy you for that. The soundtrack is good and the point and click system is very easy to use.
I really took a punt by purchasing episode 1 – 5, but if episodes 2 – 5 are as good as the first one I am in for a little treat.
Positives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Beautiful graphics
-	Good dialogues
-	Great atmosphere
-	Achievements
-	Trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	We have to wait until March for the next episode

Teenage Angst: The Game. Definitely felt like it was written by a bunch of middle-aged French dudes, for sure. The entire soundtrack was meant to be incidental but I could not imagine any teenager ever listening to such twee pap. Of course I myself am a decade removed from the age of the characters, but much of the script and music felt just a little forced.
That said, between eye rolls I did manage to examine ALL THE THINGS, make every choice, and take all the optional photos for achievements. On that note, I think it would have been a much cooler mechanic to let the player pull up the viewfinder and take photos at leisure. It would have fit in with the whole 'student photographer' theme and made the achievements feel a little more challenging than finding the thing you can use the 'take a picture' option on.
I'm interested enough to replay episode 1 and make the particular choices that will make this chapter hit all of the beats I'd prefer. Hopefully the raised stakes and (presumable) deeper exploration of the supernatural element will smooth over some of the unevenness I found in the introductory episode.
Giving this a tentative recommendation based on ep 1. It should be on the radar of anyone seeking big-budget interactive fiction. Whether to buy in now or later is left to the reader.

This was a unique experience from Dontnod Entertainment and Square Enix. A very relaxing and beautiful story about friendship and how far you are ready to go for each other. At first I didn't think much about the game as it seemed to have a lot of female influence, but after taking reliance on all the reviews, and giving it a consideration, I gave it a try. I don't regret my choice in the slightest. This game can be enjoyed by any gender. The Walking Dead meets Beyond Two Souls and Heavy Rain.
The basic principle is much like Telltale Games; You make a choice, the game will tell you that this choice will have consequences, you start to think and feel bad over what you just did. The only difference is that you can rewind important choices directly in the game and reflect on it with the help of Max's supernatural powers. If this were a game from Telltale Games you must exit the episode, and manually find the chapter had the choice which you made the mistake on. The voice acting is very well done and professional, almost as if the characters were written by writers from Telltale Games.
The only bad thing I found with the game is lip-synching. Sometimes the characters say long sentences without moving their mouth. Nothing that destroys the game, but can sometimes be annoying. As a conclusion; If you enjoyed Beyond Two Souls, Heavy Rain, and The Walking Dead, then you will definitely love Life is Strange. A well-written drama about a common girl now faced with choices that will change her and others' lives forever.

It's a little early to recommend the game on the basis of the first episode, but I certainly recommend the first episode. I have throught a lot about the game since I played it a couple days ago. The characters are interesting and have potential, even if they are one dimensional at this point (with one exception).
The time travel mechanic is an interesting addition to a Telltale-esque game like this. It gives you an in-fiction way to reload a previous save and replay a decision to see the outcome. It allows you to correct choices with negative outcomes, which might herd players toward certain choices. To pursue the story along certain paths, you have to intentionally choose paths that offend or hurt some npcs rather than stumbling blindly into decisions. I think it's an effective addition to the formula.
The time travel mechanic is used for some puzzles, including some I think I missed. I'm looking forward to it being used in more and more complex puzzles in future episodes.
Also, I find the casual bad language and drug use extremely refreshing.
In sum, the characters and story support the purchase on their own, and time travel adds an interesting tweak to the format established by Telltale.

This game might come off as pretentious and appealing to a certain specific number of target groups people will want to distance themselves from, but in truth what has been shown so far has been really quite impressive and worth trying no matter the fact it's base setting is a generic high school one.There is no underlying obnoxious moral reflection backdrop about pressing issues or anything like that, unless I'm blind and stupid, at least in EP1.
The music, just for starters, is really noticeable, effective and nice to listen to, even during loading screens. It is managed perfectly throughout EP1. The voice acting is of good quality overall, though the lip-syncing is quite flawed.
There's tension, atmosphere and mystery, 3 things most games today fundamentally fail to implement. The impact of your own choices seems to be more pronounced within even the span of episode 1 than in Telltale games. I think there's a lot of potential for branching outcomes that given my impressions of the first episode, I expect will be capitalised on.
There are some weird things like hilariously outdated teen slang/lingo (I twitched when one character went "epic win") and the now infamous comment about that movie that should not named, but generally the game really succeeds at creating a living, interesting world you can understand. Except for 1-2 occassions where you openly touch things you shouldn't be in front of people, and they make no comment. At other times, this effect does happen though.
Seriously, if you have any prejudices towards this game, drop them. If you like good stories, good characters and intricately made games, I'd heartily reccomend this game to you.

First episode in (about 3 hours) and I'm astounded by everything this game has to offer.
Because it's late and for the sake of avoiding the inevitability of an essay-level length review, I'll keep it short and sweet, and comment on multiple aspects of the game in a list.
Writing - Dear god, the writing. For the first time, in what is shockingly a long time, the setting is believeable (see: films and games in the last year with a few exceptions). The writing from the journal entries, to conversations between characters is remarkably on point for its representation of a modern high school society, filled with in-jokes reflective of the internet age and *cough* "hipster culture" taking the limelight.
Story - Through the choices I made (1 runthrough) and the relationships I've developed (and destroyed), I'm pumped for the next episode, simple. My only worry, and it's usually tied with time travel as an underlying mechanic in narrative, is my faith in the choices I've made as I progressed through the story. Made more troubling in the separation of the experience through episodes, should a game with heavier reliance on player choice be severed into parts while experimentation is expected of the player leaving them with no immediate payoff in what I would currently consider an isolated experience? Should a wide range of unanswered questions be left in the dust waiting for fulfillment in a later chapter? Or can this arguement be immediately trounced by the simple utterance of the word, "replayability". Yeah, probably, next.
Sound - Music selection from the ambient backdrop of the school grounds to Max's choice of track to calm herself is spot on, doing a splendid job of detailing the environment and the characters that occupy it. Hilariously enough I genuinely thought the track we hear through Max's earphones at the beginning was a singer hired to write the most generic, "well known locations of the world" track, accompanied by a guy tapping a cardboard box, for satire's sake. To my surprise, well known band, who knew, and now I love them.
Gameplay and presentation - Controls are simple and easy to get a hang of, with a few exceptions using the time travel mechanic with it being sometimes a little unclear when the LB option (last choice made) is viable (usually cancelled while people are talking, sometimes not) (I played using an Xbox controller). The musical stings in the menus and use of the time travel mechanic alongside the insane visual cues (watch Max while rewinding, awesome little touch), are the cherry on the cake. It's clear a lot of love went into detailing what could have otherwise been a brushed off side project.
In the end, looking forward to seeing where everything leads, and I'm interested in seeing what everyone else thinks!
Thanks for reading,
@AdamGCurtis
Edit: Forgot to mention, screw the recurring use of the "Female Protagonist" tag. If you avoid a game purely based on the gender of a character, there's something wrong with the community at large.

Overall Rating: 9/10
Gameplay Rating: 8/10
Accessibility Rating: 9/10
In Life is Strange (LIS), you are Max, an 18-year-old senior at Blackwell Academy, a special seniors-only high school where talented students go to hone their skills in a creative outlet.
The mechanics of LIS are not difficult.  The camera and movement controls are easy and generally do not interfere with gameplay.  It is occasionally difficult to properly center the mouse on an object, but this is rare.
In general, it is mostly a WASD/point-and-click game with time to make choices and a low stress level.
In LIS, the game revolve around you making decisions, some easy and some not.  These decisions have immediate and long-term effects that you discover as the game goes on.  These types of games can be fun in that you can play out your own personality or try out something much different from what you would do - sort of testing the water for what it's like to be someone different.
LIS plays out through a series of causal relationships - things happen that shape the rest of the game - and through Max's own thoughts and feelings about the events, captured in her inner monologue and in her journal, which is updated each time you go to a new 'section' of the game (i.e. crossing to a new area that wipes your rewind ability).  Max's journal entries reflect the choices you make.
Each of the chapters take around three hours for a moderately in depth gameplay style.  I really enjoy the game, even if this is not my favorite game type.  It is VERY creative, often very beautiful, and it pulls you in to the characters through development and storyline progression.  At times, both the story and character feel a little two-dimensional, but it is handled well by key moments where they begin to shape up again into more believable people.
Each chapter has improved in both the choices you have to make and the storyline.  LIS feels as though it is building to something epic.
Life is Strange is rated 8/10 for gameplay.  The story is fantastic and the effects of the decisions provide a high replay value.

What can I say about Life is Strange...
There's emotion in this games single episode so far that's made me WANT to buy the next one. It was a very polished playthrough and it didn't feel rushed or broken in any way for me give or take one or two audio and visual hitches I encountered but neither of them were game breaking and can quickly be forgotten in the grand scheme of this game.
The thing to love about this game is Max, she's an adorable, petite and socially awkward young lady who's appearence, right down to her clothes and haircut, fit her personality to a 'T'. Any choice I made didn't contradict the personality that Square Enix tried to convey be it through her actions or internal monalogue. Being Max may not be a badass experience so far but for now, being Max is just fine and if you play the game you'll fall for her too I'm sure.
My personal favorite moment is just after the first class and she's walking down the hall with her headphones in, loudly, so not to feel so nervous in a crowd as she fights back a breakdown until she can have some privacy. It added a sense of realism to the character and listening to her describe the people she knew as you walked was interesting, you get a real grasp for her personality in that golden five minutes and a little insight into the story's direction.
Then comes the introduction of her ability to Time Travel. It's a cool little trick that serves a purpose in some puzzles and events later on but my only problem with it is how quickly Max seems to grasp it. One minute she's freaking out about turning back time, the next she's fixing her broken camera just to see if she could do it again which she does with ease. She starts off big, no baby steps for Max Caufield, no sir, and to me that seemed a little off considering the fact it was freaking the hell out of her not five minutes ago.
Be that as it may Time Travel isn't just a gimick to use once or twice in a chapter, you can use it at any time to do small things like erase a reality where you broke your friends favorite snow globe right up to stopping Max from being crushed by a boulder towards the end of the episode or you can change your opinion during a conversation or even the entire outcome of an event...or you can hold the rewind button until she starts complaining about how much it hurts if your into that kind of thing but, well, You be You.
Episode One of Life is Strange is well worth downloading, I am eager for more.

After EP5...
I have no words.
"I need a new Episodic game series"
So my friend bought me a copy of LiS in February 2015, as a birthday present. I'd never heard of it, but it seemed like an interesting concept, especially after he introduced me to the Walking Dead and the Wolf Among Us. How naive I was back then...
Life is Strange is probably one of the most enjoyable linear-sort-of-interactive games I've played, that alongside the Walking Dead and The Wolf Among Us.
Gameplay-wise it's a walking sim, with an interesting twist of time travel, which allows you to do a whole miriad of things you usually wouldnt be able to do. (Read: Saying the right things ALL the time)
I overall enjoyed the narrative style, something you'll have to find out for yourself, just so I don't spoil most of the major points.
A feature I really liked about this game, which I haven't seen in other games I've played, is that at points in the story you can just sit down: listen to the music, and hear the thoughts of the protagonist on the current situation. It adds just a little bit more authenticity to the overwhelming events which have befallen our dear Max Caulfield.
Something I really enjoyed was the art style and cinematography used. It's very cohearant, and nothing seems out of place, unless it's used to enhance the jarring effect of the circumstances. Scenes are well planned, an camera angles and shots are used to enhance the content: the game comes across as very filmic. Infact at times I find that it rivals even art house films in the amount of effort put into something as simple as camera angles. The dappled pseudo-impressionist art style is something I really felt immersed me in the universe. Personally I believe having a hyper-realist game would have been far less impactful and authentic.
To wrap it up I'd like to say that on the whole I really enjoyed this game, I connected with the main character, and spent the time after an episode in complete shock. I then proceeded to tear my hair out until the next release, because I ABSOLUTELY needed to know what happened next.
So I'd rate this as my GOTY for 2015. Ofcourse it all depends on taste, and what you're looking for: but give it a try in anycase, you never know, you might enjoy it :D.

What can I say about Life is Strange...
There's emotion in this games single episode so far that's made me WANT to buy the next one. It was a very polished playthrough and it didn't feel rushed or broken in any way for me give or take one or two audio and visual hitches I encountered but neither of them were game breaking and can quickly be forgotten in the grand scheme of this game.
The thing to love about this game is Max, she's an adorable, petite and socially awkward young lady who's appearence, right down to her clothes and haircut, fit her personality to a 'T'. Any choice I made didn't contradict the personality that Square Enix tried to convey be it through her actions or internal monalogue. Being Max may not be a badass experience so far but for now, being Max is just fine and if you play the game you'll fall for her too I'm sure.
My personal favorite moment is just after the first class and she's walking down the hall with her headphones in, loudly, so not to feel so nervous in a crowd as she fights back a breakdown until she can have some privacy. It added a sense of realism to the character and listening to her describe the people she knew as you walked was interesting, you get a real grasp for her personality in that golden five minutes and a little insight into the story's direction.
Then comes the introduction of her ability to Time Travel. It's a cool little trick that serves a purpose in some puzzles and events later on but my only problem with it is how quickly Max seems to grasp it. One minute she's freaking out about turning back time, the next she's fixing her broken camera just to see if she could do it again which she does with ease. She starts off big, no baby steps for Max Caufield, no sir, and to me that seemed a little off considering the fact it was freaking the hell out of her not five minutes ago.
Be that as it may Time Travel isn't just a gimick to use once or twice in a chapter, you can use it at any time to do small things like erase a reality where you broke your friends favorite snow globe right up to stopping Max from being crushed by a boulder towards the end of the episode or you can change your opinion during a conversation or even the entire outcome of an event...or you can hold the rewind button until she starts complaining about how much it hurts if your into that kind of thing but, well, You be You.
Episode One of Life is Strange is well worth downloading, I am eager for more.

UPDATE - After playing the last episode -
Okay, after playing every episode now...
I still maintain my opinion. The strength Dontnod managed to put in this game is incredible. You feel attached to every single character and every decision has a huge impact on you, and everything you're going to do in that game is going to pressure you.
Now, after playing the last episode, I feel like the decisions you made through the entire game have little impact on the ending. In fact they have none. There is two endings, and each one is decided by the last choice you make, but your whole playthrough is changing nothing, which is disappointing.
That being said, it's probably the only bad thing I have to say about that game.
The music is awesome through every episode, great tracks and very pleasant. The graphics are in my opinion really nice, but some may dislike the cartoon-ish effect you get sometime. Last episode was a little less beautiful though.
Characters, as I already said, are touching and existant. Every one of them have a personnality and a story that drives him through his choices. In fact, they're pretty much so touching that you'll get attached to them to the point of crying at some point of the game.
The story is masterfully driven, with some plot twists that you'll expect, but some other you'll not. Last two episodes are pretty surprising in my opinion.
The concept of letting the player choose and influence the story is pretty well handled, until the last choice as I already explained.
For those who played Telltale games, it is very different from it. The choices and the story are handled very differently, in my opinion more smoothly, plus this is a story-driven game and excepted two puzzle-infiltration-ish phases, there is no action-oriented phases.
So, that brings my conclusion. Is this game worth buying? Absolutely. Is it worth every dollar you'll spend? Absolutely. Is this game one of the best I played since a long time? Absolutely. I'm personnally so fond of this game I could play it 100 times and still not be borded. I'll reiterate: this is only my opinion, but everything in this game seduced me. Everything in this game put chill in my spine and water in my eyes. Buy this game and play it. It's great. There.
It's a game where you have to chill, get in your seat, breathe, and play in one shot.
Hope this helped you!

The structure is quite similar to Tell Tale episodic games.  I would say the tone of the game is akin to films such as Juno, Perks of Being a Wallflower, The Girl Who Leapt Through Time and the adventure games, The Longest Journey/Dreamfall.  In fact, this is very similar in mood and style with the same kind of female protagonists as in TLJ/Dreamfall games...particularly the more recent Dreamfall Chapters but set in an art academy campus (like TLJ).  The setting is 2013 so a lot of the game references are relatable which gives it a nice grounded reality apart despite the time travel element.
So, if you love those wonderful games as I do, you will love this!  The time travel element is a very nice and clever integration to the game's immersion where our protagonist has the ability to rewind time and make different choices.  It might seem like just another way of going back to a save position but there are differences as you can use it for puzzle solving AND the protagonist retains the memory of the alternative paths which is an important element.  Its a wonderful plot and gaming device.
I really enjoyed this first episode and it holds much promise to be a memorable whole once all the parts are released.  I am already engaged with the real life-like characters and the storyline even has a Twin Peaks hint to it.  Parts of it also reminded me of the awesome "Left Behind" dlc for Last of Us on PS3 in terms of soulful storytelling and friendship.  The songs are a lovely reflection of the high school type angst that are ladened all over the game.
Admittedly, the narrative rules in this game while the puzzle solving is very much on the easy side.  I expect/hope the puzzle solving difficulty level to crank up in later episodes.
The first episode has a satisfying end point and whatsmore, the next episode is not far off and will be released this month, unlike Dreamfall Chapters which is being released agonizingly slowly.   I do hate this story splitting concept but if it means the only way for my beloved and endangered point and click adventure genre to survive then I am not complaining and very grateful that we are getting these sort of games with polished production values in the first place.
Of course the developers cannot spend a huge budget on this genre given its niche market so the graphics are not top end but its still immersive enough to capture the atmosphere and landscape.  The facial expressions are limiting but the voice cast make up for that with soulful nuances in their performances.
Its not really proper to rate a part game but so far, I give it a promising

As has been said by others, Life is Strange feels like a mid point between Telltale's games and David Cage's games.
This "game" feels more like the future of cinema than the future of video games, but I'm ok with that.
Life is Strange episode 1 is sublimely well presented, both in terms of visuals and audio, and the story is interesting as well as rich in subtext and symbolism.
This is a "game" which, along with other story driven games, will likely prompt conversations on the state of video games as art and, especially, the line between video games and cinema.
This is a game which will help you forget all of the disappointments of the video game industry in 2014 and start to be excited about the possibilities of the medium again in 2015.
Pros:
- sublime presentation for the most part
- well told and intriguing story, rich in subtext
- use of music throughout the game
Cons:
- occasional weird lip syncing and awkward lines of dialogue
Other:
- linear and story-driven, so may not be to everyone's tastes
Conclusion:
An excellent and intriguing start to what will hopefully continue to be a great story driven series

Like: Mixed feelings; involving blatently going through someone's things in front of them (only to be yelled at of course) then reversing time so you still know all their dirty secrets. At the same time this is fun, it also disgusted me to some degree. It feels very manipulative and somehow wrong. Using that kind of power for something so trivial.
Neutral: The protagonist Max is a "Waif Hipster" who's into photography. She's pretty indecisive and has almost no confidence. Every choice you make results in her inner monologue of her wondering she made the right choice, and reverse time to choose something else. Though it is for this reason I feel kind of proud of her when she confronts someone or stands up to a bully.
Dislike: Finding all the photo ops scattered through the chapter. I enjoy exploring around and taking in the world for the most part. Though I felt like the game was flipping me off when I saw "YOU LET THE BIRD DIE" in the chapter one summery.

This is the most emotionally intense and powerful game I've ever played.
First, lets get the fluff out of the way. The art style is unique, giving it a clean, but very beautiful look. The voice acting is at worst still great, but it's so much better than that.
The story could have easily been a convoluted mess, but they did a great job of making it easy to follow.
They did a brilliant job of making every decision feel as if it had weight and consequence. They brilliantly took advantage of our tendancy to second guess ourselves to make even the most basic choice feel like it will come back to bite you at some point. Even better, you were able to clearly see when many of those choices impacted the story later, in a way that felt completely organic.
It was able to do what another of my favorite franchises, Mass Effect, was not - create an ending that is excruciatingly painful and yet still stays true to the story. Where ME3 left me feeling angry at the sudden choice that comes out of nowhere, this made absolute sense. And even though the choices you make do not impact the outcome of the story, they impact you and what factors you will consider in your final decision.
Easily one of the best games I've ever played.

This is an absolute gem of a game.
It's not a 'true' adventure like e.g. Syberia or Longest Journey, it has more in common with the TellTale offerings or to a lesser degree 'The Vanishing of Ethan Carter'.
The comparison to TellTale is inevitable, since LiS uses the same story-rich format to do what it does.
But as opposed to TellTale, there are no QTEs (or at least not yet), and the game has no pre-defined world for you to enter.
Otherwise though, they have a lot in common. Your choices are fairly limited, the 'puzzles' aren't really puzzles at all, and I suspect that the consequence-system will be as limited as it is in e.g. Walking Dead.
So don't expect an open-world adventure, where you can influence the lives of others to any large degree.
Just like TellTale, it's not the destination, it's how you get there.
Which is why I've always been a bit puzzled when people moan about the limited consequences in the TellTale games.
TellTale (and LiS) isn't meant to be games in the traditional sense, they're inter-active novels.
The whole point is the story.
And LiS delivers story-telling in spades.
Everything just comes together in a fantastic package.
The art is absolutely superb, the dialogue at times made me laugh out loud (which is fairly hard to do), and the slew of interesting characters (yes, even Victoria) make it hard not to get emotionally involved.
And of course the fantastic sound-track that underlines the slightly melancholic mood that pervades the whole game.
Whether or not they can keep the storyline going for all five episodes obviously remains to be seen, but if they can up this level of writing, we're in for something very special.
So buy the game, make sure you're undisturbed for a few hours, and just let the story of Max roll over you.
If you have the slightest interest in good story-telling, you won't be disappointed.

Easily one of the best games I've ever played.

This is an absolute gem of a game.
It's not a 'true' adventure like e.g. Syberia or Longest Journey, it has more in common with the TellTale offerings or to a lesser degree 'The Vanishing of Ethan Carter'.
The comparison to TellTale is inevitable, since LiS uses the same story-rich format to do what it does.
But as opposed to TellTale, there are no QTEs (or at least not yet), and the game has no pre-defined world for you to enter.
Otherwise though, they have a lot in common. Your choices are fairly limited, the 'puzzles' aren't really puzzles at all, and I suspect that the consequence-system will be as limited as it is in e.g. Walking Dead.
So don't expect an open-world adventure, where you can influence the lives of others to any large degree.
Just like TellTale, it's not the destination, it's how you get there.
Which is why I've always been a bit puzzled when people moan about the limited consequences in the TellTale games.
TellTale (and LiS) isn't meant to be games in the traditional sense, they're inter-active novels.
The whole point is the story.
And LiS delivers story-telling in spades.
Everything just comes together in a fantastic package.
The art is absolutely superb, the dialogue at times made me laugh out loud (which is fairly hard to do), and the slew of interesting characters (yes, even Victoria) make it hard not to get emotionally involved.
And of course the fantastic sound-track that underlines the slightly melancholic mood that pervades the whole game.
Whether or not they can keep the storyline going for all five episodes obviously remains to be seen, but if they can up this level of writing, we're in for something very special.
So buy the game, make sure you're undisturbed for a few hours, and just let the story of Max roll over you.
If you have the slightest interest in good story-telling, you won't be disappointed.

This game is absolutely amazing! The gameplay is great, the story is great, the protagonist is wonderful and the ability to rewind time to your advantage is awesome! There's so many opportunities to use your powers to benefit you. It's great to have the ability to rewind time to make sure that you've made the choice that you want to make and see what you could do differently or give yourself another chance at something you may have done wrong.
I had a great feeling about this game when I first saw it and playing it has been so much fun. I almost expected it to be a little like The Walking Dead, but it turned out to be quite a different experience. I have often found myself excited as I play through the various events and make use of time traveling in the many different situations that allow so.
In the end, I have to say that this game is fantastic and money well spent.

Whatever your opinion of this game is after playing a couple hours, there's plenty enough nuance to rethink that opinion. Rewind time, see things from another perspective, and you just might find yourself feeling differently.
I feel liberated in this game in a way unlike any game has before. People seem to think this is a very left-wing authoritarian game for some reason, but I highly disagree. This game reminds you that actions have consequences and asks you to think about those consequences. To me left-wing politics is about escaping consequences for certain groups of people, just as right wing politics is about other groups escaping consequences. This is a very libertarian game to me, and I wonder if it doesn't subvert different ideas for both the right and the left. I also wonder if games are intrinsically a libertarian medium built on personal agency, but that's for another discussion.
I recommend this game very highly. It's the only one of its kind. While you're at it, pick up "Remember Me" from the same developer, an utterly beautiful and thought-provoking game.

Life is Strange is a very unique experience. The characters do not feel scripted, but act as if normal high school students would. The story is also quite interesting; including the amount of interaction that is in the game. I feel that there is maybe "too" much interaction over the course of the episode (but that is my personal opinion, since I got a bit bored spending time reading and looking at everything.) however whether or not you spent the time interacting with everything, doesn't really take anything away from the game itself (at least that we know so far).
There is one aspect that this game brings to the table that I felt other games do not; the ability to play Max as you would if you were in her shoes. Making decisions based off the type of personality YOU have, greatly affects everything you do. I spent a good portion of my time wondering if the decision I made was worth reversing time or going forward. "Watering your plant has consequences"....this by far blew my mind and made me question every action in this game; this is not a bad thing but a brillant way to imerse the player into Max's world.
Now the one thing I feel that would have been cool to seen, is the ability to take pictures throughout the course of the episode / future episodes, leading you to decide which picture you wanted to submit for the "Every Day Hero's" contest. Again, this isn't a con of the game, but something I felt would encourage the player to dive deeper into Max's shoes.
This is definietly worth $5, and I am very anxious and eager for the next episode...I hate cliffhangers lol.

Max is the pure 200% embodiment of a wannabe nerd, 18 year old, Seattle, spoiled hipster chick, Victoria is bascially the group of girls from Mean Girls shoved into one person, Chole is so anti-authority and rebellious that it just hurts. Characters seem to be human forms of Tumblr sections. Whoever wrote the dialog for the characters probably hasn't done much talking to real people in real life. The way some ideas are orally expressed don't make much sense with the way they were spoken. I'm pretty sure a good chunk of the words used aren't even actually spoken in person (chillax, awesomesauce, among many other words that are only used in nonserious ways, mostly online).
The world is set up well though. Everything going on, the missing girl, the mysteries of all the people around make you want to go through every sqaure foot of the maps to see what information is hidden about. The choices you make don't seem to have too much of an effect on the rest of the game, but this is just the first episode. The time reverse ability and the mystery surrounding how you even aquired it brings it's own interest. I'm pumped to find out why we get this later on.
On the technical side, the game's graphics would be considered cutting edge around 2008 and the lip syncing would have been impressive back in 2005. You occasionally get caught on some objects, the camera is sometimes in weird positions, and the characters speed is a little weird. After about 10 minutes of playing you do get used to it though, and the story begins to take over the graphical short comings.
The music is also very well done, to the point you might want to just get the soundtrack to listen to on your own time. It's on par with the game itself in terms of how Indie it is.
Overall, the game is for sure worth what it cost. The story overtakes any problems that seem to pop up, including the poor character development and personality. Hopefully some of these problems are worked on in the next episode but if not, I'm still excited to see where everything is heading towards.
It is a magical game with characters that you can relate to in one way or another.

Life Is Strange... Life really is strange is it not? This game seems to follow in those exact same foot steps. The game, or should i say movie, novel, biography of the high school girl? It is all the above. The game does not follow in Telltales foot steps, in making choices, that are completely irrelevant, as they all lead to the same conclusion. In this, Life Is Strange, your choices really make an impact. An impact that actually hold weight, that actually make you consider your actions. I had multiple times where i had to rew.... wait. You didn't know about the Time shift, or rather, for a lack of better term, Rewind Time ability?

This little girl Max Caulfield (from here on referenced as Max), has an ability to mess with the space time continuum and frame shift backwards. Correct her mistakes, help those in need, and possibly see the new episode of American Horror Story that you were fifteen-minutes late for. She is scared, she does not know what to do, and that is what is so great. This particular game gives weight to your choices, but every choice impacts Max in a different way. Each time you feel remorse, like as if you should have chosen the other option, but if you did, how will you feel with that? That is the greatness of Life Is Strange. You don't just sit there and press A, B, C, D. You have to think, you have to choose carefully. You can't blindly choose option A, as that might make Person B not give you an option for something down the road.

You meet multiple personalities in Life Is Strange. It is your typical stereotypes: The Cheerleader, the Jock(s), the Geeks, the Artsys (is that a word?), etc. Each all have their own responses, and agendas, which you can clearly find out by exploring the world drawn infront of you. It even has a bit of humor, if you can flesh it out in the conversations, or interacting with objects in the world.
So far, Life Is Strange has only given us a glimpse into its future, with Episode 1, titled "Chrysalis". This was a great entry into a series. I am down on the March 2015 release date for the next episode, but if they [the developers] can give us more material like this, i am more than happy to wait. As it stands, this game receives a big ol' Thumbs Up and a 4/5. It would receive a 5/5, but for the Achievements "Photo Optional", the 'response' to do them is quite lacking, and does not do a real good job on directing you when you should take photos. Not a big deal, just something i didn't like.

A story game to rival Telltale, blended with the "gots to looks at everything" of Gone Home, and then Prince of Persia's time rewinding thrown into the mix, this season really has promise.  The story is novel, the setting is interesting and fresh; the characters are well-defined and intriguing.  The time-rewind mechanic lets you see your options before settling on one, and whereas it could be gimmicky, it doesn't feel that way: whether this becomes the case and feels overused by the end of Episode Five - we shall see.
There are a couple of minor gripes for me, and those are that the excellent voice talent is not lip-synced to the animation (in fact, the animation on the game full stop feels much less slick than any other part of the game), and that I found bugs: but they weren't insurmountable ones thanks to the rewind device.
I would recommend this game, for sure, to anyone who has ever enjoyed a Telltale adventure, or Gone Home.  If you didn't like those, you won't like this.

Life is Strange is surely one, if not the, best story based game I ever played.
You follow or control the life of the young student Max, who is back in college for nearly a month. During her photography-class she realises that she has the power to travel in time, so that she can go back and reverse her previous decisions.
The graphic seems to be a mixture of hand painted images combined with the great visualisation of the "unreal engine". You follow the scenes in over the shoulder shots, which gives you the possibility to turn around and see the reactions in Max's face. (I'm normally a friend of 1st-person-view, but in this context the over-the-shoulder was quite the right choice to present the great atmosphere.)
The greatest thing about Life is Strange are the reliable (believable) characters. Max isn't the great Hero with muscles greater than the moon and a strong mind. No Max is withdrawn, nosey, silent, shy and helpful. The isn't sure about her photographer skills and always overthink things.
In the Blackwell Academy she has do deal with normal people, friends bullys and ♥♥♥♥♥y girls. With an elitist club and the little or bigger problems of the day.
Controlling the game is pretty easy and as usual. W,A,S,D and Mouse for movement and some extra keys/ mouse buttons for Max's skills. Objects you can interact with get shaded (what always reminds you of the drawn world) when you are near them and a dot with options around it, let you deal with it.
This game is not action based, fast or spiced with very different puzzles. It is more about enjoying the shown world, the interesting characters and the possibility to do and redo your actions with the possibility to see how the rest of the world reacts.

That out of the way, I must say I absolutely loved it: the music (oh man Syd Matters'
playing out as you begin, "wowser"), atmosphere (Pacific Northwest overload), nostalgia (rest in peace super-kitty Bongo), characters... Yes, the game striked me at first as the world's first hipster simulator, but that quickly changed as Max and the cast were properly introduced.
The graphics may not be so polished, the controls may feel clunky at times (I played this using an Xbox controller), but the story more than makes up for it. As far as I can tell though the choices you make will affect events in the upcoming episodes, not immediately. I can’t say I was that bothered by the “hip” terminology used throughout the dialogue (“chillax”, “wowser”, “blaze”, “beetch”, “oh my Lord”), it managed to get its point across. Kudos for the nod towards Twin Peaks (Chloe’s car plate reads TWN PKS), the parallel between Laura Palmer and Rachel Amber definitely feels at home.
I really liked how at the end you can replay any episode chapter in "collectibles" mode. I was really kicking myself for missing two optional photo opportunities, so I was relieved to see this.
To sum up my ramble, I wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a story-driven game, and look forward to the second episode coming up in March. Try it out, it’s well worth a fiver.

I just finished the first episode of this game last night in about two hours and now I'm sold on the other episodes. If you're in doubt, just pick up this first episode (it's only $5) and play through it, I can guarantee you'll want to play more afterwards.
This game plays like a visual novel -- or, rather, a visual choose-your-own-adventure books. You can walk around and explore but the story doesn't progress until you make choices, so if you're into Telltale games you'll feel right at home playing this. You play from the view of Max, a girl who's just moved into a boarding school to study photography. Some certain Big Things happen and Max discovers she has the ability to rewind time for short durations. This is the game's way of letting you do do-overs on decisions, basically, but they work it into the story really well, and having the main character know that she can do the do-overs is cool and sustains immersion. I can't really say much more without giving out spoilers but just think of this game as a crime-drama highschool simulator where you can also travel a few minutes back in time. It's a unique game, I know.
On to the other stuff, the visuals are pleasing in this game, but what really stands out while playing is the audio direction. The music in this game matches its  setting really well, it's very melancholy and high school sounding. Sometimes characters play their own music, too, and it helped me learn more about their personalities and styles. I found it really satisfying to listen to the music that the main character, Max, would listen to in her everyday life, and listening to it with her really helped me connect to her, I guess. Speaking of connections, this game relies on you making them. By the end of the episode you'll have so many opinions about so many characters you'll wonder how you experienced so much in two hours... actually, after this review I'm going to go back and play through the episode again to find what I missed.
The only problem I had with this game is that there was a problem with dialogue in the beginning of the game, characters would "stutter" what they were saying as their models tried to keep up with their scrips. However, this could have been a graphics/sound card issue.
TLDR; I would strongly recommend buying at least the first episode of this game, even if you feel like it might not be for you. Life Is Strange™ is an interesting switch from the usual types of titles published by Square Enix.  This game doesn't do anything that other games haven't done before, and better.  It isn't the point-and-click adventure that Myst was.  It doesn't give you the kind of time control you had in Prince of Persia: Sands of Time.  It won't wow you with its dated graphics or hipster-inspired music.  What Life Is Strange™ does very well is blend all of these elements together with the human element that Square Enix does so well.  This game would completely fall apart if the voice acting weren't so good.  In fact, it would be hard to care about any of these one-dimensional characters that fall into several different predictable categories (jock, hipster, mean girl, skater, punk) if the voice acting weren't done so well.
Choice and consequence is a central theme to the gameplay of Life Is Strange™, but we won't be able to see how many of our choices turn out because Episode 2 isn't going to be released until March 2015.  Episode 1 was an interesting taste of where this game intends to take its audience, but it was only about two hours long.  That said; those were two hours that I enjoyed very much.  At the end of Episode 1 the game will recap all of the decisions that you've made along the way and show you what percentage of people select which choices -- it's nice to see that the overwhelming majority of people out there have been opting for the moral high road, making Max a "good person" in our eyes.
I'm interested to see where Life Is Strange™ will take us as it continues in Episode 2.

What is Life is Strange?  This was the burning question that I had all through the advertisements up until I got my hands on it.  The preview videos helped little in this, but I did know that it involved time travel, saving the life of a friend, and a badass tornado....at some point.
Now that I've completed the first episode, I'm both excited and disappointed.  I was promised an interactive movie experience, and while it is certainly an interactive one, it wasn't much in the way of a movie experience.  Nothing felt timed.  You have all the time you need in a game where time should be a pressing and present concern, at all times.  The game is about time-travel.  You should be going around, doing things in the little bit of time you've got, rewinding things to the start of the scene, trying out different things, and then choosing the lesser of evil decisions to see how the various consequences play out.  That would be an interactive movie experience.  You've got two hours...make it count in whatever way you want; in whatever way you feel is relevant.
All in all, though, this game is fantastic.  I didn't feel cheated from experiencing a good game, just not a good movie.  The characters are believable, the background is plausible.  What the hell is up with that giant storm.  Episode 1 is a whole lot of setup, which is a little disappointing that you won't get to see at least one of your actions have a major consequence outside of moving someone from in front of a door.  Hopefully, the later episodes will offer a lot more of the cause and effect/butterfly effect that I'm looking for.
By the way...this soundtrack is awesome and I'm sad that it is not available for purchase separately.

Life is strange is a narrative-focused game with strong influences from contemporaries like Gone Home and The Walking Dead. What it excells at is presenting a well written story that's unfolding right along side you.
Their novel approach to choice, which  lets you rethink all of your decisions before actually committing to them, made me feel in control over my character while still retaining all the qualities of a strong, authored narrative. The game never made me feel like I just missed out on some content or want to reload to see an alternate dialogue option. That doesn't mean that there are no hard decisions to make here. They just mostly result from the dramatic events in the game instead of from a feeling of uncertainty, which I enjoyed a lot.
All of this is sold through superb art direction, character animation, voice acting and environment design. The personal spaces they present for some of these characters are among the highlights. They feel interesting and lived-in and made me want to know more about these people and their relationships. The high quality in audio-visual presentation not only makes the game an aesthetically pleasing experience, though. It also affords them the luxury of letting the player actively participate in all of the plot points and not having to rely on events told through flashback too much. This makes the story feel suspensful and immediate.
Overall I'm very impressed with the first episode and definitely will keep playing more as they are released.

Life Is Strange, but how strange is it? More importantly, is it good? The answer is yes, it's great in fact, so much so that I like it more than Telltale's The Walking Dead series, going by the same type of game both are going with.
It's an episodic games, five episodes, that's story based and has heavy decision making, and the first episode with the base game is what I'm going to talk about right now, hopefully the rest of the episodes when they come out.
Starting with how the game looks, it has a cartoon(y) warm visual style to it, that's filled with hand painted colors, and it's absolutely beautiful, filling the world, the game, with life and charm, where almost every spot in the game you'll love to look at. It has a great setting that doesn't get much attention to in games, and they nailed a really cozy atmosphere to it.
The main character you play as is good and interesting to know about, you'll like her teenage personality, I did. There's also a lot of characters that's varied and unique in characteristics, that you'll meet, and most of them are good and interesting too, finding out who they are and what they do, figuring them out, it's fun.
That, and the soundtrack is nice and calming, especially when you start it in-game with a radio or boombox somewhere. Going to the main part, it has a really nice story that has a lot of small details in the game's world, followed with simple to understand dialog, and an ending that's not that strong, or week of a cliffhanger, one that you wouldn't mind waiting for it to continue its story, waiting until the next episode to come out, which I'm eagerly waiting for.
The time reversing mechanic is great, simple, and presents a lot of opportunities to check out most of the games content, and gives you the option if you want to stick with a choice, only after you see what's on the table, if you so choose to see all the options. It pleases those who would like to stick with their first choice, and to those who want to have the worst/best route, and the choices are good enough to let you have second thoughts, even after checking all of them and choosing the one you want.
The game is simple, relaxing, beautiful, and charming, every minute I spent playing it was not wasted and I took my time exploring the world that it presented to me, rewarding interest and curiosity with nice stuff to look at, with a lot of objects that can be interfaced to have commentary over it, that's nice and informative. The game also made me realise how convenient and awesome it would be to be able to reverse time, which I'm hoping I'll dream about.

AMAZING game but not revolutionary as stated in the marketing material.
Basically, if you like ADVENTURE games or interactive movies/novels, Life is Strange is a great experience. The way the story elements intertwined with "Time rewind" gameplay elements works really well.
Life is Strange is even more awesome if you are a gamer that LOVE to SAVE and RELOAD in various adventure games or have numerous bookmarks in interactive novels to see the outcome of one choice, then reload to see other choices. Simply REWIND time, no need to have countless save points. As a bonus, your knowledge in the alternate future also can be used for your advantage.
+ Rewind time to try various choices, see the outcomes, and use it for smart dialogue option
+ Great character writing and design
+ Insight into a teenage life thats becoming adult
+ Pastel colours and watercolour art style - STUNNING!
+ Great musics and voice over.
+ Atmospheric camera angles.
+ Anti frustration feature (skip dialogues :D )
- Horrible lip-sync and stiff facial animation

This game does so many things right.
Lets talk about the cinematography - which is amazing. We don't have high end realistic character models, but who cares when the whole game looks as beautiful as it does? Everything works so well together, the scenery is simply amazing.
As is the storytelling. It sucks you in and involves you in the story. You DO care about the things happening and the amazing soundtrack takes everything - the Highly believable characters, the look of the game and the storytelling and wraps it into one big package of playable joy.
I am not kidding here - I've rarely ever played something that felt as coherent as this game. I can't wait for the next episode.
Just a great game!

Just played the 1st episode and was suprised to say the least. Everything from the enviroment to the characters felt real, walking around campus, through the halls or snooping in someones room was great. There is plenty to discover and it's up to you if you want to search around for every encounter, you dictate how you move around the enviroments at your own pace. Puzzles could be a bit better, I would like to see something more in depth then you rewind time twice and solve it. Game has a great art style and music is pretty good. World seems quite alive, walking around reading all the posters and seeing amusing graffiti really sells it. If there is one thing that I can complain about it's the lip syncing... It's actually somewhat often that you notice someones mouth is moving awkwardly while their talking (doesn't always happen but there are a few times where I felt it was kinda distracting). Also some more variety would be welcome, the whole choice A or B does get a little old. As far as gameplay it's a lot of walking around, talking and looking at things ( if you're not a fan of telltale games this game might not be for you ).
Pros
-World feels alive
-Plenty to discover
-Fun
-Story (so far it's pretty good deals with some very real problems)
-Characters
-Episode 1 was a little over 2 hours for me
Cons
-Lip syncing ( why are you ok at times and weird at other times )
-Somewhat repetitive
-Linear -> so you are free to walk around the enviroment and interact with things but theres always a main goal like "bring thing to person" I would like them to try more heres the area figure it out once in a while. Also perhaps some interactions that last longer then one coversation. Kinda like side mission.

What is Life is Strange?  This was the burning question that I had all through the advertisements up until I got my hands on it.  The preview videos helped little in this, but I did know that it involved time travel, saving the life of a friend, and a badass tornado....at some point.
Now that I've completed the first episode, I'm both excited and disappointed.  I was promised an interactive movie experience, and while it is certainly an interactive one, it wasn't much in the way of a movie experience.  Nothing felt timed.  You have all the time you need in a game where time should be a pressing and present concern, at all times.  The game is about time-travel.  You should be going around, doing things in the little bit of time you've got, rewinding things to the start of the scene, trying out different things, and then choosing the lesser of evil decisions to see how the various consequences play out.  That would be an interactive movie experience.  You've got two hours...make it count in whatever way you want; in whatever way you feel is relevant.
All in all, though, this game is fantastic.  I didn't feel cheated from experiencing a good game, just not a good movie.  The characters are believable, the background is plausible.  What the hell is up with that giant storm.  Episode 1 is a whole lot of setup, which is a little disappointing that you won't get to see at least one of your actions have a major consequence outside of moving someone from in front of a door.  Hopefully, the later episodes will offer a lot more of the cause and effect/butterfly effect that I'm looking for.
By the way...this soundtrack is awesome and I'm sad that it is not available for purchase separately.

Life is strange is a narrative-focused game with strong influences from contemporaries like Gone Home and The Walking Dead. What it excells at is presenting a well written story that's unfolding right along side you.
Their novel approach to choice, which  lets you rethink all of your decisions before actually committing to them, made me feel in control over my character while still retaining all the qualities of a strong, authored narrative. The game never made me feel like I just missed out on some content or want to reload to see an alternate dialogue option. That doesn't mean that there are no hard decisions to make here. They just mostly result from the dramatic events in the game instead of from a feeling of uncertainty, which I enjoyed a lot.
All of this is sold through superb art direction, character animation, voice acting and environment design. The personal spaces they present for some of these characters are among the highlights. They feel interesting and lived-in and made me want to know more about these people and their relationships. The high quality in audio-visual presentation not only makes the game an aesthetically pleasing experience, though. It also affords them the luxury of letting the player actively participate in all of the plot points and not having to rely on events told through flashback too much. This makes the story feel suspensful and immediate.
Overall I'm very impressed with the first episode and definitely will keep playing more as they are released.

Life Is Strange​ by Square Enix​ and Dontnod Entertainment​ is one of those games that will take you on an epic ride ..
The use of music throughout the entire game which spans 5 (five) episodes is breath takingly beautiful and heart crushing all in the same breath.
The story of a young girl and her best friend on their epic adventure through the dark underside of a fictitious version of Arcadia Bay (Oregon) and through time will leave you in tears more than once.
If you don't own the game I highly suggest getting it.
In the end will you make the right choice ?
Many people didn't like the ending .. and everyone makes different choices but I feel if you understand the emotion behid the game and an understading of basic space-time padaox then this game will leave you as teary eyed as I was.

Thought the game was pretty good, standered 8/10.
The dialogue is very, how would I put it, "cliche," but with godo reason to an extent. The main character is flawed, has social anxiety and is really expressed throughout the 60-90 minute episode. The dialogue is like the one person in your school/office who tries his/her hardest to implement internet vernacular into their everyday life, and it's kind of weird, but it adds to the cliche like feel of the school, it being one of those high schools everyone thinks of when they reminence back on or anticipate in the future(varisty jackets, bullies, football players tossing footballs, etc), and doesn't seem to take itself too serious.
The story is original so far. I'm intrested to see in where it takes us and how, in a means it breaks conventional methods of how to tell a story. Rather than focusing on reacting to a situation in a set amount of time, the rewind system allows you to explore all the possible outcomes, and lets you chose the result of it personally, whether you were curious of the outcome or morally.
Voice syncing needs work, but personally didn't bother me. The soundtrack is great aswell, mostly indie music really addding to the indie vibe the game gives off.
As a whole, if you're intrested in an off-beat story game simular to tell-tales you should check it out. For 5$, the first episode is rather short but really sets up the story and character enviroment really well.
Saw this on my newsfeed and thought I'd give it a try. Little did I know, this game would be incredibly fun and I can't wait for the next episodes. Great story and characters so far.

Althoug it ended up beeing engaging and really good I had some problems with the finale, which honstely kinda underwelmed. The beginning drags out very long, you barely have control over your character, there is lots of talking and explaining and it all comes over very cliche. There are lots of intense emotional situations, yet the facial expressions the characters displayed were very puppetlike.
The interesting stuff began when
showed up. The long intro with various inhabitants of Arcadia Bay, and
made me understand, that I do not care for the setting or the secondary characters, only the two main protagonists and this informed my final decision very much.
I have to mention the properly but not with flying colors executed stealth segments at the end, a nice change of pace, but the setting kinda did not grow on me - again the word cliche comes to mind.
I am not sure if I like the conclusion but I definetly think the game is a must play.
Touching, sad, happy and scared are feelings that acompany me throughout the whole game, but episode 4 was maybe the most intense. What strikes mostly is how authentic they seem, even when on the technical side (lip sync) things are far from perfect. But the story, the mystery and those characters you grown to like are truly special. This is one of those games that are truly outstanding and deserving of high praise.
After a rather lackluster second chapter with uninspired gameplay, here we got story first again. The repercussions from last episodes ending are felt often, but do not really play intp this chapter, and while the story did go slow there was a big "THEY DID NOT JUST DO THAT" moment at the end that made me so excited, I am not sure any game has every made me feel. And then came that final moment, which was a bit obvious, but hell... whatever... GREAT storytelling game! EPIC and MUST HAVE!
I really liked the first one and I liked, that there was more story and less puzzles. Well, now it is the other way around, and sadly, that is a downside. The puzzles use your skill of time rewind, so it is an interesting trick, but it is also a major timewaister, as you have to rewatch segments over and over again just to see how they play out for the 3rd time. There was also a tedious bottle search game that had only one purpose: prolonging the gameplay. All the puzzles seemed to me like they were uninspired gametime enhancers. I also did notice a visual lack of consistency on the first episode. This time there were some truly stunning moments mixed with very bad ones. After slogging along for 90 minutes the story did pick up and served some great moments, but in the end episode two was inferior.
This one is a 6.5/10 for inconsistent graphics, timewaisting puzzles and not enough story.
If you like Telltale, than this is the exact same sort of game, with just minor changes to the formula. The story is great and vastly diffrent to the rather pop culture offerings from them. The graphics are great, although they are not really next gen, but they are still very good, with some very realistic use of light and great emo-nation (facial animation ;) ).
The characters are based in stereotypes known from US highschool movies, but if you dig deeper you most probably will find more than a copy/paste from the last teen-drama.
Noteworthy is the use of Time-Rewind... this is a variation of the Memory-remixing from Remember Me, another great game from Dontnod, but here are no Tomb Raider like jump and run sections.
This is a game of minor puzzles, intriguing story and most of all it is about people, if you expect action... welll, move along.

This is an impressions review. As I play through the rest of the episodes, I will adjust the review accordingly, and will archive past impressions in the comment section.
So, episode two.
Obviously, the pacing was better with the second episode, as it should be, since the major, initial character development was no longer necessary.
This one focused more on providing a solid direction for the plot to follow. The rewind feature was less prominent, but the story itself took the front seat and ran with it.
This isnt to say the rewind feature was non-existent. Quite the opposite. It was used often. It was however used more as a story device and less as a unique feature.
So, this episode featured some tough choices and one definitely story changing arc depending on how you handled a specific scenario. Surprisingly so actually. The variation should cause some increasingly divergant experiences for players through the remaining episodes.
Anyway, I thought the pacing was better, the characters were obviously more familiar, and yet some of the ideas you probably had from episode one will be shattered or at least make you revisit your past assumptions. I found that to be both interesting and compelling.
So, where I thought the first episode was okay with a lot of promise, I thought episode two was actually really good and continued to keep you interested throughout. It also encourages you to at least playthrough it twice given the very, incredibly different possibilities that come from a single event in the story.
I will eagerly await episode three to see what happens next.

Life is Strange is a point and click adventure game (to be honest its more like an interactive movie) that has a time rewinding mechanic as well a setting and theme inspired by the director David Lynch.
You play as Max, an 18 year old that returns to her hometown to attend a photography school. While everything looks nice on the outside of this suburban middle class town, it is full of dark and disturbing secrets.
Not much occurs in Episode 1. You are introduced to several characters as well as their subplots and discover Max's ability to rewind time. Episode 1 serves as a nice prologue and I'm looking forward to the rest of the episodes.
There is VERY little gameplay to be had here but if you like experiencing a good story then I recommend checking it out. If you like TellTale's recent games as well as other titles like Indigo Prophey and Heavy Rain, then you know what to expect and will probably enjoy it as well.

Life Is Strange went totally under the radar for me until a few days before Episode 1 was released, and immediately caught my attention. I didn't watch any trailers, read any reviews, nothing. I just started playing knowing nothing about the game and I can say ... I adore this game!
Episode 1:
Episode one was very interesting and did a great job involving me in the backstory and giving plenty of places to interact with and explore. I went through every nick-and-crany this episode had to offer and I loved all the small additions like missing persons flyers, talking to people, etc. I just cannot get enough of the visuals either, it breaths atmosphere and is completely engulfed in personality. At times however episode one was a bit on the boring side ... in fact a lot of the time nothing was happening. Don't get me wrong I loved the peaceful adventuring I explored, but it wouldn't hurt to have a few more dramatic moments or game changing choices. I find the rewind feature is very fresh and adds a whole new element of simply rewinding and checking what the outcome of different choices would be, and pick your favorite.
Pros:
+Great introduction to features and characters/story
+Lots of places to explore
+Great visuals
+The few major choices that had to be made were very challenging and interesting
Cons:
-At times not much was going on
-Not many game changing choices
Overall I loved the first episode of 'Life Is Stange' and am very excited to see where the plot takes me. I recommened this to anyone who enjoys slower, more 'make your own story' type games. For someone who LOVED The Walking Dead and The Wolf Among Us, I adored this atmospheric adventure!
Episode 1 Score: 8.5/10
PS: Believe it or not, but Life is Stange episode 2 is probably the most anticipated game to come in the next few months. Cannot wait.

Let me start with saying, if you can't appreciate the creative, artistic elements, of a story, that portray its central theme, then this game may not be for you. Life is Strange, a 5-part interactive experience developed by
, puts you in the shoes of a seemingly ordinary teenage girl. Just as you would expect, being an 18-year-old high school student, you are encompassed by trivial drama and stereotypical teenage clichés. At first, it may seem a bit over-the-top; however, these elements are an integral part of the foundational themes, in which the story is built upon. After the first few minutes, you will quickly realize that this is not the story of a typical teenage girl, something
is happening. It is up to you to make choices, which could ultimately affect your future, and make sense of the mystery that surrounds you. It wasn't until the end of the first episode, when I caught myself staring at the credits, contemplating the many unanswered questions, that I realized how absorbed I was by the phenomenal plot. Episode one builds a rock-solid foundation that could potentially lead to a masterpiece.

I've heard nothing about this game up until now, and i'm not really sure why that is. But the game itself is incredibly relaxing, yet still compelling. When I'm gaming, I'm usually playing a game like Counter-Strike or Insurgency, so I think this game was a great change of pace.
You start this episode off in a very odd dream, waking up in the middle of photography class just at the end of it. Where? Why? What? You'll find out as you live out Max's life, who just moved back to her home town to take a course in photography led by none other than the famous Mark Jefferson.
The game looks and runs beautifully. The options menu, oh dear lord there is everything. Vsync, MSAA, FXAA, texture quality and effects, you name it and I guarantee it's there. The music is just phenomenal and the voice acting 99% of the time spot on.
I'm trying pretty hard to come up with anything negative about this game but I'm having a pretty hard time. The animations can be a bit off at times (namely, lip movements) but that's all I can really think of right now. But I'm just nit picking really, the stills look amazing an lip movement is honestly something I couldn't care less about. I mean... look at this

It took me three hours to finish this episode, and for 5 dollars I think it is well worth the purchase. Use your own judgment but I can firmly say I recommend this game. I can't wait for the other 4 episodes to come out and I hope we see more from this developer.

Really loved the first episode.  It was the best interactive adventure game i have played tops all of tellales previous work the soundtrack the choices everything is quite amazing love it. Lets hope future episodes are as good.

After the second playthrough of the 1st Episode (Chryssalis), I think that I have a pretty solidified opinion on it. It is overall a very nice start to what seems to be a great game.
>>PROS<<
-Engaging story- very suitable for this kind of games
-Great depth in characters, which is revealed through the choices you make
-The core mechanic of the game is simple and fun
-The decision-making has a lot of ethical and strategical gravity, often with these two values on opposite sides of the split decision, which adds to the replayability and overall empowerment of the player
-The photography theme (and the gameplay/ rewards associated with it) is surprisingly fitting to the time-travel ability
-A Ton of pop culture references
>>CONS<<
-As of 2/1/2015, there is a severe graphical bug throughout the game where certain objects appear to be missing textures (eg. David's eyelashes look as if he has been running a second (naughty) job at night
-Some (very little) of the dialogue seems badly-written, in the sense that it doesn't add to the character development, but merely pushes the plot forward
-They only released the first episode so far
Now, don't get me wrong, a gamer who respects him(/her)self has played games like 'The Walking Dead', 'Indigo Prophecy', 'Heavy Rain'. This title takes the 'choice' mechanic to a different level, beyond that of optimal survival, which is what the above mentioned titles are mostly about. The choices that you make in this game are for your own strategic or ethical advantage- instead for your immediate survival. This is fascinating and brings forth a new kind of genre to the table.

I've never had a game affect me as much as Life Is Strange has. Throughout the entire journey of Max Caulfield you are given so many choices that can effect everyone's life around you. It makes you question your morality, your loyalty, it makes you learn so much about yourself. The way this game is designed, its entire premise, is to allow you to undo your decisions. But is it right? Is it worth it? You have no clue what can happen later on, every miniscule thing matters. Everything you do has consequences. Near the end, it matters naught, cause there is no right or wrong. There is no happy ending. It is just the choice of the lesser of two evils. Beautiful game.

I've only played two hours of this game so far, currently on the first of five chapters, but it's probably the best £15.99 I've spent in a while.
Not only is this game cheap and great value, but it's both easy and challenging to play at the same time.
It's unique, with a great choice-based storyline, that adapts to your decisions, but also gives you the option to rewind time and alter a choice you made, or an action that you did.
It's incredibly fun to play, and is a forgiving game.
Pros:
-Unique game with a good story, beautiful graphics and music and decent voice acting. (Graphics can be a little glitchy on low quality, but higher quality does the game more justice anyway.)
-On a Similar level to telltale story/choice based games such as The Walking Dead or The Wolf Among Us. The gameplay adapts to decisions that you make, with the twist of being able to rewind time to edit or undo an action you have chosen.
-You can interact with a hell of a lot of things in the game, most of which affect the future for your charector.
-You can take selfies. 'Nuff Said.
-It has a mild puzzle element to it in some scenario's, which adds to the fun.
Cons:
-Lip sync and graphics are off in places, but it's a game, it's gonna happen.
-The ability to undo actions and redo them by rewinding time can spoil certain outcomes, but that's a player choice, not a necessity.
-Some of the charectors are frustratingly annoying.
I really, really like this game overall. 9/10

Moving, Thought provoking "Life is Strange" is not your average choice-driven story game. With riviting characters, a fantastic original score and bountiful replay value, it sets itself apart from the "tell tale" games it might have been compared to.

Life is Strange is one of those games that skew away from the normal formula of episodic games that Telltale Games has set the industry for.
In this game you play as Maxine Caulfield, an 18 year old high school senior, who has returned home to her hometown of the ficitional, Arcadia Bay, Oregon. In the first half of the game you witness the murder of a student in the bathroom by the hands of another student. This is where you learn that you can reverse time in order to change the outcome of situations. This mechanic is a breathe of fresh air to the choices in games such as the Walking Dead because you can see the outcomes of all the choices you have. While this may only be the first episode, it started off strong and cannot wait to see what DONTNOD Entertainment and Square Enix come up with in the next 4 episodes.
:
* Fantastic Characters - Believable individuals in a world that's alive
* Beautiful Visuals - Sets it apart from the other games in the genre with a beautiful landscape and art style
* Fantastic Narrative - Excellent composition of the characters, setting and story.
:
* Lip Syncing Off- Syncing of the Character's voice acting and mouth movements were off ever so slightly, hopefully improved in future episodes.
:  8.5/10
