Episode 1: I will be keeping spoilers to a minimum, but this game is definitely interesting thus far. It isn't difficult to make an impressive first episode for these Episodic games, and much more difficult to keep the momentum going. That said, 'Chrysalis' makes an excellent introduction to the world of "Life is Strange", and to the new town you'll take up residence in and its odd inhabitants. Not a whole lot more than introductions though, sadly, but with things like this that's what you can expect. The tech here is a bit jank, clearly dontnod wasn't swimming cash on this one. If you can tolerate the lack of proper facial expressions and lip-syncing, the voice acting and art style are absolutely stellar. An interesting cast and a cool power for our hero, I just hope though it goes a little more into the X-men side of things rather than living a teenage girls life who just happens to have the power of quicksave and quickload, heh. However, revelations during this episode are making me think about using my power for each little thing that goes wrong, and I'd like to play Max as someone who is more respectful of her newfound ability. Hopefully further episodes will let me play things a bit more conservatively.
All in all grade of episode 1: B+
I shall update this review after each episode.

This was my game of the year for 2015.
The story is engaging, emotional, and intriguing. The soundtrack is delightful, several times I caught myself exploring the word more just to enjoy the music and Max's insights into the world around her. On that note the roaming, point-and-click exploration is done exceptionally well, even better than in Tell Tales Games. You will never feel like you wasted time wondering around, there are pictures, backstory, and little side conversations to discover and they never feel thrown together; some writer put alot of thought into crafting each one. The writing in general is spectacular.
The gameplay is generally strong, but does falter a bit at times. The 'puzzle' parts which require you to 'rewind' are done tastefully enough, but are often too simple with every piece you can move needing to be. I was hoping for sequences more like the memory re-writing sequences from "Remeber Me". That had multiple 'fail' outcomes, and it was more of a puzzle figuring out how to engineer an event. The choice system is very well implemented in diaglouge, and I love that you can create dialouge 'world states' through clever use of the rewinding. For example snooping around and then rewinding time.
The choice mechanic itself was extremely well done. Your choices FEEL like they matter to the narative of the game. There are a few huge character moments though out the game, and the outcomes avaible to you really do feel heavily influenced by the decisions you've made in the past. What's more it's not just your dialouge choices that matter. Your choices to explore the world, to talk to characters you don't have to, to imerse yourself in the world, these all have an effect on how the game plays. This was a risky choice by the designers and it's one that I love because having spent the time to 'build relationships'; with the characters in the game I felt incredible rewared when that investment payed off later in the game.
Overall  I would highly recommend 10/10
Update:
Even a year later this is still my top recommendation to friends. Nominated for the 'I'm not crying, there's something in my eye' award without a second though.
If you love deep rich stories in games, if you are desperately craving a 'choice your own adventure' type game where you look back and actually feel like your choices mattered to the story, this is the game for you.

Big fan of the episodic game genre in general, and I enjoy a game where your choices really do effect the way the story pans out, a mechanic that seems to be truly crucial in Life is Strange. For instance,
Max at first gave me a great deal of 'not like other girls' vibes, especially when you're introduced to Victoria who is supposed to serve as her direct contrast and is of course mean-by-default, blonde, '♥♥♥♥♥♥' and wears expensive skirts in contrast to Maxs thrift store jeans and hoodie. On principle I detest the 'not like other girls' trope because it is dull, overplayed and wholly inspired by a good deal of both internal and external misogyny, as I played on Max became a bit more likeable, and more relatable when the game did glimpse into her possible symptoms of anxiety. Asides from the predictable Max-Victoria conflict, this game is very good so far for female relationships however and I hope it will continue to improve in this in future episodes.
All in all very interesting, quite intriquing. I shall be buying the season pass for 2-5.

Life is Complex, there is little doubt about that for anyone who actually lives their life. Having just finished the first episode of Life is Strange and seeing all the varied opinions on the game I feel the need to throw in my two cents.
I'll start this review with something that I feel is at the core of this game. It's no mere coincidence that the big art project is about a picture of an everyday hero. Over the course of the first episode there are a number of times where Max gets the choice to do something heroic. Do you comfort the rich ♥♥♥♥♥ Victoria? Do you step up for Katie when the security guard is harassing her for what seems to be no reason? Do you take the blame for Chole or otherwise interfere? Do you tell the Principal about the gun waving maniac? All of these choice have consequences, and sometimes it seems that doing what should be the right thing only ends up getting you into more trouble. You tell the Principal about the kid with the gun and now you are in trouble, the kid has it out for you, the Principal doesn't like you, and your mom is worried that you are lying. You defend Chole against her abusive father in law and you may end up getting into serious trouble down the road.
These choices are complex and not binary where doing good always equals a good outcome. Life is complex and so are the people in it. The people filling this episode are almost all ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s of the highest order. The only character I liked was the Friend Zoned Warren. He took a beating for the main character and has a surprising amount of depth to him for how little screen time he gets. Which is something I feel could be said for everyone in this game. If you go poking around Victoria's room, talk to other people about her, and be nice to her you find that she is more complex than just the rich ♥♥♥♥♥ role that was assigned to her. To quote Guardians of the Galaxy, “I don't believe anyone is 100% an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.” That is the thing with this game and why some people react badly to it, this game is populated by at what first blush seem to be your stereotypical archetypes of highschool roles. The Jerk Jock, The Cheerleader, and so on and so on; each being an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, but there is more to them that that, at least for the ones explored in this episode.
Now as these people are more complex than your average flawless flat character in video games it is easy to see why they rub some people the wrong way. There is no getting around it that these characters are abrasive.  I don't like Chole, I don't like David, I don't like Max, I don't like the teacher, I don't like Victoria, I don't like many people in this game. Many of them have rather extreme views (gee its almost like most of them are highschool students, I don't know about you but in comparison to my experience these characters are actually less extreme than the real people I went to school with) some of them are clearly unwell mentally: David, Chole, Max, and Nathan. Also while it was too early to tell, but I think the Principal also has issues, anyone who drinks during work has a problem.
Chances are high that there will be something in this game you do not agree with, if you are more sensitive there may be something that outright bothers or offends you. In my playthrough I encounted one anti vaccination aside, three anti gun comments, two pro vegan remarks, one anti security topic (Which could go either way based off how you see it) and there was probably stuff I missed. This is neither good nor bad in and of itself, all it does is given more detail to the world, and I must say this game is surprisingly detailed in comparison to most point and click games I have played.
There is depth and complexity to this world and not just to the characters but also to the story,
the lecture at the start of the game is an interesting foreshadow of what is to come. Diana Arbus and the little speech about how it is all ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t is in the game for a reason.  As the teacher says (or close to I can't remember the exact wording) I could place any of you in a corner and cast you in shadow and we would see a image of misery/whatever. Consider that many of the characters in this game are in fact in some sort of corner and are being cast in a certain light. As Mark the teacher says that's not really fair to them.
Also I'm sure the contrast between Frank's realism and Salvador's surrealism will come into play later on what with the small town America right next to the mysterious spooky woods with bigfoot.
So with that I will be moving away from the more touchy feely part of the game and into the nity grity.  Play this game with an open mind and open eyes and you might be surprised. Things are more complex than they first seem. Under the surface are many oddities. What's up with all the triangles and Illuminati iconography? What's the tie between the Vortex Club and the coming disaster? What do those strange glyphs on the backside of the lighthouse mean and why do they remind Max of wind? What happened to Rachel Amber? Does the now faded painting Chole and Max did have some deeper meaning?
It's all to early to say who will be who, what anything will mean, how the story will turn out. What I can say is that the game has a nice arty style that while not high end is pleasant enough. It creates a good sense of atmosphere, the character models are well done, there is a nice amount of detail, and the voice acting isn't so bad that it makes me want to kill people.
As for cons, the game is a bit buggy, not well optimized, and slow. OH LORD ALMIGHTY IS IT SLOW. The first episode is a slow burn, it starts and effectively end with the vision of a coming disaster, but everything in-between is set up for the next four episodes.  One thing that could have improved this was a bit more interaction with the game. As much as I normally hate on quick time events A Wolf Among Us showed me that they could be used well for action packed dynamic fight scenes.  Now that would be a bit out of touch with the 18 year old 90 pound waif you play normally, but it would have been interesting to at least struggle against getting choked out by Nathan. In conclusion the story of the game may be engaging the game play and mechanics of are not. Which is the biggst blow to this game.
All in all I enjoyed Hipster Girl Sim 2015 and at 5 dollars it is well worth the price, but to you HARDCORE MLG PRO gamers out there be warned. This is a slow artistic somewhat heady game that is Twin Peaks meets Gone Home with a heavy dose of hipster cred. They name drop more old movies and shows than any other game I can think of. As someone who likes those in a non hipster fashion all I can say is anyone who enjoys old school twilight zone and the work of Salvador Dali can't be all bad.

A fantastically new episodic series! (also the first one i haven't watched a youtuber play)
Life Is Strange is a game that brings something new to the choice based story system we have with Telltale Games.
You are given all the time you need to make a decision, and the ability to reverse time offers unique situations and choices that one may not have received in a game where such an ability was not possible, and because of this ability, you can actually reverse time and re-do your major choices!
Interestingly, this great ability is also a double-edged sword as now you start to doubt major choices that would be final in any other game, but aren't so in this game.
The music and simplistic style of the game really reflects the "indie" feel that the game strives for and puts you into (or back into) the shoes of an individual becoming their own independant person, i've discovered that the choices really reflect the thoughts of your own character... Do you help that person and risk facing consequences? Or do you help yourself by avoiding the problem and furthering your own success?
However, there were some issues I found in the game but they were quite minor, an npc that walked around the college campus would spontaniously change the colour of his hair and clothes, and the lip sync needs a bit of work.
For a 2 hour episode, I got a great introduction to a diverse range of characters, quality music and art, and an ever-twisting story :)

Life is Strange is very much an interactive movie in the vain of Heavy Rain or The Wolf Among Us, but thankfully it doesn't rely on QTE:s as it's primary gameplay mechanic. Instead Life is Strange use light exploration and time-shifting to move it's story forward. None of it is very challenging though and the puzzles in the game lack the complexity of producers Dontnod's previous outing, Re-member Me. By the end of the first episode there is however a hint at possibly raising the complexity in future installment. There is such great potential in this mechanic and I really hope we get to use it in more elaborate ways than being a smart♥♥♥♥♥during pop quizzes.
There are a lot of things to like about Life is Strange, though. The gameworld is quite beautiful in a low-key, serene kind of way and the music fit the game well, giving you a sense of living inside an episode of any well produced high-school tv-drama. I found Max to be a very symphathetic protagonist and her world a joy to get lost in. The main story is great and works very well in this setting where inecurities and doubt are so much a part of the day to day.
My main gripe with the game is with the script. Because while the story itself is a strength, the dialogue throughout is a clear weakness. There were just too many instances of cringe-worthy exchanges between characters, which is a shame. Instead of sounding like teenagers, characters sometimes end up sounding like parents, trying to sound like teenagers. One or two revisions would have done the game a whole lot of good.
That aside, I'm very much looking forward to the future installments and would hightly recommend the game. It might not be a giant leap, but it's still a very positive step forward for a genre in dire need of one.

To start of I don't write review that often in fact hardly at all; but for this; this is one of those few exception that really needs a mention. Now I loved this game, the story and characters is deeply immersive, interesting and awesomely portrayed. If you didn't already know this game is choice driven, therefore, every action that you take there will be some consequence -like the Walking Dead game series choice system. There is only one episode out when I wrote this and so far and that episode lasted me '4.1 hrs...'.  Think how long the other episodes are going to be! And with the story constanty ebbing back and forth due to some of the decisions that you can made and thought " I better rewind." so its not too predicable -which is top marks in my book. I recommend playing this with you imagination, creativity, nothing buggin' you, maybe a cup of coffee or tea; and that you are in a 'story mood' because it makes this game more alive and definitively adds to the awe, and to the astonishment that this game creates about the outcome of your choices and of the ending.

I have got to say, I heard this game was coming out about 4 days before its release, I pulled the trigger and got the season pass the day before it came out and DANG! I WAS COMPLETELY BLOWN AWAY! the first episode (currently the only one out. I'll be writing a full review when I've played through all of the episodes) blew me away!! I would not really consider myself "emotionally involved" with really any game I've played up to now, I just kind of played them, analyzed them; and then moved right on along to the next. But this game is truly special! I cared deeply not just for Max, but for some of the other characters as well! This is looking to be a VERY promising series! I feel like I can relate to Max in a lot of ways, and to some degree I feel for her. But enough ranting, onto the good stuff!
likes:
(for me) I felt like I could actually get immersed in the game! Like, REALLY IMMERSED to the point of actually feeling like I'm there!
the plot is very intricate.
***MUSIC! THE MUSIC IN THIS GAME IS THE BEST I'VE HEARD IN A VERY LONG TIME!!!***
another thing that I really liked was the experience! They don't really sugarcoat things at all! they lay it out, exactly like it is in college/university and that allows you to experience it fully.
The graphics:
I loved them! I could play the game on the absolute highest settings in 1080P it was GORGEOUS! a few of the textures were a little questionable and paper-like, but it was something I could easily overlook because everything else was so beautiful!
Maxs' narration was wonderful! It was beautiful, and it felt actually "real" to me. It accurately portrayed her thoughts I felt.
dislikes:
hardly anything worth mentioning here, other than I felt that the game was really holding my hand as far as doing certain things and giving clues that were very obvious as to what to do.
I guess another thing was that *FOR THE MOST PART* there were only one or two choices as far as dialogue goes.
one last thing, I know there is a TON of character interraction in this game! and I LOVE THAT! But, I think that they should have put just a bit more into it as far as there being a bit more characters to actually speak with, but thats just my opinion.
overall: 9.5/10 one of the best games I've played hand down! I think that $25 is an INCREDIBLY low price for this episodic game! I've spent $60 on other titles that I've enjoyed less than 1/10 of how much I enjoy this game!

It's a fairly different game to what DONTNOD did in the past - a combination of a classic adventure game (think Telltale, Longest Journey, etc.) mixed with visual novels (for the branching paths, etc.) - but you can tell it's the same studio. I could describe this game in one word:
. The story has a nice blend of Juno-esque teen drama, and Donny Darko time traveling concepts with a touch of the Butterfly Effect all packaged with Telltale's style of point and click adventure games like what you see in The Walking Dead. The time traveling concept is a nice touch because it lets you rewind and change your choices or you can use it to see what the other option does. It's nice because if you're trying to keep everyone happy, it makes it easier to determine what choices you'd like to stay with. I haven't finished the first episode, but I like how well the characters are written. On the surface a lot of them have cliche stereotypes, but depending on your choices you can see another side to them. Square Enix did a pretty good job of giving their characters layers.
I would say this is probably the only area the game suffers in. I like that the game has what looks like painted textures everywhere, but I would have liked to see better detailed models. The game has its own style so I'm not picky on the environments or look of the game, but the character models could have used a little bit more work. Even at max settings they look ugly.

Upon finishing the first episode of this, my first reaction was 'WOAH. That was incredible. Let's play it again!'
One of my favourite parts of any video game is talking to NPCs and choosing different responses just to see the consequences. Usually this involves a whole lot of saving and reloading which can get very tedious; needless to say I thoroughly enjoyed quick, easy rewind-and-redo being an actual part of the game mechanics. Of course this isn't much good if the characters you get to speak to aren't interesting or well rounded, but that is definitely not the case here. All of the characters I interacted with were both convincing and nuanced - even the ones I was expecting to fall into the usual 'irredeemable mean girl' archetype. While we're still on the first episode I have high hopes for the character development we'll see in future.
The visual style of the game is attractive and has a kind of indie-film feel to the lighting and colours. It has a similar, slightly melancholic feel to games like Gone Home but more in the way of actual story and interaction. It IS very story driven (some have called it an interactive movie and there is some accuracy there) and if that's something that's likely to put you off then I feel this might not be the game for you. However if you like great characters and want to support what looks like a very promising start to a fascinating story I'd recommend giving this game a whirl.

There are no barriers here - no one can say "Oh, it's a walking simulator" and pass it by. There is a game here, make no mistake.
What this game is turning out to be is
. On the one hand, for a lot of women, the story and main characters are refreshingly normal. Real life. Relatable. Almost boring in how closely they resemble (or at least call back to) experiences a lot of people had growing up.
But on the other hand, it's getting on a lot of post-GamerGate supporter's nerves. The forums for this title are littered with posts about how there should be the option to play a male character, and how there are hidden feminist agendas lurking behind every dialog option, as if the game were a propaganda film.
To be clear: This game isn't pushing anything on anyone. This is not a story about feminism. This is a story about a girl discovering something terrible is going to happen, and how she's going to navigate it.
(which seems to be isolated to a particular kind of person, if the positive reviews are any indication)
.
And this is precisely why I think you should play the game.
. This is why it's a challenge. This is why you should take up that challenge.
, and in an industry where truly new experiences are hard to come by that is a treasure.

Graphics, sound, story and game performance are top notch (cranked up everything to highest settings with x8 MSAA, 60+fps on a budget PC).
Now I spend a few more hours in the game (I'm still fairly early in the episode mind you), I must say I just love reading the journal and getting immersed in the story. There's just so much attention to detail, it's crazy. This is definitely a game you want to play slowly and explore every little thing. One negative point that I did notice though, the lip syncing is non-existent. I hope they patch it because it's the only thing about this game that looks bad.

What a joy, what really stands out in this game is the way mechanics,  story and gameplay elegantly synergize into a complete hole. In many narritive-driven adventure games you are presented with a plotline and are allowed to make choices to influence the plot. However, this often results in save-scumming and reloading in order to achieve the desired outcome. What sets Life is Strange apart is how this retreading and altering of choices is not only allowed, it is encouraged by the game through the main character Max's comments about how she should or shouldn't advise a girl to duck from a stray football. This creates an environment where the player is presented with the full knowledge and immdiate consquences of events and can truly make an informed decision. The narrative itself appears to be lacking at this early stage, although this is to be expected at this junction: there are over half a dozen characters who require introduction and positioning with more expected to appear. The narritive is amazingly scoped and all future conflicts have already infused the player with investment at the conclusion of the first episode. The conflicts are all regulated to a single town but rather from deemphasizing their gravity, the conflicts are magnified. I'm very surprised and now realize disappointed this smaller reach isn't see this more in games. I can only wait patiently for the next installment in Life is Strange which cannot be released soon enough.

If you didn't already know this game is choice driven, therefore, every action that you take there will be some consequence -like the Walking Dead game series choice system. I have got to say, I heard this game was coming out about 4 days before its release, I pulled the trigger and got the season pass the day before it came out and DANG! I WAS COMPLETELY BLOWN AWAY! the first episode (currently the only one out. I'll be writing a full review when I've played through all of the episodes) blew me away!! I would not really consider myself "emotionally involved" with really any game I've played up to now, I just kind of played them, analyzed them; and then moved right on along to the next. But this game is truly special! I cared deeply not just for Max, but for some of the other characters as well! This is looking to be a VERY promising series! I feel like I can relate to Max in a lot of ways, and to some degree I feel for her. But enough ranting, onto the good stuff!
likes:
(for me) I felt like I could actually get immersed in the game! Like, REALLY IMMERSED to the point of actually feeling like I'm there!
the plot is very intricate.
***MUSIC! THE MUSIC IN THIS GAME IS THE BEST I'VE HEARD IN A VERY LONG TIME!!!***
another thing that I really liked was the experience! They don't really sugarcoat things at all! they lay it out, exactly like it is in college/university and that allows you to experience it fully.
The graphics:
I loved them! I could play the game on the absolute highest settings in 1080P it was GORGEOUS! a few of the textures were a little questionable and paper-like, but it was something I could easily overlook because everything else was so beautiful!
Maxs' narration was wonderful! It was beautiful, and it felt actually "real" to me. It accurately portrayed her thoughts I felt.
dislikes:
hardly anything worth mentioning here, other than I felt that the game was really holding my hand as far as doing certain things and giving clues that were very obvious as to what to do.
I guess another thing was that *FOR THE MOST PART* there were only one or two choices as far as dialogue goes.
one last thing, I know there is a TON of character interraction in this game! and I LOVE THAT! But, I think that they should have put just a bit more into it as far as there being a bit more characters to actually speak with, but thats just my opinion.
overall: 9.5/10 one of the best games I've played hand down! I think that $25 is an INCREDIBLY low price for this episodic game! I've spent $60 on other titles that I've enjoyed less than 1/10 of how much I enjoy this game!

I could describe this game in one word:
. The story has a nice blend of Juno-esque teen drama, and Donny Darko time traveling concepts with a touch of the Butterfly Effect all packaged with Telltale's style of point and click adventure games like what you see in The Walking Dead. The time traveling concept is a nice touch because it lets you rewind and change your choices or you can use it to see what the other option does. It's nice because if you're trying to keep everyone happy, it makes it easier to determine what choices you'd like to stay with. I haven't finished the first episode, but I like how well the characters are written. On the surface a lot of them have cliche stereotypes, but depending on your choices you can see another side to them. Square Enix did a pretty good job of giving their characters layers.
I would say this is probably the only area the game suffers in. I like that the game has what looks like painted textures everywhere, but I would have liked to see better detailed models. The game has its own style so I'm not picky on the environments or look of the game, but the character models could have used a little bit more work. Even at max settings they look ugly.
The audio work is really well done, and I like how the developers seemed to have found the right music at several points in the game. The introduction part where you put your head phones in and listen to music as you walk through the hallway in the school was really well thought out.
Like I said earlier, I like how well the character progression was written in this game and time travel is an interesting concept, and the writers really executed it well within the story of the game. The game gets a little dorky with the teen drama stuff or just how they talk sometimes, but overall, the big picture is great.
Overall, I would highly recommend this game.

First off, it's a short episode.  I played through 3 times, making different choices each play through, and only still have 9 hours of playthrough.  This includes sitting around playing the guitar with the music.
And about the music, it's good.  I like how they even threw in a Jose Gonzalez song, one of my favorite muscians.
The atmosphere was good.  The gameplay, is your basic point and click to investigate, thrown in with rewinding time, which makes an interesting combo.  The things you learn before rewinding time remain with you even afterwards, so there is very little reason not to use the ability as often as possible to learn everything you can without the consequences of leaving mistakes behind.
Outside of all of this said, I enjoyed the short chapter of this game, and do wish for more asap.  I'm a 36 year old male, and I don't buy into the hate this game has recieved due to characters in this tale having extreme political view points like some people who haven't even played the game complain about the game having.  You're not expected to think or behave anyway you don't wish too, so complaining about side characters and their viewpoints in a video game makes little sense to myself.  I enjoy lore.  I enjoy stories and plots.  I also enjoy mystery, time travel, and sci-fi.  This game has all of those things.
My only complaint, it's too short to make us wait until March for part 2 of 6.  I've replayed all options within a day, 9 hours in fact.  I guess the only thing I would go back and do again would be playing that damn guitar all night while I'm asleep, lol.
Dontnod, please in the future, make a full length game instead of episodic content.  You have the backing of Square-Enix now, so I don't see how it would be impossible at all.  I was never a fan of TWD episodic content, but decided to give this a chance, but I can say now, I'm still not a fan of it.  I'm a fan of this story, not the way it's delivered every 6 weeks.  I also don't like mid season breaks on tv shows either, so maybe you'll get a differing view point from this review than others, or maybe I'm just another person with an opinion that doesn't matter.
Try it out if you like Twin Peaks, Donnie Darko, or The Butterfly Effect.  The game draws it's inspiration from all of the above.
Now... I'm forced to wait, then wait again, then wait again, then wait again, then finally, wait one last time.  That imho, is dumb and promotes forced deadlines/content.

As for the artwork and soundtrack, both are absolutely beautiful! The hand drawn style really makes the world come to life and the soundtrack compliments the game perfectly.
I would highly recommend this game!

I absolutely loved this game. From the moment I got to the menu screen, I was graced by a beautiful soundtrack,  and a breathtaking art design. Modern day Oregon provides a spectacular setting for a game that packs a lot of punch into a short amount of time. There were multiple moments I was left shocked, jaw wide open, with the story taking a dramatic turn. There are a few ways to play this game, but the best way would be to take it slow, absorb every moment, and truly immerse yourself into it. The production team behind Life Is Strange makes it very easy to do so. The soundtrack truly captures the vibe of the story and at a few moments I caught myself feeling emotional, connecting to the characters through the music. The graphics are stunningly beautiful, from the tornado in the beginning to the peaceful aura of the blue butterfly standing out amongst a picture perfect Oregon sunset, it's a good thing the lead character is a photographer. Few games truly capture my imagination and immerse me into them like this one did. I recommend this game to anyone with an eye for art, a dream with photography, or a knack for adventure, to check this wonderful game out. And at a mere price of an expensive cup of coffee, you can't go wrong. BUY THIS GAME.

Every time I have a misgiving about this game, it finds some other way to make up for it. It doesn't necessarily right those wrongs, but god, does it ever make up for them. The third episode of life is strange is probably my favourite and has left me impatiently waiting for episode four. The story which meanders, begs for you to explore the world, and I can't think of any other game where I've felt quite this connected to the characters. Obvious awkward slang aside, the game shines when it stops trying to think of exactly how teenagers would talk, and instead lets the characters be themselves. The world is disheartening and quiet, too small and infinitely big, filled with this desire to do better and make things right. It is so firmly grounded in reality that I thought at times, that it could do just as well even without the time mechanic. I've changed my mind on that now, but wow. I love this game. The music is spot on and when they want to hit you hard, you'll be flat on your back.
TLDR; Get this game. It's great.

What a joy, what really stands out in this game is the way mechanics,  story and gameplay elegantly synergize into a complete hole. In many narritive-driven adventure games you are presented with a plotline and are allowed to make choices to influence the plot. However, this often results in save-scumming and reloading in order to achieve the desired outcome. What sets Life is Strange apart is how this retreading and altering of choices is not only allowed, it is encouraged by the game through the main character Max's comments about how she should or shouldn't advise a girl to duck from a stray football. This creates an environment where the player is presented with the full knowledge and immdiate consquences of events and can truly make an informed decision. The narrative itself appears to be lacking at this early stage, although this is to be expected at this junction: there are over half a dozen characters who require introduction and positioning with more expected to appear. The narritive is amazingly scoped and all future conflicts have already infused the player with investment at the conclusion of the first episode. The conflicts are all regulated to a single town but rather from deemphasizing their gravity, the conflicts are magnified. I'm very surprised and now realize disappointed this smaller reach isn't see this more in games. I can only wait patiently for the next installment in Life is Strange which cannot be released soon enough.

Pros:
1) Beautiful graphics and design.  Has a good feel of high school drama/coming of age story we've seen many times yet looks quite original.
2) Cool and very soothing indie/ambient soundtrack which serves as good addition to the visuals.
3) Characters are not original but could be very interesting. I guess we have to wait and see for a couple of episodes if that is true. Max/Chloe duo potentially looking very strong.
4) Lots of points of interest. They are not so easy to find and require from the players to not respect privacy of characters at all, so I missed quite a few of them but it makes the replayability that much higher.
5) Time-bending engine is very neat and easy to use.
Cons:
1) Story has a good head start and you might anticipate it to be quite intense yet it goes into complete stop right in the middle of the episode. Appearance of Chloe saves the day but not quite so. No there near The Walking Dead level of intensity and character development. But we got to wait for at least March to make sure.
2) Camera angles are dreadful and sometimes they make it very hard to actually find clues.
3) Overall experience is not very cinematic. You don't feel like its a TV show or a movie. Rather it looks and plays like a quest for 2000s audience. Biggest con of this three.
Overall: 7/10. Definitely will play it through but I am not near as excited to do it as I am for the new Walking Dead or Game of Thrones. It has to step up it's game to draw bigger audience.

I'm not sure where the negativity towards this game is coming from....
Episode One of Life Is Strange has you experience a traumatic day in the life of Max Caulfield, a student studying photography at the prestigious Blackwell Academy.  Part Twin Peaks, part Donnie Darko, part Brick, the story is interesting and compelling, with as much extra detail on the people around you as you feel like searching for.
The choice mechanics involved are novel although I feel it will take their interaction with future episodes to truly appreciate how well they work.  Voice acting is done well on the whole, and the art style is something I personally enjoyed a great deal - not everything has to be hyper-detailed textures on billion polygon models to look good.  The music is worth mentioning too, pleasing accoustic songs with actual vocals... in a way, reminds me of the stuff in Gray Matter by the Scarlet Furies.  It's refreshing, and suits the game well.
In the run up to release (this review is written day after release) there were many comments about the feminist agenda, Social Justice Warrior=ness, anti-male stance about the game.... al complete nonsense.  I've played this chapter thoroughly - everything that exists in it exists for the sake of the story and the setting.  Just because it's a female protagonist who thinks like a female doesn't make it a feminist agenda.  It's a story.  And so far at least, it's a good one.
I greatly enjoyed the first episode of Life Is Strange, and look forwards to the others.  I spent 5-6 hours following each conversation thread and gathering all the photo opportunities, which means potentially the complete game could provide 25-30 hours entertainment - pretty good value, if you ask me, especially considering the high potential for replay of these kind of stories to see what the consequences of other actions could have been.  I urge you to give it a try and engage yourself in Max Caulfield's troubled life.

Life is Strange is firmly in the "new school" of narrative-driven adventure games, in the same vein as The Walking Dead, Wolf Among Us, Vanishing of Ethan Carter, Dreamfall Chapters, etc. You explore the environment, interact with objects to hear Max's thoughts on them, talk to people, and get told a story (with some light puzzle solving interspersed). It actually reminded me a
of Dreamfall Chapters - which is a good thing in my book. The world is richly detailed; everything looks and feels "lived in" and there's lots of stuff to interact with.
I'm enjoying the story so far, and I'm intrigued where it will go. My only real occasional issue with the game is the dialogue. It can be a bit hit-or-miss, and
can it get cringe-worthy at some points. I am admittedly a 27-year old guy, so maybe I'm not the best person to judge how teenage girls speak nowadays, but I'm pretty sure nobody uses "hella" or "epic win" unironically (though supposedly "hella" is more of a west coast thing, so maybe I'm just out of the loop). In any case, the writing and voice acting are generally pretty decent, but there are a handful of painfully awkward bits of dialogue.
If you like modern-style adventure games, I would definitely give Life is Strange a try.

An amazing game similar enough to the Telltale game style to have its great qualities but unique enough to bring something new to the table. The rewind mechanic is a wish come true with these story driven episodic games, knowing that I can say whatever I want only to rewind and say something else is almost freeing. The fact that you can learn knew information, rewind and then use that information to say something different to achieve a goal is an incredible way to puzzle solve. Not to mention I can make a huge decision only to realise I didn't like the result and to go the other way is great. No longer do I have to quit to the main menu, rewind my game save and go again, feeling like an anal retentive control freak; this game rewards me being an anal retentive control freak!
As for the story it plays out like a modern day Twilight Zone filmed by an indie director. I mean that in a good way. A little scene where the character puts her head phones in and then I get to explore the school hallways with music playing in my ears was just so reminiscent of how I tend to explore the real world I couldn't help but grin. Also the strong emphasis on being a female driven story was a nice touch and I can't help but feel in 2015 I shouldn't have to praise a game for doing this but I do and Life Is Strange deserves it. Also for the record, just because the game is centred around females doesn't mean a male won't enjoy it. Again, I shouldn't have to say that but I feel I must.
Overall this game is definitely worth playing if you enjoy story driven episodic gaming. The game mechanics make it both fun and unique. The story is great if you enjoy indie films and enjoy games for the character development rather than just lots of action.

Just finished it now and it's not what I was expected. Rather, it was more than I could have hoped for.
This is very much like a Telltales game, but it feels much larger. There is more space to roam around and explore, more collectables, more, I guess, options. It's very similar to Heavy Rain on the Playstation 3.
I like the look of it. It's not trying to hard to be realistic looking like Assassins Creed and it doesn't have to be. It works just like this, it stands out and offers for much better animation.
The choices feel vast and each choice can make or break your story. Whether you lied about being sick in class to saving a fellow class mate, it all comes back to you.
As a freelance Photographer and Digital Design student, I was really blown away by how art is so heavily involved in the story and it's refreshing to see how much research was put into that. You would think that the developers would have just googled the names and just namedropped them into the game, but no. There is so much influence involved and just too much about the art styles that are brought up. You had to have researched them to get so much detail.
One of the negatives to the game is that the voices can sound echo-y and the audio track for the voices can overlap during a conversation making things look a little awkard. It's ruined the immersion of the game for me a few times.
Other people have mentioned that the game doesn't start for them, but the Developers have addressed this in the discussion forum.
There are also a lot of Square Enix "easter eggs". It's not so bad, but hooo boy are they just pushing them in your face.
Overall, the first episode is beautifully woven into 3 hours of excitement and heartache. At first I didn't like the Teen Angst start to this, but it quickly grew on me. It may not be a game for everyone, but for me, it's a solid game that I will never forget.
I can't wait for March.

If you have finished the game, you can still replay it to change your character's destiny. May be not too much, but at least I can imagine if my life as strange as inside this game, it would be perfect. Estimated play time: 2.5 - 4 hours to complete.

Lovely iteractive story.  The actual gameplay elements are limited, though it doesn't really feel that way when playing.  It really feels like it's your story, even when playing an 18 year American old college girl whilst actually being a mid-thirties British man.  The main input you have in the game are your decisions (coversations, set pieces etc); that and the time mechanic, which I won't go into as it is a relatively minor spoiler.  There are a few simple puzzles, though they probably won't pose much of  challenge.  I'd recommend taking your time, looking at everything, talking to everyone, as that is where the flesh and blood of the world is realised. There are little or no timed events so don't feel you have to rush around.  It took me almost exactly three hours to finish this episode, but if I'd just followed the main story arc, I suspect it could have been done in half the time.
If you are looking for an action game, a puzzle game or even an traditional adventure game, this probably isn't for you.  If the idea of a beautful story with well written, believable characters in a genuinely "real" feeling world where what you say and do at least seems to make a difference appeals, pick this up and get the season pass while your at it.  Definitely for fans of the Telltale games.  I love those, but I think I prefer this. The decisions feel like they might actually make meaningful differences, though we'll have to wait for the follow ups to see how much so.

No longer do I have to quit to the main menu, rewind my game save and go again, feeling like an anal retentive control freak; this game rewards me being an anal retentive control freak!
As for the story it plays out like a modern day Twilight Zone filmed by an indie director. I mean that in a good way. A little scene where the character puts her head phones in and then I get to explore the school hallways with music playing in my ears was just so reminiscent of how I tend to explore the real world I couldn't help but grin. Also the strong emphasis on being a female driven story was a nice touch and I can't help but feel in 2015 I shouldn't have to praise a game for doing this but I do and Life Is Strange deserves it. Also for the record, just because the game is centred around females doesn't mean a male won't enjoy it. Again, I shouldn't have to say that but I feel I must.
Overall this game is definitely worth playing if you enjoy story driven episodic gaming. The game mechanics make it both fun and unique. The story is great if you enjoy indie films and enjoy games for the character development rather than just lots of action.

Having only played the first episode so far, I am still more than a little surprised at how fantastic and fulfilling this game is. It took me about 3 hours to play through once, but man, those were an AWESOME 3 hours. Although some games like this have the issue of feeling to much like a movie, I can honestly say Life Is Strange manages to actually make you feel like your choices matter, second guessing every decision you make. It also feels incredibly modern, using technology and slang in a way that is common but not cliche in our world.
My favorite part of Life Is Strange isn't the cool gameplay mechanics, the beautiful, stylistic art, or even the engaging storyline. No, my favorite part is the main character, something that is incredibly rare. While normally main characters are faceless or some different from the player, Max manages to be a relateable teenager without being annoying. I found myself laughing at least a dozen times at some of her self-analysis moments when she realized she was being stereotypical or mean. Still, her being an "anti-teenager but still a teenager" isn't the best part about her.
It's that she's an introvert. As someone who is an introvert and (somewhat) artistic, I can honestly say that the developers did a spot on job when they made this aspect of her. There were times when Max thought something and I had to stop for a second because it seemed almost exactly like something I would say or think. Her amazing wit and self reflection is what really drives home Max as a character. She's someone who I can honestly say I will remember, and that's (argueably) rare in video games these days.
Overall, I am more than satisfied with this game. I would honestly say this is a work of art more then a game, or maybe even a story. I understand this type of game may not be for everyone, but I can honsetly say I can't wait to see where this adventure leads.

I walked in expecting this to be either great or pretentious, and I walked out pleasantly waiting for the next episode.
I'm very happy to slow down and play a game this relaxing, but not detached.
It's worth noting that I thought immediately that the protagonist was a bit clicheed, but that wound up being a great canvas for me to say "no, do this, I want you to be this protagonist" and I felt like there was always the option that I was looking for. Not only that, but I really thought about some of the decisions.
There have been millions of times where I'd play a game and be like "dude, call the police!" or "don't go in the closet!" and I was actually able to do that stuff. It felt good.
Voice acting is pretty good, I'd say. The framing and aesthetics of the shots are really great sometimes. It's got its bases in real world teen culture, which I can't say I'm too huge in, but that did create a great sense of immersion.
So from where chapter 1 leaves me, I would say that I can't speak as to whether or not the next ones will be good, especially since this one felt largely like an introduction. I will say that I think the future episodes have potential to carry this story very far.

I would start writing this review by comparing it to the popular episodic series from TellTale, but it wouldn't do it justice. This game hasn't just taken what TellTale does and turned it into something unique, this game by itself stands as a testament to the genre.
Episode 1 of this game had me captivated from the get-go. It has a strong opening even if I was skeptical about it. The art style sold me over the course of the episode. In the beginning you could think the graphics are too simplistic and don't achieve anything substantial. But it's charm comes from it's simple style, and each shot you see looks beautiful in the amazing lighting this game has. It feels like you're playing inside a painting, with soft and vibrant colours. Life is Strange also boasts some of the most perfect music, as each piece fits the situation you're placed in.
The story, which is what the bulk of people thinking about buying this game will care about. You're placed in the shoes of Max, who is a shy, reclusive and socially awkward teenager at a school full of stereotypes. You have rich-kids, jocks, cheerleaders, hipsters, nerds and bullies. In the midst of this completely typical school, Max disocvers she can rewind time. At this point it is sounding like the beginning to a teen fiction novel, however, Max is slowly drawn into the politics of the school, and the darker and grittier side of the school keeps you intrigued. Everyone seems to have a secret and there are things you witness that you don't understand. The satisfaction of this game comes from searching for answers. Whether or not the answers are as satisfying as the search will remain to be seen, but uncovering secrets one by one while also learning about Max's past relationships in the town of Arcadia is what I imagine the bulk of the rest of the game will be, and I can't wait to play episode 2 in March.

Okay... So, how am I gonna start?
***Disclaimer***
Short version: This is the first time for me writing this stuff. And my English is abysmal at best. Haven't got time to read this? Go to TL;DR section at the bottom.

Long version: This is the first time I've ever written something about a game. English, in addition, is not even my first language.
That means anyone reading this incomprehensible babbling might find neither necessary "rhetoric" nor "language skills" presumably needed for this kind of writing. Watching me eating humble pie just to share my train-wrecked comment about this game shall get you some idea how awesome the game is. (Subject NP too long... sigh)
***The rig I used***
Mac Mini 2012 server (I used Bootcamp, Windows 8).
Short version: Playable (30FPS average), iff you make a compromise.
Long version: My Window rig is down atm, so I really had no choice.
The point I wanted to make is this: even with a seriously underpowered integrated GPU (Intel HD 4000, I think?), the game is somewhat playable, if you are willing to make some compromise.
Basically I cranked my resolution down to 1280*720, turned the shadow setting to the lowest, and axed antialiasing. But I set remaining gfx options (e.g. texture quality) to the highest. I got 30 FPS for the most of the time. Ground textures seemed rather blurry, though. But the problem would be on my side (Intel GFX, folks), not the game itself.
***Game mechanics***
Short version: Control-wise, you are all set if you are familiar with Telltale games. Max's time-rewinding skill lets you easily rescind your "choice", which is more than interesting.
Long version:  For those who have played games like The Walking Dead, or Wolf Among Us, you could basically use your KB+M like in those games: WASD for movements, mouse for looking up, etc.
Rewinding time is certainly a clever feature, in that you could always look for the ramification of all possible choices, and pick out the best choice. I bet Robert Frost certainly would have liked this handy dandy magic skill! She could rewind time up to certain point, however: move on to the next area, no more turning back the clock. You still have to load your autosave should that happen.
***Story***
Short version: Cool, clever, charming, captivating.
Long version: Spoiler is a felony with this kind of game (and especially when the story is great), so these lips are sealed. Suffice it to say that I've never thought angst of youth, high school life and time-reversing skill would go along well and result in the masterpiece that this game is. (Rifling through other people's stuff to progress sometimes leaves odd taste to my mouth, though!)
***TL;DR version***
Buy it. It is one-of-a-kind game, in terms of story-wise. There is a reason that I placed this incoherent wall of text!

A very strong series. The developer DONTNOD take some heavy cues from longtime episodic adventure game developer Telltale games but with their own very smart twist. Borrowing their time scrubbing mechanic from Remember Me they build a whole game around time travel and integrate it in clever ways into the puzzles and dialog. Since this is a game where you can reverse almost any choice they make the choices really hard and you won't find out the consequences of your actions till much later.
This is a game with strong characters in a setting that is rarely explored in video games. While its by no means perfect they nail a lot of smaller character moments and the story goes to some legitimately shocking places.
There are not a lot of games like this and the price is more than reasonable for the quality DONTNOD delivers.

Having only played the first episode so far, I am still more than a little surprised at how fantastic and fulfilling this game is. It took me about 3 hours to play through once, but man, those were an AWESOME 3 hours. Although some games like this have the issue of feeling to much like a movie, I can honestly say Life Is Strange manages to actually make you feel like your choices matter, second guessing every decision you make. It also feels incredibly modern, using technology and slang in a way that is common but not cliche in our world.
My favorite part of Life Is Strange isn't the cool gameplay mechanics, the beautiful, stylistic art, or even the engaging storyline. No, my favorite part is the main character, something that is incredibly rare. While normally main characters are faceless or some different from the player, Max manages to be a relateable teenager without being annoying. I found myself laughing at least a dozen times at some of her self-analysis moments when she realized she was being stereotypical or mean. Still, her being an "anti-teenager but still a teenager" isn't the best part about her.
It's that she's an introvert. As someone who is an introvert and (somewhat) artistic, I can honestly say that the developers did a spot on job when they made this aspect of her. There were times when Max thought something and I had to stop for a second because it seemed almost exactly like something I would say or think. Her amazing wit and self reflection is what really drives home Max as a character. She's someone who I can honestly say I will remember, and that's (argueably) rare in video games these days.
Overall, I am more than satisfied with this game. I would honestly say this is a work of art more then a game, or maybe even a story. I understand this type of game may not be for everyone, but I can honsetly say I can't wait to see where this adventure leads.

This review is only for episode 1 and therefore does not represent the entire 5 episode season.
This game is told from the perspective of a 17-18 year old girl attending a later grade school with a focus on photography, when out of nowhere, the character obtains the ability to ''rewind'' up to a few minutes of time. This game's genre is described as a ''point and click'' adventure, whereby the object of the game is to interact with any and all objects in the game, including other characters. This also has the branching style options to choose from, do you inform the principle of bad things happening in the school, or do you keep quiet so as to not cause yourself any trouble.
Whilst at this point in time, there is no ''effect'' for these choices it is specifically and explicitly stated that ''this choice has consequences'' after making one.
What sets this game apart is the fact that for any and all choices, be it how you respond to another character, interacting with objects or whether you interact with them at all, CAN BE UNDONE. You open a door with causes X to happen. If you dont want it to happen you can simply ''rewind'' time back to the point before making the choice to open that door - effectively negating the consequence altogether.
The trick here is, nobody knows what those consequences will turn out to be. By saving X character's life in episode 1, could in fact lead to your own character's death in episode 5!
The audio in this game is absolutely superb, with music flowing exactly where it should, audio cues right on track along with amazing delivery of lines from the cast and a sense of emotion from each character.
The graphics are what, for me personally, ended up being my only gripe. I personally am not a fan of stylised graphics such as those from Borderlands with its ''cell shaded'' imagery. It may not be a problem for you - you may even like the graphics of this game, but i found myself being constantly drawn out of the game by it.
The only other part of the game i did not enjoy was the lip syncing. O M G the timing, movement and execution of the lip syncing was downright awful. Yes the characters opened their mouths when their lines started playing and kept moving for the entire sentence, but it was quite painful to watch.
All in all, if you enjoy story far more than action and mystery more than zombies (no there is none here sorry) then this game is at least worth the price for just the first episode. If i were you, i would suggest doing what i did and only buying the first episode to pay as little as possible to determine if you want to pay the rest and experience the entire story. You can buy the ''get the rest'' following episodes for the cheaper price if you find you want to keep going.
I would recommend that this game is worth it and should be experienced by as many as possible.

Life Is Strange reminds me of an old game, Shadow of Memories, and the movie Donnie Darko, and is similar in that when you die right off the bat you discover that you can rewind time and change the outcome, and even save the world (or at least be an everyday hero.) The gameplay is a little odd in that you are a nosey photographer girl that will do things ranging from busting school bullies to looking at your friend's pregancy test and use your awesome power of time travel for everything from major events like saving lives, social events like magically making friends, and generally doing ninja stuff.  You have to use this mechanic to unlock dialogue options with various characters and get different story outcomes and events. Unlike other "decision games" like Hard Rain, this series has violence but no combat, at least in the first episode. The playtime is quite short and linear, though there is good replayability to explore other choices and make new discoveries. The game gives you hints to when you did something that will have consequences or unlock an option later on, and at the end it lists several decisions which works as a guidebook of sorts and posts your stats so you can see what percentage of people chose what.
The story is unusual in that it is a very realistic drama with events and topics like murder in a school bathroom over drug money, rich privledge, and a soldier at home with a teenage step-daughter with both of them trying to figure out how to cope with each other. But it also focuses on gossip, making friends, texting, etc. One minute you are reporting attempted homicide and the next you are responding to a text message from a friendzoned guy. Mostly this is realistic, and it is effective in the story.  But sometimes it sticks out a little too much, as there are larger story elements like a missing girl, creepy stalkers, and an impending natural disaster that makes me want to put on my fedora hat and get down to solving the big mysteries and worry a little less about who sexted whom. After all, I'm a  superheroine now, experiencing traumatic events every ten minutes, so it is a little hard to believe I would be working my normal routine and rifling through my friend's desk drawers, or at least not while they watched me, not reacting until I pull their secerets out of a box.
Overall, Life Is Strange is a title worth adding to your collection simply for the great story, and the decision making element does deliver replayability that will multiply as new episodes are released. I wish that the gameplay was more sandbox mode and less rail-like, more focused on the adventure and story elements and less focused on teens and their technology. Would you darn kids get off my lawn already?

This game tells a very engaging story that is done through a mechanic of rewinding time and trying to change possible outcomes before you become stuck with them (thereby having the chance to change your decision before exiting the zone, in which you would then be stuck with the decision).
The story centers around a young college student who is old school with photography (she's still using the Polaroid instant picture cameras). She has a vision of a tornado before soon finding out that she has the power to rewind time and put right what goes wrong. A major mystery is the disapperance of a young girl who the protagonist's friend had befriended herself. It's an engaging plot brought along by terrific voice acting that makes you feel as though you are watching an independent film, with fitting music and visual graphic art style that, while it take a moment or two to get used to it, fits every single moment of the story telling. The characters feel real, and because of that, it immerses you into it's story.
Using this power, you have the ability to learn what the right answers are to some of the questions that will help you to proceed. Furthermore, the game does a terrific job in making you doubt every single decision you make, thereby giving you some incentitve to at least see the reactions of the people who you affect (at least the immediate reactions, as you're stuck with the decision once you exit that particualr zone). Sometimes, there are a few decisions that may lead to still alterate decisions in a particular area, which furthers the depth. There are no direct failure states, but the failure states are having to deal with the decisions you choose in the story. There are also some side elements that you can find out about, and can make decisions on that you might not even realize are there, giving you incentive to snoop around and search everywhere to find those hidden elements.
Like some Telltale Games, this will be released in a episodic format, and I implore you to get the full game. It only took me a few hours to complete episode one, but you might take longer if you search for everything. By far, a very gripping story and fluid controls and mechanics make this game worthy of your time.

A point and click adventure/interactive movie along the same lines as Telltale Games' The Walking Dead or The Wolf Among Us, Life Is Strange has the added ability to immediately rewind your choices to pick other options to see how they work out. While it seems like this mostly a gimmick at first as you progress through the story you see how this ability can be used to rework events to your advantage in a way that can't be seen until you've gone through the event "normally" at least once.
You play the game as Maxine (Max for short), a shy and insecure 18 year old high school student who's recently returned to her hometown to go to a boarding school with a prestigeous photograpohy program. After witnessing a shooting in the girls' washroom after class, you discover that you have the ability to rewind time and alter events based on what you've already seen.
Additionally, unlike many oher games, we get to hear a great deal of Max's internal monologue (more than just thoughts about pictures on the wall, like what tends to be the extent of that in many of these types of games), which means we get to hear her second guessing the decisions that have been made; I found that this helped get into Max's mind more as you progressed through the story, and that may help with replayability of the game itself as you might want to go through the whole thing again once you're "more in tune" with how Max thinks.
That's kind of the basic set up, as I've only played the first episode so far, it's tough to see where the story itself is headed, because there really isn't much story that actually unfolds in the episode. Thus far we've really only seen set up and world building going on. As opposed to Telltale's adventure games, the main character is a fully realized person with a complex backstory, so decisions that you're faced with aren't necessarily "what would I do in this situation" but more of "what do I want to see Max do in this situation?" Also, Maxine clearly has a pretty complicated backstory, but very little of it is related to the player in an entertaining way (you get an 8 page journal to read that explains the last few years of Max's life, but who the hell wants to read lol?) and that leaves the first play through a little confusing  as you're frequently asking yourself "why wouldn't she do X instead of Y?"
Anyway, TLDR: The "rewind" feature is more than a cool gimmick, and a protagonist that is more than just a cipher for audience interaction in the story give this series a lot of potential, and replayability; but the first episode is mostly just set up with very little pay off.

Life Is Strange is an episodic "adventure" game. The player character is Max, a female high school senior that is attending a private high school, and she wished to become a photographer. Expect to spend a lot of time walking around, examining a variety of objects in the environment - and hearing your characters inner monologue. You also spend much of your time conversing with other characters in the game, which are generally you're classmates. The game also has some very light puzzle solving. So basically, it's a modern story-driven adventure game in the same vain as the recent Telltale adventure games.
Throughout the episode you are faced with a series of binary choices through the episode, where the game allows you to choose what you would like to do in a particular scenario. But it's not quite as simple as this - and I'll touch on that later. These choices will theoretically have consequences down the road, but as only the first episode has been released I can't actually comment how "impactful" the choices will be. If they do impact the story heavily that could potentially be quite interesting, but even If they don't - I'd say embrace the illusion of choice. Enjoy the journey of your character and the various ♥♥♥♥♥♥ situations that you will find yourself in. Much like real life you're going to be faced with choices here that don't have a particularly satisfying outcome either way.
The game also has smaller choices that the game proclaims will have consequences down the line such as whether or not you choose to water the plant in your dorm room or if you snoop and find something you shouldn't be seeing. Many of these instances are missable and in many cases not interacting with these instances is in itself a choice that will have an impact. The game has a stat breakdown at the end so you can see the statistics of the percentage of players that made each choice.
The writing of the game feels a little dated in spots. Like hella dated. Some of the characters seem a little unbelievable at this point in the story. Hopefully with some more character development in the later episodes it will make some of the characters a little more believable. Generally speaking though, the writing as well as characterization is fine. It is a bit stereotypical in its starting point for many of its side characters; hopefully it will do these characters justice in future episodes. The main character Max does seem to be written well as she seems like a believable eighteen year old high student.
I think that this game would be best played if you know as little as possible so I will say this, don't read this paragraph unless you're okay with a minor spoiler. Alright cool? You're still with me which means you're ready to go down this dark path of spoiling yourself, awesome! One of the major mechanics of the game is that the player character has the ability to rewind time in order to make different decisions with the knowledge gained from attempting something once or twice. This is utilized to allow the player to see both sides of a major decision they have to make - allowing you to decide which path you want to go down. It is also utilized by the game also to do some very light puzzle solving - which are incredibly easy but at the very least interesting usages of the time control mechanic. One particular artistic choice that I particularly enjoyed was the portrayal of photographs within the game as paintings. I generally found these paintings to be quite nice.  And, I'll just throw in here that the voice acting seems good thus far; nothing to complain about but nothing noteworthy.

This review is only for episode 1 and therefore does not represent the entire 5 episode season.
This game is told from the perspective of a 17-18 year old girl attending a later grade school with a focus on photography, when out of nowhere, the character obtains the ability to ''rewind'' up to a few minutes of time. This game's genre is described as a ''point and click'' adventure, whereby the object of the game is to interact with any and all objects in the game, including other characters. This also has the branching style options to choose from, do you inform the principle of bad things happening in the school, or do you keep quiet so as to not cause yourself any trouble.
Whilst at this point in time, there is no ''effect'' for these choices it is specifically and explicitly stated that ''this choice has consequences'' after making one.
What sets this game apart is the fact that for any and all choices, be it how you respond to another character, interacting with objects or whether you interact with them at all, CAN BE UNDONE. You open a door with causes X to happen. If you dont want it to happen you can simply ''rewind'' time back to the point before making the choice to open that door - effectively negating the consequence altogether.
The trick here is, nobody knows what those consequences will turn out to be. By saving X character's life in episode 1, could in fact lead to your own character's death in episode 5!
The audio in this game is absolutely superb, with music flowing exactly where it should, audio cues right on track along with amazing delivery of lines from the cast and a sense of emotion from each character.
The graphics are what, for me personally, ended up being my only gripe. I personally am not a fan of stylised graphics such as those from Borderlands with its ''cell shaded'' imagery. It may not be a problem for you - you may even like the graphics of this game, but i found myself being constantly drawn out of the game by it.
The only other part of the game i did not enjoy was the lip syncing. O M G the timing, movement and execution of the lip syncing was downright awful. Yes the characters opened their mouths when their lines started playing and kept moving for the entire sentence, but it was quite painful to watch.
All in all, if you enjoy story far more than action and mystery more than zombies (no there is none here sorry) then this game is at least worth the price for just the first episode. If i were you, i would suggest doing what i did and only buying the first episode to pay as little as possible to determine if you want to pay the rest and experience the entire story. You can buy the ''get the rest'' following episodes for the cheaper price if you find you want to keep going.
I would recommend that this game is worth it and should be experienced by as many as possible.

A point and click adventure/interactive movie along the same lines as Telltale Games' The Walking Dead or The Wolf Among Us, Life Is Strange has the added ability to immediately rewind your choices to pick other options to see how they work out. While it seems like this mostly a gimmick at first as you progress through the story you see how this ability can be used to rework events to your advantage in a way that can't be seen until you've gone through the event "normally" at least once.
You play the game as Maxine (Max for short), a shy and insecure 18 year old high school student who's recently returned to her hometown to go to a boarding school with a prestigeous photograpohy program. After witnessing a shooting in the girls' washroom after class, you discover that you have the ability to rewind time and alter events based on what you've already seen.
Additionally, unlike many oher games, we get to hear a great deal of Max's internal monologue (more than just thoughts about pictures on the wall, like what tends to be the extent of that in many of these types of games), which means we get to hear her second guessing the decisions that have been made; I found that this helped get into Max's mind more as you progressed through the story, and that may help with replayability of the game itself as you might want to go through the whole thing again once you're "more in tune" with how Max thinks.
That's kind of the basic set up, as I've only played the first episode so far, it's tough to see where the story itself is headed, because there really isn't much story that actually unfolds in the episode. Thus far we've really only seen set up and world building going on. As opposed to Telltale's adventure games, the main character is a fully realized person with a complex backstory, so decisions that you're faced with aren't necessarily "what would I do in this situation" but more of "what do I want to see Max do in this situation?" Also, Maxine clearly has a pretty complicated backstory, but very little of it is related to the player in an entertaining way (you get an 8 page journal to read that explains the last few years of Max's life, but who the hell wants to read lol?) and that leaves the first play through a little confusing  as you're frequently asking yourself "why wouldn't she do X instead of Y?"
Anyway, TLDR: The "rewind" feature is more than a cool gimmick, and a protagonist that is more than just a cipher for audience interaction in the story give this series a lot of potential, and replayability; but the first episode is mostly just set up with very little pay off.

This game is easily my favorite game of 2015 and one of my favorite games of all time. The art style, the tone, the sound track, the real-to-life genuine, relatable, loveable, endearing characters, the quality of the voice acting, the interesting take on the time travel genre, the touching coming of age story all combine together to create a wonderful game that I can wholeheartedly suggest to any player whether or not you've played an episodic adventure game or watched an indie movie in your life.
