This is the the first episodic game i have had the pleasure of playing, despite wanting to play some of Telltales games in the past. But after the experience i have had in the past 3 hours, i simply love this game... it is near impecable and the only problem i had with it is that some of the textures where a bit glitchy but that was most likely because i have a bad computer. This game has affected me in the small amount of time it takes to play and finish, but its length in no way makes it bad, size does indeed definetly not matter.
The world is well designed and the character building really makes you dislike or like certain characters the moment you meet them, from the shy Kate to the detestable Victoria, from the lovable teachers to the arrogant security guard. The game really made me feel what i believe they wanted me to feel while at the same time allowing me to follow the actions that i believe were right such as being kind when most would not, or keeping quiet because i know telling the truth is pointless.
Frankly ive never really believed in writing reviews and infact i never have, but Life is Strange is just one game that i would consider a must play for anyone.
Now I want to look at this from a developers view. After already daying that I do love this game this part will be rather short. This game is a testament to what can be achieved in games and why they are such a huge part of our lives today. It shows us how games effect us not in a way that they would make us change how we would act in our everyday lives but more like making us see how some things are wrong and even showing us that its okay to show your emotions some times. This game is a testiment to the power of games in the modern world. As a writer an artist and games developer I encountered alot of things in this game that inspire me as well as i'm sure will inspire many others. games like this inspire us and gives us a world where we can escape and encounter a story where our actions matter while at the same time having the safety net of knowing it isnt real, they allow us to either simply escape and live another life for a while, or while we are escaping let off some steam and destress; let go of the events of the day.
Edit after Episode two:
The Great story continues and this time it gets better, as the consequences of your actions begin to take hole. The game throws you striaght back into the thick of it. A very important thing about this episode is that once you and Max(Main char) are getting used to her newfound powers, they throw you into a scene where you're actions can cause a massive shift in the games narrative, and they take your powers away for the scene, meaning there is no retries at this scene. Throw in the cliffhangar tav series ending and you've got another brilliant episode of Life is Strange from Dontnod Entertainment
TL;DR: This is a great game, worth the money. Great story, great world design, great character bulding. No cons from me.

A charming, haunting and enjoyable story from the deliberate confusing start to its chapter ending, filled with well spoken dialogue and set to a wonderfully detailed backdrop. Oh and the music is expertly spot on for the mood.
Now having played and completed to the games ending I can honestly say this was an emotional rollercoaster experience. Not since the Mass Effect series has a game made user choice through simple story telling been more difficult thanks to the wonderful writing and the out pouring of love it's central character has for her messed up world in Arcadia Bay.
Cause and effect, wonderfully demonstrated in heart tugging fashion chapter after chapter. How your choices over the course of the five episodes and wether you really have invested yourself into this world will greatly determine how you deal with the games ending. If you see it how I perceive the developers want us to see it, then its genius. If you see it in simplistic terms without recognising that all other decisions _have_ in fact mattered to this point, then I feel sad that you missed the point they were trying to tell.
If you enjoy games that pull you in with writing, dreamy visuals and lovely voice acting that deal with every day problems, while messing with heart strings, then buy this series, avoid the Let's Plays and just experience it blind.
Bravo DONTNOD Entertainment. Bravo.

Life is Strange shows a completley original story with an amazing set of characters that never lack depth.
To top it all off, the time travel allows several very short and easy puzzles. You don't even have to do most of the puzzles if you want!
As the player, you can choose what pace you want to take the game at. Either pass by most of the "look at" options (Which I do not reccomend), or observe what's around you and it's signifigance.
Interaction with other characters is one of my favorite elements. You can mainly choose who you want to interact with and how your relationship develops with them. If you've said something wrong, you can rewind.
Choices in Life is Strange were very difficult. Some have not taken into effect yet, as this is Episode One of five. However, I was left at times very conflicted with myself on what to do.
The soundtrack is unbelieveably amazing. I loved how the music would overlay the area as I interacted with objects and other people.
Graphics at first do not appeal to most, however grows on the players as you realize how it adds to the atmosphere.
As for running this game, I have the lowest of the low laptop, and I have all settings on high. Occasionally, there is an audio bug where a dialoge is played twice, or lip sync will shift off balance. However, I've had two updates so far and it's been improving these issues each time.
If you love TellTale Games, Gone Home, or others of the sort, pick this game up. It will combine everything you love about point and clicks into this beautiful game. It's astonishing how much I am into this world and I've only played 5 hours (That's one episode length)! Can't wait until Episode 2!

This is a summary of my review video, which I encourage you to watch
if you are looking for a more in-depth review.
Life is Strange is an adventure story told in a movie style broken into
five separately released chapters.  Some of the more weighty topics explored in this game are bullying in school, climate change caused by humans, and the mental state of veterans. The music is very professional and the voice acting is well done, though I would have liked to seen some, or any of the main characters presented as something other than rail thin, as this sets a negative precedence for self image.
The story centers around a frail looking 18 year old girl who has the
ability to rewind time. The concept has a lot of potential, but it has not
been integrated well, as it is mainly only useful when there is a dialogue option,not during an actual event. You are not given the option to use or not use this ability dealing with major plot points, allowing a positive or negative side effects to occur as the lack of depth in the story comes clear when you try to go against what the game wants to happen. Instead you are forced to use it as the game dictates. Being able to go back and choose a different dialogue option has been available for a long time in computer games;  it's called quick save.
This mechanic has no real use out side of dialog, as for all the other parts of the game, giving them a scripted feel, and you are left frustrated with the games lack of depth. You have to go through the situation as it is presented to you, instead of making your own choice and dealing with any potential consequences. You are just along for the ride not actually in control of anything.
The story in itself is good, but definitely not a game with replay value;
there is no availability to skip conversations, so you must hear every conversation, and watch every cinematic whether you want to or not.  Based on the story, if all five episodes were out, I might recommend this game, but the scripted nature of the playthrough and the limited time rewind mechanic would make this a better  candidate for watching as a playthrough on youtube rather than spending the money to play through yourself.  I cannot recommend this game as it more like watching a  TV show than playing a game. It's not entertaining, and is not good game play.

This review is not supposed to focus on the good side of
. Don't consider this to be a negative review, but a warning.
I am a fan of story-based and character-driven movies, TV shows and video games.
,
and
were milestones in the interactive media.
The first episode of Life is Strange begins slow.
But what could be a chance to build up strong characters focuses almost exclusively on the protagonist Max and her friend Chloe. The dialogue is limited and the supporting characters keep a rather low profile. You are only limited to know, what the game wants you to know. You are very limited to explore these characters on your own.
Another big downfall is the incoherent flow of time and logic.
While the middle part of the first episode is designed around a date, the game shows no feedback for time. You can explore the game in your own pacing. But you don't know, whether you might be too late or too soon. No clock gives you a feeling for time. Or maybe it's irrelevant since your date will wait for you the whole day?
Logic.
The most problematic aspect of this game is the logic. Every time it is disturbed, the player becomes disturbed, too. Let's explore two examples:
Leaving a building due to a fire alarm is followed by a change of scenery. While inside the building everyone was getting out, outside everyone acts like nothing special happened a minute ago. An authority person doesn't try to get you into a safe zone but asks for your signature on a petition. Not very believable.
Max, the character you are playing, is a photography student. At one landmark she does a comment on a beautiful scenery. Why does she take no picture with her instant camera or why am I as the player not able to? On the other hand I can take pictures of much less expression for some achievements. A possible explanation would be, that Max isn't a good photographer and only takes pictures of rather unimportant objects. But why does she a comment on a beautiful scenery?
Update for Epidoe 2:
Only one minor logic problem occurred when you talk to two people and the other person doesn't recognize the third person in the dialogue. But it feels only strange for a second.
An important element of interactive storytelling is the opportunity for the player to change the story. Life is Strange has its moments, when you help people (or not) or change objects in the world (or not). The big choices are even highlighted so you can change your decision if you want.
But so far, there is no telling, if choices have any impact on the story.
Update for Episode 2:
The choices you have to make start to grow and the story starts to feel more like your way to interact with the world then a scripted story.

A charming, haunting and enjoyable story from the deliberate confusing start to its chapter ending, filled with well spoken dialogue and set to a wonderfully detailed backdrop. Oh and the music is expertly spot on for the mood.
Now having played and completed to the games ending I can honestly say this was an emotional rollercoaster experience. Not since the Mass Effect series has a game made user choice through simple story telling been more difficult thanks to the wonderful writing and the out pouring of love it's central character has for her messed up world in Arcadia Bay.
Cause and effect, wonderfully demonstrated in heart tugging fashion chapter after chapter. How your choices over the course of the five episodes and wether you really have invested yourself into this world will greatly determine how you deal with the games ending. If you see it how I perceive the developers want us to see it, then its genius. If you see it in simplistic terms without recognising that all other decisions _have_ in fact mattered to this point, then I feel sad that you missed the point they were trying to tell.
If you enjoy games that pull you in with writing, dreamy visuals and lovely voice acting that deal with every day problems, while messing with heart strings, then buy this series, avoid the Let's Plays and just experience it blind.
Bravo DONTNOD Entertainment. Bravo.

Get it. That's all I need to say.
If you're looking for a game that is all out action, move along. This is not for you. If you're looking for something fun with a great story and characters, get it. And buy the full pack. Don't just buy the first because after you've finished the first episode, you will want to get the next as it leaves you with many questions that you will want answering.
It is pretty much a point-and-click game but it's more than that and you have a lot more freedom in what you can do. You feel incontrol the majority of the time.
Episode 1:
It was a good start to the game. Will get you hooked but the time travel does not play such a huge roll. It does have some small effects to what happens later on but not much. The story is the main part of this game so that's what you are buying. They introduce charters slowly so you can easily understand who's who. A great introduction to a great episodic game series.
Episode play time - 3 hours
Episode 2:
It starts off okay. Not as big of a bang like the first episode but it soon gets into the story. Every decision you made in the last episode starts to come back to haunt you as chioces you made at the time now seem wrong. And make sure you choose wisely as some choices leave drastic conciquences down the road. The only thing I didn't like about this episode was some of the small memory games you had to play at the Diner but past that everything was fine. I'd prefer to focus more on the story and coices than that. But other than that, this episode was great, enjoyable and, well, pretty stressful at times but you will have to play the game to find out why.
Episode play time - 3 hours
Episode 3:
What? Mind. Blown.
Let's start from the beginning. There is some weird dialog like "Cowabunga" and stuff like that which sort of took me out of the experience a little. And the animation for the swimming in the pool was some of the worst I have ever seen but that isn't much of a problem. Some of the games you play to find information and progress onto the next stage can be a little hard. Well not hard, but tedious and repetitive which it did in the scene in the diner. It begun to take a little too long.
Possible spoiler
And then that ending. Well, it was certainly something. I'm just saying, make sure your last decision is the right one. I was left genuinely shocked by the choice I made. My mind was confused, amazed and upset all at the same time. I don't know what is going to happen in the next episode
Episode play time - 3 hours
Episode 4:
Welp. Need I say more? No, but I'm going to.
This episode was absolutely insane. It is beginning to wrap things up and you begin to connect the dots which leave you so confused but at the same time you understand what's going on. This episode had the most difficult puzzles so far in the series. There were parts which I even had to look up a tutorial which did take out of the experience. Expecially one part at the start. Took about 5 minutes due to a bad game mechanic but as soon as that was through, everything run smoothly with a few difficulties here and there. My PC had struggles to run the final scene at the Vortex Party. That's about my only complaint. There was also a lot more video in this episode I think compared to the last. So less game play. But that isn't a problem in my opinion. Infact, I prefer it like that. I am so ready for the last episode. Have no clue how it will end.
Episode play time - 4 hours
Episode 5:
Obviously, I had quite high expectations for this episode. It was the last episode of a brilliant series so I really wanted it to end brilliantly. At the start, I thought it was going to be a bad ending. For the first maybe 30 minutes everything was quite slow and I didn't feel like I was progressing in anyway. But then everything begun to kick off and get better. The episode then went on a drastic turn which I don't think anyone expected and felt really odd and creepy which is the atmosphere I suspect they were aiming for. I can't say much more without giving anything away. This episode had a lot more cut scenes and felt a lot more like a movie than the previous episodes.
Episode play time - 3 hours
Total play time - 18/19 hours
In conclusion, get it if you want a game with a good story and  a great soundtrack. If you just care about gameplay and graphics this is not for you.

If you have bad memories playing Remember Me, don't let that discourage you from playing this.
If you're a fan of Telltale adventure games, don't let that make you pass this non-Telltale one.
If you're one of those LISbians claiming this game is a 'Telltale destroyer' or some sort, please go away.
All I can say is that this game is DONTNOD's comeback effort and it looks, plays, and, most importantly, tells the story very, very well.
Read the lengthy review below if you want to.
When I finished the
, I immediately think this game is a cross between Telltale adventure games in terms of navigation, DONTNOD's past game Remember Me in terms of time-rewinding mechanic (more on this later), and Gone Home in terms of atmosphere.
And that is rather brilliant, with almost spotless soundtrack to go with it.
You're playing as Max(ine) Caulfield, a rather geeky teenage girl who's quite fond of photography.
She's studying at Blackwell Academy in a town called Arcadia Bay, can rewind time, and seeing weather-related premonitions.
The 1st episode basically introduces you to the quite varied cast of NPCs that basically represents most of the stereotypes in a college.
The
is where the roller coaster starts to get more intense.
Also puts way more emphasis on exploring each and every bit of things you can interact with.
This may put off even seasoned Telltale players, but these 'optionals' are where you can get more involved with the game's story and NPCs.
Because you might save a life by doing that.
The 'minor choices' you did in the previous episode actually affect quite a bit.
They mostly changes some NPCs' dialogues when talking to Max, but at times also how Max interacts with them.
The weight of your choice in this episode feels heavier due to the nature of the unfolding situation, unlike in the 1st episode where most of it were quite straightforward.
In this episode, you probably won't be sure if you picked the right 'side', or if you even have picked a 'side' at all.
And then comes the
.
Suffice to say my faith in this game hasn't been misplaced (yet).
If you thought episode 2 was a roller coaster ride, then this is probably piloting an X-Wing to blow the Death Star.
And Max has a new ability.
Just like near the end of the 2nd episode where Max could (inadvertently) freeze time.
This time she not 'only' freezes time, but she literally goes back in time.
Not the measly minutes like time-rewinding, but jumps years.
And no, that's not a spoiler because I didn't tell why and how she does it. =b
Lastly, the
.
This is where LIS gets dark...real dark.
Strangely, true to the game's title, also its brightest part.
If I said 3rd episode was like 'piloting an X-Wing to blow the Death Star', this one's like putting you as one of the light particles in the laser that hit Alderaan.
This episode's definitely not for the faintest of heart.
My emotion was flailing throughout the episode, ragdolled by the story.
I hate you, DONTNOD. =l
Navigation-wise, if you've played Telltale adventure games before you'll be in a familiar territory.
You move with WASD, hold Shift to move faster, and click-hold-drag to available actions on points of interest.
You can hold items from time to time, but it's usually area-specific; you never carry anything across different areas (aside from your camera).
Camera view is a bit different from Telltale's because it's more of a 3rd person shoulder cam rather than fixed points with fixed angles, which works well for this game.
Sometimes the action choices can be obscured by Max's body at certain places from certain angle, but that's a given with every game which cam follows the player...and usually not game-breaking.
Now about time-rewinding.
If you've played Remember Me, it works almost exactly like memory remixing in that game.
You either hold RMB or press Ctrl to rewind.
RMB rewinds to arbitrary point of time while Ctrl rewinds to certain checkpoints in the timeline.
These 'time checkpoints' are usually when you start a conversation or when you trip an event from doing something with a point of interest.
If there are time checkpoints and Ctrl reverses exactly to those, what's the point with using RMB?
Well, at certain points in the game there are events that will happen regardless of your actions.
For example, someone will be hit by a stray football regardless of what you're currently doing; it's not being triggered by any of your actions.
This is where RMB comes into play: you can rewind back time and tell the person that'd get hit to move before the football hits.
"How am I supposed to tell that person if I rewind time? Wouldn't my position be reversed as well?"
And that's one of the quirk of the time rewind mechanic in this game.
Your surroundings, including the people, moves back according to the timeline, but you stay where you're currently are.
So when you're in front of the person after the football hit, you can rewind time and you'll still be in front of that person before the football hit, thus have ample time to tell that person to move.
Another quirk of the time rewind is that you keep whatever item you obtained from the future when you rewind back to the past.
This will be explained very early in the game, and it's a key mechanic for many problem-solving events later on.
Time rewind actually allows you to make a decision, see the response and/or end result, and then go back picking the other choice if you think you're not pleased with the outcome of that decision.
Sorry, Telltale; DONTNOD got there first.
If you're wondering what would stop you from rewinding back to the start of the game in order to 'get it all right' (there's no such thing), then it's the major decision events.
Arcadia Bay is divided into several 'areas'.
You can only walk around within these separate areas but you can't go between them freely unless the story requires you to.
Usually you get a major decision event in an area before you can leave it.
You can rewind this event as much as you like to see the different outcomes but
if you stay in that area.
Getting to the next area will force the game to 'move forward' and make you unable to 'replay' the event(s) in previous area.
Now let's talk about the fluff.
First off, while the voiceovers are great, the lip sync is less so.
Characters' movements are adequate without any glaring awkwardness, including the skateboard nether region hit (yep).
Visually, it's better than Telltale's, especially the lighting effects...and that's on Medium detail preset.
If you don't want to use the presets, you can toggle VSync and adjust AA (there's MSAA and FXAA), LOD (Level of Detail), Texture, Effect, and Shadow quality.
It also runs quite smooth on my aging laptop with i5-520M and Radeon HD 5650m.
There used to be audio skips at certain points but it's virtually gone after a few updates.
There are glitches in some parts, usually involving time rewind.
Objects are occasionally 'hanging around' after rewinding time or while being engaged in conversations.
In episode 2, an item was floating because Max was using it before she rewound time.
In episode 3, a car passing in the street stopped but its tyres kept rolling when Max started talking with an NPC.
Not really game-breaking, but they're there.
So, yeah, get this game for what it is.
Not because this is made by DONTNOD.
Not because this 'beats Telltale games'.
But because this game has a story and mechanics that warrants being another worthy addition to your collection of adventure games.

Well, I just finished episode one, so this review will at start ONLY give my views on the first episode.
What is "Life is Strange"? Well, I would say Life is Strange is an story driven adventure game alá Telltale Game.
Is that it? No, that's the thing, it isn't. If it was I might have called these guys "copycats" but that wouldn't really have been fair, since I do not call Call of Duty copycats of Battlefield or the other way around.
But to return to the subject, it isn't a Telltale Games clone in that way that it actually has game play.
Telltale Games are famous for letting the player draw his or her own story by choosing different paths, and sometimes some easier puzzles (At least in The Walking Dead S1) This game has that, and a little more. This first episode has more puzzles than a whole season of Telltale Games, sure they aren't hard to do, but... The way you are doing them, that's the interesting way.
As you probably know, this game is about a girl, her name is Max and she's 18 years old, she just started going to this high-school which name I've unfortunately already forgot. It was something typical American. However, she discovers very early in the game that she can timetravel, at least a few seconds. This time-traveling is the main focus of the puzzles in Episode 1. You want to do something, you try to do something, you fail, you rewind time, see what's going on, change what you did earlier, and ta-da success!
Unfortunately this time-travel option is not available, but only when the game want it to be, which at times are a bit frustrating. I was at the time of playing talking about the game with a friend who became very interested when a certain scene happened in the game, so I said I could show him with the Steam-stream, however I wasn't able to turn back the clock at that time. Nothing big but I just wanted to state that.
How is the atmosphere of the game? Does it fit an 18 year old girls mind? Well, in a stereotypical way, yes. Do I like it? Yes. It fits perfectly to Max and her surrounding. The music is great, the art style of the game is beautiful. Not perfect though. There are quite a few graphical glitches and the faces seem... a bit... lifeless at time. But Life is Strange eh? ;)
One thing that did surprise me quite a lot was the length of the episode. Used to playing Telltale Games I thought this would be like... 1.5 - 2.5 hours at most. I spent a bit over 4 hours playing this game! I wanted to explore everything! Get to know everyone. Unfortunately I didn't even get that chance! The episode is taking your through different areas of the campus and some other places, but there are loading times between these areas, and if you enter "Area 2" from "Area 1" and you have something to do in "Area 2" you can't return to "Area 1", it simply tells you "I can't leave yet" or a similar message.
This was quite sad because I didn't explore "Area 1" fully, I missed a lot of photography possibilities, yes you can actually take pictures of things. (Only things the game wants you to take pictures of though, and there are achievements) So not only did I miss these things, but I also missed achievements. (Not that important though, I just wanted you to know)
Now I talked about quite a lot of things, but haven't really mentioned the story, except the whole time-travelling thing, which by itself is big thing but the story is more than this. A girl has gone missing, which is made known by all the "Missing person" papers everywhere, and this made me think the whole story has something to do with her, she is mentioned more and more often while the time is passing, so I guess there is something mysterious going on around her.
Either way I can't wait for the next episode! Which apparently will come in March 2015. I highly recommend this to any adventure game player.

I had high expectations from this game, just because how mesmerized I was with the promotional material released beforehand, but these expectations were far exceeded. Of course this is just the first episode, but so far I can safely tell Life is Strange is the best new adventure game I have played in many, many years. The story, the characters, the atmosphere, the artistic style is just so special, it’s actually hard to put down to words. You have to live the game to get it. You cannot just storm through it. Just walk around, explore, talk to the characters and the world you get yourself lost in will reward you. I am a big fan of Beyond Good & Evil, and although the setting of these two games could not be more different, they strike the same chords in my heart. You play a very relatable charming young female character who happens to be a photographer, you traverse a colorful world full of beauty as well as nostalgia and melancholy accompanied by beautiful music. And both games were made in France. :) The time rewind feature is very innovative and makes the game special, but it’s like icing on a cake that is very delicious anyway. The only downsides are that I would surely appreciate a Mac version of the game; and that we have to wait a cruelly long time to explore more of the poetic world, the characters and the story itself. I am very confident, however, that the team will not disappoint at this time. I am very glad I bought the season pass from the get go. The developers deserve every penny for their work and the asking price is a bargain for what you get, if this genre and style are your cup of tea. Thank you, Dontnod.

I love how the developpers gave a lot of attention to every details. Like, for example, I just went out of the school and saw a drone flying around... Started to follow it, as if I was in the game. Life is Strange is very curious and relatable narrative adventure that I would recommend to anyone looking to discover why games deserve to be regarded as a true artform, and that's only after having played Episode 1 of 5.
On the face of it, Life is Strange is your average small-town suburban drama elements of mystery and supernatural events mixed in. To say that's all the game provides would be to horribly misinform your audience though. Life is Strange feels very warm and homely with deep underlaying tones of desperation and darkness. It doesn't try to be deep and engaging, it just simply is. So many times I found myself rolling my eyes or scoffing at just how pitifully teenage everyone was acting, how pretentious and selfish every character was being, and it was only then that I realized that I was reacting to scripted characters the same way I would any other teenager I passed in the halls.
I have high hopes for Life is Strange, and I warmly invite anyone and everyone who cares about interesting narratives to purchase this game.

If you want to get right to the point, drop down to the last paragraph.
Who hasn't wished before that they could at the drop of a hat discover the ability to rewind time? To change a choice they made before, for better or for worse. The concept of rewinding time and using it as a tool to interact better with others is an intriguing concept and what drew me to the game. Not to mention my affection for decision-based games, such as The Walking Dead or Heavy Rain, which may provide me with a bit of bias towards the gameplay itself. I wouldn't exactly go so far as to call this game entirely revolutionary in itself. It's a fascinating concept, and a beautiful one as well. But as far as decision-based games, this seems to be quite similar to works done by Telltale.
In fact, you can see a lot of the games that must have influenced them, including and not limited to the story telling of Telltale's game series, the mechanics and mystery of Quantic Dream's Heavy Rain, and the delicate exploration to unravel a story as told by Fullbright Company's Gone Home. You can see a lot of the best features of their inspiration coming to light in this game.
That said, what is revolutionary about this game is the character interactions when combined with the ability to rewind time and use knowledge you received to make different choices. The ability to do this wasn't used as frequently as I expected, and was used more often outside of the main story in interactions with what appear to be minor characters. What I hope to see is even the smallest choices and use of the ability make a difference in the long run. A butterfly effect, if you will.
One of the reviews called this game nostalgic. It doesn't matter where you were involve in high school, but if you attended a public school, it's hard not to feel it. It's not just that the main character, Max, is very relatable. A new girl, the object of minor harassment, shy and not confident. Altogether, the characters are interesting and addicting, someone the player can relate to, and a proxy through which we make decisions. We get to choose what Max does with her powers.
Between characters that we can identify in, powers we wish we had, gameplay that is fantastic (though by no means original or revolutionary at this point) and a curious soundtrack that suits the soothing mood of small-town Oregon, we have a game that while is not action packed has the potential to kick off an incredible story. I'm personally a sucker for a beautiful game with well-developed characters and a complicated but sensical plot. As of chapter one, I'm completely hooked, and looking forward for more in the future. This game is for the person who wants a calming experience that interests you. I find it is completely worth the time and the money, and only hope that it can fulfill its potential.
100% recommended for Adventure-Fans
This is modern soul therapy. Outstanding work.

I've been eagerly awaiting the release of this game for some time now, as I was a fan of their previous game Remember Me and have a particular interest in French storytelling.
You play as Max who soon finds she has untold powers in the form of being able to rewind time. Now being able to rewind time is nothing new in video games, though there hasn't really been a game that details the repurcussions we would expect to see as a result of being offered the choice. This is of course due to financial constraints as well as time contraints in having to cater for each and every one of those choices.
However Life is Strange is very different. From the very beginning Dontnod encourages the player to experiment with the ability to rewind time and to see and alternate 'endings'. No longer are we confined by the need to reload a previous save game in order to do this, for they've integrated this feature into the game itself.
The parallels between an emphasis on photography with that of the game's ability to rewind time; being able to look out into the world from a camera lens whether it be a video camera or photographic camera is an interesting one, in that we're never entirely sure whether we are merely viewers of the on-screen events or actual participants. This is later reinforced by the references to George Orwell's 1984. Can everything be simply viewed from a camera lens and does the game's obvious emphasis on 'lenses', have any meaningful significance later on?
This may also lead some players to question the nature of destiny in our every day lives - do we have control over such things, or would it perhaps have been possible to go back to an earlier time to change the seemingly inevitable course of events? It really makes you think but I feel its greatest ability (and perhaps the most important), is that Life is Strange encourages you to do so while having a good time. There was never a dull moment.
A fantastic game whose other chapters I really look forward to.

(Reviewed after playing the first episode)
A fun classic adventure game with choices and consequences in the style of Telltale games, but with a time-rewind mechanic that lets you explore your other choices, effectively letting you experiment with the result before committing.  The environments are detailed and explorable, with tons of fully voiced and described interactions.  The world and characters are detailed and nuanced... and the art style is bright and mildly cartoonish.  The story so far is genuinely interesting, and I like the idea of paying per-episode actually.
Only a few negatives:
> The lip sync'ing is horrible... not even close to what you are actually hearing.  The facial expressions are also very limited.
> nVision 3D support has problems, although I suspect the community will fix that.
I would definitely recommend if you are a fan of adventure games and/or the telltale games.  I look forward to playing through the remainder of this story.
9/10

My take on Dontnod's newest game, Life is Strange. Published by Square Enix. It's an episodic, story driven adventure game where you play as Max Caulfield, a young girl who discovers she has a gift.

Have been playing for one hour, and must say I am astounded. The one thing that rings out above everything else is Max's internal dialogue of her innermost thoughts and feelings. That's how it is in real life, right? 99% of the things we think and feel are never outwardly expressed. This gives it a depth that nothing else in the history of videogames and even movies and TV have never been able to touch.
Everything else, graphics, music and how Life is Strange feels and plays is absolutely professional and polished. I'm typing this as I'm listening to the music from the Main Menu. A gentle guitar melody plays while an animated scene of a small town overlooking a beach at sunset moves about, with a nice "paint" style.
I want more games like this. And the fact that the lead is a female, struggling high school student tops it off with a quality unlike no other. Kudos to Square Enix for picking up the publishing rights, and not wanting to change a thing. As was stated on the dev's Reddit, every other company propositioned said that a female for a lead won't work.
Buy this game immediately, and prove to the industry that creativity, imagination and forward-thinking sell.

And I've always wondered what it's like to be a (sort of) hipster teenage girl with superpowers and hipster-emo friends. Seems cool enough.
Shame I gotta wait until March for the next part

Life is Strange is very curious and relatable narrative adventure that I would recommend to anyone looking to discover why games deserve to be regarded as a true artform, and that's only after having played Episode 1 of 5.
On the face of it, Life is Strange is your average small-town suburban drama elements of mystery and supernatural events mixed in. To say that's all the game provides would be to horribly misinform your audience though. Life is Strange feels very warm and homely with deep underlaying tones of desperation and darkness. It doesn't try to be deep and engaging, it just simply is. So many times I found myself rolling my eyes or scoffing at just how pitifully teenage everyone was acting, how pretentious and selfish every character was being, and it was only then that I realized that I was reacting to scripted characters the same way I would any other teenager I passed in the halls.
I have high hopes for Life is Strange, and I warmly invite anyone and everyone who cares about interesting narratives to purchase this game.

La ambientación es magnífica, un entorno pseudouniversitario en un pequeño pueblo de la costa oeste de los Estados Unidos, en el estado de Washington. Atrapa perfectamente el entorno rural, la geografía agreste, la particularidad de sus gentes... etc... Además envuelve todo esto con una banda sonora bastante guapa y adecuada.
Los gráficos, eso sí, parecen un poco toscos para lo mal acostumbrados que Square-Enix nos tiene a los jugadores, y Dontnod también ha demostrado buenas capacidades gráficas en otros momentos... Sin embargo no creo que esto sea negativo para el juego, ya que siendo una aventura gráfica lo importante es el énfasis en la historia, la narratividad, el suspense, los personajes bien definidos, buenos diálogos, y giros argumentales. Parece que Life is Strange aporta trodo eso. Ahora bien, no parece que esté muy bien optimizado, ya que a veces durante el juego comienzan a parecer artifacts (errores de procesamiento gráfico) por doquier, los píxeles se vuelven locos y perfilan las texturas de una manera rarísima. Me he dado cuenta de que, al menos provisionalmente (hasta que te vuelve a suceder) puedes solucionarlo cambiando la calidad de las texturas y volviendo al juego. Una vez regresas al juego puedes volver a poner las texturas como las tenías y parece que el juego sigue funcionando sin mostrar problemas... hasta que aleatoriamente vuelve a suceder después de un tiempo. Tendrán que sacar un♥♥♥♥♥♥parche, porque la peña paga un juego cuyos requisitos recomendados son excedidos por su máquina, y la peña LO QUIERE JUGAR BIEN. Y punto pelota. He leído también sobre gente que se queja de algo que les sucede con los menús, pero yo no he experimentado nada de eso.
Mola que esté adaptado para jugar con mando, que es el futuro de las aventuras gráficas, porque, ¿a quién le interesaría estar encorvado usando un ratón cuando en realidad desearías disfrutar de ellas recostado en el sofá como si fuesen una suerte de películas o series interactivas? Sin embargo, lo malo de que los videojuegos se parezcan a las series quizá sea el distribuirlos mediante capítulos... Telltale lleva haciéndolo bastante tiempo y yo aún sigo pensando que es mejor presentar al público una obra íntegra y que el público decida cómo se la quiere administrar, en lugar de esperar a una fecha determinada a que salga la continuación de lo que jugaste hace mogollón y quizá ya no recuerdes tan bien.
Resumiendo: Un buen objeto estético, mal vendido, pero obra de arte a fin de cuentas. No creo que sea un juego "revolucionario" como se nos vende, al final es tan lineal como cualquiera que se vende como lo contrario, pero sí que es una buena aventura gráfica con un argumento prometedor y una ambientación única. Si es lo que te gusta en un videojuego, consíguelo sin dudar y disfrútalo. :)
8/10. Have been playing for one hour, and must say I am astounded. The one thing that rings out above everything else is Max's internal dialogue of her innermost thoughts and feelings. That's how it is in real life, right? 99% of the things we think and feel are never outwardly expressed. This gives it a depth that nothing else in the history of videogames and even movies and TV have never been able to touch.
Everything else, graphics, music and how Life is Strange feels and plays is absolutely professional and polished. I'm typing this as I'm listening to the music from the Main Menu. A gentle guitar melody plays while an animated scene of a small town overlooking a beach at sunset moves about, with a nice "paint" style.
I want more games like this. And the fact that the lead is a female, struggling high school student tops it off with a quality unlike no other. Kudos to Square Enix for picking up the publishing rights, and not wanting to change a thing. As was stated on the dev's Reddit, every other company propositioned said that a female for a lead won't work.
Buy this game immediately, and prove to the industry that creativity, imagination and forward-thinking sell.

And I've always wondered what it's like to be a (sort of) hipster teenage girl with superpowers and hipster-emo friends. Seems cool enough.

After playing through the first episode, I have decided this was definitely worth the $14 I spent for the full game. There are, obviously, a few bugs that make the game a little strange to watch at times, but that's to be expected of a first day release.
Gameplay wise, I believe it is a nice change from the usual shooters/RPGs I am used to, and definitely has a calming and relaxed feel to it. The ability to realize the weight of your choices and their outcomes also gives each episode replayability, so you can see how things turn out when you betray that friend, or you don't help that stranger, or whatever it may be. The ability to turn back time can help you fix any mistakes you feel you made, and correct those relationships you so horribly destroyed for dear friend Max.
The story is nicely crafted so far, and focuses on building and maintaining relationships with others around you. Your choices carry weight, and can drastically affect how the game will progress.
I'd recommend this to anyone looking for a nice, relaxed, story driven experience that's as light on gameplay as possible. Or anyone who wants to help Max. She's cool, do it for Max. Do it.

Tibbletoads review ( a stream try will be done later today )
The game sure is something diffrent,  The graphics seem a blend between 3d and conceptual art , making some  textures ( like the principals  tie)  painted on and some of the set dressings look out of place, but somehow it fits the game .
The time rewinding is nicely implimented but  for some puzzles it feels forced,  you are forced to use it to solve a puzzle, so you first have to mess it up  the first time,  making the time rewind work like a hint system , this is not  something all adventure fans might like.
The game gave it self some big shoes to fill  by saying it would revolutionise the way decicion games are played, and so far i have to say they are doing a nice atempt at that , some of the small things you can do seem to have impact on the story, like signing a petition  or watering a plant ( no really watering a plant will have consequences in the  later chapters.
no mater how much i loved the walking dead, the choises always felt a bit black and white, and  seeing this game also has some  of those choises i cant wait to find out what they will do in the long run.
The choises here were hard hitters, not on the heartstrings , no, but more on the perseption of me the gamer.  the game seems to ike to ask you , what would you do ?
The music is gorgeus  soft tones and slow songs mark the soundtrack of the  game  and feel totaly in place in this seemingly sleepy town.
The story so far is rather simple and that is one of the down sides , but seeing that it took me a bit over 2 hours to finish the  first chapter it is a minor downside as the story is engaging enough  to want to play more.
You play Max Caulfield  an 18 year old girl who returned to her home town after 5 years  to attend the countries best photography  classes, you see Max want to be a photographer
The graphics like is aid are not the games high point , dont exept super realistic things,  trees also look pixely , but like i said it somehow works for the game, it gives the game a more unique look, it certainly is something i have not seen before.
The largest downside are the characters, they all feel a little cliche and tropey, you have seen them all before , the highly religous girl who is heavy into abstenince, the creepy weird "simple"janitor, the jerkish security guy, the good friend who clearly has a crush on max,  the rebelious punk girl , the  jerky jocks, the  spoiled rich kid with mental isseus and the asian  looking girl who has a new gadget.  One could play  trope character bingo here, even Max fits into the new girl  trope ( which is odd seeing that she is  back in her home town"
The voice acting at first sounded  a little off , Max sounded  a little bored and the religous girl  sounded like the voice actress really did not wanted to do this role.  but after a little more playing the game , the voice seem to fit the characters well  and for me added a deeper layer.
Now as some one who dabbles in to writing thrillers i could not help but  seeing some  clear hints that (offcourse) nothing is as it seems, and not everybody are  as they seem, and i seriouly hope dontnod ( the developers)  will surprice me with this game and plays with the trope characters in this first episode.
I did how ever found my self  looking at things diffrently and approach characters diffrent.
Lastly , there are some fun easter eggs in the game , (one that is kinda heavy on the phalic stroking towards square enix ) but they are none the less funny to find
Dont let the the tropey characters and the sometimes forced time travel hinty system fool you . This is a game that is definatly worth the money and time you put into it.  and when chapter  five is done  we will see how much dontnod changed the way these games are played , told and done.

(SPOILER-FREE REVIEW - No major plot points revealed.)
Someone I follow on social networks claims to have worked for Square-Enix in the past, and he said something along the lines of, "I know how their decision-making works, and the fact that this game is being published means it has to be something special." Supposedly, "Life is Strange" went through a bunch of publishers, and SE was the only one that would put it out with the creators' original vision.
Maybe I'll expand on that somewhere else, but all
the Steam buyer and player, need to know is --

I personally dove right into the season pack, refusing to spend the extra $5 ($7 because of a 10% discount) on a "test run," and it's been my best decision of 2015 so far. It came out last night; I gave it a quick play, and finished it in 2 hours.
For such a small price, you're paying for an incredible, short but sublime experience. This game easily joins other time-travel classics of our time, perhaps comparable to the cult flick The Primer, with a shamelessly indie-film atmosphere. (It even has the acoustic guitar and crooning coffee shop boy as part of the audial vibe.)
There are only two truly prominent complaints I have about this game - lip syncing, and some bugged audio in some places. (Okay, well, one thing in the game doesn't make sense, but that's the
thing in the game that doesn't make sense.) However, these are easily forgivable programming errors, even if this is a dialogue-based game.
The plot of the game itself is simple but thoughtful, using everyday interactions to make you stop and think twice about morality and social life. Does that rude teacher's pet, supposedly out to tear apart social relations, deserve your fervorous hatred? Is it better to have proof of a bad situation or to intervene at the cost of heightened tensions? Is it
worth reporting something to a principal that doesn't give a damn?
And every little thing
count -- the game makes sure you know it. (It's in the spirit of the other video game it's so far been most compared to, Heavy Rain.) It's very big on the concept of the butterfly effect, literally using a butterfly to indicate when you're making a plot-impacting decision or when you do something that will certainly affect the future -- for better or worse. The writers also a good job of making you notice the subtle things as well.
The depth at which you and your character develop depend on how deep you're willing to delve into the world. You could be like me, who basically sprinted through the game with minimal interaction. And, honestly, doing so made sense to me - Max is an introverted girl with very few friends. Why interact so much, all of a sudden? Even a fellow classmate points out your lack of social prowess.
Or, you can choose to really explore the game and all its nooks and crannies, finally using this odd, wild day to make sure you interact with basically the whole student body. And these decisions
count.
In all honesty, I was just lazy and unobservant. But the thing is, I felt that coming out of the game, even a
of action is justifiable. After all, it's your choice.
Of course, there's a lot of other things to this game than decision making, even if that's basically 50% of the gameplay. The game makes you use your newfound abilities to solve a few puzzles. These are simple tasks of observation and problem-solving, and the way they're presented make them seem basically
to the plot (I really don't want to ruin her cashmere, thanks though). The game does a good job of making them feel important, though, as they tend to lead into some plot points.
Outside of that, the gameplay doesn't really drone on as much as you'd expect "walking simulators" to. Life is Strange keeps excellent pacing, giving appropriate "air time" for you to take in the world and its inhabitants before letting you wander into the next quicktime event. It takes advantage of text messaging (being based in 2013) to fill in some of the gaps as well, letting you see the social consequences of your choices.
Even with its mid-tier graphics, the game visually presents itself excellently. The developers worked with their unfortunately mediocre graphics and came out with excellent choreography and cinematography, as well as a simple and clean (haha, Square-Enix joke) yet realistic and relatable world. There's a saying that in a good film, you should be able to take a still and come out with photography, and this game really hits that mark. Perhaps it's a bit "meta" in that sense, parading around the characters' excellent "photography" skills, but the directors clearly had a vision and met it.
And one more thought - you can feel the replayability value as the game concludes and your palate is left unsatisfied with the little things you chose against. But why should you? After all, your choices have consequences. Every choice you make in life craftfully forms a web determining your future. You can certainly use the other two save slots for this, but I'm personally going to keep to one file until the end of the series.
Play this game. In fact, buy the whole season if you're interested in even the first episode. If you're looking for a fresh experience away from the triple-A-studio circus, your expectations will be met. It's a great play, perhaps a way to fill in the time between classes, or on the plane, or whatever. After all, Square-Enix probably chose it for a reason.
I see a lot of major game reviews trying to "figure this game out," really going in with high genre expectations. Is it a thriller? Mystery? Drama? Science fiction?
Thats a gross way to look at games in general, really. In my opinion, if you go in with expectations and comparisons to whole genres like those I've already mentioned, you will be severely disappointed. This is my warning to you guys, because it has to be said.
They don't want you to look at this with a single lens. This is supposed to be an alternative, "what if" portrayal of life, a way to use the genre of video games to not just create a story, but an experience. After all, "Life Is Strange."

Edit, Episode 1: Second playthrough (2.4 hours)  On looking for the issue, I can somewhat see what people complaining about voice syncing with animation are talking about.  It is not an p rogramming or lag issue however.  It is an animation issue.  The lips do not form all of the words, and do not move acurrately.  While I have seen better lipsync animations, I also have seen much worse.  Overall it is barely noticable, because most of the voice is inner monologue.  In every situation there are many other details to draw the eye away from imperfect animations (which may exist for performance reasons).
I tryed to make this playthrough as fast as I thought it could be while still absorbing the story.  Except for in situations were I wanted to see one of the rare things I missed in my first playthrough, i only intaracted with people and objects which had been revealed to effect events.  This time is not really feasable as something to bliondly judge this game (or any gmae for that matter) on.  ONe would need to know who was important to talk to.  Where to find them.  Then every response would have to be chosen correctly on the first attempt.  I probably could have shaved the 0.4 off the end, but honestly this is close enough.
At $4-$5 per episode I feel that was well worth the money.  2.5 to 5 hours (depending on your playstyle) is not bad for a single episode at that cost.  Add to that decent writting and a fun special mechanic.
Episode 1: 4.7 hours
This game is artistic in so many ways.  I suppose that is apt seeing the protagonist.  The music fits the them well and is not horrible.  The story is compelling.  I can already see many threads being woven and interwoven.  If you take the time to read the back stories, observe the events, and let yourself fall into the story you will start to care about the characters.  If you play through as fast as you can and ignore any extraneous details, then this game will likely not be any fun to you.  The overarching theme of how minor descisions effect events around us more than we know is a wonderful theme.  I can see a point were we come to see the futility of choice, because sometimes there is no right answer.
The blurring around the edges of the screen does give me a headache, but I can see the artistic reasoning for making softer edges.  As for the people who claim to be experienceing voice lag, I have all setting turned to max and I did not experience anything like that.  The only bug that I found distracting was mirrors not reflecting environment objects that could be seen, and instead reflecting outdoor scenery.  This did break immersion somewhat, because I just had to stop and take screenshots and play with it. I quite liked LIFE IS STRANGE but, this is in no way a original game. It picks bits and pieces from other games and throws them together to create an altogether enjoyable 2,5h experience.
LIFE IS STRANGE is a story about Max, a angsty teenager with time-altering superpower, and her oh so original cast teenage friends. Buy it if you can afford, if not watch a Let's play and get the same experience.

(SPOILER-FREE REVIEW - No major plot points revealed.)
Someone I follow on social networks claims to have worked for Square-Enix in the past, and he said something along the lines of, "I know how their decision-making works, and the fact that this game is being published means it has to be something special." Supposedly, "Life is Strange" went through a bunch of publishers, and SE was the only one that would put it out with the creators' original vision.
Maybe I'll expand on that somewhere else, but all
the Steam buyer and player, need to know is --

I personally dove right into the season pack, refusing to spend the extra $5 ($7 because of a 10% discount) on a "test run," and it's been my best decision of 2015 so far. It came out last night; I gave it a quick play, and finished it in 2 hours.
For such a small price, you're paying for an incredible, short but sublime experience. This game easily joins other time-travel classics of our time, perhaps comparable to the cult flick The Primer, with a shamelessly indie-film atmosphere. (It even has the acoustic guitar and crooning coffee shop boy as part of the audial vibe.)
There are only two truly prominent complaints I have about this game - lip syncing, and some bugged audio in some places. (Okay, well, one thing in the game doesn't make sense, but that's the
thing in the game that doesn't make sense.) However, these are easily forgivable programming errors, even if this is a dialogue-based game.
The plot of the game itself is simple but thoughtful, using everyday interactions to make you stop and think twice about morality and social life. Does that rude teacher's pet, supposedly out to tear apart social relations, deserve your fervorous hatred? Is it better to have proof of a bad situation or to intervene at the cost of heightened tensions? Is it
worth reporting something to a principal that doesn't give a damn?
And every little thing
count -- the game makes sure you know it. (It's in the spirit of the other video game it's so far been most compared to, Heavy Rain.) It's very big on the concept of the butterfly effect, literally using a butterfly to indicate when you're making a plot-impacting decision or when you do something that will certainly affect the future -- for better or worse. The writers also a good job of making you notice the subtle things as well.
The depth at which you and your character develop depend on how deep you're willing to delve into the world. You could be like me, who basically sprinted through the game with minimal interaction. And, honestly, doing so made sense to me - Max is an introverted girl with very few friends. Why interact so much, all of a sudden? Even a fellow classmate points out your lack of social prowess.
Or, you can choose to really explore the game and all its nooks and crannies, finally using this odd, wild day to make sure you interact with basically the whole student body. And these decisions
count.
In all honesty, I was just lazy and unobservant. But the thing is, I felt that coming out of the game, even a
of action is justifiable. After all, it's your choice.
Of course, there's a lot of other things to this game than decision making, even if that's basically 50% of the gameplay. The game makes you use your newfound abilities to solve a few puzzles. These are simple tasks of observation and problem-solving, and the way they're presented make them seem basically
to the plot (I really don't want to ruin her cashmere, thanks though). The game does a good job of making them feel important, though, as they tend to lead into some plot points.
Outside of that, the gameplay doesn't really drone on as much as you'd expect "walking simulators" to. Life is Strange keeps excellent pacing, giving appropriate "air time" for you to take in the world and its inhabitants before letting you wander into the next quicktime event. It takes advantage of text messaging (being based in 2013) to fill in some of the gaps as well, letting you see the social consequences of your choices.
Even with its mid-tier graphics, the game visually presents itself excellently. The developers worked with their unfortunately mediocre graphics and came out with excellent choreography and cinematography, as well as a simple and clean (haha, Square-Enix joke) yet realistic and relatable world. There's a saying that in a good film, you should be able to take a still and come out with photography, and this game really hits that mark. Perhaps it's a bit "meta" in that sense, parading around the characters' excellent "photography" skills, but the directors clearly had a vision and met it.
And one more thought - you can feel the replayability value as the game concludes and your palate is left unsatisfied with the little things you chose against. But why should you? After all, your choices have consequences. Every choice you make in life craftfully forms a web determining your future. You can certainly use the other two save slots for this, but I'm personally going to keep to one file until the end of the series.
Play this game. In fact, buy the whole season if you're interested in even the first episode. If you're looking for a fresh experience away from the triple-A-studio circus, your expectations will be met. It's a great play, perhaps a way to fill in the time between classes, or on the plane, or whatever. After all, Square-Enix probably chose it for a reason.
I see a lot of major game reviews trying to "figure this game out," really going in with high genre expectations. Is it a thriller? Mystery? Drama? Science fiction?
Thats a gross way to look at games in general, really. In my opinion, if you go in with expectations and comparisons to whole genres like those I've already mentioned, you will be severely disappointed. This is my warning to you guys, because it has to be said.
They don't want you to look at this with a single lens. This is supposed to be an alternative, "what if" portrayal of life, a way to use the genre of video games to not just create a story, but an experience. After all, "Life Is Strange."

Episode 1: "Chrysalis" Review
Playtime: 2.4 Hours
Life is Strange is a point-and-click interactive adventure game that relies heavily on its storytelling. And for a game like this, storytelling is crucial to the overall scheme of how everything feels and plays out. This is not a game for everyone and plays out much like games such as Heavy Rain, Beyond: Two Souls, or any recent TellTale titles (The Wolf Among Us, The Walking Dead). The game isn't revolutionary but it does what it intends to do pretty well, though with a few flaws.
You play as Max Caulfield, an eighteen year old girl who just returned to her hometown after being away for five years. The story is pretty well told and the scenes are very well directed. The voice acting is also great but the game suffers from poor lip synchronization, which actually may or may not have been a design choice. The art style is quite nice and actually very mesmerizing in some scenes, but this also affects the characters to look somewhat bland and unemotional when delivering some pretty heavy dialogue. However, both these flaws do not retract from the overall experience of the game.
The key difference between this game and other interactive adventure games is one feature: The ability to rewind time. This supernatural element is implemented into the game and Max acknowledges this fact, although I hope there is more development and clever use for this feature in future episodes. So far in this episode, you are able to go back in time to make a different to change the outcome of how the story unfolds. This is a very neat feature and the fact that it really does have an impact on the storytelling makes it all the better.
Overall, Episode One turned out great and the story and characters definitely have my attention. I will be looking forward to the future episodes.
8/10

Life is indeed strange. What isn't though, is how much I was captured by this beautifully made and compelling adventure game, with the bonus of been so damn affordable.
It doesn't have a whole lot of features and therefore has to rely on making a rich story in which will make you want to continue playing through till the end, and here's the big secret... It does that incredibly well.
Your choices and actions actually do effect how the game plays out and there generally isn't a perfect way to go about things as it always leave you questioning yourself with a "I could maybe have done something better.. Should I go back..?" that right there is something I find to be the best thing about 'Life is Strange', it actually makes you invest into it and how you play through it. Even with the Walking Dead, I felt like your decisions, bar a couple of them, weren't nearly as weighted as they should have been, in this, it's far from the case.
Part of me wants to info-dump the plot of this adventure, but the other part of me really just wants to put out that it really needs to be experienced, especially due to the fact that it is tailored to your actions. A few things I will put out there is the main female protagonist named Max, a normal college photography student who discovers something special, a true gift that will end up weighing on her quite a bit.. Reversing time is quite a responsibility. Can you always be the good guy and hero? Sometimes you really can't and certain things aren't meant to be changed. Also, abusing this ability makes it appear to hurt Max, and visions do actually take it out of her, a little detail I happen to love. You have abilities but they take their toll to use.
It also has a nice little play on hipsters and people who are actually enthusiastic with old things like Polaroid cameras and old music.
Upon completing the episode(s), you are given a detailed card of what decisions other players globally have made compared to yours, and you then notice there are a couple of somewhat hidden things you could have done within that episode. It gives you a few more things to discover and play around with.
Graphics in this game are utterly gorgeous and it makes the already immersive world just that much better.
I honestly cannot wait for the following episodes to unlock as I am eager to see what this has in store for it. By far worth supporting the developers for it.

I quite liked LIFE IS STRANGE but, this is in no way a original game. It picks bits and pieces from other games and throws them together to create an altogether enjoyable 2,5h experience.
LIFE IS STRANGE is a story about Max, a angsty teenager with time-altering superpower, and her oh so original cast teenage friends. There is Chloe, the childhood friend with a flair for danger, the ♥♥♥♥♥y rich girl, who is really a nice girl on the inside and the quiet religious girl, with a dark secret.
It's clear that the developers DONTNOD have played the Telltale games (Walking Dead, The Wolf Among us) and thought "If only there could be a rewind button so that the player could try every option, then select the outcome they want". Because thats just what LIFE IS STRANGE is a Telltale game with a rewind button. But that doesn't make it a bad game.
Unlike the Telltale games, where I played some episodes over and over again to try different outcomes in LIFE IS STRANGE I feel there is no need to ever go back and play the first episode again ever. Maxes time-traveling-superpowers makes it possible to try everything. This power not only makes it redundant to play the episode again, I also feels like it takes away any feeling of ownership on the story. In THE WALKING DEAD every choice hade consequence and I had to live with my choice and feel the repercussion of my actions. Having the ability to undo a choice because a classmate reacted poorly takes away all the importance of the action.
In conclusion, I liked the story, the music and the atmosphere.
Buy it if you can afford, if not watch a Let's play and get the same experience.

The Following Speaks On Episode 1 Only
Well, it seems some aspects of the game have been covered in other reviews, so i'll just say some things some people might find interesting.
1. The game is not graphically intense and is quite easy to run. Even on the high preset, the highest the game could go, my 280X was just fine running a smooth 60FPS. On the flipside, the game isn't the prettiest, in my opinion due to it's similarities to other games in this genre(such as Telltale games), but on that note...
2. This is very close to a Telltale game. This is basically a TT game with a nice little time mechanic thrown in, it's interesting and at points in a game such as The Wolf Among Us in which you make a critical decision and must live with it, you can simply rewind and pick again in this game. I'd like to note I believe this little time mechanic was used a bit in the studios prior game, Remember Me, it was one of the best parts and reviews consistently highlighted it, so it's nice to see it getting fleshed out into this game.
All the same, doing this for numerous option I found myself truly questioning if I made the right choice as immediately after the decision Max(the player character) says a few lines showing she is just a bit worried about the choices she/you makes, leaving you a bit scared of said choices.
3. The story is interesting. I won't spoil much, but I just gotta say the story is quite interesting, we meet a real group of interesting characters that vary and leave me feeling as though I live in a full world, however you're fed just strings in this first episode, little hints at what could be happening and oddities you'll find which make you question numerous characters. That said, these strings just  leave me hungry for more.
4. The writing may not be for you. Oh, where to start with the writing. Yes, as I said, there are quite a few characters all different in numerous ways, however it's terribly cliche for nearly all of them. If you couldn't tell by other reviews, game previews, or screenshots, you play as a senior in high school, and this shines through in almost every teenage character. You have so many cliched character you would think the developers ripped them from a book, you have a shy plater character, a rude and snotty "Queen B" who runs the school, she is within a clique of other rich bratty children who include numerous dumb jocks, who date dumb cheerleaders, and said jocks also happen to bully a weaker kid... I can promise you you've seen this a million times before, it's ripped straight from a Disney show, some would fit perfectly into a show like iCarly or Hannah Montana, albeit they have more of a mouth on them, but still. Adult characters are few, and say few lines, I won't spoil one of the adults closest to the story but he too fits into a sad, stereotype.
It's not just the characters either, but, to a lesser extent, the teens writing. I personally don't find it grating at all but I know many people who would be turned off by lines such as "Go ♥♥♥♥ your selfie!" and "oh man, are you cereal?", that is to say "go ♥♥♥♥ yourself" and "oh man are you serious" in cutesy new age ways, honestly one of the more realistic aspects of the characters. One girl describes her step-dad as a "step♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; and "step♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;, there are many more but these are the few I remember clearly, it gets old after a bit, also it's relatively unclear if this IS a bit, or if the writing really calls for her to call her dad a "Step-" something bad, i'll go ahead and say it's just part of her character but still.
All in all the game was fun, it was polished, it was interesting, it was a similar experience to others I enjoy(such as Telltale games), I would(and will) definitely invest another $5 just to see what the next episode brings, though you truly may be turned off by the writing.
These were just a couple of thoughts I had on the game, I advise you to go read some reviews, maybe watch a youtube video or two, to get a better grasp on the game, gameplay, and story. All that said, I do recommend it.

This game has a pretty interesting concept, and the choices you make actually feel like they matter. Its actually more of an interactive story or a movie than it is a game, but I really do like the idea of watching a story and influencing what happens as it happens. Plus the ability to control time and how you can use that is pretty cool.
The story is interesting enough (I'm going to buy the other episodes to see what happens) though I already have predictions about what the surprise end twist will be.
The dialogue in the game can at times be laughable. I appreciate the attempt at trying to fit modern slang into the dialogue but when its used wrong it, its really apparent. Plus the voice acting leaves a little to be desired, the main character speaks in such a soft deadpan tone that when she says she is "Absolutely Furious" about something its really hard to believe.
The graphics are alright for a story driven game, and the particular art style they used really seems to build the world that the game takes place in. It never really got in the way for me, in fact it really to adds  to the experience. Same goes for the soundtrack, the music isn't exactly my forte but damn it does a good job of communicating a certain feel of the game's universe.
The game really shines when it gives you complete control. The game is awesome when you play with time control and talk to people to hopefully influence things that will happen later in the game. Unforuntately there is quite a bit of hand holding too. Times when you don't have control and you feel bored. Worse than that is all the expostion, the game seems to think that the players are idiots that don't understand basic gaming concepts like time control or alternate realities. Whenever I would make a decision and the character would say to herself "I wonder if that was the right decision, maybe I should reverse time to change it." it felt extremely patronizing. Did you think that I forgot I could control time? Or when the game shows you something that is clearly important to the plot and then takes the time to explain it to you. Give gamers more credit here, this isn't rocket surgery.
But these are all mostly little knitpicks that you completely forget about when they aren't obviously apparent. Overall it was a pretty cool experience, and for 5 bucks I think its totally worth it to check out on the off chance that you might really like it. I am eagerly awaiting the rest of the episodes to be released.

Episode 1: "Chrysalis" Review
Playtime: 2.4 Hours
Life is Strange is a point-and-click interactive adventure game that relies heavily on its storytelling. And for a game like this, storytelling is crucial to the overall scheme of how everything feels and plays out. This is not a game for everyone and plays out much like games such as Heavy Rain, Beyond: Two Souls, or any recent TellTale titles (The Wolf Among Us, The Walking Dead). The game isn't revolutionary but it does what it intends to do pretty well, though with a few flaws.
You play as Max Caulfield, an eighteen year old girl who just returned to her hometown after being away for five years. The story is pretty well told and the scenes are very well directed. The voice acting is also great but the game suffers from poor lip synchronization, which actually may or may not have been a design choice. The art style is quite nice and actually very mesmerizing in some scenes, but this also affects the characters to look somewhat bland and unemotional when delivering some pretty heavy dialogue. However, both these flaws do not retract from the overall experience of the game.
The key difference between this game and other interactive adventure games is one feature: The ability to rewind time. This supernatural element is implemented into the game and Max acknowledges this fact, although I hope there is more development and clever use for this feature in future episodes. So far in this episode, you are able to go back in time to make a different to change the outcome of how the story unfolds. Meet Max, a selfie-taking shutterbug who discovers she can rewind time.
The aesthetics of "Life is Strange" really stand out, and the story helpfully guides players through the game's mechanics, which are similar to the memory remix mechanics Dontnod's previous release, "Remember Me." But where "Remember Me" gives us a view of a dystopian future in late-21st century Paris, "Life is Strange" sticks us in Blackwell Academy, on the Oregon coast.
The first episode can take anywhere from two to four hours, depending on how much you choose to explore and play with the timeline. The voice acting is solid, but the characters' voices seemed a bit out-of-sync with their faces at times, which was jarring. But that's the only drawback to this technically and narratively impressive game. You'll have some tough choices to make as Max, and the choices aren't necessarily easier just because you can rewind time and see the potential consequences of each outcome!
If you're looking for a game that will challenge how you think, not just how you react, "Life is Strange" is a must-buy.
