Rex Rocket seeks to capture an older era of gameplay, and it does it somewhat well.  The monsters aren't hard to beat, but if you're not paying attention they will kill you.  The levels are set up to reward thinking things through instead of blindly jumping in.  The bosses have patterns that will kill you if you don't learn how to avoid their attacks.  All of these things are good.  The reward skill rather than just luck or blindly firing.
However, Rex Rocket also has platforming areas where virtually every single inch of the area is a death trap for you.  Acid covers the floor and if you touch it even once, you're dead and have to start back over.  Spikes might be waiting below, instant death.  Monsters will be on the ceiling, floor, and air, all waiting to touch you just once so they can knock you into whatever death waits below, and they dont have specific paths they follow, leaving you to the fate of their randomly generated movements.  Gun turrets or lasers will be positioned to fire on you and directly into your path, one touch and it's hello instant death below.  Trap boxes are placed as your only stepping stone.  Once you step on them, monsters pop out.  Mines floating in the area are positioned in areas you need to traverse over by shooting downward to float over areas.  If you hit one, they explode, sending off energy shots into your flight path.  Add on to all of this that the controls are not as precise as they should be for such a platformer.  it's very easy to feel like you've overshot your landing on a platform, attempt to correct your path just ever so slightly, and be sent off the edge of the platform because the movement is so touchy in the air, or to simply think you're going to land just slightly on the edge of the platform, safe, only to find that you fall short, and then fall to your death.
Rex Rocket is fun, but those death trap platforming areas are not.  If you use a continue, you start off with twenty (20) lives.  Not only do you have to fight your way back through several other areas, which is not only tedious and time consuming, and you're liable to lose a life or three in the process, but then you have to go back through these platforming areas sometimes even if you already completed them once before.  I've gone through three of these platforming areas so far.  Each time I've lost all of my lives.  Sometimes I had well over 20 lives because I had found extra lives before.  A few of those lives were my fault, because instead of taking the way I knew would get me safely to the next spot, I decided to experiment and try a new way.  However, the very large majority of the time it was due to a gun turret, a small slime, a land mine placed directly in my path, a slime bat, a slime on the ceiling, or, my personal favorite, a very wide open area with extremely limited space to stand on with mines between those spaces and those spaces are actually slime box traps and it seems like those safe spaces aren't even properly spaced for you to be able to make it completely without putting yourself at extreme risk of death.
Rex Rocket tries to be a game like classic mega man.  The difference is, classic mega man games were hard, but fair and reasonable.  You only died if you screwed up.  Rex rocket kills you many times when it's not your screw up.
I do not recommend this game until these areas are reworked.

Slime-san:
~~~~~~~~

San was sliming away happily in a lush garden for his morning slime as he does every single day. As he was sliming from stem to stem, the ground suddenly started shaking! From the corner of his eye, he distinctly identified a worm form, honing in on him with a wide open mouth as fast as ever! Well, you guessed it! He was gobbled up! No time to waste, he needs to get out of this worm pronto before being digested!  This is not what Slime-san was expecting for his daily morning slime!
Slime-san is a platformer game where you play a slime who has to beat one hundred levels within a worm’s digestive system in order to reach the worm’s mouth and successfully escape.
The hundred levels are divided into five sections within the worm, with twenty levels per section. The first thing you need to know is that each level has four stages to clear in order to get to the next one. Within each stage, you will probably notice a green apple which always seems to be in a rather awkward place to reach (by the way, it’s done on purpose). You will occasionally see a coin with the letter A on it; these are even harder to reach.  The good news is that you will be able to buy different shapes of slimes, outfits and side arts using your apple, and even unlock classic arcade games with your coins at the Slumptown.

The gameplay is simple, fun and very challenging. In a nutshell, you have to navigate your creature through a parkour to reach the sign with an arrow on the other side of the screen.  If you manage to complete all the stages within a specific number of seconds, you’ll be rewarded with a trophy. Rest assured, it won’t be easy; you’ll have a stack of obstacles to avoid and it will be rare to see them through on your first go. Yes, you’ll die quite a lot in this game! However, your small green thingy has a few abilities to help see him through the stages. At first he can jump, or even double jump, on walls too.  He can dash to break blocks or dash through the air in the middle of a jump to a platform which seems to be inaccessible. The one I really like is the slow motion ability – morph - which is super important on some levels. You can also pass through green walls by using it, but be careful not to land in the worm’s stomach acid, which is red.  I nearly forgot to mention the red acid wall. Yes, there is an acid wall that will come at you a few seconds after you start the stage to make it even harder and increase your death toll. In short, avoid touching or being touched with anything red!
Graphically the pixel artwork is really fun and the soundtrack is upbeat and quite catchy. As for the controls, they are very responsive either with the keyboard or the gamepad. It did take me twice as long to finish the first world by using the keyboard. Definitely easier to use the gamepad.
Positives:
~~~~~~~

-	Great pixel artwork
-	100 levels with four stages each + bonus levels
-	Super fun and challenging
-	Customise your slime, buy new outfits
-	Unlock arcade games
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Can be frustrating
It’s a fast, fun and challenging platformer!
8/10

Slime San was developed by Headup Games and released on April 7th of this year. the game is a fast paced platformer where you are a little slime that was eaten by a worm, you climb, jump, and morph your way through a variety of levels while avoiding the incoming waves of stomach acid that appear after a time limit.
This game is a fast paced platformer and a platformer is only as good as its controls, and rest assured, these controls are stellar. The control scheme is tight and responsive with full controller support and re-bindable keys. all of the keys are already bound to several options that feel comfortable, and the controls overall feel comfortable. the speed is dialed in perfectly, with the jumps and wall drags feeling comfortable and effective.
and while we are talking about speed, this game is made for speed-running. The game gives you an overhead timer and best time for each level. You can also find leaderboards, and even a speedrunner mode and this game are perfect for it. now I am by no means a speedrunner (as you can see by my level times), but even I felt the compulsion to speed through each level as fast as possible, while also fighting my urge to collect every apple of which there is one per level.
this sense of speed is encouraged by the wall of deadly stomach acid that washes towards you from one of a variety of directions based on the level after a small amount of time. This is a good way of encouraging speed, without being frustrating to the player.
the apples I mentioned earlier are a currency that you spend to purchase one of the several things. you can either buy one of many new slimes that change up your playstyle with their own unique benefits and drawbacks, or you can purchase some stunning pixel art that acts as a border for your game. There is even a full functioning arcade with minigames that you can play for tokens that are collected from secret areas, but I wasn't able to get enough because I am bad at games. This encourages replayability throughout the levels without requiring backtracking.
I would have no problem backtracking throughout these levels, however, because all of the levels feel unique. The game consists of 100 base game levels that each contain 4 rooms that all focus around a central gimmick. For Example, level NAME OF LEVEL focuses on pushing blocks around, and level 9 focuses on moving platforms that you need to maneuver through.
One of the central gimmicks is the ability to morph through green tinted objects that are used to get you through little areas. There can be green blocks to slide through, or even enemies you can move through. The morphing also slows down time and can be a useful tool when it comes to fast platforming.
The art in this game is outstanding, the game is full of great animations and colors that all look fantastic. the color scheme of using dark colors on the environment while contrasting important things with bright color, really helps the player see what they can and cannot interact with. This is paired with fantastic electronic music that really keeps the action going throughout your deaths. When the stomach acid appears, the game's music actually distorts a bit, to provide a little uneasiness to the game and encourages you to speed up. and get finished.
This game takes a lot of inspiration from Super Meat Boy with things like the trails your character leaves behind as a morbid reminder of your past lives. But, with awesome controls, tons of customization, fun gameplay, and lots of great art and music, I would consider this to be substantially better than super meat boy. Slime San earns itself a 10/10 with a label of "perfect".

Felix Jumpman has no real story, so I will be ‘jumping’ right to the main goal. As stated on the game’s description – you are tasked jump between asteroids and collect all air tanks. This is indicated by the coloured arrows and dotted squares shown on your screen. This must also be done before your oxygen bar runs out, or it will be game over.
As for the controls, this is a game that has movements and jumping. Lots and lots of jumping. In fact, you had better be skilled at making leaps if you want to progress anywhere in the game. The angle of your POV plays a big asset in how far you jump, so for beginners it may be confusing at times. The farther the asteroid, the more upwards your vision needs to be when you make the leap.
The asteroids and items are pretty basic to its design, with flat texture and shading. This isn’t too surprising to find in an Indie game, but it could have been better developed. The asteroids doesn’t fit in with how well the background was designed either. Gradient colours of blue, littered with stars made for a stunning BG imo, and really does convince the player that they are in space.
The atmospheric music also added to this. It was calming and rhythmic. The sound effects, not so much. A click sound is triggered whenever the character jumps. This can become irritating when it is running repetitively over a course of time, and I only wish there was a mute option implemented for this sound.
In conclusion, Felix Jumpman makes for an interesting concept: it did not execute the idea well with a lackluster story and character though. I had a light hearted gaming experience, provided with the serene environment and wonderful music. More detail on the character and asteroids would complete the stunning visuals.
Other than that, my interest had vanished after 1/2 hour of playing, and I simply played just to grab all the trading cards.

This could be an excellent game, but the dev dropped the ball on the main aspect of the game. Felix Jumpman revolves around jumping from one asteroid to another... and by some reason they decided that the jump will be done automatically.
I mean... I was hoping that you'd have to calculate your acceleration to not under or overshoot and become stranded in space. Maybe the gravity would change every level, according to the planet's gravity? According to each asteroid size? But no. You look to the asteroid and press space and there you go. Take off and land automatically. Boring.

I absaloutly love this game, although it's short and can be completed from anywhere between 1-2 hours it's still a gem of a game in my opinion. First off let's talk about the things that I don't really like about this game, and then we can get to the good things after. First off the game is way too short for the price that you are asking for the game. I completed the gmae in about a 2 hours, and was kind of suprised to see the game with such potential end off so short. I really didn't like that, the story wasn't all that good. With the lack of dialogue throughout the game, seemed like this game was just a shoot aliens that attack you. The way that the game tries to tell a story doesn't really work in my opinion, as the dialogue isn't presented enough for you to get pulled into the story enough. Other than some annoying jumping puzzles that's all the bad things I have about the game play of this game. But this compared with all of the really good stuff really makes it look good as there as so many good things to talk about. First off I want to talk about the variety of maps that are in this game, I really like it when a game really puts time and dedication into creating maps for levels. You can either be inside or outside and it really makes a nice change of atmosphere when shooting those robots. There are also some cool weapon designs that really fit the futuristic genre of the game. I really like the diffrenete coloured weapons that then corrospond to the colour of your bar at the bottom left of your screen. The overall pacing of the levels is good, there where some levels where walking through the corridors seemed to slow it down a little but as you got further into the game it started to pick up again. Really works well. Not only are you battling enemies on the ground with the weapon arsonale that you have collected, there are times where you can go into a tank which is really cool. Although it does change the perspective to third person when in the tank which (for me) took a little bit of the experience of a First-Person out of the game, but that's only really a small detail to complain about in my opininon. Nearer the end of the game there is a large variety of enemies and level design, which could've been used earlier in the game I guess but again another small thing I would only personally complain about. The last point I want to make, I wasn't sure whether it was negative or positive. I guess it'll be different from person to person. The game is fun, but challenge is really not a problem at all in this game. The enemies do negligible damage combined with the array of very powerful weapons and a lot of ammo you find throughout the game, it really does take the challeneging side out of this game.
The graphics of this game are really nicely polished and well presented for a retro style and feel to the game. There are custom animtions for each of the different types of robots that you encounter along your way. It's also pretty simple, anyone can play it on almost any computer whether it's a bad laptop or what. For what it looks like it seems like a big game, with it's futurstic grahpics and stuff but really isn't that big of a game. One small thing is that sometimes the graphics can glitch out a bit and make the game not as good than it actually is.
The Music for this game is really nice, again fits perfectly well with the Sci-fi genre as does it set the pacing of the gameplay as well. The sounds are a bit of a dissapointment, just generic sounds but putting into consideration all the good things about the gameplay this game really is a gem.
I definatly recommend this game to any Sci-fi fans, and anyone who likes FPS. It has some really nice game play, along with a few bad things here and there about the game play but overall very good. The music really sets the atomsphere and pacing of the game, as does the retro graphics fit well with it too.

After playing this game on my fiancee's account for almost 250 hours, I finally managed to get enough money to buy it for myself and thus further support the devs. And of course now that I have officially bought it for myself, I have also been granted the privilege of being allowed to write a review which I hereby make use of.
tl;dr
+ Very unique mechanics
+ Extremely immersive story and world design/atmosphere
+ Great sound
+ Very realistic
+ (almost) completely bug-free
- Very unique mechanics
This game handles many things, especially combat entirely differently than all other rpg-games that I have played so far. For me, it feels like a very much needed breeze of fresh air in the genre. Instead of simply pressing a button and the Character executing a certain set of moves all on his own, you have the ability to manually control every step and swing. Like I said, so far I have not seen any other game doing things like that so, at least to me, it is a completely new and fresh idea. Well, not anymore, now that I have already played for almost 250 hours, but you know what I mean.
The Ai is also very different from any other game I have played so far, as all NPCs will percieve you in a certain way and react to you according to that. Maybe you sprint down a hallway, because you want to get somewhere quickly. Then, an npc sees you and maybe he will attack you because he percieved your sprinting as threat. Maybe you have encountered a particular NPC multiple times and always been careful to not appear threatening. Then that NPC might have started to like you and maybe when he sees you fighting someone else, he will come to help you. Or maybe an NPC sees you fighting and thinks that now you will be an easy target for him so he takes the opportunity to also attack you. And right now the dialog-system is not implemented yet, so when that comes, NPC encounters might get even more interesting.
Additionally, all objects are physics based so you can interact with everything. Sometimes, objects might be too heavy for your character so you won't be able to pick them up with your mouse and drag them around. But even then, you might still be able to move them if you "push" them by sprinting into them repeatedly.
The story will not be spoon-fed to you, so you have to look for old parchments and books, and read those if you want to know what is going on. However, I do recommend that you will look for all those things, because, even though I don't fully understand it yet and it is, of course, still unfinished, it is definitely very interesting. Maybe you are the kind of person who is either not able or not willing to read a lot. In that case you will maybe not enjoy the story as much as I did. But then you probably also won't read this review.
The world is designed very well, in a very thoughtful manner. So far, everything just "made sense." I have never seen any object that made me think "what? how does that make sense? this doesn't belong here." It is a low-fantasy game, after all, so most things can be explained with logic and there are only very few things that are explained with "yeah, that's a thing now. because magic. deal with it."
The atmosphere, in my opinion, can only be compared to Stalker - Shadow of Chernobyl, which, to this day, is one of the most atmospheric games I have played. Of course, it is not better than the atmosphere in Stalker, I am not sure if that would be even possible. But it is at least getting extremely close to the Stalker atmosphere, maybe it is even on the same level (especially in the later stages of Exanima). This was also a suprise for me, because I never thought it would be possible for anyone to achieve the same quality of atmosphere.
The sound effects are done very well and the background music really fits the game.
Another drastic difference to some other dungeon rpg games is that you are not an all-powerful hero who can singlehandedly slay hordes of enemies and walk away without a scratch. Your character is no stronger than an enemy with the same skills and the same equipment. And yes, NPCs have access to the exact same skills that you have. Weak enemies maybe have only one or none unlocked, strong enemies will have various skills unlocked. But, if you have enough experience, you are able to unlock the exact same skills, so no one really has any advantage or disadvantage.
Experience is also more realistic than in other games. It is not the usual "you need [amount of exp] to level up, killing some enemies gives you [amount of exp], so you will have to kill [amount of enemies] and then you get a new skill." Instead, you first choose the skill that you want to learn and then you work towards unlocking it. You also don't get experience just for killing things (you do, but it's a very small amount of exp). Most experience comes from exploring previously unexplored areas, using new equipment, and, more generally, simply doing stuff that you haven't done before. I'd say that is more realistic, because, in rl, if you do the same thing over and over, you will also soon reach a point where you can no longer learn anything new.
Lastly, the way your equipment and weapon is handled is also more realistic. If you wear a breastplate, it will absolutely not help you at all if you get hit in the legs, arms, or head. If your weapon hits the enemy but with very little momentum, you will probably not do a lot of damage, even if the enemy has bad armour. If you stand still and face the enemies weapon, your character will automatically attempt to parry. The keyword is "attempt." The parrying still has a possibility to fail, even if you do everything correctly. this is especially true if you fight against an experienced enemy who knows how to feint, etc.
For an unfinished game, the quality is certainly unexpected. So far, I have only come across a bug once, and that bug was more a little oddity rather than being disruptive to gameplay. Especially in times where even major publishers can release games filled with gamebreaking bugs and call them "finished" this is certainly a big advantage.
Yes, you read that right in the tl;dr version. The unique mechanics are positive and negative at the same time. How is that possible? That is easy to explain. While it is certainly interesting and new, it also means that it will take some time until you finally get used to how things work (especially combat is hard to learn). This learning is made even more frustrating by the omni-present perma-death mechanics. I have to admit, after playing for about 5 hours, I almost gave up because it just frustrated me too much that I constantly died before even reaching the "noob-checkpoint" that comes after you have made it through the first half of level 1. However, once I had learned how to fight and, from reset to reset, saw myself getting further and further, it became very rewarding and now I am glad that I didn't give up. Another thing that I didn't really notice is the "practice" option that you can choose in the main menu. When you do that, you can just fight enemies and you will not feel like you lost anything of value if you die. If you can beat all 5 enemies of the beginner practice, I think you should be good enough to at least make it through levels 1 and 2.
So, I give the game a score of
. It is of course not complete and can be bad for new players, but once you have taken some time and patience to overcome the initial frustration it will be a very good experience already. And once the devs have implemented all the features, the score would probably raise to 9/10.

There is a Myst-like quality to Lifeless Planet. I mean this in the most flattering way. The game offers very little in terms of challenge, and it can get quite repetitive, but as interactive storytelling it works quite well. It helps that some of the alien landscapes on the Premier Edition, like the volcanic Inferno level, are truly breathtaking at first glance (hence the Myst comparison). I recommend this game, but with a few caveats. The original premise that I bought it for went largely unfulfilled and the game turned out to be just jumping puzzles. I bought it thinking it would be an engaging exploration story, and instead it was just endless jumping puzzles. I played a couple hours, put it down for two months, then finished it off in another two hour session.
While the game had atmosphere and piqued my curiosity, I was bored with the whole thing before it was over and playing just to finish it. What started out as an intriguing puzzle about space, time, and this planet, was quickly eclipsed by boring repetitive game play. It felt like an idea that was stretched out far beyond whatever potential it had, and left thin and wanting.
However the game was beautiful, and there were times when I did marvel at the level design and enjoy what I was playing. By the time I was done though, these positives were outweighed by boredom.
On the whole, if this is on sale it's worth a buy, but don't expect much. It also has zero replay-ability in my mind.

The problem with this game is that it is story driven. But it lacks story. Like at all - not even bad story, it simply does not have any
What you get here is merely a theme park you walk/run through, a museum of random ideas, images and references mashed together in apprenent attempt to create "mystical" and "multilayered" story. The game tries so hard to get many meanings that it fails to get even one. Most of things you will see has no point, no connection to other things (aside of exteremly vague secondary associations, that will only appear if you have read and know well enough Aelita novel by A.Tolstoy. And even then, game had to literally point you out to that novel for you to even start recognising references.
The thing that is called story here makes no stance on anything. It does not tell anything. Even main hero adventure on those planet rapidly degrades into total mess leaving you confused, scratching your head and thinking "what the hell was that?". And later on "and what was the point of all that?" because all weird stuff to happen will neven ever get any development.
The only thing that is somewhat resembles a story is overhead out-of-screen portions of interview (you have heard half of it in the trailer) that reflects on the main hero story, but it is not every interesting (because you the main hero is just a walking suit with little-to-no personality you will find hard to care about) and yes, made into mess by making totally pointless and never developed references to the game content.
So it lacks story and it was meant to lack pretty much everything else, including gameplay (it is slightly more complex version of Dear Easher and similar, gameplay wise), so yeah. But even here it manages to get annoying by horrible level design, especially closer to the end. Things like "if you die, you will respawn at last checkpoint facing the WRONG direction" (and keep in mind that many locations are quite barren and look-alike, so it is easy to get lost there) are true gems.

When that first pitch comes at you take a breath and relax. The batter will automatically adjust to the pitch. All you need to do is swing it at the right time. I played through Deus Ex for the first time in 2016, and I probably wouldn't have done so if it wasn't for Revision. Deus Ex is a remarkable, prophetic game. Its systemic game design and immersive story-telling are still a standard rarely met by today's developers (and certainly not by the sequels of Deus Ex).
There are some things to critisize about Revision. The retexturing of Hong Kong replaces all Chinese characters with gibberish, and due to the remapped level geography NPC instructions are sometimes more confusing than helpful. However, the added achievements certainly make the game more accessable for today's players who are used to being rewarded constantly.
In the end, I highly recommend every gamer to play Deus Ex as it is a historic moment in gaming history; they may decide for themselves if they do so with or without the Revision modifications. Both ways will be just fine.

People in this era of gaming seem to mistake "Hard" difficulties for "Unfair" difficulties in gaming.
Hear me out here. I've played this game for a reasonable amount of time. I know how to play platformers quite well, I've played and grown up with them; playing everything from Mega Man to Mario (the games this one claims to aspire to live up to) and I have to tell you, this game is not good. The game's bosses are either LUDICROUSLY over powered, or just blatantly unfair. Not to mention that they are extremely bland! Take the game's fourth boss, (mini-boss?) for example; he moves from left-to-right, while spamming projectiles that seem to take no path which can be learnt, or avoided, and do more damage than is necessary. When he is on the left side of the screen, you can not go behind him. When on the right side of the screen, however, he is able to be jumped behind so that you can do damage to him without him targeting you. Every blue moon he decides he should address the threat behind him, so he just fires projectiles into the wall in an attempt to hit you, with very little tell that he will do so. Not to mention the fact that your weapons do almost NO damage to any boss-type enemy in the game. You literally have to hit the boss so much that I got BORED fighting him. A platforming game, in which there are boss-fights, caused me to become bored at it's main mechanics. I love mega-man, but this game? Nah. This game isn't worthy of that title. The worst part? The game could have been good! If it was just beta-tested by someone, even if someone played through the first hour of the GAME to address that the charge-shot did almost NOTHING to the bosses in the game, or even the damn REGULAR ENEMIES, for that matter; they would have realized that the games balancing was almost non-existent! The grenades don't actually explode, rather than creating a point at which 7 projectiles come from that do regular damage, the charge-shot is worthless EXCEPT TO SERVE AS YOUR DOUBLE JUMP. Yes, you don't get a double jump. You get a gimped charge-shot that only serves to be a horribly-implemented double jump, there is a bullet-hover mechanic similar to Cave Story's, but doesn't work as well, and you get a secondary weapon system, in which you have limited, but RECOVERING ammo, which you have to get ammo upgrades for that sometimes don't even give you a full ammo for some of said weapons. There is just a myriad of horribly implemented mechanics in the game that preventing it from being what it COULD BE! It could be enjoyable, but with this many issues left un-addressed? No. This game was just a waste of $10, and I'm not one to cry over buying indie games for larger sums of cash.

The game is too frugal with it's teleporters, so you'll traverse a long way to a boss, only to get killed (it takes a while to learn their patterns) and then you'll need to work your way back. I recommend going to your Users/[your username here]/AppData/Local/Rex Rocket/ and creating copies of the save files just after you've gotten to the Boss area. This way you'll be able to reload just before the bosses. And trust me..you'll need to.
I strongly recommend using a controller as others have suggested. I also strongly recommend going to the game options to change directional control from the analog stick to the D-pad.

I was looking forward to playing this game. After 2 hours of game-time I had progressed 13% through the game.
- fun game
- but WAAAY harder than I expected
So the first 15-20 minutes was pretty easy because there wasn't really much combat. However once I got to the first boss I started to die a LOT. You start with a lot of lives, I think that is reason. In the options menu you are supposed to be able toggle 'fun mode' on and off. I think that might have actually meant hardcore mode, but this feature seemed to be broken as as there was no apply setting button and it was always back on when I returned to the menu if I'd toggled it off. The boss spammed out a lot of projectiles which I found really tricky to avoid. I think I died at least 15-20 times trying to beat it. The environment is populated by a large amount of enemies. Sometimes it's difficult to get past them with without taking damage i.e. sometimes you don't have much choice but to jump into them. They tend to surround you and appear unexpectedly when you are distracted by other hazards. Also enemies appear to have some degree of random generation so you don't always encounter the same enemies in the same place. I think that probably help keep the same areas fresh.
You don't re-spawn in the immediate vicinity are after dying instead you are taken back to a checkpoint, which there aren't that many of. This tends to set you back pretty far. So I found that I had to begin the same gauntlets from the start again and again. Sometimes after dying over and over before finally making it through sections I discovered that I'd just went to all the effort only to take me back somewhere that I had already been to! So make sure you check the map system so that you're not just taking alternative routes backwards. Also there are hidden passages and destroyable blocks which will uncover shortcuts that dramatically reduce the effort needed to navigate the ship, so be on the lookout for them. I wish I'd realized these things earlier.
I liked how the game looked. The aesthetics and sound effects remind me of lot of old console and PC games and brought back happy memories. For example I hadn't thought about ID's Dangerous Dave for a long time before playing this. That game was awesome! NPCs in Rex Rocket have little bit's of dialogue, some of which I found amusing.
So in the time that I played I felt that I only progressed a relatively small amount through the game. It was very difficult and I was having to make numerous attempts to complete small sections of the game. I struggled to reach points only to die at them and have to go back. This has potential for frustration (I’ll admit I did gripe about it lol) but surprisingly I still found that I enjoyed playing this game.

An absolutely delightful platformer, I honestly can't recommend it enough. Gameplay is super fun, and there's a great pace to it as it steadily gets more and more difficult. It certainly is reminiscent of Super Meat Boy, but I think Slime-San is different enough to stand strong on it's own. There's an incredible amount of content here for what it is, with plenty of extra modes like Speedrunning or Boss Rush, plenty of ways to customize your game experience, plenty of diverse areas, unlockable arcade games parodying games that range from Doom to Mario Kart, New Game +, and a town & home to explore and encounter so many wonderful, charming, quirky characters. Slime-San is a tough yet fair platformer reminscent of Super Meat Boy, with its gorgeous artstyle, amazing sound track, and controls that feel tight and polished.  You complete levels while collecting apples to spend in Slumptown to unlock minigames, hats, and skins that change slime-sans play style, which gives a new spin to an already refreshing game.  Most importantly, players controling Slime-san will explore levels/worlds that introduce concepts, and continue to expand upon those concepts in fresh ways. Slime-san respects your time, and rewards players for mastering their concepts.  With a couple of in-game mechanics, nothing feels impossible, with the real challenge being supported through boss rush/speed run modes and individual level speed run rewards.
For $12, Slime-san is absolutely worth the price for any gamer passionate about tight controls, well designed levels, and great sound tracks.

This is one of those games that belongs in a category I'd classify as "The one huge exception" because, for the most part, I've never cared for shmups. Too many of them have an extremely tiny margin of error allowed before you get a game over, especially if you wanna go for the SUPER SECRET FINAL BOSS kinda stuff, and the communities are generally full of people who make fun of you for playing on the easier difficulties, so that puts me off even more. REVOLVER360 RE:ACTOR is an entirely different story.
This game, on top of having different firing types, a regenerating method of destroying bullets, and a health system that lets you take a number of hits, it also has the most unique mechanic I've ever seen in a shmup, and that's camera rotation. You'd think camera rotation would be the last thing to mention in a game, but this actually makes it the center of the game's concept, where turning the camera is closer to turning a dial to adjust the playing field to your preference, because the bullets exist on a 3D plane, while you exist on a 2D plane.
This means that, on top of being able to tank a couple hits, you're also able to just turn the camera when there's a screen-wide attack, and just go around it. And the camera rotation doesn't end its usefulness there. There are enemies and items to shoot in the background to clear your path, give you health and laser items, and even just increase your score. This game gives you so many great options for keeping yourself in the game, while tying it into a mechanic that you have to master, so even if it makes the experience as a whole easier, it's still a challenge in itself.
Even if you don't care for shmups, I'd still reccommend this game, because it's really just that good, and there's a chance you'll find something to love here. Final note, that SOUNDTRACK GOD DAMN!!! A+

I really love how game progress is determined mostly by the players skill instead of what armor/weapons are equip.  Gear actually makes so little of a difference in most instances, it's even possible to get beat by a shirtless barehanded guy while you are in full armor with a sword/shield, lol.  Yeah there is a huge learning curve but if you take the time to figure it all out it becomes such a rewarding experience and incredibly fun to play.  I wish more RPG's would follow suit by making games that rely on the players skill/knowlege of game mechanics instead of how lucky they get in RNG or how much loot farming they do.  Although the game is in Early Access and still pretty basic I've still never seen another game like this and it is worth checking out.  I look forward to seeing how the actual storyline plays out and how skills will be applied to the combat when they impliment them.  I understand this is a Prelude to Sui Generis, their main project, and is probably used as a tool to "test the waters" for certain aspects they intend to use there as well as give gamers a chance to see what the future holds.  So I dont expect this to be an incredibly long game with tons of content and in depth story but I am eagerly awaiting a finished product and enjoying what content is available.

Remember SCP games? Like the endless staircase and the first actual slender game?
This here is similar to those games in a number of ways.
First one - it's made with Unity. It's also as poorly calibrated and as untested as containment project fangames are.
Second off - there's no presentation, no menu. All you get is a start menu, pause menu and a weird inconsistent way of exiting clue-screens. Also no save functionality - though it's not needed, as the game is very short.
Last point being - it's basically free. Keys are floating around seemingly everywhere. Here it's less like SCP game and more like herpes - it's kinda free but no one really wants to get it. And if you did, it's gonna stay in your library forever.
Despite this, The Next Door stands on its own. In its corner. With a dunce hat. And I can't help but feel sorry for it.
The same way I feel sorry for Kanye West. They're both as short and as shallow as they get.
Opening sequence blew me away, though. You see this dialogue happening on one black line on the screen, and immideately assume a role of a... litle sperm. In a "flock" of sperm; a whole current, if you will.
Then, after going in towards what seems like an ovary there's a sudden change.
Your spermmates are now stars. Your background music is now an Apollo radio comm. Your ovary is now the Moon.
That was so bizarre and out of context, like a dream! Sadly, it did not keep up the standard.
Every single puzzle from the get go is bland. It's as easy as: here's a clue, look at it, now go do the thing so it's the same. Floor flip, where the other part or the whole puzzle is located on the ceiling, is an interesting mechanic. But it's not elaborated on - it's present in only two rooms. Which, to be fair, is a solid third of the whole experience.
What tries to spice the blandness up is the color scheme. It tries, but it does not do a good job at it.
Half the game is set in the lighthouse from Matrix: Reloaded. I mean, everything in the background is white. Not ivory-pleasant kind of white. Sharp, eye-shanking rgb255, #ffffff kind of white.
The other half has a mix of night and twilight skies and some artificial light, which does a disservice to the spicing-up goal. It only brings attention to how dull basic tile textures are.
The stew all of this brews into is highly unappetizing. It feels like a dream of someone who had just taken occult studies course and tried to make sense of it all. An after class stomach flu fever dream that can only turn into one thing upon awakening.
Though saying so is a bit too rough. This game is more like a 30 Second to Mars album. It has bright colors and intersting symbols on the cover and it's deep for the sake of being deep. The only difference is - there's no music. There's no game.
But hey, "it's almost free and they put greenlight comments in the final room!", right?

The game can be deep as much as you like, you can play on some low EGO and just hit home runs for fun with no to very small challenge from AI, or plan upgrades for every single player on higher EGO. Fire that coach you are unhappy with and get new and better one, build your lineup like a real MLB manager, from your leadoff spot to clean up guy. Super Mega Baseball: Extra Innings is a fun if somewhat frustrating game to play.  At this I've only played the game in Exhibition mode - I haven't played a full season yet at any difficulty level - I've come away with some impressions of the game.
The pros of this game as I see them include the ease of picking up and playing with the basic control scheme, the stadiums that have a nice sense of atmosphere and depth, and the sheer addictiveness of the game.  It's easy to play a three or four-game set against the same opponent, just as they do in the bigs.  It seems as long as I stick with contact hitting, basic throwing, and pitching without worrying quite so much about trying to get a fine aim on the ball, I have good results.
The cons of this game include some of those finer points, including fine-tuning pitches before letting fly, power hitting, lack of a practice mode to get accustomed to the gameplay mechanics, and the lack of errors in the statistics.  At least in the Exhibition mode, errors are made but not counted in the stats.  This may not be true in the Season mode, and if that's the case it's a very minor nit. But if errors are not counted in Season, it takes away something from the statistical tracking, especially as the game's stats tracking is fairly deep as it is, because the players do make errors.  And not having a dedicated practice mode makes things especially frustrating when trying to bat with power or get used to making diving and jumping catches.
I was fortunate enough to pick up this game as part of a Humble Bundle deal, at a cost considerably less than the asking price here.  For what I paid, it's definitely not a bad game and it has already brought me a lot of fun.  And I suspect some of the shortcomings of this game have been addressed in the updcoming Super Mega Baseball 2.  Definitely consider this one if you like baseball and want a quick and fun experience.

How well does the Reloaded version of Al Lowe's adventure game Leisure Suit Larry in the Land of the Lounge Lizards stack up against the original?
Back in April 2012, Replay Games surfaced on Kickstarter with the news that they'd managed to convince long time conjurer of dirty jokes Al Lowe to come out of retirement for this top-to-bottom re-imagining of his 25-year-old graphic adventure game, Leisure Suit Larry in the Land of the Lounge Lizards.
The game puts the player in the driver's seat of the story of Larry Laffer, a middle-aged, balding man trying to seduce attractive women. Larry was a nerdy geek all his life and eventually became a computer programmer. He now finds himself in Lost Wages, in front of the bar Lefty's, with a bottle of breath spray and $94 dollars in his wallet.
I guess I was around 12 years old when I played the original Leisure Suit Larry in the Land of the Lounge Lizards with my friends and even though we never managed to leave Lefty's, Larry introduced us to new words from the English vocabulary, like "mount". I think we even got our hands on an uncensored version at some point, but in all its EGA resolution glory, I doubt we really noticed any difference.
What has changed from the original game? Not surprisingly, there has been a major overhaul of the graphics, sound, music and  there is now fully vocalized audio. There are also new jokes, new puzzles and even some new characters. One of the Kickstarter tiers allowed you to pay to be one of the drinkers at Lefty's, and although this was a great idea to rob someone of $5,000 (yes, that was the actually amount you had to pledge to drink at Lefty's), it introduces an element to the game that just seems shallow and unnecessary. The Kickstarter drinkers should have been replaced with over-the-top fictional characters instead.
The HD background graphics is beautiful, but the character graphics and animation have a lot to be desired. They seem rushed and most of them, expect for Larry himself, stand so much out from the backgrounds, they look a bit like something I could have drawn myself. This especially goes for the Kickstarter drinkers in the bar. Maybe they had to draw themselves, too, who knows? While we're on the subject of Kickstarter: It permeates too much of this game, Al Lowe even appears at the end, thanking the Kickstarter backers. Get off the set, Al!
Money is an important aspect of Leisure Suit Larry in the Land of the Lounge Lizards: Reloaded, and the $94 dollars in Larry's wallet won't last you long. To get more money you have to gamble, and thankfully there are slot machines, blackjacks and other mini games everywhere you look. It does, however, become rather tedious to play these games to get money, and you'll find yourself saving and loading quite a lot. To go ahead and build up a solid cash balance at the start of the game is probably a good idea, so that you don't have to back and save/load/gamble time and time again.
More often than not, understanding what you're supposed to do in the game is far from logical and your play style can easily turn into a click fest, where you try to use the hammer with the squid, the squid with the bungee cord, the bungee cord with the Tabasco sauce and the Tabasco sauce with pretty much every living and inanimate object in the casino, Caesar's Phallus. Although this is not something that is unfamiliar to point-and-click adventures, it's sort of in the name of the genre, it just feels like too much in this case. Clicking on everything will eventually pay off in the end, though, but it just seems so random. This kind of game style might not appeal to people who prefer to play adventure games where logic is in fact something that matters.
But logic is not what Leisure Suit Larry in the Land of the Lounge Lizards: Reloaded is about. It's about Larry Laffer's crazy adventure and there's nothing logic about it at all. If you laugh at fart jokes, start to drool at the thought of digital honka-honkas and enjoy clicking your mouse a lot, this is a game you should go ahead and buy.
Personally, having finished the game, I'm left with a feeling that it was 5 hours I probably could have used on something more entertaining. The jokes are OK, I laughed every now and then, but I think I expected more. Maybe the game simply isn't for the adult me. Perhaps I left Larry Laffer behind at some point in life, when I actually grew up? But all that said, it was nice to meet Larry Laffer again and realize that the first time I saw Larry Laffer back when I was 12 should have been a warning sign about become a computer programmer myself.

This game is...  interesting.  It's incredibly difficult.  I mean, absolutely, one of the hardest games I've ever played.  Mind you, I have over 1000 hours in CK2, 900 in EU4, 300 each in Vicky2, HoI4, Stellaris, etc.  I like hard, complicated strategy games and political simulations.  This one takes the cake.  Even on the easiest setting (19Q4), I can't even make it 3 years into the game.  You have to survive 10 years in order to win.  There is very limited documentation on this game, and almost all of it is only available in the form of Steam guides -- so you're kind of flying solo (as if the game wasn't already hard enough).  The game seems to be very historically accurate, though, which is definitely a plus!
Especially if you can get it on sale (and even if you can't), this game is absolutely worth the money -- but probably only if you like political simulations (like Democracy 3) and hard/complicated strategy games (like Victoria 2).  You will lose.  A lot.  But you'll still enjoy the game.  ...Probably.  I did, anyway.
NOTE:  There's a bug on Linux that prevents you from playing in fullscreen (the menus won't work).  Running the game windowed works around this issue.
EDIT:  I just started playing Dwarf Fortress.  This game is harder than Dwarf Fortress.  I'm not even sh!tting you.  DF is more complicated, but this game is harder.  At least for me.

Yeah let's get this out of the way: It's absolutely inspired by Meatboy. Instead of a trail of blood you leave a trail of slime. Instead of band aids you collect apples. This is where the comparisons to SMB will end because i never actually played SMB myself. (Hercey! Burn the witch!)
Anyway. This is a fast paced platformer with
decent design and controls. I say "mostly" because there are some issues i've come across. Firstly, the controls. You have 3 abilities: Jump, dash and slowdown. The movement controls themselves are responsive but the jump & slowdown ability can be a bit finicky. Your slime drops like a rock when not using the time slowing ability but when passing through the green obstacles (which can only be passed while using slowdown) things get hectic quickly when pressing 3 different buttons to juggle jumping, dashing and slow mow. You can remap buttons to make it more convenient but multitasking is a required skill. Also the jump itself is pretty whimpy, there are jumps that seem to be doable but only when the game feels like it. And there is this weird mechanic where you don't really have a double jump but you kinda do but only when dropping off vertically not when jumping horizontally. It's...hard to explain and takes some getting used to. Overall the dash proved a lot more reliable than the jump. Makes me wonder if maybe the game would have been better off not having a jump at all and instead be designed around only the dash. Oh well.
Another annoying thing are the collision detection and hit boxes. There are times where i swear i didn't touch the red stuff but i die and then there are times where i'm sure i should be dead but keep on living. May just be a result of the pixel graphics, some finetuning would have been appreciated in that regard.
The final gripe i have is with the level design itself. I said earlier that this is supposed to be a "fast-paced" platformer, yet there are quite a number of levels that will make you play the waiting game for a platform to lower or an obstacle to move out of the way. Kinda ruins the flow and i don't understand why the devs thought this to be a good decision in a game seemingly custom made for speedruns. Let me put it this way: When i play a 2D plaformer i wanna never have to let go of the run button. I crave constant action. I understand that this may just be my personal complaint but eh. It bugs me is all.
This seems like a long list of negatives but overall the positives outweigh for me. I really dig the pixel art and the music. The characters are cute and funny and there is hidden stuff to be unlocked here and there.
Finally, let me address the difficulty: The game is fairly challenging simply due to the fact that a single hit will kill you (there is also a time limit, if you don't clear an area fast enough acid will catch up to you). Frustration is mitigated by the fact that each area per level is only a couple of seconds long. You only have to clear an area once to move on to the next and there are never more than 4 areas in one level. Still, i can't play more than 3 levels at a time without running the danger of hurling my controller out the window. And it is designed to be played exactly like that, short levels in short bursts rather than marathons.

SHMUPOMETER Rating
EXCELLENT for Hardcore Shmup Fans | Good for Casual Shmup Fans
- Great Soundtrack, included in the game files
-Unique rotation mechanic, allowing the player to dodge otherwise unavoidable bullet patterns, elimnate background threats, and find secrets
- Laser weapon that destroys enemy Yellow bullets and rows of enemies, but has limited shots, drops your multiplier, and has a cooldown to reload
- EMP shot to destroy blue bullets/lasers and purple bullets which are even more limited than the laser, but also has a reload cooldown
- Same EMP Cooldown Meter governs the use of Overdrive mode, if full, which allows temporarily unlimited lasers and maximum score multiplier and can be used relatively frequently per level
- Relatively forgiving health system, allowing you to take many hits compared to most Bullet Hells, and inculdes health pick ups, and limited regen
- Ways to deal with difficult bullet patterns
- Stable 60fps+ gameplay
- Great port - includes support for XInput and DirectInput - I switch the input mode on my controller AND THE GAME RESTARTED ITSELF SO I DIDN'T HAVE TO
- Helpful how to play page that explains the game numerous mechanics and strategies
- Global leaderboard which includes player replays - allowing players to learn how others played
- Lovely graphics that clearly distinguish threats
-Short. Only 4 stages, meaning it can be completed quickly for somebody wanting to get through their backlog or learn the game easily to run for a better score
- Sector mode - allowing a player to practice a specific level
- Challenge mode - 50 Extra levels that are very challenging and further explain combat and score mechanics
- Inexpensive
- One life, zero continues - If you die, you have to start the whole game over
- Nearly impossible to avoid damage? While most well-crafted bullet hell games are built so that a trained player can take no damage, it seems like you will almost inevitably take damage at some point. Even the #1 ranked player took damage.
- Relatively difficult despite forgiving health system - I've lost runs many times on Sector 2, but eventually I beat it and the rest of the game on the next run.
- Potentially overwhelming gameplay. While you're dealing with an onslaught of enemies, bullets, and lasers, you will sometimes have to deal with background damage dealers if you're not paying attention and rotating the world frequently
- Rotation mechanic may be seen as an annoying gimmick to some players
- Possibly too complex gameplay for some players - Enemy Survival, along with multiple weapon cooldowns
- Stylized UI can get lost lost in the game's art style and hectic gameplay.
- High Price per hour - $10 will seem expensive to somebody only playing to beat the game which can take less than an hour or two. (dependent on player skill - a single run takes less than half an hour)
- Bright, color burn effect may be harsh on the eyes of some players
Gameplay takes place on a 2D-plane like most shooters. Shooting not only shoots standard bullets, but shoots homing missiles to the 3D background within a short range of your ship - requiring you to "hover" over enemies, environmental threats, and supply boxes to destroy them, or over parts of a boss to deal extra damage. Rotating the ship (or rather, rotating the game world) with the trigger buttons alows the player to more easily dodge some project tiles and deal with background threats or supply boxes that can provide health, weapon restore, or multipliers. You will need to balance this mechanic, along with the weapons I described in the "Pros" section to succeed. I was very concerned I wouldn't be able to beat this game because of a tough portion on Sector 2, but I got past it and found it was short work, meaning that memorizing enemy patterns might be a lass daunting task compared to shooters 2 or three times as long.

I love this game. TLDR at the bottom.
Pros:
Exanima is mechanically unique, to the point that the controls would throw anyone for a loop at first. Once I got the hang of the controls however, success in combat was sweetly satisfying, and exploring my environment left me in a constant state of wonder and eager anticipation.
Exanima is beautiful. The space around me in the dungeon felt appropriately full of objects to examine and knock around, and physics applied to almost everything I saw, from broken chairs and dining utensils to keys and weapons.
Cons:
Exanima is incomplete. I know that this goes without saying, as it is still in "early access," but i must point it out, as it is one of the only things i can find wrong with the game. Once i beat the latest level in story mode, there was nowhere for me to go, nothing for me to do, accept play arena mode, which is quite fun and challenging, but repetetive and ultimately not as interesting as the story. There is a small element of randomness to story mode runs, in the form of different loot inside containers, but that is the only variance that gives it some replayability.
The last patch was seven months ago, which is a bit long to wait for new content, in my opinion. The patches that have come always seemed to include very noticeable additions and changes, so there is that.
There is a compass, but no map in-game.
The game does not inform you in any way when you reach checkpoints. The only way to know if you have reached one is to die and realize you didnt have to make a brand-new character.
TL;DR:
Exanima is hard to master, but it also beautiful, unique, and fun. Right now, it is not complete, but it does have a fair amount of content. If you want a brand new Adventure/ Role-Playing Game experience, Exanima is probably a good purchase for you. If you want a storyline with a clear directive and a concrete resolution, pass this up for now.

It's gameplay is a mix of XCOM and WW2 with surprising attention to details, such as physics, weakpoints on tanks and enviroment destruction..
For example, once I ended up having to fight a heavy scout car, that was impervious to small arms fire. Ofc I had no AT weapons, so I hoarded a bunch of HE grenades on one guy and spammed them at the scout car to see what happens.
It's tires blew up on one side and the moment the last tire flew off, whole vehicle flipped over to theside, rendering it useless.
Buildings can be destroyed in a manner similar to Battlefield Bad Company 2, but much simpler. You can colapse them with tanks and most armored vehicles, sometimes a really good tactic to surprise attack a tank is to move behind the building trough which the enemy cant see you, boo! You're within 20 meters of the tank (preferably the backside).
Even though it has its flaws and the resolution support is a bit wonky, I have never played a more complex and realistic WW2 RTS. And yes, I have played CoH 1 (much simpler vehicle system) and 2 ("butthurt" button spam) and neither come close to this game.

Definitely one of my favorite games as of  right now. If you are a fan of sandbox city building games I would definitely check this one out. I had to watch gameplay of it on YouTube before I decided to grab it, but so far I am pretty happy with it. You can obviously tell that it is a work in progress, and the lack of content shows for that. However, that lack of content does not stop you from having a decent time attempting to build your own kingdom. This game is similar to Banished if you have ever played that, but a really really really dumbed down version of that. While I say that it is dumbed down that does not actually a bad thing. I feel like this game is more for the casual gamer who just wants to chill and watch their creation come to life. There are 3 different difficulties which allow you to play peacefully, with a little bit of a challenge, or to push yourself to the limits. The basic idea of this game is to build your kingdom starting with your castle. After that you have to make sure you have enough housing for your people as well as future people that might stop by. The people in your village have jobs (if you have built those buildings) and all need food so make sure you have plenty of that. Vikings and dragons are your enemies and will destroy everything in your path, so make sure you have plenty of defenses later on. The first few times are not too bad if you don't have any defences, but after a while your people will get tired of being picked on. You have to make sure to keep your people happy or else they're free to leave your kingdom.
So if you are a casual gamer, and want a type of city building game where you can sit back and watch your kingdom come to life. You can maybe sip on a cup of tea or coffee in the morning  and it provides good entertainment. Though the lack of content will keep your typical gamer from enjoying this for too long, I feel that casual gamers that just enjoy a quick burst of gameplay will like this, and will find the ability to build your kingdom overtime fun.
I've been playing this on a Macbook Air 2017 base-model. No problems with performance. Since banished wasn't available for Mac and won't be updated anymore; this game is a great substitute.
Be sure to check out gameplay footage (not trailers) on YouTube before you buy any game though.

Let me start off by saying while I dont normally play city builders like this I did play a fair bit of Banished. And my biggest complaint of this game, is you CANNOT manage how many people are operating a structure. Which lead to huge management issues with your peasants. Want a quarry? You HAVE to have 4 people working it, unless there are only 3 idle peasants when you turn it on. If there is 4 people working it you cannot just switch one person to a farm. This also means that if you dont have idle workers, (which you basically never do) you have to shut something down to build anything. The whole game becomes: what can I shut down to build something.
Keeping your peasant happy is a must in order to grow. A house isnt next to another house? affects your happiness. A house isnt near a well, not happy. Not enough charcoal? Not happy. Oh and it take 3 people to run a charcoal hut. And for about every 30 people you need a hut. Which means you have to have 2 charcoal huts for every 60 people. But wait theres more! To house 60 people you either need 12 hovels, 5 1x2 houses or 3 2x2 houses. The larger the houses are, the LESS happy the inhabitants are. More Hovels means more space wasted and more wells.
The game lacks a "Balance" which managing the amount of workers per building solved in Banished. I like the castle building elements, but until the games smooths itself out I cant recommend it to people that arent prepared to just click around constantly disabling/enabling buildings. Oh and the box to toggle building on and off is larger then the actual area you can select which gets INSANELY annoying after awhile. If you didnt click the exact center of that darn box.....

Compared to SMB, the control scheme is more complex, which gives it a higher learning curve at first, but I don't find it to be too cluttered - it's manageable after a while. Hitboxes are sometimes misalligned. Level design is inferior to SMB, sometimes you spend too much time just waiting around (a bother when replaying a level repeatedly) and there are a lot of environmental gimmicks that interfere with your control - a bit annoying. The two boss fights I had so far were nothing spectacular.
Overall, a pretty good effort though. If you're starved for a Super Meat Boy clone, and are willing to cut the devs some slack for a few design shortfalls, you'll have fun.

Slime-san is an unassuming 2D pixel platformer that looks pretty retro. The graphics recall the NES era, and the game intentionally uses a sharply limited color palette – blue, green, red, and white – to further reinforce the retro feeling. Most of the levels consist of four unmoving screens, with each quarter of the level starting you back over at the beginning of it, while a timer runs in the background to measure how quickly you perform.
But the graphics belie a pretty solidly constructed platformer. This is no cheapo indie game, but is rather a platformer which is reminiscent of Super Meat Boy – very solid, but very compact, level design, with simplified graphics designed to call attention to what really matters in the levels.
And this game excels at that.
The game is built around making good use of the very simple but solidly constructed platforming mechanics. You can jump, you can dash, you can jump then dash, you can dash then jump, you can wall jump, and if you jump off of a wall or run off of a ledge, you gain an additional, mid-air jump that you can use. You can become insubstantial, slowing down time and gaining the ability to move through green platforms, objects, and enemies which ordinarily block your progress or send you flying, depending on what they are. Around these mechanics, the whole game is spun.
There are environmental obstacles, but not a tremendous variety of them; there are a small number of enemies, but they don’t feel repetitive. And there are five bosses, which have simple but solid design which highlights the game’s mechanics.
What this game does well is take a number of simple elements and combine them in elegant ways to make for interesting levels. Fans blow you upwards, barrels launch you, gravity reversals… well, reverse gravity. You can be made bigger or smaller (perhaps the least interesting mechanic in the game, unfortunately, as it doesn’t feel like it generally has much of an interesting effect on gameplay, though it isn’t bad by any means). You can swim in water, in which you can dash all you want. A small number of enemy types each have their own movement range, and there are moving platforms and spawning platforms and rolling red barrels that kill you if you touch them.
The game’s very simple color palette makes the interface very intuitive and make what is going on easy to understand at a glance. Red things kill you, including the acid which spawns and creeps across the screen if you take too long completing a screen. Green things don’t hurt you, and can be passed through by the phasing ability; sometimes you need to use this ability to pass through things, while other times green objects or enemies need to be interacted with so you can bounce off of them or walk along them. White things are impermeable but are safe to touch and stand on.
Really, though, what a game like this comes down to is level design, and this game has very solidly constructed levels. They’re simple and generally present ideas in simple but interesting ways, and combine various obstacles in various ways to make navigating the levels more interesting. The game is also designed with speed running in mind, and a clever player can frequently skip off of the “intended” path in order to complete a level more swiftly, albeit often at greater difficulty in execution. The game’s mechanics are almost always very consistent, and while there were a few bugs at release, the development team is very active and quickly ironed out many of them.
Like Super Meat Boy, there are collectables in the levels. Every screen in the game contains a single apple, and thus there are four apples per level, save on the five levels in the game where the screen actually scrolls, which contain exactly one each. There are also a small number – three per world – of “arcade tokens”, which can be used to unlock simple arcade games in a shopping area.
The level select allows you to also go to a shopping area, which allows the player to buy a lot of cosmetics using the apples, as well as buy new versions of the titular slime-san, each of which have their own mechanics, somewhat reminiscent of the various characters who you can play as in Super Meat Boy. Some can double jump, but move more slowly; others are floaty, which is a double-edged sword as their higher jumps and slower fall speed can sometimes work to their disadvantage. Some run faster and fall faster; some are always dashing, making them hard to control but fast.
The game has a surprising amount of character considering what it is, with the game lampshading its own weird pseudo-japanese aesthetic at times and populated with some weird characters in the shopping area. Over the course of the game, you unlock additional areas in the shopping area, which have no purpose beyond introducing more quirky characters, as well as adding more quirky characters to the town. The story, such as it is, is very simple, but it works well enough in achieving its purpose in giving the player some direction, and the overall aesthetic of battling your way through various parts of the inside of the worm that eats you and in which the entire game is set, starting with the intestine and ending with the teeth, before finally escaping the insides of the worm entirely and having to defeat it from the outside, leads to a natural sense of progression and while it doesn’t “really” make sense in a way, it is intuitive enough and it feels aesthetically sensible.
All in all, this is a good game if you are into difficult-but-fair platformers – while this is easier than games like Super Meat Boy, it is still a fairly difficult game, and if difficulty isn’t your thing, this game may become frustrating. On the other hand, if you thought that Super Meat Boy was a good game, you’re likely to enjoy this game as well, as this hits on pretty much the same design space as that game, but feels different enough to be its own thing.

Lifeless Planet is an atmospheric sci-fi game. You won't be blasting aliens with lasers - instead of technology infused fantasy the game explores what science fiction is all about, with a psychological twist. This genre is quite a bit more demanding for game designers as it is hard to keep such games entertaining and immersive. Overall I think Stage 2 Studios did a fine job here, considering I played the game from the beginning to the end in one go. I clocked total of just under 6 hours, so the game is not very long.
So what do you do for 6 hours, then? Most of the time, walking, admiring the beautiful and sometimes mesmerizing landscape. There are also some simple puzzles to solve. Tidbits of information about what happened are found - this stuff is interesting and thought provoking. Finally, you get to jump, much more than you would like to.
Technically the game is not very impressive. The graphics look dated, especially the details, but the landscapes still look good. This just proves that graphics design can cover a lot of what old technology misses. Coupled with excellent soundtrack and somewhat sparse but fitting voice acting, the presentation is more than adequate. Controls, on the other hand, are the weak point here. Most of the time you will be walking around so you would think this is not a problem. But often you need to jump with accurate direction and timing and this is where the controls can be frustrating.
While the maps are large, there are not many things you can do. The game is heavily scripted and there is just one way you can make progress. Sometimes this creates a plausibility problem, but strangely the effect on atmosphere was small. On the plus side, the game does not hold your hand and constantly tell you what to do next. You will usually get enough hints, though. The scripting will naturally limit the replay value.

Best melee combat simulation I've ever seen. An excellent feel to each swing, completely potentially decking an opponent in a single blow, or just giving them a little love-tap depending on how well you move with it. Parrying isn't an end-all-be-all damage stopper, just slows the opponent's attack, and your shield arm gets tired at a reasonable rate, not within a few scrapes. Armor feels the best of all - you really feel the difference between cloth and leather, chain and plate. In full plate mail, battles can really feel like a total mess of "who can slowly beat the other tin can to death first" as it really should. Attacks aren't simply directional as you can get in Chivalry or Mount and Blade, you can pull any angle you like if you're good with the control scheme.
Speaking of which, whereas I've seen plenty of complaints about it, Exanima's controls aren't that hard to pick up. To perfect, perhaps impossible, but within an hour I was slugging my way into fights, if about as graceful as a little bebe. Now, I can confidently say while outmaneuvering and beating the snot out of my foe that "that -is- what I meant to do," not just flailing about wildly, hoping something happens. Well, most of the time. I'm not great with action games. You could certainly turn battle entirely into an art form as beautiful as any in here, with proper practice.
Aside from that, just about everything else works pretty well, too. The AI isn't broken, it acts about as imperfectly as a player. Perhaps slightly too... rigidly imperfect - I could see getting "too good" for the NPC opponents. But they're respectable, and can hold their own in a fight.
The weird sort of unspoken, passive diplomacy with the hall-wanderers of the adventure is pretty good, too, feeling a little unpredictable and unstable, as if navigating your way around a variety of wild animals. Like a bear, back away slowly. Wait, that was bears, right? It isn't too complex as of now, though.
The backstory seems interesting, though it really raises more questions than it answers. That's kind of part of the allure, though. The Arena is pretty solid, progress feels good, rising to the top is a pretty solid climb, not without peril.
Graphics are beautiful. Darkly beautiful. You don't get awesome landscapes or breathtaking flora or fauna, nor are the characters particularly anything to write home about (well, unless you, ah, "lose your shirt," perhaps, but that's a certain audience only), but everything you see is plenty realistic and the lighting is truly excellent. I honestly have no idea how the game runs so smoothly, either. Or perhaps, if it's no mean feat in reality, how any other game might run poorly...
Update progress, apparently, is slow - I just picked this up about a week ago, though, so I haven't felt it and in any case, pulled thirty entirely enjoyable hours out of the game within that time and don't plan on stopping now, haven't even seen all it has to offer me never mind gotten tired of what I've already seen. I could probably pull a good five hours out of dueling with basic cloth-and-quarterstaff alone. Actually, I think I did? Whatever. Five more, then.
Whether or not Bare Mettle completes this game, it's already a perfectly worthwhile purchase and experience at any price. But it's fifteen dollars. That's a pretty low price, just saying.
Also, I've got a decent idea why there hasn't been quite enough progress for some people. I'll bet a lot of the devs' time is being drained into playing the game themselves. I don't blame them. I would probably ditch everything and just play, too, if I'd created something this excellent through so much hard work.

Borderless Gaming is a piece of software which enables you to turn a windowed mode into a borderless window. It's pretty straightforward: run the desired game/program/application in the windowed mode, click on the appropriate button, and voilà. It can store your favourite applications so that you don't have to do that manually every time you start the game. It is also possible to enable and disable Steam integration which comes in handy if you want to use it offline.
So far, it has been working mighty fine for me, especially in Bethesda games which are notorious for being a pain in the neck when it comes to alt-tabbing and not having the borderless window option in the first place (Fallout 3, Skyrim). No performance issues whatsoever. It also gets updated frequently: I remember that Killing Floor was not supported by Borderless Gaming but now it is.
I recommend buying it on sale, especially since it tends to go for a buck or two.

I've written a review on Deus Ex GOTY and did not recommend it. Why, then, am I recommending Deus Ex: Revision? Well, although I don't recommend playing the game, this mod would be for people who've already decided "Heck with that! I'm still gonna play this game!" It is a fantastic mod from my time I've spent with it. The moment I started the game and glanced around the docks, I was wowed. There was a tiny little shed with panes of glass you could knock out. In it, I found the crowbar, and they had a door that looked to be very broken but still standing. It didn't instruct me to strike the door, but the item placement encouraged it without words. It was brilliant game design and something the mod creators had done all on their own while not messing with the original game since the crowbar is normally in that same area but just laying on the dock next to some boxes, offering some similar encouragement to smash them with it.
What else, though? One shed on a dock? No way! Battery Park? Y'know, the tediously long, boring paths with terrorists occasionally strolling about? It looks like a park now! The park benches have trees dotting the paths! The level no longer had me wincing and saying "This doesn't really feel like a park" as the original release of the game always had me doing, and instead I accepted it and was far more immersed for it. UNATCO was lovely. TV monitors with quiet news casts that are basically gifs of a newscaster moving his lips and many graphical improvements. Everything looks like Deus Ex but looks so much more attractive now.
The graphics were definitely an eye-sore in Deus Ex, and although it's still pretty ugly, this mod makes it SO much better-looking. I highly recommend it if you're dead set on playing Deus Ex GOTY again.

Despite the thumbs up I want to make clear that this game is a mixed bag, and I think this game makes it clear that one good idea isn't enough to make a great game.
First, the revolving mechanic, Yes it's cool, dodging bullets, lining up the enemy to wreck them, spotting background enemies. The revolver mechanic really makes the background a massive factor in the game. However, all of the enemies bullets are two dimensional. It's really hard to explain but think of it this way, you see off in the distance an enemy that is shooting a laser out, it looks like it's there to block your path but even though its far off in the background, if you move your ship in front of the laser, you will get hit by it. It can be really disorienting at times.
Second, the ship is boring, you have 3 weapons, your standard shot that shoots directly infront of you, a laser that shoots right in front of you, and an EMP that shoots right in front of you(or clears all bullets on screen if you let it charge) Lasers turn yellow bullets into points, EMP turns anything into Points. But since you can't shoot anywhere but in front of you, you can't hit anything above or behind you. This wouldn't such a problem as long as things didn't attack from behind or above, but they do, a lot. It's just angering since there is almost nothing you can do about those enemies. What would be so wrong with having multiple weapons that shoot somewhere besides infront of you? Oh yes and inorder to hit background enemies you have to get close to them in order to shoot them, so if that thing shoots you from way back in the background it will hit you instantly and you'll be "too close" to dodge.
Third, the arching paths is really a non factor, there is almost no difference between the different paths, I'm not sure why they included it. Do you want the tunnel full of enemies, or the other tunnel full of enemies, it makes almost no difference.
The Graphics are very good for an indie title and the music is great, and the game comes with the sound track. It's well polished and has no bugs as far as I can see, it's not great but it's not bad either and the price they are asking is completely reasonable. An okay game with one cool mechanic, but not much else.

-7/10-
In overall, REVOLVER360 RE:ACTOR is a great game, with solid gameplay and really, really fun to play.
The scoring and camera movement mechanics are really impressive, and construct an interesting game.
The problem I feel by playing is the lack of content. I played for 4/5 hours and I have already got half and more of the achievements, completed the story mode and won half the challenges (which can be really challenging, however).
The final level and boss are almost a joke, since the level has half the lenght of the first one, and the boss is really easy to beat, even if it's not being compared to other bosses as the second level one, which I find to be the more entertaining and difficult.
Graphics are really nice, and go along with the game.
I loved the game, but I feel like I need more to play with. More levels, sometimes more bullets, and a thougher final boss would make this a 9 or 10.
Also, I buyed it on discount, but the full price seems a little too much for the product given.
[EDIT for the steam awards: I think It should win something because its graphical awesomeness and its entertainment value!]

Leisure Suit Larry is one of those old nostalgia games with pervy humor and something I know I was amused by when I was a kid and got ahold of it.   The game has been revitalized and revamped to this new state, but remains the same game it was all those years ago.
If you enjoyed that game and want to re-experience it?  Great, this is a solid purchase for you!   But otherwise, this is just a very dated point and click adventure.  One that I enjoyed and was amused by, but I probably will never play through a second time.
